en: *Udānavarga*, Scroll One, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter One: On Impermanence (*Anityavarga*). Part One of Chapter One.
Once, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a future age, the lifespan of sentient beings will be eighty-four thousand years."

At that time, among those beings whose lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, they dwelt together in one place within this Jambudvīpa; the grain was abundant and ripe, the population was flourishing, and the cries of chickens and dogs could be heard by one another.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“You should know that at that time, when the people lived for five hundred years, a girl would marry upon reaching that age.
At that time there was a king named Śaṅkha, who was escorted by the seven treasures; he ruled and transformed the world according to the Dharma, without any crookedness.”

There was a natural chariot made of precious feathers, one thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits wide, adorned with upright and well-crafted necklaces of various jewels. In the midst of the great assembly, he distributed alms with a heart free from stinginess or regret; establishing meritorious deeds as a leader of the multitude, he provided for all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those who had attained the Way—whether traveling far, staying, passing through, or lodging—giving to them all without any sense of parsimony regarding what they sought.

At that time, when the lifespan of sentient beings was eighty-four thousand years, a Tathāgata appeared in the world named Maitreya—One Thus Come, Worthy, Perfectly Enlightened, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One;
just as I today have attained Unsurpassed, Right, and Perfect Enlightenment, fully endowed with the ten titles.
One should always protect and sustain countless hundreds of thousands of bhikṣu-saṃghas, just as I today protect and sustain countless hundreds of thousands of bhikṣu-saṃghas.

Together with the great assembly, one should extensively expound the profound Dharma—good in its beginning, middle, and end; subtle in its meaning and phrasing; complete and pure, wherein the holy life (brahmacarya) is cultivated.

Just as I today, together with this great assembly, extensively expound the profound Dharma—virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end; subtle in its meaning and flavor; and complete in its purity for the cultivation of the holy life.
The detailed explanation is as in the *Maitreya’s Descent*.

As the Buddha has taught, there is a sutra titled "The Path of the Six Spheres of Contact. If there are beings born therein, when their eyes behold forms, they see only beautiful forms and not ugly forms; they see what is lovely and not what is unlovely; they see what is venerable and not what is non-venerable; they see what is worthy of thought and not what is unworthy of thought; they see beautiful colors and not non-beautiful colors.

All sentient beings who hear sounds with their ears, smell odors with their noses, know tastes with their tongues, perceive tactile sensations with their bodies, and cognize mental phenomena with their minds—even including the Lord of Devas—are likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Great Lecture Hall by the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī. Then, many young boys of Vaiśālī each had this thought:
"We should join together and go to where the World-Honored One is to inquire after his well-being, pay our respects, and visit him."

Among those youths, some rode upon blue horses with blue canopies and wore entirely blue garments; others rode upon horses of blue, yellow, red, or white and wore entirely white garments. They struck bells and beat drums, performing music and dance as they proceeded with a retinue of attendants before and behind them to the place where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should know this: if there are those who have not seen the devas wandering for recreation and bathing in the ponds of the rear garden, you should now observe these youths; the dharma robes they wear and the palanquins they ride in are no different from those of the devas."
"The reason for this is that the robes worn by the various devas are no different from these.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of beings seated there each had this thought:

"We ought to make a sincere vow so that in our future lives we may be born among devas and humans, always wearing these Dharma robes and never being parted from them; and that in a future age when a Buddha appears, we may hear the profound Dharma, forever leave behind suffering and affliction, and enter the realm of Nirvana."

The Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings—who sought rebirth in the three realms of existence and could not escape suffering and affliction—then spoke this verse to the great assembly:
"All that is conditioned is impermanent; It is subject to decay and destruction. It cannot be relied upon, For it is ever-changing and unstable."

At that time, when sentient beings heard this single verse, incalculable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, within their present lives, exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; they all realized the fruits of the Path.
In the past, there were four brahmins who had all attained supernatural powers; they could fly through the air, their spiritual feet being unimpeded.
These four brahmacārins said to one another:

"If there are people who offer delicacies and food as alms to the śramaṇa Gautama, they will immediately be reborn in heaven and never leave the halls of merit; those who hear his Dharma enter the gate of liberation. Today, our minds crave heavenly blessings; we do not wish for liberation, nor do we need to hear the Dharma."
At that time, four men each held four pieces of sweet honey-candied sugar (*madhu-phāṇita*). One man arrived first at the place where the Tathāgata was and offered it to the World-Honored One.
Having accepted it, the Tathāgata addressed that brahmin and spoke this verse: "That which is practiced is impermanent.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin covered his ears with his hands.
Next, a second person approached the Tathāgata and offered him rock honey.
The Tathāgata again spoke this verse concerning the law of arising and passing away;
having heard it, the brahmin covered his ears with his hands.
Next, the third person arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was and presented him with rock honey.
After the Tathāgata had accepted it, he again spoke this verse: "All who are born must inevitably die.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin covered his ears with his hands.
Next, a fourth person went to the place where the Tathāgata was and offered him rock honey;
having accepted it, the Tathāgata again spoke this verse: "The cessation of this is bliss.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin covered his ears with his hands and departed from there.

The Tathāgata observed their thoughts and intentions and knew they were ready to be delivered; he then employed skillful means to conceal his form and remain invisible. The four men gathered in one place and said to one another:
"Although we have offered alms to the śramaṇa Gautama, our minds have not reached a firm conclusion. What instructions does the śramaṇa Gautama have for us?"
He first asked those who had been there before:
"What instructions did you receive upon being presented with the rock honey?
Did you not also hear the Dharma?"
He replied: "I heard a single phrase from the Tathāgata stating that what is practiced is impermanent;
having heard this meaning, I immediately covered my ears with my hands and did not accept it."
Next, he asked the second person:
"What instructions did you receive upon reaching the Tathāgata?
That person then spoke of his own experience:
"When I went to the Tathāgata’s presence to offer him rock honey, the Tathāgata spoke this verse to me concerning the law of arising and decaying;
having heard it, I covered my ears with my hands and did not accept it."
Next, he asked the third person:
"What instructions did you receive upon reaching the Tathāgata?
That man then spoke of his own experience:
"When I went to the place where the Tathāgata was and offered him rock honey, the Tathāgata spoke this verse to me: 'All that is born must inevitably die.
Having heard this, I covered my ears with my hands and would not accept it."
Next, he asked the fourth person:
"What instructions did you receive upon reaching the Tathāgata? The man replied:
"When they arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, they offered him rock honey. The Tathāgata then spoke this verse to me: 'This cessation is bliss.
After the four of them had spoken this verse, their minds were opened and their intentions were resolved; they attained the stage of Anāgāmin."

At that time, the four men, realizing for themselves that each had attained realization of the Path, reproached themselves and went to where the Tathāgata was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, stood to one side, and after a short while withdrew to sit down and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We only pray, O Tathāgata!"
"Since you have entered the path, you may become a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
"Quickly cultivate the holy life.
At that moment, the hair of the four men fell off of its own accord, their clothing transformed into *kāṣāya* robes, and they immediately attained the path of an Arhat before the Buddha.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Mahākāśyapa and Anuruddha:

“O bhikṣus, you must receive my teachings and reverently serve the words of the Buddha. You two should not enter nirvāṇa first; rather, you should first compile the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the Ratnakaraṇḍaka-piṭaka. Only after that should you enter nirvāṇa, and so forth, until the extensive account of making offerings to the śarīra.”

When the seven-day period had ended, they gathered together all these sūtras in a universal assembly. Five hundred arhats, all of whom had attained this liberation, possessed swift and sharp faculties, and were fully endowed with all virtues, assembled in one place. They then prepared a high lion throne for Ānanda and entreated him to ascend the throne.
Having ascended the high seat, he then asked Ānanda:
"In what place did the Tathāgata first preach the Dharma?
At that time, Ānanda replied:
“Thus have I heard at one time.
Having spoken these words, the five hundred arhats all rose from their rope couches and knelt on the ground, saying:
“We ourselves personally witnessed the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma; it is only today that we say, ‘Thus have I heard at one time.’”
Everyone raised their voices and wept piteously in response.
Then, Mahākāśyapa addressed Ānanda, saying:
"From this day forward, when revealing the profound treasury of the Dharma, all should say, 'Thus have I heard,' and not say, 'I saw it.'"
“The Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus:
‘This is the origin of suffering, which has never been heard before and never been seen before,’ as explained at length in the original sūtra.”
At that time, when the assembly had already compiled the Sūtras,
the Venerable Kāśyapa again asked Ānanda:
"In what place did the Tathāgata first proclaim the Vinaya?"
Then Ānanda replied to Mahākāśyapa:
“I have heard this from the Buddha.

Once, when the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, there was a son of the Kalandakas named Sucirṇa who had left the household life to study the Path and resided within the community of bhikṣus. He was the very first to violate the Vinaya, committing an offense that reached the point of being an unwholesome dharma; the details are as explained in the Prātimokṣa.”
At that time, Kāśyapa again asked Ānanda:
"In what place did the Tathāgata first teach the Abhidharma? Ānanda replied:
"I have heard this from the Buddha:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Sārandada Shrine by the side of the Markaṭahrada Lake in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having perceived the beginning and end of the circumstances concerning the son of the Vaṅgas, addressed the bhikṣus:"
"Those who are free from the five fears and the mind of resentment will not fall into the evil destinies, nor will they be reborn within the hells; this is explained in detail as in the Abhidharma."
Having completed the collection of the Abhidharma during the first watch of the night, he then recited the *Udāna* during the last watch, speaking this verse:
"Sleeping and waking—why is it said, 'sleeping and waking'?"
As the World-Honored One and other Perfectly Awakened Ones have taught:

"Sleep is a thief of life, a source of delusion, and a cause of ruin; it prevents the realization of the fruits of practice, leaves one helpless at the end of life, and fails to lead one to the realm of light."

The reason for this is that just as a person who has awakened is able to cultivate virtue and establish the roots of goodness, one who is addicted to sleep loses these qualities; therefore, such a person is called deluded and ignorant.
At that time, there was another speaker in the assembly who said:
"As the Buddha has said:
'If there are sentient beings who, regarding the various matters they contemplate while awake, remain serene and free of thought during sleep.'"
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"It would be better to sleep than to remain unawakened; how can this be reconciled?

For this reason, the Buddha taught that one should eliminate sleep and constantly maintain mindfulness of awakening. As the Buddha spoke in verse: "Regarding sleep and awakening, one should contemplate with joy. To say "joy" means that the inner mind leaps up; with a cheerful and happy heart, wholesome states of mind arise. Therefore, it is said that one should contemplate with joy.

Those who listen to what I say should focus their minds with single-minded concentration, free from distracted thoughts; with a settled mind and without error, they shall be capable of receiving and upholding it. For this reason, I say: "Listen to what I say, and record the *Udānavarga*."

Regarding what is called "Udāna" (Exalted Utterances): all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, together praised the meaning of the Udāna Dharma; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise named "Most Victorious."
What is meant by "supreme"?

It is that which surpasses all fetters and unwholesome dharmas; it surpasses lust, anger, and ignorance; it surpasses all the bonds of birth and death; and it surpasses the ninety-six types of arts of the heterodox teachers and non-Buddhist schools, such as the Nirgranthas, emerging preeminently among them. Therefore, it is called "supreme."

His exposition is fluent and unimpeded; he manifests and articulates it for the sake of devas and humans, achieving perfection in both meaning and phrasing. For this reason, he is said to have compiled and expounded the *Udānavarga*.

As the World-Honored One has spoken, his exposition is fluent and unimpeded; as the World-Honored One has taught, he possesses universal penetration. Like a seer of compassion who leaves no part of himself untouched, that which the World-Honored One speaks is expounded with fluency and without hesitation; therefore, it is called "the teaching of the World-Honored One."
"Universal penetration" means the penetration of all-knowledge, the manifestation of all things, the thorough understanding of all, and the discernment of all meanings.

One who roams through the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) accomplishes the unsurpassed path; even the Tathāgata’s six supernormal powers cannot be attained by Arhats. Because the Buddha is the most excellent and supreme among all deliverances and is able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena, he is called "one who has universally penetrated."

The "Rishi of Compassion" refers to one who fills all the hopes of those in the cycle of birth and death with loving-kindness, regarding them as one would one's own parents; one whose mind is protected by the intent of compassion. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, also call such a person a Rishi. One who cultivates the path of supernormal powers is called a Rishi; one who is fully endowed with manifold virtues is called a Rishi; and one who has practiced goodness throughout the long night is called a Rishi. For these reasons, he is called the "Rishi of Compassion."

Regarding "the body without remainder": as for what is called the "body," it is based upon the four great elements; beyond these, there is nothing further, nor does it have a limit, nor does it arise anew—just as the Buddha himself has personally proclaimed in his presence.
Ānanda! You should know that this is the final realm; it is the final state of being without a womb, and the final portion of the physical form received is like mine, Ānanda!
No longer will one see the realms of heaven and earth, nor shall one again receive such a body; this is the end of suffering, and thus it is said that there is "one body with no remainder.
All that is conditioned is impermanent, meaning it is subject to the law of arising and decaying; for all that is born must inevitably die—this cessation is bliss.

In the past, the various Brahmins each recited the teachings of their masters and divided into two schools; one school held the view that all things exist, while the other school claimed that all things are non-existent.
Regarding those who say "it exists," the Tathāgata distinguishes and removes their hesitation, cuts off their longing, and then expounds for them the practice of impermanence.
Regarding those who say "it exists," they themselves recite this praise:
"With the sharp wheel-sword, One slays sentient beings; Yet one always knows how to practice giving."
There is neither good nor evil:
the formless essence remains unchanging. Amidst the body, a sharp sword may pass back and forth without harming its life-force.
Just as the element of earth is ever-present and the realm of wind is unattached, so too does the fire-element experience pleasure and pain; the life-faculty is likewise.
Even if one were to pass back and forth with a sharp sword, one would not perceive any retribution for good or evil:
even if one were to harm one's parents, there would be no retribution for good or evil; how much less, then, could there be such a result for others?
"It is just as when a sparrow is kept in a jar; if someone breaks the jar, the sparrow flies away.
When sentient beings are harmed, their lives depart far away, leaving nothing behind that can be damaged."

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, wishing to lead those sentient beings with false views away from them, says that all conditioned activities are impermanent and cannot be relied upon; they are subject to constant flux and instability, being by nature destined for extinction. Life is like the morning dew—existing but briefly before vanishing. Therefore, he says that all conditioned activities are impermanent.
A certain group who claimed that all things are non-existent congratulated one another, saying they had achieved their own doctrine.
The Tathāgata, observing what was in their minds, told them: "This is called the law of arising and passing away.

Now, as for arising and passing away: whatever flourishes must decline; where there is meeting, there must be parting. If one has no body, then it is already over; but having received a body, what can be avoided?"
The brahmin further thought to himself:
"If this phenomenon of decay and decline does not arise again, then my thesis will be established.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke further to explain the meaning:

"Indeed, birth is immediately followed by death; the cycle revolves without ceasing. The various aggregates of sensation (vedanā-skandha) and their bases mutually receive and enter one another; it is only through the observation of the eye of wisdom that one can discern them, just as the particles of dust streaming in the sunlight are so numerous and swift that they are difficult to calculate."

"This body of the five aggregates of clinging is driven by various formations (*saṃskāra*) as it transmigrates through birth and death without ceasing; therefore, it is said that 'whatever is born must die.

As for 'this cessation is bliss,' it refers to the eternal exhaustion without remainder, the state where there is no intention of desire or attachment, the supreme bliss of constant rest and tranquility. It is the attainment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) free from the notions of arising and ceasing. It is the bliss of non-desire, the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the bliss of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the bliss of exhaustion, and the bliss of cessation; therefore, it is said that 'this cessation is bliss.'"
What joy is there, what laughter? Your mindfulness is constantly ablaze, yet you are deeply shrouded in darkness;
why do you not seek a lamp?
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

After the meal, during the late afternoon, there were many bhikṣus and the fourfold assembly of disciples—the gods, the emperors, the ministers, and the common people—who wished to hear the Tathāgata preach the Dharma of the Ambrosia.

There were also seven practitioners from other regions, heterodox brahmins, with hair and beards as white as snow, leaning on staffs and groaning as they approached the Buddha’s dwelling. They prostrated themselves in worship, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We are men from afar who have humbly received your holy transformation. We ought to have taken refuge in the Way long ago, yet our arts were limited; only now have we been able to come and behold your sacred countenance. We pray to become your disciples so that we may extinguish all suffering.”
The Buddha immediately granted them permission to receive the precepts, and they all became śramaṇas. He then instructed the seven bhikṣus to dwell together in a single room.

However, these seven men, having beheld the World-Honored One and attained the Way, failed to contemplate the law of impermanence and change; while sitting together in the room, they brooded over worldly affairs, speaking in low voices and laughing loudly without considering success or failure. Life’s span was drawing to a close, yet they did not realize it would not wait for anyone; they merely indulged in jesting and merriment, giving rein to their own dissipation and failing to reflect on impermanence.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose and went into his chamber, where he addressed them, saying:
"You who practice the Way should seek the path of transcendence and non-action; why do you laugh so loudly?"
All sentient beings rely upon five things. What are these five? First, relying on youth;
second, relying on physical beauty; third, relying on power and influence; fourth, relying on talent and capability; and fifth, relying on noble lineage.
"You seven, why do you speak in whispers and laugh so loudly? What do you rely upon?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"What joy, what laughter? Your thoughts are ever ablaze, Deeply shrouded in darkness."
"And yet you do not seek a lamp?
"What joy? What laughter?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the seven men, saying:
"You seven have not yet entered the realm of the Path, nor do you yet abide in the stages of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat."
He further addressed the bhikṣus:

"I have previously taught you that as long as one has not yet exhausted all outflows (āsrava), one must not rely on anything for security. You have received these physical forms and have not yet escaped the fetters; you dwell together with snakes and vipers within the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha). How can you speak in whispers or laugh loudly amidst such conditions?"
"One should reflect that this suffering will not be eliminated for eternal kalpas; yet you instead give rise to frivolous laughter, thereby creating defilement. Alas, it is difficult to awaken!
You all are like this. Therefore it is said: "What joy? What laughter? These are the words of the World-Honored One’s exhortation.
Regarding "mindfulness is constantly ablaze": what is meant by "ablaze"?
It is ablaze with the fire of impermanence, ablaze with the fire of suffering, and ablaze with grief, lamentation, pain, and distress.
Furthermore, by what means is one seen to be ablaze?
One is ablaze with craving, hatred, delusion, and pride; one is ablaze with envy, malice, and doubt. Therefore, it is said that mindfulness is constantly ablaze.

That which is deeply shrouded in darkness and obscurity is like a person walking at night who cannot discern colors, or one born blind who cannot see the spectrum of black and yellow; such darkness and obscurity is hardly worth mentioning.

What is called the "Great Darkness" refers to the entanglements of ignorance that pervade the entire physical form of a person without leaving a single empty space; this is what is meant by the Great Obscurity shrouding sentient beings. It prevents them from distinguishing between the essential natures of the good and evil realms, nor does it allow them to distinguish between the essential paths of white and black, bondage and liberation, or the mundane and the supramundane laws. Furthermore, they do not know the means of escape from or the cessation of the good and evil realms; therefore, it is called being deeply shrouded in darkness.
Regarding "not seeking for a lamp," what is meant by a lamp?
It refers to the lamp of wisdom. By means of the lamp of wisdom, what is illuminated?
The answer is:

Knowing the origin of the fetters and extinguishing them through the Path, one discerns the roots of the good and evil destinies and the way of escape; one can distinguish between the essential paths of white and black, bondage and liberation, as well as the laws of the mundane and the supramundane. Being skillfully able to discern the good and evil destinies, the way of escape, and their ultimate cessation, one universally illuminates all phenomena such that nothing remains unclarified. Yet, because one further relinquishes even this and proceeds toward the path of darkness, it is said: "one does not seek a lamp."
All manner of physical vessels are scattered in every direction; their bone color is like that of a pigeon—what joy is there in this?
Formerly, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who went daily to the wilderness cemetery outside the city; as he passed through another’s field on his way, the owner saw him and became incensed, saying:
"What kind of ascetic is this, coming and going here every day without cultivating the Way or its virtue?"
He then asked the practitioner,
"What kind of mendicant are you, who wanders back and forth across my field, leaving the tracks of a person?
The practitioner replied:

"I have a dispute and am seeking witnesses. At that time, the field owner, whose past karmic conditions were linked to him and who was destined for deliverance, followed the practitioner in secret. He beheld the corpses in the vast cemetery, strewn about in disarray—swollen, putrid, and rotting; scavenged by birds and beasts and scattered in various places; some partially devoured and others not yet finished; resembling roasted pigeons with maggots gnawing at them, so foul and filthy as to be difficult to approach; while crows, magpies, foxes, dogs, old vultures, owls, and screech-owls feasted upon the dead bodies.
The bhikṣu raised his hand and said to that person,
"These birds and beasts are my witnesses. That person asked:
"These birds and beasts can serve as witnesses: with whom, O Bhikṣu, are you now disputing? The Bhikṣu replied:

"The mind is a disease with many outflows and afflictions. I observed this skeleton and analyzed its foul impurities; returning to my cell, I again examined my own body from head to foot and saw it was no different from that one. Yet this mind runs and rushes in ten thousand directions, pursuing illusory and false phenomena such as form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch."
I now wish to admonish you regarding the very root of the mind; you must understand this and give rise to this thought: do not lead me into the realms of hell or hungry ghosts.

I am now an ordinary person, not yet liberated from all fetters; yet this thieving mind does not obey my commands. For this reason, I dwell daily in the wilderness, contemplating the perception of foulness and impurity, and further speaking to the mind: "The mind is violent, chaotic, and unstable; the mind must now reform and cease creating conditions for evil."
At that time, having heard the instructions of the practitioner, the field-owner wiped away his tears with his hand and sighed with a choked voice.

For ten thousand years during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha, that field-owner had cultivated the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), immediately discerning the thirty-six foul substances of the body as impure.
At that time, the bhikṣu and the landowner went together to the vast and terrifying charnel ground, where they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Then the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, beheld the two men achieving this fruit of realization. Out of consideration for their past karmic conditions, and desiring to provide an example for future disciples so that in future ages the Great Illumination might manifest and the True Dharma endure long without being extinguished, he expressed his joy and spoke this verse:

Regarding "all those with physical form": there may be hands, feet, arms, elbows, waists, hips, thighs, shoulders, knees, ankles, heels, skulls, and various limbs and joints, each situated in a different place; therefore, it is said, "all those with physical form."

Scattered in all directions, they are like wood that lacks consciousness; yet what was once cherished and beloved does not leave the heart's embrace. Adorned with ornaments, flowers, and fragrant powders that once perfumed their bodies, these are now all strewn about, each in a different place.

Regarding the phrase "the color of the bones is like that of a pigeon": originally, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings who saw [this person] with love and affection, never tiring of gazing upon them; yet now, hundreds of thousands of millions of people look down upon them with contempt, and upon seeing them, they are all struck with terror, their body hair standing on end. For this reason, it is said: "the color of the bones is like that of a pigeon."

Regarding what is called "pleasure": worldly discourse holds that where there is pleasure, there are those who are ordinary, foolish, and deluded; it is abandoned by the wise. It is what fools delight in, while the wise feel shame toward it, seeing only its ugliness. Yet the foolish indulge in and habituate themselves to it, finding it sweet and refusing to let go, concealing and cherishing it within their embrace.
If it were as at the first night, when consciousness descended into the mother’s womb, then as days pass and change occur, one would depart and never return.

As the World-Honored Buddha has expounded in his teachings, there are three conditioned states (*saṃskṛta*), and the characteristics of the conditioned are arising and decaying, changing and shifting.
Question: "If it were the case that all things possess permanence, would not corpses and skeletal remains endure for a long time?
Since one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one day and night, if physical bodies were to endure in the world for a long duration, the forms of a single person would fill the entire universe."
He replied: "Because sentient beings arise together with the sense faculties and perish together with the sense faculties, for this reason the remains do not endure for long.
If sentient beings were to perish together with the sense faculties and arise together with the sense faculties, then the bones and remains would indeed endure for a long time in the world."

Furthermore, [the body] arises together with consciousness and perishes together with consciousness; at that time, the physical form does not remain long in the world. If sentient beings were to perish together with consciousness and arise together with consciousness, then the physical form would endure long in the world.
Question: "If one were to remain in the world for a long time until reaching old age, would a person's hair not always be white from the moment they first emerge from the womb? Answer:
"That which is called 'the hair being stark white' does not have the meaning of senility.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is the meaning of this? He replied:

"When one receives the constituent parts of a physical form, there is immediately the transformation of decaying appearance, and white hair arises—just as wine, clarified butter, or sesame oil must inevitably have turbid dregs; so it is when receiving the constituent parts of a physical form: there is immediately the transformation of decaying appearance and the arising of white hair."
Therefore it is said: "As at the first watch of the night.

When consciousness descends into the mother's womb—whether it be male consciousness or female consciousness—it abides within that single moment, arising and ceasing, undergoing hundreds of thousands of transformations without rest, like the turning of a wheel, beyond all calculation; only those with the divine eye can perceive this.

When consciousness departs from the past and returns, it likewise cannot be constrained by divine spells or technical arts; having departed, it vanishes forever, and upon its return, it leaves no trace. The same is true for consciousness abiding in the mother’s womb, where birth and death ceaselessly continue: just as a river flows eastward and never looks back toward the west, so too the consciousness that has passed through the womb never returns. Only those with the divine eye can see the consciousness returning to the womb and see the consciousness departing from it.
What was seen at dawn does not appear by night; what was beheld yesterday is gone this evening.
Now that I am in my prime, I have no one to rely upon; even the young die, men and women beyond count.

In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Venerable Ānanda rose at the proper time, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. From afar, he saw a group of men outside the gate performing music and dance for their own amusement.

When the Venerable Ānanda had finished his almsround in the city and was about to depart, he saw that this musician had suddenly passed away; the crowd was carrying him out, wailing and weeping as they faced one another.
Then the Venerable Ānanda had this thought: "How strange!
How wondrous that the confrontation with impermanence has arrived; how swift it is!

This morning at dawn, when I entered the city for alms, I saw this man enjoying himself with the five pleasures like a son of heaven; how is it that he now undergoes such a confrontation and encounters impermanence?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda departed from the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī; having adjusted his robes and washed his hands and feet, he approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!

This morning, having dressed and taken up my bowl, I entered the city to beg for food. I saw a man performing music and dance, amusing himself with the five desires; I then entered the city to beg and later came out. Outside, I saw that this man had suddenly passed away, and the multitude were carrying him on a bier, wailing and weeping toward one another."
At that time, World-Honored One, I immediately gave rise to this thought:
"How strange and extraordinary! Impermanence has arrived in person; how could it have come so swiftly?"

This morning, as I entered the city to beg for alms, I saw this man enjoying himself with the five kinds of pleasure, appearing like a celestial king; how could he now encounter such retribution and undergo impermanence?
"What I have now seen is truly extraordinary; it is something never before beheld.
The World-Honored One said: "Now, Ānanda!"
"What is so extraordinary about that?
What I have witnessed in the past is truly extraordinary, surpassing what you see now.
Once, in days gone by, when the time had come, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms."

At that time, Ānanda, I saw a man outside the gate of the Jeta Grove performing music and entertainments, amusing himself with the five desires. Later, having entered the city for alms and finished my meal, I returned outside the city walls and saw this man performing music and entertainments exactly as before, without error.
"I see that you have produced something extraordinary that surpasses me.
At that time, Ānanda immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is the regular custom; what is so extraordinary about it?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Life is swifter than the wind; its departure is difficult to restrain. Now that you have only just spoken, what is so extraordinary about it?

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this meaning and investigated its beginning and end, wishing to cause the bhikṣus to clearly discern this Dharma, to manifest great illumination for future sentient beings, and to ensure that the True Dharma would long endure in the world. Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses of radiant brilliance:
"What was seen in the morning does not appear at night; what was gazed upon yesterday is gone this evening.
I am now in my youth, yet have no one to rely upon; even the young die, men and women beyond count."

Regarding those previously seen who are not seen at night: the multitude of sentient beings seen in the early morning, numbering in the thousands and hundreds, are no longer seen by evening. Since all sentient beings who contemplate and calculate find their roots of goodness complete and their minds undisturbed, they realize for themselves that life is like a flash of light from a struck stone that vanishes as soon as it appears; who then would give rise to the intention of craving attachment to this?
Only the unlearned, foolish worldlings give rise to such thoughts and harbor intentions of greedy attachment.

That which was observed yesterday is no longer there this evening; just as one saw their movements and comings and goings yesterday, even if they had entertained thoughts of contemplating the roots of goodness and planting manifold merits, their minds would have been so bold as to prevent them from reforming and repenting, and they would have internally given rise to the perception that these things are not to be relished. Therefore it is said: "What is seen in the morning does not appear at night; that which was observed yesterday is no longer there this evening."

I am now young and strong, yet I have nothing to rely upon; like a foolish person who lacks learning and knowledge, I rely on my own robustness and the intensity of my physical strength, recklessly indulging myself as I please and disregarding all future consequences.

They claim for themselves a handsome and extraordinary countenance, regarding others as lowly and unworthy of their friendship; their physical beauty, strength, and wealth surpass those of all others. Being already in the prime of youth, they walk alone without peer; whatever they desire is obtained without anyone being able to oppose them, and they act according to their own whims, showing no regard for the powerful. Furthermore, they do not contemplate the arrival of impermanence, nor do they perceive the affliction of the suffering of birth and death. Therefore, it is said: "I am now young and strong, with nothing to rely upon."

The young and strong also die, men and women in countless numbers. Even among the countless classes of sentient beings—whether male or female, large or small—who have received a physical form, possess extraordinary strength, and enjoy immeasurable wealth; who act according to their own desires and are all in the prime of youth—the number of those who meet their end while still vigorous far exceeds that of the elderly within the human world. All are subject to impermanence and are seen being trampled underfoot. Yet those who thus pass away did not cultivate merit during their time in the world and had no reliance upon the roots of goodness. From this life to the next, they rush through the five realms of existence without respite. Therefore it is said: "The young also die, men and women in countless numbers."

They perish in the womb, die shortly after birth, or pass away as infants, toddlers, children, the elderly, the young, or those in middle age, gradually and in succession, like fruit waiting to ripen.

Sixty thousand births, sixty hundred births—within these stores of births, one undergoes destruction because of harming others. Those so-called "others" include a king, ten million people, a caravan leader, merchants, parents, and *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, and *arhats*.

If one gives rise to a malicious mind and intends to harm such people, they will fall into either the Avīci Hell, or the Tapana, Pratāpana, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, or Saṃghāta Hells.

Once these offenses have been exhausted, one is born among the six classes of domestic animals, wandering and revolving through kalpas; only after this does one regain a human body. During that interval, while still within the womb, one’s life is not brought to its full term. Therefore it is said: "One perishes while still in the womb."

"Those who perish upon first emerging from the womb" refers to those sentient beings who die at the very moment they emerge from the birth canal, or those sentient beings who, while beginning to cultivate meritorious deeds but before their work is completed, meet an untimely death within the birth canal. This occurs because in a previous life they conceived the intent to harm those people who were cultivating merit; therefore it is said: "Perishing upon first emergence."

Regarding "having given birth to a son, he perishes": there may be sentient beings who exert effort to establish merit by providing gardens, fruit trees, bathing pools, bridges, and latrines at various stupas and monasteries; yet before their work is completed, they are harmed by others. This results from having harmed those of merit in previous lives, whereby upon death they enter the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. After passing through a vast duration of time, they eventually return to the human state; once born and emerged from the womb, they die prematurely within it. Therefore it is said: "Having given birth to a son, he perishes."

Regarding those who die while still infants in their mother’s arms: there may be sentient beings who, within a stupa or monastery, perform meritorious deeds and establish virtuous foundations—providing gardens, fruits, bathing pools, bridges, and latrines. Once these works are completed and but little remains to be done, they are suddenly harmed by others. This is because in a previous life, they conceived the intent to kill or harm those people who were creating merit; when their bodies dissolved and their lives ended, they entered hell. Having exhausted their retribution there, they are reborn among animals. Even if they subsequently obtain human form, being unable yet to distinguish between right and wrong, they meet with an untimely death while still in the arms of an infant.
Whether old, young, or middle-aged, all shall gradually follow one after another,
like fruit waiting to ripen.
Long ago, the Venerable Aśvajit spoke this verse:
"Some perish while still in the womb; some die once born into the world.
Even in the prime of youth, death cannot be avoided; in old age and decrepitude, one accepts it with resignation.
It is like a tree that produces wild blossoms; when they bear fruit, such instances are rare."
"Because of my resolve, I must certainly renounce; I cannot bear the summons of the Lord of Death.

This is like a fruit tree that flourishes in its season, yet its wild blossoms grow only to wither when met by the wind, and those that do form fruit are few. Some, having already borne fruit, fall due to hail; some wither before they have even flowered; and some wither once they have flowered. Among them, those that form fruit and wait for ripening before falling are but very few indeed.

These classes of sentient beings are also like this: throughout hundreds of thousands of births, whether once or twice, their bodies enter the womb and emerge from it; through youth, adulthood, old age, and sickness, all return to this path and none escape this affliction. Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, while the end of life occurs for only one or two in old age, those who die in their youth are beyond counting. Therefore it is said: "The old, the young, and those in between, gradually follow one another like fruit awaiting ripeness."
Life is like fruit waiting to ripen; one constantly fears it will fall and rot.
All that is born possesses suffering; who can achieve immortality?

Once, King Aśoka, having prepared his carriage and retinue, went to the rear garden for recreation. There, rows of various fruit trees stood in orderly alignment. According to the established custom of that land, one eats fruit only when it is ripe and never consumes it while raw.

At that time, the king issued a decree to the garden keepers: "If any fruit or melon falls to the ground, it must not be offered up; anyone who violates this regulation shall have their head impaled."
At that time, the park keeper thought to himself:

"This King Aśoka is tyrannical and unrighteous; he slaughters living beings without any heart of compassion. If I were to violate his command now, my death would come within days or nights, and I could not escape such hardship."

"However, the fruit on the trees in this garden is currently so abundant that while those remaining on the branches are few, those fallen to the ground are many. Even if you were to demand the fruit from me, there would be none left to give.
Therefore, I shall flee for now to seek ordination and study."

He immediately climbed over the wall and went to where the World-Honored One was; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he requested to become a śramaṇa. The Buddha immediately granted his request, and he entered the ranks of the Way.

He remained in quietude and non-action, neither applying skillful means to sit in meditation or recite the sūtras, nor did he practice the Vinaya or Abhidharma. He considered that practicing the Way was complete with this alone. Furthermore, he did not contemplate the twelve essential points of diligent effort—such as walking meditation and chanting in empty, secluded wildernesses; relying instead on three matters and disregarding future conditions, he rejoiced within himself:
"I have now escaped the urgent suffering of the physical form; for now I am at peace, so what need is there to know anything else?"

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the minds of those people, wishing to free them from suffering and rescue them from all calamities; wishing to establish them securely in the sublime hall of wholesome dharmas; wishing to uproot the very foundation and leave the source of birth and death behind, leading them into the path of liberation from which there is no regression.
At that time, while in the assembly, he spoke this verse of the *Udānavarga*:
"Life is like fruit waiting to ripen; One always fears it will fall.
All that is born is subject to suffering; Who can attain immortality?"

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣu reproached himself within and, harboring a sense of shame and remorse, practiced the path of contemplation on impurity in a secluded place; he immediately attained arhatship right there.
For example, as a potter kneads clay to fashion vessels, all of which must eventually break,
so too is the life of man. Once,
the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, there was a potter who fashioned earthenware vessels; he encountered no obstacles with any material and produced them according to their intended shapes without difficulty.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Kośala kingdom commanded his potters to manufacture vessels, but because that man’s affairs were numerous, he could not complete the task.
At that time, King Prasenajit harbored inner resentment and anger, and commanded his attendants:
"Go to the potter's house and destroy his wares.
Fearing for his life, the potter secretly fled to the borders of the kingdom of Kāśī, where he again began manufacturing earthenware.
When King Prasenajit heard that they were making such vessels, he again dispatched his ministers and officials to the borders of that country to have all the clay vessels they had made destroyed.
At that time, the potter fled once more to the kingdom of Kosala, where he again established himself and manufactured clay vessels.
When King Prasenajit heard that he had made such vessels, he again dispatched his ministers and officials to destroy them.

At that time, the potter’s wealth was completely exhausted and he no longer had the means to survive; his food did not suffice for his mouth and his clothing did not cover his body. Constantly fearing that King Prasenajit would seize and kill him, he fled once more into the deep mountains and went to the World-Honored One to seek ordination as a practitioner of the Way.

At that time, the Buddha silently consented and allowed him to join the ranks of the monastic community. However, that person did not reflect within himself, thinking that he had forever escaped the perils of hardship and no longer feared being harmed by the king. Dwelling in a secluded place, he did not contemplate the Way or its virtue; he did not study the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma, nor did he discern their underlying principles. He did not practice the paths that transcend the world, nor did he engage in seated meditation, recitation of scriptures, or assisting in communal affairs. Having abandoned these three activities, he did not diligently cultivate them, believing that practicing the Way was limited to this alone. He did not increase his vigor or exert himself to seek the Dharma of the Superior Man (uttaramanuṣyadharma). Thus, though he had not yet attained realization, he did not diligently seek realization; though he had not yet attained the fruit, he did not diligently seek the fruit.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observed his mind with the three types of supernormal knowledge and gradually transformed him so that his mind was freed from the net of doubt. He then told that person: "You have achieved the merit of avoiding the earthenware vessel; you need no longer fear the affliction of losing your life. However, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are the very form of that earthenware vessel; this is the great terror from which one cannot escape."

Although an earthenware vessel may be broken, it does not fear falling into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; yet the five aggregates of clinging constitute the "vessel" of the body. If one has previously failed to create various meritorious karmas or cultivate the roots of goodness, one will have nothing to rely upon and no place of refuge, remaining perpetually terrified of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this matter, investigating its beginning and end; having fully understood it, he wished to cause the bhikṣus to forever leave behind suspicion and doubt, and to enable future sentient beings to behold this great illumination so that the True Dharma might endure for a long time.
Thereupon, in the midst of the assembly, he spoke these verses: "Just as a potter, kneading clay to fashion vessels, All must inevitably break—so too is the life of man."

"All vessels, whether raw or fired, must eventually return to ruin; they gradually become heaps of filth, nothing to be craved. Likewise, all classes of living beings who receive the five aggregates of clinging—whether they be of the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, or Caṇḍāla castes—and who assume physical forms, whether short-lived or long-lived, wealthy or destitute, handsome or ugly, of noble lineage or lowly, fair-faced or disfigured, wise or ignorant—all return to death. Impermanent and subject to change, they shall all be abandoned in the wilderness among the charnel grounds."

At that time, having heard the path of instruction taught by the Tathāgata, that bhikṣu understood the essential point of impermanence, mastered the source of demerit and merit, comprehended the transformations of rise and fall, and followed the practice of parinirvāṇa; he immediately attained the state of arhatship in the presence of the Buddha.
It is like setting up the warp and casting in the weft to weave; as the threads are gradually exhausted, so too is the human lifespan.
Long ago there was a man skilled at weaving woolen cloth who had a son whose mind was constantly indolent and lazy. The father repeatedly exhorted him, saying:
"You should work at a leisurely pace; why must you be so hurried?
Once this task is finished, there will be no further work.
The father said to his son:
"Although this task is finished, there are still other duties remaining.
He spoke these words back and forth dozens of times; the boy’s consciousness became disordered, and shortly thereafter, his liver split before his father and he died.

At that time, seeing that his son’s life-force had already been severed, the father immediately abandoned his household affairs to leave the home life and study the Way. Although he was a śramaṇa, his thoughts remained fixed on his son and he could not let go of him; nor did he contemplate the Dharma and the Path, nor was he single-mindedly settled in seated meditation to seek the supreme Dharma; nor did he contemplate the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma; nor did he practice seated meditation, recite the scriptures, or assist in the affairs of the community. His mind existed solely in constant remembrance of that deceased son.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the inclinations of those people's minds with his threefold knowledge (*trividyā*), investigated their origins and ends and fully comprehended this meaning. Desiring to cause the bhikṣus to forever be free from suspicion and doubt, and so that future sentient beings might behold this great illumination and the True Dharma (*saddharma*) endure for a long time, he spoke these verses of radiant splendor amidst the assembly:
"Just as when the loom is set up, The shuttle is cast into the weaving, And the thread is gradually exhausted— Such is the life of human beings."
"All things in the universe must return to death; impermanent and subject to change, they shall all be cast away in the wilderness among the burial mounds.

At that time, having heard the path of instruction taught by the Tathāgata, that bhikṣu understood the essential nature of impermanence, penetrated the source of demerit and merit, comprehended the transformations of rise and fall, and followed the practice of parinirvāṇa; he immediately attained the state of an Arhat before the Buddha.
It is just like a condemned prisoner being led to the marketplace; with every movement toward the path of death, such is the nature of human life.
Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kosala issued an edict to the jailer: "Any thieves whose crimes warrant execution according to the law shall be taken to the marketplace and put to death. At that moment, there was a certain thief who managed to escape from among the crowd and, donning the robes of the Dharma as a pretext, lived privately as a śramaṇa.

However, that person does not reflect within themselves, thinking: "I have forever escaped the perils of distress and no longer fear being harmed by the king. Dwelling in a secluded place, they do not contemplate the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*); nor do they study the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma; nor do they discern the principles of the various paths for transcending the world; nor do they practice seated meditation, reciting the scriptures, or assisting in communal affairs. Having forever abandoned these three matters, they do not diligently cultivate them, thinking: "This is sufficient for practicing the Way," and thus they do not increase their vigor or strive to seek the dharmas of superior persons. Yet, having not yet attained realization, they do not diligently seek realization; and having not yet attained the fruit, they do not diligently seek the fruit.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observed his mind with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and gradually transformed him so that his mind was freed from the net of doubt. He then addressed that person, saying: "Because you have not escaped the calamities of the bandits of birth and death, you harbor residual resentment; your body of the five aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) revolves through the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) without end, being ravaged by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*). You shall surely fall into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals."

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing this matter and investigating its origins and conclusions, desired to cause the bhikṣus to forever leave behind suspicion and doubt, and to enable future sentient beings to behold this great illumination so that the True Dharma might endure for a long time. Before the great assembly, he then spoke these verses:
"Just as a condemned prisoner, Being led to the marketplace, Trembling as he moves toward the place of death— The life of human beings is likewise."

At that time, while staying in a secluded place, that bhikṣu reflected and deliberated, reproaching himself within. He came to understand that all things are entirely impermanent; that once born, they do not endure long but ultimately return to extinction; and that the transformations of rise and fall have occurred for a long time and are not merely a phenomenon of the present. Thereupon, before the Buddha, he repented, reproached himself, and reformed, attaining the path of Arhatship.
Like the swift current of a river, which flows onward and never returns, so it is with human life;
those who pass away do not come back.

Once, there were many people sitting by the side of a river, watching as the waters surged and receded, causing the death and injury of countless people. There were parents, wives, children, and men who fell into the water and perished in measureless numbers; among them, only one in ten thousand attained liberation.
Having attained liberation from the deep waters, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek ordination as a śramaṇa. The Buddha granted his request and permitted him to join the ranks of the disciples.

Internally, however, he did not reflect, thinking that he had forever escaped the perils of distress and no longer feared being drowned by water. Dwelling in seclusion, he did not contemplate the Way or its virtue; nor did he study the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma. Furthermore, he did not discern the principles of meaning or the essentials for transcending the world. He did not practice seated meditation, recite the scriptures, or assist in communal affairs. Having permanently abandoned these three matters and failed to diligently cultivate them, he considered his practice of the Path to be complete with this alone. He did not increase his vigor or exert himself to seek the Dharma of the Superior Man (uttaramanuṣyadharma). Thus, though he had not yet attained realization, he did not diligently seek realization; and though he had not yet attained the fruit, he did not diligently seek the fruit.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, observes their minds with the three types of supernormal knowledge and gradually transforms them so that their minds are freed from the net of doubt. He then informs those people how to escape the calamity of the thieves of birth and death. Thus, they still possess the body of the five aggregates of clinging which harbors residual enmity; as they transmigrate through the five destinies without end, they are harmed by the various fetters and will consequently fall into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this matter and investigated its origins and conclusions, desiring to cause the bhikṣus to forever be free from suspicion and doubt, and to enable future sentient beings to behold this great illumination so that the True Dharma might endure for a long time.
Before the great assembly, he then spoke these verses: *Chuyao jing*, Scroll One *Chuyao jing*, Scroll Two
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter on Impermanence, Part Two:
"Just as the swift current of a river flows onward without returning, so too is the life of human beings."

"Those who have passed away do not return. At that time, having heard these words, the bhikṣu felt inward shame and remorse; he understood that all things must return to death, that impermanence and change prevent long-term abiding, and that there is the suffering of separation from loved ones and meeting with those one hates. Contemplating the absence of self, person, or life-force, his mind became focused and upright as he turned toward the gate of Nirvāṇa. "The drifting carried by the river waters is nothing to speak of; being drowned in the River of Death, one is not released for kalpas. One must seek skillful means to depart from and leave behind this swift current."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s urgent instruction, the bhikṣu’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he became serene and free from discursive thought. Immediately before the Buddha, he escaped the perils of birth and death and attained arhatship. Three times he proclaimed, "Excellent! How joyful it is that through the ripening of merit, my aspirations have been fulfilled!"

At that time, the countless sentient beings seated there, hearing that this bhikṣu had realized the fruit of the Way and attained its realization, all gave rise to the practice of desireless purity and all attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
The merit one has created is obtained only after a long succession of ages; it is like striking water with a staff—it parts, but then comes back together.
Once, when the Buddha was in the Amra Grove at Vaiśālī.

At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus beheld a realm of earth where the country was prosperous and the people flourishing; the dwellings were level and well-ordered, grain was abundant and cheap, and they indulged their desires as they pleased. They did not follow the prohibitions of the Dharma, and those of high and low status looked down upon one another, each claiming their own way to be the true and correct one.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for their ignorance and delusion, led them toward the flavor of the Dharma through various skillful means. He immediately gathered the great assembly and addressed the bhikṣus: "Now, those who are wise understand by means of parables.

Suppose there were a realm of earth filled with water, such that there was no empty space on the ground from east to west or north to south. Within this water lived a blind turtle, having grown there for incalculable thousands of kalpas. There was also a thin wooden board, one cubit in length and breadth, with only a single hole, which was being blown about by the wind. Now, suppose that blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years to look toward the east, while the wind blows the board toward the south. What do you think, bhikṣus?"
"Would that blind turtle happen upon the hole? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
After another hundred years had passed, he was able to look toward the south again, but the wind blew the board back to the west.
What do you think, bhikṣu?”
"Would that blind turtle happen upon the hole? He replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
In this same way, it would be so for the four cardinal directions and the intermediate corners as well.
What do you think, bhikṣu? Would that blind turtle ever happen upon the hole?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
Then the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
"Will this blind turtle’s body ever again encounter the hole?
The Blessed One replied:
"This matter is extremely difficult; only at rare intervals is there an opportunity for them to meet.
To receive the body of an animal is difficult, and to seek a human among these animals is even more difficult."
In this regard, monks, it is difficult for a human body to be obtained;
even when one has obtained a human birth, life is short and fleeting, unlike the immeasurable lifespans of people in ancient times.

The World-Honored One Vipaśyin appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. From the time the Buddha passed away until the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, another Buddha appeared, named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Being, Tamer of Men and Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One.

After that Buddha had passed away, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Viśvabhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.

After that Buddha had passed into extinction, when the human lifespan was fifty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with the ten titles and meanings manifesting in the world.

After that Buddha had passed away, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, there was a Buddha named Kāñcanamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles and their meanings.

After that Buddha had passed away, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, possessing the ten titles and their respective meanings.

After that Buddha passed into extinction, when the human lifespan was one hundred years, I have now appeared in the world, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—these being the meanings of the ten epithets.

"Monks, you should know that those who live to reach a full hundred years are few; one who lives for a hundred years appears only from time to time. Therefore it is said: 'The merit one has created is only reaped after a long succession of ages.'"

In ancient times, people accumulated merit such that their lifespans were immeasurable and they were fully endowed with all virtuous practices; moreover, there were no illnesses, epidemics, or noxious vapors. Human life spanned eighty-four thousand years, during which time there were only three afflictions:
first, desire; second, hunger and thirst; and third, aging and decay.
Now, monks! The five corruptions are boiling over;
the lifespan of people in this world is extremely short, and the four hundred and four diseases envelop their bodies.
The Venerable Aśvaghoṣa also spoke thus:
"Accumulations of afflictions constitute its substance; it is watched over by old age and death.
Pressed upon by poisonous swords and blazing fires, ten thousand ailments guard its camp."
Therefore it is said: "The merit one has cultivated is obtained only after a long succession of ages;
like striking water with a staff, once separated, it immediately reunites."
"Thus it is, bhikṣus! Human life is precarious and fragile, incapable of being preserved for long; who would covet or aspire to receive such a birth?
Only the ignorant worldlings wish to be born within the three realms of existence."
At that time, when the people heard what the Buddha had said, they all gave rise to pure, non-retrogressive practice.
It is like a person holding a staff who goes about herding and feeding cattle; old age and death are likewise like this, merely nourishing the worms of life.

Long ago, when the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, he took Ānanda with him, and as they were going along with robes and bowl in hand, they saw a man driving a thousand head of cattle toward choice grass, watching for smoke.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Do you see anyone driving a herd of cattle? He replied:
“Yes, I have seen them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“This herd of cows originally numbered one thousand. Because they were not firmly guarded and tended while outside, more than half have been devoured and killed by tigers and other fierce beasts. The remainder, unaware of this, are now butting one another, leaping about, and bellowing. How extremely profound is their lack of wisdom!”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Sentient beings dwelling in the world are likewise thus: calculating for 'self' and not knowing impermanence, they greedily cling to the five desires to nourish their bodies, seeking pleasure to the utmost of their hearts while mutually harming one another."
Impermanence arrives suddenly and without appointment; being in a state of blinding ignorance, how are you any different from those herds of oxen?
Though they are nourished by fine water and grass to make their hides grow fat, it merely hastens their end and brings no benefit to themselves.

The Buddha returned to the vihāra and, on account of these events, exhorted the assembly of the fourfold disciples. Among them, more than two hundred people attained awakening upon hearing the Dharma; they acquired the six supernormal powers and became arhats.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There are some sentient beings who attain liberation by hearing urgent instruction; there are some sentient beings who attain liberation by hearing subtle wisdom and through reflection and discernment; there are some who attain liberation through parables; and there are some who, being ignorant and dark-minded, attain liberation upon hearing but a single phrase."
For those who should be instructed through parables, this verse is precisely that.
Its meaning is understood by weighing it according to the specific occasion; therefore it is said: "It is like a person holding a staff; the matter is such as this."
This day has already passed, and life accordingly diminishes; like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be in this?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When a person dwells in this world, their actions differ and their perspectives likewise vary; yet as each day passes, human life is diminished accordingly. Though one may live for a hundred years, half of that lifespan is spent lying down."
He then spoke these verses to the assembled multitude:
“If a person wishes to establish merit, They must not let day and night pass in vain.
Day and night pass as swiftly as lightning; The life of a human being is as rapid as this.”

At that time, those gathered there contemplated this meaning and practiced it with discernment. Days and nights have already passed, and the conditions for death are difficult to calculate; yet fools rely upon and cling to existence. One should reflect and exert oneself, rousing a courageous mind so as not to lose the essence of the body.
Therefore it is said: “This day has passed, and life accordingly diminishes; Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?”

"You bhikṣus, you should clearly understand this principle: even the great oceans and rivers may eventually run dry, and the great fish of ten thousand blades may be left with their backs exposed; how much more so, then, would this be the case for a small amount of water?"
Or at times, when torrential rains fill the ditches and gullies, the swift current rushes downward with a roar that resounds for miles around;
a person on the opposite bank cannot hear the voice of one calling from this side, nor can a person here hear the voice of one calling from the other side.

At times, when the water in the ditches and ravines has been exhausted with nothing remaining, the beings of the four realms of existence, though still possessing their physical forms, find their lifespans diminishing accordingly; like fish in scant water, what joy can there be in this?

There are some sentient beings whose lifespans are extremely long: the gods have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas; those in hell have a lifespan of one kalpa; animals have a lifespan equal to that of those in hell; and the lifespan of hungry ghosts is without limit.
When the Venerable Pūrṇa arrived at the time, he took his bowl, adjusted his robes properly, and entered the kingdom of Puṣkaravatī.
At that time, there was a hungry ghost standing by the city gate. The bhikṣu Pūrṇa asked the hungry ghost:
"What are you seeking here now?"
The ghost replied to him,
saying, "Do you now see me? The bhikṣu replied:
"I saw it first," she replied.
The ghost spoke again, saying, "My husband entered the city and has not yet returned; that is why I am standing here, waiting for my lord."
The bhikṣu asked, "What did your husband seek when he entered the city?
At that time, the ghost replied:

"In this city, there is a great elder who has suffered from an abscess for a long time; today it shall burst, and pus and blood will flow out in abundance. His husband will bring two people to eat together with him, so that he may sustain his life."
The bhikṣu asked again:
"How much time has passed since your husband entered the city?
Since that city was situated close to a river, she pointed her finger toward the city and said to the bhikṣu:
"This city has been destroyed and rebuilt seven times since its foundation, yet my husband has been inside it for all this time.

The lifespan of one who has taken the form of a hungry ghost (preta) is beyond measure and has no limit; however, for one who has taken human form, even a maximum lifespan of a hundred years is but a brief moment once it has passed. Therefore it is said: "Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?"
Therefore, it is said separately that a person does not fall into the four realms of existence.
The night is long for one who does not sleep; the road is long for one who is weary; and birth-and-death is long for the fool who knows not the True Dharma.
Once, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
he addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four nights upon which those who sleep are few and those who remain awake are many.”
What are the four? When a woman perceives a man, those who fall asleep are few and those who remain awake are many;
when a man perceives a woman, those who fall asleep are few and those who remain awake are many.
The third is that of thieves: those who sleep are few, while those who remain awake are many;
likewise, when a bhikṣu seeks concentration and diligently cultivates the True Dharma, those who sleep are extremely few, while those who remain awake are many.
The ignorant perceive the night as long; the bhikṣu who practices the True Dharma does not perceive the night as long.
To the weary, the path is long;
to the foolish, saṃsāra is long.
"No one knows the True Dharma!

While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Jeta’s Grove at Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin who, due to the conditions of meritorious karma established in past lives, had reached the point where he was ready for deliverance; upon briefly hearing this verse, his ignorance regarding the long cycle of birth and death was severed.

Now, that brahmin possessed abundant wealth and treasures, with a multitude of servants and attendants; his livelihood was fully established, and the wife he had taken was of exceptionally beautiful countenance, peerless in the world, her feminine charms lacking nothing.
At that time, the brahmin reflected within himself:
"I should go to where the Tathāgata is; will there be any future Buddhas?

The brahmin left the city and went to the Jeta Grove Monastery, arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was. After exchanging greetings, he stood to one side and, with palms joined, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to ask what I have in mind; if I may be granted leave, I shall venture to present my inquiry.
The World-Honored One replied, "Ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata shall expound its meaning for you."
The brahmin said: “How many, World-Honored One,
will there be in future ages who are perfectly awakened ones?”
The World-Honored One replied, "In future ages, the number of Buddhas shall be like the sands of the Ganges.
When that brahmin heard what the Buddha had said, he gazed up at him with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; a virtuous mind arose within him.

"In the future, there will be Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; at the abodes of those Buddhas, I have well cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), established merit and virtue, and performed acts of giving without weariness.

Now, while I dwell in this world, I possess abundant wealth and many treasures; my servants and attendants are complete, and my household estate is fully established. The wife I have taken is of exceptionally beautiful countenance, peerless in this world. Relying upon these merits, I shall practice the giving of alms (dāna); whatever others may seek from me, I shall not oppose their wishes."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the brahmin took it to heart, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and with hands raised in respectful salutation, withdrew and departed.
Not long after the brahmin had traveled on his way, he thought to himself:

"I have just now inquired of the Buddha regarding future Buddhas; however, as I withdrew, I forgot to ask about the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. I should now return to the World-Honored One's presence and inquire about those past Buddhas."
The brahmin immediately returned to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and stood to one side. At that time, the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How many past Buddhas have there been?"
The Buddha told the brahmin, "The Buddhas of the past were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The brahmin stepped forward again and began to weep bitterly; raising his voice, he spoke these words:
