“Fool that I am, I have been entangled in birth and death for a long time; I have not encountered even one of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—how bitter this suffering is!
He then threw himself to the ground, rolling about in self-reproach: “This is due to my negligence;

my conduct did not follow the fundamental source, causing me to fall back to the stage of an ordinary person, or to dwell in the hells of *niraya*, among animals, or as hungry ghosts, enduring suffering through the long night: upon mountains of knives and trees of swords, amidst burning chariots and glowing coals; or prostrated on the Snow Mountains until the kalpa ends before being moved; or dwelling in the Hell of Roasting, where the pain is immeasurable.”
Although I have emerged as a human being, I was born in a remote borderland; though a Buddha has arisen in the world, I have not encountered him nor beheld him.
Previously, a bhikṣu instructed me, saying, "Foolish one, birth and death are long-lasting. How true these words are!
I should now apply myself with even greater diligence and devotion to take refuge in the Tathāgata; why wait for future Buddhas?
Fields, property, and wives are but external concerns; why must I covet them and thereby bring ruin upon the holy teaching?
At that time, the brahmin joined his palms before the Buddha, knelt on one knee, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Please grant me permission to follow the sequence of the Path and practice the holy life.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Take this brahmin and instruct him in the proper deportment, then ordain him as a bhikṣu.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus immediately ordained him as a śramaṇa.

In a secluded place, he contemplated and deliberated upon practicing the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). This is why sons of noble family leave the household life to study the Way, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the three dharma-robes; out of firm faith, they leave home from the household life to practice the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacariya*), purifying their bodies to realize realization for their own enjoyment. Knowing as it truly is: "Birth and death are ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—having thus attained the Way, he dwells in the realm of no-remainder and realizes the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this meaning and reflected upon its beginning and end; he also desired to cause the bhikṣus to quickly attain parinirvāṇa, to manifest a great illumination for future sentient beings, and to ensure that the True Dharma would blaze brightly and endure long in the world. He then spoke these verses again to the brahmin:
“The night is long for one who does not sleep; the road is long for one who is weary; birth-and-death is long for the fool, who knows not the True Dharma.”
"One has no son to rely upon, nor father or elder brother; pressed by death, there is no kinsman to provide refuge.
Formerly, when the Buddha was at the Stone Chamber Vihāra to the north of the Amalaka Garden on the Site of Enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha.

At that time, there was a man who, having prepared a grand carriage and accompanied by his followers, followed the Great Guide into the sea to gather treasures; other minor merchants likewise followed him in kind, providing food, drink, and music, and bestowing gifts upon the poor, the śramaṇas, and the brāhmaṇas.
Having entered the sea and procured precious treasures, they returned to the level shore where they enjoyed themselves together, eating and drinking with unremitting joy day after day.
At that time, one man’s food and drink were coarse and poor, consisting only of parched grain; yet he did not alter his usual habits, and moreover, he acquired immeasurable wealth and treasures.
At that time, the Great Guide said to that man:
"In this world, you possess abundant wealth and many treasures, few of whom can compare to you; why do you distress yourself and refuse to eat?"
"A person living in this world should practice two activities:
first, extensive giving; second, consuming for oneself.
Having heard this, the man did not accept it in his heart; instead, he harbored resentment and gradually became distressed and haggard, saying to the guide:
"I have prepared food and drink, yet there is no way to provide for my wife, children, and grandchildren; later, when I encountered a sudden illness, I did not even reach home, passing away midway."
That Great Teacher spoke this verse:
"A person who is stingy and greedy, hoarding wealth and property, thinking only of the enmities of their household,
does not realize that their life has come to an end."
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, saw that the leader had undertaken the task of gathering jewels but met with impermanence midway.

Thereupon, for this reason, the World-Honored One contemplated this matter, reflecting upon its beginning and end, desiring to manifest parinirvāṇa to the bhikṣus and to display a great illumination for future sentient beings, so that the True Dharma might blaze brightly and endure long in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One does not rely on sons, nor on father or brothers; when pressed by death, there is no kinsman to depend upon."

At that time, when the great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, their minds were opened and their understanding awakened; they performed meritorious deeds and established virtuous foundations, rescuing the destitute and observing the fasts and precepts without fail during the three months and six periods of the year. They provided the four requisites for support—robes, food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick—and whenever anyone required clothing, they gave clothing; whenever anyone required food, they gave food. As for wealth and the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, agate, pearls, amber, and carnelian—they did not refuse the wishes of those who sought them. Whether it was those coming from afar, those staying for a long time, or travelers passing through, they supplied all their needs, providing flowers, incense, ointments, and powders without any sense of stinginess.

Countless multitudes, weary of birth and death, abandoned their greedy attachments and cultivated firm faith; they left the household life to practice the Way, cultivating the supreme Dharma with a mind free from regression, and each attained the path of Arhatship in due order.

Thousands and hundreds, not just one—men and women of noble lineage—hoard and accumulate wealth and property, yet none escape decay and loss. Living beings in this world rush about in the four directions;

greedily seeking riches and giving rise to desire without satiety, they brave the blazing heat of midsummer and tread upon the bitter frost of winter. Through hunger, cold, toil, hardship, and anxiety, they may gain one thing for every ten thousand lost, yet even then they consider themselves fortunate. It is difficult to bring the intention to give to fruition, and their minds remain unenlightened; having neither eaten it themselves nor given it to others, though they abound in precious goods, they are no different from those who have nothing.

If a practitioner of seated meditation were adorned with the seven treasures, though their eyes beheld them, their mind would find no pleasure in them; yet because of stinginess and greed, they wander through birth and death, passing from this life to the next.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, observed how sentient beings rush in all four directions, greedily seeking wealth and goods while disregarding future consequences, all of them deluded and led astray by ignorance.

The World-Honored One, investigating the beginning and end through these causes and conditions, guides the bhikṣus toward the flavor of the Dharma; he also manifests great illumination for the sake of future sentient beings, so that the blazing True Dharma may long endure in the world, and all Buddhas of the three periods of time shall fully behold and protect it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"Thousands and hundreds, not just one— Men and women of noble lineage, Amass wealth and property,
yet none escape decay and loss."

At that time, there were many tens of millions of people seated in the assembly; hearing what the Buddha had spoken, they listened with single-minded devotion and each attained realization according to their own inclinations.
"That which is constant comes to an end; that which is high must fall; meeting implies separation;
those who are born are subject to death."
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
a certain brahmin went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if I am granted permission, I shall venture to present it.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Ask whatever you wish, and the Tathāgata shall expound its meaning for you.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
"How is it, World-Honored One?"
"For what cause and condition do the beings of the present age become increasingly subtle and thin, eventually undergoing decline, such that they are not seen to flourish in the world of humans?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"There are three causes and conditions that cause the classes of beings to become increasingly subtle and thin, eventually undergoing decline, such that they are not seen to flourish in the world of humans."
What are these three?
In this regard, O brahmin, the sentient beings of the present age are greedy and lack the Way; they are firmly rooted in stinginess and envy; and they practice false and inverted views.

At that time, those sentient beings were defiled by these three matters; unseasonable winds and rains, calamities, and floods of poison occurred, such that the seeds they sowed each lost their proper timing and failed to ripen.

If the food consumed by those sentient beings—whether raw or cooked—is beset by various ailments and pestilential vapors spreading everywhere, such that the dead fill the roads beyond counting, this is called the first causal condition, O Brahmin, by which the sentient beings of the present age become increasingly minute and thin, eventually leading to their decline, so that they are no longer seen flourishing in the human world.

Wind and rain fall out of season, and calamities run rampant; the seeds sown fail to be harvested at their proper time, and the crops do not ripen nor even sprout. The people suffer from famine, and many die of hunger. This, O Brahmin, is the second cause and condition that causes the beings of the present age to become increasingly minute and thin, ultimately leading to decline rather than flourishing.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!

Suppose today the king is greedy and unrighteous, his stinginess and envy are firm, he practices perverse and inverted views, and in governing he loses the proper measure; he is insatiable in his attachment to external objects, transgresses boundaries to wage war, and they mutually inflict harm upon one another, hacking and shooting with swords, blades, spears, and arrows, so that those killed are innumerable and beyond measure. This, O Brahmin, is called the third cause and condition by which calamities arise unexpectedly among these living beings, resulting in famine, death from starvation, and unrighteous warfare.
After the Buddha had spoken these words, he addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:

“I am afflicted with back pain and shall return to my quiet chamber. You must now focus your mind on debating with the brahmin, while also ensuring that those gathered here are forever freed from their doubts.”
He replied, "So be it,
World-Honored One! At that time,

the World-Honored One folded his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) as a pillow, placed his saṃghāṭī robe beneath him, and lay on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, fixing his mindfulness on light.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well.
The brahmin replied:
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Maudgalyāyana addressed him in verse, saying:
"Behold now this land and its realm, as well as all the various fruit-bearing trees."
Mountains, rivers, streams, and springs; the ocean and its tributaries flow on without ceasing.
Where the ancients once gazed with steadfastness, what remains here today?
May you turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma, manifesting yourself to gods and men.
"I do not rejoice at the end of life; in the end, who knows to what destination one goes?
I seek those people of the past, yet now not a single one is to be seen.
As explained at length in the original text.

Upon hearing these verses, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding attained; he immediately entered the path of the Dharma. Therefore it is said: "That which is eternal must come to an end; that which is high shall also fall; meeting implies separation, and those who are born must die."
This is its meaning: Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was a certain widowed mother who had lost her only son.
She became afflicted by grief and distress, her mind clouded and disoriented, so bewildered and confused that she was like one insane, unable to regain her composure.

Leaving the city, he arrived at the Jetavana Monastery, where he further heard people say that the Buddha was a Great Sage revered by devas and humans; that he expounded the Way of the sutras to dispel sorrow and eliminate affliction; and that there was nothing he did not clearly perceive or thoroughly understand.
Thereupon, the mother of the orphan went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself, knelt for a long time, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have always had few children; I have but this one son. He suddenly fell gravely ill and passed away, leaving me behind. The grief between mother and son is such that I cannot bear it."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to manifest his divine power and transform me, thereby untangling my knots of sorrow.
The Buddha addressed the solitary mother:
"Enter the city quickly and go through all the streets and alleys; if you find a household where no one has died, beg for fire and bring it back.
Having heard this, the solitary mother was filled with joy and realization, and she leaped for joy. She entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to a certain street, where she asked at every house:
"Is there anyone here who has not died?"
"I wish to have fire so that my breath may return to life. The people replied,
"Where are our ancestors and grandparents now?"
"You are now confused and distraught; why must you go through the alleys to speak such madness?
To every house he visited, they all spoke of death.
With body and spirit exhausted and his quest unfulfilled, he returned home. Taking his young child, he went to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha:
"Having received the imperial decree to enter the city and beg for fire from house to house, we found that everyone had suffered a death; therefore, we returned empty-handed.
The Buddha told the solitary mother:
"In this world, there are four causes and conditions by which nothing can be maintained for long."
What are these four?

First, that which is permanent is necessarily impermanent; second, that which is wealthy and noble is necessarily poor and lowly; third, that which is joined together is necessarily separated; fourth, that which is strong and healthy must necessarily die.
"Moving toward death, heading toward death, and dragged away by death, one cannot escape this affliction.
The Buddha said to the solitary mother,
"Why do you not now worry for yourself?"
Why not extensively practice giving, maintain the precepts, and observe the fast?

On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, according to your capacity and strength, provide for the destitute and the solitary, as well as for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, travelers, long-term residents, and those who have arrived for a brief stay; thus you shall obtain immeasurable merit as a result.
The widowed mother said to the Buddha, “My love for my son now penetrates to my very bones and marrow; for his sake, I would not spare even my own body or life.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to transform that person and lead them to awakening, immediately manifested four great pits of fire surrounding the widowed mother’s body. As the heat of the flames pressed upon her, she shielded herself with her son; yet the child cried out, unable to endure the agony of the fire.
The Buddha said to the solitary mother:
"You have just stated that your love for your son is so profound it penetrates your bones and marrow; you would rather lose your own life than let your son perish.
Though the heat of the fire oppresses you with unbearable pain, you must simply endure it yourself."
Is it because of your children? The minor fires of the human world are hardly worth mentioning; the fires of hell burn with immeasurable suffering.

Animals suffer from ignorance and delusion, harboring folly; hungry ghosts, possessing meager merit, suffer from hunger. Those who can benefit themselves are able to practice the Way and cultivate the roots of all goodness—practicing generosity, upholding the precepts, and practicing patience—so that they do not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo various afflictions. Receiving the blessings of devas and humans, they gradually draw near to Nirvana.

At that time, having heard the extremely profound Dharma spoken by the Buddha, the solitary mother reflected upon it herself; she reproached her own heart with earnestness, grew weary of and distressed by affectionate attachment, and eliminated all conceptual clinging. She then contemplated the perception of the world as being unworthy of delight and analyzed the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Thereupon, before the Buddha, all dust and defilements were cleansed away, and she attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, becoming a *srotāpanna*.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing this principle and investigating its beginning and end, expounded this Dharma gate for the sake of future sentient beings, and spoke these verses before the great assembly:
"What is eternal must come to an end; that which is high shall also fall. Where there is meeting, there is separation;
where there is birth, there is death."
Sentient beings harm one another and thereby lose their lives; according to their actions, they fall into various states and personally experience calamity or fortune.

All sentient beings—whether flying, crawling, creeping, breathing, or possessing form—must all return to extinction and none can escape the affliction of death. According to what they have created through their conduct, they receive their retribution: by doing good, one receives blessings; by doing evil, disaster follows. Just as a shadow follows a form, how can anything be avoided?
For this reason, these verses were spoken:
"Evil conduct leads to hell; Cultivating goodness brings birth in heaven.
If one cultivates the path of goodness, One becomes untainted and enters Nirvana."
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha,
an epidemic and calamity broke out in that city, spreading in all directions with virulent poison, such that the deaths of the people were beyond counting.
With his divine eye, which is pure and free from blemish, the World-Honored One observed that those who have committed evil deeds die and enter hell.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who grew weary of birth and death; observing these four great elements as being devoid of anything desirable, foul-smelling, and difficult to approach, they entered the nirvana without remainder and attained parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this meaning and investigated its origins and conclusions, manifesting great illumination for future sentient beings and ensuring that the True Dharma would long endure in the world.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Neither in the void nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering the mountain crags—
there is no place on earth where one can dwell and escape death.

In the past, when the Buddha was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, there were four brothers who were brahmins, each of whom had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Knowing that their lives were short and that death would come before long—specifically that they were all due to pass away seven days hence—they deliberated together, saying:

"We brothers have mastered the five supernormal powers; with our own spiritual might, we can overturn heaven and earth, manifest bodies of immense size to reach out and touch the sun and moon, and shift mountains or stop flowing rivers; there is nothing we cannot accomplish. How could we possibly be unable to avoid this calamity?"
The eldest brother said:
"I shall enter the great ocean and dwell in its center, where above and below are equal; how could the ghost of impermanence know my location?"
The second brother said:
"I shall enter into the interior of Mount Sumeru and cause its exterior to close back together so that no trace remains; how could the ghost of Impermanence know my location?"
The third brother said:
"I dwell in empty space, concealing my form so as to leave no trace; how could the ghost of impermanence know my location?
The fourth brother said:

"I shall hide myself amidst the great marketplace; there, the crowd is so dense and tumultuous that no one knows another. When the ghost of impermanence comes seeking a victim, why must it necessarily choose us four?"
Having concluded their deliberations, they went together to take leave of the king, saying:
"We have calculated that our remaining lifespans are but seven days; each of us wishes to flee in order to seek great merit.
The king immediately replied:
"May you excel in virtue.

Thereupon they parted and each went to their respective destinations. When the seven-day period was complete, they all passed away from their locations; those dwelling in the void fell away naturally, like ripe fruit.
The city magistrate informed the king:
"A certain brahmin has suddenly died in the marketplace.
Thereupon, the king was awakened to realization.
“Calamity is impermanent; when four men avoid their fate and one has already died, how can the remaining three possibly escape it?

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, perceived that the four brahmins were seeking to avoid the encounter with impermanence by each seeking deliverance from the world to escape their hardship; yet their past karma could ultimately not be avoided.

For this reason, having investigated the matter from beginning to end, he wished to reveal the great illumination for future generations and to ensure that the True Dharma would long endure in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"Not in the void, nor in the midst of the ocean, Nor by entering into the mountain crags, [Can one escape death.]”
There is no place on earth where one can dwell in safety and escape death.
Seeing the suffering of old age, the mind departs at death; yet one remains bound by the prison of the household, craving the world without ceasing.
Once, when the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha,
a great number of bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what purpose and for what reason did the Tathāgata today abandon human pleasures and the ultimate beauties of the world to leave the household life and study the Way?"
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the Sūtra on Birth to the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively, reflect upon it well, and take it to heart; I shall now speak of the most subtle Dharma."
The bhikṣus replied,
“We wish to hear it with joy.
The World-Honored One said:
"At that time, the World-Honored One extensively gave the Bhikṣu-janma-sūtra to the bhikṣus:
'Bhikṣus, you should know!
King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers and assistants:'"
"I now wish to go out to the rear garden to look about; you may quickly prepare the carriage adorned with precious feathers.
At that time, the ministers and attendants went to King Zhensheng (True Purity) and said to the king:
"The prince wishes to go out to the rear garden to look about, and has been commanded to prepare the carriage adorned with precious feathers."
When the king heard these words, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;
he addressed his ministers and officials, saying, "Permit the prince to go forth to the rear garden for recreation, for it may perhaps dispel his sorrow and distracting thoughts."

He immediately prepared his carriage and assembled a great multitude of thirty divisions of troops, with fifteen divisions each flanking him on the left and right, excluding those who served as the vanguard and rearguard. O Bhikṣu!

At that time, I went to the rear garden to look about and saw an old man whose form was decrepit and complexion changed, with loose skin and wrinkled face; leaning on a staff, he groaned, his physical strength utterly exhausted. I then asked the charioteer:
"Who is this person, whose form is so decrepit and complexion so changed as to have reached such a state?"
The charioteer replied,
"This is an old man. The Prince asked:
"What is meant by 'old age'?

The charioteer replied, "What is called old age refers to the decline of the physical form and the advancing of years, where one awaits the Lord of Death from day to morning; as the nature of decay and exhaustion gradually approaches the path of death, it is therefore called old age."
"At that time, bhikṣus!
I again asked the charioteer:
'Shall I too eventually encounter such decline?'"
The charioteer replied:
"Your Majesty and all beings among humans and devas possess this affliction; none can escape it.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"Every person who receives a physical form possesses these afflictions; whether poor or noble, rich or poor, all must experience them.
He then commanded his charioteer to turn the carriage back toward the palace, where he maintained himself in purity and contemplated the Way and its Virtue.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"Did the prince’s excursion and sightseeing proceed according to his wishes?
The charioteer replied:
"The Prince went out on his excursion but did not reach the park.
The King asked the charioteer,
"For what reason did he not go to the park for sightseeing?"
The charioteer reported to the king:
"While on his excursion, the prince encountered an old man whose form had changed and whose complexion had faded; he returned filled with sorrowful reflection.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was struck with utter bewilderment upon hearing this.

"I have previously issued a command and proclamation throughout the streets and alleys, ordering that no impure or defiled things be allowed to come within the Prince's sight; should anyone violate this, those on his left and right, and those before and behind him, shall all be executed along with seven households."
He immediately dispatched a search for him, but no home was found.
This was because he had been manifested by a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
At that time, O Bhikṣus!
Again, he thought:

"Decay and old age are not something that exist only now; once a person has emerged from the womb and received their physical form, there is decay and old age. From the moment one emerges from the womb and begins to walk and move about, as the vigor and strength of youth gradually diminish, everyone is subject to this affliction."
"At that time, monks, I spoke this verse in secret:
'In youth, when the mind is full of vigor, One is beset by old age.'"
“His form has decayed to the utmost, withered and parched; his vital energy exhausted, he must rely on a staff to walk. At that time, O Bhikṣu!
As I went out for an excursion, I first beheld this transformation. After several days had passed, I again addressed my charioteer:
"I wish to go out on an excursion to the rear garden to look about; quickly prepare the carriage adorned with precious feathers.
At that time, the charioteer went to King Zhensheng (True Purity) and said to the king:

He immediately prepared his carriage and assembled a great multitude of thirty divisions of troops; fifteen divisions followed on his left wing and fifteen on his right, with the remainder serving as the vanguard and rearguard. O Bhikṣu!

At that time, I went to the rear garden to look about and saw a sick man lying there; his body was emaciated and he was vomiting, defecating, and urinating upon himself. Flies swarmed over his body, which was swollen with dropsy, jaundiced, and so foul-smelling and filthy that it was difficult to approach.
At that time, monks, I asked the charioteer: "Who is this person?"
The charioteer replied,
"He is a sick man. [The Prince asked,] "What is meant by being sick?"

He replied: "The patient’s wind-element is disturbed and his fire-element is disordered; his mind lacks joy, various ailments have gathered, and food does not digest. He finds the sound of human voices unpleasant; therefore, he is said to be ill."
At that time, I asked the charioteer:
"Shall I, too, eventually suffer from such an affliction?
The charioteer replied: [as follows].
"The Honored One, as well as humans and devas,
also have this illness. At that time, monks,
I again thought to myself:
"Since those who receive a physical form cannot escape this affliction, what is the point of going to the gardens to look about?
I shall immediately order the charioteer to turn the carriage back to the palace, so that I may cultivate myself in quietude to eliminate this affliction."
Then King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"After the prince went out to the rear garden to view it, was he pleased?
The charioteer replied:
"The Prince went out on his excursion but did not reach the garden.
The King asked the charioteer,

The charioteer replied to the king:

At that time, King Śuddhodana was bewildered by this.

He said, "I have previously issued a decree throughout the streets and alleys: 'Let no impure or defiled things be seen by the Prince; should anyone violate this, those on his left and right, and those before and behind him, shall all be executed along with seven households.'"
He immediately dispatched messengers to investigate, but there was no household to be found.
This was because it had been manifested by a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
At that time, monks! I—
He further thought:
"When a person receives a physical form, they inevitably encounter these ailments; from antiquity until now, this has always been so.
At that time, King Śuddhodana then had this thought:

"Regarding the auspicious omens the Prince has seen during his outings, he is surely distressed by the world and will find no pleasure in the household; he will inevitably leave to pursue his studies.
I must now double the number of my attendants to guard his left side and entertain his mind."
After several more days had passed, he commanded his charioteer:
"I wish to go out for a pleasure excursion; quickly prepare the carriage adorned with precious feathers.

"At that time, monks!
I went to the rear garden and saw a dead person; his kinsmen and five-fold relatives had disheveled hair and wild locks, calling out to heaven and beating the earth as they surrounded him, weeping."
At that time, monks, I asked that charioteer: "Who is this person?"
"The clan members and five types of relatives have disheveled their hair and disarrayed their heads; they call out to heaven and strike the earth, surrounding him while wailing.
The charioteer replied, "He is a dead man."
He asked, "What is meant by death?
The charioteer replied:

"What is called 'death' refers to one whose bonds of affection have already been severed and whose life-force is no more; wife, children, and five types of kinsmen are forever parted from the world. Wind has departed, fire is extinguished, water has dissipated, and earth has scattered, each to a different place. The soul transmigrates and the body becomes like dry wood, devoid of all sensation and cognition; therefore, it is called death."
"At that time, bhikṣus!
I asked that charioteer:
'Shall I too eventually encounter this death?'"
The charioteer replied:
"Venerable sir, both humans and devas are subject to this affliction;
there is no one who can escape it. At that time, O bhikṣus!
He further thought to himself:
"When a person dwells in this world, one cannot escape these afflictions; what is the use of going to the pleasure grove at the rear of the palace?
He immediately commanded his charioteer to turn the carriage back toward the palace, intending to cultivate himself in quietude to eliminate those afflictions.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked the charioteer:
"After the prince went out to the rear garden to look about, what did he find?
Was it to his satisfaction?"
The charioteer replied, "The Prince went out on an excursion but did not reach the park; seeing a dead person along the way, he returned immediately.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was struck with utter bewilderment upon hearing this.

This was because he had been manifested by a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
At that time, O Bhikṣus!
He then thought to himself:
"Alas! Old age, sickness, and death—none can escape them!
I should now seek a skillful means to leave the household life and study the Path."
"At that time, O bhikṣus!

I immediately left home and went forth to seek the unsurpassed path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. That I have now become a Buddha and deliverated the myriad people is entirely due to my accumulation of practice with a mind free from attachment; thus, having appeared in the world, I have personally attained perfect enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated this meaning, investigating its origin and its end, in order to manifest great illumination for future sentient beings and to cause the True Dharma to endure long in the world. Then, amidst the great assembly, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Seeing old age as suffering, yet death takes away the mind; Bound by the prison of the household, craving for the world is never severed."
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they were filled with joy and delight; they immediately rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
"Old age brings about the transformation of the body, comparable to an old chariot; the Dharma can eliminate suffering—one should therefore study it with diligence."
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, a great number of bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
“The Tathāgata is now advanced in years; his skin and flesh have become slack and are no longer as they were.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"So it is, so it is; it is as you have said. I am already old.

Even if a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts and practices the holy life were to carry the Tathāgata’s body upon a high couch and travel throughout the four seas, and even if he were to offer him honor, this would not repay my profound kindness."

However, I originally cultivated the mind free from pride and attained Buddhahood through my own realization; I do not speak of this as old age. Old age is a transformation of form, comparable to an old chariot. As for what is called an "old chariot": it is that which has long been used, its parts worn out, its joints loose, and its frame decayed. It is no longer fit for travel, yet it still functions by means of being pulled along. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Just so, the body of a person who has reached old age is like an old chariot: the skin is wrinkled and sagging, the hair is white and thinning, the teeth are fallen out, and the eyes are dim. The ears are dull and the nose is crooked; the limbs are bent and the joints are stiff. One walks with a stoop, supported by a staff, and can no longer enjoy the pleasures of the five senses. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Furthermore, the body of a person who has reached old age is like an old chariot: the internal organs are weakened, the vital energy is depleted, and the four elements are in decline. One cannot endure cold or heat, wind or rain, hunger or thirst, nor can one withstand the afflictions of various diseases. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Moreover, the body of a person who has reached old age is like an old chariot: it is subject to the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death, and cannot escape the cycle of the three realms. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Finally, the body of a person who has reached old age is like an old chariot: it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and cannot escape the laws of arising and ceasing. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Thus, the body of a person who has reached old age is like an old chariot; it is a vessel of suffering and a source of distress. One should contemplate it deeply and cultivate the path to transcend it. This is what is meant by an "old chariot. Even chariots crafted by royal households—some carved and inlaid with gold and silver, others interspersed with crystal and lapis lazuli—still undergo decay and ruin after many years and ages; how much more so this physical form, composed of the four great elements, bound together by sinews and drenched in blood, which is formed only through the aggregation of various conditions?

Created by one’s parents, nurtured for ten months in the womb as they are pushed through warmth and driven away from dampness, and watched over according to the seasons—one is then called a human being.

Only clear wisdom can eliminate this suffering; thus, one should lead oneself by means of the Dharma and instruct those who have not yet awakened. Furthermore, employing skillful transformations that adapt to circumstances without limit, one should apply diligent study, following the words of guidance spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One. By removing flattery and deceit, one eliminates false views; by refraining from transgressions of body, speech, and mind, one satisfies all with the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha). To nurture sentient beings such that one’s conduct is without flaw or loss and free from fear—this is what is meant by being a disciple of the Tathāgata, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He instructs his disciples to restrain themselves and prevent wrongdoing.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations within their hearts and investigating the origins and ends of things, also manifested a great illumination for the sake of sentient beings in future generations, so that the True Dharma might long endure in the world. In the midst of the great assembly, he then spoke these verses:
"With old age, the form changes, Compared to an ancient chariot; The Dharma can eliminate suffering— One should study it with diligence."
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
Alas! Old age arrives; the complexion changes and one becomes senile. In youth one acts as one pleases, but in old age one is trampled underfoot.
In the past, when the Buddha was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha,
the Venerable Ānanda adjusted his robes and straightened his garments, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One!

Now I observe that the Tathāgata’s form has changed and his complexion has faded; his faculties are relaxed and his physical appearance has grown decrepit; the faculties of his eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are no longer as they were.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.

That which is called 'aging' can cause an exceedingly exquisite and extraordinary countenance to change into a different color, and can cause the fullness of the sense faculties to become deficient and impaired; it partners with illness and flows alongside death."

He can cause the decline of physical strength, nobility, and overflowing wealth; he can cause those with upright bodies and internal vitality to become hunchbacked and forced to walk leaning on a staff;
he can cause hair that is deep blue like the color of lapis lazuli, like honey-king, or pure black, to turn white and fall out so it no longer remains;
and he can cause eyes that blink like a cow’s and have clear distinction between the white and black parts to develop cataracts and film.
The forehead is as glossy as oil, shimmering and radiant, capable of making the wrinkles on the face appear like scorched skin;

the teeth are like white jade or fresh snow, like freshly milked cow’s milk, or like the perfectly white, full-blown inner membrane of a cuttlefish, even and level above and below, such that one can never tire of gazing upon them, while they cause the decayed, worm-infested, and carious teeth to ache with pain.

To speak briefly, among the gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, [old age] can cause decline and loss, such that one no longer possesses the mind of youth; among all forms of suffering, none is more severe than old age.
Therefore it is said: "Alas! Old age arrives; the complexion changes and one becomes senile. In youth one’s will was fulfilled, but in old age one is trampled underfoot.

Even the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, who is entwined with the thirty-two marks and adorned with his body by the eighty minor characteristics, whose seven-foot halo illuminates all darkness, and whose eightfold voice resounds afar throughout the ten directions—even he is trampled by old age and illness; how much less can an ordinary person escape this?

Investigating the origins and conclusions based on these causes and conditions, he manifested great illumination for the sake of future sentient beings and ensured that the True Dharma would long endure in the world; therefore, he spoke this verse amidst the great assembly.

Chapter on Impermanence, Part Two:
Though one may live for a hundred years, one must still pass away; oppressed by old age, the various ailments reach their ultimate limit.

In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he extensively expounded the Dharma teachings for the sake of devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and all classes of sentient beings.

At that time, the mother of King Prasenajit, who was over one hundred and twenty years old, suddenly fell gravely ill. She could not be cured by medicine, nor could she be saved by deities; before even a day and night had passed, her life came to an end.
The king and his ministers performed the funeral rites according to the Dharma, making offerings of oil, ghee, flowers, and incense for every detail.

They established a shrine and appointed people to guard it. Once the funeral was completed, they returned past the Buddha’s dwelling; as was their royal custom, they removed the five ornaments and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. The Buddha commanded them to sit and asked: “From where have you come?
Your clothes are covered in dust and your appearance has changed so drastically. What ceremonies have you performed that have brought you to such a state?”
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Great Queen of the realm was over one hundred and twenty years of age; she recently fell gravely ill and suddenly passed away.
I have just finished escorting her coffin to the burial grounds, and now I have returned to the city to pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
The Buddha, knowing through his threefold super-knowledge, asked:
"How is this, Great King?
Is there anyone born into this world who does not die?"
The king said to the Buddha,
“In this world, there is no one born who does not die.
The Buddha told the king:
“From antiquity until now, there have been five great fears that cannot be avoided:
the law of aging, which one seeks to avoid by remaining unaging—this is impossible;
the law of illness, which one seeks to avoid by remaining free from illness—this is impossible;”
To wish that what is subject to death should not die is impossible;
to wish that what is subject to decay and extinction should not decay and be extinguished is impossible;
to wish that what is subject to exhaustion should not be exhausted is impossible.
Thus it is said, Great King!

These five things that cannot be obtained do not wait for human beings; all phenomena are impermanent and difficult to maintain for long. As each day passes, so too does the life of a person. Just as the waters of five rivers flow ceaselessly day and night, the swift passage of human life is likewise.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to King Prasenajit, discoursing on the essentials of non-retrogression. As for this discourse, it consisted of a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he further taught] that sensual desires are impure thoughts and that the outflows are a great affliction.
"Great King, you should know:

'Birth brings old age; sickness robs one of luster; those who meet must inevitably part. These are the constant laws of the world. As lightning flashes before the eyes or fire appears when striking stone, so too is the life of a human being; what in it is there to delight in?"
“The principle of decay and transformation makes it impossible for anything to endure long.

At that time, the World-Honored One, investigating this matter from its beginning to its end, manifested great illumination for future sentient beings and ensured that the True Dharma would long endure in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses to King Prasenajit:
"Though one lives for a hundred years, One must still pass away; Oppressed by old age, The various ailments reach their limit."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In all worlds this is the case: nothing endures forever; all must return to death, and none can escape it.
Even the kings of old, the Buddhas, the True Persons, and the seers with the five supernatural powers have all passed away; none were able to remain."
Out of compassionate attachment for the deceased, he performed meritorious deeds without weariness; his merit followed the soul as if providing provisions to a farmer in the field.
For this reason, the King extensively established meritorious works; such blessings assist a person like relying on a sturdy staff.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the king and the fourfold assembly who had gathered there were all filled with joy; they forgot their sorrows and cast off their afflictions, attaining a sudden and clear awakening. They immediately rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid their respects, and departed.
"These days have already passed, and life accordingly diminishes; like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in this?
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at Śrāvastī.

At that time, the great southern ocean suddenly surged with a massive tide, crossing its boundaries. There were three great fish dwelling in shallow waters along the upper reaches of the current, who said to one another:
"We three fish are in a place of distress; as the floodwaters have not yet receded, we ought to swim upstream and return to the great ocean."

There was a boat obstructed by water that could not be crossed. The first fish exerted all its strength and leaped over the boat; the second fish managed to cross by clinging to some grass; the third fish, its strength utterly exhausted, was caught by a hunter.
Then the hunter spoke this verse:
"First one considers what has not yet happened, And must inevitably suffer injury;
Relying on the grass for the present moment, His life escapes from death."
"The two fish both managed to escape, Saving their fragile lives from peril;
The fool who clings to his small pool Suffers distress at the hands of the hunter.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with the pure and stainless divine eye, saw those three fish being chased by the waves: two had escaped while one remained in distress. Furthermore, seeing the hunter, he uttered this verse.

Therefore, tracing back to the root and origin of these conditions, he manifested great illumination for future sentient beings and ensured that the True Dharma would long endure in the world. He then assembled the great assembly and spoke this verse:
"The day has already passed, and life accordingly diminishes; Like a fish in diminishing water, what joy can there be?"

That which is called "this day having passed" refers to whether one is a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a lay devotee; whether young, in the prime of life, old, or decrepit—all alike share this day and its common diminution and passing. Day and night do not stop; life transforms, the body becomes emaciated, the breath declines, and strength is exhausted, all more swiftly than that [previous state].

As for the fish in scanty water, they are preyed upon by birds of the air such as hawks, white herons, cranes, blue cranes, water crows, and black chickens; they are also hunted by men and women of the world and by hunters using nets, snares, hooks, and bait. Dwelling in shallow water with their lives at stake and their minds filled with myriad anxieties, they receive their form in the water and lose their lives in the water. Amidst these manifold sufferings, which are difficult to escape, what joy can there be?
Therefore it is said: Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be?
Once departed, there is no returning; day and night one must exert oneself. The fish is scorched by the heat, suffering in life and facing the peril of death.
In the past, when the Buddha was at the site of the Excellent Victory (Sudharmā) on the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, he gathered all those practitioners of the path.

Some dwelt upon high mountains, while others remained hidden within deep caves, not venturing forth. Yet these practitioners practiced the Way according to the seasons, observing the signs and the seasonal atmosphere. When spring arrived, they saw that all the trees were budding; their color was like crystal, gradually unfolding into blossoms. Furthermore, they saw that the water flowing through the gullies and ravines was clear and limpid, tranquil and without sound.
At that time, the practitioner thought to himself:
"Time does not wait; all things arise together.
Then the practitioner descended the mountain and went from house to house in the village to beg for food. He saw men and women feasting, drinking, and enjoying themselves together, and he asked them:
"Who is this person? The man before him replied, "He is from such-and-such a village and such-and-such a family; his name is so-and-so, and he is the son of such-and-such a father."
At that time, the practitioner again thought to himself:
"Now these internal things have all begun to gestate and grow.
Knowing that the myriad things increase and flourish day by day, he returned to the deep mountains to practice in silent seclusion.

Again, arriving at the autumnal season, he descended the mountain to enter the villages for alms. He saw that all the trees were gradually withering and falling; frost and snow had fallen upon them, the leaves had dropped, and they lay frozen. Furthermore, he saw that the water in the ditches and streams had run dry and parched, so that even when touched with a finger, it was not supple.
At that time, the practitioner reflected within himself:
"Now all external things are withered and fallen; the season does not return to freshness, nor do the flowers bloom again in luxuriance. How true these words are!"

Furthermore, he saw human villages and cities where men and women, both old and young, were embracing one another; with disheveled hair and hanging locks, they beat their breasts and struck themselves, wailing aloud and unable to restrain themselves.
At that time, a practitioner asked the person:
"Who is this person who wails and weeps so bitterly as to reach such a state? [The person replied:
"In such-and-such a village, from such-and-such a family, a son has perished, a daughter has died, or parents have passed away; for this reason, the entire village is mourning with such sorrow."
Having heard this, the practitioner reflects to himself:
"Now these internal things likewise wither and fall away.

Knowing that the law of internal and external decay has arrived, he immediately returns to the deep mountains. There, he calculates within himself and sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), or on a rope seat, or beneath a tree. With a concentrated mind and focused intent, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts. He contemplates that the nature of both the internal and external is truly impermanent, and thus gives rise to the perception that everything revolves like the sun, never remaining still.

What is the revolution of the sun? Calculating from spring to autumn, one reaches a year; calculating from a year to a month; calculating from a month to a half-month; calculating from a half-month to the number of days; calculating from the number of days to a season (*kāla*); calculating from a season to a day and night; calculating from a day and night to movement and revolution; calculating from movement and revolution to inhalation and exhalation; and calculating from inhalation and exhalation until they are completely exhausted without remainder. Only upon reaching this ultimate exhaustion does one come to know that all things are empty and non-existent.
Once one knows that there is no [substantial] existence, one knows that there is no basis for arising, and likewise, there is no trace of cessation.

At times, when a practitioner’s practice gives rise to traces while its cessation leaves none, they then awaken to themselves, recollecting that all things taught by the Tathāgata are impermanent and have no nesting place.

At times, when the practitioner observes the preceding formations, they may take many days and months to be extinguished; furthermore, he recalls the Buddha’s words: "The Tathāgata has also said that what is impermanent is suffering."
At that time, the practitioner reflects within himself:
"Birth and death are thus; who would be willing to delight in them?

His mind having become weary of and averse to them, he is no longer stained by the four currents. He aspires to swiftly attain parinirvāṇa in nirvāṇa, or else to attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat in the interim.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, beheld that practitioner dwelling in the deep mountains, diligently studying the Way and never ceasing his lineage of the sages. Taking this as the causal basis, he investigated its root and origin to manifest great illumination for future sentient beings and to ensure that the True Dharma would long endure in the world. He then assembled the great multitude and spoke these verses:
"The departed do not return; Day and night, exert yourself with diligence. Like fish in a seething fire, There is the suffering of birth and the calamity of death."
Human life is like the passing of day and night;
whether staying still or moving about, it is like a swift-flowing river that flows on without ever returning.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Whenever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma, they observe the proper time and circumstances and discern the inclinations of people's minds. There may be sentient beings who reckon the body to be permanent, thinking that the body of the five aggregates from yesterday is no different today. Such fools have deluded minds; they claim the aggregates do not decay, being like the swift flow of a river, where what was before is not the flow behind and what is behind is not the flow before—what departs goes forever and what comes does not remain.

It is the same for human beings: what was done previously is not the same as what is done subsequently, and what is done subsequently is not the same as what was done previously. Those who cultivate merit—whether monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen—contemplate this body of the four great elements as being like a flowing river. By discerning and reflecting upon it until they reach the realm of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), these laymen and laywomen attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, or *anāgāmin*, while the monks and nuns attain the fruit of *arhat*.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with the pure and flawless divine eye, beheld those fourfold assemblies as they discerned the arising and passing away of the five aggregates and their respective destinies.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One investigated their origins and conclusions, manifesting the Great Illumination for future sentient beings and ensuring that the True Dharma would long endure in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the great multitude and spoke in verse:
"The human life-span is like a day and night, Whether staying still or moving about,
It is like a swiftly flowing river, Which flows on and never returns."
When the fourfold assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, they departed with joy.
When one grows old, the complexion fades; as one falls ill, the body naturally decays; when the form is ruined and becomes putrid, such is the end of life.
In the past, when the Buddha was at the Universal Assembly Hall beside the Monkey Pond in the city of Vaiśālī, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"There may be sentient beings who rely on their own vigorous strength, peerless and matchless; or those who rely on being free from illness, securing their own well-being; or those who rely on their immeasurable wealth and livelihoods; or those who rely on the accomplishment of a noble and prestigious lineage. Yet there may also be the elderly gathered among the assembly, who are reviled by others and called discarded refuse."

At that time, the World-Honored One observed that there were both right and wrong within the minds of those people; wishing to cause the multitude to reform their past ways and cultivate themselves for the future, he spoke this verse.

Then, having heard these instructions, the youths of Vaiśālī conceived thoughts of impermanence and non-self, or gave rise to the mind of impurity and the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*; some reflected upon *ānāpāna-smṛti*, the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*), the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); some attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* or the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; some resolved to seek the Unsurpassed Way; and some sought the path of a *pratyekabuddha* or an *arhat*.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with this single verse, transformed countless youths of Vaiśālī. Investigating the matter from its beginning to its end for these causes and conditions, he manifested great illumination for future generations and ensured that the True Dharma would long endure in the world. He then spoke this stanza before the great assembly:
"When old age comes, the complexion fades; The body, afflicted by illness, naturally decays. When the form is ruined and becomes putrid, Such is the end when life concludes."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the youths paid their respects and departed.
This body will not last long; it shall return to the earth, for once the consciousness has already departed, only the skeletal frame remains.

In the past, when the Buddha was staying in the Amra Grove at Vaiśālī, there was a man named Āmrapālī who relied upon his own physical beauty, which was peerless in the world; it surpassed that of humans and rivaled the forms of devas. His appearance was so dignified and majestic that one could never tire of beholding him. Furthermore, his household wealth was beyond measure; he possessed abundant riches and many treasures, with all seven precious gems fully provided.

At that time, Āṭavaka adorned his chariot with feathers and jewels; having arrayed himself in finery, bathed and cleansed himself, and perfumed himself with fragrant flowers, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who had not yet severed their craving for existence and remained at the level of ordinary worldlings; upon seeing Āḍavallī approach the Buddha’s presence, they all gave rise to lustful desire and impure thoughts. The Buddha, knowing their minds, immediately addressed them, saying: "What is this, bhikṣus?"
Ābhāsvara devas receive bodies composed of the four great elements; they are foul-smelling, filthy, and not a single part of them is worth desiring.
Monks, you should know!

These Ābhāsvara devas, though remaining thus for no long time, shall lie upon a fine, high, and broad bed, their garments fragrant and worth one hundred million coins. Upon that bed, they will suddenly pass away and be carried to the cemetery to be cremated.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were struck with astonishment:

"Impermanence is so swift that it spares neither the young nor the old; yet this man, whose physical appearance was rare in the world, having received such a form, must now be cast away among the graves."

At that time, the World-Honored One, investigating the origins and the end of these causes and conditions, manifested great illumination for the sake of future generations and so that the True Dharma might long endure in the world; he then spoke these verses in the midst of the assembly:

Among them, the fourfold assembly, upon hearing this instruction, some gave rise to the perception of impermanence and non-self; some gave rise to the mind of impurity, cessation, and contemplation; some reflected on *ānāpāna-smṛti*, the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); some attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* or the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; some resolved to seek the unsurpassed path; and some sought the path of the *pratyekabuddha* or the *arhat*.
At that time, the World-Honored One transformed countless youths of Vaiśālī with this single verse.
On account of these causes and conditions, he spoke in verse:
"This body will not last long; it shall return to the earth. Once the consciousness has departed,"
"Only the skeletal frame remains.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had said, departed with joy.
Of what use is this body?
Constantly leaking and foul-smelling, one is beset by illness and afflicted by the miseries of old age and death.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
The people of that country constantly relied upon their noble lineage, wealth, and physical strength; they acted with complete freedom, boasting that they had no equals.

Among them was one man whose family was the most powerful, yet his body was covered in sores from which pus and blood flowed incessantly day and night. It was foul-smelling and impure; everyone who saw him would cover their noses, and he suffered such agonizing pain that all who beheld him were filled with loathing and distress.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, addressed them, saying:

"Indeed, all people who receive a body share the same nature as the four great elements; the six sense-gates overflow [with impurities] no differently than those [of others]. The bodies of all people are houses of illness and suffering, wherein they dwell securely amidst myriad forms of pain, affliction, sorrow, and fear."

At that time, when the Śākyas heard the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts, some gave rise to the perception of impermanence and non-self; some developed the mind of impurity through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; some practiced mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); some attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*); some resolved to seek the unsurpassed path; and some sought the path of a pratyekabuddha or the path of an arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One converted those members of the Śākya clan with this single verse.
Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
a certain elder invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus went to that house, but the Tathāgata did not go; instead, he sent a messenger to receive the food.
There are two reasons why the Tathāgata sends a messenger to receive food.
"What are these two? First, to preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas; second, to visit the sick.

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed all the bhikṣus and saw that they had all accepted the invitations. He then took his keys and opened the door of a room, where he saw a bhikṣu who was suffering from a grave and sudden illness, lying in his own excrement and unable to turn over.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the cause], asked:
"What ailment do you have that you lie upon a bed, voiding excrement and urine, unable to turn over?
Then that bhikṣu, whose nature was upright and honest and who harbored no guile within, replied to the World-Honored One:

"By nature I am dull-witted and have always harbored indolence and pride; from the beginning, I never encouraged or assisted others in their care. For this reason, there is no one today who looks after me; I am now truly destitute and have nowhere to rely."

At that time, the World-Honored One personally took him out through the gate, removed the impurities, and washed his sitting mat. He then took pure water to wash the monk’s body, dressed him in robes, spread out a new sitting mat, and returned him to the bedroom. The Tathāgata personally reached out his hand to serve as a pillow and addressed the bhikṣu, saying:

“If you do not apply yourself with diligence to seek the supreme Dharma—so as to attain what has not been attained, achieve what has not been achieved, and realize the fruit of realization that has not yet been realized—and if you do not wholeheartedly receive this Dharma, you shall instead undergo even more intense suffering and affliction.”

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the most sublime Dharma to him, using countless skillful means to exhort him to courageously contemplate the Way and its Virtue. He then rose from his seat, returned to close the door of his room, and proceeded to the Hall of Universal Assembly, where he commanded his attendant:
"Go now and quickly assemble all the bhikṣus currently residing in the city of Śrāvastī; they shall come at once to the Hall of Universal Assembly."
When the bhikṣus had assembled, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying: "O bhikṣus!

You have no father, no mother, no younger brother, no elder brother, nor sisters; furthermore, you have no kinsmen or five relations who look after one another, yet you abandon each other—this is not fitting, and it will cause the heterodox practitioners and brahmins of other schools to mock you, saying: [text continues]"

"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses not even a hair’s breadth of compassion; he regards the lives and forms of others as he would view pottery or stones, leaving the deceased destitute and without anyone to provide for them."
"In my Dharma, the superior and the subordinate are harmonious and compliant; if you act in such a manner, you will be defeated by them.

From this day forward, a disciple shall serve his teacher as he would his own parents, never abandoning him until death; the teacher shall care for his disciple as if he were his own child, nurturing him at all times and never abandoning him until death. Thus, teacher and disciple shall cherish one another, their kindness flowing through eternal kalpas. All personal belongings are to be distributed equally; if there are no belongings, they should go to a house of extensive charity and exhort them to cultivate merit."
If you have few acquaintances, you should go to the houses of merchants to beg for alms; give what is excellent to the sick and eat what is inferior yourself.
One who thus attends to the sick is attending to my own person, and the merit obtained shall not differ in degree.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the sick bhikṣu reflected to himself:
"This body is a convergence of the great suffering of the four elements; what use is it?"
"Leaking all manner of impurities, you are beset by illness and have not escaped old age and death;
you ought to exercise self-restraint and practice the Buddha’s words.
Having said this, he relinquished his physical life and entered the realm of nirvana without remainder, passing into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, many bhikṣus took the keys and opened the door; seeing that the bhikṣu had already relinquished his physical life, they immediately addressed the World-Honored One:
"The bhikṣu who was suffering from illness has now passed away; we do not know where his spirit and soul have been reborn."
"In which path-seeds does he dwell?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"That sick bhikṣu had long accumulated wholesome deeds; when I preached the Dharma to him, his mind immediately attained awakening. Subsequently, his mind became vigorous as he turned toward the Dharma, sequentially discerning the profound teachings."
"This son of noble family has already attained *nirvāṇa*; you all should offer worship to his relics.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having contemplated this matter and wishing to cause the True Dharma to endure long in the world, and to manifest great illumination for the sake of future sentient beings, spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"Of what use is this body?
"Constantly leaking and foul-smelling, one is beset by illness and afflicted by the calamities of old age and death.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the sentient beings rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
This body is a place of leaking stench, where a multitude of diseases gather in assembly. Nirvana is the foremost cessation of affliction, a state of peace and eternal rest.

Regarding "this body is a place of leaking stench": it is a locus of manifold afflictions and impurities that people loathe to behold; it is the head of all thorns, a wound from which bitter fluids and various impurities leak. It is subject to the law of impermanence and change, destined for decay. Among all forms of suffering, none is more severe than that of the aggregates (*skandhas*). One should seek skillful means to depart from this body of the four great elements; through wise strategy and expedient wisdom, one seeks the essential way of deliverance. When all manifold distresses are forever stilled without remainder, it is therefore called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).
That which has already exhausted all emptiness is void and tranquil, and is likewise free from the duality of arising-and-ceasing or attachment-and-cessation.

That which is foremost in the extinction of affliction is peaceful, free from sorrow and the perception of joy; it is a state of peace and eternal rest, the supreme Nirvana of extinction without remainder.
At that time, those assembled, having heard this teaching, received it with joy, paid their respects, and departed.
Heat ceases here; cold snow ceases here. The foolish worry excessively about the future, yet they do not know the changes that are to come.

In the past, there was an elder who constructed a residence with separate halls for each season—spring, autumn, winter, and summer. He used them according to his own whims and did not observe the prohibitions and precepts; throughout the year, he failed to exercise restraint during the three months and six periods. Possessing immeasurable wealth, he was stingy and greedy, refusing to practice charity, nor did he give anything to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.

He did not believe in this world or the next, being dissolute and self-indulgent, difficult to transform due to his greed, ignorant of the Way and its virtue, and failing to contemplate impermanence. He further built fine dwellings—a courtyard in front and a hall behind, a pavilion for the cool season and a chamber for the winter—and erected more than several dozen rooms from east to west. Yet, when the "sword-wind" dissolved his form, he suddenly met with impermanence.

With his pure and stainless divine eye, the Buddha saw that this elder had suddenly passed away; during his lifetime, he had bestowed no acts of compassion upon sentient beings, but instead merely exhausted other people with his labor, and though he planned for a great city, he never fulfilled his aspirations.

At that time, the World-Honored One, being amidst the great assembly, desired to manifest the meaning and proclaim the fundamental source, so as to enable future sentient beings to understand it well and without doubt. Furthermore, he manifested the seal of the divine mouth of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, so that the True Dharma might long endure in the world. He then gathered the great assembly and spoke in verse:
"The summer shall end here; The cold snow shall cease here. The foolish harbor many anxieties, Yet know nothing of the changes to come."
At that time, those in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

One gives birth to a child with joyful anticipation, yet becomes so stained by attachment that one cannot part from it; like being intoxicated when encountering a violent river, one is submerged and loses both body and life.

In the past, there was a layman whose wealth was beyond counting; his household storehouses were filled with the seven treasures. He possessed in abundance gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and amber—these seven jewels being fully provided. His slaves, servants, and attendants, as well as his elephants, horses, and carriages, and his granaries and treasuries of grain, lacked for nothing; yet he alone lacked a son to carry on his lineage.

For the sake of her son, she prayed and offered sacrifices to various deities—whether to the gods of the household, the city, or the crossroads; or to the gods of the ancestors, the mountains, the trees, and heaven and earth; even down to the foul spirits of burial mounds—to all of whom she knelt and prostrated herself. Yet, in the end, her wishes were not fulfilled and she did not give birth to a son; she remained in sorrowful anxiety day and night until she gradually fell ill.

"Now my household possesses countless treasures, and all rare jewels are within my home; yet I have no offspring to inherit my lineage. When my life comes to an end, all these wealth and goods will be confiscated by the state. Thinking of this, I am grieved and distressed—what can be done?"

This person was fortunate that his illness gradually subsided; before even ten months had passed, he gave birth to a son who was peerlessly handsome, a rarity in this world, with a face like a peach blossom and endowed with all the auspicious marks.

Upon seeing this, the parents were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves; they further invited the people from neighboring villages to share a feast and merriment, enjoying themselves all day long with music and song, until some became so intoxicated that they fell asleep, unconscious of their surroundings.
At that time, there was a great flood with a sudden surge and a swift current, which swept away and drowned everyone so that none survived.

Then the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, beheld the fate and destination of this elder. Based on these causes and conditions, he investigated their origins, desiring to enable sentient beings of future generations to understand well and be free from doubt. Furthermore, he manifested the seal of the divine mouth of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, so as to ensure that the True Dharma would long endure in the world. He then assembled the great multitude and spoke in verse:
"Rejoicing at the birth of a son, Attached by love, one cannot part; Yet, intoxicated, one encounters a violent river."
They drown their bodies and forfeit their lives.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Having children and wealth, the foolish are only preoccupied with them; yet life is not something that belongs to me.
How can there be wealth for a son?
Utterly deluded and ignorant, he claims, "I am wise. To be foolish yet to call oneself wise—this is called the height of folly.

Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at the High Lecture Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, there were many young boys who were skilled in the art of archery, shooting arrow after arrow so that they touched one another. In the mastery of archery, they were the foremost; they prided themselves on their noble lineage, considering themselves peerless in the world.

"Within Jambudvīpa, there is none who can equal us; even if there were those who harbor anxieties, you, my son, are now peerless in the world—how could any treacherous thieves dare to invade and deceive us?"
The son further reflected to himself:
"My father was a master of skill and would surely have surpassed all others.
Each relied upon the other, yet in the end they could not save themselves; when the encounter with impermanence arrived, they were scattered to different places.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Amidst the current of various diseases and clans, One gazes upon brothers and kin;
Pursued by the messengers of death, One is harmed without any retreat."
The messengers of death are of many kinds; though one’s kinsmen may strive to rescue them, and though their accumulated wealth is beyond counting, they are tormented by these thieves.
As a blazing fire is extinguished with water, so is that light dispelled by a covering.
Hatred is removed by the application of poison; Evil is eliminated by incantations.
A wild elephant is led by a hook; An ox is driven by a staff.
All these things have their pleasures, Yet impermanence is difficult to preserve.
"The power of impermanence cannot be relied upon; knowing that life ends in death, one does not abide for long.
All things are exhausted, yet there is no one who perceives this; reviled by the world, beings wander through the various realms of existence."
