At that time, the Śākyas of the kingdom of Kapilavastu, having heard what the Buddha had said and knowing that their skill in archery was unimpeded, fought with King Virūḍhaka, shooting arrows at one another; yet they merely grazed each other’s eyebrows or whiskers and beards, without causing any injury.
King Virūḍhaka immediately desired to retreat, but his ministers came forward and remonstrated with him:
"The Śākyas have all cultivated the precepts and attained the fruits of the Path; though they possess skill in archery, they cause no harm."
At that time, King Virūḍhaka gradually advanced, while the Śākyas retreated and firmly defended the city gates, sending a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"Today we are in dire straits, being attacked by King Virūḍhaka."
The World-Honored One replied, "If the gate is opened, there will be injury; if the gate is not opened, there will be no injury.
Then that messenger returned to the Śākyas and spoke to them, saying:
"The Tathāgata has given this instruction: 'If you open the gate, you will be harmed by the king; if you do not open the gate, you will not be harmed by the king.
Having heard these words, the Śākyas fastened the gates shut and stood guard over them with watchful eyes.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka was stationed at the city gate and said to the Śākyas, "Open the city gates quickly;
let the two houses live together in harmony so that no harm or injury shall come to either.

Among them, those Śākyas who were bound by past karmic conditions all called out for the gates to be opened, while those without such conditions followed the Tathāgata’s instruction and refused to open them.

The Śākya clan of the Śākyas, having previously fought against King Virūḍhaka outside the city, killed seventy thousand sentient beings and wounded and killed countless others by uprooting elephant tusks.
Śyāma of the Śākya clan said to Devadaha, “The son born of a Śvapākī must not be returned; I must enter the city to further prepare for battle.
At that time, the Śākyas within the city, hearing that Śyāma of the Śākya clan had caused the slaughter of countless people, immediately sent messengers to summon him, rebuking and censuring him:

"One who is not a Śākya yet claims to be a Śākya defiles my Śākya clan. You have now destroyed your reputation; depart quickly from this country. You need not remain in this city; leave at once, you need not stay."
At that time, Śākyavardhana immediately departed from the city.
King Virūḍhaka then opened the gates again, and the Śākyas who were bound by past karmic conditions said to the other Śākyas:
"Just open the gates quickly; what can this son of a slave accomplish?"
The Śākyas, including Anuruddha, spoke these words to the other Śākyas:
"The Tathāgata has given this instruction: 'If you open the gate, there will be those who are killed; if you do not open the gate, there will be no one killed.'"
At that time, King Virūḍhaka again pressed against the city gate.
Then Mahānāman the Śākya said to King Virūḍhaka:
"Grant me one request; if it is permitted, I shall then speak my own words."
The King replied to the Śākyas, "Speak as you wish; I shall not oppose you.
Then Mahānāma the Śākya stepped forward and addressed the King, saying:
"Listen to my plan for entering the water: it shall allow all the Śākyas to escape in safety.
Thereupon, Mahānāma the Śākya entered the water, tied his hair to the roots of a tree, and submerged himself to the bottom of the river; at that moment, all the Śākyas were able to flee.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka sent men into the water to see why his maternal uncle’s son, the Śākya, was so long delayed.
Upon entering the water, they reported:
"The Śākya Mahānāma has already died in the water."

At that time, King Virūḍhaka took seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan who had attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, buried them alive in the ground, and had wild elephants trample them to death; when the retribution of past karma arrived, there was no one to rely upon for protection.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the young men of Vaiśālī:
"The void may become earth, and earth may become the void; yet the causes and conditions of past karmic retribution cannot be evaded."

Investigating the beginning and end through these causes and conditions, he manifested great illumination for the sake of sentient beings in future generations, so that the True Dharma might long endure in the world. In the midst of the great assembly, he spoke in verse:
"One has no son upon whom to rely, nor father or brother; when pressed by death, there is no kinsman to trust."
At that time, the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, departed with joy.
"One should practice this; by practicing this, one accomplishes this.
Yet people exhaust themselves in toil, unaware that old age and death have arrived.
Starving and lacking water, like a weary deer rushing toward a pond,
though pierced by the hunter's arrow, one does not think to sever desire and craving.
Thus seeking skillful means, one analyzes this physical form.
Old age and death arrive suddenly, yet one does not reach the ultimate realm.

The many sentient beings differ in their aspirations and conduct, and their actions are each distinct; the roots of goodness they cultivate are too few to mention. Their minds are attached to external labors and do not contemplate internal dharmas; they do not contemplate the approach of death, and their minds constantly reckon everything as permanent.
Long ago in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there were two brothers. One left the household life and attained the path of an Arhat; the other remained at home, managing his family estate.
At that time, the elder brother frequently visited his younger brother’s house and instructed him, saying:
"Practice giving, observe the precepts, and cultivate the roots of all virtues; then you will have a good reputation while alive and fall into a favorable realm after death."
The younger brother replied to his elder brother, saying:

"One who has left home to practice the Way does not concern himself with public or private affairs, nor does he think of father, elder brother, wife, or children; furthermore, he does not think of his household business, wealth, or treasures."
"If one is insulted and humiliated, one harbors no grief; if one encounters joy and pleasure, one does not exult in it.
Though admonished and instructed repeatedly, the younger brother did not follow his elder brother's teaching.
Later, when he fell ill, he suddenly passed away and was reborn with the form of an ox, driven by others to carry salt into the city.
At that time, his elder brother, an Arhat, emerged from the city and addressed the ox with a verse:
“Carrying heavy burdens upon your back, Traversing the road without ceasing,
Driven by others at their command, Today you perform this trivial play.”
With a nose-ring for a halter, With sores from back-wounds, abscesses, and carbuncles,
And being bitten and sucked by flies— Today’s leisure is but a cruel drama.
Fed with coarse and foul fodder, And given to drink the runoff of rainwater.
The staff and whip never leave my body; today they serve as a trivial plaything.
Having received this form of an animal, what skillful means can I employ?
I shall focus my mind exclusively upon the virtues of the Samyak-saṃbuddha.
When the ox heard this, it became choked with grief and was unhappy.
The owner of the ox said to the practitioner,
"What did you say that has made my ox so unhappy?"
The practitioner replied,
"This ox originally belonged to my younger brother.
Upon hearing this, the owner of the ox said to the practitioner:
"You were indeed my close relative in the past," [the man] said.
The Arhat replied, "In the past,
my younger brother owed you the price of one coin for salt."
At that time, the owner of the ox spoke to the ox, saying, "I now release you; I shall no longer employ you for labor.
Thereupon, the ox threw itself into a deep ravine, mindfully recollecting the Buddha with all its heart, and immediately at the end of its life, it was reborn in the heavens.

There are some sentient beings who deeply covet worldly entanglements and are attached to wealth and goods; they do not cultivate wholesome conduct, and when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts.
Alternatively, there are those who leave the household life to study the Way, renouncing affection and love, abandoning the eight worldly dharmas, and cultivating a pure resolve.

It is like the case of a royal prince who desired to marry the daughter of a candāla; though she wore fragrant necklaces and was of upright countenance, appearing like a celestial maiden, the king replied:
"According to the law of kings, one does not marry outside one's own class, nor does one wed with commoners; one always marries among the elders and householders."
The Prince said to the King, "If you do not grant me this girl in marriage, I shall now take my own life; I cannot endure living in this world.
Upon hearing these words, the King was like one who has encountered a choking sensation while eating: the food neither enters his stomach nor can he spit it out.
The king sent him out; upon arriving at the house of a caṇḍāla, he said to the girl’s parents, "You should give your daughter in marriage to my crown prince.
The girl’s mother replied:
"Those of my lineage who practice the art of killing shall give their daughters in marriage to the King’s crown prince.
The King returned and said to the prince:
"If you now insist on practicing the dharma of taking life, abandoning the royal lineage to pursue such common and trivial matters, why do you insist on killing a girl for the sake of marriage?"
The Prince said to the King:
"Whatever my heart craves and delights in, I shall surely practice the art of killing without regarding it as difficult.
He then abandoned the royal palace and went to a butcher's house to arrange a marriage.

As time passed in this manner, he continued to carry firewood and grass and hold a basket to sweep; the chief minister, while out on an excursion, saw him and asked the prince, "Have you finally obtained the girl?"
The prince replied, "I have been burdened with many duties and labors; I forgot the girl long ago and no longer remember her.
The minister asked again:
"Where is that fragrant garland strung with pearls now?
The Prince replied,
"I have also forgotten it and no longer recall it."
The minister said to the prince:
"Since you have neither obtained the maiden nor the jewel, and have furthermore lost your royal throne, with nothing at all gained, what course of action would be appropriate?"
The prince shed tears, feeling deep sorrow and distress.
This is an analogy for being of benefit and excellence among the multitude.

There may be princes, elders, or householders who leave the home life to study the Way, establishing merit and virtue with the aim of becoming an arhat; they sever worldly fetters and attachments, become detached from desire, and through mutual liberation and the discernment of ignorance, achieve the meaning of precious jewels through wisdom-liberation and the liberation from doubt.
His parents and brothers rebuked and restrained him, saying to the one who had gone forth from home:
"Among human beings, nothing is more base and contemptible than the Way; begging from house to house is made one's constant practice—how can one endure or find joy in being ridiculed by others?"
People may curse you and wish to make you a beggar; it would be better to remain at home and enjoy yourself with the five desires.

Diligently practice giving and charity to create merit for the sake of those in the future, the past, and the present; provide for the solitary, the destitute, the naked, the lowly, as well as śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, guests, and travelers. Offer the four requisites—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to those who need clothing, give them clothing; to those who need food, give them food. Incense, flower garlands, hand-towels, and the six vessels can all be provided by one living at home; the life of a renunciant is extremely arduous.
Then the students said to their five kinsmen, "Our aspirations are fixed on practicing the Way; we do not delight in remaining at home to manage worldly affairs.
The kinsmen replied:
"One who does not delight in the secular world may leave home to practice the Way at will.

Thereupon, he abandoned his home to become a seeker of the Path; however, what he practiced was not essential, and he did not cultivate the right practices for some time. His five close relatives went to see him and asked the practitioners:
"Have you attained the path of an Arhat?"
The practitioner replied,
"Since I began studying the Way, it is only now that I have heard the name of an Arhat.
His five relatives asked again:

"Being without desire for desires, both [self and others] are liberated; having removed ignorance, one achieves the jewel of liberation through wisdom free from doubt. Is it not possible to attain such a multitude of dharmas?"
The practitioner replied, "We have lost all these various dharmas; we do not even know their names, let alone their principles or practice.
His five relatives then questioned the practitioner:
"Why have you abandoned your homes, wealth, and occupations; why have you cast aside your five relations and parted from those you love?
What you have practiced is not the Dharma, for it is no different from that of worldly people.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, observed the five relations as they debated with the practitioners of the Way. Knowing that they had practiced what was not the Dharma and were not in accord with the essential path, the Buddha wished to go and transform them, and thus manifested his power of the Way.

For this reason, having investigated the beginning and the end, he manifested great illumination for the sake of sentient beings in future generations, so that the True Dharma might long remain in the world. In the midst of the great assembly, he spoke these verses:
"Do this; therefore, one should practice this. By practicing this, one accomplishes this.
Yet people exhaust themselves in toil, unaware that old age and death have arrived."
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit spoke again in verse:
"Bathed and adorned in finery, the fool remains unpracticed in the good;
when impermanence suddenly arrives, it is like a mother embracing her dead daughter."

Sentient beings strike one another down and engage in mutual criticism; what they practice is erroneous and fails to accord with the True Dharma. It is like the case of a husband and wife in the past, both of whom were handsome and possessed of majestic countenances, endowed with all auspicious marks and tranquil faculties, treating each other with mutual respect throughout the day without ever growing weary.

As the days passed in this manner, the husband and wife suddenly lost their sight and could see nothing. Out of deep affection for one another, they feared being deceived by others; the husband feared losing his wife, and the wife feared losing her husband. They sat together, guarding one another, not departing for even a moment.
At that time, the five types of relatives sought out physicians from afar and brought them to the blind husband and wife; after applying medicine to treat the eyes, they were soon restored to sight.
When the husband saw that his wife’s appearance had changed and was no longer as it once was, he raised his voice and said, "Who has altered my wife?"
When the wife saw that her husband’s appearance had changed and was no longer as it had been, she raised her voice and said,
"Who has altered my husband?
Her five kinsmen then explained to her:

"The appearance of youth and vigor shifts with each passing day; as the vital energy weakens and strength is exhausted, the skin slackens and the face wrinkles, changing day by day. To look upon this aged and decrepit countenance and compare it to one's former youth is like drilling through ice to seek fire—is it not a great delusion?"
"Why do you weep, not even recognizing me?

He looked at his own reflection in a mirror and saw that his countenance had changed; he sighed, realizing that old age had arrived and that physical beauty does not endure. His once-dignified and outstanding appearance had suddenly become altered, and as sorrowful thoughts and anxieties increased, his suffering grew.
The Venerable Dharmayasas then spoke these verses:
"Just as when a person is fast asleep, A thief breaks through the wall to steal;
The owner does not perceive the loss of wealth, But upon waking, searches for it everywhere."
"The fool, having long practiced indulgence, sinks himself into the dark pool;
he does not see the thief who has stolen his wealth, for the thief of old age has rendered him powerless. Therefore it is said:
"To practice that which is not essential is to oppose the Way and lose the Dharma; one fails to realize that old age and death are approaching.
When the people heard these words, they departed with joy.
Therefore, practice meditative concentration; with the exhaustion of birth, there will be no more feverish affliction.
The bhikṣu who detests the armies of Māra shall attain deliverance from birth and death. The Tathāgata has proclaimed that all things are impermanent and subject to change;

hearing this, the bhikṣus all gave rise to a sense of weariness and renunciation. They departed from the roots of the aggregates, the bases, and the sense-fields. The World-Honored One instructed them in right action and taught them the practice of the True Dharma: whether among burial mounds or beneath trees, or in the open air practicing walking meditation or sitting in dhyāna and mindfulness, do not harbor indolence or pride. If you are not diligent now, it will be of no avail to regret it later. This, O bhikṣus, is my injunction.
Therefore it is said: "For this reason, practice meditative concentration; when birth is exhausted, there is no feverish affliction.
Whether at dawn, midday, or evening, during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Whether walking or sitting, coming or going, sleeping or waking, you should mindfully practice this samādhi so that it is not lost. One whose birth is exhausted and who has no feverish affliction has no affliction of body, speech, or mind, and is not afflicted by the fire of the fetters; such a person is courageous and diligent."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
“If one’s head or one’s robes are on fire, how does one prevent it?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"One must protect one's head and guard one's robes to prevent [the fire]; thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It is not as good as coming here to observe the head and observe the robes, but rather seeking further skillful means to extinguish unwholesome dharmas with wholesome dharmas. With firm resolve, never overstep the continuity of all wholesome dharmas; then birth will end and there will be no feverish affliction. Those who are born still exist within existence; birth, old age, sickness, and death are likewise existence. Grief, affliction, suffering, and distress, revolving and wandering back and forth, all arise from existence."
While the Chapter on Impermanence was being recited, Ānanda then spoke this verse:
"I have heard of an occurrence from the past, when the Tathāgata preached the Udānavarga;
for sentient beings harboring the darkness of ignorance, he went forth to rescue them with compassion."
One who preaches impermanence is fully endowed with the body of words, the body of phrases, the body of sentences, and the body of meanings, and their speech is flawless.

Hearing this at once, those who possess the marks of the aggregates, bases, and sense-fields are able to discern the various types of persons—namely, sentient beings, life-span, birth, form, and the body of calamity.

I heard from the Buddha at one time that the matter was as follows: with focused mind, undisturbed and without other thoughts, he sought the roots of all goodness and revealed the direct path for sentient beings shrouded in ignorance and darkness. For those beings living in the world who were born blind and sightless, he opened their eyes so they might see; out of great compassion, he rescued them from their suffering, regarding those beings as his own father or mother, and expounded upon their meaning.

By understanding the profound meaning of the words and skillfully cultivating one's virtue and conduct, one shall be able to exhaust all suffering and attain the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

One may eliminate the fetters (*saṃyojana*) through their meaning, rather than through the body of flavors or the body of phrases. The Buddha’s sūtras also state that those who do not bestow the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and equal view do not accord with the correct path; yet, for those without fetters whose outflows have departed, it is said that they will not be born again. This is the Buddha’s sūtra. Alternatively, some may recite the Buddha’s sūtras without exhausting the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); therefore, the World-Honored One taught that one should deeply understand the meaning of the words.
Then, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Then the Venerable Rāhula addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata..."
"Preach the Dharma to me, so that my mind, still subject to outflows, may swiftly attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Rāhula:
"You should contemplate the *Saṃyukta-āgama*; once you have finished reciting it, come to where the Tathāgata is."
At that time, Rāhula recited the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Connected Discourses) fluently and with ease; having reached the place where the World-Honored One was, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"Having recited the *Nidāna-saṃyukta* and the *Saṃyukta-āgama*, you have not attained liberation from the outflows.
The World-Honored One told Rāhula:
"You should recite the *Pañca-upādānaskandha-saṃyukta*."
At that time, Rāhula immediately accepted the instruction and recited the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānakkhandhā*). On another occasion, he went to the Blessed One and said to him:
"I have already recited the five aggregates of clinging, yet my mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) has not attained liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Rāhula:
"You should recite the *Ṣaḍindriyaviniścaya*.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Rāhula then recited the *Ṣaḍindriyaviniścaya*. On another occasion, he went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Having recited the six contacts, the mind with outflows (āsrava) does not attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula, saying:
"You should contemplate and examine the meaning of this."
At that time, Rāhula received the Buddha’s teaching and immediately contemplated and analyzed its meaning; he gradually exhausted the fetters and afflictions and attained the fruit of arhatship.

All this arises from the meaning of discernment; therefore, by transcending the sequential order to attain realization, one exhausts all outflows (āsrava) and achieves the state of being without outflows (anāsrava).
For this reason, Ānanda said:

"By understanding the profound meaning of the words, one skillfully cultivates the Way and its virtue; through the Way, one severs the fetters, removes the entanglements of the seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya), and brings them to permanent exhaustion without remainder."
The Way refers to Nirvana—extinction, the absence of arising and ceasing, freedom from attachment and aversion, peace, and bliss; therefore it is said: "Cultivate the Way and its virtue well."

"One who attains the exhaustion of all suffering" refers to what is called suffering: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from those one loves, and the suffering of encountering those one hates.
One attains the state of no remainder; "no remainder" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is unsurpassed and faultless.
*Udānavarga*, Volume Three; *Udānavarga*, Volume Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Two: On Desire. I know your origin, O Desire: your mind is born from conceptualization.
If I do not think of you, then you do not exist.

Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the World-Honored One, accompanied by his attendant Ānanda, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having completed his almsround, he returned and went outside the city walls.

There was a woman carrying her child and holding a water jar who went to a well to draw water; there was also a man of handsome appearance sitting to the right of the well, playing the lute for his own amusement.

At that time, the woman was excessively overcome by lustful desire and became deeply attached to the man; the man, likewise, was filled with intense passion and became deeply attached to the woman. Her mind, maddened by lust, tied a rope around the infant’s neck and suspended him in a well. She immediately pulled the child back out, but he had already died. Overcome with grief and sorrow, she cried out to heaven and shed tears, speaking this verse:
“I know your origin, O Desire: You arise from mental conceptualization. If I do not conceptualize you, Then you shall no longer exist.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The verses you have just heard were spoken by all the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; you should recite and master them well."
"At the hour of late afternoon, assemble the multitude and proclaim this verse among them.
At that time, after his meal, the World-Honored One gathered his three robes and immediately led the great assembly to the Hall of Universal Assembly, where he sat among the people.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"This morning at dawn, I took Ānanda into the city to beg for alms. Having completed our rounds and returned outside the city, I saw a woman carrying her child and holding a water jar approaching a well to draw water; not far from the well, there was another person playing the lute for his own amusement."

Upon seeing one another, both gave rise to lustful thoughts; they gazed intently at each other with unblinking eyes, mistakenly tying the child’s neck and suspending him in the well. They soon pulled him back out, but the child had already passed away.
Sorrowful and lamenting, he immediately spoke this verse:
"I know your origin, O Desire: you are born from mental ideation.
If I do not ideate you, then you shall no longer exist."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The fire of lust blazes so fiercely that it can incinerate the roots of all that is wholesome. Those who are abandoned by lust do not recognize good from evil, nor do they distinguish between pure and defiled conduct; they are ignorant of the path of bondage and liberation, and the way to transcendence."
Such people as these ultimately lack a sense of shame; they would rather lose their kinsmen and endure physical humiliation than let their lustful nature fail and thus violate their will.
Or, driven by sexual desire, they may even kill their parents, brothers, or sisters, thereby incurring such calamity.

Or perhaps due to the sins of lustful indulgence or the five heinous crimes, one may be executed by the sovereign and undergo an evil retribution; this is like a wild fire spreading that scorches the trees alongside it—once the sin is profound, it further extends to one's kinsmen.
Because people transgress the Buddha’s Dharma through lustful desire and slander the Noble Assembly, they are ridiculed by all the sages and worthies.
I shall now explain the root of committing sexual misconduct; listen well!

Long ago, there was a man whose lustful depravity knew no bounds. His parents had begotten him as their only son; one night, during the hours of non-human activity when the sky was dark with thunder and lightning, he took up a sword and arrows and went to the village of a courtesan.
At that time, the mother became aware of the situation and immediately seized him, admonishing him:

"Tonight is pitch black, overcast, and filled with thunder and lightning; if you do not succeed, you will surely be harmed by others. I have had little merit in my past lives and have only this one son; if you encounter an evil person, I shall have no one left to rely upon."
The son replied to his mother, saying, "I must go; I cannot stay any longer.
Knowing his resolve was firm, the mother bowed toward her son.
"I shall stay for tonight; I must depart tomorrow.
The son said to his mother, "Release me at once!
If you do not comply with my wishes, I shall take your life."
The mother replied to her son, saying:
"I would rather have you kill me than bear to see you harmed by another.
The son spoke again to his mother:
"You must release me at once so that I may reach him before nightfall; if you do not grant this, I shall simply kill my mother.
The mother said to her son, "Even in death, I will not let you go."

The son immediately drew his sword, seized his mother, and stabbed her to death; without considering the grave and heavy calamities and sins of future lives, he went at once to that house, knocked on the door, and called out softly.
A woman answered, saying: "Who are you?"
The man replied with a verse:
"Passion and anger weaken the faculties; One is led astray by perceptions.
Without considering one's manifold duties, One is shrouded by the darkness of folly."
"I remember how you took my mother and killed her;
though subdued, you remain like a slave, standing tall outside the gate like a guest attached to menial service.
At that time, the woman saw him from afar again and asked:
"Did you truly kill your mother?
He replied, "I truly killed her."
The woman asked, "For what reason did you kill your mother? The man replied:
"My mother did not release me to come here. The woman replied,
"There is no need to enter the house."
At that time, the woman replied in verse:
"Alas! You who have turned your back on the kindness of your nurturer, You who have committed the calamity of harming your mother— How can I bear to look upon your face?"
"You ought to depart quickly from my household.
My parents embraced and nurtured you, and as their son, you have endured manifold sufferings for them.
Yet you harm your mother while walking upon the earth; the earth does not sink beneath you because you are a killer."
"Having established myself without compassion or benevolence, I have brought harm to my own kinsmen;
as one of a different lineage, how could I possibly lead you with kindness and virtue?
At that time, the man replied again:

"Because you have harmed your mother, you have committed boundless sin; I grant you a small measure of leniency and open this door for you. You may speak with me briefly, and then you shall return home.
The woman replied: "Listen to my verse:"
"Better to cast oneself into a charcoal pit, Leap from a mountain into a deep valley,
Or seize a seven-step serpent with one's bare hands, Than to associate with the foolish."
At that time, the two parted from one another.
The man returned home, but on the road he encountered wicked bandits and was killed by them; he died and entered the Avīci Hell, where he suffered for countless kalpas.

Lust as a disease brings about immeasurable calamity; from the minute it accumulates into the great, it gradually leads to the burning of one's own body. One sinks into the Way for oneself and likewise involves others; failing to reach the ultimate goal, it is like drinking poison oneself and then giving it to others to drink.
Therefore it is said: One must not follow lust.
From love and desire arises sorrow; from love and desire arises fear. When there is nothing for which one has love and desire, what sorrow and what fear can there be?

Sensual desire gives rise to sorrow: whether one encounters the death of a wife or is robbed by others, or suffers from a chronic illness, or a husband travels far away and does not return for a long time—for these reasons it is said, "Sensual desire gives rise to sorrow."
Regarding "Fear arises from sensual desire": it refers to being stripped of one's wife by a powerful nobleman; or having long suffered from illness such that life hangs by a thread;
or departing for another land. Therefore it is said: "Fear arises from sensual desire."
Regarding "one who has no desires": how is it that one has no desires?
The Anāgāmin and the Arhat—these two distinct individuals—are without sorrow and without fear.
Why is this? Because one who has already abandoned all sorrows has nothing to fear or dread.

Those who possess sorrow and fear do so within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). For an *anāgāmin*, the sorrows and fears of the desire realm are exhausted; for an *arhat*, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of all three realms are exhausted. Within these states, they do not give rise to the notion of sorrow or fear. Therefore it is said: "When there is no craving or desire, what sorrow or fear can there be?"

Delighting in pleasures gives rise to sorrow; delighting in pleasures gives rise to fear. Having nothing to delight in, what sorrow or fear can there be? Regarding "delighting in pleasures gives rise to sorrow":

when one performs music and dance or indulges in the five desires for self-entertainment, one may be resented by a king who wishes to seize one's musical instruments; it is on account of this that sorrow arises.
Or, being sent by a king to travel far to another land, one gives rise to sorrow therein;

or, suffering from a chronic illness, one remains bedridden for a long time and loses sight, giving rise to fear at the prospect of losing one's life-force, and because of such musical instruments, one comes to lose one's body.

There may be a king whose lineage has perished and who has lost his throne; as his misfortunes are not of his own making, he recalls the places where he formerly roamed in his noble and wealthy splendor, and thus gives rise to sorrow and anxiety, eventually leading to a grave illness.

Or, if one has an old enemy who wishes to take one's life and watches for an opportunity day and night to capture or harm them, one consequently gives rise to thoughts of anxiety and distress within that situation. Therefore it is said: "Delight gives rise to sorrow; delight gives rise to fear."
What is meant by "having no fondness for pleasures"?
It refers to the *anāgāmin* and *arhat* who have abandoned all five types of sensual pleasure and delight themselves in the joy of the Dharma.
This is just as Nanda once said to the Buddha:
"I shall never find joy as long as I do not see my Sundarī.
The World-Honored One said to Nanda:
"If there is no satiety, how can there be contentment?"
If there is insufficiency, what joy can there be?
If there is no joy, what craving can there be?
If there is no craving, what pleasure can there be?
"You now indulge your desires without ever finding satisfaction; your will is constantly ablaze—when will it ever cease?
Therefore, you should now contemplate internal observation of the perception of impurity, and you shall then spontaneously awaken and attain liberation within your mind."
"The reason you have not yet attained liberation is that you do not contemplate mental objects (*saṃjñā*).
Because you do not contemplate [the foul], lust, anger, and delusion blaze up; therefore, Nanda, endure with diligence and single-mindedness, contemplating the impurity of the loathsome (*aśubha*)."

Why is this? It is difficult to obtain a human body; it is likewise difficult to encounter the worthy sages; it is likewise difficult to have one's faculties complete and unimpaired; and it is impossible to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Just as the udumbara flower appears only once in a great while, so too is it difficult to encounter the hearing of the True Dharma.
Resting in non-action, ever joyful and at peace—all these are attained by reaching the further shore through the True Dharma.

Therefore, Nanda, you should be mindful and exercise self-restraint; contemplate the True Dharma and cultivate the perception of impurity, and you shall then reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus it is said: "Delighting in [sensual pleasures] gives rise to sorrow; delighting in them gives rise to fear. When there is nothing to delight in, what sorrow and what fear can there be?"
The Buddha spoke again in verse:
"Like fruit that is sweet at first but bitter later, so too are lust and anger.
One will subsequently undergo the retribution of suffering and pain, enduring it for incalculable eons."
The fool undergoes burning and boiling, constantly within a blazing flame;
seized by the wardens of hell, he is subdued like an elephant with a hook.
Long ago, the Buddha spoke of the aggregate of suffering to his disciples.
A sutra states:
"Those who are attached to desire say among themselves:
'The śramaṇa Gautama and the brahmins constantly speak of themselves as preventing what has not yet occurred, worrying about future desires that are defiled and impure.'"
"It is not as we intend; we are stained by beautiful forms and delight ourselves in the five desires, finding pleasure in their subtle textures. What could possibly be lost?

If there are sentient beings who stubbornly rely on such teachings and commit unwholesome deeds, then when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will enter hell. Only after being born in hell do they realize it for themselves and reproach one another, saying:
"When we were human beings, we did not believe the words of the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who spoke of the defiled and impure nature of sensual desire."
"Due to this sexual depravity, one undergoes immeasurable suffering with no end in sight for seeking liberation; having created it oneself, to whom can one complain?

Therefore it is said: "The fruit is sweet first and bitter later. It is like a fruit that enters the mouth with a sweet flavor; at the time it is pleasing, but later it inevitably gives rise to affliction.

He then spoke a parable to delight and instruct those of wisdom: "There may be wise people who achieve accomplishment through encouragement; there may be wise people who are transformed by being rebuked and restrained; there may be wise people who receive instruction by having their inclinations observed; there may be wise people who attain liberation through gradual guidance and exhortation; and there may be wise people who awaken of their own accord by traveling afar to observe the world."

The World-Honored One observed the defilements according to their inclinations and administered the appropriate medicine for their treatment; thus, sentient beings gradually attained awakening of mind.

Receiving the Tathāgata’s teaching, they felt shame regarding their faults and transgressions, and as their various fetters were gradually exhausted, their minds with outflows attained liberation. Only then did they realize that sensual desire is a disease, which is sweet at first but bitter in the end.
Hard materials such as iron, copper, and tin—these prisons are not truly secure;
attachment to those pleasant forms—that is the most secure prison.

In the past, there was a man who was imprisoned for an offense in an iron cell. He devised a clever plan to escape his punishment: he might rely on the powerful, or use wealth and goods, or depend upon his clan and lineage to clear himself of his transgression.

The firm bonds of sensual craving cannot be untied by ordinary worldlings; only when the Buddhas appear in the world do they use the blazing flames of wisdom to incinerate the thickets of fetters within the mountains and wilds, and with the sharp blade of their sword, sever the very roots of the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), whereby one finally attains liberation.

Once there was a man who, having encountered a legal matter, was imprisoned. It happened that a group of monks were preaching the Dharma nearby, and the prisoner requested permission from the officials to go briefly to listen to the teaching. There he encountered a bhikṣu who, in the silence of midnight, was reciting a sutra:
“Bound by old age, bound by birth, bound by sickness, and bound by death—one is bound in this world and in future worlds.”
At that time, the person’s kinsmen sought to exonerate him from the king’s transgression, and he was immediately pardoned.
Then his relatives, acquaintances, and friends went to the offender’s house to offer their congratulations, saying:
"We heard that you have been released; we congratulate you most heartily."
The man replied: "Why have you been deceived?
As I heard the bhikṣus reciting the sūtras last evening, my imprisonment was far more severe than that of the king."
The crowd asked, "Even though you have escaped, are you still so confused and disoriented? The man replied:
"I have not made a mistake; it is only you, sirs, who have erred. That by which I am bound cannot be untied by a king.
If you, my kinsmen, truly love me, I pray that you grant me permission to leave the household life and enter the ranks of the Path."
His relatives exhorted and admonished him, speaking of the obstacles to his departure:
"Your parents and kinsmen, both male and female, are all accomplished; for what reason would you abandon them to greedily pursue the path? The man replied:
"I have previously vowed that I must leave the household life to study.
His relatives earnestly entreated him to stay and desist.

After another seven days had passed, he had recovered from his exhaustion and regained his strength; as he was leaving the gate, he encountered a practitioner in a quiet place reciting his studies, who spoke this verse:
“Hard materials such as iron, copper, and tin—these bonds are not truly firm;
attachment to those forms—that bond is the most firm.
He then returned to his house and spoke to his five kinsmen:
"I intend to renounce the household life; I pray that you will grant me permission to go forth and train in the unsurpassed holy life.
Thereupon, his five kinsmen immediately granted him permission to go forth and train.
Advancing in practice day and night without ceasing, one attains the fruit of Arhatship, forever leaving behind bondage and attachment, no longer wandering through birth and death.
Among the bonds, that which is most firm—like a flowing room with loose cords—is difficult to untie;
to be able to sever this is essential, for one who does not contemplate will fail to cut off sensual craving.

Regarding "the most firm among bonds": all forms of affectionate attachment are bonds. Only when the Buddhas arise and manifest the Vajra-holding mind (*vajradhara-citta*) is there that which is firm and difficult to destroy. Adorned naturally with a multitude of virtues, one casts away all evils; by not giving rise to the conditions for transgression, one is able to sever all evils. For this reason, it is called "the most firm among bonds."

Regarding "the stream is slow and difficult to untie": as for "the stream," it flows within the realms, within birth, and within the destinies. Now I shall provide you with a simile; through similes, the wise understand for themselves.
In the past, there was a king whose grace and bounty were so pervasive that he issued a general amnesty for the whole world, releasing all those who were imprisoned and heavily fettered.

Among these beings, those who loathed their bondage and found the prison unbearable were constantly resolved to distance themselves from it; they sought swift liberation from the jail and had no desire to remain.

Furthermore, there are beings who take pleasure in remaining within the prison; their minds are filled with longing for it, and they delight in hearing sounds of suffering. Thus, they dwell within the prison and are unwilling to leave. For this reason, it is said: "The flowery chamber is slow to escape."
The reason they are slow to leave is that, having encountered amnesty and received its grace, they are unwilling to depart.
Only by means of the accumulated goodness and various merits performed in the past can one sever these ties; therefore, it is said that being able to sever them is the essential requirement.
He disregards brothers, family estate, and kinsmen; he does not look back upon the severance of sensual desire, for sensual desire has already been severed, forever without remainder.
He transcends the eight worldly concerns by means of two vows.
What are these two? The first is the vow of wisdom, and the second is the vow of exhaustion.
By means of these two vows, one vows to deliver all sentient beings.
The world contains many exquisite forms, yet these are not called "desire";
worldly desire persists long within the world, and only the wise are able to perceive this.
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"We should rather renounce the food provided by the Sangha and beg for alms among the people. Why is this?

Because when bhikṣus who beg for alms travel and observe among the people, they behold most exquisite forms with their eyes, hear most exquisite sounds with their ears, smell most exquisite fragrances with their noses, and experience most exquisite textures with their bodies."

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure, tranquil, and stainless divine ear, heard the bhikṣus speaking among themselves, each giving rise to longing and becoming stained by attachment to worldly glory.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately sent a messenger to summon the assembly to the Lecture Hall, and the bhikṣus gathered at the hall.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think, bhikṣus?"

I have told you before that when bhikṣus who live on alms travel through the human world, they may behold most exquisite forms, hear most exquisite sounds, smell most exquisite fragrances, and touch most exquisite textures with their bodies.
"How is it, bhikṣus!
Is your mind light and fickle?

You are currently preoccupied with the phenomena of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, which are like a blazing fire already extremely intense, further augmented by the addition of fat and ghee. You are thus doubling the intensity of the phenomena of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles."
There are bhikṣus who are able to exercise self-restraint; while begging outside, their minds are constantly filled with apprehension:
"Is it not difficult to receive the offerings of others' faith?

These donors have rushed about in all directions, exhausting their feelings and laboring their thoughts to obtain these goods; they truly believe in future lives and thus set aside portions of their wealth to give as alms."
"I now possess few virtues and fear that I may not be able to digest this.

When observing the donor at the time of giving, he intends to receive the faithful offering with the thought that he does not wish to receive it; he observes his own body as if he were suffering from a grave illness; he regards the gift as medicine; he contemplates a secluded place as if he had encountered death; his mind is constantly focused on cultivating the roots of all goodness; and he views women as if they were graves. In this manner, he conducts his begging among people.
"Those who are attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, and who rely upon and depend on the path—these are called great thieves.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra asked Mahākauṣṭhila: "How is it, Kauṣṭhila?"

"Is the eye the characteristic of form, and form the characteristic of the eye? Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental objects (dharma) such that mental objects are the characteristic of the mind, and the mind is the characteristic of mental objects?
Then Mahākauṣṭhila replied to Śāriputra:

"The eye is not the characteristic of form, nor is form the characteristic of the eye. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise; the mind is not the characteristic of mental objects, nor are mental objects the characteristic of the mind."
"What is called 'characteristic' (nimitta) refers to the self-indulgence of greed; this is what is meant by 'being associated with characteristics.
To further explain this through an analogy:
it is like a white ox and a black ox tied together in one place, or yoked together under the same harness."
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Is there anyone who would say that a white ox is tied to a black ox, or a black ox is tied to a white ox, and that they are tied together as equals? He replied:

"No, Śāriputra. It is not that the white ox is bound to the black ox, nor that the black ox is bound to the white ox. What is called 'binding' refers to the rope, the yoke-tie, or the yoke; these are what constitute binding."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

The eye does not have the characteristic of form, nor does form have the characteristic of the eye; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise not the characteristics of their respective objects, nor do those objects have the characteristics of the mind. To give rise to desire within these and to act with self-will is what is called "characteristic."
Therefore it is said: "The world contains many exquisite forms; these are not what is called desire.
Human desires are impermanent, but the internal fetter of desire is constant.
When this is extinguished, one does not undergo further existence, nor is one born again in other realms."

Human desires are impermanent; desire is a phenomenon of decay and exhaustion, subject to constant change and instability, and cannot be relied upon. Human desires do not endure for long; they may perish, be lost, or be seized by others. Therefore, they are non-eternal and cannot be preserved for long.
When internal desire is deep-rooted and firmly attached, it becomes defiled by the spirit; the mind becomes the primary source of calamity, and its misfortune extends to body and speech.

Therefore, it is said: "Internal desire binds one constantly. Or, one may be harmed by powerful forces or the Lord of Death. Such desire is difficult to restrain and difficult to prohibit; it cannot be halted by one's own power so as not to lead again to the various realms of existence (*bhava*). Nor does one wish to be born in this world or in future worlds. Therefore, it is said: "Worldly desires persist for a long time in the world; only the wise are able to perceive them."

One who gives rise to untainted volition, whose aspirations are ever fulfilled, whose mind is not bound by desire, and who flows upward to the single ultimate goal—this is one who gives rise to untainted volition.
Desire is both wholesome and unwholesome; that which is wholesome desire may be either tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*).
The desire for the untainted (*anāsrava*) extinguishes all craving; herein, the tainted (*sāsrava*) is not discussed.
Regarding "the aspiration being constantly fulfilled," it means that all wholesome dharmas universally fill one's entire being.
Regarding "the mind is not bound by desires": the mind does not become stained by or attached to those desires, nor is it defiled by them; therefore it is said, "the mind is not bound by desires."
The "one who flows upward to the ultimate" is none other than the *anāgāmin*.

This is because, having spoken of the fruit of *anāgāmin*, having spoken of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), and having spoken of the severance of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), he likewise speaks here of the one who flows upward to the ultimate.
The wise do not leap over stages; gradually, by means of the subtle, the skillful craftsman gradually cuts away defilements and thoroughly purges all impurities.

Regarding "the wise do not leap over stages": being well-versed in antiquity and clear about the present, they distinguish between right and wrong; their wisdom does not diminish, and their nature is never indolent. Therefore it is said: "The wise do not leap over stages."

"Gradually and subtly" means progressing day by day without harboring any intermediate rest; it is like a skilled craftsman who removes layers of heavy grime, which is accomplished only over many days.
When a person removes the defilements of the mind in this way, they will be praised and extolled by the devas, asuras, gandharvas, mahoragas, and others.
Just as a skilled wheelwright is well able to repair raw wood,
so one who can extinguish desire according to their will shall surely thereafter enjoy eternal peace.

Just like that skilled craftsman, who inspects a dilapidated cart and repairs and adorns it so that it may carry a heavy load to a distant place without any damage, he thereby accomplishes two purposes.
What are these two? First, the widespread dissemination of one's reputation; second, the acquisition of wealth and goods.

It is the same for that skillful bhikṣu: by simply relinquishing desire, he obtains two forms of renown—the far-reaching spread of his fame and the praise of the devas—and experiences immeasurable happiness in this present life.
Therefore it is said:
"Just like a skilled wheelwright who is well able to fashion and refine the raw wood,
one who can extinguish desire according to their will shall thereafter surely enjoy eternal peace."
At that time, the entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, departed with joy.
If you wish to experience all happiness, you should renounce all craving and desire;
having already renounced all craving and desire, you will eternally enjoy inexhaustible bliss.

If there are sentient beings who wish to experience all forms of happiness, they should contemplate the bliss of the fourfold and fivefold dhyānas, the bliss of practicing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the bliss of the definitive deliverance of the Path. Such persons should contemplate the relinquishing of all desires; having abandoned all desires, they will obtain manifold merit and experience inexhaustible bliss, attaining the joy of playful mastery and encountering the joy of various meritorious deeds, such that in this present life they shall never lack worldly wealth.
In the past, non-Buddhist heterodox teachers each made this claim: "Those who unite in pairs shall attain purity, quickly find liberation, and likewise achieve the way of transcendence.

Furthermore, there were those who said: "Desire is sublime and desire is pure; one should enjoy oneself together with desire. Since there is no satiety in desire, one must eliminate that doubt regarding it. Therefore, it is said: "One can extinguish desire by following desire; thereafter, one will surely receive eternal peace."
If one does not contemplate desire with a sense of weariness, how can one cultivate meditative concentration?
One must transform regret by tracing back to the root of one's conduct; only through the medicine of wisdom will it cease.

If there are sentient beings whose thoughts of desire do not depart, and who consequently harbor defilements in their minds—just as if a person were near a great pit of fire, becoming increasingly hot the closer they draw—then to avoid that heat, they must seek skillful means to extinguish that fire.

Human beings are also like this: they eventually cease to think of desire, and desire naturally perishes. It is like a poisonous medicine that is perfect in appearance, fragrant, and sweet; if a person suffering from illness takes this medicine, their throat is cleared and it flows down easily, yet before long after it has entered the belly, their life-faculty is lost.
Lust is also like this: at that time, one indulges in unrighteous sexual desire with a pleasing mind, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, enters into hell.
Now I shall provide an analogy; the wise understand through parables.
Long ago, in the land of Jambudvīpa, King Mūrdhaja appeared in the world with a lifespan of one billion four hundred million years.

At that time, King Mūrdhaja traveled in all four directions for observation until he reached the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; because the thirty-six Śakras had met their end there, he remained in that celestial palace.
After a long period had passed, that king of men thought to himself:

"My lifespan now exceeds that of the gods; I have personally witnessed thirty-six Śakras come to their end. It would be fitting for me now to slay Śakra Devānām Indra, and thereby govern the four continents from this very place as a sovereign over the kings of men and gods—would that not be a joy?"
As soon as this thought arose, he lost his supernormal powers and fell back into the world, dwelling in Jambudvīpa; his body was afflicted with pain, and he experienced various sufferings.
Then the king’s ministers inquired after him, saying:
“The King is now gravely ill and may pass away. If there are subjects who come to see you and ask, what instructions did King Mūrdhaja give as he was about to die?”
Then King Mūrdhaja said to his ministers,
"If any people come to question you, you should answer them with these words:
'King Mūrdhaja was greedily attached to the five desires and the seven treasures, never satisfied.'"
King Mūrdhaja begot a thousand sons yet remained insatiable;
King Mūrdhaja ruled over the four continents yet remained insatiable, and then his life came to an end;
King Mūrdhaja had seven precious jewels rain down upon his palace for seven days and seven nights yet remained insatiable, and then his life came to an end.
"King Māndhātṛ traveled to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods for sightseeing; there, he conceived the intent to harm Śakra Devānām Indra and met his end. Therefore it is said:
'If one does not contemplate desire with weariness, how can one cultivate meditative concentration?'"
"By transforming regret and tracing back to the root of conduct, wisdom shall treat it until it ceases.
At that time, all who had gathered there were freed from craving and desire, their minds devoid of attachment, and they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
One who is satiated with wisdom no longer contemplates sensual desire;
because people are satiated by wisdom, they do not follow the tracks of craving.
Why is it said that one is "satiated with wisdom"? Because [wisdom] brings an end to craving.

Sharing the same Dharma-chamber as all the World-Honored Ones, together with the true persons, the Arhats, they contemplate the practice of impurity, giving rise to a mind of revulsion; they eliminate all afflictions and suffering, and come to know the original source of suffering.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, contemplate with wisdom; therefore it is said:
"One who is satiated with wisdom no longer contemplates sensual desire. Knowing the nature of desire for what it truly is, one does not associate with it."
"That which was once cherished and clung to has now been left far behind; the wise are prudent and do not become stained by desire.
At that time, having heard this teaching on desire, the assembly conceived the perception of impurity and immediately attained *dhāraṇī* while still in their seats.
People are greedily attached to sensual desires and habitually practice unrighteous conduct;
they do not perceive that the arrival of death is imminent, but instead claim that life is long-lasting.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

There was a man whose livelihood was impoverished and who lacked abundant wealth; he personally endured hardship, exerted his labor, and toiled until, after traveling throughout the four quarters, he finally obtained treasure.
Having acquired immeasurable wealth, he returned home from afar and enjoyed himself with his parents and five kinds of relatives. In the midst of the great assembly, he boasted, saying:

"I have now obtained treasures worth several hundred million; I shall now marry a daughter from a noble clan—one who is in the prime of youth, neither fat nor thin, neither too pale nor too dark, and whose feminine graces are all fully perfected."

Having naturally possessed a face as upright and beautiful as the color of a peach blossom, she further adorned her body with fragrant flowers, ointments, and powders; she took delight in him daily and could not bear to be parted from him. The delicacies and foods served day after day were never the same, and she slaughtered sentient beings beyond all counting. Indulging her passions and acting with unrestrained license, she was peerless and supreme; yet, she soon encountered an illness and immediately met her end.
Seeing that his wife had passed away, his mind became bewildered and his thoughts disordered; he consequently fell into madness and wandered through the streets and alleys, crying out in lamentation:
"How cruel and poisonous!

This murderous ghost has acted without humanity in taking my wife's life. Furthermore, these people of my clan and five-fold kin harbored hearts of jealousy; each conceived this intent to seize my wife, and fearing that their deeds might be exposed, they secretly conspired together to bring about her downfall."
Thus his complaints and accusations did not cease day after day.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and flawless divine eye, saw this man complaining in the streets and alleys, his mind deluded and unable to recognize what is correct and true.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to manifest this meaning and investigate its origin and end, in order to reveal the Great Illumination for the sake of sentient beings in future generations and to cause the True Dharma to endure long in the world, sealed it with the divine seal of the mouth of the past Tathāgatas. In the midst of the great assembly, he spoke these verses:
"Those who are greedily attached to sensual desires, Who practice unrighteous conduct, And do not perceive that the arrival of death is imminent, Deem their lives to be long-lasting."
At that time, when the assembly heard these verses, all their defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye:
"Stupid people bind themselves with greed, Seeking no way to cross to the other shore;
Because of craving for wealth and possessions, They harm others and harm themselves as well."
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was an elder named Nanda.

He possessed abundant wealth and many treasures—gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber; he had elephants, horses, carriages, and draft animals, as well as male and female slaves and servants. His clothing, ornaments, fields, and enterprises were beyond measure, and no one in the entire kingdom surpassed him in wealth.
Although he dwelt in honor and wealth, he lacked faith and was stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous.
His palace gates were sevenfold, with gatekeepers stationed at each; no one who came could enter without being strictly scrutinized.

In the center of the courtyard, he installed a sparse iron cage suspended in the air, fearing that flying birds might eat the grain; along the base of the four walls, he applied white *kīṇa*-clay, fearing that rats might burrow holes and damage his property.

However, when impermanence confronted that householder, he had only one son named Candanagandha. He immediately called his son forward and instructed him, saying: "I am now afflicted by suffering and shall certainly not survive.

Should I pass away, do not squander or waste any of my wealth or the seven kinds of precious treasures; nor should you give them to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas. If there are beggars, do not give even a single coin to them. These riches are sufficient for seven generations of ancestors to consume."

Having issued this command, he immediately passed away and was reborn within the womb of a blind Caṇḍāla woman in the city of Śrāvastī. After eight or nine months had passed, he was born into the world, born blind and without eyes.
The attendants on her left and right asked,
"Have you given birth to a son or a daughter?
The mother replied:
"A son is born.
He thought to himself:
"If it is a boy, my eyes will now grow dim, and I shall require the child's assistance and support for my care."
The attendants replied,
"Although she encountered this child, he was born without eyes.
Upon hearing this, the mother's grief and sorrow redoubled, and weeping bitterly, she said:
"The son is blind and I am blind; both of us lack two eyes.
Encountering such a decaying thing, it increases my sorrow, grief, and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by his attendant Ānanda, was walking back and forth outside the gate of the Jetavana Monastery when he raised his hand and spoke, saying:
"Calamity! Calamity! At that time, Ānanda joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just now, the World-Honored One spoke of calamity; what are the causes and conditions for this?"
"I wish to hear its meaning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Have you not heard that there is an elder named Nanda in the city of Śrāvastī?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“In the city of Śrāvastī there was once an elder who died long ago.
The World-Honored One replied:
"This elder’s spirit has returned to the city of Śrāvastī to become the son of a blind Caṇḍāla woman; he was born without eyes.
Formerly, his family estate was immeasurably wealthy; where is he now, that we might observe his whereabouts?"
"Though elephants, horses, and the seven treasures are beyond measure, yet one remains stingy, greedy, envious, jealous, and restrictive; for this reason it is said that these are calamities.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, speaking in verse:
"In the cycle of birth and death there is fear; Illusions and transformations possess no reality."
"Where there is success, there must be failure; what wise person could find joy in this?
At that time, the blind mother’s son was eight or nine years old and capable of walking about. The mother gave him a single staff and a set of eating utensils, and said to her son:
"I have now raised you until you are capable of walking about; you should seek a way to support yourself and need not remain here."
"I too am without eyes; I must beg for alms to sustain my remaining life.
This blind boy went from house to house begging, eventually arriving at the home of the elder Candanagandha. Standing outside the gate, he spoke of himself, saying:
"I am already exhausted by the pangs of hunger, and furthermore, I am deprived of both eyes."
"All sufferings have no beginning; who indeed would take pity and give?

When the gatekeeper heard these words, his anger flared up intensely. He immediately stepped forward, seized [the man] by the hand, and hurled him far into a deep pit. Thereupon he injured his left arm and struck his head until it was broken, casting all the alms-food he had begged onto the ground.
Among them was one who saw [the boy] by the pit; feeling profound pity and compassion, he went to speak with the blind mother:
"Your son has been beaten by the gatekeeper and is suffering greatly; his arm is wounded and his head is split open, such that the pain is unbearable."
When the mother heard this, she crawled on her hands and knees, leaning on a staff, to where the blind boy was; she took him onto her lap and spoke in verse:
"What fault have you committed now?"
"Son, tell me quickly now: who gave you to whom?
Why have you encountered such bitter hardship and distress?
The son replied to his mother:
“O Mother, I came here seeking alms; having reached this house of sandalwood, I stood briefly outside this gate and was then encountered by the hand of an evil man.

At that time, the World-Honored One, who nurtures sentient beings with compassion like a mother or a father, gave rise to great mercy and wished to provide salvation. After the meal, he donned his robes with dignified solemnity and, surrounded before and behind by the community of bhikṣus, entered the city of Śrāvastī and arrived at the gate of the elder Canda’s house.

At that time, the elders and the people within the city, seeing that the Tathāgata had entered the city at an unusual hour, thought, "There must surely be a cause for this; perhaps he will expound upon matters of the past, future, or present. They all followed closely behind the Tathāgata as his attendants and together proceeded to the gate of Candana, arriving at the place where the blind boy was.
When the Elder Candana smelled that the Tathāgata had arrived, he immediately went out the gate, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head and face touching them, and stood to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed that the great assembly had gathered and saw that the Elder Candana was also assembled outside the gate. He then wished to expound upon how stinginess, greed, envy, and jealousy lead to immeasurable suffering in the hells, while further teaching that the rewards for generous giving are immeasurable; he desired to cause them to transcend existence and not cling to the three realms, pointing the way toward Nirvāṇa and the path of the unconditioned.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the boy, "Are you Nanda? The boy replied:
"It is indeed Nanda. The Buddha asked again: "Is it Nanda?"
He then replied to the Buddha,
"It is indeed Nanda.
When the people of the city heard that the Buddha had asked about the name of a young boy, they were all struck with astonishment.
"How is it that the householder Nanda has received such a form?

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to uproot the suffering of hell for the householder Candana, to eliminate his stinginess and greed, and to establish him securely in the field of merit, addressed Candanagandha and spoke in verse:
"The father of old is now Nanda; Stinginess and greed wrap around his mind."
Having failed to perform virtuous deeds from the outset, one encounters these manifold sufferings and afflictions.
Should one pass away from this state, one shall enter the Avīci Hell,
becoming a denizen of that abode of evil beings, bound by the force of past conditions.
At that time, the householder Candana wept with such grief that his tears could not be restrained; prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will deliver me from the roots of my transgressions. May I receive the residual blessings bestowed by the Tathāgata. I only pray, World-Honored One!”
"I now invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation from the elder by remaining silent.

Then, when the night had passed and it was morning, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to the elder’s house and sat down in their respective order.

The elder personally served water and pure food, and having completed the offering of food and drink, he served more pure water, took a small seat, and sat before the Tathāgata, desiring to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, employing skillful means, gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the elder, discoursing upon the profound treasury of the Tathāgata. As for the discourse, it was a discussion on generosity, a discussion on morality, and a discussion on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desire is impure and that sexual lust is defiling, teaching the Dharma in such an inconceivable manner.
At that moment, while still seated upon his mat, the householder was cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having personally examined and realized the Dharma, having discerned all phenomena, and having attained fearlessness, he rose from his seat and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.

"I now take the three refuges in the Tathāgata; I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. From this day forward, may you accept me as an upāsaka; for as long as life lasts, I shall no longer kill living beings."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reprove the householder Nanda, spoke this verse:
"The fool loses his wealth and goods, Yet it does not benefit himself;
The fool covets wealth and goods, And sinks himself into a pit of hell."
Thus, this greed brings no benefit; one should know that it arises from delusion.
The fool is harmed by this and destroys the worthy, until his head is severed and cast upon the earth.
When it is said that "the fool loses his wealth," what is meant by "losing" is that it has been exhausted and extinguished, leaving nothing remaining; therefore it is said, "he loses his wealth."

The fool, lacking wisdom and devoid of discernment, may amass wealth and property, yet he neither consumes it himself nor bestows it upon others; no one among fools is more foolish than such a person.
When a person possesses wealth and goods, there are two uses for them: first, to give them away; second, to consume them oneself.
Yet that elder neither consumes them himself nor gives them to others.

That which he does not do for his own sake is stinginess and envy; these entangle the root of the mind so that one cannot liberate it or act rightly for oneself. The fool craves wealth and goods, and because the taints of affection and attachment color his mind, he is unable to relinquish them. Therefore, the wise man abandons desire and maintains tranquility. Thus it is said:
"Such is the lack of benefit in greed; know that it arises from delusion.
Fools, for its sake, harm the virtuous, until their heads are severed and scattered upon the earth.
When the great assembly heard what the Buddha had said, they departed with joy.
Even if the heavens rained down the seven treasures, one would still not be satisfied; since pleasure is little and suffering is much, it is the wise who awaken to this truth.
Long ago, the Buddha spoke this verse to King Mūrdhaja.

At that time, in King Mūrdhaja’s palace, the heavens rained down the seven treasures for seven days and seven nights; yet when the king looked upon them, his mind felt no satiety—for those possessed by craving, suffering is many and joy is few.

At that time, while that king was roaming in the heavens, enjoying the five celestial pleasures and experiencing boundless joy throughout the four quarters, he was about to face death and undergo immeasurable suffering. A wise person observes and constantly guards against such calamities before they occur; therefore it is said: "The awakened one is the noble one."
Though they possess celestial desires, they practice generous relinquishment without greed; delighting in detachment from affection and love, such are the disciples of the Three Buddhas.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park in the kingdom of Mathurā.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu sitting in meditation in a quiet room, his body unmoving. Beneath his bed, a venomous snake lay coiled and sleeping; overcome by drowsiness, the bhikṣu would now slump down and now lean back.
The venomous snake thought to itself,
"This man, terrified by my sight, will surely seek to harm me.
The venomous snake then threw its entire body forward and bit the bhikṣu who was practicing meditation.
When the bhikṣu passed away, he was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Various celestial maidens came one after another to attend upon him, and the devaputra told them:
"You sisters, do not draw near my body; if you were to approach me, you would surely violate the precepts."
The women thought to themselves, "This celestial being must have been a śramaṇa in his previous life; therefore, he has been born here to enjoy the blessings of the heavens.

Then each of the celestial maidens took a mirror and held it before him. When the devaputra saw himself in the mirror—clad in celestial garments and wearing a celestial crown—the deity thought to himself:
"Alas! My form has changed!
Why have I abandoned my human body and now been born in heaven?

He immediately wept with grief, rose from his seat, and walked through the celestial palaces. Seeing the various attendants—some handsome and some ugly—he gradually proceeded further until he reached a garden and sat beneath a tree. Sitting upright, he contemplated and sought the samādhi of concentration.

Within the waters of the pond there were various kinds of extraordinary birds, which called out to one another with mournful and resonant cries; though their forms were diverse and their colors varied, they sought to attain the Way but were unable to achieve it.

At that time, the deva-son, having completed his celestial lifespan, descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa and arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and asked about the meaning [of the teaching] in verse:
“Countless hosts of celestial maidens, Some of whom are even ugly, attend me;
In my rear garden, named ‘Delusion,’ By what means can they be rescued?”
"However, World-Honored One!

I have ultimately failed to perceive the Truth before meeting my end; though I was reborn as a deva and enjoyed celestial blessings, once that merit was exhausted, I returned to the Great Mount Tai hell. Thus I have transmigrated without end."
"Now I dwell in poverty and have nowhere to turn; I rely solely upon the Tathāgata to look upon me with compassion.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The Path is called straight and single-minded; That direction is called fearless."
"The vehicle is named 'Without Crookedness or Deviation,' for it observes the accomplishment of the Dharma.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha taught, the devaputra immediately attained the pure Dharma-eye, with all dust and defilements vanished while still seated upon his throne.
At that time, the devaputra was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he circumambulated the Buddha seven times, prostrated, and departed.

Then the World-Honored One, observing this matter and investigating its beginning and end, manifested great illumination and, so that the True Dharma might long endure in the world, spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"Though one possesses celestial desires, If one practices wise relinquishment and is free from greed, One delights in being detached from affection and love."
"Third, the disciples of the Buddha.
At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, departed with joy.
All the mountains became gold, just like the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
"This [craving] remains unsatiated; only a sage can truly perceive it.
At that time, the World-Honored One also spoke this verse to King Mandhātṛ:
"For one who has not severed desire, whatever realms and territories the mind plans to encompass, upon obtaining one, it again thinks of another; the mind's greed knows no satiety."
