Because of his greedy attachment, King Mūrdhagata found that even though nothing in the mountains was larger than this Iron Ring Mountain (Cakravāḍa), which he entirely transformed into gold so that it filled the world, he still felt no satisfaction.
If one does not contemplate the root of suffering, how can craving be distinguished?
Understanding that worldly craving is a thorn, one should advance in resolve and cultivate the precepts. Regarding "not contemplating the root of suffering":

all sentient beings rush in the four directions, encountering perils and hardships; they may meet tigers, wolves, bandits, or thieves; venomous snakes, evil spirits, thorny thickets, or deep forests where no human tracks remain; they may encounter swords and blades used for slaughter and dismemberment; they may enter the great ocean and suffer various calamities; they may encounter violent winds, swirling waves, and treacherous turns that wreck great ships; or they may encounter black mountains and malevolent ghosts, falling into the realm of rākṣasas.
For these reasons, it is said: "One does not contemplate the origin of suffering.
As for how craving arises and can be distinguished, it is entirely due to greed and desire producing one another in succession.

To understand and know the thorns of worldly craving: the fetters and afflictions are also called "thorns," and the four great elements are also called "thorns. When a person possesses these two types of thorns, they cannot escape birth and death and undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
The "thorn" is also called the thorn of craving and the thorn of views.

One who advances their intent to cultivate and study the precepts—wherein "advancing" is termed wisdom—expounds upon what is profound and obscure, abandons what is erroneous to adhere to what is correct, and thereby achieves wisdom.
*Udānavarga*, Volume Four;
*Udānavarga*, Volume Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Three: On Craving (Tṛṣṇā-varga).

If a person lacks both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, yet frequently contemplates purity out of excessive desire, their craving and attachment will increase all the more, and their fetters will consequently become ever firmer and deeper.

Regarding the statement that "if a person lacks *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they cannot reach the Path": it is like a person who does not skillfully practice contemplation; being defiled by and attached to body and mind, they are entangled and unable to be released. Within this state, they are incapable of reflecting upon wholesome dharmas. Therefore, it is said: "If a person lacks *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they cannot reach the Path."

Regarding those who observe purity while having many desires: there may be sentient beings who are attached to desires but not attached to fetters; some who are attached to fetters but not attached to desires; some who are attached both to desires and to fetters; and some who are attached neither to fetters nor to desires.
What is it for a sentient being to be attached to sensual desires but not attached to fetters?
In this regard, there is a person who initially practices sensual desire but subsequently does not transgress it again; this is called being attached to sensual desires but not attached to fetters.
Furthermore, there may be a person who repeatedly cultivates fetters without abandoning them; this is called "cultivating fetters but not cultivating desire.
What is meant by "both cultivating fetters and cultivating desire"?
There are some sentient beings who repeatedly practice desire and also practice the fetters; this is called practicing both desire and the fetters.
What is meant by neither practicing desire nor practicing the fetters?
There may be sentient beings whose affectionate attachments have been severed and who do not cling to worldly burdens, nor do they single-mindedly and repeatedly cultivate intimacy with them.

Alternatively, there may be people who, from head to foot, contemplate the myriad things of the body—reckoning the teeth to be white and pure, the hands and nails exceptionally exquisite, and the hair a deep azure-blue—and yet give rise to conceptions within this regard that they cannot relinquish; consequently, the root of craving increases, their fetters and knots become ever more firm, and they are bound by these various fetters.
Now I shall provide an analogy, for the wise understand through parables.
It is as if there were a person bound by two types of ropes:
one of leather and the other of *nāga-śīrṣa* grass.
When they approach a fire and warm themselves by it, the leather thongs become tight while the dragon-hair ropes slacken;
if they enter the water, the leather thongs slacken while the dragon-hair ropes become tight.
It is the same for sentient beings who have not yet severed desire; they are bound by two fetters.
What are these two fetters?
First is the fetter of craving, and second is the knot of views.

At times, when sentient beings contemplate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) becomes slack while the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) becomes tight.
At other times, when sentient beings contemplate mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the fetter of views becomes slack while the fetter of craving becomes tight.
Therefore it is said that the bonds and fetters become increasingly firm and deep.
If one delights in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and focuses the mind exclusively on impurity (*aśubhā*), this craving will be eliminated; in this way, the fetters are extinguished.

If there is one who delights in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and if such a person desires to abandon unwholesome contemplation and instead contemplate wholesome observation, they should constantly draw near to and practice it, never parting from focused mindfulness. First, they should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-smṛti*), personally calculating those things to which their mind was previously attached—hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth, from head to foot—all of which they considered "mine. Subsequently, they should further contemplate them as foul and impure, seeing that among the thirty-six constituent parts, nothing is worth desiring; by analyzing each part individually, they will soon attain the contemplation of impurity.
The mindfulness of the body as body pertains to the internal and external mind and dharmas.
As for "one who loves this attains its removal," it means that through wisdom one realizes exhaustion and eradicates craving.

By contemplating impurity, one is able to remove attachment and is no longer bound by it; having forever cast off all fetters, one no longer associates with them. Therefore, it is said: "In this way, one extinguishes the fetters."
Enmeshed by the net of desire, covered by the shroud of craving,
they bind themselves in prison through self-indulgence; like fish cast into a trap,
they are preyed upon by old age and death, like a calf seeking its mother’s milk.

Those who shroud themselves with the net of desire—this "net" covers and obscures the eyes of people, impairing their wisdom so that it is not clear; they are unable to emerge from the essentials and reach the Way of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This "net" prevents them from single-mindedly contemplating and deliberating, as they shroud themselves with ignorance (*avidyā*).

Those who cover themselves with the veil of craving entangle themselves in it, seeking liberation without end; they are like a fierce fire covered by ashes that does not manifest, such that an ignorant person only realizes their feet have been scorched after they have stepped upon them.

Being shrouded by craving is likewise like this: it is as if one were holding a sword with its blade pointing upward; a person without eyes, grasping it with their hand, would immediately wound themselves.

All classes of sentient beings are likewise thus: shrouded by the fetter of craving, they do not contemplate dharmas that are wholesome or unwholesome; conditioned by this, they give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, revolving through birth and death without escaping the five realms of existence. Therefore it is said: "Shrouded by the cover of craving."
Those who indulge themselves are bound in prison; all who indulge and do not comply with the True Teaching are bound by the fetters of craving.
Those who do not indulge themselves are freed from these fetters.
"Like fish entering a prison" means it is like fishermen casting nets to catch fish; once they have entered the net, there is no time for escape.

This class of sentient beings is just the same: having abandoned wholesome dharmas and practiced defiled, turbid, and non-essential paths, even when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly of sentient beings, some are like fish who have entered a prison and seek release without any prospect of doing so.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise; bound by the fetters of craving, they are unable to reach the unconditioned path of Nirvana. At that time, having heard the Buddha recite these verses, the hunters were each struck with amazement, thinking:
"The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is not for others, but is precisely for us."
Each repented their faults and reformed their practices, vowing never again to commit evil; therefore it is said: "Like fish entering a net.

The Dharma constantly taught by all Buddhas is intended to reach those sentient beings with whom they have a karmic connection, and its exposition of principles is never in vain; it is just like a physician who carefully examines the root cause of a disease before administering medicine.

At that time, the physician observes the patient to discern the severity of the illness; having examined the facial features and the complexion, he then administers the medicine. When administering the medicine, he observes with impartiality, ensuring it is neither excessive nor deficient, but precisely balanced.
The reason for this is the fear that the illness may not be cured.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, preach the Dharma for the sake of beings in the same way: they observe the inclinations of the minds of the multitude, and knowing the severity of their afflictions, they then preach the Dharma so that they may attain understanding. Their minds do not diminish [their teaching], but rather preach according to the middle way to eliminate all fetters and latent tendencies.

Observing the minds of sentient beings, he speaks one verse for those who need one verse; he provides five lines for those who need five lines; and he provides one and a half lines for those who need one and a half lines.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the mind of the hunter, spoke this verse. To those whose minds were self-indulgent and heedless, he said: "They are watched over by old age and death, just as a calf seeks its mother's milk; like a newborn calf, its heart never leaves its mother."
These classes of sentient beings are likewise thus: pursued by old age and death, as a shadow follows a form.
If sentient beings of sharp faculties skillfully examine and discern this, they will be able to leave behind these various afflictions and sufferings, increasing their roots of goodness;
if sentient beings of dull faculties do not perform such contemplation, they will achieve nothing at all.
Therefore it is said: "One is watched by old age and death, like a calf seeking its mother's milk;
one whose mind is heedless wanders here and there, just as the *mālu* tree spreads, or as a monkey roams about seeking fruit."

If the mind is heedless—whether one be a kṣatriya, a householder, a lay devotee, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā; whether young, middle-aged, or old; and as long as one has not yet attained the Path—the mind increases in heedlessness and the root of sensual desire increases. This is like a *mālūra* tree when first sprouting, which, being entwined by a creeping vine, withers and dies as it grows.
The mind of sensual desire is also like this: it causes the very roots of all sentient beings to wither away. Therefore it is said: "It is like the *mālu* tree.
As for "wandering everywhere," one wanders through the five realms of existence—hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth—like a potter’s wheel; therefore it is said: "wandering everywhere."

"As a monkey roaming in search of fruit" means that just as a macaque seeks various fruits and gourds, going from tree to tree and forest to forest; therefore it is said, "as a monkey roaming in search of fruit."
"Moistened by craving, / Thoughts grow like spreading vines;
/ Craving and desire are bottomless, / And thus old age and death increase. Regarding "moistened by craving":

this refers to the overflowing of craving, like water gushing from a spring. One dwells upon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*), recollecting past deeds and indulging in the five pleasures for one's own amusement. Therefore it is said: "Moistened by craving."
Now, regarding moisture: butter, oil, and grease do not constitute true moisture. Such things as these can be washed away and completely removed with ash and earth.
Regarding "love and desire as moisture": only when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world can they sever it with the sword of wisdom; therefore it is said, "love is the moisture."

Regarding the proliferation of thoughts: there is no fire more fiercely hot than thought; while a wound burned by fire can be treated with medicine, a wound scorched by the fire of thought cannot be healed.

If there are those who kill their father or mother, commit theft, engage in sexual misconduct, and perpetrate various transgressions such that even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot heal them, it is for this reason it is said: "Thoughts are the spreading creepers."

Old age and death increase these conditions: birth brings about the suffering of the body's disintegration; old age brings about the four hundred and four types of illness; death brings about the affliction of the "sword-wind. Therefore it is said: "Old age and death increase these conditions."
Sentient beings are entangled by craving, Like a rabbit caught in a snare;
Bound by the fetters and proclivities, They undergo suffering again and again.
Regarding "sentient beings are entangled by craving": craving constantly leads them forward, causing them to transmigrate through birth and death and unable to escape the three realms.
"Just as a rabbit caught in a snare" means that just like a rabbit in a net, it runs hither and thither with no way of escape.
These classes of sentient beings are also like this: deluded by craving, they transmigrate through birth and death, circling through the five destinies and drowning in the four currents.

Those who are entangled by the fetters—this class of sentient beings—is bound by the ties of craving and cannot escape birth and death. The fool undergoes suffering; the fool’s actions of body, speech, and mind are all neither true nor correct, and they fail to distinguish between good and evil. Consequently, they receive the forms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore it is said: "They repeatedly undergo suffering and affliction."
Sentient beings are driven by craving; They are stained and attached within the three realms of existence.
Seeking liberation through skillful means, They must rely on expedient power to attain deliverance.

As for "sentient beings are driven by craving," they are driven by the driving forces [of afflictions], bound by fetters, and shackled by bonds. Therefore it is said: "Sentient beings are driven by craving."

"Attached to the three realms of existence" refers to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); therefore it is said, "attached within the three realms of existence.
Regarding "seeking liberation through skillful means," what constitutes seeking through skillful means?

With the underlying tendency toward desire, the underlying tendency toward existence, the underlying tendency toward ignorance, and the underlying tendency toward views—since these sentient beings are thus defiled and attached to these underlying tendencies, how can they escape the suffering and affliction of birth and death?
It is just as when two oxen share a single yoke and someone strikes them from behind; how could they fail to pull the heavy load?
So it is with these classes of sentient beings: taking the four floods as their burden and being settled upon the four yokes, how could they possibly escape birth, old age, sickness, and death?

"Those who must rely on skillful means (*upāya*) to escape" refers to seeking expedient ways to remain in harmony with one's parents, siblings, and kinsmen; yet when the face of impermanence arrives, each must part from the others. Therefore it is said: "Being oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death, one must rely on skillful means to escape."
All sentient beings who have not yet exhausted their craving for sensual desire are constantly pursued by birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Those who have exhausted their craving for sensual desire no longer undergo birth, old age, sickness, or death; therefore it is said: "One must employ skillful means to emerge from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
If one can extinguish that craving, there will be no further craving within the three realms of existence;
the bhikṣu, having already abandoned craving, attains the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

Regarding "if one can extinguish that craving": craving is a disease upon which all manifold sufferings converge; it is something praised and extolled by gods and men alike. Therefore, it is said: "If one can extinguish that craving."

"One who has no further craving for the three realms of existence" means one who has already eliminated craving, eliminated feverish passion, eliminated all afflictions, and eliminated sorrow and grief.
The "three realms of existence" are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Therefore it is said: "In the three realms of existence, there is no more craving.

A bhikṣu who has already abandoned craving—one who has shattered all the fetters and latent tendencies—is called a bhikṣu; even one who wears tattered robes and carries an alms bowl is called a bhikṣu. Therefore it is said: "A bhikṣu who has already abandoned craving."

Quiescence leads to Nirvāṇa; therein there is no such mental basis. This is non-appropriation, entirely free from conceptualization and attachment; therefore one returns to Nirvāṇa. Therein there is no shadow of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), nor any shadow of renewed birth (*punarbhava*). Therefore it is said: "Quiescence leads to Nirvāṇa."
"Thinking that craving endures suffering; through greed and desire one clings to the world;
anxiety and affliction grow day and night, spreading like creeping vines.

Regarding "thinking that craving endures suffering": all sentient beings who possess a mind are unable to depart from it; they encounter manifold harms and afflictions, and there is nowhere they are not stained by attachment. Therefore it is said: "Thinking that craving endures suffering."
Those who are greedily attached to the world find it difficult to relinquish or abandon that which they cherish and do not forget.

"The world" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are also called the world, and the receptacle of feeling (*vedanā*), which is also called the world; therefore it is said, "greedily attached to the world."
The elder has been beset by anxiety and distress day and night; he constantly experiences anxiety and distress, feverish affliction, and painful illness.
Now, I shall provide an analogy, for the wise understand through analogies.
Spreading like creeping vines in the sun, spreading like creeping vines that grow;
humans are deluded by affection and love, unable to abandon their passions and desires.
Thus, with much sorrow and craving, they overflow like the rippling waters filling a pond.

When people are deluded by affection and love (*anunaya*), this affection becomes so firm that it remains indestructible throughout eternal kalpas. It is gathered within the mental consciousness and cannot be relinquished; because of this affection, one cannot transcend the stages to realize the fruit, nor can one go forth once and not return. It cannot be restrained, nor can it be extinguished. Therefore, it is said: "People are deluded by affection and love."

Thus, for one who has much sorrow and craving, these bonds of affection cause various sufferings and afflictions to increase, penetrating to the very bones and marrow; it is like flowing water entering a pond, yet like a lotus in a pond, the water does not adhere to it.

This is also like that: when the heart is bound by the deep and firm entanglements of affection, one washes away that loving attachment with the water of liberation so that it no longer clings. Therefore it is said: "The murmuring waters fill the pond."
Worthy ones, I shall now speak; let the entire assembly listen together.
Together we shall uproot the root of craving, as one selects and removes fine, fresh [weeds].
Having uprooted the root of craving, what sorrow can there be, and how could there be fear?

"Virtuous ones, when I say 'I' now, 'I' refers to the Tathāgata—one who possesses all-knowledge, the three types of supernormal knowledge, and the six superpowers, who is fully endowed with the various marks, and who discerns all phenomena."

"O worthy ones, the name 'great assembly' refers to those who have accomplished the dharmas of the noble and holy; their practiced dharmas are benevolent and virtuous, transcending the three realms, and they have fulfilled all that is to be done. Therefore it is said: 'O worthy ones, I shall now speak.'"

"All those in the assembly listen together" means that the assembly consists of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all gathered in one place to contemplate the root of the Dharma. Their aspirations and inclinations are all fulfilled according to their wishes; therefore it is said, "all those in the assembly listen together."
Regarding "together uprooting the root of craving," what is this ignorance?
It is as has been taught: for all those who proceed through these five destinies from this life to future lives, ignorance is the root; they all arise from desire.
Furthermore, there are those who say that first there is a mind of delusion, followed by the attachment of craving.
Therefore it is said: "One who uproots the root of craving.
Regarding the phrase "one who selects the fine and new," there are two causes and conditions for why one is so described as selecting the fine and new:
The first is for curing illness, and the second is for trade. One contemplates and selects the best [roots] and takes them;

the sick are healed and the traders obtain profit. The practitioner is also like this: the roots of craving are deep-seated and firm, and must be distinguished by wisdom. Those beings who are fit to be practiced upon will soon receive transformation, thereby accomplishing the great task. Once the roots of craving have been uprooted, one attains arhatship.
Therefore it is said: "Like one who selects fine and new [material].

One who has already uprooted the root of craving—what is called the root of craving? The root is ignorance (*avidyā*); the branches and leaves are the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Thus, it is called the root of craving.
If there is no sorrow, how can there be fear? Where there is sorrow, there must be fear; if there is no sorrow, how can there be fear?
Sorrow belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); it does not exist in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) or formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why is it that there is sorrow in the desire realm, but not in the form or formless realms?
The answer is:
"Because the nature of those realms is devoid of sorrow."

The reason for the arising of sorrow is that having a father, a mother, a kingdom, a city, a wife, children, servants, attendants, slaves, fields, houses, wealth, and grain—all such possessions and undertakings are likewise sources of sorrow.
One who forever lacks this will ultimately have no sorrow; therefore it is said: "Uproot the root of craving.
Where there is craving, there is death; because of it, one brings about many kinsmen and traverses the long road of sorrow, constantly falling into calamity through the suffering of craving.
One who practices the Way does not associate with the mundane; first severing the root of craving, they allow no further roots to take hold.
Do not be like one cutting reeds, only to let the heart grow back again.

That there is death because of craving is like sentient beings who have not yet severed desire; they possess all the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), with craving dwelling within them. It is said:
"All these sentient beings who greedily seek without satiety do so entirely due to the heart of craving."

Seeking existence within the three realms is likewise the mind of craving; that which the mind greedily clings to—wife, children, and wealth—all arises from this craving. Therefore it is said: "Where there is craving for existence, there is death, and one brings about many kinsmen."

Those who traverse the long road of sorrow cannot trace back what has already passed before; these sentient beings wander and revolve through the five destinies of birth and death, passing from this life to that in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Bound by the fetters of craving for this body composed of the four great elements, it is for this reason it is said: "traversing the long road of sorrow."

Bound by craving, one constantly falls into calamity; repeatedly dwelling in the womb, one assumes form in measureless ways, staying between the raw and cooked intestines, defiled by excrement and urine. Thus, one enters the womb again and again—foul, filthy, and impure—yet remains neither weary nor ashamed. Therefore it is said: "One should cultivate the Path through skillful means."

One does not associate with worldly associations. As for "repeatedly," it means birth after birth without ceasing, coming and going without end. "Born here" refers to this present body; "dying there" refers to another realm of existence. "Born here" refers to this human life; "born there" refers to the five destinies. Therefore it is said: "First eradicate the root of craving, so that no seeds may take root."

One constantly dwells within the birthplaces of the five destinies; furthermore, these five destinies possess degrees of lightness and heaviness: where there is merit, they are light; where there is no merit, they are heavy. Although there are such variations of lightness and heaviness, none can surpass the Path.

In the unconditioned Way, there is neither lightness nor heaviness, neither arising nor ceasing, neither attachment nor severance. Even if one does not seek the Way and remains defiled and impure, it is like mowing reeds or cutting tall grass; they grow back incessantly.
Without desire, there is no fear; tranquil and serene, one is free from sorrow and affliction.
By eliminating desire, the fetters are untied; this is called emerging forever from the abyss. Regarding "without desire, there is no fear":
the Sage, having already departed from desire, is fearless and without sorrow; his mind and nature are tranquil and still. Therefore it is said: "Without desire, there is no fear."

To be serene and free from sorrow and affliction means that one has already departed from all desires, which are forever exhausted without remainder. If there are sentient beings who cannot depart from craving, they are like a river flowing toward the sea, never ceasing day or night. Therefore, it is said: "Serene and free from sorrow and affliction."

Because one is able to exhaust craving, it is called the "extinction of the essence," wherein no further root remains; thus, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) are eliminated.

This constitutes a permanent emergence from the abyss, no longer dwelling amidst the burdens of existence (*bhava*), and neither performing conditioned actions nor failing to act. Therefore, it is said: "Permanently emerged from the abyss."
The devas and the people of the world dwell in dependence upon craving;
as craving departs, all fetters follow. The flow of time does not pause, and when time passes, sorrow arises again; only upon entering hell does one finally awaken.
Regarding "the devas and the people of the world," for what reason are they called devas and people?
It is because they are driven by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). If born as a deva, one is entertained by a retinue of jade maidens, forgetting the west while gazing toward the east;
if born as a human, one is deeply attached to many things, supporting a wife and raising children with a mind that cannot let them go.
If one enters hell and undergoes various sufferings and afflictions, there is no longer any affectionate mind;
although hungry ghosts and animals possess an affectionate mind, it is so slight as to be negligible.
Among all beings, the gods and humans have the greatest affectionate mind; therefore, it is said: "The gods and the people."

Regarding "dwelling in dependence upon craving": sentient beings dwell in defilement by depending on craving; they are co-existent with craving. Therefore it is said: "dwelling in dependence upon craving."
"Where craving goes, the various fetters follow" means: it is just as when someone crosses a river, a stream, or the ocean, and the guide goes straight, the followers also go straight.
Craving is likewise; wherever it tends toward the three evil realms, the various fetters also follow. Therefore it is said: "Where craving goes, the various fetters follow."

As for the statement that "the flow of time does not stop": at one point in the interim, one is born among humans in the Middle Kingdom, upon level and upright soil where one may plant the roots of goodness; a land free of mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs, abundant in rare and extraordinary treasures. One attains firm faith and develops a mind of devotion toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; with compassion for all beings, one plants the roots of manifold virtues. All Buddhas are born in such lands; yet even while situated in the Middle Kingdom, this too is from the past and cannot be maintained for long. Therefore it is said: "The flow of time also does not stop."

Regarding the phrase "When time has passed, one further gives rise to sorrow": this refers to those in the borderlands after the passing of a Buddha, who dwell in the eight states of no leisure. Tracing back to the origin and following through to the end, they feel shame that they have failed to reach the Central Land; thus they give rise to grief, distress, and affliction. Beating their breasts and crying out, they dwell upon past events. Therefore it is said: "When time has passed, one further gives rise to sorrow."
Only upon entering prison did he realize it himself, exclaiming in lamentation, "Alas! What suffering is old age!

He thought, "When we were still in the world, we heard that those who study the Way obtain blessings by practicing goodness, while those who commit evil enter prison. Those who cultivate the mind of attachment plant the seeds of disease within the three realms; even the śramaṇas say that by upholding the five precepts and practicing the ten wholesome actions, one will be reborn among gods or humans."

We were foolish and did not follow your instructions; now we have instead entered this prison to undergo various sufferings—the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, the chariots of fire, and the burning coals—all of which arise from the roots planted by our hearts of attachment.
Therefore it is said: Only upon entering the prison does one realize for oneself.

Driven by craving, one flows on without ceasing; covered by the net of desire and the faculties of the aggregates, the branches and leaves increase hunger and thirst, and the suffering of craving grows again and again.
Regarding "conditioned by craving, the flow does not cease": what is it conditioned by?

It is conditioned by hell-beings, hungry ghosts, humans, and the various devas; they are conditioned by craving for future aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as by the objects from which phenomena arise. Therefore, it is said: "conditioned by."

The "stream of craving" (tṛṣṇā-srotas) is like a swift river flowing toward the sea; this stream of craving is also like this, for it leaks out all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (dharmas). Therefore, it is called the "stream of craving."
"Non-abiding" is like a grain seed: once it enters the earth, it undergoes transformation; when irrigated according to the season, its sprout grows. The seed of craving is likewise:

it pervades the human body and, following the movement of the vital energies (*vāyu*), increases all unwholesome roots. It does not abide within the three realms, but flows through the four modes of birth and hastens toward the five destinies; therefore, it is called "non-abiding."

The "root of the aggregates" refers to the body of the five flourishing aggregates (*pañca-upādānaskandha*). This is called the five flourishing aggregates because they are deep, firm, and difficult to move. As it is said regarding the root of the aggregates, so too it is with delusion, the thorn, suffering, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; for this reason, they are called the root of the aggregates.

Regarding desire (*kāma*), there are two aspects of desire: extending upward to the limits of space and pervading downward throughout the realms of the ten directions, it is called "desire" because the craving for the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals remains uninterrupted.

Regarding "covered by a net": it is like worldly people who catch birds with nets, catch deer with snares, and catch tigers with deep pits; those birds and beasts that encounter such calamities have no time of escape.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise so: covered by the net of desire, they do not perceive good and evil; their minds constantly take pleasure in wonderful forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. Ensnared by craving, they are unable to depart from it. Any sentient being who falls into the net of craving will surely ruin the right path and fail to reach the ultimate goal; therefore, it is said that they are covered by the net of craving.
It is just as when a kudzu vine wraps around a tree until it reaches its top; once it has spread everywhere, the tree withers.
Craving is likewise: it pervades the human body from head to foot without leaving any empty space, just as when a person falls into a latrine, their entire body becomes defiled.
A wise person, wishing to save that life, searches everywhere for a clean spot on the person's body to pull them out, but finds no clean spot from which they can be pulled out.
However, this human body is filled with craving that cannot be cured; therefore it is said: "The branches and leaves increase craving.

As for hunger and thirst, the hunger and thirst of worldly people can be relieved by water and grain to sustain their lives; or one may eat roots, grasses, fruits, and gourds; or practice *xiāoxī* (regulation) and the service of *qì* (vital energy); or through medicinal herbs and divine mantras, one may prolong one's lifespan.

For one who thirsts with this craving for existence, even drinking up the waters of the four oceans would not moisten but a single foot of ground of that craving; therefore it is said that the thirst of craving is difficult to quench.

Regarding the suffering of craving: as long as craving has not been completely eliminated, it increases again and again, extending the roots of all suffering. Therefore it is said: "The suffering of craving increases repeatedly."
If one cuts down a tree but does not exhaust its roots, though it has been cut, it will grow back again;
if one cuts away craving but does not exhaust its source, suffering will arise repeatedly.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a gardener who tended the royal gardens. In the middle of the garden grew a poisonous tree; whenever men or women entered the garden to sightsee and rested beneath this tree, some suffered headaches as if their heads were about to split, some experienced pain in their waists and backs, and some even passed away right there under the tree.

At that time, the park keeper, knowing it to be a poisonous tree and seeing the multitude suffering various hardships, immediately provided an axe with a blade over a fathom long; he struck the poisonous tree from afar, yet before ten days had passed, it grew back as it was before.
However, among those poisonous trees, the branches, leaves, and trunk were exquisite; all who saw them were filled with joy.

The sentient beings therein, unaware of the danger and not having encountered such calamity, went together to run toward it to shelter themselves beneath its shade. Before their shadows had even shifted, they again met with suffering and distress.

Then, on another day, the park keeper went again with his axe to cut it down; the tree grew back as before, even more extraordinary and beautiful, and though he cut it thus many times, it grew back as it was originally.
The gardener’s kinsmen, relatives, wife, children, and servants, all craving the shade of the trees, died one after another.
Left all alone, he wandered about day and night, sorrowful and lamenting, his grief manifold. On the road, he encountered a wise man to whom he recounted his bitter suffering and its myriad pains.
At that time, the wise man said to the gardener:
"These manifold sufferings and afflictions are of your own making.
Now, if one wishes to stop a flowing stream, nothing is better than building a high embankment."
"One who wishes to fell a tree must exhaust its roots and source.
The labor you have expended thus far has merely been for planting the saplings; why do you speak of felling the tree?
You must now go quickly and dig out the root."
The man’s mind was deluded, and he further feared that death would arrive:
"If I go there to dig up the tree roots, my death is certain beyond doubt.

After my death, the authorities will surely appoint someone else to guard this garden; thus my lineage will be utterly extinguished without remainder, and there will be no successor to continue my line. It would be best for me to flee and leave the household life to study the Way."
Arriving at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, he approached the practitioners and was ordained as a śramaṇa.
However, that park-keeper had previously planted the roots of wholesome merit; they were now nearing ripeness, and it was time for him to enter the practice of the Vinaya.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned his gaze toward that bhikṣu and spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"If one cuts down a tree but does not exhaust its roots, though it has been cut, it will grow again;
If one cuts off craving but does not exhaust its source, suffering will arise again and again."

At that time, having heard these verses, the bhikṣu traced back his own past experiences; he attained awakening within his own mind, reproached himself inwardly, contemplated the afflictions of the impure outflows of the four great elements, and reflected that those poisonous trees had been repeatedly felled by him, yet their growth continued without ceasing.

Now, this body composed of the four great elements is no different from that [previous one]; the roots of craving are deep and firm, and if one does not cut them at the root, the branches and currents will not cease. One shall then be subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death—dying there and being born here, dying here and being born there—thus revolving in saṃsāra forever without rest.
Just as a poisonous tree destroys its own roots and further harms others, so too is this fetter of craving: it ruins one's own life and can also externally damage the nature of wisdom.

At that time, the bhikṣu repeatedly and deeply contemplated these five aggregates from head to foot and found not a single thing worth craving. Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat; his six supernormal powers became pure and penetrating.
Amidst the great assembly, his heart was moved with gratitude, and three times he exclaimed, "How wonderful!
The Great Way does not exclude even the most minute. Now, by the grace of the Sage, I have attained the exhaustion of all outflows."

He immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, returned to his original seat, manifested the eighteen transformations, and entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Just as one who fashions an arrow ends up wounding their own body;
so too is the internal arrow: the arrow of craving wounds sentient beings.
Long ago, the Buddha was staying in a stone cave north of the city in the Mango Grove (Amravana) in the kingdom of Magadha.
There were many hunters who entered the mountains to hunt, spreading wide nets and killing countless deer before returning up the mountain.

At that time, a certain deer fell into one of their snares and cried out loudly; hearing this, the hunters each rushed toward it, only to fall into the snares themselves, causing harm to the people beyond counting.

Although they did not die, their wounds were so severe that the pain was beyond description; supporting one another, they managed with great difficulty to reach their home, where they sought medicinal ointments to apply to their wounds.
The members of the household and their five close relatives each went to meet the corpse and funeral procession, returning to perform the *ya-xun* (the ten-day mourning rites).

Among them were sentient beings who had been wounded; they realized for themselves that their wounds had healed, grew weary of hunting, and—due to past conditions that required their deliverance and the planting of various roots of goodness—voluntarily abandoned their homes to study the Way and become śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of countless sentient beings, who stood before and behind him as he preached the Dharma.

Then, wishing to uproot the afflictions of those beings, establish them in merit, and provide them with instruction so that they might forever leave birth and death behind and dwell eternally in the Hall of Blessings, the World-Honored One spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
"Just as one who fashions an arrow for oneself ends up wounding one's own body,"
"The internal arrow is likewise; the arrow of craving wounds sentient beings.

At that time, although those hunters had become śramaṇas, they were not yet self-aware. The Tathāgata has today testified that we are indeed hunters; filled with inner shame and remorse, they reflected upon their original transgressions and, dwelling in a secluded place, practiced *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with focused and undistracted minds.

Therefore, noble son, having shaved off hair and beard and donned the three dharma robes, you have left the household life to study the Way and practice the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*). You have realized it for yourself and found joy therein; birth and death are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further undergoing of birth and death—this you know as it truly is.
At that time, all the bhikṣus had attained arhatship; their six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, free from all obstructions. Therefore, they spoke this verse:

"One who is able to awaken to this— That craving and suffering co-arise with existence, And that when there is no desire, there is no perception of existence— Such a bhikṣu, with focused mindfulness, shall cross over."
"One who is able to awaken to this realizes that craving is the foremost of all ailments. It is like a fortified city where people gather and rely upon the earth for their security.
In what way is craving the foremost of all ailments?"
As the Buddha has said:
"The sufferings endured in the hells are immeasurable in number; they are all created by craving.
All the various afflictions experienced in the hells arise from the disease of craving.
Those who take life do so because of craving;

likewise, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech—these ten unwholesome actions—are all similarly performed out of a heart of craving. These various evils are created by the mind of craving.
Having fully committed the ten evil deeds, one dies and enters hell, where thirteen fires scorch and roast one’s body.

What are these thirteen? Two volcanic mountains stand before one, entering through the mouth, piercing the spine, and passing through; two volcanic mountains come from behind, entering through the spine and exiting through the abdomen; two volcanic mountains enter through the left flank and exit through the right flank; two volcanic mountains enter through the right flank and exit through the left flank; two volcanic mountains enter from below and exit above; and two volcanic mountains enter from above and exit below. As for the thirteenth volcanic mountain, what is it?
This is created by oneself; it is craving.
While the pain of the twelve volcanic mountains may be endured, the volcanic mountain of craving created by oneself cannot be cured.
As stated in a sutra of the Buddha:
"The wardens of hell asked the various sinners,
'From where have you come?'"
The sinners replied,
"We are famished and distressed, and we do not even know from where we have come.
At that time, the hell-wardens immediately forced them to eat glowing iron balls.
In a moment, the hell-wardens again questioned the sinners:
"From where have you come? [The sinners replied:
"We are extremely thirsty, and we do not even know from where we have come."
At that time, the hell-wardens cast the offenders down and pour molten copper into their mouths; it burns through the mouth and throat, passing all the way down.
To speak briefly, the pains and afflictions in the hells are of ten thousand kinds, and those who take the form of animals undergo countless sufferings.
What is the suffering experienced by animals?
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:
"In this regard, O bhikṣus!..."
Those born as animals endure manifold sufferings and afflictions.
Bhikṣus, you should know that if there are sentient beings who fall among animals, they are born in darkness, grow in darkness, and perish in darkness. What are these?

These are what are called earth-dwelling hibernating insects. All of them, due to having craved and delighted in sensual desires in previous lives, engaged in evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; when their bodies perished and their lives ended, they died as hibernating insects within the earth. This is called being born in darkness, growing in darkness, and ending one's life in darkness. Thus it is said, O Bhikṣus!
The suffering and pain of animals are extremely intense and difficult to endure.
There may be sentient beings who are born conditioned by the four great elements, grow conditioned by the four great elements, and die conditioned by the four great elements; what are these?

What is called "the arising of blisters" occurs because, in a previous life, one was greedily attached to the taste of sensory pleasures; through evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is born among the blister-worms. One arises dependent on the four great elements, grows dependent on the four great elements, and ends one's life dependent on the four great elements. This, O bhikṣus, is what is meant.
The suffering and pain of animals is extremely intense and difficult to endure.

Bhikṣus, you should know that there are further beings born among the animal realm who, upon smelling the stench of human excrement and urine, run toward it, saying, "We shall eat this; we shall drink this."
What are these? They are what are known as chickens, dogs, pigs, boars, donkeys, wild foxes, crows, birds, and so forth.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the hungry ghosts endure extreme suffering.
What is the suffering of the hungry ghosts (*preta*)?

There are some hungry ghosts who eat and devour their own beards and hair, or eat the body hairs; others eat their fingernails, toenails, teeth, bodily impurities, thin membranes, and even thick skin; they consume the skin, tendons, bones, heart, spleen, kidneys, liver, gallbladder, large and small intestines, stomach, excrement, brain matter, marrow, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, bile, and urine.
Beings of such various kinds are the food of hungry ghosts.

They undergo these manifold sufferings because in their previous lives they were greedily attached to the taste of flavors, being stingy and eating alone; furthermore, when providing food for others, they uttered curses and insults, saying:
"When you eat my food, it shall be like eating pus, blood, excrement, and urine—and so it shall be for you as well."
"Later, he will become a hungry ghost and eat these various impurities.

Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts who, when they were originally humans, ate alone without shame and never gave so much as a single grain of rice to others; if they saw someone giving, they would suppress and obstruct them to stop them. Later, having become hungry ghosts after a vast period of time, their ears have never even heard the name of food or drink, let alone being able to eat it."
"The suffering of these hungry ghosts cannot be fully described.

The immeasurable suffering endured in these three evil realms arises because, in previous lives, one’s craving was so firm that it planted these various miseries. Therefore, the Buddha said that craving is the foremost of all ailments.

Regarding "craving and suffering arise together with existence": when there is no desire and no perception of existence, and desire has already been abandoned and departed from, forever exhausted without remainder, having been vomited out and relinquished—this is the root of all afflictions and the feverish distress of existence. Therefore it is said: "no desire and no perception of existence."

When a bhikṣu is single-mindedly intent on crossing over, the bhikṣu focuses his mind so that it is not initially distracted; departing from the extremes, he reaches the boundless. From this shore to the other shore, he enters the realm of nirvāṇa, pure and free from feverish affliction, with all hearts of attachment and craving stilled and no longer arising. Therefore, it is said: "The bhikṣu is single-mindedly intent on crossing over."
Precepts are the path to the nectar of immortality; heedlessness is the road to death.
By not being greedy, one does not die; losing the path is self-destruction.
Regarding "precepts are the path to the nectar of immortality": for a person who is not heedless, even though they die, it is not truly death.

Once there was a bhikṣu whose practice was perfected and whose virtue was full; he practiced the Way during the six periods of the day without the slightest diminution or loss, exerting himself with diligent urgency from the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, never flagging for even a moment.

After a long time had passed in this manner, his chest became congested with bound qi, resulting in the affliction of heart pain. Although various physicians treated him, it was not cured, and he suddenly passed away.

There was a lay follower (*upāsaka*), intelligent and highly talented, who knew nothing that was not understood; he went among the community of monks and spoke this verse: "For those who study meditation and cultivate concentration, though their bodies may decay and perish, it is better to let them perish and pass into the next world than to let them perish while still remaining [in this life]."
Why is this so? One who does not study meditative concentration (dhyāna) neither purifies their own mind nor delivers others.
Why do they not purify their own mind?

Having received from others the offerings of faith—robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick—one cannot fully digest or repay the kindness of such gifts; therefore, after the end of life, one must again settle this debt.

Those who cannot rescue others cause both the donor and the host to fail to obtain their karmic rewards; they are unable to propagate the Dharma, so that although the Buddha-dharma remains, it diminishes and wastes away daily until the Great Dharma vanishes and non-Buddhist paths flourish.
Such categories as these constitute the fundamental principles of the law of loss; therefore it is said: "Precepts are the path to the nectar of immortality, while heedlessness is the road to death.
Furthermore, it is reiterated: "Heedlessness is the road to death" means that a person who is heedless incurs many faults and plants the roots of unwholesomeness for both this life and future lives.
The Venerable Aśvajit also spoke thus:
"The wise abandon heedlessness as one discards a poisonous drug; for heedlessness brings many faults, both in this world and in the world beyond."
The wise return to the source and investigate the root of negligence. Alas for negligence! It is like a mouse in a jar of ghee.

Once, in the house of an elder, there was a jar of ghee kept on a high tower; because the cover was not secure, a mouse entered the jar. Day and night it fed upon the ghee without leaving the mouth of the jar, and its body consequently grew large.
Once the ghee had completely melted away, mice filled the jar, appearing as if they were the color of ghee.

When someone came to the elder’s house wishing to buy ghee, the elder went up to the upper story, took some ghee, and placed it over a fire. At that moment, a mouse inside the jar—with its head below and its body above—died within the jar and was immediately transformed back into ghee once more.
When he sold it to the buyer, the latter took the ghee by measure using pints and pecks; the bones sank to the bottom, and the skull and leg bones were each separated from one another.
Having seen this, the elder thought to himself:
"When I took the ghee, the mouth of the jar was not covered; surely a rat must have entered and eaten this ghee."
"He remains inside the jar and refuses to come out; when the butter is exhausted, the mouse will surely die—such is the nature of this matter.
The elder further reflected that negligence brings many faults, and the situation is exactly as described.
The path of the laity is not different from that of the monastics. As for what it means for the laity not to be different, the matter is as follows:

being stingy and greedy without practicing giving, failing to uphold the prohibitive precepts, and not cultivating the Eightfold Fasting Observance (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) during the three months and six periods throughout the year—never maintaining these practices—though one may dwell in the world, it is of no benefit to the Path. Upon death and passage to future lives, the spirit undergoes calamity and pain, falling into the evil destinies and the eight states of non-leisure, experiencing immeasurable suffering and affliction. This is the negligence of the laity; such are their manifold afflictions.

What is the negligence of one on the path? It refers to a practitioner of the Way who, while outwardly relying upon the dharma-robes, inwardly harbors treachery; furthermore, they do not cultivate the scriptures nor do they serve and receive the true teaching. They do not contemplate meditative concentration or reflect upon the precepts; their efforts are in vain and they obtain no reward. They fail to attain the realization of the fruit in this present life, and must wait until future lives to accumulate further practice. Therefore, it is said that negligence is the path to death.
"Those who do not covet do not die" means that even though they die, they do not speak of death.

Why is this? Because those who are heedful transfer their spirits to be born in heaven, receiving immeasurable blessings; their lifespans are extended without decline, their minds are fierce and unconfused, and they neither meet an untimely end nor suffer the anxiety of losing their lives. Therefore it is said: "Those who do not covet do not die."

"To lose the Way is to bring about one's own ruin" means that one habituates oneself to heedless conduct, failing to consider the evils of the past, future, or present; one does not cultivate a virtuous life such as that of the noble sages, yet persists in what is wrong and refuses to follow the admonitions of others. Claiming that one’s own actions are authentic while all else is false, one does not employ wisdom to sustain one’s own life. Therefore it is said: "To lose the Way is to bring about one's own ruin."
"Those who possess wisdom and guard the path excel; they never become negligent. By not being greedy, they attain joy, and from this they obtain the bliss of the Way.

Regarding "those who possess wisdom and guard the path excel": among all meritorious qualities, these are the most supreme and foremost. The wise person cultivates their own body until it is free from further defects or leaks. They are well able to discern the various realms of existence and the various paths. Being intelligent and clear-sighted, they are devoid of folly or delusion. They are constantly praised by devas and humans, and they increase the True Dharma of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken. Therefore, it is said: "Those who possess wisdom and guard the path excel."

"Ultimately not being heedless" means that because one has already abandoned heedlessness and will not create it again, the mind is joyful and the spirit is glad; regarding all wholesome dharmas, the mind never knows satiety. Therefore, it is said: "Ultimately not being heedless."

"Non-attachment leads to joy; from this, one attains the bliss of the Path. This means that for those on the noble and holy path, there is no heedless conduct. Having exhausted the habitual causes and conditions, they no longer delight in rebirth within the three realms of existence. Therefore it is said: "From this, one attains the bliss of the Path."
One should always contemplate the Way, Exerting oneself to maintain upright conduct;
The steadfast shall attain transcendence of the world— This is the unsurpassed auspiciousness.

Regarding "one should always contemplate the Way": the practitioner of *dhyāna* (seated meditation) should, from morning until night and from night until morning, fix their mindfulness before them so that the mind is free from error. From beginning to end and from end to beginning, they should contemplate the foulness of this human body—the visualization of its impurities. Therefore, it is said: "One should always contemplate the Way."

One who exerts themselves to maintain upright practice is always courageous in intent and does not harbor regret in the heart; they transcend birth and death, attaining what has not yet been attained, obtaining what has not yet been obtained, and swiftly bringing about the realization of what has not yet been realized. Therefore it is said: "Exert oneself to maintain upright practice."

Those who are steadfast attain transcendence of the world; these are the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples. Firmly abiding in the True Dharma, their minds are difficult to thwart or destroy. Having eliminated all evil dharmas and impure practices, they gradually draw near to *nirvāṇa*, which is eternal stillness and peace. Therefore it is said: "The steadfast attain transcendence of the world."

Supreme auspiciousness is that which is manifested by the Tathāgata; it is auspicious and without disadvantage, and its conduct is auspicious. It completely subdues all non-Buddhists and heterodox teachers. All of birth and death are considered inauspicious, with myriads of forms of anxiety and distress, like the tracks of a turning wheel that never cease.
Beyond this, there is no further dharma that surpasses it; therefore it is said: "Auspiciousness has nothing above it. To restrain oneself as one would ward off negligence is the mark of the wise.

Having ascended the hall of wisdom, one leaves danger and attains peace. When the man of clear intelligence observes the fool, it is like the difference between a mountain and the earth. Therefore, the wise abandon arrogance and cultivate luminous wisdom.

Therefore, those who have eyes and abandon arrogance observe that heedless conduct is neither true nor real, and is not to be relied upon; for this reason it is said: "One should mindfully abandon heedlessness."
What is called a wise person does not receive [truth] from another; they respond without external dependence and do not rely on the forms and colors of others' characteristics to awaken.

This is what is meant by wisdom. Their mental nature is swift and agile, able to respond to matters as soon as they encounter them; though they may have studied extensively within, they outwardly manifest the act of inquiring and receiving instruction. Therefore it is said: "The wise cultivate clear wisdom."
In the past, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana personally ordained two disciples who had first gone forth to study the Path: one from the family of the dyer, and the other from the family of the smith.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana gradually instructed the two men, saying:
"First inform the blacksmith that he should practice this dhyāna method, contemplating with skillful mindfulness the meditation on impurity and the foul secretions."
Next, he told the laundryman:
"You must now practice *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
These two men practiced with diligence day and night, yet their aspirations were not fulfilled; after twelve years had passed, they were still unable to attain it.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that the two men had failed to obtain their wish, said to Maudgalyāyana:

"You do not instruct your disciples with correct practice; you should instruct them according to the Dharma, yet instead you instruct them in negligence. You have not yet understood the timely practice of the Dharma."

For this renunciant who washes clothes, one should teach the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā). The reason for doing so is that this person’s mind has long been pure and clean; if they hear the teaching on the contemplation of impurity, their mind will immediately be liberated without any further hindrance.

Furthermore, one should instruct that iron-smith bhikṣu in the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing). The reason for this is that such a person constantly practices holding a bellows in his hands and understands the amount of air it contains; only then can his mind and intentions attain awakening.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana followed Śāriputra’s instructions and trained his two disciples, who immediately attained awakening.
Therefore it is said: "One who restrains oneself as if restraining negligence is truly wise."

Regarding "having already ascended the hall of wisdom and departed from danger to attain security": those worthy sages who have succeeded in ascending this hall regard all ordinary beings and practitioners as wild grasses and weeds; with a heart of great compassion that moistens all without exception, they are like the mansions of a noble clan in the human world, which the common people envy.

The various noble ones are likewise thus: having ascended the hall of the noble ones, they observe that the practices of sentient beings are not true; they feel concern for sentient beings who have not yet escaped their suffering and are habitually attached to negligence, or those who are negligent regarding wisdom—those whose minds are fixed on dhyāna and whose intentions are practiced in dhyāna, following the teacher’s instructions without transgressing their precepts; this is called "negligence regarding wisdom."
Only then do we know that those who do not practice meditation have no means of attaining liberation; therefore it is said: "Having ascended the hall of wisdom, one leaves danger and attains peace.

When the wise observe the ignorant, it is like a mountain compared to the earth; it is as if someone were to ascend a high mountain and survey those below, seeing them all clearly, while those below look up at the one above and see nothing at all.
It is the same with the fool and the wise: the mind of the fool is deluded and stubborn, unable to understand by itself; it must rely on the noble and the holy to attain awakening.

One who exerts effort and practices heedfulness, restraining oneself and disciplining one’s own mind, possesses the wisdom that can serve as a lamp for illumination, so that one does not return to the dark abyss.

To "undertake practice" means to undertake practice with an unwearied mind; even if one undertakes practice, it does not constitute true undertaking if the intention is timid or weak. Only when there is courage such that what is vowed will certainly be fulfilled is it called "undertaking practice. Therefore, it is said: "to undertake practice."
Regarding "heedfulness": although the mind may be diligent, if there is still heedlessness, one cannot accomplish the fruit of the unsurpassed path; therefore, it is said, "heedfulness."

Regarding "restraining oneself and disciplining the mind": "restraining oneself" means being fully endowed with pure precepts; "disciplining the mind" means maintaining focused intent without distraction, so that no perverse thoughts ever arise.
Therefore it is said: "restraining oneself and disciplining the mind."
Wisdom is able to act as a lamp that brings illumination; in the space of a single finger-snap, it accomplishes four matters. What are these four?
It eliminates ignorance, burns away the form of the five aggregates, kindles the fat and grease of rebirth, and forever extinguishes the root of craving.

Just as the light of wisdom acts in the space of a finger-snap, so too are these four matters accomplished; having brought these four matters to completion, ignorance is removed, the form of the five aggregates is incinerated, the fat and grease of rebirth are consumed, and the root of craving is forever extinguished.

The illumination of the noble path is likewise: in the space of a finger-snap, it accomplishes four tasks—it eliminates ignorance, produces the grease of life, eternally extinguishes the root of craving, and burns away the form of the five aggregates.

He is not cowed by fools because he has accomplished the illumination of the path of the noble ones (ārya). Possessing this illumination of the path, the various heterodox outsiders cannot shake his mind; therefore, it is said: "He does not return to enter the dark abyss."
*Udānavarga*, Fascicle Five;
*Udānavarga*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Four on Heedfulness (Part Two):
Right mindfulness is constantly aroused; practicing purity, evil is easily extinguished.
Self-restraint through the life of the Dharma prevents transgression and increases one’s good reputation.
Regarding "right mindfulness constantly arising": there may be a practitioner who gives rise to distracted thoughts, whereby the task they intend to accomplish is not fulfilled.
The Venerable Kumāralāta said:
"If one undertakes a task with a distracted mind, it will not be accomplished due to mental regret; but if consciousness is fierce, focused, and single-minded, what wish could not be attained?"

The practitioner is also like this: if the mind contemplates only what is wholesome but the body does not act accordingly, one will not reach the further shore. Therefore it is said: "Right mindfulness should be constantly aroused."
"Those whose conduct is pure find evil easily extinguished" means that their bodily conduct is pure, their verbal conduct is pure, and their mental conduct is pure.

What is impure? It is the four perversions (*viparyāsa*): to regard the impermanent as permanent is the first perversion; to regard suffering as pleasure is the second; to regard the impure as pure is the third; and to regard what is non-self as self is the fourth. That which is not associated with these four perversions is called "pure. Therefore it is said: "Those whose conduct is pure find evil easily extinguished."
When all fetters and defilements are exhausted, the body becomes cool and free from the torment of fever;

this is also called the "extinguishing of evil. Regarding "self-restraint through the Dharma for the sake of life": as for the term "restraint," it means restraining body, speech, and mind. One sustains life through the Dharma and not through what is non-Dharma; one seeks life through the Dharma and not through what is non-Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "Self-restraint through the Dharma for the sake of life."

Regarding "not transgressing increases one's good reputation": one's fame is heard throughout the eight directions and the measure of one's virtue penetrates the ten quarters. Among those who hear of this, there are none who do not receive their teachings with profound faith. Therefore, it is said: "Not transgressing increases one's good reputation."
Focus your mind and do not be negligent; by practicing the precepts of the Muni, you will ultimately be free from sorrow and suffering, and your distracted thoughts will find rest.
Regarding "focus your mind and do not be negligent": for one who desires to practice with such intense mental fervor, there may still be lapses within the prohibitive Dharma.
Formerly, the World-Honored Buddha’s disciple, the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, spoke of his own exhortation, saying:

"Among the disciples of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, I am the foremost in courageous and diligent effort; yet, regarding the untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), my mind is not yet liberated."

"If my ancestors and grandparents possessed wealth, property, and estates beyond measure, yet I now study the Way without attaining anything, it would be better for me to return home, discard these three dharma-robes, practice worldly ways, enjoy the five pleasures, and extensively give to the poor and needy. What is the use of practicing precepts and striving with such self-inflicted hardship if I do not fulfill my aspirations?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his divine ear—which was pure, all-pervading, and free from defect—heard that the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa wished to return home to practice the conduct of a layperson. He immediately vanished from the Jeta Grove and appeared before the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, asking him: "How is it, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa?"
You have conceived this thought and declared of yourself:
"Among the disciples of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, I am the foremost in courageous diligence; yet, regarding the untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), my mind is not yet liberated."

"However, my ancestors' wealth, enterprises, and estates were beyond measure; yet now that I have studied the Way, I have achieved nothing. It would be better for me to return home, cast off these three dharma-robes, practice worldly ways, enjoy the five pleasures, and extensively give alms to the poor and needy. What is the purpose of practicing precepts and diligence to bring myself such suffering as this?"
"Do you truly have these words? He replied,
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Śāriputra:
"I shall now question you on the meaning of internal dharmas; answer me point by point.
What do you say, Śāriputra?"

"When you were formerly at home, you were skilled at tuning the lute; did not the lute harmonize with the song and the song harmonize with the lute, so that their sounds, being of one kind, formed a musical piece?"
He replied, “It is so, World-Honored One.”
“Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, if the strings of a lute are too tight or too loose, will it produce music? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this so, Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa?"
"If the strings of a lute are neither too tight nor too loose,
will it produce music? He replied, "It will."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:

“A bhikṣu who practices with excessive vigor and diligence gives rise to pride and indolence; if he is indolent and not diligent, he further gives rise to sloth. Therefore, you now should neither be excessively diligent nor indolent. By practicing the Middle Way, one attains its fruit, and the mind with outflows (āsrava) achieves liberation.”
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, dwelling in a secluded place, focused his mind in contemplation and felt a profound sense of urgency. Thus, a son of good family shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three dharma-robes, leaves the household life to study the Path, and cultivates the unsurpassed Dharma; exhausting all outflows (āsrava), he realizes the state of no-outflow and attains Arhatship in the Nirvana without remainder.
Therefore it is said: "To focus the mind and not be negligent.
Regarding "practicing the precepts of the Muni": the Muni refers to the various World-Honored Ones; what are called the precepts are the two hundred and fifty precepts.

The internal restraint of dignified conduct and every word and meaning of the Buddhas' instructions are entirely prohibitions and entirely precepts. One should practice this and abandon that; one should distance oneself from this and realize that. Therefore, it is said that practicing the mind is the precept of the Muni.

Regarding "ultimately being free from sorrow and suffering": when a practitioner is indolent in their inner mind and does not cultivate the unsurpassed Dharma, they become deeply attached to worldly entanglements and fail to distance themselves from the mundane; for this reason, they give rise to sorrow and anxiety.
Furthermore, violating the Dharma and losing self-restraint also gives rise to sorrow and anxiety.

Moreover, if a practitioner receives the faithful offerings of others yet eats greedily without satiety, neither reciting the scriptures nor practicing seated meditation and mental concentration, neither cultivating mindfulness of the Way and its virtue nor teaching and assisting in communal affairs—such a person will likewise give rise to sorrow and anxiety.
What is meant by being free from sorrow and anxiety?

It refers to when the five faculties gain mastery in the methods of dhyāna without any deficiency, thereby transcending successive stages to reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One enters the Hall of No-Sorrow, tranquil and blissful; therefore it is said: "In the end, there is no sorrow, anxiety, or suffering."

Regarding "the cessation of distracted thoughts": what is meant by "cessation" is their eternal extinction so that they do not arise; it is also the absence of birth and death, attachment and severance. All the fevers of existence, the afflictions, the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*), as well as the maladies and lamentations, do not arise. Through the diligent cultivation of meditative concentration, one reaches the chamber of sorrowlessness, where mindfulness is focused and undistracted. There is always wholesome mindfulness and wholesome conditions. Therefore, it is said: "distracted thoughts attain cessation."
Do not associate with base and defiling dharmas; do not meet with negligence;
do not plant the roots of wrong views; do not grow evil in this world.
Regarding "do not associate with base and defiling dharmas," what are these base and defiling dharmas?
All fetters, all evil deeds, all wrong views, and all perversions—if there are sentient beings who associate with such things as these, they will come to possess manifold evils.

Therefore, the wise should not associate with them; they should not engage in their affairs, nor converse with them face-to-face, nor sit, rise, or walk together with them. One should always remain far removed from them, as one would avoid a conflagration. For this reason, it is said: "Do not associate with base and defiled dharmas."

Regarding "not associating with the heedless": the actions performed by those who are heedless invariably give rise to calamity and misfortune. Taking evil associates as their companions and the ten unwholesome paths as their support, they are not true intimates; they merely resemble friends. They feign weeping and shed tears while plotting their own transgressions; their words are sweet, yet their inner intent is like a sword or a halberd.

One should always distance oneself from such heedless persons and not associate with them; what is sweet at first but bitter in the end is not practiced by the noble ones. Therefore it is said: "Do not meet with the heedless."

Regarding "not planting the root of wrong views": as for the affliction of wrong views, its manifestations are manifold. As stated in the sūtras, one denies the existence of this world and the next, denies the existence of parents and the ancestral lineage, and denies the existence of arhats and others who have attained the Way. Abandoning the Buddha’s true words, one follows worldly flowery phrases, composing poems and verses with false claims and deceitful arrogance.

Having failed to practice correctly, they abandon the root for the branches; departing from reality, they dwell in falsehood and habituate themselves to perversion. They claim that the Buddha-Bhagavān, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Arhats, the Anāgāmins, the Sakṛdāgāmins, and the Srotāpannas are neither true nor existent. They slander and disparage the six perfections, declaring them not to be practices. Such as these are the most extreme of false views.
Why is this so? It is because that which is real is called unreal, and that which is unreal is called real.
When the Buddha was in the world, he spoke with his divine mouth, saying:
"Foolish people accept what should not be accepted and, conversely, slander it, asking why one would say it is wrong.
They sink themselves into an abyss and cause others to fall into the deep abyss as well; thus, neither the devas nor the people of the world accord them respect."

If one practices the external paths and heterodox teachings, such as talismans, incantations, and rites of suppression; seeks auspicious days to employ ghosts and spirits; or manifests wondrous illusions—such matters as these are all heterodox arts, which those with eyes of wisdom ought not to cultivate.

The Buddha spoke by way of an analogy: "Suppose there were a person who required snake meat for food; searching everywhere, he eventually caught a snake and grasped it by its tail with his hand. The snake turned back and bit his hand, and as the venom spread through his body, he suddenly passed away. This was entirely because that person did not know how to handle the snake skillfully, and thus lost his life."
