Now this foolish person is likewise so: taking what is false to be true and what is true to be false. Therefore it is said: "One does not plant the root of wrong views."
Regarding "not growing evil within the world," there are three kinds of worlds.
What are the three? First, the world of sentient beings; second, the world of the aggregates (*skandha*); and third, the world of the three realms.

The world of sentient beings refers to those with one foot, two feet, four feet, or even many feet; those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; and those who are neither with nor without perception—this is called the world of sentient beings.

The world of aggregates (*skandha-loka*) refers to the five flourishing aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four aggregates of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); this is called the world of aggregates.

The world of the three realms (*tridhātu-loka*) refers to the trichiliocosm up to the boundless realms; furthermore, counting from a single unit up to the trichiliocosm, this is called the world of the three realms.

If there are sentient beings who practice wrong views, they will increase their time in the world and give rise to all manner of defilements and evils, prolonging their existence in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
those who do not plant the roots of wrong views do not engage with these three worlds.
Therefore it is said: "One does not grow evil within the world.
With right view as the supreme path, examined through mundane wisdom, one will never fall into the evil realms throughout hundreds of thousands of births."

Regarding the path of the supremacy of right view: one should forever abandon all conceptualizations that are the source of false views. Even if another person were to manifest in the form of a Buddha and stand before one, preaching perversions as if they were the True Dharma, one would maintain a firm mind and never accept them.

Why is this so? Because right view is difficult to obstruct or destroy; even if the evil Māra Pāpīyān and various illusionists were to manifest numerous transformations to terrify the son of good family, they could not move his mind. He would redouble his cultivation of right view, his intention remaining unshakable. This is mundane right view, not the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Therefore it is said: "Right view is the superior path, which is examined by mundane wisdom."

Regarding "throughout hundreds of thousands of births," as the Buddha has said: "I have never seen, nor have I ever heard, a person who practices right view fall into the evil destinies throughout hundreds of thousands of births."
In whatever place one is born, one will encounter sages and holy ones, and shall never fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Therefore it is said: "Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, one shall never fall into the evil paths."
Those who cultivate heedlessness are the companions of the foolish;
those established in concentration are not heedless, like a master of wealth guarding his treasury.

Regarding "those who cultivate heedlessness": they hold fast to delusions with stubborn intent and do not accord with correct principle. They claim, "What I practice is right; what others practice is wrong. They draw near to and indulge in such habits, repeating them over and over again, as if having obtained a precious treasure they cannot bear to part with. Therefore it is said: "those who cultivate heedlessness."

That which fools habitually associate with is like a foolish, ignorant child who cannot distinguish between the true and the false, or the white and the black; they grasp at that which should not be grasped, asking, "What is fire? What is a venomous snake?"

As for the rule of non-laxity: through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gathers the mind so that both the internal and external become pure and transparent. By means of the seven great periods, the meditation-sleep, the meditation-ball, and the Dharma-staff, one restrains the mind while sitting in meditation; progressing at all times, one does not lose the methods of dhyāna.
What is called concentration?
That which is called concentration means that the mind does not regress but advances daily without retreating; for twenty-one days—three times seven—it remains tranquil and free from thought.

Regarding the "great seven": this refers to forty-nine days (seven times seven). If one applies oneself with diligence during this period without allowing the mind to become distracted, one will attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If the mind becomes distracted and loses its sequence, one must begin again from the first and proceed through the seven great weeks.
Regarding those who drows during meditation (*dhyāna*), they place a *karka* (a small shell) upon their heads and attach a cord to their ears; if they fall asleep, they will wake themselves up by it.

Regarding those who use the meditation-stick (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*), the meditation master holds a meditation-stick and watches for those who sleep; he strikes them with a ball, and once they have received the stick, they strike others in turn to awaken themselves.
The Dharma-staff is used to awaken others with the staff, so that they may successively awaken one another and seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Therefore it is said: "In concentration, there is no negligence."
Just as a treasurer guards a storehouse, so too does that meditator guard his mind without letting it go; should it become distracted, he immediately draws it back.

The treasurer likewise acts in this manner: he constantly inspects and observes the storehouse, its seven kinds of precious jewels and various treasures, its livestock such as oxen and sheep, its wealth of servants and slaves, its gold, silver, and gems, and its varieties of musaragalva, agate, pearl, and amber; he watches over them at all times so that none shall be lost or wasted.
Therefore it is said: "Like a master of wealth guarding his treasury.

Those who cultivate heedlessness are those with whom the foolish associate; yet when one is established in concentration, there is no heedlessness, and one is thus able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding "being able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*)," that practitioner reflects within themselves:

"The disease of the outflows carries many faults; these outflows and various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are spread across the three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. Due to these faults, I am bound and attached to birth and death; I have truly been deceived and have not reached the ultimate. It is now appropriate for me to decisively abandon them."
"Those who are present cause that which has not yet arisen in the future to be exhausted, do not create anything new, and furthermore do not cultivate what is old.
Therefore it is said: "One is thus able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*)."
Do not covet, do not delight in strife, and do not crave sensual pleasures; by reflecting with heedfulness, one may attain great peace. Regarding "do not covet, do not delight in strife":

this means not practicing heedlessness nor associating with those who do, and seeing others who practice it, not taking pleasure in it. Furthermore, one encourages others to abandon heedlessness and does not draw near to them. Therefore, it is said: "Do not covet, do not delight in strife."

Furthermore, do not indulge in sensual pleasures. The heterodox teachers of other schools praise and speak of sensual pleasures; these teachers themselves claim that desire is fresh, pure, and stainless. They say one should eat together to satisfy the sense faculties, that indulging in desire is blameless, and that they take defiled phenomena to be pure.
Why is this so? For those who possess form do not arise without desire; yet how could there be a self for one who is without desire?
Thus the Tathāgata said:
"This is not the true meaning; we should together disparage it—why praise it further?
For what reason? Because one desires that the mother be the mistress who gives rise to sensual pleasure."
Therefore it is said: "Do not crave sensual pleasures. By reflecting with heedfulness, one may attain great peace;

one will be completely liberated from all fetters and dwell in tranquil joy. Kings, ministers, elders, and householders amass wealth in the hundreds of millions and indulge their hearts as they please, claiming that their enjoyment is inexhaustible. Yet this practice is not a method for true peace; though one may be content at the time, one will inevitably suffer later. There is no end to seeking such things, and it is truly perilous.
One for whom all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are forever exhausted without remainder has attained what is called Great Peace. This state is immovable;

one no longer encounters the hardships of the four realms, and by means of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), even if one possesses the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi*), it cannot displace this peace to bring it to danger.
Therefore it is said: "One can thereby attain great peace.
Not indulging in self-indulgence at any time, one is able to restrain the outflows and bring them to an end;
whereas if one indulges in self-indulgence, Māra finds an opportunity, just as a lion seizes a deer."
Once, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"As long as you have not yet attained the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava), do not harbor any sense of self-reliance."
This verse also speaks of not indulging in self-indulgence according to the season, but nourishing the four great elements like dwelling with a viper.
You, O bhikṣu, should now mindfully exert yourself to seek liberation from the prison; for what reason would you be negligent and forever lose the seed of the Path?
Death involves innumerable sufferings with little joy; why, in the midst of this, do you again give rise to worldly toil?
Birth and death are ablaze with fire, leaving no place of refuge; why, in the midst of this, do you still indulge in negligence?
Therefore it is said: "Do not indulge yourselves at will according to the occasion.

One who is able to restrain the outflows (āsrava) so that they are exhausted—though you may have attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or the fruit of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin)—the outflows are not yet ended and desire-attachment is not yet dissolved. Although you do not enter the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, as long as desire is not exhausted, you must not rely on anything; there still remains great fear.
Who is it? It is Māra.
The evil Māra Pāpīyān observes the faults of people day and night; seeing those in the world who are heedless, his heart leaps with joy as he pursues them from behind, causing them to regress.
Therefore it is said: "The Māra gains an opportunity when one is self-indulgent.

It is like a lion pouncing on a deer; just as a doe, when first giving milk, cannot flee far because she is distracted by her young who follow her here and there, so too does the Māra find his chance.
At that time, the lion, king of beasts, having carefully observed that the doe could not bear to leave her fawn, went and seized them;
thus both mother and child perished. This was because the lion took advantage of the doe’s attachment to her offspring.

Those whose desires were not yet exhausted were likewise so; upon hearing this urgent instruction, they gave rise to a sense of weary detachment. They contemplated all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations. Dwelling in secluded and tranquil places, they meditated in stillness with unwavering resolve. Their craving for desire was extinguished, and they were no longer stained by worldly dust. With the extinction of sensual craving, they attained the stage of *anāgāmin*. Thereupon, they pressed forward without any mid-course regret, exhorting one another to diligently investigate the origin of suffering. Having exhausted all fetters and attachments, they attained the supernormal power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and realized the state of an *arhat*.

Therefore it is said: "One who does not indulge oneself at will is able to restrain the outflows and bring them to an end; one who indulges at will gives the Māra an opportunity, just as a lion seizes a deer."
There are four matters of negligence: taking pleasure in violating the wives of others, being in danger, lacking merit and benefit, and the fourth is being depraved and lewd.

Regarding "there are four matters of negligence": this refers to the places where those attached to desire dwell and reside; their minds are constantly delighted by the practice of accumulating and using treasures.
The wise observe it as foul and leaking, finding no virtue therein; they sleep in unease and take pleasure in reviling others.

Hell is caused by four things; for one who lusts after the wives of others, their various evils are incalculable—both in this life and in future lives—and in the present world, they are hated and envied by others.
What is meant by manifesting a body that is loathed by others?

As for why one is loathed by others: perhaps one is detained by royal law, or seized by a husband, or confined in prison; subjected to myriad forms of flogging and caning, and tortured with such bitter agony that the suffering is beyond measure; and when the body perishes and life ends, one is reborn in the Sword-Tree Hell.

While the offenders are in prison, they see upon the sword-trees (kṣuramārga) beautiful women, their countenances exceptionally distinguished like those of celestial maidens. When the offenders behold these women, peerless in their beauty, their hearts are filled with joy and delight, and they desire to have carnal union with them. They lead one another up the branches of the sword-trees, which hang down and pierce and mangle their bodies; the agonizing pain is beyond calculation, and they reach neither the trees nor their goal.

The beautiful women suddenly fell to the ground. Seeing the women on the ground from afar, the offenders were filled with joy again and climbed back down the tree; however, the sword-like branches pierced them upward, mangled their bodies until the flesh was exhausted and only bone remained. They cried out in loud lamentation, seeking death but unable to find it. Before their karmic suffering was exhausted, their flesh grew back once more. All this bitter torment is brought about by greed and lust. Thus they pass through thousands of billions of years, enduring such agonizing pain without passing away, until their retribution is fully spent.
Such are the matters regarding those who are lustful in the hells.

Furthermore, if a lustful person falls among the animals, their lust may arise according to a specific season or it may arise regardless of the season. When lust occurs according to a season, although these beings commit acts of lust, they do not violate the wives of others; their lustful intent is partial and not particularly intense.

Regarding those beings for whom sexual desire arises without regard for season: while they were among humans, their lustful intent was excessive and they violated the wives of others; now, as animals, their carnal desires are even more intense, and for this reason, their sexual activity occurs at no fixed time.
Thus do they undergo such suffering when born among the animals.

Sentient beings who are greedy for lust fall among the hungry ghosts; for the sake of their lewdness, they wage war against one another, even to the point that the asuras and the devas contend with each other—all because of greed and lust.
Those who violate the wives of others are born among the hungry ghosts (preta) and undergo such retribution as this.

As for those born among humans due to their lustful greed, they commit sexual misconduct with their own wives, daughters, and other women without restraint; they wander about and act wantonly, beyond all control.

If one further forcibly commits transgressive sexual misconduct—whether with those of high status or low status, and without avoiding kin or strangers—even if such a person is reborn as a human, they will lack a male organ; or they may possess both sexual organs, or have no organs at all; or even if they possess one organ, it will not be fully formed.
Such types of lewd individuals all arise from committing sexual misconduct without distinction of status.

If a person of lustful greed is reborn as a deva, when they encounter the calamities of the five-fold pestilence or other portents, and see their own celestial queen enjoying herself with another, the deva-king feels inner grief and sorrow as if he were being consumed by fire. Thinking, "My own body remains lustful while this jade-like woman has departed," his mind burns intensely as he gives rise to unwholesome thoughts; thus, at the end of that life, he passes away and is reborn in hell.
This arises from the failure to cultivate meritorious conduct, whereby one is born within the five realms of existence and undergoes suffering according to one's form;
thus, the offenses incurred differ. Therefore it is said: "Perilous is that which is not merit."

Regarding the fourth [offense], the destruction of the third [precept] concerning sexual misconduct: at that time, those who engage in sexual misconduct constantly harbor a sense of fear, knowing that the crime of sexual misconduct is so grave that they will not be pardoned even if it costs them their lives. They employ the three gates of body, speech, and mind to utter abusive and evil words. Furthermore, there may be a person of sexual misconduct who, having previously had no acquaintance with a woman, approaches her and commits the act, only to be reviled by the woman; or there may be one who was already acquainted with the woman and had prior conversation with her, yet when the husband sees him, he is reviled by the husband.
Therefore it is said: "Insult, humiliation, and verbal abuse make three;
hell makes four. Within the hells, there are manifold tasks for which sinners are enslaved; therefore it is said that hell constitutes the fourth.
Lacking merit and falling into evil, fearing yet finding little joy, the king’s law imposes heavy punishment—restrain the mind and stay away from another’s wife.
Regarding "lacking merit and falling into evil": one will go to the evil realms—the paths of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell—where one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Regarding the fear of those who fear and the joy of those with few desires, I shall now set forth the facts.

Formerly, King Aśoka’s younger brother, Śobhita, went out of the city to hunt and entered deep into the mountains. There he saw various brahmins, naked and exposed to the elements, seeking the state of a divine immortal; they exhausted their minds and tormented their bodies in the hope of attaining Brahma-merit, subsisting on tree leaves. Among them, those whose resolve for diligence was most courageous consumed one leaf per day, while the weak and feeble consumed seven leaves per day; some consumed six, five, four, three, two, or even one.
One who eats seven leaves should drink seven *he* of water; for six leaves, six *he*; for five, four, three, two, or one, it is likewise.
If water is unavailable, one should inhale air seven times; for six leaves, six inhalations; for five, five inhalations; for four, three, two, or one, it is likewise.
Among them, some brahmins lay upon thorns and spikes, some lay upon ashes and dust, some lay upon stones, and some lay upon pestles.
The King’s younger brother, Sunetra, asked the brahmins:
"As you practice the Way here, what is your greatest affliction?"
The brahmin replied, "Prince,

you should know that while practicing the Way here, there are no other afflictions; however, when herds of deer arrive here in pairs and couple, our lustful desires immediately blaze up and cannot be restrained."
Upon hearing this, the prince immediately conceived an evil thought:

"If these brahmins—who exhaust their bodies and torment their flesh, scorched by the sun and roasted by fire, with their very lives as precarious as if they were non-existent—still do not completely eliminate lustful desire;

how then could the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who consume sweet delicacies, sit upon fine couches, wear elegant garments, and perfume themselves with fragrant flowers, be free from lewd intentions?"
When King Aśoka heard his younger brother’s discourse, he immediately felt sorrow and distress, thinking:
"My younger brother shares in my merit; why has he instead developed a mind of wrong views?"
"I must employ skillful means to eliminate his evil intent; otherwise, I shall suffer the full retribution for my sin, and my guilt will not be small.
He then entered the palace and commanded his musicians and attendants to each adorn themselves and go to the Prince of Shanrong to enjoy their company together.
He further instructed his ministers in advance: "I have a plan. If I command you to kill the Prince of Shanrong, you must remonstrate with me."
"You must wait seven days, and then you may kill him according to the King's will.
At that time, the female attendants immediately went to amuse themselves, and before long, the King went in person to speak to his younger brother, the prince:
"Why do you take my entertainers, wives, and concubines to indulge yourself as you please?"
Displaying his fierce majesty and wrath, he hurled his wheel into the air and summoned his ministers, addressing them thus:

"Do you not know? I am neither decrepit nor aged, nor have any foreign invaders or powerful enemies come to invade my borders. Furthermore, I have heard that the sages of antiquity have this proverb:"
"When a ruler possesses merit, the four seas submit; when merit is exhausted and virtue grows thin, even those closest to one—like the flesh on one's own arm—rebel and depart.

As I observe with my own eyes, no such change has yet occurred. Yet my younger brother Shanrong has enticed my female musicians, wives, and concubines, indulging his passions and acting as he pleases until his deeds were thus exposed. Is there still any room for me?
"You shall take him to the marketplace and put him to death.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"We pray only this of Your Majesty!"
"Please listen to the words of this humble subject.
Your Majesty now has but this one younger brother, and as he has few children and no heir to succeed you, we pray that you will grant us seven days to carry out your command."
At that time, the king silently listened to his ministers' admonition. The king, again showing great leniency, commanded his ministers:

"I now permit the prince to wear my robes and ornaments; let his celestial crown and majestic appearance be no different from mine. Let him enter my inner palace to perform music and dance, and enjoy himself with us."
He further commanded another minister:
"From this day forward, don armor, take up weapons, and draw a sharp sword with your own hand; go and say to Prince Sunetra:
'Prince, do you know?'"

The seven-day period has ended and you are now due to arrive; exert yourself to enjoy the five pleasures for your own amusement. If you do not indulge yourself now, there will be no benefit in regretting it after death.
When one day had passed, the minister went again and said,
"Six days remain. In this manner,
proceeding step by step until only one day remained, the minister went and reported:
"The Prince should know that six days have already passed; only one day remains before you must face death. Strive now to indulge yourself in the five pleasures for your own amusement.
When the seventh day arrived, the King sent a messenger to summon him, saying: "What is it, Prince?"
"During these seven days, were you free in will and happy?
The younger brother replied to the king, saying,
"Great King, you should know this!"
"You neither saw nor heard anything.

The king asked his younger brother, "Clad in my robes and entering my palace, you amused yourself with various entertainers and ate sweet delicacies; why do you deceive me by saying you neither saw nor heard anything?"
The younger brother said to the king:

"A person who is destined to die is no different from the dead even before their life has ended; how could they possibly have any emotional attachment to the five pleasures or find delight in clothing and ornaments?"
The king said to his younger brother:

"Foolish one, as for what you have proposed, you now face a hundred anxieties with this single body; even a moment's rest is not permitted while this body remains. How much more so for the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who contemplate the three periods of time?"

After one body perishes, one receives another body; throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, every body experiences suffering, and as one recollects those afflictions, the mind burns with anguish.

Or again, one may remember entering the hells and undergoing immeasurable suffering; even after emerging as a human being, one is made to serve others, or is born into a poor family where food and clothing are utterly lacking.

Reflecting on these bitter sorrows, I have left the household life to pursue the Way, seeking the essential means for attaining the unconditioned and transcending the world; were I not to practice with diligent effort, I would surely have to undergo the hardships of further kalpas.
At that time, the prince came forward and addressed the king, saying:

"Now that I have heard Your Majesty’s instruction, I have attained awakening; birth, old age, sickness, and death are indeed to be loathed and feared. Grief, anxiety, suffering, and affliction flow on without ceasing. I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me leave to enter the Way, so that I may diligently and prudently cultivate the holy life."
The king said to his younger brother, "You should know that this is the time.

He then took leave of the king and went forth as a śramaṇa. Following his teacher’s instructions and admonitions without ceasing day or night, he subsequently attained the fruit of srotāpanna and the fruit of arhat; his six supernormal powers became pure and penetrating, free from all obstruction.

Therefore it is said: "One fears and fears the scarcity of joy. When the king’s law imposes heavy punishment, those who are habitually greedy and lustful and constantly practice filth and impurity are subjected to the sovereign's justice.

All their property is confiscated by the government; they are shorn, flogged, and beaten with tortures of immeasurable agony. Or they are confined in prison for years without release, further subjected to the daily application of the five bonds, whips, and staves. Their wounds are covered in pus and blood, so foul and filthy as to be difficult to approach; flies and insects swarm and sting them, leaving no place to escape, and they lie amidst excrement and urine, unable to seek death. This arises from the impure conduct of lewdness; after death, they enter hell, and it is extremely difficult to find release.
One's own nature does not create itself; one knows for oneself that it does not act of its own accord.
Without considering the paths of evil, the fool strives with his thoughts to seek [the truth].

Regarding "one's own nature does not create itself": that which ought to be created is not created, while that which ought not to be created is instead created. Thus one is censured by others, or follows the words of others rather than relying on oneself. From this arises disorder and the practice of negligence. Therefore it is said: "One's own nature does not create itself."

"To know in one's heart that one does not act for oneself" means that one personally observes that certain actions are detrimental to oneself; they ruin one's righteous practice and drag one into the dark chamber of rebirth. Therefore it is said: "To know in one's heart that one does not act for oneself."

One who does not contemplate deviant paths cannot acquire wealth and property through mere thought; if one spends day and night worrying and brooding over things without putting them into practice, one's wishes will not be fulfilled and nothing will be accomplished. Therefore it is said: "One does not contemplate deviant paths."

The fool strives with anxious thoughts; that which the fool practices lacks wisdom and insight, and he possesses no clarity of understanding. He is unable to effect any severance and lacks skillful means; dwelling in the mundane, he has no meaning of the mundane, and dwelling in the Way, he has no meaning of the Way. Therefore it is said: "The fool strives with anxious thoughts."
As when a carriage traveling on a road leaves the level, great highway for a crooked path and perishes, giving rise to the distress of a broken axle.

Regarding "as when a carriage travels on a road": in the past, there was a group of people who, accompanied by ten merchants, were returning home after gathering treasures. At that time, one man was riding in a carriage laden with treasures—countless priceless, luminous, and various jewels. The carriage was so heavy it stumbled and fell behind, losing its companions. Advancing, he could not see his companions; retreating, he feared bandits. He then followed a crooked path and drove the carriage along it, but before even a few *li* had passed, the carriage plunged into a deep ravine; the axle broke and the hub was destroyed.

Furthermore, in a desolate wilderness where no people dwell, he beats his breast and cries out in lamentation, finding no one to whom he can appeal; he weeps before the cart with no means of relief, neither seeking a way to determine whether the road is near or far, nor does he repair the dilapidated cart.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, beheld those who had lost their companions, standing in the wilderness by a broken wheel and a snapped axle, weeping beside their chariot.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that those sentient beings were ready to be delivered and liberated, immediately dispatched a manifested being to that wilderness, who sat cross-legged in the midst of the air.
The person in distress looked up and saw someone sitting in mid-air; immediately, he made this aspiration:
"I am now in the midst of calamity and suffering; I pray that you will rescue me and enable me to reach a place of peace and security."
At that time, the emanated person, by means of supernatural power, took possession of those properties and that person’s body, and suddenly appeared outside the gate of the Jeta Grove.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The emanated person who was to receive [the goods] is now outside the gate; you should lead him to where the World-Honored One is."

The bhikṣu received the instruction and immediately went to have an audience with the Buddha. Upon seeing the Buddha, that man’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he requested ordination as a śramaṇa and was immediately admitted into the Way. Hearing the subtle and wondrous Dharma, he realized that the self in the body does not exist and that all phenomena are empty. He understood that all worldly things are suffering and that only the Way is true. Within this Great Dharma, there is no further feverish affliction. He gave away all his wealth and treasures to the Triple Gem, thinking: "This is the result of my past merit in encountering a field of blessings. Neither water nor fire, nor any calamities or anomalies, can harm me. My heart is doubly joyful, and wholesome thoughts arise within me."

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the sublime Dharma—namely, discourses on giving, discourses on morality, and discourses on rebirth in heaven; he spoke of the impurity of desire and how outflows constitute defiled conduct. Through countless skillful means, he exhorted them to practice and study, and amidst the great assembly, he spoke this verse:
"Just as a carriage traveling on a road, If it abandons the level highway And follows a deviant path, it will be ruined, Giving rise to the distress of a broken axle."
At that time, having heard the verses spoken by the Buddha, that bhikṣu reflected within himself:
"Today the World-Honored One has preached the Dharma for me alone, and not for others."

The reason for this is as stated in the verse: "All the hardships and diligent efforts undergone by my body, the Tathāgata knows them all. Consequently, he redoubled his reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat. His six supernormal powers became pure and penetrating, and the fruits of his aspirations were realized; having transcended the three realms of existence, he no longer dwells within the cycle of birth and death.

At that time, there were also beings within that assembly whose resolve was not firm, who sought to violate the prohibitions and precepts, who practiced lustful conduct and deviated from dignified decorum, and who did not follow the path of true correctness.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, wishing to cause the great assembly to forget their sorrows and eliminate their afflictions, to remove those evil states of mind and dwell peacefully in non-action (asaṃskṛta), again spoke these verses to the great assembly:
"The Dharma is thus: it arises from what is not the Dharma. The fool clings to it until death, yet even so, there is the suffering of decay."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly:
"It is like those merchants who abandon the level, broad highway to take a deviant path, resulting in the distress of stumbling upon the road and the breaking of their axles."

Now, it is the same for those beings within this assembly who harbor divergent minds; desiring to depart from the True Dharma and practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, these fools cling to death and fall into the evil realms.
"O bhikṣus! How can you stand before the Tathāgata and yet deceive him face-to-face?
Is this truly so?"

When old age and death arrive and one has no one to rely upon, wailing to heaven and weeping will be of no benefit to the conscious spirit; though tears flow like rivers into the four seas, they cannot restrain the spirit from proceeding toward the evil realms.
I have now appeared in the world to eliminate all suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings.
For indeed, sensual desire burns the body and destroys one's clan; it brings no peace wherever one goes, both in this life and in future lives.
"O bhikṣus! Those who violate the precepts shall not attain liberation from the world within this present life; even the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot heal them.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, their hair stood on end in solemn awe, their hearts trembled with fear, and they reproached themselves inwardly.

The Buddha, knowing that their minds were ready to receive transformation, gradually preached the Dharma for them, causing them to eliminate all defilements and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. In succession, they realized the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*. Their six supernormal powers became clear and penetrating; they no longer dwelt within the three realms of existence and were forever freed from the eight difficulties.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
One’s conduct should also be upright; do not involve yourself in improper affairs. Deviant paths increase defilement, and the various outflows (āsrava) flourish.
When the outflows have become rampant, one must eliminate deviance so that the outflows are exhausted.
"Practice should also be correct": all roots of merit and wholesome dharmas are what is called "practice.
This is the essential treasury of all dharmas; by attending to it day and night, one ultimately reaches the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, those multitudes abandon the right and resort to the wrong; they practice what should not be practiced and forsake what should be practiced. They further indulge in unwholesome dharmas, having already cultivated what is contrary to the Dharma and departed from the path of goodness, drawing near to hell. Therefore it is said: "One's conduct must also be correct."

Regarding "do not involve yourself in what is not your business": that which is not one's business refers to negligence, greed, lust, and the practice of unnecessary actions; therefore it is said, "do not involve yourself in what is not your business."

Regarding "the wrong path increases defilement": when the mind habituates to unwholesome karma, it is like a monkey that abandons one thing only to seize another; the mind is like a flowing river, its intentions not being true and real, and it does not abide in wholesome dharmas. It is like flowers placed upon a head from which the hair has been shaved—they have nowhere to stay. Therefore it is said: "The wrong path increases defilement."

The flourishing of the various outflows (*āsrava*) is like a thicket of reeds and bamboo, or like the overflowing currents of water in mountain torrents, valleys, and streams; the mind lacks single-mindedness and is constantly dissolute, leaking forth all manner of defilements (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said: "the various outflows flourish."
Regarding the phrase "the outflows have already become intense": what is the distinction between prior outflows and subsequent outflows? The reply is:

when one does not cultivate wholesome dharmas, the mind constantly leaks and loses its integrity, increasing day by night; because one does not maintain focused mindfulness but instead indulges in negligence, the various outflows arise even more vigorously. Therefore it is said: "the outflows have already become intense."

To eliminate evil and exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*), one should forever seek seclusion and not dwell in their company. Although the Buddhas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—do not abide in the past, sentient beings who are heedless remain bound and cannot be liberated. When the wise observe this conduct, they know it to be the root of losing the Path; they must further contemplate and strive to attain wholesome dharmas. Those who wish to respect themselves first must respect the Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "Eliminate evil and exhaust the outflows."
Those who possess the wisdom of skillful means always remain mindful of the body's afflictions;
they do not engage in what should not be done, and do not abandon what ought to be done.
Possessing mindfulness, reflection, and wisdom, they shall forever be free from all outflows (*āsrava*).

For those who possess skillful means and wisdom, the Dharma constantly taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is spoken according to the needs of the individual; they do not point to matters in vain. Sometimes they speak by concealing the matter and not revealing its name; sometimes they speak with the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, householders, lay devotees, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, either manifesting their names at times or concealing their names at other times.

However, this single verse is indeterminate in its explicitness and implicitness; therefore, when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he did not speak by pointing to specific matters, but spoke this verse as a comprehensive teaching for all.

Whether acting as a teacher for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, his mind is always courageous and never timid; he does not abandon his original vow, and his mind constantly encourages those who have not yet attained the Way. Therefore, it is said: "All those who rely upon skillful wisdom."

Regarding those who constantly maintain mindfulness of the body, as stated in the Buddha’s sutras: "All who are mindful of the body are called 'immortal'; all who are mindful of the body will personally attain the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). Those who do not mindfully attend to the body violate the nectar of immortality. One who contemplates the fundamental nature of the body by analyzing it part by part will attain the nectar of immortality and ensure that their aspirations are surely fulfilled. The detailed explanation for those who maintain mindfulness of the body is as set forth in the *Sūtras*.

The Venerable Dharmasiri also spoke thus: "If, during one's entire life, a person does not destroy their various mental perceptions, that person attains a wholesome benefit and a state of great advantage."

The world is free from manifold afflictions because of the perception of the body; when in the mountains one has the perception of the mountains, and when at home one has the thought of the home. One who does not depart from the mindfulness of the body is called a supreme person. Whether walking or sitting, they do not depart from that mindfulness. Therefore it is said: "Constantly be mindful of the body as an affliction."

"Non-activities, moreover, are not performed": when a person’s mind is upright, everything they direct themselves toward is successful; as for matters that are contrary to the Dharma, they do not follow them. They do not associate with those whom they should not associate with, nor do they propagate what should not be propagated. Furthermore, they do not expound what is contrary to the Dharma to others, but constantly maintain mindfulness of renunciation and do not dwell together with such things. Therefore it is said: "Non-activities, moreover, are not performed."

One should act as one who does not abandon; always following the proper seasons and never failing to uphold the clear teachings, remaining consistent from beginning to end without initial transgression or loss. Therefore it is said: "One should act as one who does not abandon."

Regarding those who possess mindfulness, reflection, and wisdom: among all forms of existence, they concentrate their minds on one point, employing reflection and wisdom to sever the fetters through insight. It is like a farmer’s son who holds a blade of grass in his left hand while reaping with his right; the wise person is just the same. Holding fast to mindfulness with a mind that does not waver, their *jñāna* (knowledge) discriminates and their *prajñā* (wisdom) cuts through. To recognize things and distinguish the true is called *jñāna*; to eloquently expound profound discernment is called *prajñā*. Therefore it is said: "There are those who possess mindfulness, reflection, and wisdom."

To be forever without any outflows (*āsrava*) means that which is illuminated by wisdom; at that time, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are completely extinguished. Having been exhausted and eliminated, their very root is uprooted, such that there is no further birth and death. Therefore, it is said: "Forever without any outflows."
Those who are called upholders of the Dharma need not recite or study much;
if they have heard even a little and are fully endowed with the practice of the Dharmakāya,
they are called upholders of the Dharma, nourishing themselves through the Dharma.
Regarding those who uphold the Dharma, at that time the Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Kāśyapa, you should now go before the great assembly to instruct the junior disciples and to analyze and expound the meaning of the profound Dharma."
"The reason for this is that what you instruct is my instruction, and what you expound as the flavor of the Dharma is my exposition of the flavor of the Dharma.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Nowadays, newly ordained bhikṣus are difficult to awaken. This morning, two bhikṣus were disputing with one another; one argued for non-existence, and he was a disciple of Maudgalyāyana."
"One of these two speaks well; he is a disciple of Ānanda.

These two individuals each cling to their own views and mutually condemn one another. We two should now debate the meaning together to determine who prevails and whose exposition of the principles is more extensive."
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded a bhikṣu:
"Quickly summon the bhikṣu Anupama, the disciple of Maudgalyāyana, and the bhikṣu Subhāṣita, the disciple of Ānanda, and bring them to where the Tathāgata is."

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣu immediately summoned the two bhikṣus and led them to the place where the World-Honored One was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two bhikṣus:
"Have you ever heard the Tathāgata utter such instructions as to contend for victory or defeat by debating principles with others in the midst of a great assembly?"
“Do you see this or not? The bhikṣu replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
‘You fools! Why do you dispute over the Great Dharma regarding superiority and inferiority?’”

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses amidst the great assembly: "One who upholds the Dharma need not recite it extensively; if one has heard even a little and is fully endowed with the practice of the Dharma-body, such a person is called a 'Dharma-holder,' for they nourish themselves by means of the Dharma."

If there are sentient beings of sharp faculties who recite the meaning of a single phrase, contemplate and discern it, thereby exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), transcending the stages to attain realization, and obtaining the fruit of the Path such that they are forever free from craving and able to exhaust all fetters; and if they seek expedient means for what they have not yet attained so as to attain it, and seek expedient means for what they have not yet realized so as to realize the fruit—such persons are called "those of much learning" and are termed "upholders of the Dharma."

To realize the Dharma through the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, reflecting upon each point in conformity with the Dharma teachings without any omission or deficiency—this is called "upholding the Dharma. It does not necessarily require extensive recitation and study; even if one has heard little, one may be fully endowed with the Dharma-body.
Though one may recite and study many meanings, if one is heedless and does not follow the Right Path, it is like a cowherd counting another’s cattle; one shall not attain the true state of a śramaṇa.

Regarding "though one may recite and study many meanings": long ago, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, a certain bhikṣu came from a distant land to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣu withdrew for a moment, then sat down before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"I have heard of the 'much-hearing bhikṣu. To what extent is one called a much-hearing bhikṣu?
When the Tathāgata speaks of a much-hearing bhikṣu, to what limit does he define the term 'much-hearing bhikṣu'?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That which I have preached before and after is beyond measure or record. First is the Sūtra (Kṣudraka-āgama), which speaks directly through its text while the flavor of its meaning is profound."
Second is recitation (*japa*), which involves arranging the words and phrases so as not to lose the original text.

Third is memorization (*dhāraṇī*): recording the fourfold assemblies, the seven Buddhas and their seven generations of clansmen and lineages, and their parinirvāṇas; furthermore, it records that among the sixteen naked ascetics (*nirgrantha brahmacārins*), fourteen attained parinirvāṇa while two did not—namely, Maitreya and Aji.
The fourth is the verse (*gāthā*); these verses are scattered throughout various sūtras, their flavor and meaning being profound and vast, their significance abundant and their principles expansive.
The fifth is the causal condition (*nidāna*); it explains that for such reasons something is spoken, and for the lack of such reasons something is not spoken.

Sixth is the *Udāna* (Elegant Sayings). As for what is called *Udāna*, it ranges from the discourse on impermanence to that on the brahmin; it extracts the essential treasury of various sūtras and expounds and manifests them to instruct future generations, and is therefore named *Udāna*.
Seventh is the accomplishment of an act (*kṛta-vastu*). It is called "accomplishment" because, for example, a person who upholds the Vinaya records the offenses committed according to the Vinaya;

therefore, it is termed the accomplishment of an act. Eighth is the present phenomenon (*dṛṣṭa-dharma*). It is called "present" because it records events of the present that have been seen with the eyes or heard with the ears; therefore, it is termed the "present."

Ninth are the Birth Sūtras (*jātaka*). As for why they are called Birth Sūtras: it is because they recount, such as in the case of the former lives of the Bodhisattva Mṛgajā, the experiences of one lifetime, several lifetimes, up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes; therefore, they are named Birth Sūtras.
The tenth is called Vaipulya (Extensive). "Vaipulya" means that which is concise at the beginning and expansive at the end, encompassing nothing that is not included; therefore, it is named Vaipulya.
The eleventh is called Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Teachings), such as when the Venerable Ānanda praised the virtues of the Tathāgata with marvelous teachings.

Twelfth is the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Ascertainment of Meaning). As for why it is called "meaning," it refers to the thorough mastery of the meaning of the discourses (*sūtra*) and the meaning of the verses (*gāthā*), such that there is no longer any obstruction.
A learned *bhikṣu* reaches his limit at this point.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!
If a son of noble family possesses firm faith and receives the meaning of even four lines of verse;

if he recites them fluently, masters the Dharma, and achieves success in the Dharma; if he proceeds from one teaching to the next, from one principle to the next, verifying each through the Dharma itself; and if he reflects upon each point according to the Dharma instructions without any omission—then, bhikṣu, to this extent one is called "learned" (bahuśruta).

Even if one has recited many scriptures and mastered their contents, if one does not accord with those teachings or follow their instructions, but instead acts according to one's own whims in violation of the Dharma, this constitutes a detriment to the Dharma and is not called "much learning."
The Tathāgata spoke to the bhikṣus by means of an analogy:

"In the past, there was a man who tended many herds of cattle. He abandoned his own herd to count another's herd as his own. As for his own cattle, whether they encountered wild beasts or lost them in the fields and pastures, he did not realize their daily depletion. Consequently, he was ridiculed by the people, who said:
'No one in the world is more foolish and deluded than you, claiming another's herd of cattle to be your own.'"

"In the same way, a learned bhikṣu who does not himself accord with the teachings of the True Dharma, yet encourages others to practice the four kinds of offerings—robes, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicine for the sick—and further exhorts people to uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, [teaching that] one receives rewards for doing good and suffers calamities for committing sins: such a learned bhikṣu does not follow the prohibitions and discipline of a śramaṇa, and is held in derision by those of pure conduct."
They all gathered together once more and went to where the bhikṣu was, rebuking, stopping, and admonishing him, saying:
"You are one of great learning, clearly expounding and analyzing the profound and abstruse points of both ancient and modern times; yet you cannot rectify yourself—how then can you rectify others?"
One may violate the monastic discipline, contravene the law, and transgress the teachings; yet, even so, who among those born into this world does not have their will disturbed?
Who in the world is without fault?
Even the devas and immortals are heard to have their shortcomings. Only the wise man, though he may have a hundred anxieties and a thousand lapses, still practices the superior way.
At that time, Brahmācara spoke this verse:
"Though one may recite and study many meanings, If one is heedless and does not follow the right path,
Like a cowherd counting another's cattle, One shall not attain the true state of a śramaṇa."
At that time, the learned bhikṣu was naturally discerning and wise, like a new cloth that easily takes on dye.

Thereupon, the learned bhikṣu reformed his past ways and cultivated the future, purifying his heart and clarifying his mind. With all outflows exhausted, he attained the fruit of arhatship; his six supernormal powers became clear and penetrating, he attained mastery over life and death, and his aspirations were fulfilled.
*Udānavarga*, Volume Six; *Udānavarga*, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
From the Chapter on Heedlessness, Part Two:
I observe this man who has come from afar; his various marks are complete and without flaw.
He must surely belong to the world of a king, and will never revere a teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva asked the aranyaka:
"You have practiced for a long time and undergone countless hardships; what realization have you attained that brings you such personal joy?
The aranyaka replied:
"I have traveled and studied, transcending perceptions of form up to the sphere of infinite space; therein I find my own delight.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Ārāḍa is without wisdom while I alone possess wisdom; Ārāḍa is without faith while I alone possess faith. If even Ārāḍa has attained this concentration of emptiness, how much more so shall I, through diligent study, not achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated the perception of form; through repeated investigation and calculation, he immediately attained the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi). He then asked Ārāḍa:
"Is the concentration you have attained limited to this emptiness?"
"Does emptiness further emerge?
Ārāḍa replied, "The concentration practiced by a bodhisattva is limited to this alone; there is no other concentration remaining to be cultivated."
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected within himself:
"I should now go to where Udraka Rāmaputra is.
He immediately went to Udraka's place and asked him:
"You have been training here for a long time; what meditative concentration (*samādhi*) have you attained that you take as your own delight?

Rāmaputra replied, "The range of my study and practice extends from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva immediately entered meditative absorption and attained the sphere of nothingness up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Nāṭaputta lacks wisdom while I alone possess wisdom; Nāṭaputta lacks faith while I alone possess faith. If even Nāṭaputta was able to attain this concentration, how much more so could I, through diligent study, fail to achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"

Having emerged from this concentration, the Bodhisattva realized that he could not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of this dharma alone. Reflecting within himself, he spoke these verses:
"Beings lose themselves through craving; They delight in attaining worldly concentrations, Yet they revolve and fall into birth and death, Entering the darkness of the world’s calamities."
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected to himself:
"This is not the essential path to Nirvana; I must seek further the way that leads to definitive deliverance."
He then addressed Bāṣpa with this verse:
"I shall lay my body bare, Exposing the skeleton of hooks and chains;
I must by all means seek through skillful means The root of birth, old age, sickness, and death."

At that time, the Bodhisattva proceeded once more to a secluded place and applied himself with diligent austerity, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice per day. He practiced these ascetic exercises for six years; whenever he intended to rise and walk, upon rising he would fall forward, and upon sitting down he would collapse backward.

At that time, the devas of Tuṣita descended to attend upon the Bodhisattva. Observing that the Bodhisattva had no inhalation or exhalation, some said he had reached the end of his life, while others said he had entered parinirvāṇa. Overcome with grief and sorrow, they spoke this verse:
"Having originally grasped the heart of great vows To rescue the world within boundless realms, You have now abandoned that palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; Only now do you take your final breath."
At that time, a deity approached and asked the Bodhisattva:
"If you, O Honored One, find weariness with the refined vital energy of human food and drink, we shall augment the Bodhisattva’s strength with the natural vital energy of the heavens."
At that time, the Bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"If I were to receive the refined essence of the heavens today while severing my intake of human food, it would not be appropriate."
At that time, the Bodhisattva did not accept the food, drink, or vital essence offered by the devas.
Having practiced asceticism with diligent effort for six years, he reflected to himself:

"The strength within my body is now weak and depleted. To achieve the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not do so by exhausting the body through such ascetic practices."
"I should now consume human food—rice, honey, parched grain, and clarified butter—and anoint my body with oil.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke this verse:
"The root of moist craving is boiled away; It is severed and distinguished by the mind of wisdom."
"The mind is the root of all thoughts; when one calculates that the body has no enemy," at that time, the Bodhisattva did exactly as he had intended:
people offered him honeyed parched grain and milk gruel, and anointed his body with fragrant oils.

At that time, there were two daughters of brahmins attending to the Bodhisattva’s needs. Those two girls would milk five hundred cows and drink from two hundred and fifty; they would then milk those two hundred and fifty and drink from one hundred and twenty-five; they would then milk those one hundred and twenty-five and drink from sixty; they would milk those sixty and drink from thirty; they would milk those thirty and drink from fifteen; they would milk those fifteen and drink from seven; and finally, they would milk those seven to prepare food for the Bodhisattva. As the milk boiled, it rose out of the cauldron by the height of a fathom, and then returned back into the cauldron.
At that time, there was a Brahmin physiognomist who, seeing the milk in the cauldron boiling over again, remarked:
"If one who has established the faculties and attained power should consume this milk gruel, he will immediately achieve the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Then the two women filled a golden bowl with congee and offered it to the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva accepted it; having eaten and rinsed his mouth, he cast the golden vessel into the water, where Śakra-devānām-indra caught it and took it up to the heavens.
The Bodhisattva’s physical strength suffused his entire body as he crossed the Nairañjanā River.

At that time, there was a man by the riverbank named Svastika who was cutting grass with a sword; the Bodhisattva went straight up to him and said to Svastika, "Give me a little grass so that I may spread it on the ground and sit cross-legged."
Śrī presented him with grass.
He went beneath the tree, personally spread the grass, and sat down cross-legged, making this great vow:
"Now that I am seated here beneath this tree, I shall not break this posture until I have attained the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; only then shall I rise from my seat."

At that time, Māra the Wicked led eighteen billion hosts along with his son Sattva to the place where the Bodhisattva was. Some had animal heads and human bodies, some had one head and two bodies; others took the forms of monkeys, lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, venomous snakes, evil beasts, and demons in various shapes. Carrying mountains and vomiting fire, holding swords, spears, lances, halberds, and shields in their hands, they filled the void, leaping and bounding while roaring and shouting as they came to terrify the Bodhisattva.
By the power of the Bodhisattva’s compassion, not even a single hair was moved, and he immediately attained the path of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment; Māra then retreated.

At that time, the Tathāgata gazed steadily at the Bodhi tree without blinking his eyes. There were three merchants traveling from afar who wished to return to their native land, but the devas firmly obstructed them so they could not pass by. Their ox-cart came to a sudden halt, and the devas announced:
"The Tathāgata has already attained enlightenment for seven days; you may go and offer him food and drink."
He then took a vessel filled with honey, curd, and ghee and went to where the Tathāgata was to offer the food and drink.
At that time, the Tathāgata did not wish to accept it. Why was this so?
"If I were to take food by stretching out my hand, would I not be no different from the non-Buddhist brahmins?
I should now contemplate what kind of food the World-Honored Buddhas of the past used."
Just as he had this thought, the gods in the sky said,
"All Buddhas of the past have eaten from bowls.
As soon as these words were spoken, the Four Heavenly Kings presented four bowls, which were not fashioned by any craftsman but were spontaneously perfected.
At that time, the Tathāgata again thought to himself:
"Now the Four Heavenly Kings have offered these four bowls; if I were to accept one and reject three, or accept three and reject one, it would not be appropriate. I shall now accept all four bowls."
[He] struck [the bowl] once with his hand. Then, that merchant offered honey, ghee, and curd to the Tathāgata, and immediately made this dedication of merit (*pāṭihāriya*):

"May those who eat this gift obtain sufficient strength; may the donor’s family receive blessings in every generation, enjoying peace, happiness, and freedom from illness; may they preserve their lifespan to the end and ultimately attain auspiciousness; may bipeds be secure and quadrupeds be secure; may there be security for those traveling afar and security for those present; security by night, security by day, and security at midday; may all embryos be secure, and may the entire household be secure, free from disease and inwardly peaceful; may all kinsmen and retinues be secure; may there be abundant pure food and drink, and may they live for a hundred autumns and see a hundred autumns."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent for forty-nine days—seven times seven days—without preaching the Dharma, reflecting within himself:
"I wish to cause those before me to come of their own accord to request and receive it."

At that time, when the people of Magadha heard that the Bodhisattva had already attained the Way of Buddhahood, they yearned for and remembered the Tathāgata with sincere devotion day and night. Throughout the realm of Magadha, pestilence raged, yet eighty thousand sentient beings who were ready for deliverance died and were all reborn in the heavens.

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded forward gradually once more; first he converted five, then twenty-five, then thirty-seven, and then thirteen villagers. At that time, there were sixty arhats on the land of Jambudvīpa, and the Tathāgata was the sixty-first.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When you go among the people for alms, you should go in pairs as companions; be careful not to travel alone. Why is this so?
"Sentient beings living in the world may possess either sharp faculties or dull faculties; if they do not encounter a śramaṇa, they will lose the opportunity for nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded further to the brahmin village of Uruvilvā.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having subdued a thousand brahmins, turned toward the city of Rājagṛha. When King Bimbisāra heard that the Tathāgata had set out for Rājagṛha to wander for alms among the people, he immediately arrayed his fourfold army and prepared to depart from the city.
The devas closed the city gates and would not allow the king to exit. The king asked his attendants, "For what reason can we not leave the city?
The beings from the void replied:
"Great King, you should know that there are sentient beings bound in prison by their conditions; only if Your Majesty issues a great amnesty will they be able to see the Tathāgata.

At that time, the Great King immediately issued a general pardon, and all those imprisoned in the jails were released. Thereupon, the King departed the city to go forth and welcome the World-Honored One.
When the Tathāgata saw Bimbisāra from afar, he immediately stepped down from the path and sat beneath a nyagrodha tree.
At that time, King Bimbisāra descended from his carriage and approached the Tathāgata on foot; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and three times announced his own name and lineage:
“I am Bimbisāra, the king of the realm of Magadha.”
The World-Honored One replied,
"I already knew of King Māgadha. At that time,

the World-Honored One bade the king sit again and gradually preached the Dharma to him, causing twelve thousand people among the populace of Magadha and eighty thousand devas to have all dust and defilements extinguished and the Dharma-eye arise.
Therefore it is said: "The Magadhan who is not negligent, through purity attains birth in heaven.
Without desiring fame, the wise discern the meaning;
the meaning of non-negligence is abundant, and it is that which the wise inherit."

Those who do not seek fame and reputation are the virtuous and noble ones of right view; they are further praised and commended by the Buddhas and the noble disciples of the Buddhas. Such persons are able to abandon negligence and practice pure conduct; for one who is diligent, their merit in all wholesome dharmas increases, bringing great benefit to many.

When a person lives in this world from this life to the next, encountering wholesome dharmas, meeting the worthy and the noble, and receiving liberation upon hearing the Dharma—all these are attained through non-negligence and result in such renown. In every place, they perpetuate the lineage of the Buddha so that the True Dharma endures for a long time; therefore it is said: "One does not seek to attain renown."
Regarding the wise person who discriminates meanings: one who has studied extensively understands both worldly meanings and the meaning of the Path.
How does one understand worldly meanings?

Whether it be practicing agriculture and sowing crops, entering the sea to gather treasures, studying calligraphy and rhetoric, calculating mathematics and calendrical cycles, learning the carving of seals and the sealing of documents, serving as a royal envoy to communicate between distant and near regions, or mediating between two adversaries so that each may abide in non-action—all such worldly matters are accomplished through heedfulness.
How does a wise person understand the meaning of the Path?
By practicing meditation, reciting the sūtras, and assisting in communal affairs.
What is meant by practicing meditation?

Now, those who practice seated meditation and enter meditative concentration attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*). They attain the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, they attain the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—as well as the supernormal powers of psychic travel, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of past lives, thereby perceiving beings passing away and being reborn.

When a person free from arrogance enters the state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they accomplish these various dharmas and realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is due to their lack of negligence (*apramāda*); those who are negligent will never achieve accomplishment. This is called the merit obtained by one who practices seated meditation.
What is meant by "reciting the scriptures"?

It means being capable of studying and reciting the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the Khuddaka Nikāya, as well as the scriptures recited by those of external heterodox schools. When someone receives [the teachings] from him, he does not begrudge them their meaning; and if there are followers of external schools who come to challenge or question him, he is able to provide answers without any hesitation.
Those who are heedful can practice this Dharma, whereas those who are heedless cannot accomplish it.
How do they assist in communal affairs?

At such times, heedful people can exhort the fourfold assembly to serve the Triple Gem and establish stūpas and monasteries; or to construct lecture halls that are warm in winter and cool in summer, or to build dining halls, repair what is deficient, scatter flowers, burn incense, sprinkle fragrant liquids upon the ground, and provide for the Saṃgha of the past, future, and present. Heedful people can accomplish these matters, while those who are heedless cannot. Therefore it is said: "The wise discern the meaning."

Regarding the meaning of "abundance through non-negligence": a person who is not negligent possesses abundant wealth and many treasures; they lack nothing in the worldly arts and crafts. Desiring to act in a manner that surpasses others, they gather pearls, musaragalva, agate, amber, crystal, lapis lazuli, and priceless *maṇi* jewels; these are the gains obtained by the non-negligent in the secular world.

Having left the household life to study the Way, one attains arhatship, acquires the foremost sublime wisdom, realizes the vision of the body through direct experience, and attains the emptiness samādhi by entering emptiness, the wishlessness samādhi by entering wishlessness, and the signlessness samādhi by entering signlessness. Those who attain this essential path to nirvāṇa do so entirely because of non-negligence; therefore it is said: "Non-negligence brings abundant meaning."

Regarding "that which is received by the wise": as for why they are called "wise," it means they are free from outflows (anāsrava). Their speech is always accompanied by a smile, and they harbor no arrogance; thus they are able to bring forth such virtues. Those without wisdom cannot accomplish this, and for this reason it is said: "that which is received by the wise."
The meaning that exists in the present, as well as the conditions for future lives—only the brave one can expound this; such a person is called a man of wisdom.

Regarding "the meaning that exists in the present": a person who is not negligent acquires much wealth and treasure within the phenomena of the present life, naturally receiving blessings, being held in high regard by others, and having their words followed and their instructions accepted. A negligent person lacks these qualities; therefore, it is said: "the meaning that exists in the present."

Regarding the phrase "also reaching conditions in future lives": a person who practices heedfulness attains the status of a human being; they are then able to practice giving, maintain the precepts, and observe the rules of purity. Seeing those who walk the Path, they rejoice on their behalf. By perfuming their bodies with the fragrance of various wholesome dharmas, their countenance will be handsome for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes. Therefore it is said: "Also reaching conditions in future lives."

A hero who is able to expound the Dharma adapts to the occasion and does not lose the proper measure; those referred to as "heroes" are the Buddha and his disciples. Therefore, it is said: "The hero is able to expound."
This is called a man of wisdom who is able to accomplish the discerning contemplation of all dharmas, acting as a guide for others, showing them what is good and removing their evils.
The bhikṣu delights in heedfulness; the negligent have many sorrows and transgressions.
One can escape the perils of the deep sea, like an elephant emerging from the mud.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a fierce elephant that constantly entered military arrays and conquered all those against whom it campaigned.
However, that fierce elephant, having drunk too much wine, became stuck in deep mud; though thousands of people and great elephants together pulled at it, they could not move it.
A wise man saw them and asked, "What are you all doing? The people replied:
"The royal elephant, having become enraged and sunk into deep mud, could not be moved even by the combined strength of several thousand elephants and a multitude of men.
A wise man asked, "What was the strength of this elephant previously?"
The crowd replied,
"This elephant’s combat prowess is limitless.
The wise man spoke again to the crowd:
"You all must leave this herd of elephants; I can pull them out and ensure they suffer no harm.

At that time, the wise man immediately assembled drums, horns, and bells, and struck the gongs as if for battle. He further had everyone arm themselves with weapons. Hearing the sound of the drums, the elephants thought a great enemy had entered their territory to wage war against them. They immediately rushed out from the deep mud toward the military host, galloping in all four directions seeking combat.
At that time, King Prasenajit asked his attendants,
"By whose power was the elephant pulled from the mud?
His attendants replied to the king:
“There is a wise man from afar who, by devising this expedient stratagem, has escaped the peril of the elephants.
The King immediately rewarded him and appointed him as a counselor.
At that time, many bhikṣus who had seen it with their eyes and heard it with their ears began to reflect within themselves:
"An elephant is among the six domestic animals and lacks wisdom; though it falls into a place of confinement, upon hearing the sound of battle, it can extricate itself from the mud and escape.

Yet we, the multitude of beings, are submerged in the ocean of birth and death, not free from the hardships of the five realms of existence. We suffer the calamities of the poisons and terrors of birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet cannot extricate ourselves. We pursue one another until this body perishes, only to receive another body; our movements are linked to transgression, as we revolve through the six destinies with no end in sight for our escape."

At that time, the bhikṣus applied themselves with diligence day and night, finding no leisure for food or rest; they were like those extinguishing a fire or avoiding the conflagration at the end of an eon, fervently burning away all dharmas and incinerating the fetters, just as iron, when refined a hundred times, becomes a vessel that is necessarily sharp.

Human beings are also like this: when the fetters are removed and the mind abides in clarity, one attains great awakening and realizes the fruit of Arhatship; the six supernormal powers become pure and penetrating, and one gains mastery over both life and death.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye—which was pure and free from defilement—knew that the bhikṣus held fast to their resolve and maintained faith without weariness, each exhorting the others to diligence; he further knew them to be like war elephants pulling themselves out of the mud.

To act as a great torch of illumination for future sentient beings, and to ensure that the True Dharma remains long in the world, he proclaimed the Great Teaching so that it might be heard far and near. Standing amidst the great assembly, he spoke this verse:
"Bhikṣus, heedfulness is bliss; Heedlessness brings much grief and transgression.
One can escape the perils of the deep ocean, Just as an elephant pulls itself from the mud."

Regarding "the bhikṣu delights in heedfulness": a bhikṣu who maintains his practice keeps his mind from negligence; he is pure and transparent within and without, free from blemish or defilement, and his will dwells in the unconditioned, untainted and unstained. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu delights in heedfulness."

"Laxity brings much sorrow and transgression" means that laxity is the primary source of all fears and the origin of many faults. Neither the ruin of nations nor the destruction of families occurs without it. Like fire, like a thief, and like poison, the mind of one who is lax is inverted; they fall into evil realms and enter deep abysses themselves, and furthermore, they teach others to enter those abysses. Abounding in terrors, they possess no heart of joy from the outset. Therefore, it is said: "Laxity brings much sorrow and transgression."
Regarding those who can escape the perils of the deep ocean: what is meant by "the perils of the deep ocean"?

It refers to the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings; it is the inability to obtain even a hair’s breadth of goodness while seeking it from these three destinies, and the inability to extricate oneself or achieve salvation.

One who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* is able to extricate oneself from the perils of the hungry ghosts and animals; because one is free from worldly afflictions and does not coexist with transgressions, it is said that such a person can escape the perils of the deep ocean.
Regarding the elephant pulling itself from the mud: at that time, the war elephant thought to himself, "In the past and present, I have received the King's favor and patronage;

I have been the first to enjoy sweet and delicious food. In battle with the King, there is nothing I have not overcome. If today I remain submerged in the mud and do not pull myself out to advance and fight for the King, I shall lose my long-standing reputation and cause the entire kingdom to suffer disgrace."
Therefore it is said: Like an elephant emerging from the mud, a bhikṣu delights in heedfulness;
he has many sorrows and transgressions through negligence, as all evil dharmas are scattered away like leaves blown by the wind.
