The madmen of this world recklessly commit sinful deeds; some harm one another with swords and staves, committing evil in jest yet receiving agony in wailing and lamentation. They harbor malice and plot in secret, bringing calamity upon their own families and clans. Therefore, the wise person cuts off disaster before it arises and accumulates merit when it is yet formless.
Therefore it is said: "All fear death; none do not dread the pain of the staff. Taking oneself as a metaphor for others, one should neither kill nor inflict blows.
Those who commit killing will invariably have short lives; therefore, you all should avoid killing.
It is like a person who has traveled for a long time and returns safely from afar; his kin and friends are all at ease, and they rejoice upon his arrival.
Once, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man named Ghaṇṭāpaṇava (Bell-Gong). His kinsmen and relatives were beyond counting, yet he himself was destitute and lacked all property; his clothing did not cover his body and his food did not suffice for his mouth. Whenever his kinsmen saw him, they would all pass by with their heads bowed.

Zhongqing thought to himself: "In my past lives I lacked merit, and thus I was born at an unfavorable time. I know myself to be poor and destitute, with few kinsmen and little support. When I go out, I am ridiculed by others; when I come home, I am rebuked by my wife and children. It would be better for me to leave this country and seek another land; whether I live or die depends on Heaven—how could I concern myself with other matters? Even if I were to dwell in another land, I would rather die there than seek a livelihood here."

At that time, the bells and chimes immediately left the borders of his kingdom and traveled to another land. There he sold his labor as a hired servant, living by the diligent application of his strength. Remembering his former poverty and the slight he had suffered from his kinsmen, he worked tirelessly day and night, finding no leisure for food or rest. Gradually he accumulated countless riches—gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, camels, donkeys, mules, and carriages. He loaded these treasures onto the vehicles and returned to his own country.
When the five kinsmen heard that Zhongqing had returned home with much precious treasure, they all came out to welcome him.
Having been separated from their family for a long time, his hair was disheveled and his beard was long; his clothes were soiled and he was carrying money and goods on his back.
The kinsmen did not recognize him and asked, "Where is Zhongqing now?"
Zhongqing replied, "He is coming from behind; he will arrive shortly.
His five relatives stayed to wait for him and asked the person following behind: [what had happened].
"Where are the bells and chimes? A follower reported,
"The bells and chimes are at the very front."
Thus, after a long time had passed, they no longer saw the bells and chimes.
The one who had the bells said they were behind him, while the one with the chimes said they were ahead; consequently, as they reached their home, they did not know where the bells and chimes were.
At that time, his five relatives seized the slave who was ringing the bells and chimes; pointing out the bells and chimes, they were able to see one another.
"We have been parted from you for a long time and no longer recognize each other; though the person remains, the form has changed to such an extent as this."
"Now my five kinsmen have come specifically to welcome you; why do you deceive me face-to-face by saying you will follow behind?
Zhongqing replied, "I am not Zhongqing;
it is the carriage behind carrying the treasures and goods that is Zhongqing."
"In the past, when you were poor and destitute, you were held in contempt by your kinsmen; they would look at you face-to-face and pass by with their heads bowed.
Why do you now seek out bells and chimes?"
The five kinsmen replied, "How could we have acquired such wealth today by merely attending to you?

Although it was so, their wealth was not as much as before and did not reach its former fullness; nevertheless, they went outside the city to exchange greetings with one another, bathed and washed themselves, put on new clothes, and entered the city to return home.

When morning dawned on the following day, he took leave of his five relatives, saying, "I have been far removed from the Tathāgata for a long time; I wish to go and pay my respects, behold him, and inquire after his well-being.
His relatives replied:
"We also wish to follow you.
At that time, the five kinsmen went together to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, when the World-Honored One saw that the assembly was seated, he spoke these verses:
"Just as a person who has traveled for a long time returns safely from afar, his kinsmen and friends feel at ease, and they rejoice upon his arrival."

At that time, the bells and chimes rang out, and his five kinsmen were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as wholesome thoughts arose within them; they immediately rose, knelt on their right knees, and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to their home to offer a meal.
The Tathāgata accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

When the time arrived the following day, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded before and behind by the assembly of bhikṣus, went to the house of Ghaṭīkāra and sat down in their respective places.

He personally handled the bells and chimes, serving sweet delicacies and various foods; when the meal was finished, he served water for rinsing the mouth, then took a small seat before the Tathāgata to receive his words of blessing.
The Tathāgata spoke this verse:
"Those who delight in practicing merit, go from here to there; they themselves receive blessings and fortune, just as one rejoices when a kinsman arrives."
Arising from the noble teachings, one restrains what is unwholesome; draw near to those who see and love the Path, and distance yourself from those who leave it.
Those whom you approach and those whom you do not—their destinations differ: by approaching the Path one ascends to heaven; by not approaching it, one falls into hell.
At that time, Zhongqing and his five kinsmen, hearing what the Buddha had said, had their minds opened and were awakened; they immediately attained the Dharma of Perfect Faith while still seated.
Delighting in the precepts of the Dharma and achieving them, practicing with sincerity and faith, and being able to discipline oneself—such a person is loved and respected by others.
Regarding those who delight in the Dharma and achieve precept-perfection: among the various classes of sentient beings, they practice the teachings of the Dharma and cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
What is meant by "achieving precepts"?

If there are sentient beings who uphold the prohibitive precepts without the slightest transgression, and through the merit of maintaining these precepts are reborn in the Brahma Heaven to receive inexhaustible blessings—yet [if] this [rebirth] is actually due to a deficiency in precepts and a failure to follow the prohibitive laws, [then it is not true precept-perfection].
Why is this? It is because they trade away their heavenly blessings.

Furthermore, if there is another person who upholds the prohibitive precepts without losing even a hair’s breadth of them, yet does not seek to be born in heaven as a Brahmā or Śakra, nor seeks to become a Māra king, nor seeks to become a Wheel-Turning King ruling over the four continents—saying instead, "I now uphold these precepts seeking only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—this is what is called the accomplishment of morality (*śīla-saṃpad*).
Therefore it is said: "Delighting in the Dharma and accomplishing the precepts.

One who sincerely delights in and practices [the Dharma] maintains firm faith and constantly delights in cultivation; their mind is without fear and free from distracted thoughts. They possess profound faith in every action as being truly real, always abiding in that which is determinate (*vyākṛta*) rather than indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Their speech is ultimate sincerity, never speaking of "this" or "that. Therefore it is said: "Sincerely delighting in and practicing."
How can one discipline oneself? One who practices goodness does so for their own sake;

by bestowing gifts upon others, they themselves receive the merit. By upholding the prohibitions and precepts, they abandon heedlessness and seek the salvation of their spirit, acting as a bridge for future lives. They study the sutras and expound their meanings, extensively examining various interpretations to benefit themselves as well. Therefore, it is said: "One can discipline oneself."
To be loved and respected by others means that wherever a person of virtuous conduct travels, they are honored by people and their virtues are praised.
Fortune is magnified by others, and one's reputation spreads abroad; therefore it is said, "to be loved and respected by others."
Being loved and respected by others arises entirely from what one has created oneself;
in this present life one gains renown, and in future lives one is reborn in the heavens.

As for being loved and respected by others: when a person’s conduct is complete, their reputation becomes manifest; they are honored and revered by tens of millions of outsiders who come to see them, and their words are followed and put into practice, making them a leader among men. This is because their accumulated deeds have been without flaw or deficiency. Therefore it is said: "Being loved and respected by others."

"All is produced by oneself" means that when a person cultivates wholesome conduct to seek liberation from calamities and hardships, and receives from others the offerings of the faithful—clothing, bedding, food, seats and bedding, and medicine for the sick and infirm—they do not violate the prohibitions and precepts. With sincerity within, they are able to digest [the offerings] externally; therefore it is said, "All is produced by oneself."

That which is praised in the present life is extolled by devas and humans; its virtue is worthy of reverence and esteem, and in whatever direction one travels, there is no obstruction. Therefore it is said: "praised in the present life."

Regarding those who are later born in the heavens: when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in a good destination, the heavens, where they enjoy natural blessings within palaces made of the seven treasures; therefore it is said, "later born in the heavens."
"Instructing so that they may receive [the teaching], Restraining unlawful conduct, This is what the virtuous keep in mind; The wicked should keep far away from it.

Regarding "instructing so that they may receive": it refers to teaching the True Dharma within the merits of the Dharma, expounding the instruction according to whatever is required by others. Therefore, it is said: "instructing so that they may receive."

To restrain those who act unlawfully: those who act unlawfully are loathed by others and give rise to much turbulent thought; they are the source of all evils and cause people to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore it is said: "Restrain unlawful conduct."

That which is contemplated by the virtuous refers to those who cultivate goodness and are fully endowed with virtuous merit; they never cause others to fall into the evil realms. Therefore, it is said: "That which is contemplated by the virtuous."

Regarding the statement "one should distance oneself from the evil": evil associates are themselves evil; their conduct does not reach the essential goal and they always move in the company of evil. What is conceived in their minds takes evil as its primary focus. Therefore it is said: "One should distance oneself from the evil."
Regarding the wholesome and the unwholesome: these two are not the same.
Through the unwholesome one is born in hell; through the wholesome one is born in the heavens.
The wholesome and the unwholesome are each distinct from one another.
First is the sublime, second is the non-sublime;
first is concentration, second is distraction;
first leads to the good realms, second leads to the evil realms.
First, one gains a good reputation; second, one incurs slander. Therefore it is said:
"The wholesome and the unwholesome. As for these two being indistinguishable:

from this human world, at the end of life, one likewise dies according to the ground of one's conduct; from this, one creates karma that leads to future transformations. Therefore it is said: "These two are both indistinguishable."

Regarding those who are born in hell due to unwholesome deeds: these are people of evil character who cultivate unwholesome conduct and desire that others likewise act as they do. Therefore it is said: "The unwholesome lead to birth in hell."

Regarding those who are virtuous and are reborn in the heavens: these refer to the four pairs and eight ranks of noble persons, the twelve worthy ones, who cultivate the roots of goodness and roam in the void, finding no pleasure in worldly entanglements; therefore it is said, "The virtuous are reborn in the heavens."
*Udānavarga*, Scroll Eight; *Udānavarga*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Seven: On the Precepts The wise person guards the precepts;
through this merit, they reach the Three Jewels. They gain renown and profit, and in the future, they ascend to celestial bliss.
Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“A wise person who seeks three dharmas should always guard the prohibitive precepts.”
What are these three dharmas?
First, when one is praised by the virtuous, one regards it with caution according to the law and discipline.
Second, even if one obtains gain and offerings, one is unable to be obstructed or deterred by them.
"Thirdly, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens.
These are the three dharmas practiced by those who maintain the precepts, through which they ultimately receive their blessings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
“The wise person guards the precepts; through merit, they reach the Triple Gem. Renown and profit are gained, and later they ascend to celestial bliss.
Constantly dwelling in the sphere of the Dharma, guarding the precepts serves as their illumination; attaining true vision, they are auspicious among their peers.”
"One who upholds the precepts dwells in peace, causing the body to be free from affliction; lying down at night they are tranquil and serene, and upon waking they are always joyful.
At that time, the assembled multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Through precepts, one finds peace in old age; through precepts, one dwells in well-being. Wisdom is a treasure for humanity; fortune cannot be stolen by thieves. Regarding "through precepts, one finds peace in old age":

although a person who upholds the precepts may reach an advanced age and become decrepit, devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly follow, protect, and assist them. Asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and rākṣasas—all such classes as these constantly guard the elderly person who upholds the precepts. They provide watch and ward day and night, like a shadow following a form. Therefore it is said: "Through precepts, one finds peace in old age."

Regarding "abiding securely in the goodness of the precepts": if there are sentient beings who have faith and inclination toward the Tathāgata and have perfected the faculty of faith, such faith possesses two aspects:
first, faith free from doubt; second, faith rooted in the fundamental [truth].

Among all assemblies—whether the assembly of śramaṇas, brahmins, or brāhmaṇas, or the assembly of Brahmās or Māras—one who maintains the precepts cannot be turned toward evil; such a person is venerated by devas and humans. Therefore, it is said: "Virtuous conduct brings peace and stability."

Regarding "wisdom is the treasure of humanity": wisdom is also called light, also called clarity, also called a torch, also called a lamp, also called the eye, also called the sun, also called the moon, also called a great mass of fire, and also called the radiance of all dharmas. Just as a person in the world must possess abundant wealth and precious treasures to be established in a village, so it is with the person whose treasure is wisdom; one who possesses both merit and the illumination of wisdom is called a treasure of humanity. Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom is the treasure of humanity."
Meritorious thieves do not take it, as stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* Sūtra:
"A deity approached the Tathāgata and asked about this meaning:
'What is it that fire does not burn?'"
What thing does the wind not blow?
What thing does the wind not move?
What thing does water not soak?
What is it that the earth cannot destroy?
What is it that kings, thieves, and violent thunder cannot damage?
What is it that remains in a storehouse, neither guarded nor diminished?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to that deva:

"The fire of merit does not burn; the wind of merit does not move it; the water of merit does not soak it; the earth of merit does not destroy it; kings and thieves do not plunder the merit; and violent thunder cannot harm it. Merit brings forth all treasuries, which remain undiminished even without being guarded."
At that time, the devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they further praised the Tathāgata with these verses:
“Excellent, O Most Victorious One in the world! You manifest the light of the world for us.
We have cultivated virtuous deeds And have obtained the blessings of the devas.”
At that time, the devas again questioned him with a verse, saying:
"What is it that ultimately constitutes goodness?
In what goodness does one find secure rest?"
"What is the treasure of a person?
What is it that a thief cannot steal?
The World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Through precepts one reaches peace in old age; through precepts one dwells in goodness and tranquility. Wisdom is a treasure for humanity;
even a thief cannot take away such merit.
When that celestial being heard what the Buddha had spoken, he took it to heart, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and suddenly vanished, returning to the heavens.
Cultivating precepts and practicing giving, one creates merit and performs meritorious deeds; from this, one proceeds to that, always arriving at a place of peace.

Regarding the cultivation of precepts and the practice of giving, there are two matters: if one maintains the precepts firmly while concurrently practicing giving, one will naturally receive good retribution within the heavenly world; if one gives to those who uphold the precepts, one obtains abundant fruit and reward.
Therefore it is said: "One who maintains the precepts and practices giving.

Regarding "one who creates merit for the sake of merit": there may be someone who maintains the precepts in their entirety but lacks extensive learning; the merit such a person obtains is indeed insufficient to mention.

However, if there is another who maintains the precepts in their entirety and further possesses great wisdom, extensive learning, and the practice of giving, that person shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Therefore it is said: "One who performs merit creates merit.

As for "going from here to there," this means going from the present life to future lives; with a mind that is always joyful and free from regret or stinginess, therefore it is said: "Going from here to there."

"One who constantly reaches a state of peace" means one who hopes for fulfillment, naturally experiencing joy and delight with a serene mind; knowing that their precepts are complete and their giving is pure, they will certainly receive the karmic reward and not fall into the ranks of the heterodox. Day and night they rejoice without harboring any feverish affliction. It is the same for those who give to those who uphold the precepts and those who are learned; therefore it is said: "One who constantly reaches a state of peace."
The bhikṣu establishes the precepts, guards and restrains the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, and awakens the mind to make it responsive. Regarding "the bhikṣu establishes the precepts":

he maintains his resolve with such firmness that it cannot be broken or destroyed; he is not led astray by forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. Therefore, it is said: "the bhikṣu establishes the precepts."

To guard and restrain the sense faculties means to be fully endowed with the faculty of the eye, as well as the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; to be complete in all of them without any deficiency or omission; for the mind to be neither confused nor distracted by other thoughts; and to cultivate sublime conduct in accordance with all these faculties. Therefore, it is said: "guarding and restraining the sense faculties."
"One who knows moderation in eating" means eating according to the capacity of one's stomach, neither hoarding food nor being gluttonous.
The Venerable Dharmanandi said:
"Eating too much leads to suffering; eating too little causes the decline of physical strength. One who eats with moderation is like a scale that is neither high nor low."
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣa, in composing the *Pratipattisūtra*, also says:

"It is like catching many birds and hiding them in a large vessel, watching over them at all times and feeding them at the proper intervals; once their feathers and tails have grown long, they are trimmed as needed, and the fattest ones are selected daily for the kitchen."
Among them, one bird reflected within itself:
"If I eat too much and become fat, I shall die; if I starve and do not eat, I shall likewise lose my life. I should exercise self-restraint:
by eating sparingly, though my flesh may waste away, my feathers and down will remain lustrous, and I shall be able to escape from this cage."
"According to what he thought, he immediately ate little; his body hair became lustrous, and thus his wish was fulfilled. It is the same for that practitioner of the path:

he reflects within himself, "If I eat much, I will become dazed and unable to cultivate the Way; I shall not obtain the contemplation of wholesome dharmas, and all unwholesome dharmas will increase day and night. Greed, hatred, and delusion all arise from eating too much, and one will not attain the ultimate goal."
In the Buddha’s sūtras it is said that those who eat excessively suffer from five afflictions.

What are these five? First, frequent defecation; second, frequent urination; third, excessive sleepiness; fourth, physical heaviness that renders one incapable of engaging in spiritual practice; and fifth, a multitude of ailments due to indigestion.

Those who eat excessively suffer these five hardships; they fall into the abyss of suffering and fail to reach the ultimate goal. Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should know moderation in eating. To awaken the mind so that it accords with the Way:

day and night one should remain vigilant, binding the mind to *dhyāna*. If sleep is about to overcome you, you should extend one foot down from the bed. If sleep persists and cannot be dispelled, you should extend both feet down from the bed. If sleep is too heavy, you should practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). If sleep remains heavy while walking, sprinkle water on your face. If you still cannot wake up, gaze upward at the stars to rouse your resolve. Thus, during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, let there be no indolence.
Therefore it is said: "Awaken the mind and make it responsive;
keep the mind constantly alert, studying with diligence day and night. When the outflows are exhausted and the mind is liberated, one may attain Nirvana."

"One whose mind is always awake" means that body, speech, and mind are constantly awakened; when lust, anger, and delusion arise, they are immediately severed. One does not encounter afflictions and dwells in peace and security. Therefore it is said: "One whose mind is always awake."

One studies with vigor day and night: practicing by day as one does by night, and practicing by night as one does by day; likewise during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night. One maintains the mind with single-minded concentration, free from other divergent thoughts, contemplating only the dharmas that accord with the Path. Therefore it is said: "Study with vigor day and night."

Regarding the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of outflows: it is only when the mind is courageous and firm that one can exhaust the outflows. Those who maintain a mind of indolence and arrogance cannot exhaust the outflows nor can they apply themselves with diligent practice; therefore, they regress and fall into the category of ordinary worldlings.

Yet that practitioner exerts themselves with diligence day and night as if their head were on fire; maintaining a courageous mind, they do not hesitate before perils and difficulties, prioritizing the lofty resolve to sever the fetters and extinguish the outflows. Therefore it is said: "The outflows are exhausted and the mind is liberated."

That which can lead to *nirvāṇa* means that all practices have been perfected; the various afflictions of worldly suffering shall never arise again. Seeking entry into *nirvāṇa*, one transforms the great array of fetters; those who are bound, attached, and defiled become obscured and do not arise. Proceeding toward the realm of *nirvāṇa* without obstruction, one abandons present karma and enters the realm of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said: "That which can lead to *nirvāṇa*."
The wise establish the precepts, Devoting their minds to practicing wisdom;
Such a bhikṣu, free from feverish affliction, Can realize the end of suffering.

"The wise establish the precepts" means that their morality is unshakable; they dwell securely and firmly, and cannot be moved. The wise eliminate the darkness of ignorance and never remain within the midst of delusion. It is like a valiant general clad in heavy armor who, if lacking a sword in hand, cannot defeat a powerful enemy; likewise, one with a sword but no armor cannot also subdue that powerful enemy.

If a valiant general were to don heavy armor and grasp a sharp sword, fighting the enemy amidst secure and perilous terrain both in front and behind, he would certainly achieve his objective without any doubt.

It is the same for those who practice the path: one whose body is armored with the precepts but whose mind lacks the sword of wisdom cannot destroy the roots and heads of the fetters (*saṃyojana*); likewise, even if one possesses wisdom but lacks the armor of the precepts in the body, one cannot destroy those fetters.

If that valiant general dons the armor of the precepts upon his body and grasps the sword of wisdom in his mind, he will surely be able to achieve success even when facing the formidable and perilous enemy of the fetters (saṃyojana) in battle.
Therefore, it is said: "The wise establish the prohibitive precepts."

One who practices with single-minded devotion uses wisdom to refine the mind and investigate all defilements; it is like ore and iron repeatedly entering a furnace of a hundred refinements, whereby the supple becomes firm and the counterfeit becomes authentic. It is also like the great ocean, which seethes and surges day and night, causing turbid dregs to sink and transform into precious jewels.
Human beings are also like this: if one exerts the mind day and night without ceasing, one will attain the realization of the fruit.
Therefore it is said: "Dedicate the mind to practicing wisdom.

As for the bhikṣu who is free from feverish affliction, even if heaven and earth were to melt and burn away, though he remains within that form, he would ultimately never experience feverish affliction nor suffer any injury.
Why is this? Because a bhikṣu establishes the faculties and gains power; his resolve does not retreat, and what he aspires to must surely bear fruit.

A bhikṣu destroys all fetters and defilements until they are forever exhausted without remainder; he wears the kāṣāya robe and holds the alms-bowl in hand; when the time comes, he goes to households with a face of true shame and modesty; whether the offerings obtained are coarse or fine, his aspiration is for parinirvāṇa—therefore, he is called a bhikṣu.
Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu is free from feverish affliction.

Regarding "one who can bring about the end of suffering": having exhausted the source of suffering so that it is forever extinguished without remainder, one no longer undergoes further hardships; from this extinction of suffering, merit and virtue increase daily. Therefore it is said: "one who can bring about the end of suffering."
Subdue the mind with the precepts; maintain the mind in right concentration; internally cultivate cessation and contemplation, never forgetting right wisdom.
Regarding "subduing the mind with the precepts": one constantly binds the mind so that it is not lost, nor does it wander or run wild. Therefore it is said: "Subdue the mind with the precepts."

Regarding "guarding the mind through right concentration," there are three grades of concentration: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. One who guards wholesome concentration does not allow unwholesome concentration to find an opportunity;
they constantly recollect and reflect: "I have now attained right concentration and must reach its ultimate source; for what reason would unwholesome concentration cause confusion within it?"
Therefore it is said: "Guarding right concentration.

As for one who internally studies *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they constantly maintain mindfulness and fix the mind upon clarity, removing darkness and acting as a lamp to illuminate. They observe the root of craving and seek out the source of delusion; by bringing them to rest, they do not arise. Therefore it is said: "Internally studying *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*."

Regarding "unfailing right knowledge" (*asampramoṣa-samyagjñāna*): the illumination of wisdom reaches everywhere; the mind’s thoughts follow wisdom like two oxen yoked together by a single harness. It is like the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), which governs the body’s lightness and heaviness. Holding the mind with the body and holding the body with the mind, once the body and mind are in accord, there is no obstruction; even stone walls are passed through. This is refining the mind to enter the subtle, and refining the subtle to enter the body; as the mind’s thoughts follow the form, there is nothing that can touch or obstruct them.
Therefore it is said: "Do not forget right wisdom.
Eradicate all defilements; exhaust pride so that it does not arise. Seek the Dharma throughout your life, never for a moment parting from the Noble Ones.

To "remove all defilements" means that the various defilements within the mind—the fetters, bonds, and attachments—as well as the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements of sensation, have been exhausted and extinguished, leaving no further trunk, nodes, branches, or leaves; therefore, it is said: "to remove all defilements."

"Exhaust all conceit and do not give rise to it" means that one should restrain the mind and the mental states of arrogance, overweening pride, and dogmatic attachment; by subduing conceit, one causes its extinction, so that both the traces of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the traces of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are extinguished together. Therefore, it is said: "Exhaust all conceit and do not give rise to it."

Regarding those who seek the Dharma for the rest of their lives: as for what is called "body," it refers to all things categorized as physical forms and instruments; the knots [of affliction] are also called body; the aggregates of the five skandhas and the activities of nourishing life are also called body; and even the fourfold military forces—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—are also called body.

Among all things within the body, none are more severe than the fetters that bind it. One who can destroy these fetters and seek the True Dharma is said to be liberated from bondage. Such a person does not dwell in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and does not fixate on the seven stations or the three contemplations. A true disciple of the Buddha is endowed with firm faith and firm Dharma; they are able to destroy the accumulation of fetters. Therefore, it is said: "Throughout one's life, one seeks the Dharma."
Do not be separated from the Noble Ones for even a moment; always keep in mind that you are a successor in the lineage of the Sages, which is what your heart delights in.
There are three kinds of knowledge regarding the dwelling place of the Sages:

first, the knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*); second, the knowledge of the realm of *nirvāṇa* with remainder; and third, the knowledge of the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Therefore it is said: "Do not for even a moment be separated from the Noble Ones.
One should properly contemplate morality, concentration, wisdom, and liberation; having completely abandoned all defilements, one will be free from calamity and eliminate existence.

Regarding those who possess morality, concentration, and wisdom: that practitioner, having fully equipped the three types of action—morality, concentration, and wisdom—as their own adornments, destroys the mass of fetters and afflictions; where could they go that would not be overcome?

It is just as when a king possesses great wealth, power, and talent that surpasses others; he is then able to provide peace and relief to his subjects, and external invaders do not attack. Now, this practitioner is also like this:

when the three karmas are fully perfected, there is no doubt or difficulty in destroying the thieves of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Precepts establish one's resolve, concentration restrains the distracted mind, and wisdom cuts off the fetters. Therefore, it is said: "Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation."

"One should practice wholesome reflection" means that one should contemplate the three categories day and night, putting them into practice without ever departing from them; therefore it is said, "one should practice wholesome reflection."

"Those who have already left behind all defilements" refers to those who propagate the ultimate truth; they understand the suffering of birth and death and deliver beings from within it. Being utterly pure, without flaw, and free from all taints, it is for this reason that it is said: "They have already left behind all defilements."

"Free from calamity and having eliminated existence" means that one has already departed from the affliction of suffering and turmoil as boiling water; having exhausted all three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) so as never again to undergo conception, one knows this as it truly is. Therefore, it is said: "Free from calamity and having eliminated existence."
"Through understanding and liberation one is delivered; nothing further arises. One transcends all realms of Māra, as clear and bright as the sun.

Regarding "through understanding and liberation one is delivered": there are six categories of conduct. These are the fetters, bonds, and defilements of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; specifically, the delusion, pride, folly, and confusion arising from the desire realm that entangle and ensnare oneself. Therefore, it is said: "Through understanding and liberation one is delivered."

Regarding "the remainder shall not arise again": that practitioner contemplates and observes it as it truly is and knows it accordingly; he then seeks the skillful means to seek the extinction of those fetters. Birth and death are exhausted, and he will no longer undergo conception; the holy life has been established and what was to be done has been accomplished. Therefore it is said: "the remainder shall not arise again."

Regarding "transcending all realms of Māra": from the six heavens below upward, all are realms of Māra; they abound in various sufferings and afflictions that obstruct the mind for the Way, preventing people from reaching the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta).

Within Jambudvīpa there are beings of a different species called Makas; by day they hide themselves between the raw and cooked intestines, falling into the realm of Māra. This is what is meant by the desire realm being harmed by Māra and abounding in calamities and misfortunes.
Noble and sagely persons transcend the realms of the heterodox; therefore it is said, "they transcend all realms of Māra.
"Like the sun’s clear brightness" means that the brilliance of the sun is free from the five obscurations.
What are the five obscurations?
First, clouds; second, smoke; third, dust; fourth, mist; and fifth, the hands of the asuras.
When these five afflictions are absent, the sun and moon are clear and bright.
The practicing bhikṣu is also like this, being free from the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

What are the five hindrances? First is the hindrance of sensual desire; second is the hindrance of ill will; third is the hindrance of sloth and torpor; fourth is the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth is the hindrance of doubt.

A practicing bhikṣu who is free from these five hindrances immediately attains clarity and purity, with inner and outer penetration like that of purple-polished gold; therefore it is said: "Like the sun, pure and clear."
Madly deluded and self-indulgent, the bhikṣu avoids them from without; in the practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom, he seeks fulfillment and shall not depart from them.

Regarding "madly deluded and self-indulgent": this refers to the sudden and violent conduct of ignorant, deluded worldlings. It is like a monkey that abandons one thing only to seize another; their minds are like a swift wind, racing through ten thousand thoughts. Therefore it is said: "madly deluded and self-indulgent."

A bhikṣu who avoids the external is one whose conduct is like water and whose forbearance is like the earth; such a bhikṣu does not rely on noble families, is able to restrain his own emotions, and closes off the six sense-gates—only then is he called a bhikṣu. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu avoids the external."

Regarding the practice of precepts, concentration, and wisdom: one must diligently apply oneself day and night to the categories of precepts, concentration, and wisdom without giving rise to negligence. Just as one who wishes to cross a vast ocean must board a great vessel, so too one who seeks to proceed toward Nirvana must rely on the practices of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. One should diminish unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas; those who violate this correct teaching and do not accord with the Dharma and Vinaya will thereby bring harm upon themselves within the Buddha’s Dharma and the Noble Sangha.
Therefore it is said: "In the practice of morality, concentration, and wisdom, seek fulfillment and do not depart from them.
Since one does not indulge in self-indulgence, nor harbor discursive thoughts, one thus abandons pride;
in this way, it does not arise.
As for "not being self-indulgent," it means not racing toward forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; therefore, it is said, "not being self-indulgent.

Furthermore, as for "not forming mental images," it means that regarding the phenomena contemplated by the mind, one cultivates only the concentrated mind (*samādhi*) therein, and does not form mental images of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; therefore, it is said, "and not forming mental images."

Therefore, one who abandons arrogance internally contemplates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to restrain and eliminate mental distraction, constantly entering a concentrated state of mind. One must not manifest through the six sense objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—the outward signs of pride. For this reason, it is said: "abandoning arrogance."

In this way, that which is "not produced" is like those things that do not exist—namely, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*). The mental objects contemplated by the mind are likewise so; what the mind contemplates is like rain from heaven or grain spilled from a cart overturning, yet the evil contemplated by the mind is even more abundant than that. Therefore, it is said: "In this way, it is not produced."
The wise person’s learning is firm; Regarding all the prohibitions and precepts, They proceed directly on the path to *nirvāṇa*, And swiftly attain extinction.

As for "the wise person’s learning is firm": following the Buddha’s exhortations and receiving the teacher’s instructions, they abandon the deviant and follow the correct. Their mind is always steadfast and not corrupted by a depraved mind. Therefore it is said: "The wise person’s learning is firm."

Regarding "the various prohibitions and precepts": this refers to practicing the path and guarding the prohibitions and precepts at all times; it is what the wise cultivate, not what fools practice. Therefore, it is said: "regarding the various prohibitions and precepts."

To proceed directly upon the path to Nirvana means to eternally rest in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is without beginning or end, quiescent, and non-arising; therefore, it is said: "proceeding directly upon the path to Nirvana."

"To swiftly attain extinction" means that there are no obstacles along the way; it is like a river in flood, which flows entirely toward the sea. Therefore, it is said: "To swiftly attain extinction."
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind; The scents of lotus and sandalwood do not travel against the breeze.
But the fragrance of virtue perfumes even against the wind; A person of virtue is smelled everywhere.
Long ago, when the Buddha was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Now, Mahākāśyapa had been born and raised in a noble clan; his body was delicate and his food had always been sweet and refined, never coarse or rough. Since he was inclined toward compassion for the poor, when he went to a poor household to beg and received coarse and unpalatable food, he immediately fell ill. His internal winds were disturbed, resulting in a violent diarrhea.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Now follow me and inquire after the sick. He replied:

"So be it," the World-Honored One replied, and he led Maudgalyāyana to Vulture Peak. At that time, Mahākāśyapa was sitting alone in a quiet room with no one to attend to his illness; the Tathāgata then proceeded directly to Mahākāśyapa’s cave.
When Kāśyapa saw the Buddha and wished to rise from his seat, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"You are currently suffering from illness; remain seated and do not rise. I have my own sitting mat that I carry with me."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked Kāśyapa:
"Now you dwell alone in an empty room with no one to attend to you when you are ill; how can you find joy in these empty mountains?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was standing behind Kāśyapa. Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, speaking this verse:
"Having renounced the throne of the Heavenly King, He practices virtue without weariness; With a heart full of joy, Kauśika gazes upon him."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra Devānām-indra, speaking these verses:
“The nature of the celestial body is pure, Anointed with the fragrance of incense;
Why do you lower your noble spirit To gaze upon this foul and impure body?”
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, repeating these verses:
"O Most Victorious One, please know this now: The fragrance of the precepts is peerless.
I now smell this merit; I no longer regard my own ugly form."
"However, World-Honored One!

The various incenses of the heavens increase and intensify the roots of bondage, further augmenting the dust and toil of affliction (*kleśa*). The fragrance of the precepts of the worthy and holy ones cuts off all fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana*), closing the gates of calamity so that no desires leak through."
However, World-Honored One!

Such ordinary fragrances circulate within birth and death throughout the succession of kalpas, yet they cannot cause people to enter eternal tranquility; the fragrance of the precepts of the noble ones appears only once in every hundreds, thousands, or millions of kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having subtly observed Śakra Devānām Indra, spoke this verse:
“Excellent, O Lord of Devas, is your cause; Your present intention is most rare.
Amidst negligence, you are able To restrain your mind and cultivate the roots of virtue.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, based on this fundamental teaching, spoke these verses while seated amidst the great assembly:
"Flowers and incense do not go against the wind; The fragrance of lotuses and sandalwood likewise.
But the fragrance of virtue wafts even against the wind; A person of virtue is smelled everywhere."
"Furthermore, while the various flowers and fragrances of the world all diffuse with the wind and not against the wind,
the fragrance of the virtue of precepts diffuses both against the wind and with the wind."
The fragrances of worldly flowers permeate only the desire realm and not the form realm; or they may permeate only one direction and not the other three.
But the fragrance of upholding the precepts pervades the ten directions.
The fragrance of flowers can only be distinguished when one is close to it;
the fragrance of those who uphold the precepts reaches upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Therefore it is said: "The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, but the fragrance of a virtuous person is smelled everywhere."
The many fragrances of sandalwood and the blossoms of the blue lotus, though said to be genuine, are not equal to the fragrance of the precepts.
As for "the many fragrances of sandalwood," these are what is spoken of by the world: aloeswood, *kālānusāri*, sandalwood, and *turuṣka*; these are fragrances derived from roots.

As for the fragrance of flowers—blue lotuses, water lilies, campakas, *sugandhika* powder, *sugandhika* blossoms, up to and including the *vimukti* flower, the *sūryaprabha* essence, and the *puṇḍarīka* flower—these various flowers numbering in the tens, hundreds, and thousands of kinds cannot, even by way of metaphor, be compared to the fragrance of one who maintains the precepts; it exceeds them a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and a hundred-millionfold, beyond what the mind can conceive or the intellect can fathom.
Now, these fragrances of various scents provide entertainment for people in this present life, yet they cannot accompany them into future lives;
the fragrance of upholding the precepts brings blessings in the present world and has never been in vain throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Therefore it is said: Though one may call this "true," it is not equal to the fragrance of the precepts.
The scent of flowers is faint and cannot be called true; the fragrance of upholding the precepts reaches the heavens and is most excellent.
As for the fragrance of flowers that is faint, such as that of sandalwood or aloeswood, it is prized in the central lands but absent in the borderlands;

yet the fragrance of the virtue of the precepts wafts upward beyond the heavens and penetrates downward throughout the ten directions, filling the entire world so that there is no one who does not perceive it.
Therefore it is said: "The fragrance of flowers is faint; it cannot be called true.

The fragrance of upholding the precepts surpasses even that which reaches the heavens. Even the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—who indulge their passions and follow their whims with complete freedom—still praise those who uphold the precepts. They recognize that practicing good brings merit while committing evil leads to transgression. Those who abide in the categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the vision and knowledge of liberation, and the analytical knowledge of liberation, are worthy of reverence and honor as they pursue the unsurpassed path.
Why is this? Such a person acts as a guide for others, leading them along the correct path and dispelling their ignorance so that they may perceive the light of wisdom.
Therefore it is said: "The fragrance of upholding the precepts reaches the heavens, most excellent."
Perfected in the fulfillment of the precepts, liberated through concentrated mind, Māra is lost and bewildered;
Māra does not know the Way.

Regarding those perfected in the fulfillment of the precepts—the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—these possess precepts that are pure and without the slightest flaw or omission. Although the King of Māra possesses great power and is uniquely exalted as he rules over the realm of desire, he cannot know the fruits of realization attained by the fourfold assembly, nor does he know by which path or fruit they have brought their outflows and fetters to an end.
At that time, the evil Māra spoke with his own mind:

"These men in black robes, with shaven heads, bare arms, and right shoulders bared, practice meditation and cultivate concentration. Some advance until they depart from my turbid realm; some come and go without following my instructions; some achieve eternal extinction, unaware of where their consciousness resides; and some, having relinquished their life-force, are unknown as to where their knowledge and perception have gone."
Therefore it is said: "Māra is deluded regarding the Path; Māra does not know the Path.
This Path is ultimate; this Path is unsurpassed.
By attaining this, one can fathom the source; meditative concentration is that which binds Māra."
This path is the ultimate; it is secure, unconditioned, and its bliss is inexhaustible. It leads toward the single way to the gate of Nirvana. Therefore, it is said: "This path is the ultimate."
This path is unsurpassed; there is nothing higher than this path, for which the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas serve with reverent hearts and present offerings.
The Venerable Śāriputra had a novice named Cūḍapanthaka, who was eight years old and possessed the six supernormal powers; he flew through the air to the Anavatapta Spring.
There was a brahmin possessing the five supernatural powers named Subhadra who also arrived at that spring.

At that time, the blue-clad yakṣa who guarded the Nodaka spring drove away the brahmin with five supernatural powers, pelting him with tiles and stones so that he could not approach the divine spring. When the śrāmaṇera Cunda arrived through the air, the several hundred members of that assembly of blue-clad yakṣas all came forward to welcome him: some went before him to gather up his robes, some brought pure water to wash his hands and feet, some used clean towels to wipe his head and face, and some bathed his body with fragrant water.
The brahmin Subhadra raised his voice and declared:

"I have now attained the five supernormal powers; my spiritual merit is immeasurable, and my strength is such that I can move mountains, stop flowing waters, and turn heaven and earth as easily as one turns a bead upon the palm of one's hand."
Since I began studying the Way more than one hundred and twenty years ago, I have toiled my body and exhausted my spirit until both form and mind were utterly fatigued.

At times I pursued the five sciences, maintaining four fires that blazed around me while the sunlight shone from above; at other times I lay upon ashes and excrement, or upon thorns and brambles. Amidst such hardships and perils, there was no path I did not study.
Yet they continue to drive them away so that they cannot reach the spring.

Furthermore, these small children in black robes are only seven or eight years old and have not yet weaned from nursing; their bodies remain filthy and foul-smelling, yet [the others] still wait for them with great reverence, welcoming them, meeting them halfway, and serving them.
"For what reason? At that time, the blue-clad ghost said to the brahmin:
"Although this scholar’s physical age is small, his conduct transcends the three realms, and he has attained the eightfold path of the noble ones."
"You do not possess such [qualities] now; therefore, you do not arouse reverence.
There was a brahmin named Yakṣa who established a monastery also named Yakṣa, and he constantly provided ghee and oil to supply lamps for the monastery.

At that time, a brahmin from a distant land came to the Yakṣa Monastery; having heard that the brahmin Yakṣa was of eminent talent and illustrious virtue, and that he particularly believed in the Buddha-dharma and had established a shrine therein, he went to meet him and exchanged greetings with him.
At that time, a śrāmaṇera came forward again to meet them, taking oil and ghee to provide for the lamps of the monastery. A great multitude of brahmins said to the yakṣa-brāhmaṇa:
"Did you truly pay homage just now to the person in the dyed robe?"
Before he had finished speaking, the śrāmaṇera arrived and immediately paid his respects again.
A great multitude of brahmins said to this brahmin:

"You are of the four castes and your talents surpass those of men; there is no astronomy or geography you have not studied and mastered; your divine incantations move the spirits, and there is nothing you do not accomplish."
Now, as for this man in colored robes, he has emerged from many lineages and castes that are not pure; why do you violate the fundamental law by paying him respectful homage?

Furthermore, O Brahmin, you maintain a life of purity, having mastered the inner treasuries, diagrams, prophecies, and secret records; in practicing the Way to achieve merit, what wish could you not fulfill? In matters of writing, characters, and seals, there is nothing you do not fully comprehend. Compared to this, the Buddha’s conduct is meager and rarefied—what is there in it to be precious?

To abandon the root and grasp at the branches is what I loathe. I have heard that śramaṇas are of lowly and humble origin, yet they abound in craftiness and deception; they delude the people of the world, and their conduct is short-sighted. They seek glory for a single lifetime and cannot extend it to bring about the merit of Brahma. Even if we were to meet, it would be sufficient merely to join our palms; why should one prostrate oneself with the five limbs touching the ground in respectful salutation?
"We have personally witnessed this most extraordinary occurrence; how much more so for a great man who was formerly a scholar—how could he possibly forgive you for such a crime?
The yakṣa replied to the many brāhmaṇas:
"All of you, remain silent and listen to the verses of the sublime gāthās that I shall speak."
“The virtues of the noble ones are immeasurable; the Eightfold Straight Path is the unsurpassed way.
This is the *brahman* of the śramaṇa, as proclaimed from the mouth of the Tathāgata.”
"Behold this form, though small; yet by means of it, one attains the path of the noble sages.
Therefore, I now take refuge in it; O Brahmin, why do you mock it?
For this reason it is said: "This path has none above it."

Regarding those who have attained the ability to investigate the root: the Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin are able to sever the fetters, the various entanglements, and the aggregates of the sense bases within the desire realm; therefore it is said:
"One who has attained the direction toward the exhaustion of the root."

Regarding "dhyāna-concentration binds Māra": for one who enters meditative absorption and practices seated dhyāna, delighting in seclusion and tranquility with a mind dedicated to a single purpose, and counting the inhalations and exhalations with firm resolve, they are able to sever the bonds of Māra; yet, by conversely binding Māra, the one who has entered absorption can employ ghosts and spirits at will, so that they arrive immediately.
The Buddha’s sūtras also state:

“I have observed throughout the heavens and the human realm that among all bonds, none is more firm than the bond of Māra; yet it is shattered and humiliated by Arhats who have exhausted their outflows, such that they shall no longer undergo rebirth in the future.”
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way: you must seek skillful means to sever the firm bonds of Māra.
Even if the teaching of the Dharma is slight, listen and receive it with single-minded devotion;
such a person is called a protector of the Dharma, who has removed lust, anger, and delusion.
One for whom the multitude of fetters is forever exhausted is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Although his teaching may be slight, it is essential; its meaning and flavor are in perfect accord.
In the past, there were two bhikṣus studying in the deep mountains; one was widely learned, while the other was of little depth.
At that time, the one of meager learning maintained his precepts perfectly, yet he recited only a single sentence of scripture, chanting it daily without seeking to receive any more.
At that time, the deities of the void and the deities of the mountains and forests daily exclaimed, "Excellent! We wish to hear what the man of the Way has to say.

Then that learned bhikṣu chanted aloud with a resonant voice the various profound and wondrous meanings and sūtra passages he knew; yet the deities of the mountains and forests remained silent, offering no response nor exclaiming "Excellent! again.
At that time, the learned bhikṣu, immediately harboring anger, said to that mountain deity:
"Now this junior bhikṣu has studied but little and recites only a single phrase, yet you, O Deva, immediately praise him, saying, 'Excellent!'"

"I am now deeply learned in the profound principles of meaning; I have gathered the exquisite phrases and words from various sūtras to recite and practice with you. Yet, even the celestial deities neither respond nor praise them."
The deva replied: "The bhikṣu does not reproach himself, yet he reproaches me instead.
This bhikṣu of little learning is consistent in his words and his actions; you, however, though you recite the Tripiṭaka, your conduct contradicts the sūtras."
In the *Udānavarga* expounded by the Buddha, there is also this verse:
"Though the teaching may be slight, If one listens and receives it with single-minded devotion,
This is called a protector of the Dharma, Who removes lust, anger, and delusion."
"This bhikṣu is in accord with the Dharma; although he has not yet exhausted lust, anger, and delusion, he employs skillful means to bring them to exhaustion.
Although you are learned, day and night you practice lust, anger, and delusion, and you are greedily attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena."
This bhikṣu of little learning contemplates in dhyāna day and night without distraction; for this reason, he is always praised as virtuous.
Although you are of great learning, your mind is not single-minded; for this reason, you are not praised as virtuous.
At that time, having heard the words of the devas, the bhikṣu was immediately filled with shame and felt self-reproach for his actions, thinking:
"If even a mountain spirit perceives my impure conduct, how much more so one who has attained the Way through supernormal powers?"
"I shall now personally reform my thoughts and cultivate sublime wisdom, never again giving rise to thoughts of attachment to lust, anger, or delusion.
As his conduct thus accorded with his words, the devas praised him immeasurably day after day.
When a person practices in accordance with the influence of friends, they attain full accomplishment in the wholesome Dharma.

At that time, a bhikṣu who practices with diligence attains mundane sublime dharmas: the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the four foundations of mindfulness, the stage of heat, the stage of summits, the stage of patience, and the stage of the supreme mundane dharma; through these, he successively realizes the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Having attained the Way, the bhikṣu offered his gratitude to the devas, saying:

"I have been favored by your exhortations and drawn forth from the muddy depths. That I have now attained the Way is entirely due to the power of the deities; it has brought me great benefit and great accomplishment."
He further preached the Dharma to the various devas again, and their minds were opened and their intentions liberated, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Therefore it is said: "Though the teaching may be slight, one who is not heedless gains renown; through heedlessness, one incurs slander."
The people of Magadha who are not negligent, by virtue of their purity, shall be born in heaven.

Long ago, in incalculable ages past, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having lived in the world to teach and transform, and having completed his work of delivering all sentient beings with whom he had a karmic connection, he entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of sentient beings enshrined the śarīra relics and erected stupas made of the seven precious substances, offering them veneration and offerings.
After several more generations had passed, the stupas eventually fell into decay, yet there was no one to repair them.

At that time, there was an assembly of ninety-two thousand people from the town of Arthasiddha, with King Bimbisāra as their leader. King Bimbisāra addressed the great multitude: "Each of you should exhort yourselves to together cultivate meritorious virtue.

A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter, and a human birth is difficult to obtain. Even though one has obtained a human form, one may fall into a remote region or be born into a family of wrong views. Why, then, do we remain greedily attached to worldly pleasures?"
"It would be better to open your minds and restore these dilapidated stūpas and monasteries.
The people followed this instruction and, together with the king, repaired the ruined stūpas and monasteries. They then made a collective vow:

"We, all of us, being of one mind and one purpose in restoring this monastery, if we possess even a hair’s breadth of merit, may we not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions; instead, may we be reborn together in the heavens or among humans, dwelling in the same place without distinction."

Furthermore, I have heard that in the future there will appear a Buddha named Śākyamuni; when he first preaches the Dharma, he shall cause my great assembly to attain liberation first, with the king at their head.
At that time, ninety-two thousand people, according to their respective lifespans, each passed away and were all reborn in the heavens, dwelling in the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

After several more lifetimes had passed, within Jambudvīpa there appeared a Buddha in the world named Śākyamuni, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles; possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his purple-golden body was surrounded by a halo seven feet in diameter, and his voice had eight qualities like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
At that time, ninety-two thousand devas, having exhausted their celestial merits, each passed away and was reborn within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha.

King Bimbisāra was eight years old when he succeeded to the throne; he governed according to the Dharma without any crookedness, cultivating the True Dharma with benevolence extending even to his subordinates, refraining from harming living beings, and distributing alms to relieve the destitute and aid those in distress, providing for all travelers who paused to rest on their journeys.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrīkumāra abandoned eighty thousand court ladies and relinquished his royal station. During the night, at a time when humans were not abroad, he left the kingdom to seek the Way. He shaved his own hair and cast off his precious robes, handing over the white horse he had been riding to Chandaka to return to the kingdom and inform the King:
"The sufferings and anxieties of birth and death are countless. I shall now study the Way to seek the realization of its fruits; if I fulfill my aspiration, I shall return to deliver you, O King."
At that time, the Bodhisattva proceeded further along the road when he encountered a hunter wearing religious robes and appearing like a śramaṇa. The Bodhisattva asked the hunter:
"What is the name of these religious robes you are wearing?"
The hunter replied, “This is called a *kāṣāya*.

When I wear it while hunting, the deer, seeing me, think I am a practitioner of the Way; they all come to pay their respects and remain free from fear. We then take them one by one and kill them to sustain our own lives.”
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s compassion and pity redoubled:
“Those who rely on the four immeasurables To rescue and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings— The kāṣāya is the robe of the Tathāgata; Yet they remove defilement while creating it.”
"I now possess these celestial robes worn upon my body, which are extremely fine, soft, and beautiful; we may trade them for one another.
The hunter replied, "The Prince was raised in the deep inner palace; his body is delicate and tender, unaccustomed to cold and hardship. I fear they might harm the Prince's person."
The Bodhisattva replied, "There is no hardship in merely trading; this is the established custom of the ancient sages.
The hunter replied:
"The prince’s precious robes are worth an incalculable sum, whereas these monastic robes (kāṣāya) are of no value for giving; why do you wish to trade so hastily?
The Bodhisattva replied, "Whatever one requires depends on one's intention; it does not matter whether something is expensive or cheap."
The hunter replied, "I do not dare trade for this garment; it is filthy, a place of putrid pus and blood.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Once the foul and the fragrant have been distinguished, one shall naturally wash them clean.
The hunter immediately took off his own garment to trade for the Bodhisattva’s precious robe.
At that time, the Bodhisattva donned the dharma-robe, held a lotus leaf in his hand, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
At that time, a multitude of many tens of millions gathered together in one place; they encountered the Bodhisattva raising his hand in praise, some saying, "Welcome!
and others saying:
"Sun and Moon.
Some pressed their palms together in self-surrender, while others exchanged greetings, asking, "Are you a deva?
Or a Brahmā?"
"Is this Śakra Devānām Indra?

Surrounded by the multitude, with no room left to beg for alms, he immediately took up some flower petals and returned outside the city, heading straight for the Eastern Mountain; the crowd pursued him, following one after another from front to back.
At that time, King Bimbisāra was atop a high tower; seeing from afar the multitude pursuing the Bodhisattva, he immediately asked his attendants:
"Why is this great crowd all rushing toward the mountain? What is the reason for this?"
A certain high minister, who clearly recognized the Bodhisattva, addressed the king, saying:
"This is a scion of the Śākya clan who left his home to study and has been wandering abroad; he may be plotting against the affairs of state, and we should go and execute him."
Having heard this, Bimbisāra said to that minister:

"Protect your lineage and do not utter such words! Even if the son of the Śākyas succeeds to the royal throne and becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rājā*), we shall serve as his ministers and assistants; but if he renounces the world to study the Path and attains Buddhahood for himself, we vow to be his foremost disciples."

The first instance of preaching the Dharma occurred in this manner: King Bimbisāra, laden with food, drink, and various delicacies, went into the mountains to meet the Bodhisattva. He immediately prostrated at his feet and announced his name and lineage:
"I am the one who is King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha."
The Bodhisattva replied, "I recognized him long ago; why should I pay him homage?
King Bimbisāra then addressed him, saying:
"Now I present this humble offering; from what remains after my own meal, I pray you will accept it to manifest my sincere devotion.
The Bodhisattva silently accepted the food.
When he had finished eating, the pure water was offered, and the king stepped forward and said:
"If the Prince should attain the Unsurpassed Way, I shall see him first deliver me, so that I may forever be free from worldly suffering.
Then King Bimbisāra prostrated at his feet and took his leave; the Bodhisattva proceeded on his way to the hermitage of Ārāḍa.
The various disciples of Ārāḍa saw the Bodhisattva approaching from afar and said to their teacher:
"A man of exceptionally handsome and distinguished appearance is now heading straight for our master's gate; he must surely seek to become a disciple."
At that time, Ārāḍa addressed his disciples and spoke this verse.
*Udānavarga*, Fascicle Nine; *Udānavarga*, Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Training.
Guarding against bodily misconduct, rectifying one’s own bodily conduct, and guarding against what is evil in the body.
Regarding "cultivating bodily good conduct and guarding against bodily evil conduct": for what reason is it called "bodily evil conduct"?

It is so named because one recognizes one's own internal faults and recognizes the faults of others. Once evil has fully taken hold, the facial expression changes; one may strike with hands or fists, destroying the physical form. These various evils result in a lack of peace and security in both this life and future lives, or lead to rebirth among hungry ghosts or animals with hideous appearances.
If one is born among humans, one’s talent may fall short of others.
There was once a certain brahmin who was bitten by a dog; filled with rage, his body and mind were ablaze, and he vowed to punish the wicked dog so that it would no longer be violent.
The parents said: "Brahmin!
Suppose a dog bites a brahmin; would it be appropriate for that brahmin to bite the dog back?"
The brahmin replied to his parents,
"I must certainly treat the dog so that it no longer unleashes its venom.
His parents said to their son:
"Since you do not follow my instructions, do as you please.
At that time, the brahmin seized the dog, bound its limbs behind its back, and beat it with a staff.
In beating it, there were two points of impropriety:

Just as a grass rope injures a dog’s paw and causes it to lose its dung, so too it is with these classes of sentient beings: they provoke small disputes that lead to great calamities, thereby harming themselves.

Although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow their great compassion and instruct sentient beings not to engage in contention, sentient beings do not follow their teachings. Ensnared by anger, they further give rise to two kinds of unrighteousness and are bound by manifold sufferings. They shall again undergo the afflictions of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; even if they obtain a human form, their appearance will be hideous. Such various afflictions are beyond reckoning. For this reason, the World-Honored One taught the protection against evil conduct of the body.
Having guarded against misconduct of the body, what merit is obtained?
The answer is:
"One obtains two merits: reputation and the roots of goodness."
What are these two?

If one dwells in a celestial palace where blessings are received spontaneously, with halls of the seven treasures suspended in mid-air; or if one is born among humans with a handsome and upright countenance, such that all who see him rejoice and come to revere and look up to him, being honored and venerated by tens of millions in the great assembly—just as the moon alone shines brightly while the multitude of stars revolve around it.
Therefore it is said: "Guard against evil conduct of the body.
What merit does one obtain by personally rectifying one's bodily conduct?
What renown does one acquire?
He replied:
"One may gain renown in the present life, and one may also gain renown when the body perishes and life ends.
How does one gain renown while in this present body?
In this present life, whether moving or staying, coming or going, they will be seen and honored by tens of millions of beings;
and when the body perishes at the end of life, they will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens above.
What further merit is there in rectifying one's own physical conduct?
The answer is:
"Evil, depraved, and malevolent spirits, as well as violent and wicked ghosts and deities, cannot find an opportunity to harm them; enemies who lie in wait to capture them cannot seize them."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Enmity fills the world; though one seeks to seize it, The seeds of evil return to strike oneself, Just as a snake turns back to poison itself."
"The body is the root of suffering and the mind is the head of calamity; therefore, the World-Honored One said: 'One should rectify one's own bodily conduct.
Why is it said that one must guard against evil in the body?"
The destination of evil conduct is not true, as has been taught.
Evil wealth, evil sons, evil clothing, evil places, and evil lands—all these are called "evil.
Whether one commits evil by relying on those who are known as kin, or commits evil by relying on those who are not known as kin, for this reason the Tathāgata spoke of guarding against bodily evil.
Regarding the cultivation of bodily wholesome conduct, there are two types of wholesome conduct as previously described.

One who possesses good wealth, good sons, good clothing, a good dwelling, and a good land cultivates wholesome conduct with the body; toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Noble Sangha, parents, and elders, they practice complete reverence without any transgression or negligence. For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke of the cultivation of bodily wholesome conduct.
Guarding against verbal misconduct, rectifying one’s own verbal conduct, and protecting oneself from verbal evil—
this is the cultivation of virtuous verbal conduct.
Why is it said that one guards against verbal misconduct?

To know one's own internal faults and to know the faults of others is what is called "evil conduct. If, out of anger, one utters verbal abuse and falsely imputes blame, causing tens of millions of beings to conceive evil thoughts, yet remains unaware and ignorant of this, they will later undergo an evil retribution as all share in their resentment. That abuser shall subsequently enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals to suffer immeasurable pain.
If one is born among humans, they will frequently be slandered and their words will not be trusted;

however, those who can guard their speech will personally attain meritorious retribution, and if born in the heavens, they will experience natural happiness, and if born as a human, they will not be subjected to harsh words.
Therefore it is said: "Guard against evil conduct of speech.
What kind of merit is obtained by one who rectifies their own verbal conduct?
The answer is:

"He is seen and praised by tens of millions of people, who pass the word along to one another, saying: 'This person is upright and prudent, his conduct being consistent with his character; his speech is not coarse or harsh; he does not seek out the faults of others nor disparage their shortcomings; his teeth are well-proportioned and his speech is not stammering.'"
Therefore it is said: "One rectifies one's own verbal conduct.
Regarding the phrase "guarding against evil in speech," there are two meanings:
either remaining in the noble silence of the sages, or speaking in accordance with the Dharma and its meaning.

Now, one who wishes to speak must first regulate oneself; that speech has led to the ruin of one's person is not limited to a single individual. If one utters coarse words, one will be loathed by others, and whether advancing or halting, moving or coming, no one will show one respect or hospitality.
Therefore it is said: "One who guards against verbal evil.

As for one who cultivates verbal good conduct, those who practice such wholesome deeds harbor benevolence and compassion in their hearts; the words they utter are gentle and do not wound the minds of others, and thus they are loved and cherished by the multitude. Therefore it is said: "Cultivating verbal good conduct."
Guard against misconduct of the mind; rectify your own mental conduct. One who guards against mental misconduct cultivates wholesome mental conduct.
Guarding against misconduct of the mind is the foremost among the three types of mental action; in a single moment of thought, the mind can turn cities and villages entirely into desolate wilderness.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "How is this, householder!
Have you perhaps heard of the wilderness of shifting sands, the wilderness of wandering śramaṇas, and the wilderness of secluded tranquility?"
The householder said to the Buddha,
"I have heard of the Flowing Sands Wilderness, the Wandering Śramaṇa Wilderness, and the Tranquil and Empty Wilderness.
The Buddha told the householder:
“How is this, householder?
Who created these desert wastes and wildernesses that follow the śramaṇa’s wilderness?
The elder addressed the Buddha:

"It is all because of the evil intentions of the immortals that they employ incantations and sorcery to create these flowing sands and desolate wildernesses, following the tracks of the śramaṇas' wildernesses. As stated in the *Caryā-sūtra*:

"Of nineteen people who uphold and practice correct conduct, only one person should not be in a secluded place; because his verbal karma and mind are evil, those who maintain the practice do not permit this person to remain in the wilderness."
He then addressed that person, saying:

"Your mind harbors evil and your thoughts are unwholesome; you ought to recite and study the scriptures among humanity and assist in various affairs. By exerting your mind and disciplining your distracted thoughts, you shall attain the fruit of the Way."

"If you, while in the midst of emptiness, wish to seek the meaning of emptiness, your mind will immediately become distracted and constantly give rise to unwholesome states; you will bring about your own destruction and fail to reach the path of goodness.
