Rāhula, you should know this!

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who practices in such a manner; there is no evil he will not undergo and no suffering he will not encounter, just as water defiled by impurities cannot be used for purification.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally poured water onto the ground and said to Rāhula:
"Do you see me pouring this water upon the ground?
"Indeed, I have seen it."
"If one possesses such sincerity that they persist in false speech, lacking a sense of shame and having no sense of disgrace—such conduct encompasses every kind of evil.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a water vessel in his hand, turned it upside down upon the ground, and said to Rāhula:
"Do you see me turning this vessel upside down?"
“Yes, I have indeed seen them.

“If there are those who, with sincere intent, persist in speaking falsehoods, lacking a sense of shame and having no sense of disgrace—such as these, there is no evil they will not involve themselves in.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula, saying:
"You should now train yourself in this way: you must not speak falsely even for the duration of a finger-snap or a moment of playful laughter, much less when speaking falsely with full sincerity."
"Thus it is, Rāhula! You should train yourself in this way.
Therefore it is said: "One dharma has passed away: namely, the person who speaks falsehoods."

Within the majestic conduct of the two hundred and fifty precepts, seven laws are specifically prohibited; whoever violates even one of these laws shall incur its retribution. Therefore it is said: "One law has passed away," referring to the person who speaks falsehoods.

"To fail to escape future lives" means that one has already abandoned the meritorious roots of virtue for future lives. When a person speaks falsely, it is witnessed and known by all; how much more so when they speak of having repeatedly committed sins? They will experience hardships and sufferings without exception. Therefore, it is said: "One fails to escape future lives; there is no evil one does not undergo."
"Better to eat glowing iron and swallow molten copper than, lacking precepts, to consume the faithful offerings of others.

As for "better to eat glowing iron," it is like taking a ball of iron that has been heated red by a fierce fire and swallowing it; it burns the lips, the tongue, the throat, and passes down through the belly, causing such suffering that one brings about one's own death. Yet, because of this, one does not enter the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm to undergo immeasurable suffering. Therefore, it is said: "Better to eat glowing iron and swallow molten copper."

Regarding those who do not observe the precepts yet consume the faithful offerings of others: these are people who, while outwardly bearing the dharma robes, inwardly harbor deceit and guile; they possess no sincere practice yet are arrogant and haughty toward others; knowing but little, they boast to the world and praise themselves, claiming that it is only natural for them to receive the faithful offerings of others, without considering that in future lives, myriad poisons will be inflicted upon their bodies.

Seeing those who maintain the pure conduct of Brahma-practitioners, they give rise to a mind of contempt; upon death, they invariably fall into evil realms. Their body, speech, and mind are incomplete, and they do not cultivate dignified deportment or ritual propriety; in their coming and going, they violate established prohibitions and limits. Seeing others obtain sustenance, they harbor a mind of jealousy;
upon death, they invariably suffer distress, for there is no sin that does not bring its retribution.
Therefore it is said: "One should not consume the faithful offerings of others without observing the precepts.
If a person fears suffering and does not delight in suffering, they should not commit evil deeds;
should they do so, they must immediately feel regret.
If a person fears suffering, they must not inflict suffering upon others, for one who inflicts suffering upon others will later receive its retribution.

This body is like the earth: according to what is sown, each receives its own fruit. It is the same for all classes of sentient beings; according to the sins they plant, they later receive their retribution. Human minds differ just as reflections do; when the suffering of sin pursues the body, there is no escape.
Therefore it is said: "If a person fears suffering, they should not take pleasure in suffering.
Do not commit evil deeds; do not inflict evil upon others. For when one benefits oneself, one thereby benefits others; how can one benefit others without first being able to benefit oneself?"

Whether in the midst of bustle or in quiet seclusion, whether great or small, visible or invisible, one should distance oneself from evil as one would avoid the conflagration at the end of an eon; therefore it is said: "Do not commit evil deeds; reflect upon them and repent immediately."
To commit evil with utmost sincerity—whether it has already been done, is being done, or is yet to be done—one cannot escape suffering; what benefit is there in seeking to avoid it?

As for those who commit evil with utmost sincerity, there may be some who have already done it, are currently doing it, or are about to do it. Having done it belongs to the past, doing it now belongs to the present, and about to do it belongs to the future. Committing evil throughout these three periods of time while remaining ignorant that suffering will arrive—for this reason it is said: "To commit evil with utmost sincerity, whether it has already been done or is yet to be done."

Regarding "one cannot escape suffering": among the various classes of sentient beings, their minds delight in doing evil and they do not realize that the retribution for future sins will arrive. Just as one who violates the prohibitions of a king in this present life is judged and punished according to the gravity of the offense, so too is it with the prohibitions of this internal Dharma. One practices evil without self-awareness, indulging the passions and relaxing the mind; therefore it is said: "One cannot escape evil—what benefit is there in seeking to avoid it?"
The King of Death, Yama, dispatches the jailer Ābāng to welcome the soul of the offender; with the body bound by five fetters, he is led before the King Yama.
The King asks the offender:
"Did you not see the first divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
The king then questioned the criminal:

"O man! When you were born among humans, as you passed through villages, towns, cities, and districts, did you see men and women with their parents holding them in their arms—unable yet to leave behind the discharge of urine and excrement—while their parents pushed aside the dry bedding to place them on the damp, bathing and washing them and rinsing and laundering their clothes? Did you see this?"
He replied, "I have seen it.
The king said to the criminal:
"Why do you not consider this?
Seeing the retribution for good and evil within this very life, you should exercise self-restraint and cultivate all wholesome dharmas by purifying your body, speech, and mind."

The sinner replied, "While dwelling among humans, I gave rein to my desires and acted with self-indulgence; being foolish, I did not recognize the truth. What I originally created, I now receive as its retribution.
The King said to the sinner:
"As you have said, you yourself originally created this; now you must undergo its retribution, so that those who are heedless may know that prohibitions are difficult to violate.
The karmic offenses you have committed were not created by your parents, nor by your brothers, your five kinds of relatives, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas."
At that time, King Yama instructed him with this first divine messenger; he then further instructed him with the second divine messenger:
"Have you seen the second divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
The king then questioned the criminal:
"O man! As you travel through villages, districts, towns, and cities in the human realm, have you seen men and women afflicted by severe illness, sitting or lying upon couches and mats?"
The sinner replied, “I have seen them. [The Buddha asked,] “How so, man?”
Why do you not reflect thus:
"Since the fault within these present phenomena is such as this, I shall be diligent and prudent, purifying my body, speech, and mind, and cultivating all wholesome dharmas"?
The sinner replied: "While dwelling among humans, I was negligent and self-indulgent; being foolish, I did not recognize the truth. What I originally created, I now suffer as its calamity."
The king said to the offender:
"As you have said, you yourself originally created this karma and must now receive its retribution; let this serve to make heedless people know that restraint is difficult to violate."

The offenses you have committed were not wrought by your parents, nor by your brothers, kinsmen, or relatives; they were not created by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor were they instigated by gods or people of the world.
At that time, having instructed him with these words regarding the second divine messenger, the king then further instructed him with the third divine messenger:
"Have you not seen the third divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
The king then questioned the criminal:

"O man! As you travel through villages, cities, towns, and districts in the human world, have you seen those who are elderly—walking with the aid of staffs, groaning, their backs bent and hair white, their teeth fallen out, their food and drink failing them, and their lives hanging by a thread?"
“Did you see it? The sinner replied, “Indeed, I saw it.”
The king asked the criminal:
"How is this, man! Why did you not think to yourself: "
"In this present life, such is the case; you should therefore be prudent and, purifying body, speech, and mind, cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
The sinner replied: "While dwelling among humans, I was heedless and self-indulgent, ignorant and failing to recognize the truth; what I originally created, I now suffer as its calamity."
The King said to the offender:
"As you have said, you yourself originally created this karma and must now receive its retribution; let those who are heedless know that prohibitions are difficult to violate."

The transgressions you have committed were not wrought by your parents, nor by your brothers, your five kinds of relatives, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas; nor were they instigated by the gods or the people of the world to be done by you.
When King Yama had thus instructed him with this third divine messenger, he then further instructed him with the fourth divine messenger:
"Have you seen the fourth divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
The king then questioned the criminal:
"What do you think, man?

As you travel through the human world, passing through cities, prefectures, counties, villages, and hamlets, have you seen men and women who have passed away, whose bodies—having been dead for one day, two days, or even up to seven days—are bloated, from which pus and blood flow, or who are being devoured by crows, magpies, tigers, and wolves?"
“Do you see it, or not? The sinner replied, “Indeed, I see it.”
“O man! Why do you not reflect thus:
‘In this present life, matters are such as these; I should be prudent and, purifying my body, speech, and mind, cultivate all wholesome dharmas.’”
The sinner replied: "While dwelling among humans, I was heedless and self-indulgent; being foolish, I did not recognize the truth. What I originally created, I now suffer as its calamity."
The king said to the sinner:
"As you have stated, you yourself originally created this karma and must now receive its retribution; let those who are heedless know that prohibitions are difficult to transgress."

The sins you have committed were not created by your parents, brothers, five types of relatives, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas; nor were they instigated by the gods or the people of the world to be done by you.
When King Yama had thus instructed him with this fourth divine messenger, he then further instructed him with the fifth divine messenger:
"Have you seen the fifth divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
The king then questioned the criminal:

"O man! As you travel through the human world, passing by cities, prefectures, counties, villages, and hamlets, have you ever seen men who were thieves and robbers caught by the king, and for whom his hands were severed, his feet were severed, his ears were cut off, or his noses were sliced away; who had their skin flayed alive, or had the sinews of their heads pulled out, or had their necks sawn with a saw, or had long stakes driven through their loins so that they protruded from their mouths, or had molten copper poured over their bodies, or had their limbs dismembered, or were hung upside down from trees for seven days before being shot to death with arrows, or had their heads bound with raw leather and were tied backhand on the bare earth and cast away into the wilderness, or had their bellies ripped open and their entrails drawn out and stuffed with grass?"
“Did you see it? He replied, “Indeed, I saw it.”
“O man! Why do you not reflect thus:
‘In this present life, matters are such as these; I should be prudent and, purifying my body, speech, and mind, cultivate all wholesome dharmas.’”
The sinner replied: "While dwelling among humans, I was heedless and self-indulgent; being foolish, I did not recognize the truth. What I originally created, I now receive as its retribution."
The King said to the offender:
"As you have stated, you yourself originally created this karma and must now receive its retribution; let those who are heedless know that prohibitions are difficult to violate."

The transgressions you have committed were not created by your parents, brothers, five types of relatives, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas; nor were they instigated by the devas or the people of the world to be done by you.

When King Yama had finished instructing him with this fifth divine messenger, he immediately handed the sinner over to the hell-wardens and led him to the place of the boiling cauldrons. Depending on the gravity of his offenses, he was made to enter one of the thirty-six boiling cauldrons, where he endured immeasurable suffering for kalpas.
Therefore it is said: What benefit is there in seeking to avoid [karma]?
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering among the rocks of the mountains, can one find a place where one may escape the calamities of past evil deeds.

In the past, when the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, Śrāvastī, King Virūḍhaka assembled the fourfold army and intended to march against the Śākyan kingdom. Leading his retinue, he deposed his father, the former king, and established himself as monarch.
There was an evil minister named Yeli who addressed King Virūḍhaka, saying:

"When Your Majesty was formerly a prince, you went to the home of your maternal relatives among the Śākyas; having arrived at the Buddha’s vihāra, you were insulted and humiliated by the sons of the Śākyas."
At that time, the king saw the decree:
"If I am to become king, I shall then reveal this matter.
Now the time has arrived, and the troops and horses are flourishing.
He immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared, intending to go and take revenge.

The Buddha, knowing his intention, arrived first at the side of the road and sat beneath a withered tree. At that time, King Liu-li personally led his troops to invade the country of Śākyas; encountering the Tathāgata on the way, he went forward to pay his respects and addressed the World-Honored One:
"There are many fine trees here with lush foliage; why have you abandoned them to sit beneath this withered tree?"
The Buddha told the king:

"The protection provided by one's five close relatives is profound and cannot be abandoned. In the past, when this tree was lush with flourishing branches and leaves, I once passed by here and obtained the strength of its shade."
The king immediately retreated and returned to his troops, addressing those above and below:
"We ought to turn back and not advance further. Why is this so?"
"The Tathāgata has today come for the sake of those five kinsmen; surely he must rely on his supernatural power and cannot be attacked.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"How could the Tathāgata remain seated beneath a tree forever?"

After the Tathāgata saw King Virūḍhaka depart, he knew that this karmic connection from past lives could not be avoided; using his knowledge of past lives, he observed its origins and perceived that the Śākya clan would inevitably suffer.
He immediately rose from his seat and departed, returning to the assembly of bhikṣus where he sat among the multitude.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw that the Tathāgata was feeling compassion for his five kinsmen as if he were filled with sorrow and anxiety; he went to the Buddha’s presence and addressed him, saying:
“Now King Virūḍhaka is attacking the kingdom of Śrāvastī; mindful that its people will suffer hardship, I wish to employ skillful means to rescue and protect that country.”

First, he lifted the country of Śrāvastī and placed it in the midst of empty space; second, he lifted the country of Śrāvastī and placed it within the great ocean; third, he lifted the country of Śrāvastī and placed it inside the belly of Mount Sumeru.
"Fourth, lift the people of the kingdom of Śrāvastī from beneath this ground and place them in another world-system,
so that King Virūḍhaka shall not know their location.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:

"Although you possess such wisdom, virtue, and immeasurable supernormal powers, you have merely brought peace and security to the people of Śrāvastī; how could you possibly remain at ease when facing an adversary?"
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana prostrated and withdrew.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, expounded upon this meaning, desiring to cause the True Dharma to endure long in the world and to demonstrate that past karmic retributions can never be avoided.
Upon hearing what he said, the great assembly was despondent and wept with grief; pitying King Liuli for the retribution of his past karma, they spoke these verses before the assembly:
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, Nor by entering the mountain clefts— Nowhere can one find a place To escape the calamities of past evil."
Sentient beings suffer affliction, unable to escape old age and death;
only those who are benevolent and wise do not dwell upon the faults or evils of others.

Regarding "sentient beings suffer affliction": if one sees another person engage in unrighteous deeds, a awakened bhikṣu should focus his mind on the five dharmas, and only thereafter inspire the resolve of others.

What are the five? First, being unable to fluently recite the sūtras for others; second, not having accomplished the precepts; third, not possessing concentration of mind; fourth, being foolish and lacking discerning wisdom; and fifth, not having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore it is said: "Sentient beings experience suffering and affliction; they cannot escape old age and death.

Only those who are benevolent and wise, wishing to restrain others, should first exercise self-restraint. If one is personally defiled yet seeks to restrain others, their actions will be mocked and ridiculed by others.

Therefore, the wise ultimately remain far removed from it. Among all bonds, none is more firm than the bond of objective conditions (*ālambana-pratigha*). The place of such bondage is the hells (*niraya*); yet there is no one who is truly bound—each receives their retribution according to the lightness or gravity of their offenses.
Therefore it is said:
Only those who are benevolent and wise do not dwell upon the faults or evils of others.
To falsely testify for the sake of seeking bribes, to conduct oneself with impropriety, and to slander and defame the virtuous—these are the ways of the unwise.
To punish the scholar with injustice, one binds this person with guilt and casts oneself into a pit.

Regarding those who seek bribes through false testimony: there may be sentient beings who do not measure themselves, who lack internal reflection, and who constantly seek out the faults of others; they rejoice at seeing what is wrong and do not follow what is good. In all their actions, they take the perverse to be right. Therefore it is said: "Seeking bribes through false testimony, one conducts oneself improperly."

Regarding those who slander and calumniate virtuous men: there may be good and benevolent people whose intent is to pursue learning, yet whose clothing does not cover their bodies and whose food does not suffice for their mouths; they are thus despised by the foolish, and their virtue is obstructed so that it cannot manifest. Because of this, they incur guilt and shall further pass through one hundred and thirty-six hells, going from one hell to another, where the suffering endured therein is beyond measure.
They take molten copper as food, boiling water from cauldrons as their dwelling, pus and blood as their fine meals, and marrow and brain as their unguents.

Once they have exhausted those karmic retributions, they enter the realm of animals, receiving various forms with differing dispositions—some high and some low—and subsisting on fodder and grass while bearing heavy loads; all this results from their aggressive and violent conduct in previous lives.

If one is born among the hungry ghosts (preta), they fill their bellies with air and pierce them with needles; the air within is released, yet it immediately fills the belly again, just as when looking through thin gauze, both the interior and exterior are clearly visible.
Therefore it is said: "To slander a virtuous man is to unjustly punish a gentleman.

For one bound by such offenses, the retribution follows the person like a shadow follows a form; they rush through the five realms of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering. Wherever they go, they are not free from the four bonds and five fetters. Even if they are born as humans, they are perpetually confined in prison and shackled; though their bodies are subjected to torture and flogging, they cannot find death.
Therefore it is said: "Bound by their own sins, they cast themselves into a pit."
Now, when a person cultivates conduct—whether it be good or evil—it is for their own sake, and thus they shall never come to ruin. As for what is meant by "a person cultivates conduct":

it refers to all classes of sentient beings who possess form; their mental thoughts, verbal expressions, and the actions of body, speech, and mind. Therefore, it is said: "A person cultivates conduct."

Regarding "the liked and the disliked," whether it be good or not good, beautiful or ugly, painful or pleasant, or even the pain of suffering and the pain of pleasure—all these are termed good and evil, and they all arise from one's conduct. Therefore it is said: "The liked and the disliked."

"Each acts for their own sake" means that when a person performs good or evil deeds—whether resulting in suffering or happiness, beauty or ugliness—they shall all receive the retribution thereof; no one can escape it. Good leads to rebirth in the heavens, while evil leads to entry into hell. Therefore it is said: "Each acts for their own sake."

In the end, there shall be no ruin or extinction; for the conduct of good and evil follows one another like a form and its shadow. Retribution arises from one's actions and never perishes. Even if heaven were to burn away and earth to melt, Mount Sumeru to collapse, the waters of the ocean to dry up, the sun and moon to fall to earth, and the stars to wither and fall, the retribution for good and evil would still never perish.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“In movement, turning, bending, or stretching, The shadow is ever closely attached; Whether rising or staying still, It never leaves its form.”
Not only does the shadow follow, but the form also follows the shadow; likewise, when one performs good or evil deeds, they are ultimately never separated.
Therefore, it is said that in the end, there is no destruction or extinction.
The person who is fond of grasping considers themselves capable; yet by grasping at others, they themselves perish. As for the person fond of grasping:
one should cultivate one's own person well, not dwell upon the faults of others, nor mock or disparage them, but rather choose the ground and grasp what is essential.

If one deceives others with falsehoods and untruths, throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes—dying here and being born there—one will constantly be deceived by others; transmigrating through successive retributions, one remains bound by attachments, receiving now the fruits of the actions performed in the past.
Just as planting a fruit tree yields bitter fruit from bitter seeds and sweet fruit from sweet seeds, so too is the retribution for good and evil:
goodness receives celestial blessings, while evil is rewarded with the hells.
Therefore it is said: "The person who delights in grasping considers themselves capable; yet they sink along with that which they grasp, and others likewise perish.
When one commits evil without ceasing, it is like being severed by a weapon; dragged away without awareness, one falls into an evil realm.
Only later, when suffering the retribution, does one realize one's former habits."

Regarding "one who commits evil does not arise": the deliberations of a fool do not coincide with the wholesome; day and night he gives rise to thoughts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, committing the ten unwholesome actions. Therefore it is said: "one who commits evil does not arise."
Just as when one is severed by a soldier, there is never again a mind that turns back to look;
why is this so? Because the foolish person forms this thought:
"The donor and patron were originally poor and destitute, yet those who are stingy and envious have instead become wealthy and noble.
Because of this, when the foolish see such a transformation, they cling to their views even more firmly and their minds do not open to awakening.
Therefore it is said: "Committing evil without ceasing is like being severed by a weapon.

To be "dragged away without awareness and already fallen into the evil realms" means that one does not recognize the good and evil deeds performed in this life and the next, nor does one consider that in the future there will be no protection; therefore it is said, "dragged away without awareness and already fallen into the evil realms."

Later, when he experienced the retribution of suffering, he finally realized his former habit: Long ago, there was a lay practitioner who instructed his family to eat pheasant meat. He would first place the pheasant meat in a cauldron and then seek fire to boil it; unaware, a snake fell into the cauldron.
Regarding the proper method for a layperson to eat, one must consult the teacher. If the teacher says,
"This is not to be eaten," yet the person does not follow the teacher's instruction and proceeds to eat it anyway.
After one night had passed, the snake venom manifested within him, and he finally questioned his teacher.
The teacher said, "Since you did not follow my instructions, what do you expect to happen?
At that time, the physician spoke a verse to him:
"Craving the taste, he consumed the poison; / Not following my former words, / He was beset by that poison, / And only later did he awaken.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly:
"One should do this and abandon that; for when a person commits evil, they die and enter hell, whereas those who practice virtue receive the blessings of the heavens.

Yet these sentient beings have existed for a long time, failing to reckon with the reality of impermanence and change; they do not accept the Tathāgata’s true and ultimate teaching, taking evil to be good and right to be wrong."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The mind of the fool is not awakened; Practicing evil, he does not follow my teaching.
He suffers the agonies of the hells, And only later does he remember the true instruction."

"Only after experiencing the retribution of suffering does one come to know one's former habits: the agony of being scorched and roasted in hell, the misery of hunger and famine as a hungry ghost, and the constant heavy suffering of an animal. Therefore it is said: 'Only after experiencing the retribution of suffering does one come to know one's former habits.'"
When a wicked person commits cruelty, sinking deeper into it repeatedly, they take pleasure in doing so;
yet the retribution for their sin follows naturally.
Long ago, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kosala was in a secluded hall and an empty chamber when this thought arose within him:
"What kind of sentient beings do not think of themselves?"
At that time, the king reflected again:
"Those who harbor evil and inverted thoughts in body, speech, and mind are said to be people who do not mind their own welfare.
How, then, does a sentient being mind their own welfare?"
"If there are sentient beings whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure, such persons are said to be mindful of themselves.

At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his secluded hall and quiet chamber, prepared his carriage adorned with precious feathers and gems, and set out with his retinue for the place where the World-Honored One was. Upon arrival, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and after a short while, withdrew slightly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just now, while in my secluded hall and quiet chamber, a thought arose within me:"
"Which sentient beings think of themselves?
Which sentient beings do not think of themselves?
At that time, World-Honored One!
Again, he reflected deeply:
"Those who harbor evil and inverted thoughts in body, speech, and mind are said to be people who do not mind their own affairs.
How, then, should sentient beings mind their own affairs?"
"If there are sentient beings whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure, it is said that such persons are mindful of themselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Prasenajit: "It is so! It is so!"
As Your Majesty has said:
those whose actions of body, speech, and mind are impure do not truly regard themselves;
whereas those whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure do indeed regard themselves.
Why is this so? Great King, you should know that those who do not mind their own welfare bring about their own decline and give rise to unwholesome states.
Those whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure act for their own true benefit.
"Why is this so? It is because that person has cultivated pure conduct.
At that time, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa spoke these verses:
“Those who habitually practice evil do not consider the conditions of future lives;
having committed evil, they themselves receive the calamity, and that calamity shall never perish from their bodies.
Therefore it is said: “The violent person commits cruelties, sinking deeper and increasing them again and again.”

If one is about to commit such acts and the retribution for their sins manifests naturally, they will receive that evil retribution wherever they are born: in the hells, they will suffer immeasurable flogging and whipping; among the hungry ghosts, they will suffer from ignorance and delusion; among animals, they will suffer as they repay their debts for their offenses; and if born among humans, they will suffer from deficient conduct.
Therefore it is said: "If one acts with a sense of pleasure, the retribution for the offense follows naturally.
When ordinary people commit evil, they cannot perceive it themselves; being foolish and seeking gratification, they later suffer the bitterness of torment.

When ordinary people commit evil and are unable to awaken to it themselves, these foolish commoners constantly harbor delusions; they indulge their passions in committing evil without being able to reform, nor do they know that they will receive retribution for it later. It is like a person traveling through a perilous mountain pass, with steep precipices on both sides, who passes through with eyes closed, unaware of the danger to his life and perhaps meeting his end.

This ordinary person is likewise so: born blind and devoid of wisdom, they do not know that they shall receive retribution in the future. Therefore it is said: "When an ordinary person commits evil, they are unable to awaken to it themselves."

Those who take pleasure in folly will later suffer the bitterness of distress. A wise person with clear vision beholds this as being like a great pit of fire on a path; when travelers pass by, they may not yet know the way. The one with clear sight points it out and says to the travelers:
"There is a great pit of fire in the middle of the road that cannot be crossed. You should rest your minds here and do not proceed further."

The men, their minds bold and arrogant, did not believe his words; they all stepped forward together and fell into the fire pit. Suffering extreme agony, they cried out to heaven, but even with their lamentations it was too late.
They said to one another: "We did not follow the instructions of the wise man; now that we suffer this pain, whom can we appeal to?"
The perversity of these sentient beings is likewise thus; they single-mindedly pursue the path of human existence, which is censured and halted by those of wisdom, who say:
"The path is full of hardships and is plagued by oppressive, poisonous pains; if you intend to press forward, you will inevitably encounter these afflictions and cannot escape their perils."
Therefore it is said: "The fool finds pleasure [in evil], yet later suffers the bitterness of its poison.
When a person commits evil, they set themselves ablaze; with tears streaming down their face, they later receive the retribution for it.
When a person commits evil, it is purely wicked and unwholesome; they neither reflect upon it nor take pleasure in it. For this reason, it is said that "the person who commits evil.

As for "burning oneself," if a person harbors a mind of regret and recognizes the affliction of sorrow and anxiety, they will dwell on these worries day and night until they become feverish with distress. Therefore, it is said: "The person who commits evil burns themselves."
"Tears flow down his face" means that he weeps in sorrow day and night; with disheveled hair and wild locks, he raises his voice in lamentation. Therefore it is said, "tears flow down his face."

As for receiving its retribution later, it is immeasurably bitter and painful, not to be desired or enjoyed; furthermore, there are countless sorrows, afflictions, hardships, and hundreds of thousands of anxieties. Therefore, it is said that one receives its retribution later.
When a person of auspicious character practices virtue, it accumulates and increases as they follow along; they perform it with a willing heart, and blessings respond naturally.

As for "a person of auspicious character practicing virtue," it is like someone who acts so as to reach their destined goal, being honored by devas and humans, praised for their virtue, and having their good reputation extolled until it is heard throughout the four quarters. Countless people come to make offerings to them; therefore, it is said: "A person of auspicious character practices virtue."

Regarding "growing together through association": day and night there is joy and celebration without any sorrow; the mind is glad and free from distress. Therefore it is said, "growing together through association."

To do so with a willing heart, such that blessings respond spontaneously, is like being born with a celestial body where blessings respond spontaneously: one’s palaces and dwellings number in the billions, colored in the five hues of black, yellow, blue, red, and white, with joy that is limitless. Or, if born among humans, one naturally enjoys the five pleasures, performing songs and music to delight oneself; the mind is serene and no disordered thoughts arise. Therefore it is said: "To do so with a willing heart, blessings respond spontaneously."

Committing evil in jest, having performed such bodily actions, one receives retribution with wailing and weeping; as the transgression follows, the punishment arrives. Regarding "committing evil in jest":

good and evil deeds all have varying degrees of gravity; they are created through body, speech, and mind, and are not of a single type alone. Sometimes, relying on one's own person, one commits evil in jest, harassing sentient beings so that they find no peace in their abodes; or using tiles, stones, knives, or weapons, one mutually inflicts injury upon others; or bringing others together to cause strife and litigation—just as people in the world delight in fighting rams, fighting cocks, fighting camels, fighting oxen, fighting men, and fighting elephants.
If one encounters others coming and going with insults and abuse, yet sees them with such joy that one cannot restrain oneself, then at the end of one's life, one will weep and suffer.

Therefore it is said: "One who commits evil in jest, having performed such bodily actions, shall receive retribution with wailing and lamentation; as the deed was done, so does the transgression arrive."
Evil does not manifest immediately, like milking a cow; the retribution for sin lies in wait, like fire covered by ashes.
"Evil does not manifest immediately" means that when a person performs an action, the retribution does not respond at once.

In the past, there was a foreign land where a plant called "immediate-effect" grew; if that grass were placed in milk, it would instantly turn into curd without the passage of time. Therefore it is said: "Evil does not manifest immediately, like the milking of a cow."
If it were not so, what would the meaning be? He replied:
"The fool is burned, and only then does he awaken."

"Sin lies in hidden observation, like fire covered by ashes. This means it is as if one covers fire with ashes; people do not perceive it, and when they step upon it with their feet, the heat gradually penetrates until they realize their feet are being burned.

These classes of sentient beings are also like this: while they are committing evil, they take pleasure in it with a willing heart; yet when their lives end and their bodies fall into the evil realms where the five poisons inflict torment upon them, they only then awaken to realize that their transgressions have reached their fruition.
Therefore it is said: "Sin lies in waiting in ambush, like fire covered by ashes.
Though evil does not manifest immediately, it is like that sharp sword; one must receive its retribution, for no thought was given to future lives.

Regarding those whose evil does not bear fruit immediately: there may be sentient beings who habituate themselves to the roots of evil; though their lives span a hundred years, they rely on their longevity and claim to be without fault, saying to one another:
"People say that committing evil brings retribution, yet we personally practice it and find our lives thus prolonged."

There were butchers and hunters who themselves gave rise to slander, saying: "The śramaṇa Gautama practices what is not true; he delights in practicing falsehoods and empty words of every kind. He instructs his disciples, saying:

'All those who kill living beings or harm people will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, enter the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo immeasurable suffering.'"
Therefore, the World-Honored One himself spoke this verse:
"Evil-doers are entangled by evil; Committing evil, they do not perceive it themselves.
When evil reaches its culmination, they realize evil has arrived; They receive suffering as the root-source of evil."
At that time, the butcher heard what the Buddha had said but still did not reform; therefore it was said:
"Evil does not manifest immediately, like that sharp sword; yet one need not worry about future lives, for its retribution shall surely be received."

When retribution arrives suddenly, one then realizes the consequences of evil; furthermore, one must undergo the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore it is said: "If one does not consider the future life, one shall receive its retribution."
Just as rust arises from iron and consumes its own body, so too do evils born in the mind return to destroy one’s own form. Regarding the phrase "just as rust arises from iron":

it is like pure iron or a bright, clear mirror that has been polished until it is immaculate and free of dust and grime. Yet, if the person who possesses it fails to store it securely—perhaps leaving it in the earth or in damp ground—then thick rust will soon arise; upon contact, it crumbles and scatters, becoming unfit for its original purpose.

It is like a sharp sword that people cherish and revere, which one constantly guards and keeps close to one's person; yet, through negligence or forgetfulness, it is placed insecurely and soon becomes covered in rust until the original iron is no longer present. Reflecting on this sword, one realizes it has become worthless; once ruined, it can no longer be used. Therefore it is said: "Just as iron produces rust, it consumes its own body."

That practitioner is likewise: shrouded and obstructed by greed and desire, they disregard the calamities and afflictions of future lives; they associate with evil companions and do not take the virtuous as friends. Because of this, their own calamities destroy their very roots; they do not cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), but are licentious and impure, thus inviting misfortune for themselves and reaping its retribution.
Therefore it is said: "Evil arising in the mind returns to harm one's own form.
*Udānavarga*, Volume Eleven; *Udānavarga*, Volume Twelve.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: On Faith Faith, shame, morality, intention, and wealth— These qualities bring praise from the noble.
This path is taught by the wise; in this way, one ascends to the heavenly realms.

Regarding those who possess the wealth of faith, shame, virtue, and intention: if among the people of this world there are sons or daughters of noble family who possess this wealth of faith, as well as the wealth of shame, conscience, virtue, and intention, they shall become uniquely honored and noble among hundreds of thousands of millions of beings. They will be revered by others, and beings will joyfully follow them, unable to part from them.
Therefore it is said: "Faith, shame, and the precepts are the treasures of the mind.

These dharmas are praised by the refined gentleman; for all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas, have attained the infinite perfections and possess no deficiency in their various practices, and are thus praised by the sages and saints. For this reason it is said: "These dharmas are praised by the refined gentleman."

Regarding the phrase "those of clear wisdom who expound this Way": those of clear wisdom are intelligent, astute, and sagacious; they are able to manifest that Way and eloquently explain its essential tenets.
What is meant by the "Way"?

Who is this "Path"? That which is called the Path is formless and soundless; its traces cannot be seen when sought. It is that which the wise tread, not that which the foolish practice; it is that which the pure cultivate, not that which the defiled and turbid perform. Therefore it is said: "This Path is what the wise proclaim."

Thus, for those who ascend to the world of the heavens, if people desire to seek merit and dwell in the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta), then faith, a sense of shame, learning, generosity, wisdom, and knowledge—all these constitute the path to birth in heaven.

There may be someone who possesses faith exclusively; if they are reborn in heaven because of that faith, their merit is not extensive. Or, one may be reborn in heaven because of a sense of shame and dread of blame, or because of precepts, or because of learning, or because of generosity, or because of wisdom. In such cases, their merit is not extensive, and the blessings they receive are so slight as to be hardly worth mentioning.

There are some sentient beings who, by merely observing the precepts, are reborn in the heavens; there they have only one celestial maiden, one musical performance, and their own body—these three—and sometimes the various devas share a single vessel of food.

If one is born in heaven by practicing a single deed, they raise their hand to eat black food and consume it while covering their mouth. If one is born in heaven by fulfilling a multitude of deeds, they raise their hand to eat white food and appear openly among the assembly without concealment. Those born in that heaven who have fulfilled the various precepts, possessing shame, modesty, virtue, and learning, are attended by innumerable celestial maidens; in palaces of the seven treasures, they indulge in all desires at will, performing music and song with supreme joy.
Therefore it is said: "Thus one ascends to the world of heaven.
The fool does not cultivate heavenly conduct, nor does he praise the giving of alms;
yet he who has faith and assists those who do good will go from this state to that peace."

The fool who does not cultivate the heavenly path is characterized by stinginess, envy, jealousy, and doubt; his mental nature is narrow and limited, and he lacks a mind for giving. Furthermore, he does not create the excellent field of merit that brings blessings in future lives, nor does he possess the courageous roots of various wholesome virtues. Therefore it is said: "The fool does not cultivate the heavenly path."

Nor do they praise those who practice giving; these foolish people do not give themselves, and when they see others giving, they become angry. They take pleasure in cultivating unwholesome karma and do not practice wholesome dharmas, instead associating with and following foolish teachings.

As it has been said: the fool does not delight in giving and is shunned by the wise. The foolish person clings to their own mind and nature with stubbornness; though they wish to bestow gifts, their mind ultimately does not awaken to it. The person of wisdom discerns that this is not essential; therefore, it is said: "Nor does one praise the act of giving."

Regarding "Faithful giving assists in goodness": when a wise person practices the giving of material wealth, their mind is not timid or weak; they believe that such giving brings merit, whereas stinginess and envy are considered diseases. Therefore it is said: "Faithful giving assists in goodness."

"To go from here to that peace" means: if one ascends from this world to the heavens and becomes a sovereign king there, or is born into the infinite nobility and wealth of the world, and by virtue of this attains entry into the extinction of *nirvāṇa*, being free from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death; being tranquil and eternally stilled, yet neither clinging nor falling into nihilism—it is for this reason it is said: "To go from here to that peace."
Faith is the leader of true persons; mindfulness of the Dharma brings peace of abiding;
those who draw near attain excellence of mind; wisdom is the life-span among all lifespans, the most noble.

Formerly, when the Buddha was dwelling in the realm of the Ālavī spirits, there was at that time in that country a violent spirit named Āḷavaka, who constantly devoured living people by the dozens every day until his slaves and servants were completely exhausted.
At that time, the people within that realm said to one another:

"We have been devoured by this evil ghost; those who have died are numerous, while those remaining are few. We ought to seek his pardon, and every household should provide one person each day for his kitchen as an offering; only then will there be a way to survive."

Then, according to what had been said, those people sought out the spirit and obtained its favor; they sent one person every day, first dispatching their slaves and servants until none remained, and subsequently sending their own children.

At that time, there was an elder named Naulāyana, who had always been childless. On that very day, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was exceptionally distinguished and rare in the world; his face was like a peach blossom, and one could never tire of gazing upon it. Furthermore, it was also the day when the *piśāca* (hungry ghost) to whom he was next due for a meal was due to appear. At that time, the elder possessed abundant wealth and many treasures; elephants, horses, and the seven precious gems were beyond measure, and his storehouses were filled with gold, silver, jewels, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli—priceless objects in abundance.
The elder went in person through the streets and alleys seeking to buy male and female slaves to provide for that ghost, but he could find none.
At that time, the elder turned toward Heaven, Earth, and all the deities, seeking their compassionate pity, crying out:
"Alas! How can you let me lose my heavenly protector!"
"Today I have given birth to but one son, fulfilling my vow; today, I shall next feed that evil ghost.
She then called out from afar to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One:
"May you look upon me with compassion and deliver me from this suffering and distress."

At that time, the World-Honored One, possessing the three insights and six supernormal powers, knew that the householder’s mind was burning with distress and that he had no one to rely upon. By means of his spiritual power, he went to that realm of ghosts, arriving just as the Āḷavaka ghost was gathering a great assembly of ghosts and proceeding to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings.
At that time, there was a Kettara ghost who, while traveling through the air above that realm of ghosts, was unable to pass despite exerting all his strength and power. He thought to himself:
"By my own strength and power, I can move mountains and fly over peaks, overturning heaven and earth; wherever my divine power reaches, there is no obstruction."
"I have often passed by this way before without any difficulty; why is it that today I have met with such an obstacle?

He then descended from the air and approached the demon's dwelling. Seeing from afar the World-Honored One’s radiant marks clearly manifest, he immediately came forward, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew. Arriving at that realm of the Great Assembly of Demons, he spoke to the demon Āḷavaka:
"O worthy one, you have now quickly obtained a great and wholesome benefit."
"Why is this? Because the Great Śramaṇa Gautama dwells within your realm.
Upon hearing this, the evil spirit’s wrath flared up, and he spoke to himself with both mind and mouth:
"While I was away, I was treated with contempt by those śramaṇas.
He said to that Kheṭaka ghost:
"I shall now return home to fight with the śramaṇas; if I am victorious, there will be no more śramaṇas; but if I am defeated, I shall simply perish and cease to exist in this world."
The yakṣa general Ālambā returned to his own realm, and having arrived, he said to the World-Honored One:
"Depart quickly, śramaṇa!
There is no need to remain."
The Tathāgata emerged according to those words.
“Return and enter as a śramaṇa!
The Tathāgata entered according to those words.
This was repeated three times.
The World-Honored One said:
"I have followed your wishes by coming out and entering three times; however, there are further advances and retreats that do not follow your wishes."
The ghost said:
“World-Honored One!

If this śramaṇa does not come forth, I shall question him on the meaning [of the Dharma]. If he does not answer the meaning, I shall split open the śramaṇa’s belly and drink his blood; I shall cause boiling blood to gush from his mouth and face, and I shall seize your arm and shake you across the river.”
The Tathāgata replied,
"I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Brahmā, Māra, noble being, deva, or non-deva who could pierce my belly or cause boiling blood to gush from my mouth and face."
"If you wish to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma, now is precisely the right time; I shall explain it to you one by one.
He then addressed the Tathāgata in verse, asking:
"Among human karmas, which is supreme?"
What practice leads to joy?
What is the essential for one seeking liberation?
What is the supreme life among all lives?
The World-Honored One addressed him with a verse:
"Faith is the foremost of true persons; Abiding in mindfulness of the Dharma, one dwells in peace.
One who draws near attains excellence of mind; Wisdom is the life-span among all lifespans, and is the most noble."

At that time, having heard the true meaning of the Buddha’s teaching, the spirit Āḷavaka’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened. He immediately prostrated himself before the Tathāgata with his five limbs touching the ground and took refuge, saying:

“I now take refuge at the feet of the Great Śramaṇa; I take refuge in the Dharma and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. From this day forward, I shall no longer kill living beings; may I be accepted as an upāsaka.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Welcome, worthy sir!
You may receive and practice the five precepts from the Tathāgata, whereby you shall obtain immeasurable karmic fruits in this present life."
The ghost said to the Buddha:
"Since I have received this ghostly body, I have always eaten living people and not the flesh and blood of the dead. If I were to practice and uphold the five precepts, how could I preserve my life?"
The Buddha told the spirit:

"To the north of here, there are immeasurable sentient beings. In that land, it is customary for the sovereign, ministers, parents, and kinsmen to scarify their faces with knives when someone dies, or to scarify their chests and lips until blood gushes forth like a spring. You may eat this; thus you shall not violate the precepts and will preserve your life."
He immediately received the five precepts.
As an upāsaka, for as long as his life lasted, he did not kill living beings, nor did he conceive thoughts of killing, nor did he instruct others to kill.
The capable one replied:
"Uposatha. As an upāsaka, for the duration of his life, he must not take what is not given, nor think of taking it, nor instruct others to take it.
The capable one replied:
"I can. As an upāsaka, for the remainder of his life, he shall not engage in sexual misconduct by violating the wives of others, nor shall he incite others to engage in sexual misconduct.
The capable one replied:
"I shall. As an upāsaka, for the remainder of his life, he must not speak falsely, nor must he teach others to speak falsely or incite strife between this party and that.
The capable one replied, "Yes, I will.
Having become an upāsaka, for the remainder of his life he must not drink alcohol, must not taste alcohol, and must not teach others to drink alcohol.
The capable one replied, "Ubin.

Then the householder Āḷavaka, the father of Naūlā, personally took his son in his arms, bathed and washed him, dressed him in new clothes, and brought him to the realm of the spirits to hand him over to the General of the Spirits.

At that time, the ghost, having received it, presented it to the Buddha; the Buddha, having received it in turn, presented it to his father. They passed it from hand to hand, and it was called "Hand-Jewel" (Hastaratna).
On account of his son, he spoke this verse:

"The one with faith is the elder among true persons; dwelling in mindfulness of the Dharma, they abide in peace. Those who draw near find their minds uplifted; wisdom is the life-span among those who live."
The Buddha’s sūtra says:
“He addressed the bhikṣus:

‘If you see a wealthy and noble elder who possesses abundant riches and many treasures, complete with the seven precious gems and lacking nothing, you should think to approach him and speak subtly of the teachings of the Way, discussing generosity, discipline, and the virtues for rebirth in heaven; such various practices have faith as their primary source.’”
Therefore it is said: "Faith is the foremost of true persons.
As for "dwelling in peace through mindfulness of the Dharma," one who is mindful of the Dharma shall receive happiness.
Happiness has two meanings:
first, worldly happiness; second, ultimate happiness.
Worldly happiness refers to that of the heavens and the human world.
The bliss of the ultimate truth is that which takes the four dhyānas of the noble ones as its joy.
One who contemplates the Dharma attains these two kinds of bliss; therefore it is said: "One who dwells in the contemplation of the Dharma abides in peace."

Recently, I have come to understand that within the cycle of birth and death’s continuous flow, which revolves again and again, only integrity, trustworthiness, and truthfulness are held as supreme. If a person speaks falsely, while alive their own clan will never be harmonious; after death they enter hell, where a thousand plow-oxen till their tongue. They undergo immeasurable suffering among hungry ghosts and animals, and even if they are reborn as humans, they are constantly subjected to slander and their words are not trusted.
Therefore it is said: "The one who is near attains the superior mind.

Among those whose life is wisdom, the wise person receives various fruits of realization throughout the world without limit; they forever relinquish the life of birth and death and advance toward the life of the noble sages.

The noble and sagely one whose life is wisdom constantly dwells in hundreds of thousands of meditative concentrations; when questioned according to the capacity of others, he is able to provide the appropriate response.
Therefore it is said: "Among those whose life is wisdom, the wise are the most noble."
"Through the wealth of faith one attains the Path; by oneself one reaches the Nirvāṇa of the Dharma.
Through hearing the good, one obtains wisdom; all bonds are thereby released. Regarding "through the wealth of faith one attains the Path":

the noble ones possess unwavering faith and never depart from the Triple Gem. They single-mindedly recollect the Buddha and cultivate the practice of an Arhat. With a sincere heart, they recollect the Buddha and the merits therein created. If a person with a faithful heart were to direct their faith toward a hundred persons practicing for the fruit of Srotāpanna, a hundred persons practicing for the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, or a hundred persons practicing for the fruit of Anāgāmin, it would not equal directing their faithful heart toward a single Arhat. While those practicing for the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Anāgāmin all attain rebirth in heaven, one who has faith in an Arhat believes in the path to Nirvāṇa. Therefore it is said: "Through the wealth of faith one attains the Path; by oneself one reaches the Nirvāṇa of the Dharma."

"Regarding 'one who gains wisdom through hearing well': this refers to one who receives the teacher’s instruction from beginning to end, thoroughly investigating and clarifying its meaning and flavor, upholding the doctrine through contemplation so as not to lose the original limit.

Long ago there was a bhikṣu named Vajra, who delighted in practicing the extraordinary and sought out wondrous arts; he received the Dharma from his teacher and did not lose its underlying principles."

The bhikṣu had not yet fully mastered his teacher’s instructions. One evening, after the teacher had met a guest outside and returned home intoxicated, he sat down upon the bed; the leg of the bed immediately broke. Fearing that his teacher would fall over, the bhikṣu took up the bed with his body and carried it for the entire night until dawn.
He asked his disciple, "What are you doing? The disciple replied:
"The Master returned yesterday evening drunk and sat upon his bed; the leg of the bed broke, and I supported the bed with my body.
The Master was moved by his intent and said, "I possess certain skills that I shall teach you in their entirety; I will never begrudge them to you."
The technique having been mastered, the Master again tested his resolve.
The Master drank a salt broth and immediately spat it onto the ground, commanding his disciple to eat it; the disciple was then about to eat it.
The Master seized him and stopped him, saying, "Your arts are now perfected; all will be auspicious and nothing unfavorable.
He then recalled the words of the Buddha’s admonition: "By hearing the good, one attains wisdom."

Truly significant are these words: "All bonds are liberated. This means that those who have attained liberation are able to sever all seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and nine fetters (*saṃyojana*). Having eternally exhausted them without remainder, they have abandoned and detached themselves from all bonds and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Therefore it is said: "All bonds are liberated."
Faith and precepts—if one possesses wisdom and can practice them, the steadfast man crosses over anger and is thereby liberated from the abyss. Regarding "faith and precepts":

when that practitioner upholds faith, observes the precepts, and maintains a mind free from distracted thoughts, being fully endowed with these two practices, he is honored and revered by sentient beings; he strides alone among the great assembly without peer, like the full moon amidst the host of stars.

If one draws near to and cultivates sincere faith, in whatever place one is born, one will abound in wealth and treasures; with elephants, horses, and the seven precious gems, one shall never suffer from lack. This is because such faith is difficult to obstruct or destroy.

Furthermore, if a practitioner maintains the precepts without deficiency, cherishing and practicing them with diligent effort day and night—like one who carries a sword or treads upon ice, guarding the prohibitions and precepts without any lapse—they shall become a leader among countless sentient beings. Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they will be reborn in a good realm, in the heavens. Therefore, it is said: "Faith and the Precepts."
One who can practice with a wise mind ensures that body, speech, and thought are not harmed; through contemplation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they gather all distracted thoughts.
The Tathāgata spoke this verse:
"To be complete in the three karmas, to sit upright with single-minded focus, to recite much without weariness, and to assist in the performance of duties—these are called the three."
Furthermore, there are three types of action:
first, giving; second, observing precepts; and third, contemplation. These are called the three. Faith belongs to giving;
the precepts encompass non-killing; and meditative concentration encompasses contemplation. Therefore, it is said that wisdom enables the mind to act.

"The heroic man crosses over anger": the "heroic man" refers to one who has established the faculties and attained mastery, having entered the realm of the noble ones (ārya). His resentment and wrath have forever ceased and do not arise; he is pure within and without, like celestial lapis lazuli. Having accomplished what was to be done, he will not again dwell in a womb. Endowed with all wisdom, his inner self is already purified, and he tirelessly transforms others externally. Therefore it is said: "The heroic man crosses over anger."
Those who emerge from this abyss and are able to possess these manifold virtues are rare indeed. Why is this so?

Because they have been liberated from bondage and attachment; even when their lives come to an end, their reputations will spread far and wide. Therefore it is said: "From this, one emerges from the abyss."
Faith causes precepts to be perfected; it also brings longevity and wisdom. Wherever one can practice them, one will be nurtured everywhere.
As for "faith causes precepts to be perfected," who is it that accomplishes faith and precepts?
He replied:
"The noble ones are the srotāpanna and the sakṛdāgāmin.
As for ordinary persons, what they have already attained is lost again."

The reason for this is entirely due to greed, hatred, and delusion; it is caused by associating with evil associates and failing to associate with virtuous teachers, thereby losing the proper time, losing the fruit, and losing the person.

Those who have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin are not trodden upon by such things; even if one were to manifest in the form of a Buddha to test them, performing various transformations, their minds would not waver, nor would they be overcome by him.

Formerly, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a preeminent householder who possessed abundant wealth and treasures; his elephants, horses, and seven kinds of precious goods filled his storehouses. Yet, being stingy and greedy by nature, he was unwilling to practice charity.

Whenever anyone came to beg, he would not allow them to enter the inner quarters; he guarded the gates with great firmness, installing seven layers of double doors. He plastered the walls with stone dust for fear that mice might burrow through them, covered the roofs with iron cages to prevent birds from flying in, and kept no dogs in the house for fear they might damage the rice and grain.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Go to the house of the householder Jayanta.

Then, respectfully receiving the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the city of Śrāvastī, arriving at the householder's home where he addressed him:
“The Tathāgata constantly teaches that when a person gives alms to those who are destitute, they obtain five merits. What are these five?
First, longevity; second, physical beauty; third, strength; fourth, happiness; and fifth, eloquence.”
"Those who give alms shall obtain these five virtues.
The elder thought to himself:

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is of lofty talent and vast learning; the sūtras he expounds would not be surpassed even by eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of elephants carrying them. Yet today, when a disciple renowned for his great learning comes to my house, he speaks only of giving alms and is greedily attached to wealth and goods. This is the way of a beggar, not that of a wise and virtuous man."

At that time, Ānanda extensively gathered the meanings of the sūtras and adapted them to suit the occasion for that elder; however, the elder’s mind was as hard as steel and could not be moved, so he said to Ānanda:
"Is there a place where you have been invited today?"
"Is it because you wish to go begging for alms?
Ānanda replied, "There is no place where we have been invited; we must now go begging for alms."
The householder then said to Ānanda, "The sun is already approaching midday; you should know that it is time.
Ānanda immediately rose and departed, going to other houses to beg for food.
Returning to the place where the World-Honored One was, he said to the World-Honored One:
"The householder Mātsarya is firm in his resolve and cannot be subdued.
On the following morning at dawn, the Buddha addressed Aniruddha, saying:
"Go to that place and subdue the miserly and greedy elder.
Having received these instructions, Aniruddha went immediately to the elder’s house and met with him. He gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the elder, saying:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha constantly teaches this Dharma: if a person practices giving to those who are destitute, they shall obtain immeasurable merit; in both the present life and future existences, they will receive natural abundance as their reward."
The elder thought again:

"I have heard that Anuruddha abandoned his noble status to leave the household life and practice the Way, yet he constantly receives offerings of five hundred bowls of food without ever feeling satisfied. Now he has come to my house to urge me to give alms; he is merely a beggar, not acting according to the dharma of a worthy man."
He then said to Anuruddha, "The sun is about to reach its zenith; you should know that it is time.
Anuruddha immediately rose and departed, going to another house to beg for alms.
Returning to the place where the World-Honored One was, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Elder Mātsarya is firm in his resolve and cannot be subdued.
The Buddha then spoke again to Mahākāśyapa:
“Go and subdue the stingy and greedy elder.
Kāśyapa accepted the instruction and went to that elder’s house to meet him. He then preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the elder, saying:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha constantly teaches that if a person practices giving, they will obtain five merits and will be loved and respected by others wherever they are born.”
The householder thought to himself:

"When this man was formerly a layman, he plowed his fields with nine hundred and ninety-nine oxen, possessed sixty baskets of gold and grain—each basket containing three hundred and forty *hu*—and had as his wife the foremost virtuous woman of the country of Kāmpilya. Having renounced such wealth and status to become a śramaṇa, why does he now go to other houses like a beggar, praising the merit of giving while remaining attached to material goods?"
Kāśyapa employed countless skillful means to preach the Dharma for him, yet his mind remained unopened and he did not change his resolve. [The Buddha] said to Kāśyapa:
"Is it noon today? Is there a place where you have been invited to receive offerings?"
"Is it because you wish to go begging for alms?
Kāśyapa replied, "There is no place where I am invited; I shall now go begging for alms."
The householder said to Kāśyapa,
“Please know that now is the time.
He immediately rose and departed to visit other households, then returned and informed the World-Honored One.
"That man clings to his mind and heart; he is difficult to deter or break.
The Buddha again addressed Maudgalyāyana:
"Go to that stingy and greedy elder."
Maudgalyāyana accepted the instruction and immediately went to that elder’s house. Upon meeting him, he spoke to him about giving:

“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha constantly teaches this Dharma: ‘If a person gives alms to those who are destitute, they will obtain immeasurable merit; in both the present life and future existences, they will receive natural abundance as their reward.’”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there are sentient beings who understand the karmic fruit of giving, and having left behind the remnants in their final alms-bowl, they do not consume them but instead open their minds to bestow them as a gift—encountering a field of merit that is a worthy, noble, and auspicious one—I bear witness that their virtue is immeasurable."
The elder thought to himself:

"I have heard that this man possesses unimpeded supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), able to move mountains and fly over peaks, overturning heaven and earth, or even bringing worlds from other quarters into this land while the beings therein remain unaware. Yet he cannot manifest even a single supernormal feat for me; instead, he speaks only of the blessings of giving. This must be because he harbors stinginess and greed in his heart. He is a beggar, not a worthy sage."
Maudgalyāyana continued to preach the Dharma, yet he did not clarify its meaning. [The other] said to Maudgalyāyana:
"It is now midday; is there a place where you have been invited?
Or do you intend to go for alms?"
"You should know that this is the time.
He then went to another household.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
"Go to that stingy and greedy householder.
He then accepted the instruction and went to the householder; having met with him, he sat to one side and addressed the householder, saying:
"A man of wisdom and discernment should distinguish four things."
What are the four knowledges?
First, the discernment of giving; second, associating with virtuous friends; third, remaining free from stinginess and envy; and fourth, the mindful cultivation of wisdom and penetration.

The elder thought to himself: "I have heard that this man, at the age of eight, surpassed all others in debate; by sixteen, he had mastered every book in Jambudvīpa such that nothing remained unopened. He has extensively studied the past and present, elucidating the profound and abstruse; he has attained complete mastery in astronomy, geography, records, chronicles, and portents, as well as the Brahminical arts of calendrical calculation. Among the disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama, he is foremost in wisdom. I expected him to preach the subtle teaching of wisdom, yet now he speaks instead of the virtue of giving. He is but a beggar, not a worthy sage."
He said to Śāriputra: "Is there a place where you have been invited?
Or do you wish to go for alms?"
"You should know that this is the time.
Śāriputra immediately returned to where the World-Honored One was, approached the Buddha, and said:

"That man is stingy and greedy, his mind firmly grasped; he has piled wood as high as the heavens and set it ablaze, yet because his mind has not been melted away, his disposition has not changed. I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to descend in person to that elder’s home, manifesting the Buddha’s majestic power to remove his stinginess and dispel his ignorance."

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the brief interval it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm, arrived at the house of the elder and sat in the central courtyard. When the most excellent elder saw the World-Honored One arrive, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the householder:
"When a person practices giving, they obtain five great merits.
The householder addressed the Buddha:
“How does one obtain the five great merits through giving?
The Buddha told the householder:
“The first gift is that which consists of not killing living beings; this, householder, is called the first gift.”
If there are sentient beings who uphold the precept against killing, they will cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and shall have no fear; this is called the foremost gift.
The elder thought to himself:
"People kill living beings because of poverty and low status; now that my household abounds in wealth and treasures and I may indulge in whatever I desire, why should I go on killing living beings?"
"These words are excellent; we shall follow their teaching.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to take refuge in person and receive the Buddha's precepts; for the rest of my life, I dare not commit the taking of life."
The Buddha again addressed the householder:
"One does not commit taking what is not given.

If there are sentient beings who uphold the precept against taking what is not given, they will cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and will have no fear; this is called the second great gift."
The elder thought to himself:

"Those who steal the property of others do so because of poverty and low status. Now, within my own home, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, gold, silver, and various jewels—musaragalva, agate, coral, and amber—fill my storehouses. Why would I steal the property of others?"
"These words are excellent; I shall follow your teaching.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to take refuge in the Buddha's person and receive his precepts; for the rest of my life, I shall not violate the precept against stealing."
The Buddha again addressed the householder:
"If there are sentient beings who do not commit theft, they will cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and will have no fear; this is called the second gift."
The Buddha again addressed the elder:

"One must not engage in sexual misconduct by violating the wives or daughters of others. If there are sentient beings who uphold the precept against sexual misconduct, they will cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and will have no fear; this is called the third great gift."
The elder thought to himself:

"One who has no wife commits adultery; yet within my own household, the female attendants and retinue already number in the tens of thousands, and even if I wished to take more as my favorites, my desires would still not be satisfied—how much less should I violate the wives and daughters of others?"
"These words are excellent; we shall follow their teaching.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to take refuge in the Buddha personally and receive his precepts, and for the rest of my life, I shall not commit sexual misconduct."
The Buddha again addressed the elder:
"If there are sentient beings who do not commit sexual misconduct, they cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and are free from fear; this is called the third great gift."
The Buddha again addressed the householder:
"Not to speak falsely—this is called the great gift.
The householder thought to himself:

"As for why people in this world engage in false speech, it is because they are poor and lowly and cannot sustain themselves; thus, they take up the practice of empty claims, deceit, and guileful artifice, and so they speak falsely."
"I now possess countless accumulated wealth within my home, extending for one hundred million *li*; how could I speak such a falsehood?
These words are excellent; I shall follow your teaching.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I vow that I shall personally take refuge and receive the Buddha’s precepts, and for as long as my life lasts, I shall not commit the offense of false speech.
The Buddha told the elder:
“One who does not commit false speech covers all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and is free from fear; this is called the fourth great gift.”
The Buddha again addressed the householder:
“One must not drink alcohol; this is called the fifth great gift.
The householder thought to himself:
"A person who drinks alcohol incurs thirty-six faults; there is no ruin of states or destruction of families that does not stem from wine.
If I drink, when guests arrive, there will be clamor and disturbance; furthermore, it wastes my wine and leads to quarrels and strife."
"These words are excellent; we shall uphold the Buddha's teachings.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to take refuge in person and receive the Buddha’s precepts, and for as long as my life lasts, I shall not commit the transgression of drinking alcohol."
The Buddha told the householder:
"If there are sentient beings who do not consume alcohol, they will cover all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and shall have no fear; this is called the fifth great gift."
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
