"According to the prohibitions observed by us non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners, when a disciple serves a teacher and receives their instructions, they must repay the teacher's kindness regardless of its magnitude; they should provide wealth and treasures to supply whatever the teacher requires."

He personally entered the storehouse to select white cotton cloth, intending to take the inferior quality for an offering to the Buddha; however, whatever he grasped would invariably turn out to be of the highest quality. After repeating this process dozens of times, he could not find even a single piece of poor quality. His mind and mouth contended with one another, as his stinginess and greed were so deep-seated that his resolve remained unopened.

At that very time, the asuras and the Trāyastriṃśa devas were engaged in battle; sometimes the asuras prevailed while the devas were defeated, and sometimes the devas prevailed while the asuras were defeated.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and stainless divine eye, beheld the gods and asuras engaged in battle; he further saw the mind of generosity and the mind of stinginess contending within the elder, wherein sometimes the mind of generosity prevailed while the mind of stinginess was defeated, and at other times the mind of stinginess prevailed while the mind of generosity was defeated.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Giving and fighting do not coincide; the mind of wisdom does not dwell in such karma.
This is the time for giving, not the time for fighting. Give quickly—why hesitate?"
When the eminent householder heard these verses spoken by the Tathāgata, he felt inward shame and remorse; he immediately brought out white cotton cloth, knelt down, and received the blessing.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One gradually expounded for him the subtle and wondrous Dharma, discoursing upon sublime conduct.

As for the discourse, it was the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he taught that] sensual desire is impure, and the outflows (*āsrava*) are a great affliction.

Having heard this, the householder immediately, while still seated, had all dust and defilement cleansed away and attained the pure Dharma-eye. He attained the Dharma, acquired the Dharma, became perfected in the Dharma, and having discerned all phenomena, he reached fearlessness regarding the Tathāgata’s teaching. Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I wish to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*); for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing."
The Tathāgata silently gave his consent.
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Having received the three refuges, the Tathāgata immediately rose from his seat and departed.

Not long after the Buddha had departed, the evil Māra Pāpīyān transformed himself into the likeness of the Buddha and came to the house of the elder. His body was endowed with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor signs, and his purple-golden halo extended seven feet around him. Upon seeing this, the elder thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has just left; how can he have returned so quickly?"
He paid homage to him with the same reverence as if he were seeing the Buddha himself and asked,
"I wonder what instructions the Tathāgata has for me?
The counterfeit Buddha replied:

"I said that you, Elder, possess lofty talent and vast wisdom, discerning the nuances of the faculties; yet, upon careful reflection, I see that you are deluded and devoid of wisdom. The Four Truths I previously expounded were not actually the ultimate truths; they were merely the inverted doctrines practiced by the non-Buddhists."
The elder immediately perceived that this was a deception and replied to him:
"Stop, stop! Do not speak further!
I have attained the eye of wisdom and stand upon firm ground; even if you were to manifest a thousand million bodies and come before me, wishing to cause my mind to regress, it would be impossible."

How could one compare the light of a firefly to the brilliance of the sun? How could a mound in a farmer’s field be likened to Mount Sumeru? While owls, vultures, crows, magpies, and golden birds fly together, you, with your defiled form and deceitful, false body—if you are a magician, you should not linger long; if you are Pāpīyān, you ought to return at once.
When the evil Māra Pāpīyān heard these words, he was ashamed of his form and his shadow; he immediately restored his body and departed by the same path.

If sentient beings who have accomplished faith and precepts are never thwarted by Māra, how much less could there be any falling back for those who have attained the stages of Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin?
This matter is not so.

Abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has not yet been examined by the Path; thus, upon seeing this illusory form, there may be regression, and consequently, no accomplishment.
An ordinary person might first achieve [a state] and later regress; therefore it is said: "Faith causes precepts to be accomplished."

Furthermore, one who possesses longevity and wisdom is able to practice giving to its ultimate conclusion; during this process, they harbor no distracted thoughts. Regarding the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the Truths by a *srotāpanna*, these are permanently severed without remainder through the mind of giving. With the exception of seven deaths and seven births in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and one death and one birth in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), all other future births are forever exhausted without remainder.

As for the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner): by means of the mind of giving, they have attenuated the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths, as well as lust, anger, and delusion; having eliminated one death and one birth within the desire realm, all other future births are forever exhausted without remainder.

The *anāgāmin* has, through the mind of giving, eternally exhausted without remainder the fetters abandoned by insight into the truths within the three realms and the fetters abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm. Having relinquished birth in the desire realm, with the exception of one death and one birth in the form and formless realms, they will never again take birth in any other state. Free from stinginess and envy, their minds harbor no thoughts of craving or attachment to worldly glory; they are endowed with manifold wisdom and do not meet an untimely death. For this reason, it is said that they possess both longevity and wisdom.

"Wheresoever one is able to practice": the wise person who practices takes edification as their fundamental purpose; wherever they intend to go—whether east, west, south, or north—they invariably bring benefit and initiate Buddhist activities. Therefore, it is said: "wheresoever one is able to practice."

"Seen being sustained everywhere" means that once one has reached that realm, one is seen and provided for by sentient beings; wherever one may be, one distributes the transformative teachings of the Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "seen being sustained everywhere."
As for worldly profit, wisdom and faith constitute true knowledge; these are the supreme treasures, whereas family wealth is impermanent.
Regarding "as for worldly profit," worldly profit refers to the human body within the land of Jambudvīpa.
For what reason is it called "worldly benefit"?

It refers to the people of Jambudvīpa, because within this Jambudvīpa appear the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and divine immortals who have attained the Way and practice the *pāramitās*. If people in this world perform good deeds of body, speech, and mind, and further achieve the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) here, knowing the existence of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they will no longer be deluded or defiled by worldly dust and toil; even when their lives end, they shall leave behind no lingering affliction.
Therefore it is said: "Wisdom and faith constitute wisdom.

One who possesses both faith and wisdom is able to fulfill the eighty thousand practices. Faith governs the root of the mind, while wisdom adorns the body; faith leads to great wealth, while wisdom results in the realization of the fruit. Therefore it is said: "Wisdom and faith constitute wisdom."

Regarding this "supreme treasure among riches," that which is the truest among treasures is the treasure of wisdom. It is the most excellent and supreme, with nothing surpassing it; it is the highest and most subtle, beyond all analogy for comparison. Therefore, it is said: "This is the supreme treasure among riches."
Regarding those whose family fortunes are extraordinary: though their worldly wealth may be vast, there will inevitably come a time of decline and loss.
Within the city of Śilāgṛha, there were three householders; the first was named Śreṣṭhin, a man of a different surname.
The second was named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and the third was named Vappa.

These three were brothers by birth. They possessed abundant wealth and jewels, with property beyond measure; they lacked for nothing in elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, and neither government officials, thieves, nor calamities such as water and fire could infringe upon or deceive them.
There was a brahmin who observed the *elāpattra* dragon fast, hoping for wealth, nobility, abundant riches, and many treasures.
At that time, the dragon manifested his form and said to the brahmin:
"Why do you now exert your body and afflict your person, eating only wind and drinking only dew, cutting off grain and eliminating flavors? For what purpose do you observe this fast here?"
The brahmin replied,
"The reason I observed the fast with the dragon at the divine spring was in the hope of attaining great wealth and acquiring precious treasures.
The Dragon King replied:
"Do you not hear? I have two names: the first is Elāpattra, and the second is Asaṃtuṣṭa."
"Since you are named 'Insatiable,' do you still have further requests from me? The brahmin replied,
"If you do not grant me a favor, I shall die right here and be unable to return home empty-handed."
The Dragon King immediately brought forth fine purple-gold and gave it to the Brahmin, saying:

"Within the city of Śilāgṛha there is a wealthy and influential elder, a native of India whose family name is so-and-so and whose personal name is so-and-so. Go to his house, give this gold to him, and seek wealth from him."
Then the brahmin, having received the gold, departed and went to the house of that elder, where he brought out the gold and showed it to him.
Upon seeing the gold, the elder said to him:
"Hide this away so that no one sees it."
He then went to the inner quarters and summoned his five kinsmen, saying, "This man escorted me a great distance and gave this gold to me.

His kinsmen feasted and enjoyed themselves, storing the gold within their treasury; however, all the miscellaneous items in the treasury sank into the earth and returned to that dragon’s treasury. Not only one family, but the wealth and goods of seven households on either side likewise sank entirely into the earth.
The news spread among the śrāvakas and reached the three householders.

They further heard that the Dragon King and the brahmin Jin had gone to the city of Śilāvatī, where they caused the treasuries of seven aristocrats to sink entirely into the earth and return to the dragon palace.
At that time, the three householders said to one another:

"The wealth of our three families is immeasurable and our treasuries are full; we have acquired it through the Dharma and have not wronged or overstepped upon others, so it shall never be seized by water, fire, thieves, or the king's law."

When the people of the country heard this, they considered it boastful talk, claiming that his words and deeds were at odds. They gathered together en masse and went to those three houses, asking the householders:
"The wealth and treasures of the seven families have all entered the dragon palace; we have heard that you three said among yourselves:
'Our family wealth and treasures were acquired through the Dharma, and we do not seize the property of others.'"
"What proof can be given so that this may be known?

At that time, the three householders each took ten *jin* of gold and divided it into six portions. Together with the people and the owners of the seven families who had lost their wealth, they went to the Dragon Spring and cast the gold into the spring; the water immediately surged and boiled like the broth in a cauldron.
The Dragon King, struck with alarm and fear, immediately dispatched his daughter to return the gold; she then returned to report her thanks and bid the messenger farewell.
Wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma is accomplished through principle and will never be plundered or deceived by water, fire, or thieves;

whereas wealth not acquired through righteousness is obtained by wrongfully usurping the property of others through unrighteous means, and it is subsequently seized by thieves, fire, water, or the king—this refers precisely to the aforementioned seven types of households.
Therefore it is said: "Family wealth is impermanent.
To wish to see the true ones, to delight in hearing the preaching of the Dharma, and to be able to abandon the defilement of stinginess—this is called faith.

Those who wish to see the various *satyavādins* (truth-tellers) should, if they possess firm faith, go to visit the worthy sages (*āryas*), construct monasteries and stūpas, pay homage to and seek audiences with eminent Dharma masters, inquire after their well-being, listen to and receive the teachings, and joyfully hear the exposition of the Dharma. As stated in the *Sūtra*:
"If there is a person who is attached to worldly pleasures and lacks nothing at home, yet builds [such structures], they will incur five deficiencies."
What are these five?
In this regard, such a person delights in domestic conversation; yet when they enter a gathering, they hear the Teacher’s instruction:
"When a person practices the path, they should maintain the noble silence of the *āryas*."
That person felt regret in his heart and vowed not to go to the assembly, thinking:
"What I find pleasant and enjoyable is what others criticize; it brings me no benefit, so why should I go to the assembly again?"

Because they do not approach the assembly, they do not see the Noble Ones; because they do not see the Noble Ones, they do not hear the Dharma; because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall into the realm of ordinary beings and the three evil destinies.
This is called the first deficiency of such a person regarding the discipline of the noble ones (*ārya-vinaya*).

Furthermore, whatever things this person loves and desires are always present before him; yet when he happens to enter an assembly and hears various Dharma masters speak of their impurities, that person feels regret and vows not to go to assemblies again, thinking:
"What I delight in is censured by everyone; it is of no benefit to me, so why should I go to the assembly again?"

Because they do not go to the assembly, they do not see the Noble Ones; because they do not see the Noble Ones, they do not hear the Dharma; and because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall into the state of ordinary beings and the three evil realms.
This is called the second deficiency of such a person regarding the discipline of the noble ones.

Furthermore, suppose this person knows that a relative has traveled far away and his heart is constantly filled with love and respect for them; yet when he goes among the assembly, he hears the Teacher’s instruction:
"Wandering afar hinders one's happiness; though one knows of the longing of a relative, by leaving the Teacher and leaving the assembly, one will not reach the ultimate goal."
That person felt regret and vowed not to go to the assembly again, thinking:
"What I find pleasing is criticized by the multitude; it benefits me nothing, so why should I go to the assembly again?"

Because they do not go to the assembly, they do not see the Noble Ones; because they do not see the Noble Ones, they do not hear the Dharma; and because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall into the realm of ordinary beings and the three evil paths.
This is called the third deficiency in this person regarding the discipline of the noble ones (*ārya-vinaya*).

Furthermore, suppose this person knows that his relatives have been expelled by the community; when he goes among the assembly, he hears the teacher’s instruction and reprimand concerning those relatives. His heart feels remorse, and he vows not to go to the assembly again, thinking:
"What I delight in is censured and discussed by the multitude; it is of no benefit to me, so why should I go to the assembly again?"

Because they do not go to the assembly, they do not see the Noble Ones; because they do not see the Noble Ones, they do not hear the Dharma; because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall into the realm of ordinary beings and the three evil paths.
This is called the fourth deficiency in the discipline of the noble ones for such a person.

Furthermore, when this person learns that a relative has passed away, they are overcome with grief and longing, unable to set aside their eating or resting; yet when they go among the assembly, they hear the Teacher’s instruction:
"When the body dies and the spirit departs, one must undergo rebirth in a womb."
That person did not believe it and thought it was total extinction; he felt regret and vowed not to go to the assembly again, saying:
"What I hold dear has been criticized by that man; it is of no benefit to me, so why should I go to the assembly again?"

Because they do not go to the assembly, they do not see the Noble Ones; because they do not see the Noble Ones, they do not hear the Dharma; because they do not hear the Dharma, they fall into the state of ordinary worldlings and the three evil realms.
"This is called the fifth deficiency in the discipline of the noble ones.
These are the five deficiencies that prevent one from reaching the great assembly.
Therefore it is said: "Those who wish to see the True Ones delight in hearing the teaching of the Dharma."

Regarding those who can abandon the defilement of stinginess: among all defilements, stinginess and envy are the foremost; they pollute the human mind so that it does not reach the Path. They obstruct the intent to give and sever the roots of all virtues—all of this arises from stinginess and envy.

If that practitioner’s mind is like extinguished ashes and his will is as steadfast as the earth, even if he encounters wealth and treasures, he will never harbor greed; he regards such riches no differently than pottery shards or stones. Believing only in the Way and not practicing perversity—for this reason it is said: "To be able to abandon the defilement of stinginess is what is called faith."
Faith can cross the river; its merit is difficult to take away. It can restrain theft; this is the delight of the wilderness-dwelling śramaṇa. Regarding "faith can cross the river":

faith is a direct path that proceeds without obstruction wherever it is directed. For example, suppose one travels near or far and is deceived by others; though the way ahead is truly difficult, if there is no affliction from deceitful words, such a person, having already placed their faith, will advance along the road. Even if they encounter hardships, they will pass through them unharmed.
There was a person of upright faith who, having reached the bank wishing to cross the river, asked a traveler:
"Is the water deep or shallow?
The traveler replied:
"It is only up to the ankles.

When he held onto the boatman's word and crossed over, it was exactly as he had said. Even though this man had withheld his payment, the place where he was reborn after his life ended did not contradict his words; the multitude honored him, saying, "This is a person of merit."
Therefore it is said: "Faith can cross the river.

Regarding "whose merit is difficult to seize": long ago, there was a man who violated the king's law; his family estate and all possessions were confiscated by the government. The king commanded the man:
"Take a complete inventory of your family’s property and wealth and present it to the authorities."
That man brought the register of his merits and virtues to the official.
The king asked him:
"I commanded you to deliver the register of your family estate and wealth; why have you instead delivered a register of your merits and virtues?"
The man replied, "The register of household property for future lives is this very register;
as for the register of household property for this present life, it follows whatever Your Majesty has recorded."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he ceased his pursuit and no longer recorded [the offense].
Therefore it is said: "That merit is difficult to seize.

One who can restrain theft—formerly, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who had profound faith in the Triple Gem. Compassionate, benevolent, and generous, he nurtured all sentient beings and provided for those in poverty.

At that time, amidst heavy rain, lightning, and thunderbolts, thieves suddenly arrived to plunder his wealth. The elder soon became aware of them and said to the robbers, "Do not take it away; I wish to give it to the śramaṇas."
Upon hearing these words, the bandits' eyes were shrouded in darkness and their hands could no longer be raised; the bandit leader signaled to his men, and they immediately retreated and departed.
Therefore it is said: "One who can restrain from theft finds joy as a wilderness śramaṇa."
The frequent arrival of śramaṇas is what the wise delight in, as well as for those of firm faith;
between them there is joy.

As for "the frequent arrival of śramaṇas": upon seeing the śramaṇas, their minds open and their intentions are resolved; they provide whatever is required, inquire after them at appropriate times, and offer the four requisites: clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick and infirm.
Therefore it is said: "The frequent visits of śramaṇas are what the wise delight in.

As for "and other persons of firm faith," when those living in nearby villages see them performing meritorious deeds, they all assist with joy and together cultivate goodness; therefore it is said, "and other persons of firm faith."

Regarding those who rejoice therein: some come from afar to personally attend upon him, sharing in his joy; as they enter and exit, walk and come and go, they observe his majestic deportment and ritual decorum. Therefore it is said: "Those who rejoice therein."
If a person harbors anxiety and covets the food and clothing of others, that person shall not attain a concentrated mind day or night.
Regarding "if a person harbors anxiety": in the past, before the Buddha appeared in the world, ninety-nine kinds of paths were all flourishing.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, all heterodox views naturally perish, and his disciples and followers all receive offerings.

Yet those of external paths and divergent studies harbor malice within and give rise to envy; seeing others obtain gains and sustenance, they act with resentment, affliction, and slander. This is what is meant by externalists giving rise to a jealous mind.

Furthermore, there may be someone who, though having left the household life and entered the path within the internal Dharma, does not apply themselves diligently to that path; outwardly they appear to observe the precepts, yet inwardly their conduct is impure. Seeing others receive offerings and sustenance, they give rise to a mind of envy, thinking:
"I too have left the household life, and you too have left the household life; yet you alone receive blessings while I do not obtain such sustenance."

It was as if there were two arhats whose merit was equal and whose practice perfected, with neither increasing nor decreasing; yet one received offerings that followed him without leaving, while the other went from house to house begging and could not provide for himself. Thereupon, he conceived a thought and gave rise to a doubt similar to this:
"Why alone am I not provided with offerings?"
"How can that person alone possess such merit as to constantly receive offerings and sustenance?
Even one with a stainless mind for the Path still gives rise to such thoughts; how much more so would an ordinary person not feel envy?

Only one who has attained Buddhahood is uniquely honored throughout the three realms; he does not grieve when insulted, nor does he feel excessive joy when honored. He maintains a mind like the earth, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore it is said: "If a person harbors anxiety and covets the clothing and food of others, that person, day and night, shall not attain a concentrated mind."
If a person can sever [the defilements], exhausting them to their very root, that person will, day and night, attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As for "if a person can sever": fearing future transgressions, they do not create conditions for subsequent lives; by exhausting the roots and sprouts, there are no further signs of rebirth. This is likewise true: if one can sever the fundamental basis of the mind's intentional thoughts, then day and night one will dwell in peaceful concentration with an undisturbed mind. Whatever the mind intends, it is attained according to its wish. Therefore it is said: "If a person can sever, exhausting them to their very root, that person will, day and night, attain meditative concentration."
Lacking faith and not practicing, one delights in stripping away right speech; like a clumsy person drawing water, they dig at the spring and stir up the mud.

"Lacking faith and not practicing" means that one neither draws near nor serves [the wise]; even if one engages in conversation or undertakes activities together with them, wholesome qualities diminish and unwholesome qualities increase.

It is like a clumsy water-drawer who seeks it from a high mountain; his labor is in vain and he does not obtain water. Even if he were to dig the earth and find water, it would be muddy and unfit for drinking.
Therefore it is said: Those without faith do not practice and delight in tearing apart the true words, like the clumsy one who draws water by digging at the spring and stirring up the mud.
The wise man practices wisdom and delights in looking up toward the clear stream; like the skillful one who draws water, he seeks the coolness without disturbance.

The wise man who associates with those who possess wisdom—here, "the wise man" refers to a disciple of the Buddha—should constantly draw near to, serve, and make offerings to them; by attending to them at the proper times so that they lack for nothing, he shall obtain great merit. One whose aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) is not yet complete will thereby be able to fulfill the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the vision and knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).

It is like a person who thirsts for the Dharma, contemplating it day and night until their lips and mouth are parched and cracked as they pursue it without ceasing; it is like water that is clear, cool, and unpolluted.

The practitioner is also like this: fully endowed with manifold virtues, the four immeasurables of compassion, and kindness that extends to all beings and reaches far among sentient beings, yet never for his own sake. The defilements and fetters have been exhausted and do not arise again; the burning heat of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases has no further root. Having received the cool aggregates, there is no longer any lingering heat. Therefore it is said: "The worthy man practices wisdom and delights in looking up to the clear stream, just as one who skillfully draws water seeks the cool and remains undisturbed."

Trust does not defile others; it belongs only to the wise and the benevolent. That which is not good, one should distance oneself from; that which is good, one should learn. Regarding "trust does not defile others":

those who are defiled are burdened by heavy fetters (*saṃyojana*); they are fully possessed of lust, anger, and delusion, which penetrate to the bone and reach the marrow. One should always remain far removed from such defilement.
The reason for this is that such afflictions are so grave as to be unfit for habitual practice.
Therefore it is said: "Faith does not defile others.

Only the wise and the benevolent, having attained the Way of the Immortals and departed from the eight worldly dharmas, cultivate purity within themselves; being undefiled, they do not defile others either.
The reason for this is that what is defiled is fundamentally unfit to be approached.
Therefore it is said: "Only with the wise and the virtuous.

As for "if one does not like them, one stays far away," this refers to a corrupt friend whom one distances oneself from as if abandoning a latrine, avoiding a vicious dog, fleeing a runaway bull, leaving behind a wicked horse or a mad elephant in rut, or shunning a treacherous path or bandits. Thus it is said: "If one does not like them, one leaves them."

Regarding those who "may be excellent through learning," such individuals as these are all worthy and holy persons who uphold the precepts; they are worthy of reverence and esteem, honored by both devas and humans. They are like clear, cool, and sweet water; like one suffering from thirst and exhaustion seeking Vaiśravaṇa and thereby obtaining wealth and treasures without any cause for regret; or like one needing flowers who should go to a garden, or one needing precious jewels who should go to the great ocean. Therefore it is said: "One may be excellent through learning."
*Udānavarga*, Volume XII; *Udānavarga*, Volume XIII.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on the Śramaṇa Having crossed the stream and reached the further shore,
free from desire like Brahmā, knowing that all conditioned things have been exhausted,
he has attained immeasurable virtue.

Regarding those who cross by cutting off the stream: the "stream" is the root of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Outflows (*āsrava*) consist of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*), just as all the currents of rivers flow toward the ocean.
The fetters and afflictions of ordinary worldlings are likewise thus; they leak out into the dust and toil of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
When that practitioner grasps the sword of wisdom to sever them and bring them to rest, the fetters and entanglements no longer leak out. Therefore it is said: "He cuts the stream and crosses over."

Regarding those who are desireless like Brahmā: they contemplate the severance of desire, just as a brahmin exerts himself day and night, toiling his body and mortifying his flesh, exposing his corpse to the elements, and standing on one foot day and night while gazing upward at the sun and moon, vowing to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven to enjoy its celestial blessings as a noble and honored Brahma. Thus, in this very life, he concentrates his mind with single-minded devotion, contemplating the severance of desire and cultivating pure conduct.
Therefore it is said: "To be without desire is like Brahmā.

Regarding the phrase "knowing that [craving] has been exhausted": one who is without desire is pure both internally and externally; having refined the essence of their mind so that there is no further defilement, it is therefore said, "knowing that [craving] has been exhausted."
Regarding those who have attained immeasurable virtue: the offerings received by such a person are immeasurable; giving to all ordinary worldlings is not equal to giving to a single *srotāpanna*.
The reason for this is that they shall eventually exhaust all birth and death and will no longer dwell within the three realms of existence.
The *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin* possess perfected practices and immeasurable merit;
giving to a hundred *srotāpannas* is not equal to giving to a single *sakṛdāgāmin*, and giving to a hundred *sakṛdāgāmins* is not equal to giving to a single *anāgāmin*.
Therefore it is said: one attains immeasurable merit.
When the wise establish their practice and apply themselves with diligence, they obtain the fruit; but when practitioners grasp with laxity, their defilements increase all the more.

The wise establish their practice; at times they recite and study the subtle and profound, enter meditative concentration, sit in dhyāna, chant the sūtras, and assist in communal affairs. They maintain a courageous and steadfast resolve, harboring no timidity or weakness, and strive diligently day and night without weariness. Therefore it is said: "The wise establish their practice; through diligent effort, they attain the fruit."

Regarding the practitioner who clings to laxity: when one has left the household life, the essential requirement is still diligent effort—walking meditation by day and meditative concentration by night. If one cannot comply with the Buddha’s teachings, assist in communal affairs, or pay homage at stupas and temples, instead becoming even more indolent and failing to apply oneself to the three karmic actions, one will consequently fall among the ordinary worldlings and fail to reach the ultimate goal. Therefore it is said: "The practitioner clings to laxity."
"To further increase the dust" means that the practice of ordinary persons is not firm, and lust, anger, and delusion increase.

Having left the household life to study and receive the offerings of others' faith, they are unable to contemplate the Way and its virtue; instead, they engage in myriad empty discourses. Their conduct is neither true nor correct, and they do not recite, practice, or receive the teachings. For this reason, it is said: "They further increase the dust."
Now, regarding laxity in practice: whether it be good or evil, if one’s holy life (*brahmacarya*) is impure, one will not attain the great fruit.
As for those whose practice is lax, when a person wishes to establish a practice, they must bring it to completion; their aspirations should reach fruition without ever withdrawing midway.

However, that practitioner’s mind and intentions are sluggish and unable to reach completion; furthermore, they are unable to recite or practice until something is accomplished, nor do they sit in meditation, recite sutras, or assist in communal affairs. For this reason, it is said: "The practice is lax and slow."

Regarding good and evil: when a person desires to practice and act either for good or for evil, they must establish their resolve so that it is surely fulfilled according to their wish. If the mind intends to incline toward good, good will certainly be accomplished; if the mind intends to incline toward evil, evil will certainly be accomplished. Those who habitually cultivate defilement find their fetters following them; those who habitually cultivate goodness find their fetters extinguished accordingly.

Furthermore, some practice asceticism and observe various codes of decorum; they exhaust their forms and torment their bodies, exposing their carcasses to the elements, worshiping the sun and moon, and subjecting themselves to the austerity of the five fires. They sleep upon thorns, abstain from grain, and practice breath control, or subsist on fruits and gourds, desiring to fulfill their aspirations.
Therefore it is said: "Regarding good and evil. As for impure brahmacarya:

some observe the precepts in order to trade for celestial blessings and seek rebirth in the Brahma Heaven; others seek to become Śakra, the gods of the six heavens, or the Māra King; furthermore, they employ the merit of their precepts to seek the status of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) who presides over the four realms. Therefore it is said: "impure brahmacarya."

Regarding "not attaining the great fruit": among fruits, the supreme is the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), which is most excellent, most honored, and peerless. However, [this person] only receives the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*) and does not receive the fruit of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-phala*). For this reason, it is said that they do not attain the great fruit.
It is like grasping a bundle of *śara* grass: if one holds it too loosely, one will wound one's hand.

A śramaṇa who does not exercise restraint brings about his own imprisonment; he is like one who has mastered the arts of combat and strategy, or the skills of riding horses, driving chariots, flying wheels, throwing lassos, crossing bridges, and treading with horses—all of which he must fully understand.

Furthermore, one should next learn the affairs of a householder’s farming: gathering and storing the harvest while anticipating the burning of wild fields; reaping the grain and recognizing whether the stalks are stiff or supple—holding firmly when they are stiff, for if too loose they will injure the hand, and holding loosely when they are supple, so as not to cause damage.
Therefore it is said: "It is like grasping a bundle of *kusa* grass; if one grasps it too loosely, one will wound one's hand.
It is the same for a śramaṇa practicing the path: if his cultivation of the precepts is not firm, he will violate and lose the prohibitive laws, whether through practice or through abandonment.

If there are practitioners who have not previously studied the precepts, yet possess the clarity of discerning wisdom regarding the path for entering meditative concentration, they may either completely lose the root of the precepts or omit half of them; this is entirely due to their failure to follow virtuous friends and their association with evil friends, whereby they will be reborn in the hells.
Therefore it is said: "The śramaṇa who does not exercise restraint is his own thief, imprisoned by his own records.
Just as when pulling up *caṇḍā* grass, one holds it firmly so as not to injure the hand;
so too, the śramaṇa who restrains himself through the precepts gradually approaches the path to Nirvāṇa.

For example, one who handles *śara* grass: the method of study requires that one exhaustively master the teacher’s arts; all skills and the six arts must be fully prepared. It is like engaging in battle where one must have the necessary equipment—planting one's feet firmly, steadying the mind, and grasping the bow and arrows—with which one will surely achieve one's heart's intent wherever one goes. Furthermore, just as one gathers and stores the harvest of household property, so too it is with the sprouts and grain of the *śara* grass.
Therefore it is said: "Holding firmly so as not to injure one's hand; the śramaṇa’s restraint through the precepts gradually approaches the path to Nirvāṇa.

When a śramaṇa upholds the precepts, he is as immovable as a mountain and cannot be shifted; he is not thwarted or destroyed by external evils. Having already distanced himself from evil associates, he attends to steadfast virtuous friends, knowing the destination of Nirvāṇa. This, too, is the śramaṇa’s restraint through the precepts that leads to the extinction of Nirvāṇa.
Hard to understand and hard to realize; śramaṇas with little wisdom encounter much disturbance, and the foolish bring suffering upon themselves.

"Hard to understand and hard to realize" means that it is difficult to study the Path and seek Buddhahood, and difficult to leave the household life and meet a teacher; this is truly what is meant by being hard to understand.
The supreme Dharma, wondrous deeds, and that which is studied by the noble ones are therefore said to be difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand.

Those śramaṇas of little wisdom—those people of little wisdom—are not true śramaṇas; they may dwell as householders, being defiled by and attached to what is non-essential and unable to abandon it; or they are like cooking pots and stoves that are leaking, broken, and incomplete, yet they cannot abandon them; or they are like beds and mats that are filthy, leaking, and impure, yet they cannot abandon them.

Suppose there is a woman who is blind, lame, and emaciated, such that she cannot leave her [husband]; for this reason the Buddha said: "A fly is trapped by a spider's web; a bird is trapped by a net; an elephant is trapped by firm shackles; and a wicked horse is trapped by the whip."

Having contemplated this, the seeker is able to forever renounce their home and occupation, cast aside wife and children, eliminate the five desires, and remain eternally free from the eight worldly concerns; thus they are able to practice the Way without being attached to worldly entanglements.
Those of little wisdom are like flies thrown into a net or birds caught inside a snare; it is extremely difficult for them to escape. Therefore it is said: "The śramaṇa has little wisdom.

As for those who cause much disturbance, one may use countless hundreds of thousands of skillful means and exhort others with the aspiration for the Path, urging them to leave the household life and study the Dharma, yet they refuse to believe or accept it, their minds being like lotus leaves upon which water does not cling or stain them.
Not only do they refuse to leave the household life when exhorted, but they also refuse to believe or accept the observance of the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) when urged to do so.

Not only did he fail to encourage others to observe the eightfold precepts, making them contemplate their own goodness for even the duration of a finger-snap, but he did not even believe in them; how much less could he abandon his home to study the Way? Such a thing was simply impossible.

It is like a sovereign who pardons prisoners and releases those bound in the prison; those who loathe the prison immediately seek release upon hearing the news, as if fleeing a fire, while fools delight in the prison and long for it, refusing to leave.

The Tathāgata appears in the world and radiates great compassion and forgiveness; furthermore, throughout the trichiliocosm, he unties the firm knots of worldly attachment, so that beings may gradually depart from birth and death.

Among them, those who were wise and possessed of vision, upon hearing the sound of the Great Compassionate One’s amnesty, immediately abandoned their household affairs to leave the home life and pursue the Way;

whereas the foolish and those with little merit, whose minds were not awakened, remained stained by worldly entanglements and refused to leave the home life, so that although they heard the sound of the amnesty, it did not enter their hearts.
Therefore it is said: Amidst much turmoil, the fool brings suffering upon himself.
What does the śramaṇa practice when he cannot restrain his own will?
At every step he is caught by attachment, merely running after his thoughts.

What is the practice of a śramaṇa? One cultivates the dharma of a śramaṇa by calming the mind so that it does not arise; yet the foolish person gives rise to delusion, asking: "What path should a śramaṇa pursue?"
Among these, one whose mind is stilled does not delight in leaving the household life; therefore it is said: "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?

As for one who cannot restrain their will as they wish, they should exercise restraint so that forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena do not gain entry. This is like a farmer who constantly keeps out livestock to prevent them from ravaging his crops, or like using a hook to tame an elephant. The human mind is also like this: one must always guide and control it so that forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena find no opportunity. Therefore it is said: "One who cannot restrain their will as they wish."

Regarding "counting at every step with attachment": the practitioner therein lacks firm resolve; they are like a light garment drifting east and west with the wind, or like a light feather that moves when caught by the breeze. Their thoughts arise in abundance, racing in ten thousand directions, led astray by the three perceptions.
What are the three? First, the perception of desire; second, the perception of ill will; third, the perception of stinginess and envy. These are called the three perceptions.

They are difficult to restrain and difficult to control; they depart without leaving a trace and arrive without manifesting form. Perception acts as the servant of the mind, making it difficult to attain concentration.
Therefore it is said: "At every step one is counted, attached, and stuck; one merely follows after the wandering of thought.

Learning is difficult, abandoning transgressions is difficult, living as a householder is also difficult, and meeting to dwell together in shared benefit is difficult; there is no hardship that exceeds existence.

A bhikṣu who has left the household life but whose mind remains constantly attached to worldly matters, who pursues thoughts of family affairs instead of cultivating meritorious deeds, may in the interim develop a heart of regret, thinking: "Why have I left the household life to practice the dharma of a śramaṇa?"
He harbors anxieties as if he had encountered a funeral; like a startled deer fleeing in haste, his mind is full of errors and as restless as a monkey.

His mind is likewise unsettled, dwelling only on forms, sounds, scents, tastes, textures, and mental objects (*dharmas*). He violates the precepts; advancing, he lacks the mind for the Path, and retreating, he dwells on domestic burdens. Thus he accumulates sins for himself and fails to reach eternal tranquility.
Therefore it is said: "Training is difficult, abandoning evil is difficult, and living as a householder is also difficult.
It is difficult to assemble and dwell together in shared benefit. As stated in a sutra:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:"
"To dwell as a sojourner in a foreign land is difficult; to beg for sustenance while naturally poor is difficult; to assemble and abide together with shared interests is difficult.

You, O bhikṣu, when entering homes to beg, should always maintain a humble mind and not follow after their provocations; whether you receive what is fine or coarse, do not give rise to judgments of right or wrong."
Therefore it is said: "It is difficult to assemble, cease, and share in common benefit.
That which is no more than hardship refers to passing through the existence of hell-beings, the existence of animals, and the existence of hungry ghosts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The reason you have left the household life is that you wish to sever the three realms of existence and not be reborn within them; you have abandoned your family affairs and forever forsaken wife and children, desiring in all cases to extinguish existence and having no wish for birth in existence."
"O bhikṣus, since you have accumulated [karma] from time immemorial, you have traversed countless ages and undergone immeasurable suffering.
Therefore it is said: "There is no hardship that exceeds existence (bhava).
Though the saṃghāṭī robe is draped over the shoulders, if one does not abandon evil, then one is an evildoer who practices evil."
Such people fall into the evil realms.
As for those who wear the *kāṣāya* draped over their shoulders: there may be those who study the Way, yet while wearing the *kāṣāya* on the outside, their internal conduct is not pure.
Long ago, there was a great number of bhikṣus dwelling in mountain thickets and desolate places where no humans lived; villages, districts, and counties sent them boundless offerings.
Among them, the bhikṣus were attached to cleanliness; their robes were exceedingly fine and exquisite, and day and night they engaged in discourse, their minds never departing from desire.

At that time, the deity of the tree and the deity of the mountain observed the inclinations of the bhikṣus' hearts and, wishing to restrain them from giving rise to thoughts of desire, immediately manifested a human form and spoke these verses:
"Fearing death and harboring dread, You merely bear the name of śramaṇa."
"Clad in the saṃghāṭī robe, you are like an old ox with a long tail.
At that time, when the many bhikṣus heard the verse spoken by the deva, their anger flared up, and they immediately replied to the deva:
"Are we old oxen to you?"
Then that deva addressed the messenger with this verse:
"I do not mention names or surnames, nor do I select specific individuals;
it is because of their defiled conduct therein that I speak of such people."
Therefore it is said: "The saṃghāṭī robe is draped over the shoulder. Regarding "those who do not abandon evil":

such practitioners of the path have accomplished unwholesome dharmas; they are greedy and lack restraint, failing to guard the faculties of body, speech, and mind. They are incomplete in their discipline, acting wantonly and according to their own whims without self-restraint. Therefore it is said: "those who do not abandon evil."
Regarding those who practice evil and do evil: day and night they commit evil with diligence and without slackening, as the Buddha taught in the Gautama-sūtra.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In a future age after my parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus of various names and lineages who do not cultivate or establish the precepts but instead practice various unwholesome dharmas; though their bodies are clad in the *kāṣāya*, they exercise no self-restraint."
Therefore it is said: "Those who commit evil and practice evil deeds fall into the evil realms.
Because they entangle themselves with evil and cannot leave it behind, after death they enter the three evil paths; therefore it is said, "They fall into the evil realms."
The person who ultimately violates the precepts is like a tree withered by entangling vines;
this is what they have done for themselves, being consumed by the fire of hatred.

Regarding "the person who ultimately violates the precepts": not even a hair’s breadth of the precepts remains in their heart, nor do they possess any pure and wholesome dharmas, as described in that sutra.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I do not see even a hair’s breadth of pure and white dharma existing in Devadatta’s mind. Had there been even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma existing in his mind, I would not have declared that Devadatta would enter hell."

It is like a person who has fallen into a deep latrine and is unable to move; another compassionate person, wishing to save his life, observes that person's body to see if there is any clean spot not defiled by excrement and urine, thinking, "I wish to seize him and pull him out."
"Observing that person thoroughly, there is no part that is not defiled; there is not even a hair’s breadth of purity.
Ultimately, the offense of one who violates the precepts is the same as that [of the former], and for this reason it is said: "one who ultimately violates the precepts."

"A tree entwined by creepers withers" means that just as a *sālu* tree, though once lush with branches and leaves, becomes withered and dies when entwined by creepers; therefore it is said, "a tree entwined by creepers withers."

When one acts for the sake of oneself, one invites calamity upon oneself and brings about one's own destruction; one becomes envied by others and their virtues are not praised. Therefore it is said: "This action is done for oneself."

Regarding those who are consumed by the fire of hatred: on the northern Snowy Mountains there is a grass named Elaka; it contains poison distributed by the gods, and wherever the wind blows upon it, all plants and trees perish.

In the ocean there is a fish named Svayaṃghātin (Self-Destroyer). It lies on its side in deep grass by the water's edge; when the wind blows and moves the grass, it touches the body of that fish, causing the poison of its wrath to flare up and its body to swell. When the grass touches its body a second and a third time, its body breaks apart and it comes to its end.
Therefore it is said: "One is consumed by the fire of hatred.
As for what is called an "elder," it is not by advanced age; though the body be mature and the hair white, one may still be merely dull-witted and foolish.

What is called an "elder" is not defined by advanced age, nor by a physical frame grown decrepit and separated from youth. One who does not know the prohibitions of the Dharma, nor the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, or what is beautiful and ugly, or how to advance; one who does not know what constitutes restraint and non-restraint, or transgression and non-transgression; one who does not know the gravity of offenses, nor the majestic deportment and advancement prescribed by the two hundred and fifty precepts; whose form is matured, whose face is wrinkled, and whose skin is slack like that of an old ox or an old elephant—though such a person has reached an advanced age, they are merely dull and foolish. This may be called the age of eating, not the age of wisdom; for failing to recite the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and failing to contemplate the three meanings, they merely undergo suffering in vain.
Therefore it is said: "One is called an elder not merely by the aging of years.

Though one's form may be mature and hair white, if one is merely dull-witted and foolish—meaning that while the physical frame has ripened, life remains but for a morning or an evening—one shall go before King Yama; there, interrogated by the King, one will have no words with which to respond.
While existing in this world, such a person’s foolish mind entangles itself, failing to produce wholesome fruits; they merely endure their lifespan in the world without observing the three karmas."
Therefore it is said: Though one’s form is mature and hair is white, one is merely dull-witted and foolish.
One who has abandoned both evil and merit, purely cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and is wise, far-sighted, and pure—such a person is called an elder (*sthavira*).

That which is called "being able to relinquish both demerit and merit" means that being born among gods or humans is called merit, while entering the hells or the animal realm is called demerit. When a person has severed these and they no longer arise—having exhausted their root source and not planting the seeds for future existence—it is for this reason it is said that one is able to relinquish both demerit and merit.

Regarding the "pure cultivation of the brahma-faring": the Noble Eightfold Path is also the brahma-faring; by relying on this brahma-faring, one attains the excellent destination and reaches the ultimate exhaustion of the source of suffering. Therefore, it is said: "the pure cultivation of the brahma-faring."

Regarding those who are wise, far-sighted, pure, and clean: that elder has accomplished the qualities of an elder. Formerly, when King Prasenajit governed his realm without external opposition and was respected and attached to by both the distant and the near, the six teachers led one another to King Prasenajit’s presence and earnestly instructed the king, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama boasts to the world and claims for himself that he is the foremost, walking alone without peer. Your Majesty should go to the śramaṇa’s place and say to that śramaṇa:
'Gautama, have you now truly attained the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?'"
If he replies that he has attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, the King should respond with these words:

"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and the others left home at a young age to study, yet even now, in their advanced years, their bodies are worn out and their spirits exhausted, and they have still not attained the Way of the Buddha.
You have been studying for only a short time; you left home at twenty-nine and claim to have practiced asceticism for six years—how could you possibly have attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

At that time, King Prasenajit, having received the instructions of the six teachers, went to where the World-Honored One was. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side. After a short while, he withdrew slightly from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama, have you truly accomplished the path of Perfect Enlightenment?"
The Buddha replied to the king, "It is as you say; I have attained equal and perfect enlightenment.

"The six heretical teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the others, left home at a young age to study the Way, yet after many years their bodies and spirits are both exhausted, and they are unable to attain the unsurpassed Way. How much less so for Gautama, who spent his youth in the royal palace, indulging himself in the five desires and never undergoing cold or hardship; at the age of twenty-nine he left home to seek the Way, and now he boasts before the world, claiming to have attained the unsurpassed Way?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"There are four things in the world that must never be underestimated. What are these four?"

First, when a venomous snake’s wrath is at its peak, it spews poisonous fire from its mouth that incinerates mountains and valleys; all living beings with form are afflicted by its venom. This is called the first reason one must not treat it with contempt.
Second, although fire is small, it must not be underestimated; it burns and consumes all things—this is called the second thing that must not be underestimated.

Third, although a bhikṣu may be in the prime of his youth, he must not be underestimated; his supernormal powers are sovereign and his transformations are manifold, and his skillful wisdom in transforming others is likewise inexhaustible—this is called the third thing that must not be underestimated.

Fourth, although a prince is young, he must not be treated with contempt. Why is this? Because he possesses the power to sever [obstacles] and issue commands according to his will, such that none fail to obey. This, O Great King, is what is meant.
"Fourth, one must not treat others with contempt.

When King Prasenajit heard these instructions from the Buddha, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and then withdrew.
Therefore it is said: One who is wise, far-sighted, and pure is called an elder (*sthavira*).
As for what is meant by a *śramaṇa*, it is not necessarily one who has shaved his hair; if one speaks falsely, greedily takes, and possesses desire like an ordinary person, [he is no *śramaṇa*].

What is called a śramaṇa does not necessarily mean one who has shaved his hair. Formerly, when the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground in the city of Rājagṛha, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The realm of Magadha has attained a most excellent benefit, having encountered the Tathāgata surrounded by his noble disciples."

During the ninety-day summer retreat in the city of Rājagṛha within this realm, his fame spread throughout the sixteen great kingdoms. Hearing that the Tathāgata had praised the noble disciples and the community of bhikṣus, the people of the realm redoubled their joy; they gave rise to reverence and made offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick.

There were immeasurable sentient beings living at home who were impoverished and destitute; day and night they struggled to save their lives, unable to sustain themselves. Seeing that the bhikṣus received spontaneous offerings and, having already provided for themselves, were free from both public and private obligations, they reflected on this expedient means and each led others to leave the household life to practice the Way.

Having become a śramaṇa, one is unable to compile and practice the Dharma teachings, nor to recite the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; furthermore, one neither practices dhyāna, recites scriptures, nor assists in communal affairs, but instead accepts the faithful offerings of others while discussing trivial matters.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When you were formerly at home, you did not attend to your household affairs and lacked clothing. Seeing that the bhikṣus received spontaneous offerings, you left the household life to practice the Way out of greedy attachment. Your outward form is that of a śramaṇa, but your mind is like a starving tiger; what virtue or conduct do you possess to enrich my Dharma?"
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"The world calls you a śramaṇa, and you also call yourself a śramaṇa;
though your form resembles that of a śramaṇa, you are like a crane waiting for fish."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

“To shave off the hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and accept the faithful offerings of others while claiming it is the way of the Dharma—when the retribution for such an act arrives, even a hundred million Buddhas could not save you.”

"Among them, those of sharp faculties and swift wisdom immediately rectified their past ways and cultivated themselves for the future, receiving the Tathāgata’s teaching; however, those of dull faculties who were unable to reform themselves subsequently brought calamity upon themselves."
Therefore it is said: one who is called a śramaṇa is not necessarily one who has shaved his hair.

If one speaks falsely, greedily grasps at things, and possesses desires like an ordinary person—“O bhikṣus, you who are associated with evil wisdom and have forever abandoned wholesome dharmas are not truly śramaṇas; though you call yourselves śramaṇas, you appear to others as śramaṇas merely because of your dharma robes.”
The Tathāgata further spoke this verse:
“As one who is detached yet not truly detached, Who wears the kāṣāya yet does not truly remove [defilements],
Who holds the alms-bowl yet does not truly hold it— Such a person is neither a layman nor a śramaṇa.”
"Thick clouds without rain, The crops flourish but yield no fruit;
A bhikṣu separated from other bhikṣus Is like a lamp without light by day.
Therefore it is said: "Lying and covetous grasping—having desire like an ordinary person."
What is called a śramaṇa is one who expands and propagates the Great Way, quiets the mind and extinguishes the will, so that coarse fetters do not arise. Regarding what is called a śramaṇa:

long ago there was a foolish man whose nature was wayward and dissolute; he could not distinguish between right and wrong or good and evil. He saw dozens of people carrying out a corpse from the city, and further encountered a multitude scattering incense and flowers over the dead body.

At that time, the foolish man returned home and lay down to sleep. Previously, a bundle of saffron flowers had been suspended from the rafter of the house; the rope broke, and the flowers scattered and fell upon the foolish man. The foolish man raised his voice and called out to his family, saying:
"I am now dead; why do you not carry me away and discard me?"
The family members asked, "How did you die? He replied:
"Do you not see the flowers scattered upon my body? His family replied, "We do not consider scattering flowers upon the body to be death.

What is called 'death' is when there is no inhalation or exhalation; when the body is like withered wood; when the wind has departed and the fire is abandoned, such that consciousness is severed; when the body becomes rigid and can no longer function—it is by such criteria as these that we define death."
"Though you say he is dead, he is like the dead but not truly dead.
It is the same with this assembly of bhikṣus: you who are now like bhikṣus are not bhikṣus.
A true bhikṣu is fully endowed with dignified deportment; seeing even a small transgression, he feels dread, how much more so for a great one?
His manifold practices are without deficiency, and his aspiration is directed toward the three paths: the path of the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Arhat.
One who is fully endowed with dignified deportment and the precepts in such a manner is called a śramaṇa.
You, however, have shaved off your hair and beards and wear the saffron robe on the outside, yet harbor treachery within;
what is truly meant by "śramaṇa" is one who broadly expands and propagates the Way.

"Quieting the mind and extinguishing volition so that coarse fetters do not arise" means that all corrupt and evil dharmas have already been exhausted and extinguished, never to arise again; "coarse" refers to the roots among the fetters, and once the roots are removed, there are no branches or leaves.
Therefore it is said: "When the mind is stilled and the will extinguished, coarse fetters do not arise.

This means being able to abandon evil; this is called a śramaṇa. A brahmin eliminates evil, a śramaṇa practices the conduct, and by removing one's own defilements, one may be said to have attained the Way.
This means that one who is able to abandon evil is called a *śramaṇa*; having already stilled all evils, as stated in the Sūtra.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Just as people address you, all say, 'Śramaṇa, śramaṇa.'"
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is, World-Honored One!
Fools all say, ‘Śramaṇa, śramaṇa.’”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you are to be so, you should maintain the conduct of a śramaṇa; if you are to be a brahmin, you should maintain the conduct of a brahmin.
Therefore, bhikṣus!"
One's conduct should be like that of a śramaṇa and also like that of a brahmin. Why is this so?
Because the conduct of śramaṇas and brahmins is pure; whatever they desire and aspire to will necessarily accord with their thoughts.
What is the dharma of the śramaṇa and brāhmaṇa?
That which is called the dharma of the śramaṇa and brāhmaṇa is the purity of bodily conduct.
Or again, one might think thus:
"Whatever was to be done has been accomplished and fulfilled; my speech and mind are likewise so, and thus I have attained the preservation of life.
This is called the Dharma of the śramaṇa and brahmin.
The brahmins who practice the conduct of evil śramaṇas, whose constant mode of cultivation is pride, rely on their own technical skills and say to one another:

“We brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā; those of the kṣatriya caste were born from Brahmā’s chest; those of the vaiśya caste were born from Brahmā’s sides; and those of the śūdra caste were born from Brahmā’s feet. With Brahmā as our father, we are arrogant and boastful, claiming ourselves to be supreme.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The dharma of the brahmins is not actually so. Those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) remain pure to the end, eliminating unwholesome dharmas; yet now these brahmins bring calamity upon themselves, keeping wives and raising sons and daughters who fill their halls. Their own conduct is impure, yet they conversely claim, 'I am born from the mouth of Brahmā.'"
Therefore it is said: "The brahmin removes evil; the śramaṇa practices the path.

One who removes their own defilements may be called a follower of the Way. A bhikṣu who practices the path removes his own defilements, such that all evil and unwholesome dharmas are forever exhausted without remainder, and he sports in the Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore it is said: "One who removes their own defilements may be called a follower of the Way."

There are three grades of defilements: superior, middling, and inferior; specifically, superior-superior, superior-middling, superior-inferior, middling-superior, middling-middling, middling-inferior, inferior-superior, inferior-middling, and inferior-inferior. Such fetters and entanglements defile the human mind; one should abandon them all and cultivate pure conduct.

There may be certain brahmins who give rise to wrong views, thinking that because there is no dust or defilement within, illness comes from without; they enter the Ganges River or the Three Lotus Pools, or enter springs frequented by humans and non-humans, bathing and washing themselves to remove external filth, yet they cannot eliminate the fetters and attachments of the mind.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a person practices the path until it reaches ultimate purity and removes all dust and defilements, they should maintain the unsurpassed wisdom that is capable of eliminating those defilements."

Why is this? While external dust and grime on the body are despised by others, those who eliminate the defilements of the mind through the ultimate truth (paramārtha) are revered and honored by gods and people of the world.

The defilements of the human realm cause one to fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; though these human defilements may be perfumed with incense and flowers, they continue to arise as before. However, once one has abandoned all fetters and is perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, that fragrance will ultimately be so pervasive that there is no one who does not smell it.
Therefore it is said: "To remove one's own defilements may be called the Way.
The Eightfold Right Path is the most direct path; the Four Truths are the traces of the Dharma.
This Way is named the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), by which the lamp extinguishes the darkness of craving."
Regarding the Eightfold Right Path, what is meant by "straight" (ṛju)?
It refers to the Four Noble Truths. Are these four the objective bases?
Are they four because they are conditions for results?
Are they four because they are aggregates?
If they are four by way of meaning, then this refers to three.
To designate suffering means there is no accumulation; to designate accumulation means there is no suffering. These are called the first exhaustion, the second path, and the third suffering.
When the conditions and the fruit are taken as the fourth, these are called the five.
Because suffering has existence as its condition and also conditions the fruit of existence, and the Path is likewise, the Truth of Cessation constitutes five [factors].
If these are grouped into four, they are called the Eightfold [Path].
First, one abandons suffering within the desire realm; subsequently, the form realm and the formless realm constitute the second [set]. This applies likewise up to the path.
Having established this principle, there are further proponents who say that they are called "five" in the sense of being conditioned by results.
Suffering arises both from conditions and from results; it is collectively termed the trace of suffering, the trace of existence, the trace of craving, and the trace of stinginess.
To those who raise an objection, the path also has conditions and results; it is collectively termed the trace of suffering, and is also termed the trace of existence and the trace of stinginess.
Why is it that the Two Truths are not established herein?
The answer is:

"There is indeed a reason for this, as it is intended to refute those other treatises. In those [treatises], two theories are raised regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); yet there is neither suffering nor origin. Because one wishes to refute these two theories, [it is said here] that there is suffering and there is its origin."

The Path possesses conditions and fruits; if one were to give rise to a discourse claiming that the Path does not exist, it is for the purpose of refuting such a discourse that the Path is affirmed to exist. Therefore, it is said that there are four truths, not five.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: because they are aggregates (*rāśi*), this treatise establishes that there are eight [truths].
The answer is:

"Because the meaning of an aggregate is a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); once the suffering of the desire realm and the suffering of the form and formless realms have all been gathered together, and once the formations conditioned by the desire realm and the formations conditioned by the form and formless realms have all been gathered together, the characteristic of arising (*utpādalakṣaṇa*) is produced."

The exhaustion of formations pertaining to the desire realm, and the exhaustion of formations pertaining to the form and formless realms—when these have all been gathered together, it is called the sign of rest (*vissama-nimitta*).

When the counteractives (*paṭipakkha*) to the formations of the desire realm, and the counteractives to the formations of the form and formless realms, have all been gathered together, it is called the sign of the way out (*niyyāna-nimitta*).
Therefore it is said that these are called the Four Noble Truths.

As they are contemplated by wisdom, one knows what is with affliction and what is without affliction, and through mindfulness one knows the way of escape; therefore it is said that the Four Noble Truths are the tracks of the Dharma.

This path is called "unconditioned" because it is the secure nirvana—the cessation and unconditioned state where all suffering is utterly relinquished; therefore, it is said that this path is called unconditioned.

Regarding "extinguishing the darkness of craving with a lamp": there are three kinds of existence (bhava) within craving—existence in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-bhava), existence in the realm of form (rūpadhātu-bhava), and existence in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-bhava). One is firmly bound and attached by that craving, which gives rise to deluded thoughts and manifold sufferings. By what means is it severed?
The answer is:
"The Noble Eightfold Path eternally severs [craving] so that it does not arise.
Therefore it is said: "By means of the lamp, one extinguishes the darkness of craving."
Wisdom leaves all abysses behind, like the wind dispersing clouds; having extinguished conceptual thought, this is called the vision of wisdom.

Regarding "wisdom leaves all abysses behind": it is not that there is only one kind of abyss, for there are many. Some speak of wind-blown dust, others of deep waters. Dust defiles the human body, making no distinction between old and young; it causes the eyes to see unclearly and clothes to become soiled with grime. Above, it obscures the sun and moon, depriving them of their brilliant radiance; it hinders people from seeing from afar, preventing them from distinguishing the true from the false.

At that time, the Dragon King, out of compassion for the world’s deluded and ignorant beings and wishing to free them from these various calamities, sent down a cool breeze and a fine rain; he suppressed the dust, extinguished the mists, and brought forth a vast, brilliant light.
Therefore it is said: wisdom leaves behind all abysses, just as the wind disperses the clouds.
That practitioner who applies himself with single-minded concentration extinguishes internal perceptions of dust.
There are three such perceptions:
There are the perceptions of desire, ill will, and delusion.

These three perceptions do not allow one to master sensory objects, giving rise to distracted thoughts that ruin wisdom and prevent it from reaching its ultimate goal. They obstruct the eye of wisdom so that one does not behold the Four Noble Truths, defiling the Dharma-body and rendering it unclear.
One who can restrain this mind and cause these various perceptions not to arise is therefore said to have "extinguished conceptual thought; this is called the vision of wisdom."
Wisdom is the elder of the world; it delights in non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Through wisdom one receives the true teaching, whereby birth, old age, and death are exhausted.
That "wisdom is the elder of the world" means it is the most eminent, the highest, the subtlest, and the most wondrous; these are also called the three meanings.
What are the three? First is the meaning of the objective basis (*vastu-artha*), second is the meaning of the view (*dṛṣṭi-artha*), and third is the meaning of the condition (*pratyaya-artha*).
They are also called the meaning of the eye, the meaning of the head, the meaning of the path, the meaning of awakening, and the meaning of the noble ones' way of escape.
By means of this, one universally illumines all phenomena, just as external objects are illuminated.
External objects refer to the sun, moon, stars, clothing, and palaces; they are termed entering into one realm, entering into one base, entering into one aggregate, and entering into one path.
To enter one realm is to enter the realm of form;
to enter one base is to enter the base of form;
to enter one aggregate is to enter the aggregate of form.
To enter the One Path is the path of the present.

By means of this light of wisdom, one illuminates the eighteen realms, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates; through wisdom, one universally illuminates the future, the past, and the present, bringing great benefit and great accomplishment.
Therefore it is said: "Wisdom is the elder of the world.

Those who delight in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) ride upon this wisdom to distance themselves from birth and death; they are well able to discern things without harboring hesitation, and likewise discern the Four Noble Truths without harboring doubt. Therefore it is said: "They delight in the unconditioned."

To know how to receive the true teaching and bring an end to birth, old age, and death: that which causes one to experience suffering arises because of birth; if there were no birth, how could there be suffering?

Just as when many arrows are shot in competition from a training mound, so too is this body defiled by manifold sufferings; therefore it is said: "The wise one who receives the true teaching brings an end to birth, old age, and death."
The Path is the wondrous Eightfold Straightness; The Noble Truths are supreme among the four phrases.
The Dharma of desirelessness is the most excellent; The One with Clear Eyes, the Honored One among bipeds. Regarding "The Path is the wondrous Eightfold Straightness":

the followers of external paths and heterodox teachings intend to practice the Path by severing grains and cutting off food as a means of pure conduct; some lie on ashes or excrement and do not wear ornaments; some remain naked and barefoot with their bodies uncovered; some lie on thorns, use stones for pillows, or rinse with flowing water; some braid their hair for clothing; some observe tree leaves and practice calculation or incantations; some serve fire, water, the sun, moon, stars, and constellations; or they throw themselves from high mountains or enter deep waters, claiming these acts constitute the attainment of the Path.
The World-Honored One said:
"This is not the true path, nor is it the essential point; it is not that which is practiced by those of good knowledge.
This path is not sublime, nor is it that which is practiced by the noble ones."
"Among all such paths, the Noble Eightfold Path is the most supreme. Therefore it is said:
"The Path is the eightfold, straight, and wondrous. Regarding the four noble truths as supreme:
