Bhikṣus, you should know that from the time I began accumulating practices throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, when I cultivated the six perfections—practicing the perfection of giving by offering my head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children—and when I maintained the precepts, practiced patience, and applied myself with diligence and single-mindedness, it was all because I desired to eliminate greed, eliminate anger, and eliminate thoughts of malice.
Therefore it is said: "When one's bones are broken and life ends, the kingdom perishes.
If a person reviles me, whether I triumph over them or they triumph over me, if I follow after the impulse for gratification, enmity will never cease.
If someone reviles me, one should reflect for oneself:
"That person reviles me, yet he does not follow the prohibitions and precepts as he unjustly encroaches upon the virtuous.
Therefore it is said: "If someone reviles me."
Regarding "the victor over those who do not conquer," he reflects to himself:
"If one acts according to the Dharma, I am victorious; if one does not act according to the Dharma, I am not victorious."
Therefore it is said: "It is better for me not to be victorious.

As for those who follow their own pleasure, they engage in such reflections; consequently, their enmity increases because they do not reflect with discernment. Therefore it is said: "Those who follow their own pleasure."
Regarding those for whom enmity never ceases: such persons possess minds as hard as steel that cannot be broken or destroyed; therefore it is said, "enmity never ceases."
One should not repay enmity with enmity; In the end, one will find rest.
By practicing patience, one brings enmity to an end; This is called the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Regarding "one should not repay enmity with enmity," at that time the World-Honored One addressed the assembled multitude:

"I recall that since countless kalpas past, it is through enmity that enmity can be stilled. A human body is difficult to obtain, and the appearance of a Buddha in the world is even rarer, occurring only as rarely as the udumbara flower appears from time to time. To have attained a human birth and yet be able to leave the household life to study the Way is likewise difficult to achieve."

"You have already obtained a human body; with your faculties unimpaired, you are capable of receiving transformation through the teachings. Why, then, do you contend and quarrel with one another regarding the True Dharma?
For this reason it is said: "One should not overcome hatred with hatred; only thus will there be ultimate rest."

"Practicing patience brings an end to enmity; this is called the Dharma of the Tathāgata. Now, for one who practices patience, silence is paramount. If, upon hearing another's reply or being reviled by them, one returns the revilement in kind, such as this, enmity will never cease. To be weak is called "patience," and to overcome the strong is also called "victory. Therefore it is said: "Practicing patience brings an end to enmity; this is called the Dharma of the Tathāgata."

If one finds a virtuous friend with whom to roam the world, One will not accumulate surplus possessions, but will focus the mind in accord with their intent. Regarding "if one finds a virtuous friend":

there may be sentient beings who are perfected in etiquette, unerring in conduct, perfected in the flavor of meaning, and perfected in the practice of patience; all these arise from the perfection of physical conduct through friendship. Therefore it is said: "If one finds a virtuous friend."

Regarding "wandering together through the world": such virtuous friends follow one another from kalpa to kalpa without regarding it as a hardship; therefore, it is said that they "wander together through the world."

Regarding "not accumulating so as to have a surplus": for a person whose mind is equanimous, they do not calculate wealth and goods, nor do they discriminate between those who are known or kin. Even if a friend is of lowly or humble station, whether their appearance is good or bad, or whether they are handsome or ugly, one must not discriminate. Therefore it is said: "not accumulating so as to have a surplus."

To be single-mindedly mindful and to share the same intent means that one’s resolve and practice are aligned with others in their goodness, and that one has sincere faith directed toward the Buddha; therefore it is said, "to be single-mindedly mindful and to share the same intent."
Even if one does not find friends, Wandering alone without companions, One should observe all quarters of the world; Being virtuous alone, one commits no evil.

Regarding "even if one does not find friends": those called "friends" are those whose conduct is equal and whose virtue is the same, who together perform wholesome deeds; those who do not practice wholesome deeds are not called friends.

As it is commonly said in the world, when a person has no companion, they are like a donkey and an ox together; one who practices unwholesome deeds cannot be called a virtuous friend. Therefore it is said: "Even if one does not obtain a close friend..."

Regarding "wandering alone without a companion": it is better to wander alone and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds than to be accompanied by those who are corrupt and evil; therefore it is said, "wandering alone without a companion."

Regarding "extensively observing the realms of all directions": when a person wishes to observe and transform, they see various categories of phenomena which gradually increase their wisdom; thus, upon hearing words, they are not deluded. For this reason, it is said: "extensively observing the realms of all directions."
To practice virtue alone and refrain from committing evil means that the wise delight in tranquility and do not dwell amidst chaos and clamor.
Long ago, there was a great king of a rival state who raised an army to attack another; when a neighboring state heard of this, a minister addressed the king, saying:
"An enemy invader has approached our borders."
The king said,
"I have no suffering, nor is there anything for me to endure.
The bandits advanced further, and the minister again addressed the king:
"The bandits have already approached and arrived at the city.
The king said,
"None shall be able to invade me."
The rebels then entered the city and fortified the walls.
The minister again addressed the king:
"The rebel invaders are drawing near; Your Majesty should prepare for defense and go out to engage them in battle."
The king said, "Do not worry; it shall never harm me.
As the outer crown advanced further, proceeding directly toward the palace, the minister spoke again to the king:
"The raiders have now arrived; what does Your Majesty intend to do?
At that time, the king bathed and changed into new clothes; he carried his own provisions and went out to meet the neighboring king of the enemy state, addressing him thus:

"The city walls, the palace, and all else are yours. I wish to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way and its virtue; food shall suffice to sustain my life, and clothing shall suffice to cover my body."
At that time, the king spoke in verse:
“I now offer these robes and food, seeking only to remain hidden from view;
I relinquish the throne so that you may become king, while I seek to accumulate great merit.”
It is better to dwell among the crags and rocks, wearing coarse garments and eating meager food,
subsisting on fruit while practicing breath-counting meditation, and finding joy in the company of deer;
it is not to occupy the throne of a king, which brings the bitter suffering of torture and interrogation.
The wise, fearing the world to come, never create the conditions for evil.
Seeing that you have raised a great host of troops, wishing to come and harm me—I am but a decaying vessel; kill me at once, but do not wrong the multitude.
When the king of that hostile nation heard these words, he reflected deeply within himself and replied with this verse:
"How wonderful! The Great Awakened One, Leading himself according to the Dharma, Armed with the arrows of all virtues, Has shattered my military host."
"Though an enemy may be wise, what benefit is there in a friend who is foolish?
Therefore, wisdom is the foremost; through wisdom, one brings about vast deliverance.
At that time, the king of the enemy nation immediately withdrew his troops and led his own army back to his own country, returning the palace and all the dwellings to the original king.
Therefore it is said: "One should broadly observe all directions and realms, remaining solitary in virtue and refraining from evil.
Patience overcomes enmity; goodness overcomes the unwholesome; the victor is able to give;
and sincerity overcomes deception.

Regarding "the patient overcomes the enemy": when two swords meet, there will inevitably be injury; when encountering poison, it must be treated with antidotes, yet death remains certain. Only the patient can eliminate enmity; therefore it is said that patience overcomes the enemy.
"What is it that overcomes the unwholesome?
Have you ever heard, sirs, that the inherent nature of fire possesses the quality of cold?
They replied, "No."
This is also the case here: one who harbors enmity can never bring that enmity to rest.
What is it that can bring it to rest?
Only the good can truly bring it to rest.
Therefore it is said: "The good triumphs over the unwholesome. One who triumphs is able to practice giving;
a person who cultivates goodness acts without flaw or omission, their mind free from conceptualizing thoughts, and thus they are able to bestow gifts.

A person who harbors resentment brings calamity upon themselves; after death they enter hell to undergo immeasurable suffering, harming one another in cycles of death and rebirth. If they are later born among humans, their appearance will be ugly and deformed; they will be treated with contempt by others, and their wishes will not be fulfilled.
Therefore it is said: "The victor is able to bestow. To be sincere is to surpass the deceitful.

The wise person acts with their body so as not to commit verbal transgressions; their speech accords with the Dharma and causes no provocation. Even at the cost of death, they do not seek a precarious livelihood through false or frivolous speech. Having experienced birth and old age and undergone immeasurable suffering, one sees and hears that enmity is the most grievous thing. Therefore it is said: "To be sincere is to surpass the deceitful."
If one has no companions in study and cannot find virtuous friends, it is better to maintain virtue alone than to associate with the foolish. Regarding "having no companions in study":

when a person studies extensively, they must rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). From the first resolution for enlightenment until the attainment of the Way, everything is accomplished by relying upon spiritual friends.
If one encounters evil companions, one's conduct will inevitably become foolish and wicked.
Therefore it is said: "In learning, there are no such associates.

As for "failing to obtain good friends," this refers to when a student encounters an evil teacher (pāpamitra) who spends day and night in quarreling and litigation, making the practice of evil their profession; therefore it is said: "Failing to obtain good friends."

"It is better to guard one's own goodness alone than to associate with fools" means that even if one lacks companions, one should establish one's own resolve; one's thoughts should dwell in seclusion and quietude, remaining far removed from confusion and turmoil. If one hears of quarrels and disputes, one should always keep far away from them and never take pleasure in them. Therefore it is said: "It is better to guard one's own goodness alone than to associate with fools."
Delighting in the training of the precepts, what need is there for companions?
To be solitary and virtuous is free from sorrow, like an elephant in the wilderness.
As for one who delights in the training of the precepts: the practitioner’s mind finds joy in seclusion and stillness, and they constantly adorn their body with the prohibitive precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣu Koṭṭhika:
"Exhort and admonish him to cease the dispute.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu did not accept the Buddha's instruction.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately rose from his seat, soared through the air twelve yojanas, and returned to the original vihāra to join the great assembly, where he spoke these verses:
"Delighting in the training of the precepts, what need is there for a companion?"
"To practice virtue alone and be free from sorrow is like an elephant in the empty wilderness.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The Kauśāmbī people delight in quarreling and litigation, slandering and reviling one another. I have now departed from them; even if I hear that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are in that region, I shall avoid them and proceed to another land."
At that time, there was an elephant king who had separated himself from his herd and lived in solitude, wandering alone in the wilderness. He thought to himself:
"Having been freed from all other elephants and my kinsmen, how joyful it is to wander here all by myself!"
"When I was among the herd of elephants, they were unrestrained and many in number; only after they had trampled the water and grass could I eat.
Today I travel alone, and having obtained clear water and fine grass, I am free from anxiety."
At that time, the World-Honored One, perceiving what was in the mind of that elephant, spoke these verses before the great assembly:
"Among a multitude of elephants, there is one elephant Who is fully endowed with six tusks;
His thoughts are identical to mine: He delights in solitude and tranquility."

Regarding "a single elephant among a herd of elephants": the body of the Tathāgata is called a nāga-elephant, and that [other] elephant is also called a nāga-elephant. The Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, is uniquely honored throughout the three realms; the elephant is uniquely honored among nāgas. For this reason, it is said that there is one elephant among a herd of elephants.

Regarding "possessing six tusks," the tusks represent the majestic wrath of the elephant manifesting from its neck-ornaments; "merit" refers to the *lakṣaṇas* and *anuvyañjanas* of the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata beheld that Bhikṣu Kuṭaṃbī, he felt a sense of weary detachment; the elephant represents one who is weary of the multitude. Therefore it is said: "Being solitary and virtuous, one is free from sorrow, like an elephant in the empty wilderness."
*Udānavarga*, Volume Sixteen; *Udānavarga*, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 16: The Chapter on Mindfulness Mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation, Fully perfected through thorough reflection,
From beginning to end, made clear and proficient, Just as taught by the Buddha.
Regarding mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation: *āna* refers to the entry of the breath, and *apāna* refers to the exit of the breath.
That practitioner should skillfully observe two gateways to the nectar of immortality:
first, *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), and second, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

There may be practitioners who cultivate only ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing) or who cultivate the contemplation of impurity. Among them, those who cultivate ānāpāna contemplate and discern the exhalation and inhalation; they know when the breath is long and they know when it is short; they know when the breath is warm and they know when it is cool.

If the mind becomes distracted, begin again from the start; distinguish and understand [the body] from head to foot. If it should become distracted again, begin once more from the start. Proceeding in this manner through repeated cycles, one knows for oneself that the mind has reached its destination: "Now, as I grasp the breath, I have attained mastery."

If one wishes to cause the breath to exit through the left ear, it is not difficult to do so as one pleases; entering through the left ear is likewise. Exiting and entering through the right ear, or exiting and entering through the nose, can all be done according to one's will. Finally, when the returning breath exits from the crown of the head, if this is accomplished according to one's will, the method of counting the breaths (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) is perfected. Should it not be accomplished, the cranial vault will burst and one will immediately meet their end.
Thus, after the practitioner has trained for twelve years, some may achieve success while others do not.

Furthermore, the practitioner should analytically contemplate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); going outside the city to a desolate cemetery, they observe the corpses of the dead and examine them with thorough discernment: "What difference is there between these corpses and my own form?"
Returning again to the vihāra, he either sat upon a couch, spread out a seat, or sat in the open air, reflecting within himself:
"Recalling the corpses exposed in the cemetery that I have remembered from the sūtras, my own body is no different from them."
Thus, after twelve years had passed, there were those who attained concentration and those who did not.
For this reason, it is said: "Mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation."

Regarding "one who is fully endowed with thorough reflection": when a person’s mind is concentrated, they skillfully examine and discern [the breath] through the six stages—first counting, second following, third settling, fourth observing, fifth returning, and sixth purifying. Therefore, it is said that one is "fully endowed with thorough reflection."
Regarding those who have mastered [the practice] from beginning to end, they strive day and night without ever ceasing; should there be any deficiency in their count, they begin again from one.
This mastery means that they are not defiled by the external dust and grime of the six sense-faculties.
Therefore it is said: "From the beginning until the end, one attains thorough mastery.

As for what is meant by "according to what the Buddha has taught": the reason the Tathāgata bequeathed the twelve divisions of the sūtras and analyzed their essential meanings was solely for the sake of future generations who have not yet attained awakening, so that they might attain mastery over all wisdom and eliminate all expectations. Therefore it is said: "According to what the Buddha has taught."
This illuminates the world, like the sun appearing when the clouds disperse;
whether rising or resting, one should practice contemplation, never abandoning it while sitting or lying down. Regarding "this illuminates the world":

it is like the bright moon in autumn, free from the five obscurations, whose radiance shines uniquely among the multitude of stars. This is likewise so for one who has attained the concentration of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing); among all practitioners, their majestic power is uniquely manifest, and their countenance is so radiant that none can equal it. Therefore it is said: "This illuminates the world, like the sun appearing when the clouds disperse."

Regarding the phrase "beginning and ending the training in contemplation": by attaining the concentration of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), the body and mind become firm and immovable, such that they cannot be thwarted by external evils. The mind is likewise; it does not follow external sensory objects to give rise to perverse thoughts. Therefore, it is said: "Begin and end the training in contemplation."

Regarding "not neglecting or forgetting while sitting or lying down": that practitioner of the path, having already attained the concentration of samādhi, constantly maintains contemplation; whether sitting or lying down, they study throughout the entire day without ever abandoning it for even a moment. Therefore, it is said: "not neglecting or forgetting while sitting or lying down."
The bhikṣu establishes this mindfulness: What is beneficial before will be good afterward;
What is attained at the beginning will surely be victorious at the end. He vows never again to behold birth and death. Regarding "the bhikṣu establishes this mindfulness":

the so-called bhikṣu forever stills myriad thoughts so that his mind does not wander. He holds fast to his resolve with firmness, uprightly restrains all sensory emotions, and keeps his mind constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), seeking no other thoughts. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu establishes this mindfulness."

"Beneficial at first and good in the end" means that one first attains the meditative concentration of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), and subsequently, by transcending the stages, realizes the fruit and surpasses the three realms. Within the body, all fetters are forever exhausted without remainder; it is as pure as refined gold, forever free from even the slightest blemish. Therefore, it is said: "beneficial at first and good in the end."

Regarding "having attained the beginning, one will surely prevail at the end": this means that one has already fully understood and exhausted the conditions for transformation; having crossed over oneself, one shall no longer receive a future form. Therefore it is said: "Having attained the beginning, one will surely prevail at the end; one vows never again to behold birth and death."
If one perceives where the body dwells, The six spheres of contact are considered foremost;
With a stilled mind and constant single-mindedness, One will personally attain Nirvāṇa.

Regarding "if one perceives where the body dwells": whether they be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, those who are newly trained—whether male or female novices, upāsakas or upāsikās, or those of the kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, householder, or merchant castes—if they hold their resolve firmly, it will not be difficult for them to advance toward the Path. Therefore it is said: "If one perceives where the body dwells."

Regarding "the six contacts are considered supreme": this means closing off the various sense faculties; when the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind are clear, pure, and undisturbed, one guards the six emotions and does not accept various views. Therefore it is said, "the six contacts are considered supreme."

"One whose mind is stilled and always single-minded" refers to that practitioner who, through the meditation on inhalation and exhalation, observes each and every pore, distinguishing them one by one without ever erring. This is like a person with clear vision beholding their own facial reflection in a bright mirror; therefore it is said, "one whose mind is stilled and always single-minded."

"To personally attain nirvāṇa" means that by severing all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and outflows (*āsrava*), one is forever detached from the mundane world; thus, one reaches nirvāṇa—immovable and unchanging—no longer returning to or becoming defiled by attachment to the various realms. Therefore it is said: "one personally attains nirvāṇa."
Because one possesses these various thoughts, one constantly establishes practice within oneself;
if one were not thus, one would ultimately fail to attain the conduct of the mind.

Regarding "because one possesses these various thoughts, one constantly establishes practice within oneself": it is like that person who practices with resolve, exerting diligent effort day and night without confusion, advancing forward to seek the Way as if rescuing their own head from a burning fire during a world-ending conflagration. From the beginning of the night until its end, they do not neglect or forget [their practice]. Therefore it is said: "Because one possesses these various thoughts, one constantly establishes practice within oneself."

If it were not thus, one would ultimately never attain the practice of the mind; for birth and death are long and far-reaching, having no beginning or end. Once one understands and realizes Nirvana as being already detached from the three realms—past, future, and present—it is therefore said: "If it were not thus, one would ultimately never attain the practice of the mind."
"One who follows their original practice thus crosses over the toil of craving;
if one can awaken the mind's attention, there is the bliss of liberation through single-mindedness.

'One who follows their original practice' refers to a beginner on the Path: at times they are first taught mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), and at times they are first taught the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). One must observe the practitioner's own inclinations; therefore it is said, 'one who follows their original practice.'"
Thus, for those who cross over the toil of craving, craving is the root of disease, difficult to dig up and difficult to pull out. Why is this?

Because craving is difficult to dig up and craving is difficult to pull out; it is because this root of craving traverses birth and death, pervading the three realms, increasing the four modes of birth, and revolving through the five destinies—who is able to awaken to this?
Only those of keen wisdom are able to fully awaken to and comprehend the afflictions of suffering endured within the three realms and five destinies;
therefore it is said, "Thus one transcends the toil of craving."
If one can awaken the mind, one attains the bliss of liberation through single-mindedness;
by practicing the Dharma appropriately at the proper time, one crosses over the realm of old age and death.

Regarding "if one can awaken the mind": that practitioner binds the mind to clarity and does not dare to sleep. The attainment of the various fruits of the path depends fundamentally upon awakening; it is not attained through slumber. Even if one is awake, if the mind is not focused and concentrated, the fruits of the path will not be achieved. Once the mind is awakened and the application of the heart is focused and correct, one transcends the three realms of existence and reaches the realm of Nirvana without remainder.
Therefore it is said: "If one can awaken the mind of intention.

Regarding "the joy of a liberated one-pointed mind": that practitioner has already attained a concentrated mind and is fully endowed with its manifold virtues; one who has not attained concentration cannot be complete in these various virtuous qualities.

In the past, there was a man of licentious indulgence whose mind was so fixed on the beauty of women that he could not distance himself from them even in his waking hours. He longed for their features and wished to converse and have intimate relations with them; even in sleep and dreams, he envisioned their countenances and imagined walking hand-in-hand with them. At that time, his wife fell ill; her bones wasted away and her flesh was consumed until only her skeletal frame remained standing.
At that time, spiritual friends and practitioners were constantly coming and going to that household.

The wife said to one such practitioner, "I am currently afflicted by an illness that leaves me exhausted and emaciated day and night. I wish to express my situation with you; would it be permissible?"
The practitioner said, "Speak freely;
there is no need for concern. Even if there are matters you wish to conceal, I shall keep them hidden and not allow them to become public.
The woman replied:
“My husband is by nature excessively lustful; he harasses me day and night, allowing me no time for food or rest. Because of this, I have fallen ill and fear I shall not survive.
Then the practitioner said to the woman:
“If your husband draws near to your body, you should say these words to him:”
"Is it proper for one who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* to behave in this way?
Later, exactly as she had said, her husband approached his wife and immediately asked her:
"Since you have attained the path of *srotāpanna*, is it appropriate to act thus?"
Upon hearing his wife’s words, he was deeply ashamed and reflected within himself:
"Could it be that I am not actually a *srotāpanna*?
He immediately stilled his mind and dwelt in a secluded place, where through contemplation and deliberation, he attained the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*.
Knowing for himself that he had attained the path, he no longer engaged in sexual relations with women.
His wife asked her husband,
"For what reason do you now forever stifle your desire and no longer engage in relations with me?"
The husband said to his wife, "I have clearly seen you already; for what reason would we ever go back and forth together again?
The wife said to her husband:
"You say you have clearly seen me; what fault is there in me?
I am always chaste and virtuous, never violating the proprieties toward women; why do you revile me to such an extent?"
The woman immediately assembled her five kinsmen and the extended clan, and addressed them, saying:

"Now my husband has become cold and indifferent; he has forever ceased our kinship and no longer communicates with me, and moreover, he insults me, addressing me by name. You may now speak of this before the assembly."
The husband said,
"Wait! I must first cite evidence before I can prove my own innocence."

The husband returned with a beautifully painted jar, filled it to the brim with filth, and sealed its mouth firmly; yet he perfumed it with fragrant flowers and incense. Returning to that assembly, he said to his wife:
"Do you truly love me?"
"If you love me, you may embrace and play with this jar as you would my own body.
The wife followed his words, embracing and fondling the jar without letting go.
When her husband saw that his wife was so attached to the jar, he immediately struck it and broke it; foul stench overflowed and maggots emerged. He then spoke to his wife again:
“Are you still able to embrace this broken jar? The wife replied, “I would rather die than ever come near this broken jar;
I would rather enter a pit of fire, throw myself into deep water, or cast myself down from a high mountain with my head and feet in different places, but I could never come near this jar.”
The husband said to his wife:
"When I spoke of seeing you earlier, I was referring precisely to this very thing.
When I contemplate your body from head to foot, analyzing it as the thirty-six constituent parts, what is there in it to be craved?"
At that time, he further spoke in verse:
“The valiant one enters meditative concentration and observes the defilements arising from body and mind;
having seen them, he conceives revulsion, as if looking at a painted jar.”
Therefore it is said: "Liberation is the joy of a single-minded focus.

Regarding those who practice the Dharma with timely equanimity: a practitioner relies upon virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and being protected by the devas, external evils cannot enter; thus, seeking the Way becomes exceedingly easy, free from fear or difficulty.
It is like a traveler on a long journey who has lost the great highway and instead followed a minor path;
a wise person tells him, "This is not the correct road; you should now repent and follow that right path."
At that time, the one who had lost his way followed those instructions and returned to the main road, reaching home in safety.
It is the same for the practitioner: by relying on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they attain the Right Path. Therefore it is said: "One should practice the Dharma at the proper time."

This "crossing over the realm of old age and death" is like a person traveling along a road filled with many terrors: perhaps encountering tigers, wolves, or bandits; perhaps meeting wicked demons and malevolent spirits; or perhaps encountering dangerous and precipitous terrain where one must pass by leaning sideways. Amidst such hundreds of thousands of various hardships, they further encounter a shortage of water and provisions.
That person thinks to themselves: "If there were even a single difficulty on this road, it would still be impossible to pass; how much more so when there are so many perils?"
Thus, from the moment he resolved his mind, he proceeded day and night without ceasing; having overcome those difficulties, he returned in safety without losing his wealth and treasures.

That practitioner contemplates that the three realms are all ablaze with fire; desiring to distance himself from them, he seeks the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore it is said: "This is crossing over the ground of old age and death."
A bhikkhu awakens his mindfulness; he should act in accordance with this mindfulness.
Having utterly abandoned birth and death, he is able to make an end to suffering.

Regarding "a bhikkhu awakens his mindfulness": once, there was a merchant traveling through a wilderness. Exhausted from the journey, he slept throughout the night. A band of thieves, having gathered together, intended to come and plunder him.
Then that deity of the void, from within the sky, addressed the merchants with a verse:
"Who is awake among those who sleep?
Who is asleep among those who are awake?"
"Who knows? Who discriminates?
One perceives the retribution according to its true nature.
At that time, among the merchants was an upāsaka who was a disciple of the Buddha’s five precepts; he immediately replied to him, saying:
“I am awake, yet I think I am asleep; I am asleep, yet I think I am awake.
I know, yet I discriminate—desiring to know the meaning of this.
The deva asked again:
"How is it that awakening is sleep?
How is it that sleep is awakening?
How does one know discrimination?"
"I wish to hear the meaning of this.
At that time, the upāsaka replied to the deva:
"The Noble Eightfold Path is what the Three Buddhas have expounded."
While they are practicing the dharma of awakening, I am as if asleep;
I do not perceive the Eightfold Path, as taught by the Three Buddhas.
When they are sleeping while practicing the dharma of awakening, I am as if awake.
"This is what is called the divine power: 'I am awake while others sleep; I am asleep while others are awake; I know and I discern'—this is the meaning one should seek to understand."
The deva spoke again:
"Excellent is awakening while asleep; excellent is sleeping while awake.
Excellent is knowing how to discern; excellent is hearing this meaning."
When the upāsaka heard this teaching, he immediately replied to the deva:
"By the grace of the deva, we have returned safely.
The deva had confounded the thieves so that they did not know where the merchants were staying, thereby enabling the traders to cross the perilous path.
Therefore it is said: "A bhikṣu should awaken his mindfulness.

One who should apply this mindfulness is that practitioner who maintains his resolve with diligent effort; whatever he aspires to in his mind will not fail to be accomplished. Pure and free from blemish, he does not engage in negligence; clad in the garment of diligence and harboring the light of wisdom in his heart, the darkness of ignorance has no way to appear. Therefore it is said: "One should cause him to apply this mindfulness."

Regarding "casting off everything along with birth-and-death": that practitioner further employs skillful means to sever all fetters and attachments; having cast off the heavy, peeled away the heavy, and struck down the heavy, they depart from and distance themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore it is said, "casting off everything along with birth-and-death."

To be one who can bring an end to suffering means that, within this present life, one transcends the dharmas of ordinary worldlings and does not abide in parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāṇa*), parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāṇa*), parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāṇa*), or parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāṇa*), nor parinirvāṇa by ascending to the ultimate limit (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Such a trainee attains parinirvāṇa within this present life, having set aside these five types of parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? As stated in the Buddha’s sūtra, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
“Monks, I do not say that there is even a slight portion of birth, not even for as long as a finger-snap; how much less so for more?”
Why is this? Because the suffering inherent in the process of birth causes one to transmigrate and remain unable to escape suffering.
A bhikṣu should contemplate it as being like excrement: if even a small amount is constantly foul-smelling, how much more so a large quantity?
Therefore, monks! You should seek skillful means to sever the factors of rebirth and forever leave the three realms of existence. Thus it is, monks!
"One should train in this way: uproot the root of birth so that it does not spread its tendrils.

When practitioners hear what the Buddha has taught, they receive his instructions; within this very life, they uproot the source of birth so as never to experience it again. Therefore, it is said: "One is able to bring an end to suffering."
One should always listen to the subtle and wondrous; awaken one’s own mind through self-awakening.
To be able to awaken is to be a worthy person, who is ultimately and eternally free from fear.

Regarding "one should always listen to the subtle and wondrous": it is extremely rare to encounter those who preach the Dharma to others; likewise, it is difficult to possess all the faculties in their entirety. To meet a worthy one or an enlightened sage occurs only once in billions of lifetimes. Thus the World-Honored One said:

"I have accumulated meritorious conduct for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas before I was able to hear the Dharma; yet even having heard the Dharma, it is difficult to encounter its analytical meaning and flavor again.
He addressed those gathered there, saying, "Listen with single-minded concentration to this subtle and wondrous Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "One should always listen to the subtle and wondrous."

Regarding those who awaken to their own intent: while the World-Honored One was in the world, surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, he was preaching the Dharma.
At that time, there was a person among that great assembly who fell into a deep sleep.
A certain bhikṣu said to that sleeping bhikṣu:
"Why do you not awaken to listen to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma?
Instead, you continue to sleep and disturb the great assembly."
"Why do you not contemplate the Tathāgata’s sublime Dharma?
It is more exquisite than ambrosia and eliminates the myriad afflictions of humanity.
Having heard this, the man remained silent and did not respond.
Therefore it is said: "One awakens one's own mind. To be able to awaken is to be a worthy person;

awakening from this sleep is like the difference between heaven and earth—ten million, ten billion times greater than anything that can be illustrated by analogy. There may be practitioners obscured by the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances), dazed and clinging to sleep, while the gods assist them by frequently coming to awaken them, for the mad elephant of the Lord of Death (*Yama*) tramples the sprouts of the three roots of goodness, and the blazing fire of impermanence burns the roots of all living beings.

The Honored One among Men has appeared today, universally illuminating the three realms so that none fail to receive his light. The bandits of the fetters plunder the wealth of goodness; such manifold transformations are beyond reckoning, all arising from the failure to awaken from sleep.
Therefore it is said: "One who is capable of awakening is called a worthy one. Regarding "being without fear from beginning to end": when a person awakens, no myriad evils can interfere.

It is not only those who practice the Way who are considered worthy for their awakening; even ordinary worldly people accomplish various tasks through awakening. At times, a layperson may lose wealth and property while asleep, only to be seized by creditors, robbers, or threatened by fire and water. Or at times, a practitioner may fall into a daze of sleep; when they ought to hear the Dharma, they instead fail to hear it, and when they ought to realize the fruits of the Path, they instead fail to attain them. They should recite and study the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), yet within sleep, all of these are utterly lost.
Therefore it is said: from beginning to end, there is nothing to fear.
By attaining responsiveness through awakened mind, one should day and night aspire to study and practice;
one shall understand the essential nectar of immortality and cause all outflows to be exhausted.

Regarding "attaining correspondence through wakefulness of mind": that practitioner reflects and contemplates, praising the virtue of staying awake day and night; whereas the indolent person likewise praises the essentials of sleep. Therefore it is said: "one attains correspondence by awakening the mind."

Regarding "day and night longing for learning and practice": that practitioner exerts themselves with diligence, never ceasing day or night; they do not lose the proper sequence in the beginning, middle, or end. Therefore it is said, "day and night longing for learning and practice."

That which should be understood as the essential nectar is the Noble Eightfold Path; this is called nectar. The cessation and extinction of *nirvāṇa* is also named nectar. Those practitioners who study and train in the Noble Eightfold Path to advance toward *nirvāṇa*, who depart from the eight states of non-leisure and the mind’s craving for pleasure and desire, and who abide in tranquility, detachment, non-action, and non-activity—for this reason, it is said that one should study the essential nectar.
Regarding the phrase "causing all outflows (āsrava) to be exhausted," what is the meaning of "outflow"?
For what reason is it called "outflow"?
The answer is:

"The meaning of 'abiding' is the meaning of 'outflow'; the meaning of 'soaking' is the meaning of 'outflow'; the meaning of 'dripping' is the meaning of 'outflow'; the meaning of 'predominance' is the meaning of 'outflow'; and the meaning of 'being possessed by non-human beings' is the meaning of 'outflow'."
Regarding the meaning of "abiding as an outflow" (*āsrava*): by what is the abiding of sentient beings in the desire realm restrained?
The answer is:
"By the outflows."
"By what are the sentient beings of the form and formless realms restrained and sustained?
He replied: "By the outflows (*āsrava*)."
Therefore, it is said that "abiding" (sthiti) has the meaning of "outflow" (āsrava).
What is the meaning of "soaking" (parisravaṇa) as "outflow"?
The answer is:
"Just as when soaked with water, the sprouts of grain are able to grow, so it is with these classes of sentient beings:

by means of the three waters, they soak the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of their past actions, and the sprouts are able to grow. This is what is meant by 'soaking' in the sense of 'outflow' (*āsrava*)."

Regarding the meaning of "drip" as "outflow" (*āsrava*): it is like a gushing spring, a leaking roof, a deep channel, or a mountain torrent; it is also like the natural overflow of a mother's profound compassion. This is what is meant by "drip" as the meaning of "outflow."

Regarding the meaning of "outflows" (*āsrava*) as being "predominant": it is just as among human beings there is mutual respect, where the noble and the base, the honorable and the humble, each have their respective places; above there is an enlightened ruler, and the subjects below may not wander freely to the east or west. These classes of sentient beings are likewise so constrained and held fast by the fetters (*saṃyojana*), that they cannot escape the three realms, the four modes of birth, or the five destinies. This is what is meant by the meaning of outflows as being predominant.

Regarding the meaning of being possessed by non-human spirits as constituting an outflow (*āsrava*): it is like a person who, when possessed by a non-human spirit, speaks in a state of madness; they avoid what should be avoided, do not avoid what they should leave, do not hold onto what should be held, and grasp what should not be grasped.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise thus: being possessed by the *saṃyojana* (fetters) and non-human spirits, they speak with madness; therefore, it is said that being possessed by non-humans constitutes the meaning of *āsrava* (outflows).

One who is able to sever these outflows is uniquely honored among humans and devas; whatever the mind intends will surely be accomplished without difficulty, and one attains the knowledge of cessation. Having uprooted the foundation of suffering to reach the ultimate state, one no longer undergoes future existence and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore it is said: "One can sever these various outflows.
When a person attains a true benefit, they come to take refuge in the Buddha;
for this reason, day and night, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.

Regarding what is called "attaining good benefit," the worldly benefits consist of elephants, horses, carriages, national wealth, wives and children, gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber. Although these are called good benefits, they are not true benefits; they deceive and delude the people of the world, leading to resentment and causing the ruin of nations and the destruction of families. One cannot escape the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals through them. However, if one can cast aside their life and take refuge in the Tathāgata, one will be able to escape the calamities of hell and the animal realm.

Those who take refuge in the Buddha sever existence down to the desire for non-existence; they leap over stages to realize the fruit, attaining their respective vows according to the practice of the three vehicles, and if born among devas or humans, they receive spontaneous blessings.

If one who has first resolved to revere the Buddha-way further attains the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Therefore it is said: "A person attains a wholesome benefit.
A question is asked:
"For what reason do you speak only of a person attaining the realization of the fruit, and not of devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, or spirits?"

He replied: "The human realm is the most honored and most sublime among all destinies; by focusing the mind with single-minded intent, one can sever the outflows, exhaust the fetters, and transcend to realize the fruit. Because the human realm is capable of receiving the teachings of the noble ones and the sages, it is called 'human'."
Regarding "therefore one comes to take refuge in the Buddha," what is meant by "taking refuge"?
For what reason is it called taking refuge?
The answer is:
"Protection is the meaning of refuge.
Furthermore, fearlessness is the meaning of refuge, and liberation from calamity is the meaning of refuge.
Therefore it is said: "One comes to take refuge in the Buddha."

Therefore, one should single-mindedly practice mindfulness of the Buddha day and night. The thoughts of a person’s mind flow and race in ten thousand directions; in the mere snap of a finger, immeasurable karmic actions are created. What is contemplated day and night never ceases. To extricate oneself from within this state and turn the mind toward the good—single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha so that no other thoughts ever arise—is why one should single-mindedly practice mindfulness of the Buddha day and night.
A person who attains such wholesome benefit as to come and take refuge in the Dharma should, therefore, day and night, single-mindedly contemplate the Dharma.
What is called the Dharma is the extinction of Nirvana; for those who are fearful, it leads to the Unconditioned.
For one who is free from fear, what difficulty could there be in attaining the Path?

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, and death; whereas Nirvāṇa, which is cessation, is free from birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore it is said: "A person obtains a true benefit when they come to take refuge in the Dharma."

Regarding "day and night, with a single mind, one contemplates the Dharma": as for what is called the Dharma, it brings blessings in the present and eliminates all feverish afflictions; it is that which the wise practice, not that which the foolish perform. Therefore it is said: "Day and night, with a single mind, one contemplates the Dharma."

A person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha; therefore, day and night, one should single-mindedly keep the Saṅgha in mind. Regarding the statement, "A person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha," it is asked: [The Buddha said: "A person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha. Why is this? Because the Saṅgha is a field of merit for the world, including gods and humans. Just as a well-planted field yields an abundant harvest, so too does the Saṅgha, when properly cultivated, yield great fruit. Furthermore, the Saṅgha is a field of merit that is pure, stainless, and free from defilement. It is a field of merit that is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration. By making offerings to such a field of merit, one obtains great rewards. Therefore, a person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha. For this reason, day and night, one should single-mindedly keep the Saṅgha in mind. Why is this? Because by constantly recollecting the Saṅgha, one’s mind becomes upright and focused, and one gradually approaches the path of liberation. Thus, one should always maintain mindfulness of the Saṅgha. This is called the third refuge. One who takes refuge in these three—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—is called a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgata and dwells within the fold of the Buddha’s disciples. They are able to abandon the evil destinies and are certain to attain the bliss of heaven and the ultimate peace of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, one should always take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Thus it was said. The Buddha having spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard his words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. This concludes the Discourse on Taking Refuge in the Three Jewels. Therefore, one should always take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Thus it was said. The Buddha having spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard his words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. This concludes the Discourse on Taking Refuge in the Three Jewels. The third section is finished. The fourth section follows. [The Buddha said: "A person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha. Why is this? Because the Saṅgha is a field of merit for the world, including gods and humans. Just as a well-planted field yields an abundant harvest, so too does the Saṅgha, when properly cultivated, yield great fruit. Furthermore, the Saṅgha is a field of merit that is pure, stainless, and free from defilement. It is a field of merit that is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration. By making offerings to such a field of merit, one obtains great rewards. Therefore, a person attains a wholesome benefit when they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha. For this reason, day and night, one should single-mindedly keep the Saṅgha in mind. Why is this? Because by constantly recollecting the Saṅgha, one’s mind becomes upright and focused, and one gradually approaches the path of liberation. Thus, one should always maintain mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
If fearlessness is the meaning of taking refuge, why is it said that one who has fear within the great assembly takes refuge in the assembly?
The answer is:
"There may be a great assembly that has already abandoned the five difficulties and is no longer subject to fear."

What are the five hardships? First is the hardship of birth; second is the hardship of old age; third is the hardship of illness; fourth is the hardship of death; and fifth is the hardship of not delighting in the assembly.
"Only after one has departed from these five difficulties may one take refuge.
What is meant by "the assembly"?

There are various other assemblies of heterodox practitioners and naked ascetics, numbering from one to ten, even up to the infinite; yet among all such assemblies, the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme.
Therefore it is said: "If a person attains a true benefit, they come to take refuge in the Saṅgha; for this reason, one should day and night, with a single mind, keep the Saṅgha in mind.
Those who are able to know and awaken for themselves are disciples of Gautama;
day and night they should keep this in mind, and with a single mind, take refuge in the Buddha."

Regarding "one who can know through self-awakening": initially, taking refuge in the Dharma was not yet fixed in its meaning; now, this mindfulness of the Buddha is called "fixed," for it is directed toward the Buddha with such firmness that it cannot be shifted. Therefore, it is said: "one who can know through self-awakening."

Regarding those who are disciples of Gautama: the Tathāgata, having emerged from the Gautama clan, spoke this meaning in order to observe future events yet to come. In a future age, there will be sentient beings of the Vatsa clan who are parentless, born suddenly, and who, being arrogant and self-important, will boast of themselves in the world. Desiring to stop their slander, the Tathāgata therefore spoke of "disciples of Gautama."

Day and night one should keep this in mind; with a single mind, one should be mindful of the Buddha. For one who is single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha, the hosts of evil spirits and ghosts dare not approach or invade them. Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should be mindful of this Buddha; with a single mind, one should be mindful of the Buddha."
Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened are disciples of Gautama;
day and night they should keep this in mind, single-mindedly mindful of the Dharma.
"Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened"—thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
"One should personally examine the essentials of all phenomena and eliminate distracted thoughts.
Therefore it is said: "Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened are disciples of Gautama; day and night they should maintain mindfulness, with a single mind mindful of the Dharma."
Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened are disciples of Gautama;
day and night they should keep this in mind, with a single-minded focus on the assembly.
To those who are well-awakened and self-awakened, the Buddha addressed the great multitude:
"You all see this entire assembly; you see it with wisdom, not without wisdom, and you observe it with discernment, not without discernment. You also know whether my assembly is pure or impure."
Therefore it is said: "Those who have awakened well and are self-awakened are disciples of Gautama; day and night they should keep this in mind, with a single-minded focus on the Sangha."

Mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of impermanence, mindfulness of precepts and the virtue of giving, mindfulness of heaven, mindfulness of *ānāpāna*, and mindfulness of death—one should contemplate these day and night.

That practitioner maintains the precepts in their entirety, pure and stainless; they are as indestructible as a diamond and as immovable as Mount Sumeru. Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of impermanence, mindfulness of precepts and the virtue of giving, mindfulness of heaven, mindfulness of *ānāpāna*, and mindfulness of death—one should contemplate these day and night."
Regarding what is called "mindfulness of giving," there are two kinds of giving:
the gift of material wealth and the gift of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The gift of the fetters is called ultimate; it is a giving that does not change or regret.
The gift of material wealth is not the ultimate gift, for after giving it, one may later regret it;
therefore, it is said that one should be mindful of giving.

As for what is called being mindful of the devas: the noble disciples are mindful of the devas day and night, thinking, "By maintaining the precepts here, I shall be reborn in those realms. They cultivate meritorious deeds without severing the faculty of faith, and they fulfill the roots of all virtues by accomplishing the prohibitive precepts. Therefore, it is said: "One should be mindful of the devas day and night."

Regarding the practice of mindfulness of the body: one should constantly contemplate that this body is composed of various impurities and is filled with filth; therefore it is said, "one should be mindful of the body.
This remains true even up to the point of death.
"One who is well-awakened and self-awakened is a disciple of Gautama;
day and night they should contemplate this, with single-minded focus on non-harming.

Regarding "one who is well-awakened and self-awakened is a disciple of Gautama": all sentient beings cherish their own lives, are attached to their wives and children, and are greedy for their household affairs. Only those who cultivate their body, speech, and mind so as not to harm others are called wise men. Therefore it is said: "Day and night they should contemplate this, with single-minded focus on non-harming."

Day and night one should contemplate this so as not to give rise to anger. For when a person gives rise to much anger, they produce many distracted thoughts; the mind becomes like a sword or a halberd, difficult to restrain and difficult to maintain. One who gives rise to anger fails to obtain its fruit. Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should contemplate this so as not to give rise to anger."
Day and night one should contemplate this: one should desire to leave the household life and take no pleasure in dwelling at home with attachment to the five desires.

Although that practitioner remains within the household, they view desires as fire and their mind is constantly weary of them; day and night they reflect upon and dream of leaving the household life. Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should contemplate this," meaning one should always be mindful of the desire to leave the household life.

Day and night one should contemplate this: sit in meditation with a single-minded concentration. For the beginner, the three dhyānas are primary; through dhyāna, the mind is restrained so that the fetters and afflictions do not arise. When all discursive thoughts are stilled and concentrated, mindfulness does not wander or race away. Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should contemplate this: sit in meditation with a single-minded intent."

Day and night one should maintain this mindfulness; by maintaining it, one does not receive the dust [of defilement]. Always delighting in tranquility, one does not dwell among worldly people; wearing coarse clothing and eating poor food, one does not cling to ornamental finery. Striving merely to sustain the physical form, one finds sufficiency in practicing the Path. Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should maintain this mindfulness; by maintaining it, one does not receive the dust."

Day and night you should contemplate this: emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness; constantly observe that the body of the five aggregates is void and not real, and cannot be relied upon. It is a phenomenon subject to change and cannot endure for long. If one calculates that there is no self, how much less can there be a body?
Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should contemplate this: emptiness, non-aspiration, and signlessness. Day and night one should contemplate this:

to depart from and abandon the mind of seeking and desiring. That practitioner seeks the Way and its virtue not for their own sake; they do not aspire to the forms of male or female, nor do they aspire to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharmas*). Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should contemplate this: to depart from and abandon the mind of seeking and desiring."

Day and night one should contemplate this, training in the mind of non-conception; when a practitioner attains the state of non-conception, they are fully endowed with the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.
A question is asked:
"While a practitioner dwells in the various stages, they do not perceive a self or a non-self."
"Why is it that you do not speak of the complete and perfect Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones, but speak only of the attainment of non-perception? He replied:
"The attainment of non-perception is the secret chamber of the noble ones; those who enter this chamber hear no more of the mixed and defiled conduct of ordinary worldlings."
Therefore it is said: "Day and night one should keep this in mind, training in the mind of non-perception.
Day and night one should keep this in mind: entering the chamber and reflecting, that practitioner, when first beginning his practice, trains in two types of reflection:
first, the severing of fetters; second, finding delight in the present life.
Therefore it is said: One should contemplate this day and night, entering meditative concentration and reflecting upon it.
Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened are disciples of Gautama;
they should contemplate this day and night, finding delight in the bliss of Nirvāṇa.

That which is called Nirvana is, from beginning to end, free from sorrow; nor does one perceive its arising, its existence, or its exhaustion. It is forever detached from all afflictions and devoid of feverish distress. It is without seeking and without conceptualization; there is no longer the five aggregates or name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). There is no sense of "I," nor does one perceive name-and-form as "mine. To state it in brief: it is empty, non-existent, and beyond all mental construction.
The wise teach and train [others]; therefore it is said: "Those who are well-awakened and self-awakened.
These disciples of Gautama should contemplate this day and night, delighting their minds in the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
One should mindfully awaken oneself; be careful not to let one’s conduct decline.
Conduct that is practiced leads to peace; by not practicing such conduct, one receives its retribution.
Regarding "one should mindfully awaken oneself": when a person engages in any action, they should first reflect within, deliberate, and contemplate it thoroughly.
Reflect well before you act; be careful not to lose your proper course.
He who considers how not to lose his way avoids the pain and grief of having lost it.
Therefore it is said: "One should mindfully awaken oneself."

Be careful not to let your practice decline. For when a person undertakes an action, if the matter has already become manifest yet they again become lax and indolent—failing to investigate its principles or engage in meditative reflection, or if their recitation is sometimes neither fluent nor proficient, and when the time for testing arrives, they abandon the assembly and flee—this is what is meant by having a decline in one's training.

For those who practice meditation, if their mindfulness does not abide in concentration but wanders among myriad objects—like a monkey that abandons one branch to leap to another—it constitutes a great hindrance to the Dharma and Vinaya of the Noble Ones. Therefore, the masters of old instructed their juniors to bring their path to completion without allowing it to leak away or be lost. For this reason, it is said: "Be careful not to lose what you possess."

Regarding "being mindful so as not to lose one's place": there may be a person who recites ten thousand [verses] a day and understands a hundred thousand meanings; reciting and chanting day and night without losing the preceding or following words and phrases, each part being distinct and clear, such that the principle does not deviate from the meaning. Entering the stillness of *dhyāna*, even when celestial thunder and earthquakes produce ten thousand simultaneous sounds, they cannot disturb their spirit. For this reason, it is said: "being mindful so as not to lose one's place."

Those who lose what they cherish and suffer the pain of grief do so because their conduct is not focused on themselves alone; they give rise to envy together with others and thus fall into the abyss. All this is due to the rectitude of their conduct. Therefore it is said: "They lose what they cherish and suffer the pain of grief."
A person should seek skillful means to personally attain wealth and treasure;
by observing its significance for themselves, their wishes will immediately bear fruit. Regarding "a person should seek skillful means":
many people in the world long to travel in all four directions, striving diligently at every step to save their own lives, yet they do so out of greed for wealth and goods.

The bhikṣus further sought skillful means, reciting the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and the various miscellaneous collections (Kṣudraka-piṭaka). Those bhikṣus practicing meditation entered deeply into dhyāna-concentration; whether for seven short periods or seven long periods, they did not lose their sequence. Having acquired the wealth of the Dharma through the method of "the ear-hammer," their merit increased and their practice was strengthened. Therefore it is said: "A person should seek skillful means to bring about the attainment of wealth and treasure for themselves."

He observes the meaning for himself, and his wishes are immediately fulfilled. People in the world reflect: "Who is there among the wealthy and noble who possesses tens of millions in accumulated riches that can spend such treasures at will? Yet the one who studies the Way renounces wife and children and departs from honor and glory; he knows that his merit is fully perfected, and when the principles of the Dharma are analyzed, he is able to answer any inquiry.

That practitioner of dhyāna further observes for himself the tranquility of meditative concentration; he attains the six supernormal powers, soars through the void, and performs the eighteen transformations with the mastery of appearing and disappearing at will. Those who do not yet believe in the Way gain faith upon seeing this, while those who already believe in the Way advance further without regressing. Therefore it is said: "He observes its meaning for himself, and his aspirations are immediately fulfilled."
Sitting and rising, he seeks skillful means, seeking for himself the clarity of meditative concentration;
like a craftsman refining pure gold, he removes the darkness of dust and grime.
No longer obscured by gloom, he is forever freed from the affliction of old age and death.

"Sitting and rising, seeking skillful means, one seeks for oneself the clarity of concentration. Regarding what is meant by "sitting and rising," these refer to the various doubts and fetters. A person who harbors indolence and arrogance does not investigate their own karma; though such an indolent person may say they are rising, it is no different from sitting. A person of diligent application, though they may say they are sitting or lying down, it is no different from standing. Therefore it is said: "Sitting and rising, seeking skillful means, one seeks for oneself the clarity of concentration."

One should always single-mindedly seek meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for its luminous clarity is inexhaustible and there is nowhere it does not illuminate; therefore it is said, "seeking the light of concentration.

It is like a smith refining pure gold to remove dust and impurities. When those master craftsmen and artisans have gathered among the great assembly, it is as if objects covered in dust are obscured by that grime; until they are swept away, the defilement only increases.
The mind of this person is likewise so: defiled by the stains of lust, anger, and ignorance, it lacks brilliance and cannot shine forth.
Therefore it is said: "Just as a craftsman refines true gold, removing dust and darkness."

Not obscured by darkness and forever free from the affliction of old age and death—such is the practitioner who has cleared away the dust and grime of defilements and is devoid of all fetters. He is ultimately not subdued by birth, not distressed by old age, and not summoned by impermanence. Therefore it is said: "Not obscured by darkness, forever free from the affliction of old age and death."
Not feeling shame where one should feel shame, and feeling shame where one should not;
not fearing what is fearful, and fearing what is not fearful—one gives rise to false views in life and enters hell after death.

Regarding "those who are not ashamed where they should be ashamed": there may be practitioners who, being advanced in years, are unwilling to receive instruction from junior bhikṣus. When a junior bhikṣu speaks in accordance with the Dharma teachings, the elder feels ashamed and reflects within himself:
"To be instructed by a young bhikṣu—this fills me with extreme shame; I have nowhere to hide my face."
In that regard, one should feel shame where there is no cause for shame; therefore it is said, "one feels shame where there is no shame.

As for "feeling shame where there is no shame," this refers to a practitioner who does not recite, study, or master the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and the various miscellaneous Piṭakas, yet in vain accepts the offerings of the faithful—robes, food and drink, medicine for the sick, beds, mats, and bedding; therefore it is said, "one feels shame where there is no shame."

Those who do not fear what they ought to fear are those who, facing the cessation of all things—Nirvana, which is tranquil and unconditioned—instead fear it and fail to apply themselves to its practice. Within that Nirvana there is no birth, no aging, no sickness, and no death; nor are there the realms of gods, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals. Yet they fear it as described.

Those ordinary persons have never heard of this: that which was originally non-existent, is now non-existent, has already ceased to exist, and will never exist; nor do they possess fearlessness or tranquility, nor are they free from various harms and transformations. Having abandoned all hardships, they yet fear them further. Therefore it is said: "To manifest fear when there is no fear."

To fear what is manifest yet not fear it means that one is being burned by the blazing fires of lust, anger, and delusion within the cycle of birth and death across the five realms; furthermore, one does not fear the ever-increasing suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress—which are beyond description—nor does one fear further attachment to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Therefore, it is said: "to fear what is manifest yet not fear it."

To be born with wrong views—what are called wrong views—is to feel no shame where one should feel shame, and to feel shame where one should not; to feel no fear where one should feel fear, and to feel fear where one should not. All such instances are termed wrong views.

To create karma of wrong view is called being born with wrong view; upon death, one enters the evil realms. Those who have committed much sin enter the evil realms; those who have committed middling sin enter the animal realm; and those who have committed slight sin enter the realm of hungry ghosts.
Therefore it is said: "Those with wrong views fall into evil realms.
If a person commits a transgression first but later ceases and does not offend again, they illuminate the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished."
Once, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there lived not far from the borders of the kingdom the son of a brahmin named Ahimsaka.

He constantly followed his teachers and friends to study the brahminical scriptures. His teacher was an elderly elder over eighty years of age who had taken a wife; she was young and vigorous, with a beautiful and upright countenance, and her feminine decorum and dignified bearing were fully perfected. The brahmin youth Ahimsaka was likewise handsome, a man whose physical appearance was peerless in the world.

At that time, the woman’s lust was intensely inflamed; she immediately seized the hand of the Brahmin youth Ahiṃsaka and said, "I revere your virtue and desire to unite with you in passion; would this be acceptable to you?"
Upon hearing this, Wu-hai covered his ears with his hands and said,
"I would rather lose my life than ever dare to listen.
The woman replied to him:
"If one provides food and drink to a person who is hungry and thirsty, is that not an act of profound kindness?
Now, the fire of lust within me is blazing fiercely; I require your water of lust to extinguish it—would this not be most agreeable to my heart?"
"If you were to cause me to lose my life-force, what would be the use of studying this scripture? Ahimsaka replied,
"If I were to die by violating the Brahmin law according to my mother's will and fall into hell, would that not be a great injustice?"
Then Ahiṃsaka dragged himself out through the door.
At that time, the Brahmin’s wife, with disheveled hair and her head covered in dust, tore her clothes, sat upon the ground, and wept aloud.
When the elder brahmin returned from his journey and saw this, he asked his wife,
"Who took you and beat you so severely?
The wife replied to the brahmin:
"He is your trusted disciple.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin reflected within himself:

"It is not appropriate for me to reveal this matter now; that man has heard everything and will undoubtedly harm me. I must employ a skillful means to entice him forward subtly, so that I may seize his person and sever the root of his life-force."

He immediately called the son of the brahmin and said to him, "The incantations you have studied from beginning to end are now all complete and without deficiency; however, you must select an auspicious day to sacrifice to the various deities before the incantation can be performed."

Holding a shield in his left hand and a sword in his right, he proceeded to a narrow and perilous path; whenever he encountered a person, he would slay them, and upon reaching a total of one thousand, he would take a finger from each to form a garland—only then could the incantation be successfully performed.

At that time, Māra the Evil One again dispatched kumbhāṇḍa spirits to protect that person so that they might commit evil deeds; he cut off the paths for people so that no one traveled them anymore, until gradually, even the Ārāmavatī Garden was deserted, the populace was sparse, and the entire kingdom suffered calamity; furthermore, he was short of one finger, so as not to complete the required number.
Ahiṃsaka’s own mother constantly thought to herself:
"My son has been in the wilderness for a long time; it is certain beyond doubt that he suffers from hunger, cold, and toil.
At that time, the mother went in person to that grove to bring him provisions. Seeing her from afar, Ahiṃsaka immediately had this thought:
"I have received my teacher’s instruction that I must complete the finger-garland; now, with one finger missing, the count is insufficient.

Now that I encounter my own mother coming to deliver provisions, if I were to eat first, the incantation would not succeed; yet if I were to kill my mother first, I would commit a crime of immediate retribution."

"The son of the brahmin is one who should attain liberation through the Buddha. With his three types of supernormal knowledge, the Tathāgata perceives that he intends to commit the five heinous crimes without hesitation, including killing his mother.

If this is indeed the case, even a hundred million Buddhas could not save him. It would be well if I were now to go and rescue him from his suffering, so that both mother and son may be preserved whole."

He immediately transformed himself into a bhikṣu, holding an alms-bowl in his hand and walking while looking at the ground; following that path, he went straight toward that garden. As he walked, the travelers and cowherds by the roadside said to him:
“Stop, stop, śramaṇa!”
"Do not take this road; ahead lies a violent bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who has already harmed and killed countless people. We dread him and do not travel this path."
"The śramaṇas are weak; if we were to be harmed by bandits, would that not be a great tragedy?
The transformed man said, "Do not worry;
the bandits will not harm me. I possess incantations sufficient to restrain them and prevent them from harming me."
He advanced further still, intending to reach the garden.
Aṅgulimāla saw a bhikṣu approaching from afar; he leaped for joy, unable to contain himself, and thought, "My wish has been fulfilled!"
"I must certainly achieve the *añjali-mālā* [finger-garland] rite; furthermore, I shall not harm my mother.
Once the incantation is accomplished, I will temporarily set aside my mother and this food; only after killing that bhikṣu will I be able to eat."
Grasping a sword and holding up a shield, Ahiṃsaka went out to confront the bhikṣu.
Being naturally a powerful man, he ran as fast as a galloping horse toward the Buddha;

however, by the Buddha’s supernormal power, Ahiṃsaka was made to shrink suddenly into the ground, while the ground where the Buddha stood expanded and widened, so that he became utterly exhausted and unable to reach the Buddha.
Aṅgulimāla raised his voice and called out to the śramaṇa, saying:
"Stop, stop, śramaṇa!
I wish to ask about the meaning of the Dharma."
The bhikṣu replied, "I have long been abiding; it is you yourself who do not abide.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke a verse to the bhikṣu, saying:
“The śramaṇa acts contrary to his words when he says ‘I abide,’ and I abide while he says ‘I do not abide.
The śramaṇa should explain this meaning: how is it that you abide while I do not?”
At that time, the Buddha again answered in verse:
"Aṅgulimāla, I abide in harmlessness toward all people;
you are a violent man—why do you not reform your transgressions?"
The full explanation is as set forth in the verses of the *Sūtra*.

At that time, the bandit Aṅgulimāla cast his sword, shield, and the garland of fingers upon his head into a deep ravine; with palms joined in reverence toward the Tathāgata, he repented and further praised him with these verses:
*Udānavarga*, Volume XVII.
*Udānavarga*, Scroll 18,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty;
Section on Miscellaneous Matters, Part Two.
“I take refuge in the Great Sage Hero; desiring to behold the Honored Śramaṇa, I now wish to repent for the transgressions I have committed over a long time.

At that time, the World-Honored One again manifested his physical form, his majestic spiritual power resplendent and manifest. Holding Aṅgulimāla by the hand, he proceeded to the Jetavana Monastery and addressed the bhikṣus:
"You all shall ordain this Aṅgulimāla as a bhikṣu.
