Accordingly, he received the teachings of the Buddha and became a practitioner of the Way; at dawn, he dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, inside the city gate there was a female elephant who was pregnant and about to give birth, yet she could not bring forth her offspring.
Seeing the bhikṣu approaching from afar, the owner of the elephant immediately rose to meet and welcome him.
“Monks, if one can cause an elephant to give birth, one may enter the city to beg for alms;
if one cannot cause an elephant to give birth, one must not enter the city, lest one commit a *pācittiya* offense.”
The bhikṣu replied, "I have not previously recited this spell.
Please wait a moment while I return to the World-Honored One to receive the divine incantation; once I have returned, I shall recite it so that she may give birth."
Then the monk Aṅgulimāla went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Blessed One:

"Just now, as I entered the city for alms, I encountered an elephant about to give birth inside the city gate. They demanded my incantations, saying that only after the elephant had given birth would they grant me alms."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously accept this divine spell, so that the elephant may give birth and be able to cross over.
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Go to that place and recite this spell over it, saying: [insert spell here]."
"Now, by this spell of utmost sincerity— having never since birth taken the life of a living being—
I hold this word of utmost sincerity so that the elephant may give birth safely and without harm.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla received the incantation from the Buddha and immediately went to recite it over the elephant, which then gave birth in safety.
At that time, all the people exclaimed:
"Excellent! There is indeed such a marvelous thing in the world."

Although this Śaṅgharakṣita had previously killed countless beings, he now swore an oath that from birth until now he had never once taken life; by the power of these words of utmost sincerity, he caused the elephant to give birth without harm.

He was then able to enter the city. When the people of the streets and alleys saw Aṅgulimāla approaching, those among them whose parents, brothers, wives, or children had been killed by him all came forward to avenge their grievances. Some struck Aṅgulimāla violently with swords, staves, tiles, and stones until he was thoroughly battered; they broke his head, wounded his body, and tore his robes to shreds. His alms bowl was also shattered, so he immediately fled out of the city and did not beg for food at all.

Returning to the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and recounted the origins of his circumstances. The Buddha, knowing his intent, said, "Mālādhāra, how swift is the ripening of karmic retribution!

Thereupon, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him; immediately upon sitting, he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and eventually reached Arhatship, with the six supernormal powers becoming perfectly clear.
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately assembled the fourfold army—the cavalry, the elephant corps, the chariot corps, and the infantry—and intended to go to that grove to fight with Aṅgulimāla.

Having departed from the city of Śrāvastī, he heard on the road travelers say that the great bandit Aṅgulimāla had received the instruction of the Tathāgata and become a bhikṣu; he immediately halted his troops and entered the Jeta Grove Monastery to meet with the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the king was about to arrive, immediately used his supernormal powers to conceal Aṅgulimāla’s form so that it would not be visible.
When King Prasenajit reached the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. Then the World-Honored One, knowing the situation, asked:
“The King has prepared weapons of war and assembled the fourfold army; for what purpose have you come?”
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,

“Within our borders there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla who dwells in the mountains and commits robberies with such cruelty and lawlessness that we have gathered an army, intending to go and attack him.”
On the way, I heard people say:
"Aṅgulimāla has been converted by the Buddha's coming to teach him and has attained the Way.
I do not know where that man is now?
The Buddha, knowing the king’s thoughts, immediately withdrew his supernormal power so that the king might see Aṅgulimāla.
Upon seeing him, the king was struck with terror and fell face-down upon the ground; his ministers raised him up and sprinkled water over him.
The Buddha said to the king:
"It is by great good fortune that Your Majesty has encountered this minor terror; for that man has already attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Had you gone to that deep garden and seen him in his true form—with a garland of fingers upon his head, his body smeared with human blood, holding a sharp sword, and his countenance fierce and enraged—upon seeing him, Your Majesty’s heart and liver would have been shattered and your life-force would have perished."
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata today brings down those who have not yet been brought down and delivers those who have not yet been delivered.
Yet, World-Honored One, how could that man—who killed countless people—attain the fruit of Arhatship?”
The Buddha said, "Do not grieve;
conditioned phenomena have sequence, some are matured and some are not, and there is beginning as well as end.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the causes and conditions of past lives, spoke these verses before the great assembly:
"To commit evil before others and extinguish it with goodness illuminates the world, like the moon when the clouds have vanished.

Regarding "committing evil before others and extinguishing it with goodness": it is like Aṅgulimāla, who killed countless thousands of people, yet extinguished that evil through the Noble Eightfold Path; all evils being exhausted, they were forever without root, ultimately pure, and attained the state of non-arising.
Therefore it is said: "If a person previously committed evil, they may extinguish it with goodness.
Regarding the phrase "this illuminates the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished," the term "world" (loka) has three meanings:
first, the world of sentient beings; second, the world of the vessel (the physical environment); and third, the world of the aggregates (skandhas).

Just as the autumn moon, surrounded by the multitude of stars, shines uniquely bright among them, its light illuminating both the near and the far; so too, when a wicked bhikṣu has exhausted all evils and cultivates pure conduct, he brings widespread salvation and deliverance to the great assembly.
Therefore it is said: "This illuminates the world, like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
If a person has previously committed evil, they should extinguish it with goodness; regarding worldly attachment, one should contemplate the meaning of emptiness.

Regarding those who commit evil in public and seek to extinguish it with goodness: for all acts of evil arise from attachment; when that brahmin’s wife gave rise to malice toward one who was harmless, it was entirely due to her heart of attachment.
Therefore it is said: "If one has previously committed evil, one extinguishes it with goodness.

Regarding the phrase "the world's attachment; contemplate emptiness as its meaning": because the heart of craving is deep and firm, beings transmigrate through the three realms, undergo the four modes of birth, and revolve through the five destinies. All this arises from attachment that cannot be relinquished. Practitioners may differentiate these things as empty and unreal, yet they do not truly know them. Knowing that all are empty and quiescent, and cannot be relied upon, it is therefore said: "The world's attachment; contemplate emptiness as its meaning."
Having renounced the home life in youth, he diligently cultivated the Buddha-dharma; he illuminates the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:

“By way of the parable of the elephant trainer, there was once a young elephant that the trainer sought to discipline while it still delighted in the wilderness; it died in the wilderness before being tamed. Furthermore, there was a middle-aged elephant that was not disciplined and met its end there as well.”
It is the same for a young bhikṣu who passes away without having received instruction, as it is for an elder bhikṣu who passes away without having received instruction.

"Monks, you should know that it is just like this: a young elephant dies while being trained; a middle-aged elephant dies while being trained; a young bhikkhu dies while being instructed; and an elder bhikkhu dies having been instructed and having attained the noble Dhamma."
A young and vigorous bhikṣu practices the Buddha’s teachings with great intensity, without any loss or deficiency, fully perfecting the Buddha-dharma.
What does it mean to be "fully perfected"?

It means to transcend the gradual stages to attain realization and achieve the unsurpassed fruit; therefore it is said: "The young and vigorous leave home and practice the Buddha’s teachings with great intensity."
"This illuminating of the world is like the moon when the clouds have vanished" means that it is like the light of the autumn moon shining far and wide.
Having abandoned the home life in youth, one vigorously cultivates the Buddha's teachings; regarding worldly attachments, one contemplates the meaning of emptiness.

Those who leave the household life in their youth and vigor desire to sever attachment; they are seen and respectfully attended by devas and asuras, and the garuḍas, gandharvas, and others all serve and make offerings to them. Therefore, it is said that one should contemplate the meaning of emptiness regarding worldly attachment.

To cause no affliction while living, and to feel no grief at death—this is the courage of one who has seen the Path; one should remain composed in the midst of it and not grieve. Regarding "to cause no affliction while living, and to feel no grief at death":

from birth until now, such a person has refrained from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and committing various evils. At the time of death, their consciousness is clear and tranquil, free from alarm or fear. Furthermore, they do not see the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor do they see malevolent spirits; they see only auspicious and favorable omens. Therefore it is said: "To cause no affliction while living, and to feel no grief at death."

Regarding the statement, "One who is firm upon the Path of Vision should not grieve amidst it": such a person who has realized the Truths (satyadarśin) has already transcended the five difficulties; thus, even while amidst sorrow and distress, they remain serene and inactive, neither wailing nor weeping to give rise to various afflictions. Therefore it is said: "One who is firm upon the Path of Vision should not grieve amidst it."
Not causing distress while living, nor grieving at death—this is seeing the Path with courage;
being alone and clear among one's kin.

Regarding "not causing distress while living, nor grieving at death": from birth until now, one has not practiced unwholesome dharmas on account of parents, brothers, or the five clans of one's lineage. Therefore it is said: "being alone and clear among one's kin."
Severing turbid and dark dharmas, one trains only in purity;
crossing the abyss without returning, abandoning reliance and coming to rest, no longer stained by pleasure, one severs desire and is free from sorrow.
Regarding "severing turbid and black dharmas," what are called turbid and black dharmas?
The answer is:

"All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*bandhana*), and defilements (*mala*); all unwholesome dharmas that lead to retrogression and falling, and all attachments to birth and death—these should be severed, have been severed, and are forever severed."
Therefore it is said: "One cuts off turbid and dark dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "training in what is purely white," what is meant by "purely white dharmas"?
The answer is:

"The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and whatever other dharmas there may be that transcend birth and death and provide the means of deliverance, are also called pure and white dharmas."
Therefore it is said: "One trains for the sake of purity alone.
As for "crossing the abyss without returning," why is it called an "abyss"?

What is meant by an "abyss" is that one's flow remains within the realms and destinies, increasing birth and death; because of this abyss, one wanders through birth and death beyond measure, falling into the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties. For this reason, the World-Honored One said: "One should extinguish the four abysses and seek the unsurpassed path."
Therefore it is said: "Having crossed the abyss, one does not return.
Regarding the phrase "abandoning reliance and bringing practice to rest," what is meant by "reliance"?
What is called "reliance" refers to relying on unwholesome dharmas of desire. For this reason, the Tathāgata said: "Abandoning reliance and being without attachment is what is called true practice."
Therefore it is said: "Abandoning clinging, one comes to rest.

As for "no longer being stained by pleasure," this means not being defiled by the five pleasures, drawing near to the discipline of the noble ones, and never abandoning it; therefore it is said: "one no longer delights [in them]."

Regarding those who wish to sever sorrow: for a person not to reach the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is all due to the presence of desire. Being defiled by and attached to female form, one gives rise to mental conceptions, dwelling upon her appearance—her hair, eyebrows, teeth, and fair, upright features.
When a practitioner holds their resolve and eliminates such thoughts, the desire-conception ceases and no longer blazes forth.
Therefore it is said: "One who desires to sever sorrow has no grief.
With the mind of craving as the field, and lust, anger, and delusion as the seeds—thus, by giving to those who have transcended the world, one obtains immeasurable merit.

Regarding the statement "the mind of craving is the field": it is just as when a field is overgrown and its soil is defiled, failing to be cultivated and tended; weeds grow in competition, harming the fine seedlings, so that the grain does not flourish and the harvest is not bountiful at its time. When a person is stained by and attached to craving, it is also like this. Therefore it is said: "the mind of craving is the field."

Regarding "having lust, anger, and delusion as seeds": when a practitioner cultivates their practice, they constantly observe themselves; if a person plants merit, in what place does one bestow it so as to obtain its karmic fruit?
The answer is:
"Those who give without entering emptiness are few; those who give while entering emptiness are many.
Why are those who give without entering emptiness few?
He replied:

"As for those among the various non-Buddhist heterodox sects, such as the naked ascetics and the Nirgranthas, who are foolish people fond of giving and hope to gain merit therein—they do not obtain even one-sixteenth part [of the merit] compared to this."

"Just as a field infested with weeds harms the healthy seedlings, so do the defiled practices of a brahmin harm the roots of goodness; being shrouded by lust, anger, and delusion, one does not produce the fruits of the Path."
Therefore it is said: "Because lust, anger, and delusion serve as seeds, one gives to those who have transcended the world.

Regarding the phrase "obtaining immeasurable merit," this praises the reward for giving to the noble assembly of the Tathāgata. Among the great assembly, there are those who have severed desire; though what is given to them may be small, the merit obtained is immeasurable, and the resulting retribution is beyond calculation. Thus it is said: "Therefore, by giving to those who have transcended the world, one obtains immeasurable merit."
Just as in a field of filth and impurity, where anger grows and spreads like a creeping vine, one should therefore abandon anger; the reward for such giving is immeasurable.
As for the phrase "just as in a field of filth and impurity, where anger grows and spreads like a creeping vine," why is it called "filth and impurity"?
The reason they are called "corrupt and evil" is that they both destroy themselves and further destroy others.
As for how they destroy themselves: when their hatred is blazing and intense, their facial expression changes and their innate nature is altered; this is what is meant by destroying oneself.
Furthermore, regarding those who disparage others: with the fire of hatred blazing intensely, they cause harm to others, even to the point of depriving them of their life-force.
Therefore it is said: "It is like a field of filth, where hatred grows and spreads like creeping vines."

Therefore, one should abandon anger; the retribution for giving is immeasurable. Because people harbor anger, they later receive the retribution of anger; because people are driven by hatred, they lose their nations and destroy their families—all this arises from hatred. When a benevolent person practices the merit of giving, if they give without anger, they obtain immeasurable blessings. For this reason it is said: "One should abandon anger when giving; the retribution is immeasurable."
Just as in a field of filth, the filth of ignorance arises;
therefore, one should abandon ignorance, and the reward obtained will be immeasurable.

Regarding the line "just as in a field of filth, the filth of ignorance arises": it is like a blind person whose eyes do not perceive high ground or level plains, nor do they see beautiful or ugly forms, blue, yellow, red, or white.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise so: entangled by the darkness of ignorance, they do not perceive the Four Noble Truths or the dharmas of the wholesome and unwholesome; their wisdom-light and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are shrouded and obscured.
The heterodox teachers, followers of different schools, and various brahmins are shrouded by ignorance and do not recognize the truth of the Path.
Among the noble assembly of the Tathāgata, such afflictions never exist.
Therefore it is said: "It is like a field of filth, where folly grows and spreads like creeping vines."
"Therefore, one should abandon folly; the merit obtained shall be immeasurable. Regarding this, if a practitioner wishes to seek freedom from folly, from whom should they seek it?
The answer is:
"One should seek it from the noble assembly of the Tathāgata."

Why is this? Because the noble assembly has already observed the beginning and the end—whether great or small, beautiful or ugly—and through their discernment of the Four Noble Truths, their vision is clear and their wisdom awakened without missing even a hair’s breadth. Since they bestow [this merit] upon that noble assembly of Tathāgatas, who are free from all delusion, they shall obtain immeasurable retribution.
Therefore it is said: One should give while remaining free from delusion, for the retribution will be immeasurable.
Just as in a field of filth, where arrogance grows like spreading vines, one should therefore abandon pride;
by doing so, one shall obtain immeasurable retribution.
"Just as in a field of filth, where arrogance grows and spreads like a creeping vine"—for the arrogance of non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners is most extreme, the Tathāgata spoke this verse:

"The Brahmins are full of excessive arrogance; from the end of their lives in this world, they shall be reborn among the six realms of existence: the fifth being the five hells, and the sixth being chickens, pigs, dogs, wolves, and donkeys. One who gives to such people shall not obtain its reward."
Therefore it is said: "Just as a field is defiled by weeds, so too is pride exceedingly abundant.

Thus, one should abandon arrogance to obtain immeasurable retribution. Within the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata, one must eliminate pride; whether at times wearing robes and carrying an alms-bowl to enter a village for alms, one should humble oneself and lower one's mind like a *caṇḍāla* girl. Even if one’s body is clad in precious garments worth hundreds of thousands, if one approaches another’s house, one should stand leaning against the gate and wait, not daring to enter the residence.

To treat a bhikṣu with contempt is likewise so. Originally from a noble clan, he has brought hardship upon his own form to practice the dharma of a mendicant; he governs his mind and disciplines his will as if wielding a sharp sword, and holds his alms bowl in hand like a pauper of the world. While the people of Jambudvīpa adorn themselves with hair, we śramaṇas shave it off; while the people of Jambudvīpa are greedy for fine garments, the pure śramaṇa dyes them to change their color. When those among the people of Jambudvīpa who have committed crimes flee to the deep mountains, the śramaṇa takes the mountain thickets as his home. If such is the conduct of one who is free from desire, how much more so for one who has attained the fruits of the path—could his mind ever be swayed?
Therefore it is said: one should abandon arrogance, and the reward obtained will be immeasurable.
Just as a field is defiled by weeds, so greed acts as a spreading vine;
therefore, one should abandon greed, and the reward obtained will be immeasurable.

"Just as a field is defiled and overgrown with weeds, so too is greed. When a person harbors stinginess and greed, they do not abandon them until death; or, due to such stinginess and greed, they may even bring about the premature destruction of their life-force. Therefore, the wise distance themselves from stinginess and greed. Thus it is said: "Just as a field is defiled and overgrown with weeds, so too is greed. For this reason, one should abandon greed; the reward obtained shall be immeasurable.
The six sovereigns are stained; stain is their chief. To be unstained is to be free;
those who are stained are called fools.
Regarding these "six sovereigns," what is meant by "sovereign"? It refers to the following: [the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind].
It is said: "It is the mind (manas).
Counting forward from it, there are six; counting backward, there are likewise six. As for its supremacy:
when the mind moves, the other five follow in their activity as the five feelings (pañca-vedanā), enlisting the various sense bases (āyatana); all are produced by the mind."

As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras: "Just as the five faculties each have their own respective domains, which do not intermingle nor encroach upon one another, the mind reaches these five locations as their primary source;
it invades those five realms and employs the five feelings so that they cannot remain stationary. Among the five objects, it is the most supreme and most subtle; therefore, it is called the 'King'."
Therefore it is said: "The six are the sovereign lords.
Regarding the statement, "Defilement is the head of defilements," what constitutes defilement?
That which is called defilement refers to the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*). Therefore it is said: "Defilement is the head of defilements."
"Being unstained, one is liberated. What is meant by "unstained"? One who is unstained is the Arhat.
Although it is said that for the Srotāpanna all defilements are exhausted and they attain the purity of the Dharma-eye, they have not yet attained ultimate purity.
An Arhat has attained eternal purity; therefore it is said: "Being unstained, one is liberated. To be stained means to be deluded.

That which the deluded person habitually practices is attachment to the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. They do not contemplate what should be contemplated, and they instead contemplate what should not be contemplated; therefore it is said: "To be stained means to be deluded."

"The skeleton serves as the city wall, smeared with flesh and blood; all the gates are wide open, and the bandits of the fetters run wild. Regarding "the skeleton serves as the city wall, smeared with flesh and blood":

what is called a "city" here takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its ramparts. The skeletal frame is the enclosure wall, which is stained with blood. If one were to contemplate how internal substances are exposed to the exterior, one would then give rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), becoming detached from the body and conceiving the thought that it is not to be relished. Since the skin merely covers the bones to form a shape for adornment, the wise observe that there is not a single thing therein worth craving. Therefore it is said: "The skeleton serves as the city wall, smeared with flesh and blood."

"When the gates of the sense faculties are all wide open, the thieves of the fetters gain license to run wild. This means that when the eye-faculty is opened and receives external forms, one asks: "Who opens it?
The answer is:
"It is due to a lack of reflection that allows the thieves of the fetters to enter and plunder the wealth of the roots of virtue."

The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. When the faculty of the mind (manas) is opened wide, the thieves of the fetters (saṃyojana) gain entry. Therefore it is said: "When the gates of the faculties are opened wide, the thieves of the fetters run rampant."
When conditions exist, suffering increases; observing those three causes of bondage, one extinguishes them through the assembly of the virtuous, for they are not removed by external fools.

Regarding "when conditions exist, suffering increases": when there were causal conditions previously, suffering subsequently arose and increased; if there had been no causal conditions previously, from what could suffering have arisen?

Just as a spring source produces water that forms rivers, so it is here: because of prior conditions, there is the limit of suffering, which gradually increases until it reaches the four hundred and four ailments. Therefore it is said: "When there are conditions, suffering increases."

To contemplate those bound by the three causes is like a laborer confined within a workshop, compelled to toil without rest; it is the same with this body of the five aggregates in full bloom, which is bound by the fetters of afflictions (*saṃyojana*). Grief, sorrow, and suffering compel the consciousness to remain restless, and one must further undergo the four hundred and four diseases. Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate those bound by the three causes."

Regarding "extinguishing [defilements] through the assembly of the virtuous": one who wishes to practice faithful giving should approach the great assembly; though the gift be small, the merit obtained is vast. This is just as a valiant and strong man who can repel external enemies and crush their hosts is called "valiant," and furthermore receives rewards that surpass those of all others.

The Tathāgata’s assembly of noble ones is also like this: just as the ocean receives ten thousand rivers without rejecting even the smallest streams, when those who come to offer worship do so, he feels no joy; and when they do not offer worship, he likewise feels no sorrow or distress. Therefore it is said: "Its cessation is due to the assembly of noble ones."

"Those who do not eliminate external delusions" refers to those worldly fools and deluded people who have long been subject to inverted views, clinging to a self (*ātman*). They are attached to the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), reckoning it as a real body. This is like a person who, having never been bitten by a venomous snake, does not avoid it; or one who, having never been bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*), yet engages in such conduct and is defiled by external objects. For this reason, it is said: "They do not eliminate external delusions."
For what reason is it called "Miscellaneous"?

It is termed "Miscellaneous" because the meanings of the verses are expounded in various ways that differ from one another; other verses contain single, unified meanings not shared by these, and for this reason they are called "Miscellaneous. The seventeenth chapter, "The Miscellaneous," is hereby concluded.
With a pure mind one attains mindfulness; there is nothing to be craved or delighted in. Having already crossed the abyss of delusion, one is like a swan leaving a pond.

Regarding "with a pure mind one attains mindfulness; there is nothing to be craved or delighted in": this means fixing the mind upon purity, constantly seeking skillful means with the desire to attain liberation. One contemplates this cycle of birth and death as being like an illusion or a magical transformation, always harboring fear as if the mind were a blazing fire. Therefore it is said: "With a pure mind one attains mindfulness; there is nothing to be craved or delighted in."

As for "like a goose abandoning a pond," this means that knowing the waters of that pond are full of many fears and are further terrified by hunters coming repeatedly, the bird immediately abandons the pond and flies high to avoid these manifold perils; therefore it is said, "like a goose abandoning a pond."

"Having crossed the abyss of delusion" means that when the abyss of delusion obscures one so as to penetrate to the very bone and marrow, one seeks expedient means to extinguish it forever without remainder; therefore, it is said, "having crossed the abyss of delusion."
It is like a wild goose that descends briefly from the sky, seeking to escape the evil realms and reach the state of non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for "like a wild goose," it refers to one who fears the various birds flying in the void; to avoid these perils and seek the non-conditioned for oneself, it is therefore said, "like a wild goose."

Regarding "descending briefly from the air": the body is able to fly, moving to and fro over near and far distances without obstruction, departing from danger and proceeding toward safety; for this reason, it is said that one "descends briefly from the air."
It means seeking deliverance from the evil realms and reaching the state of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The noble disciples of the Tathāgata, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, remove evil for the sake of others and seek deliverance from the evil realms; they cultivate wholesome karma and detach from all fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore it is said: "Seeking to leave the evil realms, one reaches the state of unconditioned."

It is also called the extinction of *nirvāṇa*, which is without birth, cessation, attachment, or annihilation; it is eternally unchanging and indestructible. When practitioners who have attained that concentration are beset by old age and illness—when the four hundred and four ailments constantly afflict their bodies—they grow weary of this body of the four great elements, cast off the form of the five aggregates, and enter the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One does not cultivate the holy life; one does not accumulate wealth in youth; the fool sleeps, guarding what he has rather than creating anew.
Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and, accompanied by his attendant Ānanda, saw two elderly men in Jambudvīpa whose forms had changed and whose complexions had faded as they walked with bent backs. Having seen them, the World-Honored One smiled.
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes once more, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must be a reason for this smile. I pray that you will explain its meaning."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these two venerable elders? Their forms have changed and their complexions have faded."
If these two individuals, who have accumulated wealth since their youth in this city of Śrāvastī, were the foremost among the wealthy in Śrāvastī;
yet, if they were to renounce their wives and children, abandon their livelihoods, leave the household life to study the Way, they would immediately become arhats.
If he had accumulated small amounts of wealth until it was sufficient for today, he would now be in a second household within this city of Śrāvastī;
however, since he has left the home life to study the Path, he has attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
If these two individuals were in their middle age, they would have accumulated wealth sufficient by this day; they are now in the third house.
Had they left the household life to study the Path, they would have attained the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
"Pity these two who have contravened their former vows; abandoning the fundamental for the derivative, they are beset by myriad afflictions such as hunger, cold, and arduous toil.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing this meaning and in order to expound the Great Illumination for future sentient beings, spoke these verses amidst the great assembly.
Failing to cultivate the holy life and failing to accumulate wealth in one's youth—what benefit is there in clinging to the past, like a crane by a pond?

Just as an old crane stands waiting by the edge of a pond, hoping for a fish to come ashore so it may seize it as food, its thoughts are occupied all day long without fulfilling its wish; yet, never ceasing its efforts, it brings about its own destruction.

The aged have the ways of the aged, while the strong possess the strength of the young. A crane, though employing the methods of old age upon its youthful vigor, achieves nothing all day long; it merely thinks of catching fish in its prime, unaware that senescence has already arrived.

Now this elderly elder is likewise; thinking himself strong and vigorous, he indulges in song, dance, laughter, jesting, board games, and diversions, without considering that today his years have advanced and he is decrepit, crouching with his knees drawn up.

To recall what one has experienced without practicing the dharma that transcends aging, but instead to dwell on youth and its myriad forms of deception—this is why it is said: "Like a crane by a pond, what benefit is there in guarding the past?"
Do not despise small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
All transgressions reach their full measure through accumulation from the smallest beginnings.

"Do not underestimate small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity. When a person commits an evil deed, however small it may be, it must not be disregarded. Even a small viper, though tiny, can bite a person until its venom spreads throughout their body, causing them to lose their life-force. Likewise, even a minute dose of poison, if someone comes to eat it, causes death upon the sight of the toxin.

This is also like that: although an evil deed may be small, it obstructs one’s right practice; until reaching the ultimate goal, one does not consider that one will later receive its retribution. Day after day, one refuses to reform, and failing to contemplate the need to distance oneself from evil, it continues to grow. Therefore it is said: "Do not treat a small evil lightly, thinking there will be no calamity."

Although a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel; this is like a large vessel held upright to catch dripping water, where each successive drop follows the last until the vessel overflows and is full. Therefore it is said: "Although a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."

Regarding the statement that "all sins, when they reach fulfillment, are accumulated from small beginnings": the foolish person practices and acts starting from small things and proceeding to great ones; day by day they indulge in these habits without realizing that calamity is approaching. Therefore it is said: "All sins, when they reach fulfillment, are accumulated from small beginnings."
Do not despise small virtues, thinking they bring no merit; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
All blessings reach fulfillment through the accumulation of even the most slender beginnings.

"Do not despise small good deeds, thinking they bring no merit. For instance, there may be virtuous people who go to stupas and monasteries to pay homage and seek merit; they may offer bright lamps, burn incense, sweep and sprinkle water, perform music and dance, or hang silk banners and canopies. Starting from even a single coin, they further encourage others to give rise to a mind of generosity, offering even a single lump of food to the holy assembly; or they provide willow twigs and pure water for cleanliness; or they replenish the oil in lamps to maintain their light.

Even such small things must not be disregarded; based upon that consciousness, one obtains immeasurable retribution. It is like lighting a single lamp to dispel the darkness of a house, leaving no trace of the darkness behind; or like burning an extremely subtle incense, which completely eliminates foul odors so that their location is unknown; or like a sharp sword, though small, which can sever a poisonous tree.

This is also like that: though virtuous conduct may be slight, it can eliminate grave sins; one will travel between the realms of humans and devas without further suffering or distress. From here to there, one receives immeasurable blessings that can be known even in the present. Just as drops falling without ceasing eventually fill a large vessel, so too does the courageous person gradually accomplish the perfection of merit through their practice.
Therefore it is said: All merit, when fully realized, is accumulated from the smallest beginnings.
It is like a person crossing a river who binds a raft together with great firmness;
others may say they have crossed or not crossed, but only the wise can truly be said to have crossed.

As for those who bind rafts so that they are secure: it is like sentient beings who wish to cross a deep abyss; whether they cross by means of a raft, or cross by means of a waist-boat, or float on a gourd, or carry a small boat, or use grass and wood as a raft, they all reach the shore without hindrance.
Therefore it is said: "It is like a person crossing a river who binds a raft so that it is secure.

Regarding what is called "crossing" or "not crossing": the abyss of craving is like a deep chasm from which a river flows forth; it fills the world and flows toward the three realms, proceeding through the four modes of birth and pervading the five destinies. It further flows toward forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*). Therefore it is said: "Regarding what is called crossing or not crossing."
As for the "wise one" mentioned as crossing over, the wise ones are the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas; that they cross the abyss of the world is not to be considered extraordinary. Why is this?
The abyss of the world is inexhaustible; those who cross the abyss of craving and desire are called extraordinary.
Therefore it is said: "The wise are said to have crossed.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already crossed; the Brahmin has crossed to the other shore; the bhikṣu enters the abyss to bathe; the śrāvaka binds a sturdy raft.

In the past, there were two great brahmin teachers who established the great city of Pāṭaliputra. Once the construction work was completed and the city was fully adorned, they invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks to enter the city for offerings.
Before the various gates had been given names, the brahmin thought to himself:

"If the śramaṇa Gautama exits through a certain gate, that gate shall be named 'Gautama Gate'; and if the Tathāgata crosses the Ganges at a certain point, that crossing shall be named 'Gautama Crossing'."
At that time, the brahmin again had this thought:
"I wonder whether the Tathāgata intends to cross the river by carrying a raft, or by using a waist-tethered boat, a floating gourd, or a small boat?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that brahmin, immediately used his supernormal power to cross over together with the community of bhikṣus in an instant, standing upon the opposite shore.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already crossed over; The brahmin has reached the further shore.
The bhikṣu enters the deep pool to bathe; The śrāvaka binds a sturdy raft.”
Having spoken these verses, they each returned to their monasteries.
When the brahmin heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
"What is the use of this spring? [the Buddha asked.]
The water is always still and full; having uprooted the very root of craving, what more could one hope for?

What use is this spring, whose water is always still and full? The "three realms of existence" (triloka) are metaphorically called a spring, and craving is also called a spring. The water is always still and full because all fetters (saṃyojana) gather within the spring of craving. Therefore it is said: "What use is this spring, whose water is always still and full?"

"Having uprooted the root of craving, what further hope could there be? means that when a practitioner is able to uproot the root of craving, they will no longer undergo birth and death. It is like a poisonous tree whose roots have been completely destroyed; it can no longer sprout, nor will it have branches or leaves. Craving is likewise: once its root is uprooted, it has no further branches or leaves.
"What further hope can one have? means that there is no further grasping at existence and no further rebirth; therefore it is said, "What further hope can one have?
A sailor adjusts his boat, a bow-maker adjusts his horn, a skilled carpenter adjusts his wood, and the wise person adjusts his body.
A boatman who adjusts his vessel repairs its sturdy rigging and seals all leaks so that no water enters, enabling living beings to reach the far shore from this side;
a bow-maker refines sinew and horn so they are properly tempered, such that when heated by fire and put to use, the sinew does not snap.
Therefore it is said: "The boatman adjusts the boat, and the bow-maker adjusts the horn.

As for the skillful carpenter adjusting the wood, he uses ink-lines and plumb lines to ensure they are straight, and levels and heights are made uniform; his intention is to construct a palace or dwelling so that it is successfully completed. Therefore it is said: "The skillful carpenter adjusts the wood."

The wise person who disciplines the body always follows the correct teaching without violating the laws and precepts; they seek out the profound meaning and flavor of the Dharma and strive for the qualities of a superior person. Therefore it is said: "The wise person disciplines the body."
Just as a deep spring is clear and transparent both within and without, so it is with hearing the Dharma;
the wise rejoice.
Regarding the lines "just as a deep spring is clear and transparent both within and without," this verse was spoken so that the wise may understand through analogy.

There may be deep springs that are not clear and are constantly turbid; yet there are also springs that are both deep and clear, wherein one’s own facial reflection appears in its entirety. Therefore it is said: "Like a deep spring, transparent and pure from top to bottom."

Regarding the statement, "Hearing the Dharma thus, the wise rejoice": Long ago, there was a king who grew weary of worldly treatises and exhausted by mundane affairs; he went to a stupa-temple desiring to hear the True Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu Hastibala had attained the path of arhatship and was next in line to preach the Dharma.
Then the king of that country entered the assembly to listen to the Dharma with a cloth covering his head and wearing sandals on his feet.
The Arhat bhikṣu said to the king, "In the past,
the Buddha established a precept that one must not preach the Dharma to those wearing shoes.
The king’s inner resentment flared up, and he immediately removed his sandals.
The Arhat Bhikṣu further addressed the king, saying:
"In the past, the Buddha Tathāgata also established this restriction, stating that one must not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered.
Upon hearing these words, the king gave rise to anger and reflected within himself:
"Alas! I have been humiliated by this bhikṣu; it is because this bhikṣu sees my head as white and bald that he wishes to insult me.
If this bhikṣu’s preaching of the Dharma does not enter my ears, I shall take up my sword and cut off his head."
At that time, the king immediately pulled back his head-covering and said, "Śramaṇa, quickly preach the Dharma to me.
The bhikṣu replied, "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has also taught this instruction: one must not preach the Dharma to those who are full of anger."
"Your Majesty is now filled with anger; how can you hear the Dharma?
Your Majesty should straighten your mind and listen to this parable:
it is like a turbid spring that surges and boils without ceasing; Your Majesty is just like this—your mind is so inverted and confused, how can you hear the Dharma?"
At that time, the king felt deep personal shame and immediately gave rise to a heart of reverence, thinking:
"This bhikṣu must surely be a sage, for he is able to perceive with profound insight and penetrate the minds of others."
Immediately rising from his seat, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and prostrated himself with his head at the feet [of the Buddha], addressing the bhikṣu:
"I only pray that the Holy One will preach the Dharma to me, so that this defiled body may forever receive your protection."
The king then took his seat, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the king with this verse:
"Just as a deep spring is clear and transparent both within and without, so it is when one hears the Dharma."
"The wise rejoice.
At that time, the bhikṣu again preached the Dharma to the king, causing the king’s heart to leap with joy; his roots of the Path and his faith became firm and unshakable.
Therefore it is said: Hearing the Dharma in this way, the wise rejoice.
Their patience is like the earth; they are as immovable as Mount Sumeru;
they are as clear as a pure spring; the wise are without confusion.
"One whose mind of patience is like the earth" means that just as this earth receives both the pure and the impure, yet the earth does not form the thought:
"I shall reject this and accept that."

The practice of the wise is likewise: if someone praises them, they do not take pleasure in it; if there are those who revile them, they harbor no grief or distress; seeing good, they are not delighted, and hearing evil, they do not become angry.
Therefore it is said: "The mind of patience is like the earth.
Regarding "immovable as Mount Sumeru": it is just as Mount Sumeru, standing alone among all mountains, cannot be shaken or toppled by violent winds.

The person of noble and holy realization is also like this: their mind neither increases nor decreases even when the four requisites are lacking; therefore it is said that they are as immovable as Mount Sumeru.

"Serene and still like a clear spring; the wise person is undisturbed. Just as a serene and still spring is transparent both within and without, and is not troubled or turbid by small streams, so it is with the wise: since there is no internal fault, external evils cannot enter; their mind is like a diamond, indestructible. Therefore it is said: "Like a clear spring, the wise person is not disturbed. This concludes the eighteenth chapter on Water.
*Udānavarga*, Volume XVIII; *Udānavarga*, Volume XIX.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: On Flowers Who is able to select the ground,
Discarding the mirror and taking up the heavens, Speaking only the phrases of the Dharma,
Just as one selects choice flowers?
The reason the Tathāgata recited this verse was to provoke a challenge through words; yet, no one was able to pose a reproof.
The Buddha then spoke for himself: "Who can choose the ground, rejecting the mirror and taking the heavens? Only by speaking the phrases of the Dharma is it like selecting fine flowers."
The Buddha replied with a verse:
“The learner chooses the ground; Discarding the mirror, they take up the heavens. Skillfully expounding the phrases of the Dharma, They are able to gather the flowers of virtue.”
"The learner who chooses the ground" refers to one who is heading toward arhatship.
What is called "ground"?
That which is called "ground" is the seed of craving.

The seeker who adheres to faith and discriminates to select the wholesome ground removes the root of craving and thereby attains the realization of the Path. Therefore it is said: "The seeker discriminates the ground. Regarding "abandoning the mirror and taking up heaven":

when a practitioner cultivates, they search from this world upward through the various heavens to strip away and seek out the root of craving, severing it forever without remainder. Even among the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—and their generals, those who possess craving can all be made to abandon and sever it. Therefore it is said: "Abandoning the mirror and taking up heaven."

One who skillfully expounds the phrases of the Dharma and is able to gather the flowers of virtue analyzes and discerns the meanings and principles of both the phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) and the words (*pada-kāya*), using unimpeded wisdom to unravel all fetters and attachments. This is like a student who gathers various flowers to fashion them into a garland; once it is sold, those who behold it never tire of it. The skillful exposition of the phrases of the Dharma is likewise: it unfolds the profound and subtle while extensively gathering all that is wondrous; therefore, it is called the "skillful exposition of the phrases of the Dharma."
Cut down the forest, do not cut down individual trees; for in the forest there arises much fear.
When the forest is cut down, the name "forest" ceases; one who is without a forest is called a bhikṣu.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to an immeasurable multitude, who surrounded him on all sides.
Then there was a man of firm and steadfast faith who abandoned his home, wife, children, and five kinsmen to leave the household life, study the Path, and seek to become a śramaṇa.

At that time, while among the great assembly, that man’s mind dwelt upon his former indulgence in the five desires for his own amusement; he recalled the features of a woman as if they were present before his eyes, and his organ immediately became aroused.
Filled with shame and remorse, he went at once to a secluded place and severed it with a knife; blood flowed out profusely, and he fell into a state of stupor, unconscious of himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Observe this foolish person: what he ought to obtain, he does not obtain; and what he ought not to sever, he severs."
"One who wishes to sever [suffering] should sever the fetters and all bonds; why then do you seek to sever this physical form?
For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke these two verses repeatedly:
"Sever the forest, do not sever the trees; Within the forest, fear arises in abundance. Until the forest has been severed,"
This increases human bondage.
Cut down the forest, not merely the trees; for within the forest much fear arises. When the mind is bound and lacks release, it is like a calf longing for its mother.

As long as the forest has not been cut down, one's fetters and attachments increase; as long as the fetters of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and various perceptions have not been severed, the mind’s underlying tendencies run wild and cannot be concentrated. Therefore it is said: "As long as the forest has not been cut down, one's fetters and attachments increase."

"Those whose minds are bound have no liberation" means that ascetics always delight in mountains and thickets; the reason for this is that it is by virtue of those mountains that they attain the Way. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is bound and has no liberation."

"Just as a calf yearns for its mother" means that just as a newborn calf’s mind never departs from its mother, so too it is with these classes of sentient beings: as long as their various fetters are not yet exhausted, they are pursued by doubt. Therefore it is said, "like a calf yearning for its mother."
"One should sever one's own attachment, like a lotus in an autumn pond; ceasing from worldly traces and receiving the teaching—this is what the Buddha calls Nirvāṇa.

Regarding "one should sever one's own attachment, like a lotus in an autumn pond": the affliction of love that stains the spirit has no discernible beginning. It is just as a lotus flower, whose color is fresh and beautiful, which all who see it cannot help but love and delight in. Yet when the autumn flowers wither, people’s hearts all turn away and no longer crave them. For this reason it is said: "One should sever one's own attachment, like a lotus in an autumn pond."

Regarding "those who follow the traces of tranquility and receive the teaching": those who follow the traces of tranquility are the noble and holy ones; they receive the correct instructions and admonitions without the slightest deviation from the beginning, such that wholesome dharmas increase daily while unwholesome dharmas recede daily.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that Nirvāṇa is bliss; within Nirvāṇa there are no afflictions or various calamities that touch the body. For this reason, it is said that the Buddha teaches Nirvāṇa as bliss.
"Just like that pleasing flower, Beautiful in color yet lacking fragrance, So it is with the flower of eloquent speech: Without fruit, one receives no reward.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all living beings and wishing to expound the teachings of the Dharma, spoke this verse. As for those who preach the Dharma, their words are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and their principles are profound; yet if their conduct contradicts their own words, they shall not obtain the reward. For this reason, the World-Honored One said that they do not attain its fruit.

The reason the Tathāgata spoke this verse was to instruct future disciples and to ensure that teachers provide strict and earnest instruction, while disciples fulfill their duty by receiving and upholding such admonitions. Sometimes, however, disciples are unable to endure such teaching and correction; it is for this reason he said: "Just as those pleasing flowers which have beautiful colors but lack fragrance, so too is one who is skilled in eloquent speech but bears no fruit—such a person receives no reward."

Just as that pleasing flower, Beautiful in color and pure in fragrance, So too is skillful speech; One will surely obtain its fruit and retribution. At that time, the World-Honored One repeatedly preached this Dharma before the assembly.

That preacher’s voice was clear and resonant, his speech free from hesitation or difficulty. He taught the Dharma to sentient beings—excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; complete in meaning and phrasing; a pure cultivation of the holy life with profound principles. The wise discerned it, and having practiced it with single-minded correctness, he likewise instructed others. All followed the Dharma without contradicting the principles; the World-Honored One declared that such a person would fully obtain the fruit and retribution. Therefore it is said: "Just as that pleasing flower, beautiful in color and pure in form and fragrance, so too is skillful speech; one will surely obtain its fruit and retribution."
"As a bee gathers from a flower, Unperturbed by its color or fragrance, Taking only the nectar and departing— So it is when a benevolent person enters a village.

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse for the sake of the bhikṣu Piṇḍola. When the one who provided him with food went to observe him, he saw whether the other’s complexion was good or bad, handsome or ugly; he gazed at his appearance without looking away. If he saw someone who was not upright, he did not look at them; if he smelled their fragrance, he sniffed it with his nose; and if he saw someone who was filthy, he turned his back and abandoned them. Recalling that fine complexion and fine fragrance, he returned to his cell and contemplated it day and night.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the minds of the bhikṣus were each thus, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Why do you not act like bees gathering from flowers?
They take only the nectar and depart, without disturbing the color or fragrance."
"O bhikṣus! Whether it be pleasant or foul odors, beautiful or ugly forms—whether good or bad—what benefit do they provide?
Whether one is a great family or a small family, wealthy or poor and lowly, you should simply carry out your duties toward those people according to your own conscience."
"If you act as you do, why not act in this way?
Therefore it is said: "As a bee gathers from a flower, undisturbed by its color or fragrance, taking only the nectar and departing; so too should you enter a village."

Those who frequently create precious flowers and fashion exquisite, jeweled garlands are like those skilled disciples of flower-garland makers who collect many various flowers to craft garlands, sustaining themselves through their value.
When the bhikṣus saw what he had done, they each fashioned unprecedented flower garlands themselves. The World-Honored One said:
"Each of you should fashion flower garlands; it is thus that you should act."

This is precisely the time for practice; only by performing countless deeds does one obtain a human body. Why do you not cultivate merit, personally practice giving, contemplate the instructions, and diligently cultivate the precepts while maintaining pure brahmacarya?
Therefore it is said: "One who creates many jeweled flowers, binds together precious ornaments, and extensively accumulates merit will be reborn in increasingly excellent states.
A fool may recite a thousand chapters yet not understand a single phrase; a wise person understands a single phrase and thereby comprehends a hundred meanings.

Regarding the statement, "The fool recites a thousand chapters but does not understand a single phrase": the fool lacks wisdom, lacks practice, lacks vision, and lacks the eye; he has not cultivated learning. Possessing only shallow and coarse intelligence, he greedily consumes those thousand phrases without understanding even one. Therefore it is said: "The fool recites a thousand chapters but does not understand a single phrase."

Regarding the statement, "One who understands a single phrase immediately understands a hundred meanings": the wise possess eyes and vision; they are able to contemplate that single meaning in detail, examining its implications from all sides as to whether such a principle is appropriate or inappropriate. Therefore it is said: "One who understands a single phrase immediately understands a hundred meanings."
"Just as when it rains, the flowers bloom, And the sprouts are just beginning to unfold;
so too with lust, anger, and delusion, the bhikṣu attains liberation.

Regarding the line, "Just as when it rains, the flowers bloom, and the sprouts are just beginning to unfold": it is like the celestial flowers that bloom during the rainy season without diminishing; though their petals fall away, the emerging sprouts become even more beautiful. Therefore it is said: "Just as when it rains, the flowers bloom, and the sprouts are just beginning to unfold."

Regarding lust, anger, and delusion in this way, a bhikṣu attains liberation. "O bhikṣus, you have become practitioners of the Way not out of fear of kings, nor out of fear of bandits, nor out of fear of punishment, nor out of fear of illness, nor out of fear of corvée labor."

Is it not so that you have become practitioners of the Way because you were weary of and disgusted by the sufferings of the world, and that you became practitioners of the Way because you desired to escape birth, old age, sickness, and death?
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is, World-Honored One! [The Buddha said:
“Why do you not reflect upon the removal of lust, anger, and delusion?”
One should remain far removed from the fetters and not engage with them; one should vomit them out, eliminate them, extinguish them, and attain [liberation].
What are the two types of karma to be attained?
Those performed for oneself and those performed for others.

One who acts for oneself perfumes the body with virtue; one who acts for others—if they receive from others gifts of faith, such as clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for illness—incurs no loss whatsoever.
Therefore it is said: "In this way, through lust, anger, and delusion, a bhikṣu attains liberation.
It is like a field ditch bordering a great road, wherein a lotus grows—fragrant, pure, and pleasing to the mind."

It is like a field ditch situated near a main road. As for what is called a field ditch, all manner of impurities and filth flow into it; people find it loathsome and refuse to approach it. When walking, they avoid it and do not wish to look upon it. Therefore it is said: "It is like a field ditch situated near a main road."

In the midst [of the mud], a lotus flower grows—fragrant, pure, and pleasing to the mind; perfected in color and perfected in fragrance. When people see it, they rejoice and form this thought: "Without asking about its ground, I shall simply observe its flower."
"How is it that such exquisite flowers have grown in this place?
It is truly extraordinary and rare in the world.
Therefore it is said: "In their midst grow lotuses, fragrant, pure, and pleasing to the mind."
Birth and death are thus; the ordinary person dwells on the periphery, while the wise delight in emerging [from it] as disciples of the Buddha.
Once, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed throughout six periods of a single day and night, seeing that there were sentient beings who ought to be delivered by the Buddha, yet instead fell back into the stage of ordinary worldlings; this constituted a great deficiency and decline within the Buddha-dharma.
With his divine eye, the World-Honored One saw within the city of Śrāvastī a son of the caṇḍālas who supported himself by clearing away refuse as a hired laborer.

At that time, when it was time for the meal, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms; proceeding step by step, he arrived at the house of that caṇḍāla.

At that time, the guest who was clearing away refuse saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar; inwardly feeling shame and embarrassment, he immediately avoided the World-Honored One and went toward another alley, but the Tathāgata suddenly went back to meet him there.
The man thought to himself:
"I am carrying filth, stench, and impurity; by what means can I today have an audience with the World-Honored One?
He then wished to flee and go to a marshy place, where he found a rope that had snapped and a broken jar, defiling the clean ground. Fearing the owner’s anger, he intended to run away.
The Buddha called out from afar, saying, "I have come here specifically for you;
where do you wish to go now? The man replied:
"My body is defiled, and I did not dare approach your venerable countenance; that is why I wished to avoid you.
Your Honor should know this: I lost my parents early, my five relations have perished, and I have no wife or children. Left alone and destitute, I support myself by working as a hired sweeper."
"I do not understand what the World-Honored One intends to instruct;
how is it that you can compassionately converse with such a sinner?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:
"Follow me; I wish to ordain you as a śramaṇa.
The man addressed the Buddha, saying, "How so, World-Honored One?"
"Can those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals also attain the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to that person:
"Since the beginningless past, I have cultivated countless practices to seek the realization of the Buddha-way precisely for the sake of those suffering from transgressions."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately employed his supernormal powers to take the man by the hand and ascend into the air. He went to the banks of the Ganges River and bathed the man’s body until it was fragrant and pure. Then, using his supernormal powers again, he brought him back to the Jetavana Monastery and commanded the bhikṣus:
"Take this man and ordain him as a śramaṇa."
Having received these instructions, he was immediately ordained as a śramaṇa.
Once he had attained the state of a seeker of the Way, he reflected within himself:

"I have emerged from a cold and lowly station; fortunately, by a small measure of merit, I have been able to partake of the flavor of the Way. If I do not now seek for myself that which is sought in the Way, I shall later fall back into the state of an ordinary person, and my condition will be even more wretched than it is now."

He immediately exhorted himself to diligent practice with daily renewal; before ten days had passed, he attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*. His six supernormal powers became pure and transparent, and he moved through space at will. He then went to a large square rock, sat upon its center, and mended his old robes with patches.
At that time, King Prasenajit, hearing that the Buddha had ordained the son of a Caṇḍāla, a hired sweeper, thought to himself:

"The Buddha has emerged from a noble clan of the Śākya lineage, and his attendant disciples all come from the four castes—the Vaiśyas, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and [others]—who enter our palaces to receive our offerings and gifts of faith, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and bowing at his feet;
yet now I hear that the Tathāgata has ordained one of the Caṇḍāla caste. How can we possibly humble ourselves to pay him homage?"
"I shall now go to reprimand the Tathāgata.

The king personally prepared his carriage and set out for the place where the Tathāgata was. Before he had yet arrived, he saw a bhikṣu sitting upon a large square stone, mending an old robe with patches, surrounded by five hundred gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven who were paying him homage.
The king stepped forward and said to the bhikṣu,
"I now trouble you, bhikṣu, to go and inform the World-Honored One:
'King Prasenajit is outside and wishes to have an audience with the World-Honored One.'"
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately sank into the stone, emerged from the ground of the Tathāgata’s vihāra, and approached the Buddha, saying:
“King Prasenajit is outside and wishes to see the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Now go back from this place, emerge from that rock, and say to the king:
'You should know that the time has come.'"
"Then, in accordance with the Buddha’s instruction, [the water] gushed forth from the rock and addressed the king, saying:
'The Tathāgata has given this teaching; Great King, you should know that now is the time.
King Prasenajit then thought to himself:

"The reason I have come here now is that I wish to question that man who cleans away refuse; however, let that be set aside for a moment. First, I ask this bhikṣu: how is it that he is able to enter and emerge at will within these hard, rigid stones?"
"One should also ask what kind of person this bhikṣu is.

At that time, King Prasenajit removed his royal regalia and proceeded to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and after a short while, withdrew slightly from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What was the name of that bhikṣu who was just here?"
"It is because he possesses such supernormal power that he can pass back and forth through the stone without any obstruction.
The Buddha told the king,
"This is a guest scavenger who now possesses such supernormal power as this."
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these two verses:
"Just as fragrant and pure lotuses grow from a foul and evil field, a ditch, or a deep pit."
"What do you think, Great King?
Would a man with sight take this flower?
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

Flowers that are exceedingly fragrant and pure should be taken to adorn [the body]; those that are foul and filthy should be viewed as like a mother’s womb, for within that womb, the flowers of merit are born.”
At that time, King Prasenajit joined his palms together and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!

That person has swiftly attained a great benefit; having received the holy instruction, he has entered the ranks of the Path. Now that he has become a practitioner of the Way, his supernormal powers and transformations are inconceivable."
"From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I request to provide offerings to this bhikṣu, ensuring that the four requisites are never lacking.
Therefore it is said: "The wise delight in leaving the household life to become disciples of the Buddha."
"Just as one gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted, / Village-slumber and the waters' drift lead one to death's dragging.

/ 'Just as one gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted': Long ago, there were many people in the wilds gathering flowers; they chose the exquisite and vied for the beautiful. Therefore it is said: 'Just as one gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted.'"

Regarding the phrase "The village sleeps while swept away by water, dragged off by death": at that time, the people, exhausted from gathering flowers, returned home and fell asleep; then a sudden flood surged forth and swept them all away and killed them. Therefore it is said: "The village sleeps while swept away by water, dragged off by death."
As when gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted, one’s desire is insatiable and one is beset by exhaustion.

Regarding "as when gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted": at that time, the people gather exquisite flowers, vying for the finest ones as they rush east and west, seeking to obtain wonderful fragrances to celebrate with joy. Therefore it is said: "As when gathering flowers, with focused mind and undistracted."

Regarding the statement, "The mind of desire knows no satiety; one is thus constrained by destitution": the reason for gathering flowers is the desire to amuse oneself with the five sensual pleasures and to indulge in self-indulgence. One does not know of the changes to come nor observe what has not yet occurred. When these changes advance and the day of death draws near, one then realizes one is constrained. Therefore it is said: "The mind of desire knows no satiety; one is thus constrained by destitution."
It is like one gathering flowers, focusing the mind without distraction; yet before obtaining wealth or property, one is beset by poverty.

"As one gathering flowers, focusing the mind without distraction" means that at a time when the people are destitute, impoverished, and lacking much, one gathers flowers and goes to sell them to sustain oneself. Therefore it is said: "As one gathering flowers, focusing the mind without distraction."

Those who have not yet acquired wealth or occupation and are thus beset by poverty will diligently seek riches wherever they may be; yet when their efforts do not match their wishes and fail to satisfy their hopes, they are driven by destitution. Consequently, they cast off this present form to receive another body, all because they lacked foresight in abandoning one life to take up another. Therefore it is said: "Those who have not yet acquired wealth or occupation are beset by poverty."
Contemplate the body as being like an unbaked clay vessel, an illusory phenomenon like a mirage; sever the blossoming flowers of Māra, and you shall not behold the King of Death.

"Contemplate the body as being like an unbaked clay vessel" means that it is like an unbaked earthenware pot—perilous, fragile, and unstable, destined for destruction. It is subject to the law of annihilation and cannot be relied upon; it must all eventually reach its end. Gradually accumulating, it becomes a mound of earth.

This body composed of the four great elements is likewise so: it cannot be relied upon and must all return to extinction; it is subject to the law of decay and destruction. Before long, it shall be cast away amidst the graves. Therefore it is said: "Contemplate the body as being like an unbaked clay pot."

The "phantom phenomena like a mirage" refers to how the shimmering flames of a mirage deceive the eyes of people; when people wish to go toward it to investigate its location, they do not know where it is, merely exhausting themselves in vain without gaining anything.

To understand that all phenomena are thus—neither strong nor firm, and not to be relied upon—is why it is said: "illusory phenomena are like a mirage. Regarding "severing the blooming flowers of Māra": what is called Māra is the Devaputra Īśvara.

The fetters to which he is attached are severed by seeing the Truths and contemplating the Path. Having been severed, they are to be severed; having been stripped away, they are to be stripped away; having been struck, they are to be struck. Therefore, it is said: "severing the blooming flowers of Māra."

"To not behold the King of Death" means that one who has seen the Truth and contemplated the Path has exhausted all fetters that ought to be abandoned, leaving none remaining; such a person no longer advances toward the realm of the Sovereign Deva (Īśvara), nor are they further entangled by the devas. Therefore it is said: "To not behold the King of Death."
This body is like foam; the nature of illusory phenomena is such that one cuts off the blooming flowers of Māra and no longer beholds the King of Death.

Regarding "this body is like foam": it is just like a mass of froth that cannot remain for long and is not to be relied upon; as soon as it is grasped, it dissolves and cannot be maintained. This body composed of the four great elements is likewise: it has no power, no strength, and no solidity. Therefore it is said, "this body is like foam."

The natural state of illusory phenomena is like magically conjured objects that deceive others; they are neither true nor real. The foolish become stained by attachment and claim them as their own, yet the wise, upon observation, find not a single thing therein worth craving. Therefore it is said: "Illusory phenomena are natural."

"Severing the blossoming flowers of Māra" means that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths and through cultivation are forever exhausted without remainder; one no longer accords with their words nor draws near to them. Therefore, it is said: "severing the blossoming flowers of Māra."

"Not seeing the King of Death" means that one who has seen the Truth and contemplated until the fetters are exhausted reigns alone over the three thousandfold world system; having mastery over both life and death, they are no longer constrained or recorded by the Sovereign Deva. Therefore it is said: "Not seeing the King of Death."

Understanding that the body and craving are one and not different, one who trains is able to relinquish firm existence, like selecting an *utpala* flower; such a bhikṣu crosses from this shore to the other, like a snake shedding its old skin.
Regarding "the learner who is able to relinquish the firm existence": what is that which is "firm" within existence?
It may be said that the five desires are it.

When the mind and thoughts become defiled and attached, one cannot relinquish them; this causes sentient beings to give rise to defiled attachment, causing them to transmigrate through the five realms of existence, beginning again and again, as one form is destroyed and another form is received.
Furthermore, what in this world is most firm?
It is that which is called the body of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Moreover, it causes the various classes of sentient beings to indulge in it day and night, unable to abandon it; yet, those practitioners who study [the Dharma] hold their resolve with firm determination.

One who is able to relinquish this solid existence may be called a noble sage; one who can relinquish the body of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) as well as the five desires is said to be practicing in accordance with the conduct of the noble sages. Therefore it is said: "Train in being able to relinquish solid existence."

Regarding the phrase "like selecting the *utpala*": a person skilled at discernment may select exquisite flowers in search of the *utpala*, yet their body and spirit become exhausted and they fail to obtain it; their mind then becomes weary and they abandon the effort and depart. Therefore it is said, "like selecting the *utpala*."

Regarding the bhikṣu who crosses over from this shore to that shore: what is called a bhikṣu is one who has destroyed all fetters and defilements, who has discarded the physical form [of worldly attachment], and who, wearing the robes and holding the alms bowl, goes on almsround to deliver others.

"To cross over this shore and that" refers to the six internal and external sense bases—the six internal sense faculties and the six external sense objects. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu crosses over this shore and that. "Like a snake shedding its old skin":

the noble and holy person for whom the three realms of existence are a prison follows the path of the noble and holy; such a sage is able to abandon the path of the noble and holy and enter the city of Nirvāṇa, which is unconditioned. Therefore it is said: "Like a snake shedding its old skin."
Like a horse well-tamed and gentle, going wherever it wills, One who possesses faith, precepts, diligence,
and the essentials of concentration and dharma, With patience, harmony, and a settled mind— this is the severance of all suffering.

"Like a horse that is well-tamed and compliant, going wherever it is directed": this refers to a skilled horse trainer who controls a horse with a whip; wherever the horse goes according to his will, it does not lose its fundamental purpose.
