Because the horse's nature is stubborn and upright, and fearing the lash of the whip, it constantly guards itself for fear of making a mistake. Therefore it is said: "Like a horse that is well-tamed and compliant, going wherever it is directed."

Regarding those who possess faith, precepts, diligence, concentration, and the essential factors of the Dharma: the conduct of such a bhikṣu is like that horse. Internally, he constantly reflects, fearing the occurrence of transgressions and further fearing that fellow practitioners of the holy life might come and reprove him. With faith directed toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, his diligence is firm and indestructible; his mind is constantly in meditative absorption, and he discerns all phenomena without omission or loss. Therefore it is said: "Possessing faith, precepts, diligence, concentration, and the essential factors of the Dharma."

Regarding "patience harmonizes the mind and stabilizes concentration": when a practitioner in training progresses, they discipline their sense faculties so as not to become heedless, attaining complete mastery over the gates of the senses and being fully endowed with the power of patience. Whether others treat them with disparagement or praise, honor or revile, suffering or pleasure, they do not give rise to anger nor harbor notions of right or wrong. Therefore it is said: "Patience harmonizes the mind and stabilizes concentration."
This is the one who severs all suffering; having severed it—whether with remainder or without remainder—one enters parinirvāṇa. Therefore it is said: "This is the severing of all suffering.
Abiding in this concentration, like a well-trained horse, one severs anger and becomes free from outflows, thereby experiencing celestial bliss.

Regarding "abiding in concentration from this": that practitioner of meditation withdraws the sense faculties, maintains mental focus without distraction, and remains free from extraneous thoughts; the phenomena contemplated by the mind likewise do not wander. Therefore, it is said: "abiding in concentration from this."

"Just as one who trains a horse": it is like a horse trainer who, seeing a wicked horse that is stubborn and untamed, fastens it with a halter and bit and further applies the whip and lashes until it is finally tamed; thereafter, it goes wherever it is directed without hesitation or obstruction. Therefore it is said, "just as one who trains a horse."

Regarding "having severed ill will and being without outflows": all ill will has been exhausted and there are no further outflows; one no longer undergoes future existence and shall not be born again hereafter. For this reason, it is said that one has severed ill will and is without outflows.

Regarding those who enjoy celestial bliss: the devas guard the Arhats day and night and proclaim their merits; casting aside their lofty celestial positions, they come to the human world to extol the virtues of the noble and holy ones, spreading them far and wide so that there are none who do not hear them. For this reason, it is said: "These enjoy celestial bliss."
Not indulging in indulgence, Awakening much while amidst sleep, Like a feeble horse compared to a fine steed— Only by abandoning evil does one become a sage.

Regarding "not indulging in indulgence, awakening much while amidst sleep": it refers to those practitioners whose minds are free from negligence, who praise the virtue of heedfulness, who delight in seclusion and do not dwell in turmoil, and who, upon seeing those who are negligent, exhort them to eliminate greed.

Now, a person who is heedless fails to acquire the roots of virtue and loses much of their wealth. Regarding sleep, they should be frequently awakened, as the Buddha’s sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata states:

"If a person sleeps excessively, there is much that is damaged; things that ought to be accomplished instead go to ruin, while things that ought not to be accomplished are instead brought to completion—all such transformations arise from sleep."
Therefore it is said: "One who does not indulge in negligence, but remains awake amidst sleep, is like a weak horse compared to a fine one;

by abandoning evil, one becomes a noble person. It is as if two horses were heading in the same direction: one is well-fed and swift, while the other is weak and inferior and cannot keep pace with its companion. Yet that weak horse first reaches the straight path and is on the verge of reaching the goal, whereas later the fine horse, having advanced, surpasses the inferior one."

It is the same with these classes of sentient beings: there are those of sharp faculties who are attached to sleep and refuse to practice and study, while there are those of dull faculties who apply themselves diligently to study and do not indulge in negligence. Therefore it is said: "As a weak horse is compared to a fine steed, so one who abandons evil is considered noble."
One who possesses a sense of shame and modesty achieves wisdom; such a person is easy to guide forward, like urging on a fine horse.

One who possesses a sense of shame and modesty and has achieved wisdom is like a person practicing a discipline who feels ashamed that they have not kept pace with the multitude; they strive for every single goal and turn toward further progress. If they find even one omission in their practice, they feel personal shame, thinking: "By what karmic conditions from my past was this practice undertaken yet not brought to fruition?"
"Anxious and self-reproachful as if they had lost both parents, their minds constantly desire to depart from evil and unwholesome dharmas.
Therefore it is said: 'The person possessed of shame and remorse achieves wisdom.'"

Such a person is easily led forward, like one who guides a fine horse; they are fully capable of extinguishing all evils, forever uprooting their source so that no further dust or obscuration remains. Because such a person can easily advance toward the Way, it is said: "They are easily led forward."

A "good horse" refers to one whom a horse-tamer trains and disciplines from being wild until it becomes well-behaved; such a horse anticipates the direction of the rider's intent. Therefore it is said: "Like a good horse urged by the whip."
Just as a well-trained horse may be fit for a king’s mount, so too one who is disciplined is honored among men and receives the seal of trust. Regarding the phrase "just as a well-trained horse":

suppose there are three kinds of horses in a royal stable—first, the superior; second, the middling; and third, the inferior. In providing fodder and sustenance, there is no distinction made between them. Yet the superior horse is inspected frequently by the king himself, the middling horse is sent to be looked after by an attendant, and the inferior horse is sent to be looked after by a slave.
Therefore it is said: "It is like a horse that has been well-trained.

Regarding "fit to be ridden by a king": adorned with various ornaments and necklaces of gold and silver, when ridden to wherever one must go, its gait is steady and composed; it never deviates from what the king intends. Therefore it is said, "fit to be ridden by a king."

One who is disciplined is honored among people; dwelling amidst the multitude, they are the most venerable and supreme, with none surpassing them. They are the foremost, beyond comparison, and without peer. Therefore it is said: "The disciplined one is honored among people."

As for "accepting sincerity and faith": when one hears such slanders and does not harbor sorrow or distress, but instead feels compassion for that person, thinking they will later suffer calamity, and never becomes resentful or angry, nor gives rise to an evil mind toward the other person—for this reason it is said, "one accepts sincerity and faith."
"Though well-trained for a long time, like a horse newly broken in, even the most excellent elephant is not equal to one who has trained himself. Regarding "though well-trained for a long time":

it is like a horse-trainer who, having known horses since his youth, understands them all—whether they are noble or dull, and whether a particular one is easy to train or difficult to train, or whether its temperament is impetuous or slow. One who can distinguish these qualities is called a skilled examiner; therefore it is said, "though well-trained for a long time."

Just as that novice driver, realizing that the wild horse could not yet be tamed, began to instruct it in riding and galloping from east to west; within ten days, it became well-trained and docile. However, if its will remained so stubborn that it could not be tamed, he would immediately hand it over to others to carry firewood and grass. Therefore it is said: "It is like that novice driver."

He is also the most excellent of elephants. As for the most excellent of elephants, his mind is subdued and his heart is tamed; though his body is coarse and rough, he is the greatest among beasts, beloved by men, and those who behold him never tire of the sight. Therefore it is said: "He is also the most excellent of elephants."

It is not as good as self-taming. When a person can tame themselves, subduing what is improper and removing what is evil, they are seen and honored by the devas, worldly people, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and those who have attained the Way through supernormal powers. Therefore it is said: "It is not as good as self-taming."
They cannot mount that which those others have not reached; only those who have disciplined themselves reach the realm of discipline.

They cannot mount that which those others have not reached means they cannot mount this vehicle to reach the state of fearlessness, nor can they mount this vehicle to reach the place of peace and security, nor can they mount this to reach the place free from calamity and affliction; therefore it is said, "they cannot mount."

"Only those who discipline themselves reach the realm of discipline. When a person can discipline and control themselves, their consciousness swiftly reaches the state of peace and security. One who is undisciplined can be made disciplined; one who is not upright can be made upright. Abiding forever in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they no longer undergo sorrow, grief, joy, or anger. Therefore it is said: "Only those who discipline themselves reach the realm of discipline."
They cannot ride that which people have not reached; only those who have disciplined themselves extinguish all evil.

Regarding "they cannot ride that which people have not reached": they cannot ride this vehicle to depart from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, nor can they transcend the eight difficulties. Therefore it is said: "they cannot ride that which people have not reached."

"Only those who discipline themselves extinguish all evil. When a person can discipline themselves, all manner of virtues will gather; they attain the highest mastery over all fetters and afflictions, and are able to completely eliminate the traces of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore it is said: "Only those who discipline themselves extinguish all evil."
They cannot mount that which no one else has reached; only those who have disciplined themselves are freed from all suffering.
They cannot mount that which no one else has reached—by mounting this vehicle, one cannot exhaust the root of suffering and proceed from this shore to the other shore.
Why is this? Because that vehicle is not a vehicle that reaches the ultimate end, nor is it the vehicle of the primary meaning (paramārtha).
Therefore it is said: "He cannot ride it; it is a place not reached by men."

Only those who discipline themselves are liberated from all suffering; having forever exhausted suffering, they no longer undergo birth and death. Therefore it is said: "Only those who discipline themselves are liberated from all suffering."
They cannot mount that which no human has reached; only those who have disciplined themselves can reach Nirvana.
They cannot mount that which no human has reached because they do not know its track; how much less could they know Nirvana as something visible?
This matter is not so; therefore it is said: "He cannot ride that which men have not yet reached.

Only one who has disciplined himself can reach Nirvāṇa, for he understands that Nirvāṇa itself is empty and tranquil. With single-minded focus and no other distracting thoughts, he attains it; therefore it is said: "Only one who has disciplined himself can reach Nirvāṇa."
Constantly self-restraining, like halting a galloping horse, one is able to exercise self-control and contemplate crossing over the source of suffering.
Regarding "constantly self-restraining," it means contemplating self-restraint to abandon evil and embrace goodness, as stated in the Sūtra where the Buddha told Cunda:
"Since one who has not disciplined themselves and whose mind is not focused cannot discipline others, this is impossible; if you wish to discipline others, you must first discipline yourself."
Therefore it is said: "One should always discipline oneself.
This is like one who stops a galloping horse; just as a horse-tamer tames a wild and runaway horse, making it avoid danger and seek safety, so it is said: "Like stopping a galloping horse."

"One who can personally restrain themselves and mindfully seek to cross over the origin of suffering" means that once all practices are complete, one no longer treads upon suffering but transcends the realm of suffering.
What is the "realm beyond suffering"?

It is the extinction of *nirvāṇa*; therein there are no further manifold sufferings or burning afflictions. Therefore it is said: "One mindfully restrains oneself, mindfully seeking to cross over the origin of suffering."
One is one's own protector; one seeks refuge in oneself to achieve liberation.
Therefore, one must personally exercise vigilance, like a merchant examining a fine horse.
Once, when the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Jīvaka the King of Medicine invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, with the single exception of Pāṇḍava.
The reason for this was that during the four months [of the rainy season], Pāṇḍava had been unable to memorize even the names of the broom.

At that time, the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus went to that house and each sat down in order. Jīvaka then rose and proceeded to offer pure water, but the Tathāgata did not accept the pure water. Jīvaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand for what reason or cause the Tathāgata does not accept the water?"
The Buddha told Jīvaka, "In this assembly there is no bhikṣu named Paṇḍita; for this reason, he did not accept the water.
Jīvaka addressed the Buddha:
"It is not that those who sweep the floors cannot recite this verse within four months; even those who walk the roads, herd oxen, or tend sheep can all recite this stanza."
"For what reason did you invite this man?
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"If you had not invited Pūrṇa, I would not have accepted the pure water."
At that time, Jīvaka, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately sent a messenger to summon Pūrṇa.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Hand the bowl to Pūrṇa."
The Buddha again addressed Pāṭika:
“Do not rise from your seat; reach out your alms bowl from afar and place it in the hands of the Tathāgata.
At that time, seeing such supernatural power, Jīvaka repented and reproached himself:
"Alas! I have made a great error, bringing disgrace upon the noble and holy ones; today I finally realize that one must not violate their spoken words.
He immediately conceived a heart of reverence toward the bhikṣu Pañcika, and no longer showed such zeal for the five hundred men.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively explained a past causal connection:
"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, Jīvaka himself was a horse trainer by profession, engaged in the trade of buying and selling horses."

At that time, he drove a thousand horses toward another country. On the way, one horse gave birth to a foal; its owner immediately gave the foal to another person and continued driving the horses along the road.
He soon traveled to another country and had an audience with the king. The king asked the horse trainer:

"I have now observed these thousand horses; they are ordinary steeds. Yet among them is one horse whose mournful neighing differs from that of the others. This horse will surely produce a dappled colt, and if that colt grows to maturity, its value shall equal that of these thousand horses."
"If I obtain this colt, I shall purchase all the horses; if I do not obtain the colt, I will not buy any horses.
The horse trainer replied, "Since we set out on the road, I do not recall any mare giving birth to a colt."
The king said to that man:
"I recite the marks of horses; by hearing the sound of a mare's mother, I can certainly know whether her foal is good or bad.
As the horse was being led away, it recalled these words and turned back, thinking to itself:
"Near the road, this mare gave birth to a dappled colt; I shall give it to the master on the way.
Before ten days had passed, the colt spoke in human speech and said to its owner:
"If someone comes seeking me with horses, you must give me away only if they bring five hundred horses; do not give me away unless they have five hundred horses."
Within a few days, the horse-master arrived of his own accord; leaving the foal nearby as a trust, he said:
"You have undergone the hardship of raising this horse; I shall now redeem it with one fine steed, and I pray you return it to me."

The man replied, "I did not originally force you to part with the colt; rather, since you left, I have raised it with great toil and hardship. If you now redeem it for five hundred horses, only then shall I return it to you."
He then redeemed it exactly as he had said, using five hundred horses, and thus recovered his original colt.
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"In the past, you first treated the colt with contempt and gave it away to a beggar, but later you ransomed it back for five hundred horses; it was first base and later became precious."
Now it is the same here: you invited five hundred bhikṣus but retained only Pāṇṭaka; yet now you instead hold Pāṇṭaka in high esteem while treating the five hundred with contempt.
"This condition has existed for a long time; it is not something that began only today.
Therefore it is said: "Like a merchant and a fine horse. The twentieth chapter, "The Parable of the Horse," is concluded.
*Udānavarga*, Volume Nineteen.
Udānavarga, Volume 20, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 21: On Anger (Krodhavarga). Chapter Twenty-one: On Anger.

Eliminating anger and casting off pride, Transcending all fetters and afflictions, Untainted by name-and-form— What more could there be to eliminate? Regarding "eliminating anger and casting off pride":

when a person harbors anger, it ruins those who practice the good. Thus, competing for profit, whether great or small, leading to the ruin of families and the destruction of nations until entire lineages are extinguished—all this stems from anger. Through pride, one has been destroyed, is being destroyed, and will be destroyed; therefore, it is said: "eliminate anger and cast off pride."

Regarding the transcending of all fetters (*saṃyojana*): anger and pride are the roots of these fetters; when the root is removed, there are no branches or leaves. Therefore it is said: "transcending all fetters."

"Not being stained by name-and-form" means that although name-and-form have been entirely eliminated, they still persist; yet sentient beings harbor notions of pleasure because they engage in mutual disparagement regarding name-and-form, saying, "My physical appearance and reputation surpass yours," or "Your physical appearance and reputation do not surpass mine. For this reason, it is said: "Not being stained by name-and-form."

"What exists when existence is removed? refers to that which is called "existence"—namely, the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*). One who has not yet been able to transcend existence to reach non-existence is driven by the afflictions, bound by the fetters, and constrained by the bonds.

That practitioner, through the tranquil cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of emptiness and stillness, exhausts them forever without remainder, transcending existence to reach non-existence. Therefore it is said: "What exists when existence is removed?"
Subdue anger so that it does not arise; when desire arises, one should restrain it.
Gradually severing the root of ignorance, cultivate the Truths—the supreme bliss.

Regarding "subdue anger so that it does not arise": anger blazes like fire; one should mindfully strive to extinguish it quickly. If allowed to grow, it causes much injury and ruin. When anger arises, calamity follows, just as a person holding a torch against the wind burns his own body. Therefore it is said: "Subdue anger so that it does not arise."

Regarding "one should restrain desire as it arises": as soon as a thought of desire arises, one should immediately seek skillful means to prevent it from arising. This is like a venomous snake that is just about to emerge from its hole; one must immediately control it so that it does not become violent and run wild. Desire is just like this: as soon as it arises, it should be extinguished so that it does not grow and flourish. Therefore it is said, "one should restrain desire as it arises."

Regarding "gradually severing the root of ignorance": ignorance is the great darkness of the world; it shrouds the mind and consciousness, preventing them from expanding and unfolding. One should seek skillful means and, with a courageous mind, sever its root so that it does not arise again. Therefore, it is said: "gradually sever the root of ignorance."

Regarding "cultivating the truths is the foremost happiness": the reason a practitioner does not quickly accomplish the Path is that their body and mind are defiled by lust, anger, and ignorance. These three fetters are severed through the Four Truths; one who has not attained the person of the Truths cannot eliminate these three matters. Since beginningless ages, they have never experienced the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); only upon attaining the Four Truths does one find true happiness. Therefore it is said: "Cultivating the truths is the foremost happiness."
Having severed ill will, one sleeps in peace; with ill will exhausted, one harbors no sorrow.
Ill will is the root of poison; for a bhikṣu, it is sweet.
The noble ones are able to eliminate it entirely; having severed it, they sleep well.

Regarding "one who has severed ill-will sleeps well": when a person is full of anger, they cannot sleep day or night; this state of anger is like being bitten by a snake, like the onset of a disease, or like the loss of wealth and property—such are the characteristics of ill-will.

When a person is free from anger, they do not perceive the various afflictions; they sleep peacefully and wake at dawn without distress. Their consciousness is as serene as if they had consumed ambrosia (*amṛta*). Therefore it is said: "By severing anger, one attains sleep."

"Having exhausted anger, one harbors no sorrow" means that when a person harbors anger and it manifests before them, they grieve day and night as if they had lost a close relative or lost wealth and treasures. Once anger has been eliminated, there is no further sorrow, grief, or affliction; therefore it is said, "having exhausted anger, one harbors no sorrow."

Regarding "hatred is the root of poison": among all poisons, none surpasses hatred as the root. When a person’s hatred is intense, it obscures all meritorious qualities so that they cannot manifest. Therefore it is said: "hatred is the root of poison."

To be sweet is for a bhikṣu who has already uprooted the root of poison so that no poisonous sprout remains, and who produces beautiful medicine; like that nectar which removes all impurities and evils, it is therefore said: "To be sweet is for a bhikṣu."

The noble ones are able to eliminate it entirely; they sever that which allows for sound sleep. Those called "noble ones" are the disciples of the Buddhas. Having eliminated all evils and gathered all virtues, they extinguish the root from which anger arises and no longer create new karma. Their minds do not give rise to thoughts, nor do they harbor such perceptions of anger. Thus they attain sound sleep, free from further anxiety. Therefore it is said: "The noble ones are able to eliminate it entirely; they sever that which allows for sound sleep."
When a person gives rise to anger and performs both wholesome and unwholesome deeds, later, once that anger has been removed,
they recall those past events as if a fire were blazing fiercely.

When a person gives rise to anger and performs both wholesome and unwholesome deeds, it is as if that person is entangled by anger such that their mind is inverted and they lack all discernment. Just as a blind person cannot perceive a high bank or level ground, so too is the angry person: entangled by anger, they do not see what is wholesome or unwholesome, nor what is good or evil. Therefore it is said: "When a person gives rise to anger, they perform both wholesome and unwholesome deeds."

Later, once the anger has been removed, to retrospectively recall past events as if they were a blazing fire is like a traveler who has lost their way finding a timely change of course; for one who harbors resentment, swift repentance is paramount. Internally harboring shame and remorse, one should immediately reproach oneself:
"Anger is hollow and deceptive; why did I give rise to this fury?"
"Anger and anger met with retaliation never cease; it is like a blazing fire.

When the mind undergoes remorse and feels shame for being driven by hatred, it is for this reason that it is said: "Once later hatred has been removed, one reflects upon past events as if they were a blazing fire."

Lacking shame and lacking remorse, Furthermore prone to anger and rage, Ensnared by hatred, they are like those who have lost their sight in the darkness. Regarding "lacking shame and lacking remorse":

when a person’s anger is rampant, they fail to distinguish between the honorable and the base, possessing no sense of shame or modesty. Like one who is dazed and deranged, though surrounded by a crowd that mocks them all day long, they remain unaware of themselves. They conceal their deeds yet expose them, and their deceitful words lack any foundation. Therefore it is said: "lacking shame and lacking remorse."

Furthermore, regarding those who are prone to anger: such angry persons act without purity and harbor defilement in their hearts; they have no means by which to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Therefore it is said, "furthermore, they are prone to anger."

Enveloped by hatred, one is like a blind person in the darkness; when that angry person’s wrath blazes forth, they perceive the day as night and the world as entirely dark. Having no light from their own body, what benefit is there for them even if a thousand suns were to shine together?
Therefore it is said: "Enveloped by anger, one is like one who has lost their sight in the darkness.
That strength is not true strength; for those who take anger as their strength, anger is a base and decaying dharma, and they do not perceive the resonance of the wholesome."
That strength is not true strength; those who take anger as their strength give rise to hatred through what is unrighteous, thinking within themselves:
"What I do is right, and what he does is wrong."
When the time came for the assembly to interrogate him, he was put on the defensive and mocked by the children.

Only then did he realize his error and regret his conduct; as it is said, when the noble and virtuous are upright in principle, they prevail, for the power of anger is not to be relied upon—it lacks stability and ruins one’s virtuous nature.
Therefore it is said: "That strength is not true strength; it is the taking of anger as strength. Anger is a base and decaying dharma.

For one who does not perceive the resonance of wholesome responses, all roots of goodness are extinguished; their speech becomes evil, they disregard what precedes or follows, and they provoke insults toward whatever they encounter, their words always coarse and vulgar, with hatred and anger as their primary motive.
When a person possesses virtue, those far and near offer congratulations, and their good reputation inevitably spreads wherever they go.

Now, when we speak of this person, we hear only an evil reputation and no sound of goodness; though there may be some slight merit, it is obscured by anger and cannot manifest. Therefore it is said: "Anger is a base and decaying dharma; one does not perceive the resonance of one's own goodness."

The powerful draw near to weapons; the powerless draw near to gentleness. Patience is supreme; one should always be patient with the weak. Regarding "the powerful draw near to weapons; the powerless draw near to gentleness":

those who rely on their own strength and power consider themselves the foremost. When faced with the weak, they treat them with contemptuous patience and do not retaliate; even if they are struck or beaten, they do not give rise to anger. Thus, the strong follow after the strong, and the weak approach the weak. The powerful never direct their intent toward the weak, whereas the weak, conversely, often turn their intent toward the strong. Therefore it is said: "The powerful draw near to weapons; the powerless draw near to gentleness."

Patience is supreme; one ought always to be patient with the weak. What is called patience is not seeing faults or judging right from wrong; this is what is termed patience. It is not relying on one's own strength to treat the weak with contempt. If one were to treat the weak with disdain, one would be mocked by all people. Therefore it is said: "Patience is supreme; one ought always to be patient with the weak."
The entire multitude despises him; those with strength must endure it. Endurance is supreme;
one should always endure the weak.
Regarding "the entire multitude despises him": perhaps there is one person who is despised by the multitude, and among them, one who possesses wisdom is able to endure it.
Why is this? That person is solitary and weak, having no one to turn to for refuge; how could one direct anger toward such a single individual?
Therefore it is said: "When the multitude holds one in contempt, the powerful should endure."

Patience is supreme; one should always practice patience toward the weak. Patience is the foremost power, and there is nothing in the world that surpasses it. Even the supernormal powers, the clear discernment, the attainment of the Way, and the marks of physical excellence are all the result of the power of patience. To achieve thorough understanding of this life and future lives, and to possess penetrating insight without limit, is also due to the power of patience. Therefore it is said: "Patience is supreme; one should always practice patience toward the weak."
"Between oneself and another, there is great fear from which there is no rescue;
if one knows that the other is angry, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself.

Regarding "between oneself and another, there is great fear from which there is no rescue": when a person reflects, they first examine themselves and then observe the other's countenance to discern their character. One can thus distinguish whether this nature is corrupt and evil or whether it is virtuous and good. One should always be cautious and refrain from committing unwholesome deeds, fearing the retribution of future lives where one would suffer immeasurably, having no liberation from this life until the next.
Therefore it is said: "Between myself and that person, there is a great peril from which there is no rescue.

If one knows that the other is full of anger, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself. Knowing that the other’s angry countenance is fierce and intense, one should remain silent and reflect inwardly:
"If I were to compete with him, it would not be proper for me; I should now remain silent—why should I contend with him?"
Therefore it is said: "Just as one knows the anger of another, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself.
When both practice this principle, myself and the other are likewise so;
just as one knows the anger of another, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself."

Regarding the statement, "Both practice its meaning; so it is for me and for others as well": this means that one acts both for oneself and for others, and protects both one's own person and the persons of others, constantly reflecting upon the avoidance of two matters:
first, the fear of suffering calamity in the present life; second, the fear of retribution in the future.
Therefore, it is said that both [parties] act according to the same principle; "I" and "the other" are likewise so.

As for knowing that the other is angry and thus one should extinguish the flaws within oneself: suppose one personally sees another person filled with fierce rage, or sees them grasping tiles and stones intending to come and cause harm; one then likewise prepares tiles and stones to resist them. It is like a person who, holding a white staff, intends to go and engage in a fight, but the staff in his hand immediately transforms into a sword; seeing this, the person immediately throws the sword to the ground.

At that time, a king atop a high tower saw this man from afar; he first saw him grasping grass, which then transformed into a sword, and immediately upon seeing it again, the man threw it to the ground.
The king soon dispatched a messenger to summon him for interrogation, asking:
"For what reason did you previously grasp the grass as if it were a blade,
and why did you cast the blade upon the ground?"
The man said to the king:
"I have heard it stated in the Buddhist scriptures that the Buddha told his attendant:

'When I am about to pass away into the void of nirvana and the unconditioned, during the future age when the five grains boil over, sentient beings will contend with one another; as they seize tiles and stones, these will immediately transform into swords and spears.'"
"Your servant has accumulated merit for a long time and did not dare to be the primary instigator of evil; therefore, I threw my sword to the ground.
When the King heard these words, he was deeply moved and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, immediately rewarding the man by granting him a household of subjects.
Therefore it is said: "Just as one knows the anger of another, one should extinguish the flaws within oneself.
Practicing both principles—acting for myself as I do for others—the fool deems himself powerless;
yet the observation of the Dharma is likewise so.

Regarding the statement, "Practicing both meanings, I act for the sake of the other": one constantly protects oneself and protects others as if protecting precious goods. Internally reflecting, one subdues one's own mind so as not to disturb others, and ensures that others do not come to harm oneself. Thus, both parties guard one another so that neither suffers loss; therefore it is said, "Practicing both meanings, I act for the sake of the other."

Regarding the statement, "The fool says there is no power, and so it is when observing phenomena": the mind of a fool is dark and fails to perceive future changes; he thinks that those who fight will always fight and never cease, while those who harmonize will always harmonize and never engage in dispute. The wise, however, observe that for one who does not fight, there is inevitably loss; though one may be called victorious, it is better than having no fight at all. Therefore it is said: "The fool says there is no power, and so it is when observing phenomena."
If a fool defeats one of superior wisdom with coarse words and evil speech, yet desires to always remain victorious, he should maintain silence regarding such talk.

If a fool defeats one of superior wisdom with coarse words and evil speech, he will constantly associate with wicked companions who ruin the virtuous; his speech is so full of malice that throughout the entire day nothing good comes from it. Evil follows evil as they accumulate sins like mountains; though their peers may praise them, each contends for superiority. This is called being defiled and turbid, failing to reach the ultimate goal. Therefore it is said: "If a fool defeats one of superior wisdom with coarse words and evil speech."

For one who desires constant victory, it is appropriate to remain silent in speech; the noble and wise praise such silence. When evil is inflicted upon oneself, one does not regard it with resentment; when receiving honor and favor, one does not regard it with joy. Not repaying abuse with abuse, one practices patience as one's vocation; if struck or beaten, one accepts it silently without retaliation. Therefore it is said: "One who constantly desires victory should remain silent in speech."
One should practice the teachings of the wise and not associate with fools;
one can endure foul and leaking words, and for this reason, patience is said to be supreme among virtues.

One should practice the teachings of the wise and observe those who are superior to oneself, carefully refraining from contravening their instructions; if one does not even dispute with those who are inferior, how much less would one dispute with those who are superior?
This is not so. Why? Because a person of wisdom is honored and supreme; there is none who surpasses them.
Therefore it is said: "One should practice the teachings of the wise. One does not associate with fools, for like attracts like:

the virtuous enter into good assemblies and the wicked enter into evil friendships. When the virtuous hear evil views, they avoid them; when the wicked hear what is good, they wish to disparage and belittle it. The Buddhas, the noble sages, and all those who have attained the Way praise the virtue of non-contention. Therefore it is said: "One does not associate with fools."

One who can endure foul and leaking words considers that those who are base and evil do not cherish themselves; they are loathed by others due to their violent nature and conduct. To engage in dispute with such people is to become an object of ridicule; one brings disgrace upon oneself, causes friends to lose joy, and incurs the reproach of others. How, then, could one trade this body of gold and jewels for their mere shards of clay?
Therefore, the wise take patience as their silence.
For this reason it is said: "One is able to endure foul and leaking words.

Thus it is said that among those who practice patience, the noble and holy person is supreme; they are fully endowed with all karmic actions, and having perfected the roots of goodness and the outflows-free states, they restrain their own minds when beholding the foul conduct of others.
"Why should I now again associate with them?

Having encountered countless sages, one achieves success through patience. One should remain on guard day and night as if dwelling in a blazing fire, cultivating wholesome thoughts so that they increase daily, while ensuring that transgressions and evils diminish and are extinguished. Therefore, it is said that patience is supreme among virtues.
One who is angry does not speak; though dwelling among the multitude, they are as if in a secluded place.
When a person’s anger blazes forth, they ultimately do not realize it themselves. Regarding "one who is angry does not speak":

having received this human form after accumulating countless practices, one has finally attained its fulfillment. Having obtained a human body with a complete faculty of speech, one should constantly praise and speak of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha; serve one's parents; honor and revere teachers and elders; and day and night recite and study the profound and wondrous sūtras.

Why is this? The Buddha also cited a metaphor: the tongue is like a sword or halberd that brings about calamity and misfortune; through the coarse words of the tongue, one may cause the extinction of one’s clan. The tongue has ten titles, and speech is considered extraordinary; it is a heavy responsibility for humanity, from which one has never been separated.
Therefore it is said: "The angry person does not speak. Regarding "being as if in private even when among the multitude":

a practitioner who trains himself always maintains vigilance to guard against verbal transgressions. Whether in a great assembly or in private, his speech is gentle and does not wound the minds of others; his preceding words cover what follows so that the reasoning is neither cumbersome nor redundant. Therefore it is said: "Being as if in private even when among the multitude."

When a person’s anger burns fiercely, they remain unaware of it until the end; just as that wicked man, when moved by joy or anger, is shrouded by the veil of hatred and cannot see clearly for himself, he only brings harm and disgrace upon himself without benefiting the world. Entangled by his own defilements, he does not seek to cleanse himself; committing evil for a single day accumulates calamities for billions of kalpas, let alone a lifetime of practicing evil—how could one hope to attain the Way? It shall never be possible.
Therefore it is said: When a person is consumed by the fire of anger, they remain unaware of it until their end.
One who speaks the truth without malice, and when asked, thinks only of giving—these three things have a fixed destination;
such a person will naturally dwell in the celestial palaces.

To speak truthfully and without anger means that one acts with utmost sincerity and is revered by others; such a person is remembered and esteemed by tens of millions of people, all of which results from the virtue of being free from anger.
When a beggar thinks of giving and harbors no stinginess, such that when someone comes to beg they do not resist with ill will, this person is called one who is open and magnanimous.

The beggar does not act out of greed for the sake of conditions in future lives; rather, by accumulating merit through goodness until it is full, they naturally attain the Noble Path. Therefore it is said: "The beggar thinks of giving."

Regarding the phrase "three parts have fixed locations, naturally dwelling in celestial palaces": these three types of karma constitute conduct that does not wither or decay; one will inevitably be born among gods or humans, circling through rebirths without remaining in lowly or base conditions.

It is like a person who goes from one pleasure grove to another, from one garden to another, delighting themselves with the five kinds of music and never experiencing grief or sorrow; they are thus able to close the gates of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, open the path to the heavens and humans, and by advancing further in their meritorious deeds, reach the state of unconditioned liberation (*asamskṛta*).
Therefore it is said: "Three things have their fixed places; naturally they dwell in celestial palaces.
When the mind is stilled, how can there be anger? By self-restraint, one finds clarity within life;
through equal wisdom and meditative liberation, having known this, there is no more anger."

"When the mind is stilled, how can there be anger? This means that a practitioner who has stilled the heart and subdued coarse and depraved thoughts has a mind like extinguished ashes and a body like withered wood. When encountering anger or joy before them, they do not harbor these in their hearts; their minds are as stable and clear as Mount An-ming, incapable of being moved. Therefore it is said: "When the mind is stilled, how can there be anger?"

Regarding "one who is wise and self-restrained within their lifespan": the practitioner examines and nourishes their own life, constantly honoring and protecting it through the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, without craving worldly glory or harboring expectations. Therefore, it is said: "one who is wise and self-restrained within their lifespan."

"Equanimity-wisdom is the liberation of concentration; having known this, there is no anger. This practitioner attains equanimous liberation rather than non-equanimous liberation. One who possesses non-equanimous liberation is merely a worldly person who has severed desire. A person of equanimous liberation never harbors anger or resentment; all stains of the fetters of anger have been forever eradicated. Therefore it is said: "Equanimity-wisdom is the liberation of concentration; having known this, there is no anger."
Now, as for those who commit evil: when anger meets anger, there is a retribution of anger; if one does not return anger for anger, one triumphs over the one who fought and lost.

Regarding the statement, "As for those who commit evil: when anger meets anger, there is a retribution of anger": a person who practices evil brings calamity upon both themselves and others. It is like a wild fire that, as it spreads, encounters what lies before it and sets it ablaze. One who is first provoked to anger causes anger to arise in another; one who is first possessed of an evil mind causes an evil mind to arise in another. Therefore it is said: "As for those who commit evil: when anger meets anger, there is a retribution of anger."

Not returning anger for anger is to triumph over those who lose in combat. Formerly, King Prasenajit favored and maintained many slaves; he dispatched them as envoys to attack and conquer other kingdoms, and because they were skilled in the arts of war, all whom they encountered submitted.
Later, the wives invited monks to provide offerings and seek their prayers; the monks further preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for them, and they all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
When the soldiers returned from their expedition, the wives said to their husbands:
"After you departed on your campaign, we invited various monks to provide offerings and seek our prayers, wishing that you might return home safely and soon."
"Preach the Dharma for us; we have already attained the stage of Srotāpanna, so you all should further request him.
They then followed their wives' words and invited the practitioners to provide them with offerings and preach the Dharma, whereupon the husbands also attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
In that realm there were also bandits and marauders, and the king commanded his various groups of slaves to go and attack them. Upon hearing this, the slaves reflected within themselves:
"Each of us has attained the Truth of the Path; we are compassionate toward all and do not harm living beings. How could we go to wage war against those enemies?"
He further reflected:

"If I do not accept the king's command and respond to his summons, my life will perish and the calamity will extend to my wife and children; it would be better to face death there than to remain here alive and bring sin upon my wife and children."

They immediately prepared their carriages and set out toward the enemy; through the responsive power of the devas, nāgas, and spirits, they shattered the opposing host and returned home in safety. The sovereign rejoiced, and peace prevailed throughout the four quarters.
Therefore it is said: Not returning anger for anger surpasses the defeat of combat;
patience conquers enmity, goodness conquers evil, the victor is able to give, and sincerity conquers deceit.

Regarding "the one who overcomes enmity through patience": Formerly, King Ajātaśatru assembled the fourfold army and went to attack Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit also assembled his fourfold army and went out to battle; he crushed the great host and captured King Ajātaśatru alive. Leading him to the presence of the Tathāgata, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "My sister’s son, Ajātaśatru, was rebellious and unrighteous, recklessly giving rise to evil intent to invade my kingdom.

Where there was originally no enmity, he created enmity of his own accord; where there was originally no strife, he created strife of his own accord. I now grant him amnesty for his crimes and release him to return to his own country."
Why is this? Because my elder sister has released me.
For this reason it is said: “Patience triumphs over enmity.”
Regarding "the virtuous overcoming the non-virtuous": those devoid of merit delight in self-aggrandizement, saying, "What I know is much, while what he knows is little.
Though they possess no actual skill, they claim to have it; though they possess no actual strategy, they claim to be versatile. When the moment of action arrives, they shrink back like a centipede.
If one observes the wise, they stand solitary and unmoving, like a heap of dead flesh devoid of consciousness.

For this reason, the wise urge people to accumulate learning; learning is the precious abode that sustains the spirit. When the mind and will are at ease, one attains mastery throughout the four quarters; that one achieves success through study, and that the laws and standards for managing households and establishing states distinguish between the right and the wrong—all these arise from learning.
Therefore it is said: "The good triumphs over the unwholesome.

As for "the victor who is able to give," this means that the victor triumphs over that stinginess and greed. A person who does not establish the roots of virtue is envious of others and jealous of the worthy; seeing someone practice generosity, they feel as if they were personally losing their own wealth, constantly thinking:
"If I give to them, what will I have to look forward to in the future?"

Only those who have established faith are able to practice giving; they do not discriminate among recipients nor do they seek a karmic reward. When beggars fill their gates, they impose no restrictions; when people gather from all quarters like clouds, they do not reject even the lowliest. Therefore it is said: "The victor is one who can give."

Sincerity surpasses deception; those who practice sincerity are honored by their kin and retinues, and there is no place where their renown is not heard. Those who speak falsehoods are unhappy to be seen by others and are detested and envied by them. Therefore it is said: "Sincerity surpasses deception."
"Without anger and without harming, always mindful of truthful conduct;
the fool gives rise to anger within himself, and his resentment remains ever-present.

He who is without anger and without harming, and who is always mindful of truthful conduct—that practitioner knows the proper time and the Dharma; he knows what should be avoided and avoids it, and knows what should be pursued and pursues it. His speech is truthful and is honored by the world, for he does not deceive others. Therefore it is said: 'Without anger and without harming, always mindful of truthful conduct.'"

"The fool gives rise to anger within himself, and the knot of resentment remains ever-present" means that among the habits of a fool, hatred is foremost; it persists within his mind and is never abandoned. It is like carving characters into stone, where the inscriptions are distinct and cannot be obliterated by violent winds. Therefore it is said: "The fool gives rise to anger within himself, and the knot of resentment remains ever-present."
"One who can restrain their own anger is like one who stops a runaway chariot; this is called a skilled driver, who leaves behind darkness and enters into light.

'One who can restrain their own anger, like one who stops a runaway chariot' means that if one can immediately subdue anger as soon as it arises, such a person is called a hero among men. It is just as when a horse-drawn chariot bolts away, a driver who can bring it to a halt is called a skilled driver. Therefore it is said: 'One who can restrain their own anger is like one who stops a runaway chariot.'"

This is what is meant by being a skilled driver—one who leaves darkness and enters light. This "skilled driver" does not merely drive a chariot, nor does he drive elephants or horses. What is called a driver is one who can restrain his own thoughts so that they do not scatter, who calms the mind so it does not arise, whose will is directed toward non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), and who is unattached to worldly burdens. He serves as a great responsibility for others, acting as a virtuous field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); he is worthy of respect and honor, and is the supreme object of offerings. Therefore it is said: "This is what is meant by being a skilled driver—one who leaves darkness and enters light."
The śramaṇa and the Way: practicing this loving-kindness, mingled with water, flowers, and incense, with the horse’s resentment as the tenth.
The Most Perfectly Awakened One has attained it by himself; he is unstained by any phenomena.
The All-Knowing One is fearless; he is self-enlightened without a teacher or protector.

Having attained the Most Perfect Awakening by himself, [the Buddha] appeared in the world. Formerly, when the six teachers were in the world, they were greedily attached to gain and offerings, competing with one another to claim that they alone were supreme. Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world, his divine virtue and power surpassing those of men, the six teachers gathered like clouds and each made a vow together:

"We six men have no equals in this world. Recently we have heard that a Buddha has appeared in the world, whose divine virtue and majestic power exceed our own. We should deliberate together with unified hearts and equal intentions, our words not contradicting one another, so that we may then defeat that Gautama."
He immediately dispatched one man to observe whether the Tathāgata’s countenance and gaze were those of a human being.
Upon going to observe him, the man found that his gaze was never tiring to behold; he returned and reported to the six teachers exactly what he had seen.
"Gautama’s countenance is rare in this world; his majestic power and radiance surpass those of the sun and moon. As I see him, there is no simile by which he can be compared.
The six men then thought:
"This man is born of a royal lineage; it is only natural that he should be handsome, so why should it be considered strange?"
"Now let us send another person to observe Gautama’s appearance and demeanor to see if he is fearless, or if he is agitated and constrained.
They went at once to observe his features; he was like a lion king among the beasts, possessing no fear or difficulty. Returning, they informed the six teachers:
"Gautama is in the midst of the assembly like a king of beasts, possessing no fear or difficulty."
The six men thought again:
"This fool merely circles him because he is eager for a new experience and covets that radiance; this is his natural disposition, so why should it be considered strange?"

That Gautama came from a royal palace; though he was entertained day and night by sixty thousand court ladies, he has not yet undergone the teachings of a master nor ever engaged in study. It would be better to send someone to listen to what he says, to see whether he possesses any principles or if he is merely like an ordinary man.
He immediately dispatched one person of clear intelligence to go and observe him.
Having heard in full what was being taught, he returned and reported to the six men:

"That Gautama’s exposition is thorough regarding the past and knowledgeable regarding the present; his foresight is boundless and his retrospective vision is infinite. He adjudicates meanings and analyzes principles with such clarity that they are neither redundant nor cumbersome."
Having heard this, the six teachers again thought to themselves:

"There are many people in the world whose eloquence is swift and who can please the hearts of others; yet they do not abide by principle and are impossible to fathom. We should send someone to observe Gautama to see whether the multitude, upon hearing what he says, listen to him in silent reverence."
"Is it because of the commotion that you could not listen?
He immediately went to observe and listen.
Seeing that the great assembly was thirsting for the Dharma with focused minds, gazing up at the Tathāgata with eyes never blinking, he returned and informed the six teachers:
"What Gautama expounds is as sweet as ambrosia; the multitude yearns for it and listens without ever being sated.
The six men then thought again:
"When a person gathers a following, their initial resolve is extremely fierce, yet they will surely retreat and disperse after a long time. Why, then, should we find this strange or suspicious?"
"Let us send another person to observe Gautama: is his doctrine profound and subtle, or is it shallow and incoherent?
He then dispatched a man of superior standing to go and examine Gautama.
Having heard what was said, he returned and reported to the six teachers:

"What Gautama has expounded is like a shoreless ocean, while what we have seen is like water in a cow's hoofprint. Now, I alone wish to go to him and seek to become his disciple; how could I know what the others would do?"

The attendants from both the front and the rear each escorted one another to the place where the Tathāgata was. Furthermore, countless sentient beings gathered like falling clouds, vying with one another to reach the presence of the Tathāgata. There they immediately heard the Buddha speak this verse:
“Self-attained by the Most Perfectly Awakened One, Untainted by any phenomena, All-knowing and fearless, Spontaneously realized without a teacher or protector.”

"The Most Perfectly Enlightened One who has attained self-realization" means that he has awakened to all phenomena; there is nothing too subtle that does not enter his awareness and nothing too minute that he does not examine. Through the power of supernormal knowledge, he knows them as they truly are. For this reason, it is said: "The Most Perfectly Enlightened One who has attained self-realization."

To be unstained by all phenomena means not being defiled by these eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, defamation and praise, renown and insignificance, suffering and pleasure; therefore it is said, "one is unstained by all phenomena."

One who possesses the fearlessness of omniscience is free from all afflictions and no longer subject to manifold distress; they cannot be overwhelmed by water, fire, or wicked bandits, but transcend calamities to dwell alone in goodness and without sorrow. Therefore, it is said: "The Omniscient One is fearless."
Being naturally without teacher or protector, he alone rules over the three thousandfold world system; having no peers or equals, how much less could there be anyone who might surpass him?
Therefore it is said: Spontaneously self-arisen, without teacher or protector;
his resolve solitary and peerless, he has personally attained the True Path.
The Tathāgata, Honored One among gods and men, is fully endowed with all powers of wisdom.
As for his resolve being uniquely peerless: with my divine eye, I have surveyed the three thousandfold world system to see if there were anyone of such a kind as myself;
yet, though I searched everywhere, I found no one equal to him, much less anyone who could surpass him.
This matter is not so. Therefore it is said: "The will is solitary and without equal.

Regarding "having personally attained the Right Path": when I sought the Path, I did so without a teacher’s instruction and attained it spontaneously; furthermore, having no companion, I walked alone without fear. For this reason, it is said: "Having personally attained the Right Path."
The Tathāgata, the Honored One among devas and humans—why is he called the Tathāgata?

Because as the past Samyaksaṃbuddhas came, I have come from them; having practiced with diligent austerity for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, whether giving away my kingdom, wealth, wife, children, head, eyes, marrow, or brain, I was able to deliver myself. Because I have come from within that [path], I am therefore called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, because one accords with the world’s conventional meaning based on the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata, one is called a "Tathāgata.

Just as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, were fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique and sublime qualities, and possessed great loving-kindness and great compassion to universally deliver all beings without departing from the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), so too am I now; therefore, I am called a Tathāgata.
For what reason is he called the Honored One among Gods and Humans?

It is said that he is called the Honored One among Gods and Humans because gods and humans rely upon him to cultivate the roots of goodness, transcend successive stages to realize the realization of the Noble Path, exhaust all outflows to achieve the state of no-outflows, and attain the three types of perfect knowledge and supernatural powers without any obstruction. Therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata is the Honored One among Gods and Humans."

Regarding "endowed with the power of all-knowledge" and "possessing the strength of the Tathāgata’s physical body": this body consists of one hundred and twenty joints, and each joint has one hundred and twenty-eight arms. This divine power is the strength of his physical constitution, not the power of supernatural *ṛddhi*; therefore, it is said that he is "endowed with the power of all-knowledge."
I am the World-Honored One; having severed the outflows and being free from lust, I am followed by a multitude of devas and worldlings who follow my mind.
Regarding my title as "World-Honored One," there are three kinds of worlds: [the world of beings, the world of phenomena, and the world of space].
First is the world of the aggregates (*skandha-loka*), second is the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), and third is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
For what reason is it called "non-attachment"?
It is called non-attachment for three reasons:

First, it is called non-attachment because of the severing of fetters; second, it is called non-attachment because of being worthy of receiving the offerings of others; third, it is called non-attachment because there are no seeds in the three realms, nor any root, and thus there is no further rebirth.
Therefore it is said: "I am one who is unattached.

Regarding the phrase "having severed the outflows and being free from lust," this refers to the meaning of the Unsurpassed, which has nothing superior to it and possesses no peer; it awakens to all phenomena, penetrating the most minute and reaching the most subtle. Furthermore, in order to resolve the doubts of the sentient beings within the assembly, he speaks of the meaning of the Unsurpassed.

In the past, there were countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whose lifespans were exceedingly long and whose assemblies of disciples were beyond calculation; their lands were pure and free from any blemish. One might say that the spiritual power of those past Buddhas was greater than my own today.
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
The power of supernatural penetrations and wisdom is one and not two; it is only that the minds of sentient beings themselves possess increase and decrease.
Therefore it is said: "He has severed the outflows and is free from lust.

Among the gods and the people of the world, he alone follows his own mind; among the gods and the people of the world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, or the celestial beings such as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings—I am the sole honored one, the sole awakened one, without equal. Therefore it is said: "Among the gods and the people of the world, he alone follows his own mind."

At that time, when the disciples of the six heretical teachers heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, those whose minds were firm immediately sought the Way; those whose minds harbored hesitation returned to their masters and reported in detail what they had heard: "He who is uniquely honored throughout the three realms and presides over the ten directions truly has no equal. It is fitting that we each disperse and seek our own peace."
Since I have neither teacher nor protector, and am likewise without companion,
I have attained Buddhahood by accumulating a single practice, spontaneously penetrating the Holy Path. At that time, the World-Honored One,
having been entreated by Brahmā beneath the King of Trees, rose from his seat and proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the brahmin Upavāna saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar and thought to himself:
"Today Gautama’s countenance is joyful and his appearance is serene, both internally and externally clear and translucent; what could be the reason for this?"
"Who is your teacher? From whom did you learn the Way?
What Dharma do you study, and what techniques do you cultivate?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse to the brahmin:
“I have no teacher or protector, Nor do I have any companion;
Having perfected a single practice, I attained Buddhahood, Spontaneously penetrating the Holy Path.

Regarding the line “I have no teacher or protector”: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—having observed and penetrated the three periods of time with nothing he does not know—spoke this verse for the sake of future sentient beings who have not yet awakened.
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be two bhikṣus: one named Mahāsāṃghika and the other named Vatsīputrīya; they shall be known as Mañjuśrī."
The Teacher Śākyamuni spoke this verse in order to eliminate their doubts.

Furthermore, some say that various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers each maintain the argument that the śramaṇa Gautama attained enlightenment only after hearing the Dharma from Ārāḍa Kālāma; wishing to eliminate such doubts, he declared, "I have no teacher or protector."

Furthermore, regarding those who are solitary and without companions: the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, perceives and penetrates the three periods of time—the future, the past, and the present—and there is nothing he does not examine. As for the two groups of bhikṣus in the future, one shall be named Mahāsaṃghika and the other shall be named Vatsīputrīya.

Setting aside the root to focus on the branches: when there is a realm of human beings and lands, a Buddha appears in the world. Yet those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts below, as well as those in the heavens above who delight in their own pleasures, never emerge to meet the Buddha. The transformations manifested by the Tathāgata are not limited to any single place; if he were not to pervade every location, he could not be called a Buddha.

Those two groups are said to be incomplete; for by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, he ascends to the summit of a single Sumeru mountain and thus proceeds through his travels, teaching and transforming beings without end. Therefore it is said: "He is also solitary and without companion."

Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood through the accumulation of a single practice: one achieves supreme perfect enlightenment within these three periods of time. When a Buddha appears in the world, it is primarily in Jambudvīpa; he is born in the central lands and not in the borderlands. As for why he is born in this Jambudvīpa: among the billions of Jambudvīpas in the east, west, south, and north, this particular Jambudvīpa is situated at the very center. Its terrestrial realm possesses spiritual power superior to other regions, whereas the lands of other directions do not compare to it. Therefore, it is said that one attains Buddhahood by accumulating a single practice.

One who naturally penetrates the noble path abandons the feverish afflictions and fetters, becoming cool and free from heat. A person with a mind of sorrow always has a face that is not joyful, whereas one without a mind of sorrow always has a face that is harmonious and serene. The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise: all ailments have been exhausted and there is no further feverish affliction. Therefore it is said, "He naturally penetrates the noble path."
At that time, the brahmin Upavīta came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Do you now claim for yourself to be the most supreme?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied to the brahmin in verse:
"Victorious over oneself, one does not receive evil; Victorious over all the world, with wisdom vast and boundless, Opening the eyes of the ignorant—I am the victor.
Regarding "victorious over oneself, one does not receive evil": to be victorious over all the world and able to overcome enemies is what the world calls victory.

This victory is not the true victory; rather, it is the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) and the eradication of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), wherein all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are forever extinguished, that is called victory. Such a one reigns alone as king over the world, with none able to equal him. Therefore it is said: "The self-victorious does not receive evil; he is victorious over the entire world."

"Wisdom is vast and boundless; I have opened the delusions of others and am thus the Victor. For those in the world who fall into evil dharmas and commit transgressions, I have eternally extinguished them and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The future reception of birth, existence, craving, and the twelve links of dependent origination are eternally extinguished without remainder. Therefore it is said: 'Wisdom is vast and boundless; I have opened the delusions of others and am thus the Victor.'"
At that time, the brahmin Upavāna came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama, where do you intend to go today?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Now I am going to Vārāṇasī, / Desiring to beat the drum of the Deathless;
/ I shall turn the Wheel of Dharma, / A wheel never before turned.
Thus the brahmin questioned the Buddha.
"Is this indeed so? The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The words of the Tathāgata are without duality."
Having heard this, the brahmin nodded his head, sighed in admiration, and departed.
The wise do not dwell among the foolish; observing the world, they transform it accordingly.
They proclaim the stainless path, wherein there is eternal rest, unsurpassed.

The wise do not dwell in folly; those who observe the world and transform beings accordingly refer to the Buddhas and their disciples, who first observe the world to see who should be delivered and who should not be delivered. They examine everywhere who is capable of receiving transformation and who is not, and who has planted the seeds for liberation and who has not.
Therefore it is said: "The wise person does not dwell in folly; observing the world, they transform it accordingly.

Regarding the statement, "To speak of the stainless track, the eternal cessation which is unsurpassed": the "stainless track" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path; "eternal cessation" refers to the extinction of *nirvāṇa*. When sages descend into the world to receive and deliver sentient beings, they always do so by means of the Noble Path, never departing from untainted (*anāsrava*) practice. Therefore it is said: "To speak of the stainless track, the eternal cessation which is unsurpassed."
The valiant one roars a great roar; the Tathāgata of the True Dharma explains the Dharma and explains its meaning;
the Awakened One is eternally at peace.

Regarding "the valiant one roars a great roar; the Tathāgata of the True Dharma": the "valiant ones" are the Buddha and his disciples. Śākyamuni Buddha was valiant enough to transcend nine *kalpas*; therefore, he is named "the Valiant One."

The six teachers are unrestrained and fond of practicing what is not the Dharma, failing to follow the correct discipline; whereas that which the Tathāgata has expounded and practiced is in accordance with the Dharma and transcends worldly dharmas. Therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata of the True Dharma roars the great roar of the brave."

"Teaching the Dharma and teaching its meaning, the awakened one attains eternal peace": when what is human or what is of the world is not treated as the true Dharma, it is ridiculed by people and loathed by the multitude. But that which is spoken by the Tathāgata—teaching the Dharma and teaching its meaning—brings joy to those who hear it; it removes sorrow, feverish affliction, and brings about the eternal absence of suffering and distress. One constantly attains tranquility, and the mind becomes serene. Therefore it is said: "Teaching the Dharma and teaching its meaning, the awakened one attains eternal peace."
The courageous and steadfast establish themselves in single-mindedness; Having gone forth, they extinguish [defilements] day and night.
The devas constantly provide protection, And they are praised and prophesied by the Buddha.

Regarding "the courageous and steadfast establish themselves in single-mindedness": that practitioner maintains a concentrated mind in single-mindedness, free from other thoughts. Endowed with all virtues, their resolve cannot be broken. For one who enters meditative absorption, whatever they aspire to will surely bear fruit. Therefore it is said: "The courageous and steadfast establish themselves in single-mindedness."

Regarding "the renunciant extinguishes day and night": what is called renunciation does not merely consist of abandoning wife and children and departing from the five desires; rather, it involves seeking liberation from the realm of desire to cultivate the paths of the higher realms. In the first dhyāna, one brings to rest the activities that arise and cease. Therefore, it is said: "The renunciant extinguishes day and night."

Regarding "the devas constantly guard him": when a person enters meditative concentration, the devas guard, serve, and pay homage to them, desiring to increase their merit; therefore it is said, "the devas constantly guard him."

Regarding those who are praised and prophesied by the Buddha: from this world up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, he extols those who have established the faculties; the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have swiftly obtained excellent benefit, as the Tathāgata, being present, extensively expounds the flavor of the Dharma. The number of sentient beings delivered is beyond measure or limit; therefore it is said, "they are praised and prophesied by the Buddha."
Among gods and humans, he praises and proclaims the Perfectly Enlightened One;
he swiftly attains self-awakening and, at last, leaves behind the body born of a womb.

Regarding "among gods and humans, he praises and proclaims the Perfectly Enlightened One": the gods and people of the world constantly chant the virtues of the Buddha, each offering a virtuous mind until the attainment of Buddhahood, never departing from it. Therefore it is said: "Among gods and humans, he praises and proclaims the Perfectly Enlightened One."

Those who quickly attained realization and awakened for themselves marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming, "The merit of the Tathāgata is most marvelous and extraordinary! We all thought the Tathāgata was sitting right here; how could we have imagined that the Tathāgata travels through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worlds, teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever becoming weary?"
Therefore it is said: "One swiftly attains and awakens for oneself.
Regarding the final body born from a womb: when the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa* after receiving his last physical form, he sighed and spoke to Ānanda, saying:
"This body of the Tathāgata shall not undergo further birth; it is unconditioned, eternally quiescent, and shall no longer arise or cease."
Ānanda, you should know this!
I have observed the regions of the world and the space above; there is no further rebirth for me, for my destiny as a being has reached its end. Ānanda!
"I am no longer defiled by the mundane; amidst the turbulence of the world, I shall not return again.
Therefore it is said: "This is the final body emerging from the womb.
All those who were called Buddhas of the past, as well as those yet to come,"
The Present Perfectly Enlightened One removes the many sorrows of the multitude.
As stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*: Once, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is truly a great suffering when people of the world gather together yet do not show one another respect!
I constantly harbor this thought:"
"Are there perhaps among the world’s śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas anyone superior to me, whom I should serve, support, and pay homage to?
Thus, I have observed whether among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas there is anyone worthy of veneration.
At that time, Bhikṣus, I further thought to myself:

"In the past, when I attained Buddhahood, it was by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Now, I serve and make offerings to them as I would to honored elders. All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, also attained supreme perfect enlightenment through these dharmas. All the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the future, shall likewise attain the Way by relying on these dharmas. I, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, have also attained the fruit of the Way by relying on these dharmas; I now personally contemplate and discern these dharmas."
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas of the past, those yet to come, and the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the present, have largely removed the sorrows of the multitude.
All together they revere the Dharma—those who have revered it, those who do so now, and those who shall henceforth revere it;
this is called the essential core of the Buddha's teaching."
Desiring to inspire reverence for the Three Times, he spoke this verse:
"If you wish to seek what is essential for yourself, Making right conduct your foremost priority,
Reverently honor the True Dharma And keep the Buddha’s exhortations in mind."

"If one wishes to seek the essential for oneself, rectifying the body is foremost": when a person desires to achieve the Way, they must necessarily seek the essential for themselves; they advance toward the Way and show reverence for all dharmas, recollecting the instructions and admonitions spoken by the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, as if they were present before them, without any loss or omission. Therefore it is said: "If one wishes to seek the essential for oneself, rectifying the body is foremost; one should revere the True Dharma and mindfully recollect the Buddha’s instructions."
*Udānavarga*, Scroll Twenty; *Udānavarga*, Scroll Twenty-One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Those who do not believe in the Tathāgata— such beings as these—
shall fall into the path of calamity, like merchants who encounter rākṣasas.
