Regarding those who do not believe in the Buddha: in Jambudvīpa there were many merchants who, having joined together in a caravan, entered the sea to gather treasures. They encountered a swirling eddy and a fierce wind that wrecked their great ship; furthermore, other people on a dilapidated vessel were driven by the wind and cast adrift, falling into the realm of the rākṣasīs.
A great multitude of rākṣasīs, with handsome features and their bodies adorned with various precious jewels, came forward to welcome the merchants:
"Welcome, sirs! This place abounds in wealth and many treasures;

take as much as you desire of priceless pearls and miscellaneous gems according to your pleasure, for there is no one here to guard them. Since we have no husbands and you have no wives or concubines, you may stay here and enjoy yourselves together. Later, when a favorable wind arises and you find good companions, it will not be far to return home."
Furthermore, sirs, you should know this!
The waves of the ocean ebb and flow day and night without a fixed direction. If you see a path on the left, be careful not to follow it; even if you see such a path in a dream, do not speak of it.
At that time, there was among the merchants one who was wise and discerning, and he thought to himself:
"The heterodox teachings spoken by these women are not for naught; there must surely be a karmic connection here."

He immediately devised a deceptive stratagem and secretly plotted an intrigue; toward evening, he lay down with the woman to engage in intimacy. Waiting until she had fallen asleep, he rose stealthily and proceeded along a heterodox path for several li. Along the way, he heard tens of millions of people within a city crying out in lamentation, some calling for their parents, brothers, sisters, wives, or children, saying: "Why have you abandoned the land of Jambudvīpa to meet your end here?"

Upon hearing this, the merchant’s hair stood on end; he restrained his mind and proceeded directly toward the city. He surveyed it from all sides and saw that the city was enclosed by walls of cast iron, with no gates or entrances for coming and going. Not far from the city stood a *śirīṣa* tree, both tall and vast in size.
He immediately went to climb the tree and saw tens of millions of people inside the city weeping and wailing;
from afar, he asked the people in the city, "Why are you crying out for your parents and brothers?"

The people within the city replied, "We entered the sea to gather precious treasures, but were driven astray by the winds and deceived by rākṣasīs; we have fallen into this realm of ghosts and are confined within this prison-city."
Previously there were five hundred people who were gradually taken and killed; now only two hundred and fifty remain.
Do not call this woman a human being; she is merely a rākṣasī demon!
Having heard this, the man immediately descended from the tree and went to her village, where he secretly approached the woman as she lay down.
At dawn the following morning, he said to his companions:
"I have a secret matter I wish to discuss with you; let us each go to a secluded place, and take care not to bring your wives along."
The people responded in unison and each went to a secluded place, where they immediately said:
"Do you all know? Last night, this thought suddenly arose within me:"
"Why do these women so earnestly say, 'Do not take the path on the left'?
Seeing the women asleep, he rose furtively to observe; he beheld a great iron city where several hundred people were confined, wailing and crying out in distress.

I climbed to the top of the tree and asked from afar about the cause of this matter. The people replied to me: "Our ship was wrecked by a makara fish; driven by fierce winds and waves, we have fallen into this realm of ghosts and are confined within an iron city several tens of zhang high. We urge you to return home and seek skillful means."
"What do you intend to do today, sirs? The people replied,
"Why did you not ask that man again last night whether there might be some expedient means by which we and our bodies could return home in safety?"
The man replied, "I retired last night without asking about this matter; I shall rise secretly this evening and go to inquire further.
Having said these words, they each returned to their respective places.
When that wise man had finished his union with the woman at dusk, he rose furtively while she slept and went up into the tree.
He asked the people of the city, "Is there any expedient means by which you all, as well as myself, might return to the land of Jambudvīpa?"

The people within the city replied, "Just now we conceived the thought of returning to Jambudvīpa, but this iron city immediately became many layers thick and indestructible; those who die here day by day have no way to escape.
Only you, an outsider, possess some skillful means by which we may be delivered and return to our own land."

On the morning of the fifteenth day, there was a horse-king who, having eaten naturally grown non-glutinous rice from Uttarakuru, came to this realm of hungry ghosts and stayed atop a high mountain peak, calling out three times:
"Who wishes to return to Jambudvīpa?"
“If you all hear the voice of the Horse-King, go forth to pay him homage and request to return to your own land.
Having heard these words, the man immediately returned to his companions and related the situation in detail.
The crowd replied, “Should we go now?”
The wise man replied, "Fifteen days must pass before the Horse King arrives; only then may you depart.
Before many days had elapsed, the Horse King arrived at the summit of a high mountain and called out three times:
"Who wishes to return to Jambudvīpa?
The sound echoed far and wide.
Upon hearing it, the merchants all went to where the horse-king was and addressed him, saying:
"We all wish to return to our own native lands; we pray that you will take us in so that we may return to the state of non-action.

The Horse King replied, "You must listen with single-minded attention to what I say. If you each desire to go home and return to your native lands, you shall attain it provided your minds are focused and upright; if your minds are not focused and upright, you shall not attain it."
"These women, each cradling a son or daughter, are pursuing you from behind, wailing and crying out.
Those among them who harbor feelings of longing and attachment would not be able to leave even if you were upon their own backs;
yet if you can cast aside affection and love, with a right mind and single intent free from all clinging, and grasp a single hair of mine with a sincere heart, you shall be able to return home."
When the women arrived as they had been told, each said to her husband:
"Truly, you may abandon my lowly body, but why must you forsake our children?"
First, he instructed his children to go and embrace their father’s neck, weeping and crying out:
"Why do you abandon us? Where do you wish to go?
Those whose hearts were bound by attachment were unable to return; only the one of great wisdom, Siṃha, returned in safety.
Therefore it is said: Those beings who do not believe in the Buddha will surely enter upon a path of calamity, like merchants who encounter a rākṣasa.
Those beings who have faith in the Buddha will return safely and in peace, all having been delivered by the Horse-King.
Only Sīha alone returned in safety; the others, due to their hearts of longing and attachment, all fell into calamity.
At that time, the rākṣasī took her son and daughter and went in pursuit of the merchant Sīha, visiting every place he might be. She announced to the various villages:
"Sīha is my husband; we together begot this son and daughter, yet he has abandoned me and fled, and I know not where he has gone."
Having heard this, the people asked Siṃha,
"Observing the nature, appearance, and features of your wife— she is the most exquisite among women— and considering your children who are so pitiable, why have you abandoned them?"
The Lion replied, "This too is not a human, but a rākṣasa demon.

He dwells on an island in the sea and slaughters and devours merchants beyond counting; my companions, numbering several hundred, are confined within an iron city, and I alone have fortunately escaped."
"Now this female ghost is again pursuing me from behind; she intends to harm me, and I fear I shall not escape her.
Having said these words, he continued forward and returned to his own country, while the ghost also followed him to that land.
The ogress went to inform the king, saying:

"I have been married to the lion, and after giving birth to these children, I hoped to receive their strength; I did not expect to be abandoned forever today. If the lion has no use for my person, he should at least take the children. I am still young; could I not find another husband?"
The king summoned Siṃha and questioned him regarding the facts:
"Your wife is young and of beautiful countenance; the man is extraordinary and possesses the marks of a gentleman. Why did you abandon her and refuse to accept her?"
The Lion addressed the King, saying:

"These are not human forms; they are rākṣasa demons who devour men. They have manifested as a man and a woman to pursue me from behind, hoping that my mind would incline toward them so that they might seize and kill me."
"Previously, I led five hundred merchants into the sea to gather treasures, but they were all devoured by rākṣasas; I alone was spared and reached safety.
Now I am being pursued once more—what do you think will happen?"
The king said to the lion,
"Even if you do not need it yourself, you may take it and give it to me. The lion replied:
"This is truly no human, but a rākṣasa demon; having committed such transgressions, do not harbor resentment toward him later.
The Lion King further addressed his ministers:
"When this ghost arrives here, he will surely cause harm to the King."
"Now that you do not believe me and wish to enter the inner palace, before long both the King and the women of the harem shall be utterly consumed by ashes.
The King, filled with further rage, said to Siṃhaka:
"The beauty of this woman is like that of a celestial jade maiden; for what reason do you call her a rākṣasī demon?"
"Quickly go outside and observe for yourself.
The king took the female spirit into the inner palace, secured the gates and chambers, and remained there for one night.
On the following day at mealtime, the palace gates did not open; the ministers then deliberated together:
"The King has recently taken a wife; because his mind is preoccupied with sensual pleasure, the gate remains closed.
Siṃha said, "Let us come and discuss this further."
"The King, the Queen, and all the court ladies must have been devoured by rākṣasas;

that is why the gate remains closed. He then set up a high ladder, climbed over the wall, and entered the inner palace. He saw the skeletal remains of the dead filling several rooms, and he also saw pits where fresh soil had been excavated.

The ministers asked Siṃhala, "The King has now died and the inner palace is in ruin; the bones have formed a heap that cannot be distinguished. How shall we perform the funeral rites for the King's body?"
The Lion replied, “Gather all the bones together in one place and cremate them; let it be said only that the King has been buried, while the rest shall not be included in this rite.
Once the funeral rites were completed, the ministers rebuked the Lion, saying:
"Sitting upright before you is a rākṣasa who has killed the king, caused the loss of the kingdom, and brought about the destruction of the palace. What do you intend to do now?

The Lion replied, "I previously made a covenant with him, saying: 'This is not a human being, but a rākṣasa; since he is fully possessed of transgressions and faults, do not harbor resentment toward me later.'"
"Why do you all continue to reproach me?
The ministers and the people came forward and said to Siṃha, "The King has now passed away and there is no heir.
We pray only that Siṃha will ascend the throne to govern the people so that they may forever enjoy peace and security, providing us ministers with a sovereign to revere."
The Lion declared: "If you wish to appoint me as your king, you must follow my instructions; should you not comply with my instructions, you shall all be devoured by rākṣasas."
The people, though of diverse appearances, responded with one voice, all praising it as excellent, and immediately followed the King’s instructions.
The King told his ministers:
"Those rākṣasa women sleep at specific times; we must assemble our troops, board our ships, and enter the sea to launch an attack."

He immediately went to attack and kill the rākṣasas—men, women, and children of all ages—in numbers beyond reckoning, leaving none remaining. He then went to destroy the iron city and brought forth the people from within it; because of their settlement there, the place became flourishing, wealthy, and naturally prosperous, with marvelous and extraordinary objects in immeasurable abundance.
For this reason, that city was named Siṃhala (Lion).
Those Rākṣasa demons who were cast out and did not fall within the regular order were moved to the west of the mountain.

According to the customary law of the people on the eastern edge of the Cakravāḍa mountains, if there is even a single person who does not serve the Buddha, they shall be sent to the west of the mountain to be delivered to the demons to devour them.
From that time forth, the Buddha-dharma flourished and countless beings attained the Way.
Therefore it is said: "All those who have faith in the Buddha—beings such as these—return safely to their destination, all having been delivered by the Horse King."

Furthermore, it is the constant custom of that country that when a king fathers sons—whether ten, a hundred, or even countless in number—they all leave the household life to practice the Way. They study and recite the Buddhist scriptures, fully mastering the Three Piṭakas. Only after they have returned from their religious life and ascended to the throne do they rule. If one is不通 (unproficient) in the Sanskrit language and fails to master the scriptures, he shall not be permitted to ascend the throne.
Because he dwelt on an outer island, it was called the Kingdom of Siṃhaladvīpa.
The Tathāgata, peerless and unequaled, contemplated the two types of meditative practice;
having skillfully observed the two forms of seclusion, he dispelled darkness and transcended to the state of a divine sage.

The Tathāgata is peerless: the Tathāgata abides in the world with immeasurable divine virtue; his conduct transcends space and his transformations are limitless. He universally guides sentient beings, leading them to the light of wisdom; through the four immeasurables he nurtures all, and those who behold him attain liberation. Therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata is peerless; contemplating the two types of observation and skillfully discerning the two forms of tranquility, he dispels darkness and transcends the realm of immortals."

Well-attained and having attained mastery, with craving exhausted and nothing accumulated, liberated and free from outflows, he bestows grace upon gods and men. Regarding "well-attained and having attained mastery":

sentient beings dwell amidst the flames of suffering, transmigrating through the five destinies and the surging waves of the seven fetters. When they seek the Path, they do not know by which way they may reach it.

Therefore, the Tathāgata does not abandon his heart of great vows, but rescues those in suffering and hardship, universally leading all classes of sentient beings to point toward the Hall of Sovereignty; for this reason, it is said that he has "skillfully attained sovereignty."

Regarding "the exhaustion of craving and the absence of accumulation": having attained the four fearlessnesses, one eternally exhausts craving; therefore it is said, "the exhaustion of craving and the absence of accumulation. Regarding "the liberated mind free from outflows":

the mind attains eternal liberation without any obstruction, and further acquires the state of being free from outflows, eternally removing all defilements; therefore it is said, "the liberated mind free from outflows."

One who bestows grace upon gods and humans is one toward whom all sentient beings come to turn for refuge and look up in devotion. Therefore, the Sage responds to the times and adapts his transformation to rescue and provide for them without lack; hence it is said, "one who bestows grace upon gods and humans."
Like a person standing on a mountain peak, Beholding the villages of men from all sides;
To examine the Dharma thus is like ascending a tower to view a garden.
The person’s anxieties are removed and sorrowless; It causes one to know the destinies of birth and death.

It is like a person standing on a mountain peak who sees villages all around; just as a person with sight perceives a village in its entirety—those walking and those sitting, those entering and exiting, coming and going, weeping, singing and dancing, and laughing—all of these are clearly observed.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise: standing upon the summit of the mountain of wisdom, he observes the sentient beings of the five destinies—whether they be clever or foolish, those who have attained or those who have not—and is able to discern them all and go forth to transform them.
Therefore it is said: "It is as if a person standing on a mountain peak sees all the villages and hamlets.

To examine the Dharma in this way is like ascending a tower to view a garden. With the divine eye, the Tathāgata sees everything everywhere; from atop his high tower, he discerns each individual case—those who are difficult to deliver and those who are easy to deliver. He speaks with those with whom he may speak, and remains silent toward those with whom he may not. According to the inclinations of those before him, he brings them to the realization of the Way. Therefore it is said: "To examine the Dharma in this way is like ascending a tower to view a garden."

"Human sorrow is removed and sorrowlessness attained, causing one to know the destination of birth and death. This means that the Tathāgata observes those with sorrow and those without sorrow, those with little wisdom and those with great wisdom, discerning them all. He instructs and guides sentient beings so that they may know the destination of birth and death; therefore it is said: "Human sorrow is removed and sorrowlessness attained, causing one to know the destination of birth and death. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, "The Chapter on the Tathāgata."
One who hears well and practices well, who delights in solitude and whose conduct is not perverse, dwells in peace like a śramaṇa.
One who hears well and practices well—the learned scholar praised by others as "Excellent! Excellent!"—is truly such a one.
When a person has learning, their conduct will necessarily be good; therefore it is said: "One who values learning and delights in practice.

One who values and delights in seclusion and tranquility seeks deliverance from the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; finding no pleasure in clamor and being unbound by attachments, their aspiration is directed toward seclusion and tranquility. Therefore it is said: "One who values and delights in seclusion and tranquility."

"Whose conduct is not perverse" means that the actions of body, speech, and mind always accord with correct principle and never go astray; it is most excellent and most sublime, with nothing superior to it. Therefore it is said: "whose conduct is not perverse."

One who is "peaceful like a śramaṇa" follows the conduct of a śramaṇa and does not oppose the conduct of a śramaṇa; because they act and cultivate themselves exactly as one should, it is therefore said that they are "peaceful like a śramaṇa."
The fool does not perceive it, yet delights in practicing the way of immortality;
the one who well understands the Dharma knows that illness is like the plantain tree.

The fool does not perceive it—this "delight in practicing the way of immortality" means that the fool’s habitual practice is always a base conduct; he cannot distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, nor does he perceive whether things are good or foul. He does not reckon with the laws of impermanence and change, but instead provides for his own body, thinking it will last for a thousand years without end, and maintains material things as permanent and enduring, believing they will never diminish. Therefore it is said: "The fool does not perceive it, yet delights in practicing the way of immortality."

Regarding the statement, "One who well understands and knows the Dharma is like a plantain tree when ill": although such a person has a thorough understanding of the Dharma, it passes through their ears as if by rote; just as a plantain tree sheds its leaves when struck by the wind, the patient is suddenly brought to the brink of collapse when further afflicted by a toxic decoction. Therefore it is said: "One who well understands and knows the Dharma is like a plantain tree when ill."
"Just as when a house is tightly roofed, it is dark and nothing can be seen;
though there be many wondrous colors, one with eyes cannot perceive their brightness.

Regarding "just as when a house is tightly roofed, it is dark and nothing can be seen": it is like constructing a dwelling and closing off the windows and doors so that both inside and out are sealed tight and shrouded in darkness such that no light is seen. Therefore it is said: "Just as when a house is tightly roofed, it is dark and nothing can be seen."

"Though there be many wondrous forms, one with eyes may not see the light. This means that although within that house there may be many wondrous forms arranged in beautiful display, a person with eyes who enters therein will never see those forms. Therefore it is said: "Though there be many wondrous forms, one with eyes may not see the light."
Suppose there is a certain person who is wise, erudite, and of broad learning;
yet without hearing, they do not know wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas.

Suppose there is another person who is wise, erudite, and of broad learning—whether among the world’s laymen (*upāsaka*), laywomen (*upāsikā*), kṣatriyas, elders, householders, or commoners—who possesses a clear and brilliant mind and wisdom. If such a person has not previously heard [the teachings], they will know wholesome and unwholesome dharmas. However, even one of supreme wisdom, if they have not previously heard the Dharma, will have no means of discerning them. Therefore it is said: "Without hearing, one does not know wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas."
"Just as a person holding a candle sees all forms and appearances, having heard [the teaching], one is able to fully know the destinations of both good and evil.

Regarding "just as a person holding a candle sees all forms and appearances": it is like a person of wisdom and insight who, holding a bright lamp in hand, is able to discern all beautiful and ugly forms. Therefore it is said: "Just as a person holding a candle sees all forms and appearances."

"Having heard, one is able to fully know the destinations of good and evil": this means that when a practitioner hears the Dharma, they immediately understand all dharmas—both good and evil, proximate and remote, determinate and indeterminate—and can fully comprehend them. Therefore it is said: "Having heard, one is able to fully know the destinations of good and evil."

Though one may be called "learned," if one's precepts are not complete, one will be censured by the Dharma and Vinaya, and what one has heard will then be deficient. Regarding "though one may be called learned, if one's precepts are not complete":

although one possesses extensive learning and broad wisdom and is skilled in discerning the Dharma, if one is not earnest regarding the precepts, one will commit transgressions upon contact with them and thus fail to possess the full Vinaya. For this reason it is said: "Though one may be called learned, if one's precepts are not complete."

Regarding "being censured by the law and having deficiencies in learning": when those who uphold the precepts raise a formal objection according to the Dharma, it means this person has violated the Vinaya and does not practice the True Dharma; being reviled by others, they must perform acts of shame and remorse. Therefore it is said: "being censured by the law and having deficiencies in learning."
"Though the practitioner has heard little, If they are fully complete in the prohibitions and precepts, They are praised by the Dharma and Vinaya; Yet in their learning, there is still deficiency.

Regarding "though the practitioner has heard little, they are fully complete in the prohibitions and precepts": this means that while their observance of the precepts is perfect and without flaw, they have not extensively studied or practiced; therefore it is said, "though the practitioner has heard little, they are fully complete in the prohibitions and precepts."

Regarding the phrase "praised for his adherence to the law and discipline, yet deficient in learning": when a person who maintains the precepts is praised by others, saying, "In such-and-such a village, there is a person who maintains the precepts, worthy of respect and honor; he practices the Path with diligence day and night without ceasing," yet he does not study extensively, nor does he master the ancients or understand the present, and is thus deficient in learning—it is for this reason it is said that he is "praised for his adherence to the law and discipline, yet deficient in learning."
Though one has heard much, if one’s observance of the precepts is incomplete, both are subject to reproach and that which was wished for is lost.

As for one who, though having heard much, is incomplete in observing the precepts: since they have heard little themselves and their discipline is not complete, they are ridiculed by the multitude. When a person cultivates the human foundation, they must perfect every practice; how can such a person utterly uproot all roots of goodness?
Some may give rise to thoughts of compassion for such a person, considering that after death they will suffer immeasurable affliction throughout the long night.
Therefore it is said: "Though one has heard much, if one's observance of the precepts is incomplete, both shall be rebuked and what was desired will be lost."
One whose wisdom is vast is called "widely learned"; one who maintains the precepts in their entirety is likewise complete.
Both attain renown, and all that they wish for is fully obtained.

When one is both widely learned and fully endowed with the precepts, refraining from all evils, they are seen by gods, humans, nāgas, ghosts and spirits, asuras, gandharvas, and mahoragas, all of whom pay them respect, serve them, and honor them. Therefore it is said: "One whose wisdom is vast is called 'widely learned'; one who maintains the precepts in their entirety is likewise complete. Both attain renown, and all that they wish for is fully obtained."
One who is learned can uphold the Dharma; with wisdom, their mind is always settled.
Like that Jambu-river gold, who could say it has any flaw? Regarding "one who is learned can uphold the Dharma":

one contemplates the True Dharma without deficiency or omission. One can analyze the meaning of a single phrase and expound upon it infinitely, yet again be able to summarize it back down to a single phrase. Therefore, it is said: "one who is learned can uphold the Dharma."

"One whose wisdom is always settled in mind" refers to one who, through the clarity of discerning wisdom, seeks to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and reach the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, without any further effort, they accomplish the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the noble ones; their minds are perpetually tranquil in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and free from distracted thoughts. Therefore, it is said: "One whose wisdom is always settled in mind."

Just as that Jambū-river gold, compared to other inferior and base metals which are full of flaws, this Jambū-river gold has no flaws within or without, nor does it have any dust or grime; therefore it is said, "like Jambū-river gold."

Who can speak of faults? It is like a person whose conduct is pure, who is transparent both internally and externally, whose actions are without blemish or flaw, and who has committed no transgression; such that no one is able to censure that practitioner. Therefore it is said: "Who can speak of faults?"
Those who praise their own physical form, And those who extol their reputation and virtue,
All these are said to be driven by desire, Yet they themselves do not realize it.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, must first accomplish two tasks:
First, the eye perceives forms; second, the ear perceives sounds.
The ignorant hear this erroneously: first, they claim that the Tathāgata is attached to forms; second, they claim that the Tathāgata craves sounds.
"The voice of the Tathāgata is like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
The Buddha said: "It is not so."
What I have taught differs; the meaning is not as you think.
The wise analyze and understand the meaning of the Tathāgata:

having accumulated practices for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the Tathāgata first purified his eyes and ears and their respective objects, and only thereafter cultivated the remaining practices.
Therefore it is said: "Those who praise their own physical form, or extol their reputation and virtues—all these are called craving, yet they themselves do not realize it."
Internally there was no self-awareness, and externally there was nothing seen;
seeing no fruit within, he followed the sound.
Formerly, King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army and went out from the city to wander during the night, at an inauspicious hour.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Rāvaṇabhadra, who, in a state of profound stillness and seclusion, chanted with such a clear and penetrating voice that none among the fourfold army failed to hear it.
At that time, King Prasenajit, amidst that assembly, had this thought:
"If tomorrow I see this bhikṣu who recites these verses, I shall grant him three hundred thousand pieces of gold."
The king again drew closer and thought to himself:
"The sound seems to be near, yet I do not see [the person].
As he stepped forward further, he saw that the man's body was inside a casket; he then bestowed upon him three pearl shells. Therefore, it is said:
"If one knows [the truth] within but sees nothing without, yet perceives the fruit within,
one follows the sound and goes.
If one does not know within but sees something without, and both fruits are accomplished, one follows the sound and goes."
"Internally there is that which is known; externally there is that which is seen. He possesses brilliant wisdom and does not follow after sounds.
Then King Prasenajit came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, "Where is the practitioner who was just now chanting?"
"I wish to behold it.
The Buddha said to the king:
"If you wish to see it, do not give rise to indolence or arrogance."
The Buddha immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the bhikṣu.
Upon seeing him, the king felt a sense of remorse and regret for the extreme extravagance he had permitted that night; he promptly gave him three pearl shells, yet his mind still desired to repent.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What virtues did this bhikṣu practice in the past to obtain such a wondrous voice?
And what deeds did he perform to receive such a small body?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, using his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), observed the future, the past, and the present, and then addressed the king:

“In times long past, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the people treated one another with mutual respect, humility, and service. At that time, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa; having completed his worldly travels, transformations, and instructions, he entered parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the king, his ministers, and the people conceived a heart of longing and reverence, and immediately erected a stūpa that was both high and wide.
That man was also there by their side at the time, and he exclaimed:
"Why is this stūpa being made so high and wide?"
That very night, he hung a single bell upon the mast of the stupa and immediately made this vow:

"In whatever place I may be born in future lives, may my voice be clear and penetrating, reaching up to the Brahma-heaven; may I encounter that Sage and exhaust all outflows, and among his disciples, may my voice be clear and penetrating."
"Because in the past he spoke with disdain regarding the vastness of the temple, as a result of this karma he received an extremely small body;
yet because he hung bells upon the temple, through the fruit of this merit he has attained such a wondrous voice."
"One who has internal knowledge observes their own body internally and finds that there is nothing therein; whatever is pleasant, they are able to discern it all.
One who knows internally knows the six internal sense bases."
Therefore it is said: "One knows this within oneself.

As for that which is seen externally, one contemplates the external body by analyzing each part individually; even if seeing it being flayed, cut, or pierced, there is no sensation, for one understands it to be empty and deceptive.

Furthermore, as for the statement that there is something seen externally, it refers to seeing the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) externally. Therefore, it is said that there is something seen externally.

As for those who possess clear wisdom, they discern the internal and external body, contemplating each part with thorough investigation and without obstruction. They understand all that exists; yet when observing it with wisdom, they see that nothing at all exists. Therefore, it is said that they possess clear wisdom.

Regarding "not following after sounds": the vocal sounds of others are the primary source that disturbs one's wholesome thoughts. For one who has entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), external sounds do not enter and internal disturbances do not arise; they understand those sounds to be equal to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore it is said: "Do not follow after sounds.
The meaning of each of these four verses is as follows:
The auditory consciousness hears much; The visual consciousness sees much.
What is heard and seen is not firmly established; matters are analyzed according to their principles. Regarding the ear-consciousness that hears much:

one may hear Buddhist scriptures, or the heterodox teachings of outsiders, songs, and poetic recitations; what is pleasing is accepted, while what is disliked is rejected. Therefore it is said, "the ear-consciousness hears much."

Regarding "eye-consciousness sees much": eye-consciousness indeed sees much—whether it be the beautiful or the ugly, whether it be pleasant forms or unpleasant forms. Therefore, it is said that "eye-consciousness sees much."

Regarding the statement that "hearing and seeing are not firm, for matters are analyzed according to their meaning": if one is able to fully discern what is seen, heard, thought, and known—stating "this is seen" when it is seen and "this is heard" when it is heard—therefore it is said: "hearing and seeing are not firm, for matters are analyzed according to their meaning."
"Skillful speech by one firm in wisdom is a joy; knowing through hearing and having a concentrated mind is a joy.
But for those who do not employ knowledge and concentration, they quickly practice heedlessness.

Regarding "skillful speech by one firm in wisdom is a joy": such a person reflects well and their speech is not confused. Having received and retained [the teaching] without loss, they act accordingly. Therefore it is said: "Skillful speech by one firm in wisdom is a joy."

Regarding the statement, "The joy of knowing through hearing and concentration arises from hearing": it is because one first attains concentration by means of hearing that, once concentration is attained, there is no obstruction in whatever one directs the mind toward; therefore it is said, "The joy of knowing through hearing and concentration."

Those who do not employ the concentration of knowledge and instead swiftly practice heedlessness—such heedless persons are able to commit further evil, disregarding future conditions and failing to consider the next world. It is like throwing grain seeds into a fire while hoping for stalks and ears; such a thing will ultimately never happen.
It is like trying to stop the current of a river by blocking it with a small clod of earth; such a thing can never be achieved.
When a person who is negligent in mind conducts themselves with violence and cruelty, I do not see how they could ever seek even a hair’s breadth of goodness.

Therefore it is said: "He who does not employ knowledge and concentration, but swiftly practices heedlessness, though he delights in the Dharma as a noble one, his actions will not correspond to his speech.
Only by means of patience, reflection, and concentration can the mind become firm through what is heard."

Those who are noble and holy find delight in the Dharma; they take pleasure in that which accords with the Dharma of the noble and holy. From the very beginning until the end, they never abandon it, but constantly practice and study it without ever becoming weary or satisfied. All of this has been expounded by the Buddhas and the noble ones; therefore, it is said: "The noble and holy find delight in the Dharma."

Regarding "conduct that accords with speech": one’s actions accord with the prohibitive precepts without any transgression or failure; therefore it is said, "conduct that accords with speech. Regarding "attaining concentration through patient reflection":

one receives the teacher’s instructions and practices them with single-minded devotion, giving rise to no feelings of resentment or jealousy toward others. Hearing their virtuous words, one accepts them with a willing heart, reciting and practicing them day and night without departing from a concentrated mind; therefore it is said, "attaining concentration through patient reflection."

Regarding "the intent of what is heard becomes firm": the Dharma taught by the Buddha, from beginning to end, with its superior, middling, and inferior meanings, is recited throughout the day without ever being forgotten. For this reason it is said, "the intent of what is heard becomes firm. The twenty-third chapter, "The Chapter on Hearing," is concluded.
One should learn well-spoken words; as for the śramaṇa’s sitting and rising, he finds delight in a single seat, seeking to bring the mind to rest.

Regarding "one should learn well-spoken words": day and night one should recite and practice well-spoken and excellent words, gathering the various subtle essentials for transcending the world. Therefore it is said: "One should learn well-spoken words."
Regarding the sitting and rising of a śramaṇa, a bhikṣu should constantly maintain this thought:

"Distinguishing between superior and inferior seats, I shall not encroach upon another's seat; 'this is a seat for eating,' 'this is a seat for walking meditation,' 'I shall sit here,' or 'I shall leave this.'"
Therefore it is said: "The śramaṇa sits and rises.

That which one delights in while seated is to concentrate the single mind in pursuit of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), to discern all mental states, and to master the sense faculties. One who is distracted in mind while seated does not truly sit; only when the mind does not wander outward can one transcend and pass beyond the realm of Māra.
Therefore it is said: "The joy found in a single sitting.

Those who seek to still the mind harbor mental consciousness; those who do not restrain their minds possess manifold discursive thoughts. If they again receive a physical form and fall into the three evil realms—among hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—they will not encounter the Three Jewels or the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, nor meet pure practitioners of the holy life. Lacking a sense of shame, they shall pass from one birth to hundreds of thousands of births.
One who seeks to still the mind is free from birth and death; therefore it is said: "Seeking to still the mind."
Sitting alone and lying down alone, walking solitary without companion, one should subdue oneself and find joy only in the mountain forests. Regarding "sitting alone and lying down alone":
this refers to subduing the blazing fires of birth and death within and without; yet, even if one sits or lies alone, if the mind is not settled, it does not constitute true sitting or lying.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the hardships of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and constantly fix the mind so that it does not become distracted.
Therefore, it is said: "Sitting alone and reclining alone. As for "walking alone without a companion":

whether among a crowd or in the wilderness, the mind is always fixed; whether walking or sitting, the mind does not wander. Like that practitioner who begs for food at the proper time, he reflects inwardly on the origin of the food; he receives alms while seeking to repay the kindness of the donor, knowing contentment and moderation. Furthermore, he should recollect the Buddha’s physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and merits, maintaining his resolve with patience so that it does not scatter.
One who possesses such a mind may enter a village to seek the salvation of sentient beings; without giving rise to distracted thoughts, they remain no different from those in the mountain forests.
Therefore it is said: "Walking alone without a companion."

"One who should subdue themselves" means they constantly quiet their own minds so that they do not wander or scatter, and are always able to examine all internal and external things. Because they are able to subdue themselves, they are served and provided for by devas and people of the world; the eight classes of spirits and deities protect them at all times, and they are praised and extolled by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Therefore it is said: "One should subdue oneself.

Those who find solitary joy in the mountain forests maintain their minds with single-minded focus and constantly delight in seclusion; though they enter among the great assembly, their minds remain as empty as space. Even amidst thunder from heaven or earthquakes on earth, their minds are not disturbed. Only then do they accord with the sacred scriptures of the Tathāgata.
Therefore it is said: "To find joy alone in the mountain forests;
though a thousand times a thousand may be one's enemies, a single man may conquer them, yet nothing is equal to subduing oneself—the victory supreme among all battles."

As for one man who conquers a thousand enemies: there may be sentient beings who conquer a thousand by themselves, yet if they do not subdue themselves, this is not true victory; it is merely a downfall that fails to reach the ultimate goal.

One who is able to restrain the mind within and subdue it without, thereby transcending all stages to reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), surpasses all enemies and enmities without fear or dread—this is called "victory. One who can extinguish the roots of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the triple world so that they are forever exhausted without remainder is called a "valiant man" (*dhīra*); having already extinguished the roots of the fetters of the triple world without remainder, one no longer creates new karma.
There may be sentient beings who surpass a thousand people, or even ten thousand people, yet they are not considered heroic men.
Why is this? Because they still dwell within birth and death and are not far from the eight difficulties.
Therefore it is said: "To defeat a thousand men a thousand times, and for one man to conquer them all, is not as good as conquering oneself; this is the victory in battle.
To conquer oneself is supreme. Just like those sentient beings, the practitioner who has subdued himself is fully endowed with all virtues.

Regarding "To conquer oneself is supreme": When a person lives in the world, if they can subdue themselves so that their spirit is not deluded, they will further be honored by devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kinnaras. Even though the celestial Māra Pāpīyān rules over the six heavens, he cannot find an opportunity against them. Therefore it is said: "To conquer oneself is supreme."

"Those sentient beings" refers to those practitioners who, having themselves aspired to study, are further able to cause others to practice accordingly. When defilements do not arise within their minds and external dust does not enter, they then accord with the state of pure, untainted non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Therefore, it is said: "those sentient beings."

Among those who have brought themselves under control and are fully endowed with all practices, there are ten designations for people that differ from one another. Some are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*); the categories of self, person, life-span, and those with form are all termed "sentient beings. Such individuals as these, being able to subdue themselves and not giving rise to external thoughts, realize the ultimate truth of the primary principle (*paramārtha*), which is formless and invisible. Those who seek the Way of Non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) should contemplate self-subjugation and not give rise to the eighteen fundamental graspings (*upādāna*). Being without outflows (*anāsrava*) across all realms, they are likewise called "those who have brought themselves under control."

With all faculties complete and merits fully endowed, one practices the Path according to the proper time without missing its season; therefore it is said: "The self-subdued person is one whose various practices are complete."

Neither devas nor gandharvas, neither Māras nor Brahmās, are superior to one who has abandoned all that is excellent—the wise bhikṣu. Regarding "neither devas nor gandharvas, neither Māras nor Brahmās":

there are those among worldly people who sacrifice to various devas seeking blessings and merit; some serve the gandharvas practicing their pure conduct; some serve the Māra-devas hoping to attain noble status; and some serve Brahmā, regarding him as the Way. Those of external paths and heterodox studies conceive of Brahmā in their minds, believing that the root of all sentient beings is born from Brahmā; for these reasons, they serve Brahmā.
The Tathāgata said:
“This is not the true path; it deludes oneself and further leads others onto a deviant course. It is neither firm nor can it be relied upon.”
That which is called the true Path refers to the wise bhikṣu.

He maintains a pure mind that does not leak through the fetters; he preaches the Dharma for others without a sense of self or other; his intention is like space, indestructible; his faculties are sharp and swift, never obstructed; and whatever his mind intends, there is nothing it does not achieve.
Therefore it is said: Neither gods nor gandharvas, neither Māras nor Brahmās, are superior to one who has abandoned all that is excelling—the wise bhikṣu.
First rectify yourself, and only then rectify others; indeed, one who rectifies themselves is called superior.

As for "first rectifying oneself and then rectifying others," it means that when a person cultivates the practice of self-restraint as their primary concern—admonishing themselves by day and walking in meditation by night, striving with diligent and tireless effort throughout the entire day—they can subsequently instruct sentient beings and establish them securely in the Great Way.
As stated in a sutra of the Buddha, the Buddha told Cunda:
"It is as if a person, having themselves sunk into deep mud, wishes to use expedient means to pull out another who is drowning; this is not possible."
It is like a person who, lacking precepts themselves, wishes to instruct others; such a thing is impossible. As explained at length in the Sūtras:

"Just as a vessel that is complete and intact does not leak when filled, so too a person whose spirit is serene and tranquil is capable of receiving the profound Dharma and can also transform and guide all sentient beings. Those who hear the Dharma will have no lack of faith and joy. Therefore it is said: "First rectify oneself, and then rectify others. One who rectifies themselves is called superior.
First rectify yourself, and only then rectify others. One who rectifies themselves does not encroach upon the wise. When a person practices their conduct, they do not let their efforts go to waste;

they bring their learning to completion without shirking toil and hardship. With what they believe to be impartial and non-dual, they apply diligent effort so that their practice is renewed daily. They draw near to those of clear wisdom and do not associate with corrupt friends.

When a person possesses wisdom, it arises entirely from the sagely insight that perfects human intelligence; this cannot be achieved without a teacher. Therefore, it is said: "One does not offend the wise."
One should discipline oneself and practice accordingly, following its teachings and instructions. If one has not been disciplined oneself, how can one instruct others?

Regarding "one should discipline oneself and follow its teachings and instructions": it is like a person who practices and perfects all deeds, adorning themselves with precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom; through mindfulness, concentration, and samādhi, they exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*). Only then are they able to instruct all beings, so that those who hear the Dharma take refuge in it with sincere faith and harbor no doubt.
Therefore it is said: "One should discipline and cultivate oneself, following its instructions.

If one has not been instructed oneself, how can one instruct others? It is like a person who studies without ever having had a good teacher; lacking guidance, they will inevitably encounter obstacles. One who meets a good teacher and is able to discipline and examine themselves will surely obtain their aspirations, succeeding in every endeavor.

It is just as a skilled horse trainer follows the nature of the horses: he nurtures those that are good and applies the whip to those that are evil. Only then does one come to know the distinction between good and evil. This is no different when applied to the wise and the foolish: the good are born in heaven, while the evil enter hell. There, they must undergo all manner of karmic suffering until it is exhausted; how could the hardships encountered therein ever be fully described?
Just as a person setting out on a journey must seek auspicious blessings so that their destination may be reached without failing to obtain what they desire, it is therefore said:
"One should cultivate oneself and follow the teachings; if one has not been trained oneself, how can one train others?"
Reflecting upon one's own self-discipline and cultivation, one causes others to attain faith and understanding; with one’s own mind focused, this is what the wise practice.

"Reflecting upon one's own self-discipline and cultivation" means that one should always be diligent and focused so as not to let the mind become distracted. One should extinguish the ten paths of unwholesome action and bring them into accord with body, speech, and mind, so that countless sentient beings do not fail to look up to you with longing thirst, and they eagerly desire to hear what is taught, wishing to cultivate and practice it.
Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness and self-discipline.

To cause others to have faith and understanding means that when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and lay devotees hear the correct teaching, their minds will believe and rejoice in it, never going against it; therefore it is said: "To cause others to have faith and understanding."

I have focused my mind; as for that which is practiced by the wise, it is like a person learning a craft who achieves mastery only through single-minded concentration. If one loses a good teacher, they will fall away and be unable to extricate themselves. My every movement—whether entering or exiting, advancing or halting—is seen and respected by gods and humans; even when I reach other regions or distant lands, those who see me rejoice in their hearts and never turn back midway.
Therefore it is said: "I have focused my mind; this is what the wise practice.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, many fail to achieve success.
But those who realize this first rectify themselves and only then instruct others.

Whether acting for oneself or for others, there are many who do not achieve success. When a person practices by means of the karma of their own false views and then imparts their own wisdom to others to study, they will fall into ruin and fail to reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Conversely, if another person is themselves single-mindedly upright and practices correct reception and conduct, and teaches and instructs others according to what they have realized, those who receive these teachings will believe and understand them, and their efforts will not be in vain.
Therefore it is said: "Whether acting for oneself or for others, many fail to achieve success.
One who perceives this understands that a person’s practice must investigate their fundamental conduct; as the Buddha taught: "If one cannot benefit oneself, how can one benefit others?"

Those who practice and cultivate should contemplate and observe, reflecting on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; fully understanding that all things are non-existent, devoid of self, and empty—how could there be a body?
Therefore, the sage demonstrates the rules for others and guides them with subtle teachings, while manifesting and strictly prohibiting [what is harmful].
Thus it is said: "He who awakens to this rectifies himself and then instructs others."
The body remains whole and the Way is preserved; at such a time, how could there be room for others?
Having already been subdued, the wise expound its meaning.

Regarding "the body remains whole and the Way is preserved": because those who practice this path are single-minded and self-disciplined, they become honored, noble, and unsurpassed. In their coming and going, whether advancing or retreating, they do not encounter misfortune or cruelty. They are constantly venerated by gods, humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kumbhāṇḍas, and mahoragas, who protect their bodies so that they do not suffer affliction.
Therefore it is said: "If the body is preserved and the Way is attained, how could there be room for that [defilement] at such a time?

Having already been subdued, the wise expound its meaning as follows: just as a person who yearns to cultivate the profound and subtle Dharma attains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and transcends the three realms, thereby accomplishing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the noble eightfold path. This is called the Tathāgata’s gateway to the nectar of immortality (*amṛta-dvāra*); through it, one obtains all that is wished for: the four requisites of offering—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick and infirm.
Therefore it is said: "Having already been subdued, the wise expound its meaning. To state the essential point:
the verse consists of three lines, the wording of which is identical; however, for those of increased wisdom, they obtain the single line: "They have attained the Dharma."
"Dharma" has two meanings:
first, the meaning of the substance of names; second, the so-called ultimate truth, which refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
"The wise person attains its precepts" constitutes these two phrases; as for the precepts, there are two kinds:
The first is called the two hundred and fifty precepts; the second is called the untainted body-precept (*anāsrava-kāya-śīla*).
These are the three phrases by which the wise are praised.
This also has two meanings:
First, they are praised by the worldly; second, they are praised by the inner treasury.

As for the "worldly," it refers to eloquence in speech, a gentle and pleasant countenance that does not wound others' feelings, such that those who hear the Dharma receive it with joy and delight in hearing its teachings.

Regarding the untainted precepts of the body: one’s conduct is never improper, and one constantly encounters sages and saints; being free from the eight unfavorable states, those who see such a person find their minds opened and their intentions resolved, and they inform one another while praising and extolling that person's virtues.
"The wise hear its name" refers to these four lines; there may be practitioners who hear its name in the mundane world or hear its name on the Path.
"The wise obtain its joy" means that there are two kinds of joy:
mundane joy and the joy of the Path.

While remaining in the secular world, they receive its blessings and merits; they are remembered and honored by donors and patrons, receiving their offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the treatment of illness.

The joy of the Path consists of receiving the blessings of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the Noble Eightfold Path.
The wise person attains its wisdom; there are two kinds of wisdom:
either mundane wisdom or supramundane wisdom.
What is called worldly wisdom (*loka-prajñā*) is the discernment of names and designations without being hindered by them.

What is called the wisdom of the Path (*mārga-prajñā*) is the attainment of the path of the *srotāpanna*, the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the path of the *anāgāmin*, and the path of the *arhat*, as well as the attainment of the perfection of the faculties and the [three gates of] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Therefore it is said: "The wise obtain their wisdom. The wise obtain their mind;

for the mind is the root of all practices. If the mind is not upright, it flows and races toward myriad ends, externally attaching itself to forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*). If one can subdue and collect the mind so that it is not distracted, one will be able to accomplish the fruit of the unconditioned path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga-phala*).

However, that practitioner brings his mind under control and reflects that in the past he was deluded by the mind; throughout immeasurable kalpas, his experience of birth and death has all arisen from the mind.
However, today I have awakened to what the mind does; I shall no longer create new karma nor be driven by the mind.

The wise attain this path, whereas sentient beings wander through kalpa after kalpa in numbers beyond reckoning. As stated in the sūtras, those sentient beings who enter hell are more numerous than the dust and soil of the great earth.

Just as I have today transcended the three realms and, with the divine eye, observe the various classes of sentient beings—how they mutually harm one another, from the flying insects to the crawling worms, without end—just as a potter’s foot kicks the wheel to turn it and produce earthenware vessels, some being broken while on the wheel, some being broken while on the ground, and some being broken once they have entered the kiln; so too are human beings. Therefore, those who train should mindfully aspire to practice.
Furthermore, he cites a sutra:
"With my divine eye I observe sentient beings; those born in the heavens are like the dust upon a fingernail, which is truly insufficient to mention.
Therefore it is said: "The wise one attains the Way."

While dwelling long in the heavens and wandering about in contemplation, he saw that those sentient beings who had been born in the heavens for a long time possessed three qualities superior to those born there later. What are these three?
First, celestial lifespan; second, celestial appearance; and third, merit and prosperity.
Therefore it is said: "Dwelling in heaven for a long time, one wanders in observation.

Dwelling in heaven for a long time, one receives blessings and enjoys mutual entertainment, looking to the east while forgetting the west; therefore it is said: "Dwelling in heaven for a long time, one receives blessings."
Amidst his clan, he was like the sun piercing through the clouds as it rises; he was seen and cherished with love and respect by his parents, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen.

He severed all fetters, fully able to cut off all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); all bonds and attachments were forever exhausted without remainder, and all defiled cravings were completely cast aside.
Therefore it is said: One is able to completely sever all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Dwelling in sorrow, one does not personally grieve; the mind understands right from wrong and realizes that impermanence, the separation from loved ones, and the constant laws of the world are such that:
where there is pleasure, there must be suffering; birth must be followed by death; if there is no birth, there is no death; how then can death be avoided?
Inferring from this principle, for whom does sorrow exist, and from where does joy arise?
Therefore it is said: "Abiding in sorrow yet free from sorrow, the mind is like extinguished ashes; tranquil and non-active."

One completely extinguishes all evil destinies; those already categorized as evil destinies include the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals, as well as the borderlands and among the barbarians, which are also termed evil destinies.
Therefore it is said: "Extinction of all evil destinies.

It is liberation from all suffering and affliction, liberation from the eight roots of suffering: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the loathed, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one desires; in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Within this, the practitioner is liberated from these manifold sufferings; Nirvana is supreme, being unconditioned, uncreated, and devoid of all transformations. Therefore, it is called Nirvana. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Self."
*Udānavarga*, Scroll Twenty-one and Scroll Twenty-two,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-five: Extensive Exposition Though one may recite a thousand chapters, what benefit is there if they lack righteousness?
It is better to understand a single phrase; by hearing it, one may attain the Way.

"Though one may recite a thousand chapters, what benefit is there in that which is not righteous? This means that when people in the world recite much and study extensively, yet do not understand the principles of meaning, nor comprehend the flavor of the meanings or the significance of the phrases, they are like someone who carries hundreds or thousands of loads of grass and wood; it is merely exhausting and of no practical use.
Therefore it is said: "Though one may recite a thousand chapters, what benefit is there if they lack righteousness?

It is better to understand a single phrase through which, upon hearing it, one may attain the Way. This is like a man of old who stored up vast wealth and abounded in grain. Desiring to travel afar, he sold his household grain to exchange for treasures, accumulating immeasurable riches. Later, finding even those treasures excessive, he traded much of them for fine silver. Still dissatisfied with that, he exchanged the fine silver for *cāmpeya* gold (*purpāṣa*). Finding even that too much, he then traded the fine gold for a priceless *maṇi* jewel that grants all wishes (*cintāmaṇi*), whereby his every aspiration was fulfilled without fail.

This is also like that: although one may have studied extensively, if one does not understand the meaning of the phrases, whereas one who understands even a single meaning will surely achieve success.
Therefore it is said: "It is better to understand a single phrase than to hear many without attaining the Way."
Though one may recite a thousand chapters, possessing the fullness of the Dharma’s meaning, hearing but a single phrase of the Dharma can lead to the cessation of the mind.

Regarding "though one may recite a thousand chapters, possessing the fullness of the Dharma’s meaning": many people cultivate and study until they achieve mastery over the flavor of the meaning; yet, if they fail to contemplate its underlying significance, they will fall away and fail to reach the ultimate goal. Therefore it is said: "Though one may recite a thousand chapters, possessing the fullness of the Dharma’s meaning."

Regarding the statement that "hearing a single dharma-phrase can lead to the cessation of the mind": in the world there are many who are extensively learned and well-informed, capable of contemplating a single phrase to derive hundreds or thousands of meanings. As these meanings follow one another in succession without losing their thread, they gradually reach the Unconditioned Great Way. Therefore it is said: "Hearing a single dharma-phrase can lead to the cessation of the mind."
Though one may live for a hundred years, if one violates the precepts and the mind is not settled, it is not as good as spending a single day making offerings to one who upholds the precepts.

Regarding "though one may live for a hundred years, if one violates the precepts and the mind is not settled": a person who transgresses the precepts does not protect the three matters [of body, speech, and mind]. Such individuals—those who do not practice seated meditation, recite the scriptures, or provide assistance—are not to be approached. Although they remain in the world for a long time, they accumulate immeasurable evil; upon death, they enter hell and undergo countless sufferings, such as the burning chariots, the glowing coals, the mountain of knives, and the forest of swords. The same applies to rebirth as animals or hungry ghosts. Therefore, it is said: "Though one may live for a hundred years, if one violates the precepts and the mind is not settled."

It is not as good as, for even a single day, making offerings to one who upholds the precepts. Such a person who upholds the precepts practices meditative concentration; the merit of a single day is countless and immeasurable, beyond the reach of analogy. Abiding long in the world, they accumulate immeasurable virtue; if they are reborn in the heavens, they naturally receive blessings. Therefore it is said: "It is not as good as, for even a single day, making offerings to one who upholds the precepts."
Though one may live for a hundred years, if lacking wisdom and lacking concentration, it is not as good as living for a single day with discerning wisdom and concentration.

Regarding "though one may live for a hundred years, if lacking wisdom and lacking concentration": in the world there are many who do not know shame or remorse; they are no different from the six domestic animals—such as camels, mules, donkeys, elephants, horses, pigs, and dogs—having no distinction of noble or base, high or low.

The analogy for a person lacking wisdom is likewise: shrouded in the darkness of folly, they do not know their own brilliance. Therefore it is said: "Though one lives for a hundred years, if there is no wisdom, there is no stability."

It is not as good as spending a single day possessing wisdom and meditative concentration. A person of wisdom enters deeply into the scriptural teachings; from the meaning of a single phrase to a hundred thousand meanings, they contemplate them repeatedly without finding it difficult. Therefore, it is said: "It is not as good as spending a single day possessing wisdom and meditative concentration."
Though one may live for a hundred years, If one is indolent and lacks diligence, It is not as good as a single day Of diligent effort without cowardice.

"Though one may live for a hundred years, if one is indolent and lacks diligence" means that there are people in the world whose minds are constantly indolent and whose aspirations remain unfulfilled. Having fallen themselves, they cause others to sink into birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Those who have submerged themselves lose the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*) and do not reach the state of the unconditioned Great Way (*anupādāya-mahāmārga*). Being themselves deluded regarding the Path, they further teach others to sink into birth and death.

If one receives food, drink, bedding, seating, or medical treatment for illness from a donor but cannot digest it, one will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals from birth until death; even if one subsequently attains human form, one will be born in a remote land, during a period when no Buddha has appeared, or in one of the eight difficult conditions where wisdom and eloquence are lacking.
Why is this so? It is entirely because in previous lives one did not accumulate merit.
Therefore it is said: "Though one may live for a hundred years, if one is indolent and lacks diligence."

It is not as good as spending even a single day with diligent effort and without cowardice; for there may be those among worldly people who are courageous and energetic, understanding that the world is impermanent, that a human body is difficult to obtain, and that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare to encounter. Furthermore, it is difficult to be born in a central land, and it is likewise difficult to have all one’s faculties complete.
To seek to become a śramaṇa within the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones is not easily achieved, and to hear the words of the True Dharma is likewise not easily achieved.

Those of wisdom who can understand this should mindfully apply themselves with diligence to seek the fruit of the Way; it will not be difficult for them to reach Nirvana, and having already prepared what is necessary, they shall be able to accomplish the untainted Dharma-body.
Therefore it is said: It is not as good as, for even a single day, to be diligent and free from cowardice.
Though one may live for a hundred years, if one does not understand the matter of arising and ceasing, it is not as good as understanding the matter of arising and ceasing for even a single day.

"Though one may live for a hundred years, if they do not know the matter of arising and ceasing": a person in the world is bound by ignorance and cannot attain liberation; throughout a hundred years, they accumulate immeasurable sins and likewise remain ignorant of that which arises and that which ceases. Even if they leave the household life to pursue the Way, if within the Dharma of the Tathāgata they do not understand arising and ceasing, they will forever remain on the level of an ordinary person and fail to reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is not the practice of a bhikṣu or śramaṇa; it is far from the *tathāgatagarbha* and does not approach the Buddha’s casket. Therefore, it is said: "Though one may live for a hundred years, if they do not know the matter of arising and ceasing."

It is not as good as living for a single day and thoroughly understanding the nature of arising and ceasing. When a person dwells in the world, they observe that all phenomena (*dharma*) are individually empty and non-existent; they do not know why things arise, nor do they know why they cease. By discerning each one separately, they can understand their fundamental source. On the day of death, they will feel no fear or dread. Their consciousness will not be confused regarding their future rebirth; they will encounter the worthy and the sages, hear the Dharma, and attain liberation. Therefore it is said: "It is not as good as, within a single day, thoroughly understanding the nature of arising and ceasing."

To state the essential point: one contemplates the origin from which suffering arises. Generally, people living in the world do not know where the cessation of suffering originates; even though they may be bhikṣus, they do not comprehend the conduct of a śramaṇa. Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate the origin from which suffering arises."

One should contemplate the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*); if people’s habitual practices do not lead to the cessation of outflows, they will remain stagnant within the three realms and five destinies, transmigrating through birth and death with no time of escape.

The wise practitioner cultivates the practice of observing these outflows (*āsrava*); they know from whence they arise and where they cease. If one does not know why they arise when they arise, nor why they cease when they cease, one will gradually attain the realm of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, one should observe the track of immovability. If there is someone who cannot observe the track of immovability, they will fall and descend into the cycle of birth and death; though they dwell as a śramaṇa, they do not practice the conduct of a śramaṇa, and though they dwell as a brāhmaṇa, they do not practice the conduct of a brāhmaṇa.

By virtue of four causes and conditions, even one who possesses profound and subtle teachings—if they are a practitioner who observes and fully understands the track of immovable conduct, their mind will neither waver nor shift, and they will gradually reach the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, one should contemplate the path of immortality: just as a person in this world does not know of death and birth, when death occurs, the spirit departs, the wind and fire cease, and the soul disperses; the body becomes rigid and straight, no longer possessing its former vitality.

However, these practitioners who follow this path, though they wear the dharma robes, shave their hair and beards, and don the three dharma garments, are unable to contemplate death as death and life as life; nor are they able to cultivate the pure brahma-faring.

What is called the "path of the deathless" is the extinction of *nirvāṇa*; by means of this, one enters that unconditioned state where there is no birth, no aging, no sickness, and no death—a state of serene bliss.
Therefore it is said: "One should contemplate the practice of immortality.

Furthermore, one should observe the path of purity; the purity of the Way is not that which is studied by the defiled, and the Way can remove impurities, being not that which is studied by those habituated to defilement."

Next, one should contemplate the nature of celestial forms: one cannot perceive the tracks of those who have practiced the path of the superior man; that which is supreme and most honored among all dharmas, beyond which nothing can surpass it, is what is called the extinction of *nirvāṇa*.

The practitioner observes the traces of the ambrosial path; they have no thought of hunger or thirst, nor any thought of affliction or fever. Those who do not behold it will fall forever into birth and death; those who fail to reach fundamental non-being and obtain the ambrosia lack sufficient meritorious karma. Having already bestowed [the merit] upon others, they harbor no stinginess.
Though one may live for a hundred years, Offering sacrifices to the fire in mountain forests, It is not as good as for even a brief moment, To practice and cultivate oneself with devotion.

"Though one may live for a hundred years, offering sacrifices to the fire in mountain forests" refers to a story of the past: there was a brahmin who exhausted his body and tormented his flesh, performing fire sacrifices in the vast wilderness and deep mountains. He worshipped the fire deity at the proper times without deviating from the ritual texts; he selected clean firewood, gathered fine flowers, and burned various kinds of incense as offerings, hoping thereby to obtain grace and merit.
At that time, the brahmin withdrew and thought to himself:

"I have stayed on this mountain practicing extraordinary arts and attending to this fire for a hundred years. Now I shall test it to see if the merit of the fire's kindness can be known; if the proof of its gratitude and nourishment is to be seen, then so be it, but if not, what is the use of continuing these sacrifices?"
At that time, the brahmin, lacking foresight, reached out with both hands toward the blazing fire. His arms were immediately scorched, causing a pain beyond description.

The brahmin thought to himself: "I have performed this fire sacrifice for so many years; my labors have been in vain, resulting only in loss and no benefit. It must be that my own body has brought about this suffering."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu practicing the path not far from that mountain who, knowing [the situation], asked:
"Brahmin, you should know!
Fire is hot by nature; it does not distinguish between those who have shown kindness and support, nor between the noble and the lowly."

"If you wish to know, I have a holy teacher who is uniquely honored throughout the three realms: when he walks, he treads upon the void without any obstruction; when he sits, he radiates light that penetrates the ten directions. Would it not be fitting for us to go there together to pay him our respects and fully hear his profound and subtle Dharma, so that we may cross from this shore to the other shore?"

Having heard this, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding attained; he then went with the practitioner to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the brahmin was ready for deliverance, spoke these verses amidst the great assembly:
“Though one may live for a hundred years, Performing fire sacrifices in the mountain forests, ... [the verse continues]”
"It is not as good as for a brief moment practicing and cultivating what one admires.
At that time, the brahmin’s mind was suddenly enlightened; all defilements were exhausted, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"In the past, you spent a hundred years in the mountains tending the sacred fire and making offerings to various deities; your labors were in vain, for they did not reach the ultimate goal.
Now that you have come to know the locus of the True Way, it would be better for you to practice and cultivate yourself for even a brief moment."

The people of the world cling to folly until death and fail to overcome it; for a hundred years they have served fire without awakening to their own condition. Embracing ignorance, they cast themselves into the darkness and cannot reform themselves.
