If one could awaken to this and know that [the object of worship] is not real, constantly reflecting upon where the illness arises, from whence it comes, and whither it goes, one would fully realize that these are not true dharmas.

Furthermore, if one receives from others clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for illness, and is able to digest them without waste, and serves and makes offerings of famous flowers, powdered incense, blended incense, silken fabrics, banners, and streamers—the merit of such deeds is beyond measure.

To tend the sacrificial fire for a hundred years is not equal to practicing a single act of loving-kindness for the briefest moment, such as the snap of a finger; the merit of the latter is most exalted and unsurpassed, difficult to describe and impossible to measure, beyond the reach of any analogy.

It is like comparing a mustard seed to Mount Sumeru, or contending for measurement with the waters of the ocean using the water in a cow’s footprint; it is like claiming that the dust on a fingernail is superior ground, or competing with the sun for brilliance as a firefly. Such is the nature of the virtue of a compassionate heart—how much more so when one has cultivated such virtue fully for a hundred years?

Riding upon this merit, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he has never fallen back into the stage of an ordinary person; all people look up to him with reverence and worship, all of which results from the accumulation of practices performed in previous lives.
Therefore it is said: It is not as good as practicing loving-kindness for even a single moment.
Even if one were to consume solid food month after month, if that fool does not place faith in the Buddha, he shall not obtain even one-sixteenth of its merit.

From month to month, those who are foolish and subsist on solid food—beings who, out of craving for food, nourish their physical forms without considering the calamities and misfortunes of future lives—do not realize that the four great elements of the body are of differing natures, while the spirit dwelling within them distinguishes right from wrong. The wise recognize the truth, whereas the foolish hold perverted views; they do not understand the good and evil deeds of this life or the next, and thus they wander through the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties with no time of escape in sight.
Therefore it is said: "From month to month, the fool consumes morsel food.

If one does not place faith in the Buddha, they shall not obtain even one-sixteenth [of the merit]. If there are sentient beings who, for a single day or half a day, for a single hour or half an hour, or even for the duration of a finger-snap, maintain profound faith in the Buddha with an unwavering mind, their merit will be immeasurable and incalculable; it cannot be compared by means of analogy. This merit reaches its retribution in the unseen realm, being formless and imageless, yet arriving spontaneously and suddenly, with its blessings and rewards being inexhaustible.
Therefore it is said: "He who does not have faith in the Buddha shall not obtain even one-sixteenth [of the merit]. To speak briefly:

he who does not have faith in the Dharma shall not obtain even one-sixteenth [of the merit], even if he hears the sound of the Dharma for hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* of eons. That which is called the Dharma is the extinction of cessation, *nirvāṇa*.
As stated in the sutra, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now declare to you the three who are the most supreme:
first, the Buddha is the most supreme; second, the Dharma is the most supreme; third, the Saṃgha is the most supreme."
In what way is the Buddha the foremost and most honored?

Among all classes of sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, one-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or without form; with perception or without perception; and even those who are neither with nor without perception—the Tathāgata is the honored one, the supreme one, and the unsurpassed among them.
Therefore, monks! Any sentient being who possesses profound faith in the Buddha has the foremost honor as their object of faith;
by having the foremost honor as their object of faith, they shall receive the foremost merit.
Because he has received the foremost merit, he is born as the most eminent and honored among humans and devas.
This is why he is called the Buddha, the Foremost Honored One.
What, then, is the Dharma that makes him the Foremost Honored One?

What is called "Dharma" refers to conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; among these, the dharma of cessation, the dharma of desirelessness, the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, and the dharma of Nirvana are the most honored, the most supreme, and unsurpassed.
Those who revere the Dharma revere that which is most supreme;
by revering that which is most supreme, they obtain the foremost merit;
by obtaining the foremost merit, they are reborn in the heavens as the most eminent and honored among the noble.
This is what is called the Dharma being the foremost and most honored.
What is meant by the Sangha being the foremost and most honored?
Among all great assemblies, vast gatherings, and retinues of followers, the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is the most honored, the supreme, and unsurpassed. Therefore, O Bhikṣus!
If there are sentient beings who have profound faith in the Sangha, they are foremost and most honored;
because they believe in that which is foremost and most honored, they receive the foremost merit;
because they receive the foremost merit, they are reborn as the most noble and honored among devas and humans.
This is what is called the Sangha being the foremost and most honored.

As for those who do not possess a compassionate heart, they do not obtain even one-sixteenth [of the merit]. Beings of all kinds harbor poison day and night; ensnared by anger, they devour one another. Since they harbor such wrath even toward their own parents, how could they ever bestow compassion upon other sentient beings?
This matter is not so. Therefore it is said: "One who does not possess a heart of loving-kindness obtains not even one-sixteenth [of the merit];
one who does not pity sentient beings obtains not even one-sixteenth. This is like a realm or territory where the names, titles, and surnames of the sentient beings within cannot be fully enumerated.

If there is a practitioner who has entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and therein teaches and transforms others to provide for the destitute and relieve the needy—without discriminating between the beautiful and the ugly, nor giving rise to conceptual thoughts such as "this may be given" or "this may not be given"—but remaining equal, non-dual, and undifferentiated, this is called true giving.
Therefore it is said: "For one who does not possess a mind of loving-kindness, one gains not even a sixteenth part.

There may be a land where its sentient beings are called the class of crawling creatures; therein, one acts with courage and does not shrink from toil, providing for their needs in that realm so that nothing is lacking—this is called the mind of giving.

Among the wriggling and crawling species, not even one in sixteen is saved because of spirits or deities; nor are they saved because of the True Dharma, for sentient beings fall of their own accord, descending into the heterodoxies and divergent teachings.

The Nirgranthas and others claimed for themselves the title of "Venerable," binding their bellies with iron plates as they walked through the world. They said among themselves: "These Śākya śramaṇas and practitioners are madmen of the world;

they go about with their heads bare and their garments fastened on the left, yet claim for themselves the title of 'Venerable. We observe that this is truly an omen of misfortune. The people of the world are deluded and confused—why do they treat these men as venerable?"

If there are sentient beings who give to such a person, they will later receive the retribution of foul, evil, and impurity; they may see such a one in dreams, and upon waking encounter misfortune—how much more so when walking the Path and meeting them face to face!
Therefore, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:

"One who can maintain unbroken faith in the True Dharma, whose mind remains unchanging even when encountering hundreds of thousands of hardships and difficulties, who directs their intent with single-minded devotion toward it and does not practice inverted views—it is only such a person who may be called one who upholds the Tathāgata’s True Dharma."

Those who lack faith have not attained even one-sixteenth part [of this merit]; whereas those who possess faith and turn toward the True Dharma, their merit is immeasurable and incalculable—hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and hundreds of millions of times greater—such that it cannot be compared by means of analogy.
Why is it said that "not even one-sixteenth part" is obtained?

The reason for discussing the number sixteen is that these refer to the sixteen great kingdoms; within this realm of Jambudvīpa, where benevolence and righteousness reside, there is no place beyond these sixteen great kingdoms. One who is erudite in antiquity and comprehensive in the present may expound upon the profound and subtle, resolving matters according to the time to forever eliminate doubt and leave no room for hesitation.
The names of these sixteen kingdoms are as follows: the first is Aṅga;
the second is King Makhādeva Piṅgala.
Third, Kāśī; fourth, King Prasenajit of Kośala; fifth, Soma.
Sixth was Suratha; seventh was King Caṇḍapradyota;
eighth was King Prasenajit.
Ninth is Āpa. Tenth is King Aśvatarāyaṇa. Eleventh is Kauru.
Twelfth is King Pañcāla-Akuli; thirteenth is Droṇa; fourteenth is Yavana.
The fifteenth is Jianfu; the sixteenth was originally missing.

These sixteen great kingdoms encompassed the myriad affairs of state with comprehensive knowledge, remaining unconfused amidst them; their eloquence was swift and agile, their learning neither redundant nor burdensome; they mastered subtle meanings and investigated both the root and the branches; they expounded the immeasurable, such that one could never exhaustively fathom them—these emerged from among these sixteen great kingdoms.

Now, for a practitioner who cannot direct their mind toward aspiring after the sublime meaning, they should simply travel through and visit the sixteen kingdoms; there, their majestic deportment and ritual etiquette will naturally be perfected, requiring no further instruction from a teacher and no external models to follow.

If a person prays to spirits and sacrifices, hoping for blessings throughout the year, they will not obtain even one-fourth of what is promised. Regarding the phrase "if a person prays to spirits and sacrifices, hoping for blessings throughout the year":

it is my thought that those of external paths and heterodox schools, with their inverted and false views, are stubbornly ignorant and fail to awaken; they perform sacrifices at shrines for as long as a year, and the wealth of the common people expended therein is beyond measure.

To burn various kinds of sweet delicacies and food in fire, believing one thereby gains merit, only to encounter instead calamity—this arises from clinging to folly and refusing to reform oneself, leading to entry into the dark gloom after death, where one beholds neither the Great Light nor the brilliance of wisdom.
Therefore it is said: "Among these four parts, one does not obtain even a single portion.

For this reason, the Sage instructs by gradual stages and guides by way of the path; by leading the ignorant and deluded to the place of peace and security, practicing virtue for even a brief moment surpasses that of doing so for an entire year.
The "Chapter on Extensive Exposition" concludes.
Those who lack faith and harbor malice and envy, who incite strife between this person and that, are shunned by the wise;
the foolish practice such ways as their pleasure.

Those who lack faith, harbor hatred and jealousy, and incite discord between people—such individuals have no firm foundation of faith while in this world. They likewise do not believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, True Suchness, or the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Even if they accumulate wealth as vast as the heavens, it cannot be relied upon; on the day their life ends, wealth does not follow them. This is all because, in this present life, they did not practice generosity nor cultivate merit, thus exhausting what was done in the past without creating anything new.

It is like a bird that is habitually greedy for meat; when there are leaves on a mountain tree that resemble the color of meat, it watches day and night, stretching its neck upward in expectation. While perched upon the tree, what it perceives as meat falling is actually just a leaf. Ensnared by such delusion, it fails to awaken, and thus, without ceasing, it loses its life there.
Why is this so? It is entirely because they do not reform their greedy minds.

What is heard here is transmitted there, and what is heard from there is transmitted back here; they incite strife between these and those, preventing them from achieving success. Envy arises within their hearts, further producing defilement. Therefore it is said: "Lacking faith and harboring hatred and envy, they incite strife between these and those people."

That which is shunned by the wise refers to those who, knowing propriety and etiquette, avoid suspicion and distance themselves from doubt; they do not dwell amidst confusion and turmoil, and will not engage in such matters for even the duration of a finger-snap, let alone spend their entire lives wandering together with them.

What is called a wise person is one who understands the past and knows the present, is broadly versed in all matters, and foresees what has not yet occurred so that their actions never go astray. Their mind and speech correspond, their words are without error, and they discern profound meanings without confusion. From a single phrase, they can expound upon the infinite; yet these are the things that delude the foolish. Therefore it is said: "These are what the wise discard."

Regarding "the fool practices what he takes for pleasure": suppose there is a person who, with a virtuous mind, exhorts, advises, and encourages a child, training them in the Way so that they may perceive the gateway to the Path. Yet, instead of following these instructions, the child becomes further confused; they treat hell as their own hall and chamber, taking no account of the roots of calamity and retribution in future lives. They are taught to practice evil deeds and refuse the good teaching, eventually falling back into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. For this reason, it is said: "The fool practices what he takes for pleasure."
Possessing faith and free from malice and envy, diligent, faithful, and possessed of much learning—such a person is honored and respected by the wise, and the noble ones (āryas) find joy in them.

Regarding "possessing faith and being free from malice and envy": suppose there is another person who has deep faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; who with a sincere mind believes in and understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; who harbors no flattery and whose mind is supple; who serves and respectfully attends to fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārins); who diligently receives instruction by day and practices walking meditation by night; who exerts himself tirelessly without losing his dignified demeanor; and who maintains a gentle and pleasant countenance, speaking after first smiling so as not to offend the minds of others. It is for these reasons that it is said: "possessing faith and being free from malice and envy."

Regarding "diligent, faithful, and learned": among people’s practices of cultivation, diligence is supreme; how much more so for one who extensively studies and gathers great learning, widely disseminates precepts, hearing, generosity, and wisdom to all, abides peacefully in the state of non-action at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and expounds what they have seen to others. Therefore, it is said: "diligent, faithful, and learned."

Those who are honored and treated with respect by the wise should always draw near to them and receive their instruction. They should cause those whose aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is incomplete to become complete; they should cause those whose aggregates of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the vision of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*) are incomplete to become complete. Therefore it is said: "Those who are honored and treated with respect by the wise."

That which the noble and holy take as joy means that when a person practices the path, they pursue the worthy and the holy without shrinking from cold or suffering; even if they encounter seven thousand billion hardships requiring the sacrifice of body and life, though they meet such misery, they do not waver in their resolve. Therefore it is said: "The noble and holy take this as joy."

Do not associate with evil associates; do not join in unlawful assemblies. Associate with virtuous friends and always join in the assemblies of the True Dharma. Regarding "not associating with evil associates":

when a practitioner encounters an evil associate, their evil conduct increases day by day, leading them to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Even if one’s actions are pure and the mind is clean, following an evil person will stain one's natural character. It is like someone who loves dogs, pigs, and sheep and does not distance himself from them; the pigs and dogs follow him closely and never leave. What these pigs and dogs delight in is excrement as their highest food and latrines as their bathing pools, and they defile one another. One who associates with evil associates is just like this: they pursue one another until finally there is no goodness left.
Therefore it is said: "Do not associate with evil friends. Regarding "not meeting with those who act contrary to the Dharma":

those who act contrary to the Dharma have five kinds of unforgivable offenses—lacking precepts, lacking faith, lacking learning, lacking wisdom, and lacking generosity. Such persons must not be approached; whoever pursues them as companions will fall into the evil realms and never reach a good destination. Therefore it is said: "Do not meet with those who act contrary to the Dharma."

To associate with virtuous friends means that one's learning improves daily, one’s speech is gentle and harmonious with the mind, and even in what one does, one does not harm the feelings of others; one speaks after first smiling, and one’s words are consistent with their meaning. Therefore it is said: "Associate with virtuous friends."

"Constantly attending the assembly of the True Dharma" refers to what is called the assembly of the True Dharma: namely, the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. There are no sentient beings who arise superior to the Buddha; apart from the Buddha, there are no sentient beings who arise superior to the Pratyekabuddha; and apart from the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, there are no sentient beings who arise superior to the Śrāvaka. Those who have faith directed toward these three will attain the ultimate goal and shall not fall into the calamitous realms of the three evil paths. Therefore, it is said: "Constantly attending the assembly of the True Dharma."
When traveling on a road, one should maintain mindfulness and caution;
those who uphold the precepts and possess great learning contemplate immeasurable realms, and having heard those excellent teachings,
each understands their distinctions.

Regarding "one who travels while mindful of precaution": when a group of people is on the road, they must speak with caution. In the midst of vast wildernesses, there are many spirits and deities; if one utters evil speech, these spirits will find an opportunity to act against one, but if one speaks of what is good, the spirits and deities will provide protection. Thus, wherever one goes, one will not encounter wicked people, nor will one meet with robbers or thieves. Therefore it is said: "One who travels while mindful of precaution."

Those who uphold the precepts and possess great learning do not allow the Buddha’s teachings to depart from the forefront of their minds; as the Buddha has taught, he told the bhikṣus that they should cultivate samādhi and right concentration, whether walking or sitting, never allowing them to falter. Thus, they will be seen and protected by devas and spirits.
Why is this so? It is entirely because they have received and upheld the true teachings of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is said: "One who upholds the precepts and is possessed of much learning."

Regarding "contemplating immeasurable objects": day and night one contemplates sitting meditation, reciting the sutras, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom; therefore it is said, "contemplating immeasurable objects."

Hearing those excellent teachings, each comes to know their distinctions. Just as a student who hears those excellent instructions does not allow the mind to become confused and ensures that the words and phrases correspond correctly, they thereby attain the fruits of the path—the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), and the fruit of arhatship—increasing their roots of goodness until they reach the unconditioned path. Therefore it is said: "Hearing those excellent teachings, each comes to know their distinctions."

"Associating with the wicked leads to one's own ruin; practicing the good brings forth renown. That which is sublime remains ever sublime; this is due to the integrity of the body. Regarding "associating with the wicked leads to one's own ruin":

suppose there is another person who associates closely with evil friends; they suffer daily decline and never reach fulfillment. This is just as during the dark fortnight of the moon, when there is obscurity and no great radiance. Associating with evil friends is also like this: one’s roots of goodness diminish daily while unwholesome dharmas increase. Therefore it is said: "Associating with the wicked leads to one's own ruin."

Regarding "practicing goodness brings forth renown": those who practice what is superior gain daily renown, just as when the moon is about to reach its fullness, its radiance shines afar beyond all bounds. A person who cultivates goodness is likewise so; their good reputation becomes vast and their fame spreads far and wide. Therefore it is said: "Practicing goodness brings forth renown."

The "excellent" (miāo) are those who are perpetually excellent themselves; their conduct is exclusively upright as they cultivate the unsurpassed path. This is like the family of a *srotāpanna* looking up to cultivate the path of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, the family of a *sakṛdāgāmin* looking up to cultivate the path of an *anāgāmin*, the family of an *anāgāmin* looking up to cultivate the path of an *arhat*, and the family of an *arhat* further increasing all their own wholesome merits. Therefore it is said: "The excellent are perpetually excellent themselves."

Regarding "this is due to the body being upright and true": one should seek skillful means to adorn the body with all manner of meritorious ornaments. If one desires that one's reputation be widely disseminated within the mind, and wishes to be honored and received by devas and the people of the world, one must be personally cautious and refrain from associating with worldly defilements, thereby bringing forth the Way. Therefore it is said: "This is due to the body being upright and true."
The virtuous end in goodness, for they associate with the virtuous;
wisdom is supreme, and through the precepts, there is eternal quiescence.

The virtuous end in goodness because they associate with the virtuous; the wise seek wisdom to accomplish the Noble Path. It is like the finest *cāmpeya* gold, clear and translucent both inside and out, which, when fashioned into vessels, is never unsuccessful.

The wise are likewise; through the mutual cultivation of the noble ones, they leave their teachings in the world to remain imperishable for all eternity. Therefore it is said: "The good end well, because they associate with the good."

"Wisdom is supreme; through the precepts, one attains eternal tranquility. This means that when a person practices the path, they should first seek the Dharma of the Noble Ones; therefore it is said: "Wisdom is supreme; through the precepts, one attains eternal tranquility."
Just as fish swarm together in haste, so do people greedily seize them;
their minds are so attached that they do not perceive the stench, and the habituation to evil is likewise.

"Just as fish swarm together in haste, so do people greedily seize them" means that just as a school of fish gathers in one place that is foul and difficult to approach, so too the human mind is greedily attached and disregards the filth. The fool clings to his intent, deeming it sweet and delicious, unaware that over time it will be detrimental to the body, its foul odor overflowing and manifesting on the outside.

It is the same for those who habituate themselves to evil: by associating with them, one becomes evil, diminishing one's roots of goodness and increasing the faction of evil. Therefore it is said: "Just as fish gather in a turbulent pool, people greedily seize them; their minds are so attached that they do not perceive the stench. Habituation to evil is likewise."
The leaves of the agallochum, chrysanthemum, and *huò*—sentient beings go there to gather them;
the fragrance of the leaves spreads afar. Practicing goodness is also like this.

Regarding "the leaves of the agallochum, chrysanthemum, and *huò*, sentient beings go there to gather them": suppose there is a person of refined discernment who goes to gather their fragrance; although they do not obtain the roots, they acquire the fragrant leaves whose scent is exquisite and pervasive, such that even when discarded from their original place, they still remain fragrant.

It is likewise for one who follows a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): they cultivate human virtue, and their merit accumulates day by day. Therefore it is said: "The leaves of the *mukha*, *kāśa*, and *horaka* plants—when sentient beings go to gather them, the fragrance of the leaves spreads far and wide; so too is the practice of goodness."
Having personally refrained from practicing evil, yet associating with those who practice evil, one is slandered and ridiculed by others, and one’s ill repute grows ever more intense.

Having personally refrained from practicing evil, yet associating with those who practice evil—there are many in the world who do not commit evil deeds such as lewdness or theft, whose nature is not to drink alcohol or to gamble for pleasure; yet if such beings sit in a tavern, enter a village of prostitutes, or sit in a gambling house, they may be seen by the owners, who, thinking that this person practices such unrighteousness, will harbor doubts about them.
"This man was previously chaste and pure; why does he now practice such unrighteousness?
Consequently, his ill repute spread far and wide, and as hundreds of thousands of sentient beings spoke of it to one another, his infamy increased day by day.

Therefore it is said: "Having not practiced evil oneself, yet associating with those who practice evil, one will be slandered and ridiculed by others, and one's ill repute will increase and blaze ever more fiercely."
Observe what is practiced and practice it; know what is near and draw close to it.
When a poisoned arrow is within its quiver, the pure are defiled by it;
the brave man can remove the stain, casting away evil and not making it his companion.

Those who observe what they practice and then practice it accordingly, and who know what is near and draw close to it, are many in this world yet remain unrestrained by the Way; their resolve is not firm as they associate with evil, and being untrained, they practice according to whatever they encounter. Seeing evil, they practice evil; seeing good, they practice good. Taking what they themselves have seen and showing it to others—how can those whose own persons are not upright bring others to rectitude?

Just as a poisoned arrow defiles those around it, so too does one who commits evil themselves and teaches others to practice it; the wise, having observed this, never commit such evil. Therefore it is said: "Observe what is practiced and then practice it; know whom you associate with and draw near to them. A poisoned arrow lies within its bundle, and the pure are defiled by it; the courageous man can remove the defilement—cast away evil and do not be its companion."
Therefore, knowing the fruits of retribution, the wise person discerns them all:
do not associate with those who are not kin, but associate with the virtuous.
A bhikṣu practicing the Path endures suffering to exhaust all outflows.

"Therefore, it is known that the wise fully discern the fruits of retribution" means that the karmic results produced by sentient beings differ: some offenses may be slight yet require profound remedies, while others may be grave yet easy to cure;

only the Awakened One can utterly extinguish them. What the wise practice they examine with clear self-awareness; if they commit a transgression, they are immediately able to admonish themselves for their error. It is like a horse that stumbles and falls: only after being struck with a whip does it become tamed. The practice of the wise is likewise: as soon as a lapse occurs, they feel regret for their failure. Therefore it is said: "The Sage knows the fruits of retribution; the wise fully discern them."

Do not associate with those who are not kin; rather, you should associate with and draw near to the virtuous. Those who are called "not kin" act contrary to righteousness; though they utter words and teachings from their mouths, in the end there is no sound of goodness, as they spread poison among people, taking this as their pleasure.

If there are sentient beings who habitually indulge in this, they will wander through birth and death for a long night, undergoing immeasurable affliction; their consciousnesses will become inverted and their minds will be feverish with distress.

What is called a "worthy one" (bhadra) is one who encompasses and understands all matters and myriad affairs without confusion; serving as a model for others with unimpeded eloquence, they demonstrate the teachings to sentient beings through their own clear wisdom, so that those who hear their voice receive deliverance.
Therefore it is said: "Do not associate with those who are not kin; one should associate with and draw near to the virtuous.

When a bhikṣu practices the Path and endures suffering to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), the practitioner maintains his resolve and perfects the various karmas—the Eightfold Noble Path of the Sages, which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly practice. Furthermore, by means of the Dharma of noble patience regarding suffering, he exhausts all outflows and achieves the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu who practices the Path endures suffering to exhaust all outflows.
Though a fool may serve a person of wisdom for as long as his life lasts, he still does not know the True Dharma, like a ladle that merely scoops up food.

Though a fool may live in this world for a hundred years alongside a wise person, his mind remains clouded and he cannot distinguish the true Dharma. For this reason, the sages employ the metaphor of a ladle: though it scoops up substances all day long, it does not know whether they are salty or sour. This illustrates how a fool, even when encountering sages and saints, has a deluded mind and a confused heart that fails to comprehend the correct teaching; he merely exists as a parasite in the world, rendering no benefit to the age.
Therefore it is said: Even if a fool serves a person of wisdom for as long as his life lasts, he will not understand the True Dharma, just as a ladle cannot discern the flavor of food.
But if a wise person serves a noble and holy one for even a brief moment, they will know the True Dharma in every detail, just as the tongue perceives all tastes.

The will of the wise person is swift and agile; hearing one thing, they understand ten thousand, and they anticipate what has not yet occurred. Their conduct in accordance with the times is never erroneous; they can discern all things without obstruction, just as the tongue tastes flavors and can distinguish sweet, sour, salty, and bland.

What the student practices is a thorough mastery of the beginning and the end, distinguishing the white from the black dharmas. They know the origin of illness and know how illness is extinguished; they can fully discern what is not inverted and what is inverted, and apply the sacred medicine accordingly. Therefore it is said: "In a mere moment, the wise serve the noble sages; they know each true dharma, just as the tongue knows various flavors."

To speak briefly of the matter: that which is practiced by the ignorant who lack the wisdom to understand it can only be thoroughly investigated by the wise. Those who lack eyesight are what we call the foolish;
"eyesight" refers to the eyes of the noble ones (ārya), and only the wise possess them.
They do not understand the true Dharma spoken by the Samyak-saṃbuddha; those who do not understand the true Dharma are the foolish.
The wise person, by investigating a single phrase, can expound upon a hundred kinds of meanings;
the foolish person may recite a thousand phrases, yet fail to understand the meaning of even a single one.

Regarding the statement, "The wise person seeks out a single phrase and brings forth a hundredfold meanings": the wise person maintains a resolute mind and clearly understands the Way and its arts; through meditative seclusion they remain undisturbed, refining their spirit and consciousness until they are forever free from defilement and fully possess the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). When asked about the meaning of a single phrase, they can penetrate hundreds of thousands of chapters. Therefore it is said: "The wise person seeks out a single phrase and brings forth a hundredfold meanings."

If a fool recites a thousand phrases but does not understand the meaning of a single one, his mind is deluded; he goes from darkness to darkness and does not behold the Great Light. Although he recites a thousand chapters, he does not comprehend a single principle; therefore, the wise person should always keep such a person at a distance and have no dealings with him. For this reason it is said: "The fool recites a thousand phrases but does not understand the meaning of a single one."
The accomplishment of the meaning of a single phrase is what the wise cultivate and study, while the foolish prefer to distance themselves from it; this is what the True Buddha has taught.
Once, there was a bhikṣu who went to where the Buddha was and, approaching him, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Indeed, World-Honored One, out of your great compassion and pity, please awaken us who have not yet attained understanding. We pray that you will preach the Dharma in a way that is suited to our capacities; having heard the Dharma, our minds shall be awakened and we shall receive deliverance.”
At that time, the World-Honored One briefly explained the meaning and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If it is not yours, then relinquish it.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"I have understood it.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"In what sense did you understand my teaching?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Form is not mine; I have relinquished it.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! It is just as you have said.
Therefore it is said: "The accomplishment of the meaning of a single phrase is that which the wise cultivate and study."

The fool delights in distancing himself from what the True Buddha has taught: the Great Path of equality through which the Sage dwells in the world to instruct sentient beings. Yet the mind of the fool is deluded and his consciousness is difficult to transform; some, upon seeing the Tathāgata, close their eyes; some, upon hearing the preaching of the Dharma, plug their ears; and some, seeing the wheel-marks of the Tathāgata’s footsteps upon the ground, trample them to ruin. Such types as these have deeply rooted defilements and stains that are difficult to reform or change.

The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, have all finally completed their preaching of the Dharma within the realm of no-remainder; yet, because sentient beings have long been bound by delusion and ignorance, they neither see nor hear the descent of the nectar-like rain. Thus, they cast off one form only to receive another, revolving through birth and death with no prospect of escape, all because they are entangled by the folly of ignorance.
One who harbors resentment but possesses wisdom triumphs; Such a person does not follow the influence of friends or kin.
The fool is instructed in what is not the Path, And gradually proceeds along the road to hell.

Regarding "one who harbors resentment but possesses wisdom triumphs": a resentful person recognizes their own faults and transgressions. Being naturally intelligent and discerning, they provide for the future and constantly reflect:

"If I were to practice unrighteousness today, I would only bring ruin upon myself without harming that person; what should I do when there are many enemies and one desires to retaliate but lacks the power to do so?"
"It is not as good as practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), for by doing so one may attain victory.
Therefore it is said: "The wise conquer those who harbor enmity and hatred. As for "not following the way of friends":

when the hearts of friends are intimate and they share what their minds delight in, they teach the other person and rejoice together; yet if they share in evil, they share in evil, and if they share in good, they share in good. Later, when they receive the retribution for these actions, they enter hell. Therefore it is said: "Not following the way of friends, the fool is instructed in the non-path, gradually treading the road to hell."

The fool who calls himself a fool should be known as one of good intelligence; the fool who calls himself wise is said to be the most foolish among fools. When a fool calls himself a fool, one should know him to be of good wit and discernment.

The fool reflects upon himself with regret for his former inadequacy: "What I formerly practiced was truly contrary to the Dharma. I have planted the roots of various evils, opening the gates to hell and blocking the path to Nirvana. Day and night I reproach myself: 'I now dwell in the world, bound by my own fetters and defiled by dust and grime. From body to body, I transmigrate through birth and death, never leaving the three realms of existence. Thus, he reproaches himself and seeks out teachers and companions, gradually attaining the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Therefore it is said: "The fool calls himself a fool; one should know that this is truly wise. When a fool calls himself wise, he is the most extreme among fools.

Such a person, born into the world, constantly praises himself, saying, "I am noble and honorable, while others are not my equal. Failing to comprehend the calamities and transgressions of both this life and the next, he proclaims his own renown while suppressing the virtues of others. Unaware of the hardships of birth and death, he practices the conduct of an ordinary worldling. Therefore it is said: "When a fool calls himself wise, he is the most extreme among fools."
If one further praises the fool and reviles the body of the wise, though reviling the wise may still leave room for excellence, praising the fool is not supreme.

If one further praises the fool, it is because one praises what the fool habitually perceives; such a person fails to distinguish between the noble and the base, or between good and evil conduct. Thus, regarding that which ought to be praised, they instead revile it. Therefore it is said: "If one further praises the fool."

As for one who reviles the person of the wise, though they are slandered, they do not feel sorrow or distress, knowing that this is brought about by the conditions of karmic retribution. Therefore it is said: "Even when the body of the wise is reviled, there is still something superior."

Regarding the statement, "To praise the foolish is not supreme": when sentient beings dwell in the world, they join the ranks of the ignorant and are deluded by them; upon hearing their names praised, they rejoice and leap for joy, unable to restrain themselves, unaware that this will prove disadvantageous to them in the long run. Therefore it is said: "To praise the foolish is not supreme."
Do not see the fool, nor hear his voice; do not dwell with the fool.
To dwell together with a fool is difficult, like living with an enemy.
Once, when the Buddha was at Rājagṛha, he traveled along the road accompanied by a single attendant named Ānanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar that Devadatta was advancing along the same path. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"We should take another road together; why should we meet with this foolish man?"
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Why, World-Honored One, does the Tathāgata today fear this Devadatta?
Why do you wish to avoid him and take another path?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“I recall from my own memory that through the merit I originally cultivated, I have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; furthermore, I have never seen any Māra, deva, follower of external paths, heterodox teacher, śramaṇa, or brahmin who could cause the Tathāgata to experience fear.”
This matter is not so.

In the past, while I was beneath the King of Trees and my various fetters were not yet exhausted, the evil Māra Pāpīyān led a host of eighteen billion beings—having the forms of humans with animal heads, monkeys, lions, tigers, rhinoceroses, venomous snakes, and malevolent ghosts—who carried mountains, spat fire, and brandished swords, spears, halberds, lances, armor, and shields; they raised their voices in roars that filled the void and came to terrify me, yet they could not move even a single hair on my body. How much less, now that my body has attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment and I am the sole Honored One of the Three Realms, should I fear the foolish Devadatta?
"This matter is not so.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Do not see the fool, do not hear his voice, Nor dwell together with the fool."
"Dwelling with the foolish is difficult, like living together with an enemy;
one should choose those with whom to dwell, as if meeting with one's own kin.

When a person lives in this world, they should dwell with those who are wise. When going out, they should have a pleasant countenance; when returning, they should share in mutual joy. They should treat one another with respect, no different from a father, an elder brother, or one's own body. Just as the hearts and minds of close kin are sincere and profound, so should such mutual respect lead to the state of *asaṃskṛta* (the unconditioned).
Therefore it is said: One should choose with whom to dwell, as if meeting with one's own kin.
Thus, one should associate with those who are learned and likewise uphold the precepts;
such persons are the highest among men, like the moon among the stars.

Therefore, one should attend upon those who are learned and likewise those who uphold the precepts. Such learned beings understand that the world is impermanent and clearly discern the three realms of existence; they know the retributions of this life and future lives, and they know for themselves that they are fully endowed with all virtues. They constantly associate with noble persons who have achieved ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation.
It is said: For this reason, one should cultivate much learning as well as maintain the precepts.

Such a person is supreme among men, like the moon among the multitude of stars. While the fivefold Dharma-body has not yet been fully perfected, they cause it to become complete; standing alone and most honored within the great assembly, they have no equal. They are like the bright moon among the multitude of stars, whose radiance shines afar beyond compare.
Therefore it is said: "Such a person is supreme among men, like the moon among the stars. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, "The Chapter on Kinsmen," from the second volume of the *Udānavarga*.
[End of] Volume Twenty-two of the *Udānavarga*. Volume Twenty-three begins.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-seven: On Nirvāṇa Just as a tortoise hides its six limbs, The bhikṣu should restrain his thoughts and perceptions.
Without attachment and without harming others, one attains *nirvāṇa* beyond all verbal expression.

Just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs, so too does the bhikṣu who restrains his thoughts. Like that divine tortoise who fears for its life—should it encounter an enemy, it withdraws its six limbs within its shell and reflects within itself:

"If I do not withdraw these six limbs, I shall be captured by a hunter; my head may be decapitated, my front left or right legs may be wounded, my hind left or right feet may be severed, or my tail may be destroyed. If I do not guard myself now, my death is certain beyond doubt."
The practice of a bhikṣu is likewise: fearing and loathing birth and death, he restrains his distracted thoughts and constantly reflects to himself:

"Though one has attained human birth, the time remaining is but brief; if I do not restrain myself now, I shall allow the evil Māra Pāpīyān, the Māra of sensual dust, and the sovereign son of heaven to gain the advantage over me."
Therefore it is said: "As the tortoise hides its six limbs, so the bhikṣu restrains his thoughts.

To be without reliance and without harming others, and to attain nirvāṇa beyond verbal expression—this means not relying on the various fetters, attachments, wrong actions, or perversions. If one wishes to rely upon anything, one should rely only on the Noble Truths; if one wishes to reach a state of peace and arrive at that goal, it is like a person long afflicted by illness, emaciated and bedridden, lying in their own excrement and unable to move, or like one who is so extremely aged and frail as to be unable to rise or sit up, requiring a strong man to support them under both armpits, desiring to reach a place of safety and arrive there.

The analogy for the various classes of sentient beings is likewise so: their faculties are dull and dark, and they do not apply themselves with great diligence toward profound meanings. Even if they encounter a virtuous friend and find a place of reliance, they gradually manage to escape the realm of birth and death. For this reason, the World-Honored One expounded the teaching for future generations: do not rely on birth and death to give rise to a mind of malice; by not relying and not harming, one then accomplishes the traces of the Path.
Therefore it is said: "Without dependence, one does no harm to others.

That which is extinguished and beyond verbal expression is like a blazing fire whose flames are fierce; it burns away the mountains, wilds, trees, and branches and leaves until nothing remains, and once the fire is extinguished, there is no further sign of its fierce glow.

Ordinary people are just like this: with the blazing fire of greed, the blazing fire of hatred, and the blazing fire of delusion, they burn away their roots of merit and goodness until they are forever exhausted and gone. Having thus lost their own blessings, they further prevent others from reaching the ultimate goal.
If one attains arhatship, all defilements are exhausted; the fires of lust, anger, and delusion are never seen again, and having attained the Way oneself, one is further able to deliver others.
Therefore it is said: "Nirvana is beyond words."
Patience is the foremost; the Buddha has declared Nirvana to be supreme.
One who harbors no burning afflictions and does not harm others is a true śramaṇa.

When Śākyamuni Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva, he dwelt in deep mountains in uninhabited places, toiling his spirit and mortifying his body to practice patience; internally binding his own mind, no manifold signs arose.

At that time, King Kālābu was out on an excursion for recreation, accompanied by his palace ladies and court maids, delighting himself with the five kinds of music. Playing the lute and the harp, they performed songs and instrumental music at their leisure and will; becoming weary from listening to the music, he fell asleep immediately.

The palace attendants and court ladies each hurried away to gather exquisite flowers; from afar they saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree, his countenance upright and beautiful with the color of a peach blossom. All who beheld him were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, like the newly risen sun whose light shines everywhere, or like the moon in the sky surrounded by stars and towering peaks.
When the maidservants saw him, they rushed toward him and knelt, each standing on one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva slowly opened his eyes and gazed upon them with dignified and composed bearing; he gradually led them forward and preached the sublime Dharma to them.

“Unchaste conduct is impure; the outflows (āsrava) are a great affliction. For a person whose body is defiled by craving and desire, one will later fall among birds and beasts, such as pigeons and sparrows; being foul, filthy, and impure, one falls into the evil destinies. This is not that which is studied by the noble ones or true persons.”
"Sisters, you should know!
As for sexual desire, one shall receive the retribution of being burned in fire-chariots and glowing coals.
In this way, the Bodhisattva used countless skillful means to speak of the defilement of desire.

At that time, King Kalmāṣapāda awoke from his sleep and looked around; not seeing the assembly of court ladies, he immediately drew his sharp sword, mounted a swift horse, and galloped forth to search for them. After a long while, he finally saw them from afar: the Bodhisattva’s countenance was serene and majestic as he sat surrounded by the court ladies.
The king thought to himself: "This man is so handsome, a rarity in this world; he must have engaged in amorous dalliance with my ladies."
Internally giving rise to a mind of anger, resentment, and malice, his fury blazed so fiercely that he disregarded all reason and stepped forward directly to ask:
"You are a practitioner of the arts here; have you attained the first dhyāna?"
He replied, "No, Great King!"
He asked again:

"Have you attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
He replied, “No, Great King.”
The King said to him:
"You are now here studying the arts of the Way, yet you have not attained even one of these various virtues; why remain here wasting your days and months?"
The Bodhisattva replied,
"The reason I have abandoned my family estate to study here is that I wish to cultivate the concentration of forbearance.
The King then thought to himself again:

"This person has studied under me for a long time; seeing that my countenance was stern, he perceived the intensity of my anger and thus reported to me that I was practicing patience. I shall now test him to see whether this is indeed the case."

Now, as for the method of testing patience, one cannot know it through food, drink, delicacies, or the performance of music and dance; rather, it is through the afflictions of fierce anger and piercing pain that wound the flesh that its manifest verification is known.
The king said to the seer, "If you truly practice patience, quickly extend your right hand; I wish to test it.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva joyfully extended it. Then the king, his anger reaching its peak and disregarding the consequences in future lives, immediately drew a sharp sword and severed the right hand, followed by the left hand. He then cut off the right foot and then the left foot, and sliced off the ears and the nose. The king asked the seer:
"What do you seek now? The seer replied, "I am currently practicing patience without abandoning it for even a moment;
even if the King were now to take my body and crush it into pieces as small as mustard seeds, I would never regress or lose my compassionate patience."

When that lady, with a mind defiled by anger and hatred, disfigured my body, immeasurable blood flowed from it; now that I have attained patience and been empowered, milk flows from all the pores of my wounds. It is for this reason that I practice patience, taking this as proof.

Not far from there, several hundred other sages were practicing the Way; hearing that this Bodhisattva had been reviled by the king, they all came running to him, surrounding him and inquiring after his well-being:
"We wonder, O sage, whether your pain is not too severe?"
He replied, "No. The various worthies and seers asked again:
"You have now divided your body into seven parts; how can you say that there is no pain?

The Bodhisattva replied, "If the mind suffers while the body does not, one falls into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; if the body suffers while the mind does not, one attains the Unsurpassed, Most Perfect Enlightenment."
At that time, each of the sages exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
The patience of the divine seers is supreme and unsurpassed; it is swift and sharp-witted, nourishing one's merit, and its vow will surely bear fruit before long."
Therefore it is said: "Patience is the foremost.

When the Buddha says that Nirvāṇa is supreme, he means that among all dharmas, nothing is more subtle and wondrous than Nirvāṇa. Now, Nirvāṇa is without birth, aging, illness, or death; it is tranquil, non-active, and free from the notions of arising and ceasing. Among all dharmas, there is nothing superior to it.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddha says that Nirvana is supreme. As for those who do not harbor the fever of affliction:

they abandon their homes and renounce their wives and children; they eliminate the five desires and discard the eight worldly concerns; disregarding worldly glory, they leave the household life to cultivate the Way. Why, then, would one cause distress and heat to sentient beings therein?
Therefore it is said: "One should not harbor the fever of affliction.

As for one who harms others while claiming to be a śramaṇa: a true śramaṇa should accord with the primary meaning [of his vocation], following the dharma of a śramaṇa without transgressing the proper order; he should be free from hatred, envy, deceit, or fraud toward others, protecting them as he would himself, and should not fail to follow the instructions that lead to progress in learning.
Therefore it is said: "One who harms others is a śramaṇa.
One's speech should not be coarse or harsh; what one says should be eloquent.
If one of little learning engages in debate, one will instead suffer defeat at the hands of the opponent.
Regarding the instruction "one should not speak roughly or harshly," the Buddha, while in the world, taught the Dharma to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana, today! When preaching the Dharma, one should preach it in accordance with the Dharma."

Regarding the principle that there must be no admixture of extraneous matters therein: when expounding the True Dharma, one’s mind and intentions must be upright; one must not look left or right, nor should one ever engage in frivolous talk on matters of no urgency.
Why is this so? For coarse speech abounds in flaws and rifts; later, when one receives another form, one will have a hundred heads in a single body, no different from that bhikṣu Kāpiśa.
Therefore it is said: "One's speech should not be coarse or harsh. Regarding that which is said to be "fit for eloquence" (*pratibhāna*):

one who knows the celestial bodies, geography, and the variations of the stars from which portents and anomalies arise; who is proficient in the six arts (*ṣaḍaṅga-vidyā*) and thoroughly versed in the classics; yet who acts without cause and is thus suspected by the wise—if such a person is summoned and reproached, their anger increases manifold. One should not associate with such a person as this; therefore it is said, "that which is spoken should be fit for eloquence."

When those of little learning engage in debate and are instead defeated and humbled by their opponents, the practice of judging right and wrong among people has long existed. "What I have said is correct; what you have said is incorrect"—as they thus vie for superiority and inferiority, anger arises. This is just like two people slandering the Buddha, one of whom has received the teachings but does not examine them with care.
One person lacks faith and has dull faculties;

these two types of people receive the seeds of rebirth as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals. Even if they are born as humans, their six sense organs will be incomplete and their speech will be stammering.
Therefore it is said: When one of little learning engages in debate, he is instead defeated and subjugated by the other.
Frequently giving rise to afflictions within himself, he is like a broken vessel;
transmigrating through birth and death again and again, he remains submerged for long without hope of escape.

"Repeatedly giving rise to afflictions oneself is like that broken vessel. This means that just as a person clings to folly until death without reforming, being bound by fetters and attachments, possessed by inverted and chaotic thoughts, and entangled by false views and deceit—just as a broken vessel leaks out its contents so that nothing remains fit for use, and becomes defiled by dust and grime—therefore it is said: "Repeatedly giving rise to afflictions oneself is like that broken vessel."

Regarding the phrase "repeatedly transmigrating through birth and death, long submerged with no time of emergence": if one does not contemplate beforehand, one will inevitably suffer its calamities. It is like a potter’s wheel, revolving without ceasing; dwelling long within birth and death, it is difficult to achieve liberation, for which there is no adequate analogy. Therefore, it is said: "Repeatedly transmigrating through birth and death, long submerged with no time of emergence."

If one does not afflict oneself, like a vessel that is complete and sturdy, one will thus reach Nirvāṇa, forever free from the obscuration of dust and defilement. Regarding "if one does not afflict oneself, like a vessel that is complete and sturdy":

if one can be self-disciplined, not giving rise to various attachments, and removing all fetters and bonds, one shall then attain the faculty of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñānendriya*), as well as the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Just as a complete vessel is capable of holding [its contents], those who see it cannot fail to love and delight in it. Therefore it is said: "If one does not afflict oneself, like a vessel that is complete and sturdy."

Thus, reaching up to *nirvāṇa*, there is forever no dust, defilement, or obscuration. When a person is free from these blemishes and impurities, they attain the state of extinction, *nirvāṇa*, which is eternally tranquil and eternally stilled, where nothing arises or ceases. Therefore it is said: "Thus reaching *nirvāṇa*, there is forever no dust, defilement, or obscuration."
Health is the supreme benefit; contentment is the supreme wealth;
knowing one's kin is the supreme friend; Nirvana is the supreme bliss. Regarding "health is the supreme benefit":
in this world, there are many people who have few ailments from their youth, all of which result from the retributive fruits of their past lives.

In the past, there were two merchant travelers who braved perilous terrain to seek their livelihood in another country. Before many days had passed, they had accumulated countless riches. One man, by the turn of events, suddenly encountered a grave illness;
his entire fortune was exhausted in treating the ailment, and though he was impoverished and critically ill, he received no cure. The other man remained free of illness and spent no wealth;
yet, despite having secured great profit, he harbored resentment and complained: [The text continues with the second man’s lamentation regarding the loss of his companions and the hardships endured.]
"What I have gained now is not even worth mentioning.
Having returned home safely without any loss, he lamented day and night over his failure to obtain wealth. His kinsmen exhorted him, saying to the merchant:
"You have now arrived home safely and free from illness; why do you wail and cry out that you have gained no profit?"
"To possess a body and preserve one's life is the supreme among treasures.
Therefore it is said: "Freedom from illness is the foremost benefit;
contentment is the greatest wealth. As stated in the Buddha’s Vinaya Piṭaka, there are two types of people in the world who are difficult to satisfy.
What are these two? First, obtaining wealth and squandering it; second, obtaining wealth and hoarding it deeply.
Even if the heavens were to rain down the seven treasures upon Jambudvīpa until this world was filled with them, these two types of people would still remain unsatisfied.

Those who have not severed their desires are greedily attached to wealth and goods; having acquired them, they seek more again, never knowing contentment. Only those who tread the Path clearly understand that all things are impermanent and that worldly phenomena are not real; thus, they disregard such treasures, understanding that they are illusory transformations that cannot endure for long.
It is like sparks seen when striking flint, or a flash of lightning passing before the eyes; such is the nature of change and transformation, which never remains still.
Therefore it is said: "Contentment is the supreme wealth."
Regarding the knowledge that kin are the foremost friends: people universally recognize that kinship is rooted in sincerity; only when trust precedes righteousness can one dwell together.

It is like the story of a man whose affection was so profound that he attended only to his friends and did not speak with his own brothers. When an official sent to arrest him arrived, the man, intoxicated with wine, killed the official’s messenger. He then fled to seek refuge with his friend, recounting the full truth of his situation:
"I am now in peril, with nowhere to set foot; only by your acceptance of me may I escape this distress."
When his friends heard this, they were all struck with astonishment and said:

"Alas! Your great matter cannot be kept hidden; you should simply return home at once and no longer linger here. If your deed becomes exposed, our guilt will not be small. You have brothers and a flourishing clan—why do you turn against us, your own flesh and blood?"
Upon hearing this, the man immediately returned home and prostrated himself before his brothers, surrendering his body and life; he then candidly confessed the transgressions he had committed.
When his kinsmen heard of this, they all comforted him, saying:
"Do not be afraid; we shall devise skillful means to ensure you are spared from this calamity."

The five types of kinsmen gathered like clouds; they prepared their carriages and traveled, each proceeding on his way to the borders of another kingdom. There they established residences where they treated one another with mutual respect and hospitality far exceeding that in their own country; their wealth and treasures flourished daily, and their attendants were beyond counting.
Therefore it is said: "Knowing one's kin is the foremost friendship.

Regarding "Nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss": within Nirvāṇa there is ultimately no suffering or affliction; the various fetters of worldly toil are forever non-existent, having been brought to rest and extinguished. Therefore it is said: "Nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss."
"Hunger is the foremost affliction; action is the foremost suffering.
One who knows this as it truly is finds Nirvāṇa to be the foremost bliss.

Regarding "hunger is the foremost affliction": formerly, King Bimbisāra was imprisoned in a deep dungeon by his son Ajātaśatru. Cut off from news of the outside world and deprived of provisions, he remained there in hunger and distress, with no one to whom he could appeal for help.
The King suddenly reflected, bringing the Buddha to mind and recollecting what had been previously taught; he then spoke these verses within the prison:
"The most supreme teaching, Spreads forth without limit; The world transmits and practices it together, Truly never wearying of it."
"Like that which is peerless, the excellent teaching he has proclaimed asks: when one is oppressed by bodily suffering, what exceeds the affliction of hunger?
Among all forms of suffering, none is greater than hunger; therefore it is said: 'Hunger is the foremost affliction.'"

Regarding the fact that action is the foremost suffering: when a person dwells in the world, their aspirations differ and what they practice varies. The severity of hunger, cold, and diligent toil cuts to the very core of one's being. If a person receives a physical form, they must endure the affliction of dwelling in the dark chamber of the womb; furthermore, upon descending into this world, there is the distress of bodily injury. When all the sensory faculties are complete, one will inevitably be beset by decline, death, old age, and sickness. Once the body receives [the retribution] and the spirit follows, one must then undergo the rewards and punishments of good and evil; this is brought about by the actions one has created.
Therefore it is said: "Action is the foremost suffering.

One who knows this as it truly is [realizes] that Nirvana is the foremost happiness. When a person practices the path seeking eternal stillness and eternal liberation from all afflictions, they dwell securely in the unconditioned, free once again from the affliction of various pains and sufferings; therefore it is said: "One who knows this as it truly is [realizes] that Nirvana is the foremost happiness."
Those who incline toward the good are few; those who incline toward evil are many.
One who knows this as it truly is should swiftly seek *nirvāṇa*.

In the world, those who cultivate goodness are few; though one may practice virtue, their aspirations may not be fulfilled. Even if one should possess all wholesome deeds, at that time the various devas regard humans alone as the place where goodness resides, while humans regard the heavens as the hall of merit.
As it is said in a miscellaneous sutra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The devas, knowing for themselves that the five auspicious omens were about to arrive, all gathered together like clouds.
He then addressed those sons of heaven, saying:

“May you, passing away from here, be reborn in a good destination; reaching that place and arriving here, may you swiftly obtain excellent benefit, and through obtaining such benefit, may you abide in the unconditioned.
At that time, a bhikṣu came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One?”
“The devas in their excellent abodes have swiftly attained wholesome benefit and dwell securely in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the meaning of these three phrases?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

“Endowed with the faculties of the path, he has shaved off his hair and beard within the True Dharma, donned the three dharma-robes, taken no pleasure in family life, and gone forth to study the Way.”
"This, O bhikṣus, is called the excellent abode of the devas.
What is dwelling in the unconditioned?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"To attain the contemplation and discernment of the Four Noble Truths—
this, O bhikṣus, is what is called [the path]."
"The devas dwell securely in the unconditioned.
Those who practice the Way and cultivate goodness while in the world are few; those who incline toward the good are few.
Why is it that those who incline toward evil are so numerous? What is the reason for this?

Among the various classes of sentient beings, those who cultivate evil are many; they do not recognize the Buddha, nor the Dharma, nor the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Furthermore, they fail to distinguish between good and evil, or the beautiful and the ugly, planting only the seeds for rebirth in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. From darkness they enter further darkness, with no prospect of escape, like a blind man holding a candle to illuminate others while remaining unenlightened himself.
Therefore it is said: "Those who incline toward evil are many.

One who knows this as it truly is and swiftly seeks *nirvāṇa*—for people differ in their capacity for benefit and speed of awakening—may awaken upon hearing the teaching, or may attain understanding by beholding its form. For this reason, the Sage disseminates various teachings; he administers medicine according to the illness and the individual, never in vain. Among them, those of sharp faculties observe that the myriad transformations of the world are difficult to endure in common with others; they seek the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) above all, as if their hair were on fire. Why is this so?
That place is empty, still, secluded, and peaceful; it eternally accords with the void, clarifying the spirit so that it remains unmoving.
Therefore it is said: "He who knows this as it truly is shall swiftly seek nirvāṇa."
There is a cause for birth in a good destination; there is a condition for birth in an evil realm;
there is a condition for parinirvāṇa—all such things likewise have conditions.
Regarding "there is a cause for birth in a good destination," what constitutes its condition?

What is called "condition" refers to generosity, precepts, learning, wisdom, and reflection; the deportment of a lay follower of pure faith, the deportment of one who has gone forth, and the deportment of a great practitioner; and the relinquishing of unwholesome conduct. These are the bases for proceeding toward the Path through causes and conditions; therefore it is said: "By means of causes, one is born in a favorable realm."
Regarding those who have conditions for rebirth in the evil realms, what are the causes and conditions?

It is like a person who harbors hatred and envy within, whose mind of generosity does not open, and who violates the precepts by killing and taking what is not given; unable to reform such tenfold unwholesome actions, they ultimately fall and descend into the three miserable paths. Therefore it is said: "There are conditions for rebirth in the evil realms."

Regarding those who attain *parinirvāṇa* through conditions: the *nirvāṇa* spoken of is entirely by means of the true path of the noble ones (*ārya*), severing all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proceeding toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Apart from this category of the noble ones, it cannot be attained. It is just as the non-Buddhist Brahmins say among themselves:
"In the world there are no causes and conditions, nor is there beginning or end; that which exists exists spontaneously, and that which does not exist exists spontaneously."
How do we know this is so?
It is like thorns growing in a vast wilderness; could there have been a skilled craftsman who fashioned those sharp needles?
Or consider deer among the various beasts and birds perching in trees; their coats are of diverse colors and their forms are different—could anyone have painted their bodies?

If one examines their categories, the natures of their sensations differ: the nature of earth is inherently soft, while the nature of stone is inherently hard; how could there be anyone who creates this hardness or softness?
All of these arise spontaneously, without causes or conditions.
"Those of such a kind have been obstinately deluded for a long time, and they continue to instruct one another without ceasing even to this day. For this reason, the World-Honored One said:
'That which occurs has its conditions; it does not come from empty suffering.'"
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does this occur?

When sentient beings practice the ten wholesome deeds, the ground where they dwell becomes level and even; at that time, pits, ravines, high embankments, thorns, and overgrown weeds naturally become leveled and smooth.

However, when there are sentient beings who practice evil, then the entire earth everywhere produces thorns, high embankments, and deep chasms, and venomous snakes and poisonous insects breed and multiply in great numbers—all of which results from the accumulation of evil in their previous lives.
Therefore it is said: "All such things have their conditions.
The deer returns to the wild; the bird returns to the void; meaning returns to discernment;
the True Person returns to extinction."

In the past, when the World-Honored One was at the Indrasailaguha near the Mango Grove in the realm of Magadha, he beheld with his pure, tranquil, and stainless divine eye a herd of deer that had encountered a hunter; filled with alarm, they fled toward the midst of steep and rugged terrain.

At that time, the World-Honored One again used his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and saw a flock of birds avoiding a net by soaring high and rushing toward the void. With his divine eye, the Tathāgata further saw a bhikṣu whose speech was eloquent and whose meaning was gentle and fluent; that very night, he contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), thoroughly investigating them in both forward and reverse order from beginning to end, which the Tathāgata’s divine eye likewise observed. Furthermore, he saw another bhikṣu who, throughout the entire night, repeatedly contemplated and entered the meditative concentration of liberation (*vimukti-dhyāna-samādhi*). As the night drew to a close and the darkness was about to vanish, he attained parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*); this too was witnessed by the Tathāgata’s supernatural vision.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the causes and conditions from which this meaning arose, wishing to cause his disciples to propagate his teaching and to cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world, so that future generations of living beings might behold its great illumination, the World-Honored One then spoke these verses:
"The deer returns to the wild; The bird returns to the void; Meaning returns to discernment;
The True Person returns to extinction."
"Without a mind of indolence, nor reaching a state of cowardice,
one who desires to reach Nirvāṇa shall burn away all fetters and attachments.
Regarding "without a mind of indolence, nor reaching a state of cowardice," as stated in the *Madhyama Āgama* (Middle Length Discourses), a sutra of the Buddha, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This Dharma is practiced by those who are diligent, not by those who are indolent; yet, if one is indolent by nature and cannot advance oneself, how could one possibly attain Nirvana through skillful means?"
It is just as if there were a person whose nature was inherently timid and weak, and who had never possessed two eyes; how could such a person intend to sleep out in the open wilderness?

With many thieves and bandits and difficult roads to traverse, one who wishes to cross over those perilous places must have strong men and heroic warriors to achieve self-deliverance and abide in peace without exertion;
yet one who harbors folly, a perverse nature, and believes in inverted views will ultimately never be able to cross over those perilous places.
"One must possess the eye of wisdom and the methods of the noble ones before one can reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore it is said: "One should not, with a lazy mind or a timid spirit, fail to reach the goal; desiring to attain *nirvāṇa*, one must burn away all fetters and attachments."
"Monks, bale out the boat quickly; by baling it out, it shall become light.
Having forever severed the passions of greed, you shall thereafter reach Nirvāṇa.
In the past, there was a monk who wished to cross a river and encountered a dilapidated boat that was old, rotten, and unrepaired. At that time, the boatman said to the monk:
"The Daoist wishes to go somewhere; you may drain this stored water with your own strength. Once the boat is lightened and you are safe, where will you not succeed?
At that time, the bhikṣu exerted all the strength of his suckling years and drained the water from the boat until it was exhausted, whereby he was able to cross over to the opposite bank.
He adjusted his robes, composed his demeanor, and gradually approached the World-Honored One. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
The Tathāgata, knowing that this person was ready to be delivered, gazed upon him with a steady, penetrating look; such a power is not within the reach of Pratyekabuddhas or Arhats.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"O bhikṣu, bale out the boat quickly; by baling it out, it shall become light.
Sever forever the passions of greed, and only then will you reach Nirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You now worry about immediate hardships, yet you instead fear the taboos of future lives. A boat is the common feature of this perilous world;

it is used as a provisional means to ferry sentient beings across without weariness. Its form is like a vessel filled with pure impurities—why not cast it aside? By emptying out the foul leakage of disease and severing lust, anger, and delusion, one may board the vessel of the noble ones and reach Nirvāṇa."
"What I have was originally non-existent; what I originally had is now non-existent.
It is neither non-existent nor existent, and as it is now, it cannot be apprehended.

Regarding "What I have was originally non-existent; what I originally had is now non-existent": the various views held by the heterodox teachers and followers of different schools differ, each claiming their own position to be correct. [They claim] that my original surname was such-and-such and my given name was such-and-such; though existing, it is non-existent, and though non-existent, it exists; it arises spontaneously from non-existence. Therefore it is said: "What I have was originally non-existent; what I originally had is now non-existent."
