"Neither non-existent nor existent": "neither non-existent" refers to the past; "nor existent" refers to the future; and "as it cannot be apprehended in the present" refers to the present.
How could those who cling to folly depart from the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, yet follow this deviant path without reforming themselves? Why is this so?
It is because they do not understand the supreme meaning of the Way of Nirvāṇa; they believe in false views and do not believe in Nirvāṇa.

Therefore it is said: "That which I had as a basis no longer exists; that which once existed as a basis is now gone. It is neither non-existent nor existent, for it cannot be apprehended in the present."

The Truth is difficult to see and unshakable; one should observe it well and discern it. One should examine the source of the exhaustion of craving; this is called the limit of suffering. Regarding "the Truth is difficult to see and unshakable;

one should observe it well and discern it": the extinction of *nirvāṇa* is supremely subtle; it is formless and invisible. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) shift and do not remain still, but that which is formless cannot be moved or shifted. Only the Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, by means of the eye of wisdom, can observe it well, discern it, and understand each point with certainty. Therefore, it is said: "The Truth is difficult to see and unshakable; one should observe it well and discern it."

One should examine the source of the exhaustion of craving; this is what is called "the limit of suffering. Knowing that the root of craving gives rise to manifold afflictions, one extricates oneself from within them, severing them forever without remainder. Therefore it is said: "One should examine the source of the exhaustion of craving; this is what is called 'the limit of suffering.'"
"Sever craving and eliminate desire; exhaust the river so that no sign of flow remains. One who can clearly understand the root of this craving—this is called reaching the limit of suffering.

To "sever craving and eliminate desire": craving is a disease, the very foundation of manifold afflictions. By uprooting the source of craving, its branches and leaves will not flourish. Having severed it from within oneself so that nothing remains, the root of desire is extinguished of its own accord and shall never arise again. From craving, the flow of desire arises, just as a swift river sweeps away living beings; hundreds of thousands of millions lose their life-force and find no means of salvation. Once the river is exhausted, sentient beings may come and go without the threat of harm. Therefore, it is said: "Sever craving and eliminate desire; exhaust the river so that no sign of flow remains."

"To clearly understand this root of craving is what is called reaching the end of suffering. Craving constitutes the essential substance, desire constitutes the branches and leaves, and delusion constitutes the moisture and sap. If a practitioner of the path contemplates with sublime insight and can sever this [craving], they transcend the limit of suffering. Therefore it is said: "To clearly understand this root of craving is what is called reaching the end of suffering."
To see and truly see, to hear and truly hear,
and to know and truly know— this is called reaching the limit of suffering.
Why is it said that one sees and truly sees?
Why is this? It is because one does not see reality, yet it is not that one does not see.

For example, suppose there is another person who, when seeing forms with the eye, discerns the fundamental nature of form and contemplates the conditions of consciousness such that no conceptual attachment arises.

To see without truly seeing refers to those deluded and ignorant people who, upon seeing forms with their eyes, give rise to visual consciousness; although they see, it is not the same as not seeing at all.
Why is this? It is because visual consciousness arises from seeing with the eye.
Therefore it is said: "One sees, and one sees what is real."
"To hear and yet truly hear" means that when a person hears a subtle and wondrous sound, they do not give rise to conscious attachment; therefore it is said, "to hear and yet truly hear."

To know by knowing it as it truly is, is as follows: suppose there is another person who discriminates within the body of consciousness, extracting the roots of goodness and abandoning the roots of unwholesomeness, such that all defilements are forever exhausted and no new ones are created. Therefore, it is said: "To know by knowing it as it truly is—this is called the limit of suffering."
I-niṃ mi-ni, ta-ppe da-ra-ppe, ma-śe gau-śe, all vi-rā-ri;
this is called the end of suffering.
In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the Dharma to the Four Heavenly Kings, two of them understood the language of Madhyadeśa while two did not.
To those two who did not understand, he spoke in the language of the country of Tāmraliptī to proclaim the Four Noble Truths.

Although he spoke in the language of Tāmraliptī, one of them understood and one did not; to the one who still did not understand, he further spoke in the language of Mālava, namely *maśe gauśe sarva-vilīra*.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all attained realization of the Four Noble Truths; immediately upon their seats, they obtained the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Their sense of self was extinguished, their perceptions ceased; all sensations became cool and serene, and all conditioned activities were forever stilled. Consciousness and perception no longer arose.

This is called the limit of suffering. Regarding "one who is bodiless extinguishes their perceptions": this body is not solid; it is subject to decay and destruction. This body is not firm and must inevitably disintegrate. Only the Dharma-body of the five factors is truly solid. Since the mind arises from perception, and perception gives rise to myriad ailments, one who can extinguish that perception accords with the true Way. Therefore, it is said: "One who is bodiless extinguishes their perceptions."

Regarding "all pains attain coolness": these classes of sentient beings wander through the ocean of birth and death, casting themselves into rivers, lakes, and the four great waters without ever feeling satiated. This arises because they suffer distress due to the root of pain; that sentient beings harm one another and kill each other all stems from pain, which leads to such calamities. Only the wise do not create such pain; therefore it is said, "all pains attain coolness."

Regarding "the permanent cessation of all formations" (*saṃskāra*): a person's reception of consciousness arises from formations; formations grow and develop into myriad ailments. Wholesome formations lead to the wholesome, and unwholesome formations lead to the unwholesome. The wise person practices formations without creating the root of formations. Therefore it is said: "the permanent cessation of all formations."

"Perceptions and thoughts do not arise again" means that perceptions and thoughts flow and race about, giving rise to ten thousand kinds of afflictions. Therefore, the sage restrains his consciousness so that it does not scatter. When people give rise to consciousness, they mostly do so from the root of delusion; thus, one uses three hundred medicines to extinguish the hundred types of consciousness—using one hundred medicines in the morning, one hundred at noon, and one hundred in the evening—to extinguish perceptions and thoughts.

Furthermore, one uses the methods of the untainted noble practice and the stage of "Summit Patience" (mūrdha-kṣānti) to extinguish perceptions and thoughts. For this reason, it is said: "Perceptions and thoughts do not arise again."

Where there is dependence, there is movement; where there is movement, there is no cessation. When there is no cessation, one knows there is no weariness. Because one knows there is no cessation, one does not perceive past, future, or present. Because there is no past, future, or present, there is no birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because there is no birth-and-death, there is no sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction. From this aggregate of suffering arise all manner of maladies; these arise from habitual proliferation and are enveloped by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In the practice of cultivation, a person must necessarily have something upon which to rely.

That which is called "reliance" refers to the category of things with form, such as mountains, rivers, rocks, and cliffs—whatever is perceived by the eyes is all considered a reliance. One who can extinguish these [attachments] accords with the primary truth (*paramārtha*). Within the primary truth, one perceives no coming or going, nor any circling about;

because there is no coming, going, or circling, there is no birth and death. Those who do not understand this give rise to worldly toil (*rajas*); birth, old age, sickness, and death increase day by day, from which arise myriad forms of sorrow, grief, and affliction. Seeking their source, one finds no beginning; they revolve and mutually produce the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the suffering body. That which can extinguish these is none other than the Way of Nirvāṇa.

There may be bhikṣus who have arising, reality, and conditioned existence; there may be bhikṣus who have no arising, no reality, and no conditioned existence. A bhikṣu who does not practice for the sake of the unconditioned likewise has no arising. If one has no arising, no reality, and no conditioned existence, then it is by reason of arising, reality, and conditioned existence that the unconditioned is spoken of.
If sentient beings were free from this affliction, the Tathāgata would never have spoken of the bliss of extinction and nirvāṇa.
Knowing the beginning and end of birth, one understands the conditioned and the unconditioned;
though enshrouded by birth and old age, the decaying state is exceedingly difficult to restrain.

Regarding the knowledge of the beginning and end of birth, it is as explained in that *Sūtra* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, specifically in the discourse on the beginning and end of Great Affection (*Mahāmaitrī*), where the Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there were no such thing as birth, I would not have taught the Dharma of birth to others, even down to the various classes of beings such as fish and water-dwellers; nor would I have taught it to dragons possessing the nature of dragons, ghosts possessing the nature of ghosts, devas possessing the nature of devas, or humans possessing the nature of humans."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
Because I know there is birth, I speak of birth.
Therefore it is said: "Knowing the beginning and end of birth."

To know the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) by means of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) means that it is formless and imageless, and cannot be perceived within the phenomena of change; therefore, it is said: "One knows the unconditioned by means of the conditioned."

Regarding "being enveloped by birth and old age": when a person dwells in the world, they know that with aging comes death; being pressed by these two matters, one cannot escape their affliction. Therefore it is said: "enveloped by birth and old age."

That which is in decay and exceedingly difficult to restrain arises from the various practices of lust, anger, ignorance, pride, jealousy, and resentment; it is driven by old age and sickness and originates from these causes. Therefore it is said: "That which is in decay is exceedingly difficult to restrain."
Without food, life cannot be sustained; who then could refrain from contemplating food?
Indeed, one must first establish food as the priority, and only thereafter can one reach the Way.

Among the myriad classes of sentient beings dwelling in this world, all depend upon food; if a person lacks food, they have no means to practice the Way. Therefore it is said: "Without food, life cannot be sustained."

Who can refrain from reflecting upon food? One who awakens to the fact that this is impermanent, who knows the origin of food with certainty and without doubt, and who practices receiving it without any hesitation—therefore it is said: "Who can refrain from reflecting upon food?"

Food, as a substance, is a phenomenon of the turbid dregs of birth and death; once it takes form, it burdens one with the need for sustenance. Therefore, it is said: "The establishment of food comes first."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I know that the various bases (āyatana) are neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor wind; they are not consciousness, nor space, nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor this world, nor the next world, nor even the places reached by the illumination of the sun and moon. Such categories as these are beyond the reach of causal conditions."

Among them, those with inverted views seek liberation through the sun; the Nirgranthas and others who instruct one another in seeking liberation must enter a chamber sixty cubits deep and one hundred *yojanas* wide, for whoever enters this chamber shall attain liberation.

Having contemplated this meaning, the Buddha, wishing to sever doubts regarding birth and death, wishing to block the inverted conceptions of the Nirgranthas, and wishing to eliminate doubts concerning future lives, spoke of this matter.
"The sun and moon do not shine together; the heterodox and the orthodox do not flourish in competition.
This matter is clear. Therefore, bhikṣus!
I do not speak of wandering through birth and death or of arising and ceasing; this is called the root of the end of suffering."
When the elements of earth, water, and fire [are present], at that time the wind does not blow and light does not shine; thus, its reality is not seen.

Those who are to be transformed by means of their nobility, or those who are to be saved through some assistance—those to be delivered by their noble status do not require the addition of words or sounds; those to be delivered by relying on something else awaken suddenly of their own accord without needing a teacher; and those who are humble and lowly naturally attain awakening. Therefore it is said: "Where light does not shine, its reality is not seen."
"It is not the moon, yet it possesses light; it is not the sun, yet it possesses brilliance.
One who examines this with discerning clarity is truly acting in accordance with the conduct of a brahmin.

Regarding "it is not the moon, yet it possesses light; it is not the sun, yet it possesses brilliance": this is like the light of the sun and moon being obscured by various clouds, such that they cannot widely disseminate their teachings and commands. It is also like the heavens of the Trāyastriṃśa and the Ekaniṣṭha gods, where they illuminate one another with their own radiance without the need for the light of the sun or moon. All of this is brought about by the accumulation of past practices. Therefore, it is said: "It is not the moon, yet it possesses light; it is not the sun, yet it possesses brilliance."

One who observes this with thorough discernment is one who accords with the practice of a brahmin. As for what is called a "brahmin," it is so named because he has transcended the three realms and his conduct is filled with and perfected in virtue; therefore it is said: "One who observes this with thorough discernment accords with the practice of a brahmin."
"Handsome form and composure—by these one attains liberation from all suffering;
neither form nor non-form—by these one attains liberation from all suffering.

The arising of suffering has its root in both the realm of form and the formless realm; one who can escape this suffering shall be liberated from among all sufferings. Therefore it is said: 'Handsome form and composure—by these one attains liberation from all suffering.'"
Ultimately free from fear, Transcending bonds without doubt,
yet not having severed the thorns of sensual desire— how could such a one know that the body is a source of affliction?
Regarding "ultimately free from fear," there are two aspects to this ultimate state:
The first is ultimate through intentional application; the second is ultimate through spontaneity.
When the mind is upright, one does not fear its crookedness; therefore it is said: "Ultimately, there is no fear."

"Transcending bonds and being free from doubt" means that all fetters have been severed and exhausted without remainder. Having long wandered through birth and death, cycling through the five destinies for boundless eons, one was ignorant of the principles of shame, modesty, and disgrace; therefore it is said: "Transcending bonds and being free from doubt."

As long as the thorn of craving for existence has not been severed, how can one know that the body is a source of affliction? Indeed, when people dwell in the world, their practices of the Dharma differ; there are three matters concerning those who have not yet attained the severance of craving for existence:
first, existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); second, existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); and third, existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

What is called the "thorn of desire" is the thorn of the deviant path; it strikes and beats, and its blows are heavy and its damage grave. Therefore it is said: "As long as the thorn of desire has not been severed, how can one know that the body is a source of suffering?"
What is called "ultimate" is that for which the cessation of traces is foremost;
it is the total severance of all conceptual attachments, wherein words and phrases are free from error.

Regarding the statement, "What is called 'ultimate' is that for which the cessation of traces is foremost": what is called "ultimate" is that which is supreme among all dharmas and beyond surpassing; it is the most grievous of ailments, wherein the fetters of attachment and the mind of desire are forever exhausted without remainder. Therefore it is said: "What is called 'ultimate' is that for which the cessation of traces is foremost."

"Having completely severed all conceptualizations and ensuring that words and phrases are not erroneous"—as for what is called "conceptualization," it refers to the conceptualization of desire, the conceptualization of hatred, and the conceptualization of delusion, as stated in the *Miśraka-sūtra* where the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Gautama, you should know!..."

Desire, anger, and delusion—these are the roots of conditioned activity. When all such perceptions have been extinguished without remainder, one no longer gives rise to thoughts or intentions regarding them; thus, the words and phrases one utters are never erroneous.
Why is this so? Because there are practices that reach their ultimate conclusion and those that do not; for this reason, the teachings were established to instruct future generations.
Therefore it is said: "Exhaustively sever all conceptual attachments and thoughts, so that words and phrases are free from error."
Knowing moderation and not knowing moderation: the Most Victorious One abandons conditioned activities and contemplates within himself, like a chick breaking through its shell.

"Knowing moderation and not knowing moderation": moderation refers to conditioned activities; those who do not know moderation long harbor afflictions and are unable to contemplate the Path. Their six sense-faculties are blocked and closed off, such that the meaning of the Dharma cannot pass through. Therefore it is said: "knowing moderation and not knowing moderation."

Regarding those who practice the relinquishment of existence, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the most supreme; he has relinquished the three realms of existence and does not perform further karmic actions. Therefore it is said: "The most supreme relinquishment of the practice of existence."

Internally reflecting upon his own practice, he was like one who breaks through the shell of an egg; as if entering into meditative concentration or non-concentration, he attained the concentrated mind and realized the fruit of the Way.

Just as the species that hatch from eggs or are born from moisture cast off their skins to assume their true forms, so too now does he cast off his former practices to pursue the practice free of outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore it is said: "Just as a chick breaks through its shell, among all gifts the gift of Dharma is supreme;
among all pleasures the pleasure of Dharma is foremost;
among all powers the power of patience is greatest; and the truth of the extinction of craving is wondrous."
Regarding the statement that "among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme": why is it that, among all gifts, the gift of Dharma is considered supreme?

It is because this so-called gift of Dharma is excellent, beautiful, and free from all afflictions; for those sentient beings who hear the Dharma therein, their minds are awakened and there is none who does not attain liberation.

Regarding what is called the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*): if it is sufficient for one person, two people will harbor resentment; thus, the intention behind giving and the resulting matters differ.

For example, when the subtle and wondrous Dharma was preached to King Bimbisāra, eighty thousand devas and twelve thousand Magadhan beings [attained realization]; furthermore, when the subtle and wondrous Dharma was preached within the stone chamber to Śakra Devendra, eighty thousand devas all attained the subtle and wondrous Dharma, their various faculties becoming thoroughly penetrating and free from any form of obstruction. Therefore, it is said that among all gifts, the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is supreme.

Regarding what is called the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), one receives it today and must seek it again tomorrow; however, as for those who seek therein even the path to the heavens, such people hear the Dharma from kalpa to kalpa without end. Therefore it is said: "Of all gifts, the gift of the Dharma is supreme."

Regarding the various forms of pleasure, the supreme among them is the pleasure of the Dharma. Worldly pleasures are the root of distracted thoughts; those who pursue them to the ultimate end create the karma for hell.
As for the pleasure of the Dharma, it flows freely through eloquent exposition so that questions are never obstructed; its clarity of insight and meaning is vast, entering the ears with abundance.
Therefore it is said: "Among all pleasures, the pleasure of the Dharma is supreme.

Regarding the statement that "among all powers, the power of patience is foremost": Long ago, there was a king of a neighboring country who raised an army and mobilized his hosts to attack an enemy state.
His attendants and ministers said to the king, "The neighboring country has raised an army and now approaches us closely; we pray that Your Majesty prepare yourself to join us in the assault."
The king said to his ministers, "This is a minor matter; why must I personally go to face the enemy?
As the bandits drew near and attacked the city gates, the ministers addressed the king:
"The bandits are now outside; Your Majesty should deeply contemplate this matter.
The king told his ministers:
"Although the bandits are outside, there is no need for far-reaching anxiety. They merely attend to their own private interests; why worry about public affairs?"
At that time, the bandits, acting with increasing cruelty, entered the city. Those around him reported, saying:
"The bandits are now drawing near; we do not know what precautions Your Majesty has ultimately taken."
The King said to his ministers, "This matter is so trivial; why should it be reported to me?
At that moment, the Great King of the neighboring state advanced further until he reached the palace hall, whereupon the ministers informed him:
"The king of the neighboring country now oppresses us; we do not know what the Holy One intends. The King replied: "I am now dwelling in this world where change never ceases:

that which rises must surely decline, and meeting is inevitably followed by parting. It would be fitting for me to cast off my robes, alter my appearance according to the manner of a mendicant, and retire alone to the deep mountains. There, contemplating the Way and its Virtue, I may find self-delight."
Should this tyrannical king wish to seize my person and kill my body, I shall not shrink from the transgression.

Why is this so? The ruin of a nation and the loss of its territory all stem from a single individual; if I now undergo death, the myriad people will be free from suffering—would this not be a great blessing for me?
At that time, the king of the enemy state marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and cried out in a loud voice:
"Excellent, excellent, Great King!
From antiquity until now, nothing has ever been like this. Although I have achieved victory, it does not compare to yours; you have opened your heart with great wisdom, disregarding worldly glory."
"From this day forward, you shall return to rule your own kingdom; we shall receive you together with the King in our governance and administration, treating you no differently than ourselves.
Therefore it is said: "Of all powers, the power of patience is supreme."

"The excellence of the Truth of Suffering through the exhaustion of craving": Craving is the root of all fetters. A practitioner training in the Path first severs the fetter of craving, and only thereafter gradually advances toward the restraint of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). Therefore it is said: "The excellence of the Truth of Suffering through the exhaustion of craving. This concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on Nirvāṇa.
*Udānavarga*, Fascicle Twenty-three and Fascicle Twenty-four,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter 28: The Chapter on Contemplation Carefully examine your own flaws and vulnerabilities, so that you do not expose them to others.
Others have their own vulnerabilities, just like the light dust that flies about.

One who skillfully observes their own flaws sees only the faults of others and not their own transgressions; thus they engage in mutual disputes and slander one another. This is like a person winnowing grain: what is light is scattered far away, while what is heavy remains near. Therefore it is said: "Skillfully observe your own flaws so that you do not expose them outwardly; others will have their own flaws, like those flying particles of light dust."
If one claims to be faultless while both [faults] arrive together,
seeing only the flaws of others yet constantly harboring a harmful intent,
one perceives what is distant but fails to see what is near.

Generally, people in this world often deceive themselves by praising their own reputation, claiming that their merit and virtue are peerless in the world, asserting that their practice of precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom is supreme, unique, and without equal; it is for this reason that it is said: "If one claims oneself to be without flaw."

Regarding "when both matters arrive together": this refers to those who engage in gambling, where the one who acts contrary to the rules wins and the one who follows them always loses. It is the same for those who practice the Way and cultivate virtue: they recognize their own faults and do not expose those of others. Therefore it is said: "When both matters arrive together."

"Only seeing the vulnerabilities of others, one constantly harbors a harmful intent": this means that people do not examine themselves but instead focus only on external phenomena—the various unwholesome dharmas and the afflictions of evil. Consequently, they fall into the miserable realms and fail to reach the good destinations, planting the seeds of suffering for hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Therefore it is said: "Only seeing the vulnerabilities of others, one constantly harbors a harmful intent."

Space and earth are each separate from one another; one does not perceive true dharmas, nor does one perceive non-true dharmas. Therefore it is said: "Looking from afar, one does not see what is near."

"Knowing shame is the highest form of longevity; The vulture seizes and strikes out of greed, and the strong man has no fear or restraint; such as these have short lives. Regarding 'knowing shame is the highest form of longevity':

when people live in the world, if they do not know shame or remorse and have nothing to fear or avoid, they are like a violent and unruly ox that has nothing to fear or avoid. Such foolish and deluded people are also like this; they act according to their whims with no sense of fear or restraint. Therefore it is said: 'Knowing shame is the highest form of longevity.'"

"The hawk seizes and strikes because of greed" means that just as a soaring hawk is insatiable in its gluttony and seizes upon people and things without restraint or consideration, so too it is with the various classes of sentient beings; they are greedily attached to wealth and sensual pleasures without ever reaching satisfaction. Therefore, it is said: "The hawk seizes and strikes because of greed."

Regarding "the wrestler who has no fear or restraint": just as that strong man has nothing to fear or find difficult, acting at will amidst the great assembly with none able to equal him, he immediately conceives anger and severs the life-root of anyone who comes to reprimand, admonish, or exhort him. Therefore it is said: "The wrestler has no fear or restraint."

Those whose lives are brief and short-lived are those who, dwelling in this world, hold others in contempt while esteeming themselves; they persist only in inverted views and delusion without awakening, and they encroach upon the property of the Triple Gem, relying on their own arrogance and violence. For such as these, life does not endure long; therefore it is said: "The lives of these people are brief and short."
Knowing shame, one does not exhaust one’s lifespan; constantly seeking pure conduct, with dignified deportment free from deficiency, one should contemplate the truly pure lifespan.

Regarding "knowing shame, one does not exhaust one’s lifespan": that person of shame and remorse is not overly diligent regarding food and clothing. Whatever wealth they obtain, they distribute to others; wearing coarse garments and eating poor food, they do not indulge in adornment. They merely preserve their life in this world, harboring no hope for worldly glory. Therefore it is said: "Knowing shame, one does not exhaust one’s lifespan."

One who constantly seeks pure conduct acts with purity and does not create heterodox factions; their body, speech, and mind are pure, corresponding to the supreme practice. Furthermore, they know external purity, such that their speech is appropriate to the occasion and causes no harm. Therefore it is said: "Constantly seeking pure conduct."
Regarding "one whose deportment is without deficiency": it means to restrain the sense faculties so they do not flow outward in distraction;

therefore it is said, "one whose deportment is without deficiency. One should contemplate true and pure longevity: whether moving or staying, coming or going, speaking words, or taking food and drink to sustain one's life; therefore it is said, "one should contemplate true and pure longevity."
The world is universally blind and dark; those with eyes are but few indeed.
Like flocks of birds falling into a net, rebirth in heaven is not even worth mentioning. Regarding "the world is universally blind and dark":

it is like a person born blind who cannot see beautiful colors or ugly colors, nor level ground or high cliffs. These classes of sentient beings are just the same; covered by lust, anger, and delusion, they do not see good or evil conduct, they do not know what is beautiful or ugly, nor do they understand the teachings of white and black (virtue and non-virtue). Their minds are self-deluded and they do not seek a wholesome state. Therefore, it is said: "The world is universally blind and dark."
Those with eyes who possess but little hearing are as described in the *Dīrgha Āgama* Sūtra, where the Buddha told the brahmin Dīrghanakha:
"In this world, those who cultivate goodness are exceedingly few."

To speak briefly, sentient beings who harbor perverted views outnumber the particles of dust upon the great earth; they do not recognize the Buddha, nor the Dharma, nor the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus, nor their own parents, and furthermore, they cannot distinguish between the honorable and the humble, the high and the low.
Sentient beings who possess right view are like the soil on a fingernail; though their vision is not mistaken, their aspirations and pursuits differ.

They are like the non-Buddhist Brahmins and Nirgranthas, who have left home to study the Way, each claiming their own path to be supreme. Their scriptures are distinct as they seek liberation, yet they cling to folly and their minds are deluded, failing to reach the Great Way; compared to them, those with right view are hardly worth mentioning.
Therefore it is said: "Those with eyes are exceedingly rare.

As for the birds falling into the net: just as a hunter spreads out a net and sets snares to capture birds, obtaining countless species of birds and beasts, while those that escape are but one or two;
so too it is with the multitudes born in the heavens—only one or two obtain the blessings of heaven.
As stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The sentient beings who enter hell are more numerous than the particles of earth; those who pass away from hell and are reborn again in hell, as well as those in the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, are likewise so numerous.
Those sentient beings born in the heavens are like the particles of dust upon a fingernail."
Therefore it is said: "Just as birds fall into a net, so too do those born in heaven.
Observing the laws of worldly decay, they see only the transformation of various forms;
the fool binds himself, enveloped by darkness."

Regarding the contemplation of the laws of decline and decay, one sees only the transformation of various phenomena; for a person dwelling in the world undergoes thousands of turns and ten thousand variations, with their conduct differing accordingly.
There are three realms in the world:
first, the realm of the vessel (the physical environment); second, the realm of the aggregates (the five skandhas); and third, the realm of sentient beings.
What is called the "receptacle world" refers to the trichiliocosm.
The "sentient-being world" refers to the sentient beings of the three realms, the four modes of birth, and the five destinies.
The "aggregate world" refers to the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formlessness.
Regarding the realm of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, why is it said that they are subject to the law of decay?

What is called the law of decay refers to being worn away by lust, anger, and delusion; it is like a merchant traveling a long distance who encounters bandits and loses the wealth and treasures he has acquired, being plundered by those thieves.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise so: they are plundered by lust, anger, and delusion, who rob them of the wealth of their roots of goodness. While all people see that they are wasting away, only a few among billions escape; therefore it is said: "Observing the law of worldly decay, one sees only the transformation of outward appearances."

"The fool binds himself, enveloped by darkness" means that among the many people in the world whose paths of conduct differ, they are constantly bound by two fetters: first, the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), and second, the bonds of the aggregates (*skandha-bandhana*).

Bound by these two matters and shrouded by the veil of ignorance, they are likewise incapable of transcending the stages to realize the fruit, exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) to achieve the state of no-outflow (*anāsrava*).

It is just as a criminal confined in a prison who cannot behold the light of the sun and moon; these classes of sentient beings are also like this, enveloped within the dark chamber of ignorance. Bound by desire, anger, and delusion, it is difficult for them to seek liberation.
Therefore it is said: "The fool binds himself, being enveloped by darkness.

He does not perceive his own conduct; though he observes, there is nothing there. Through such investigation of his nature, he perceives no root of merit at all. Furthermore, even if one possessed the knowledge of others' minds and wished to escape this peril, there would be not a single root of goodness by which to be saved.

It is like a person who has fallen into a deep latrine and been defiled by excrement; another compassionate person, wishing to rescue him from that distress, searches for a clean spot to reach out and pull him out, but after examining everywhere, finds not a single clean place and thus abandons him and departs.
The one free from outflows observes sentient beings, wondering: "Is there even a hair’s breadth of roots of goodness that can be healed?
Having observed them thoroughly, he finds no roots of goodness that can be healed. The Sage thinks to himself: "Alas!
This multitude is in decline; their transgressions are so grave as to reach this state."
Therefore it is said: "One does not perceive even in conditioned formations; though one observes them, they are non-existent.
Sentient beings all possess a self, and because of that, suffering arises.
When each [element] is not seen as such, one does not behold the thorn of false views."

"All sentient beings possess a self; it is for their sake that I experience suffering. In this world, many people harbor perverted views, claiming that the various classes of sentient beings are created by a "self" or arise from a "self.
Furthermore, there are those who say they arise from another or exist because of another.
Therefore it is said: "All sentient beings possess a self; because of that, suffering arises.

As for the phrase "each does not see the other, nor perceive the thorn of wrong views": "each" refers to the non-Buddhist brahmins who do not contemplate right view but instead believe in perverted and inverted doctrines. Therefore it is said: "Each does not see the other, nor perceive the thorn of wrong views."

Contemplating these thorns and their causal conditions, which sentient beings are stained by and attached to—what I have created does not exist in them, and what they have created does not exist in me.

Regarding "contemplating these thorns and their causal conditions": the so-called "thorns" refer to the thorns of wrong views. As for "causal conditions," these are the various distinct realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas, each having different seeds of karma. Therefore, it is said: "contemplating these thorns and their causal conditions."

Sentient beings are stained by and attached to [false views]; non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners strive and toil day and night, each claiming their own [views] to be true while holding perverted and inverted views. Unable to abandon these and proceed upon the correct path, it is for this reason that it is said: "Sentient beings are stained by and attached to."

Regarding the statement "I create, but that does not exist; that creates, but I do not exist," each party claims to be correct while mutually contradicting one another. Among the classes of sentient beings, some think: "What I have done and what I have created is not possessed by that [other]; furthermore, they reflect:
"What that [other] has done and what that [other] has created is not possessed by me."
Therefore it is said: "I have created this; that does not exist. That has created me; I do not exist.
Ensnared by conceit, beings are stained by arrogance;
deluded by views, they do not escape the bounds of birth and death.
Sentient beings are entangled by pride; those who are stained by and attached to arrogance think to themselves that their own mental disposition is haughty:
"I am now the most honored and supreme among the assembly; in terms of lineage, social standing, house, fields, servants, and household wealth, none can equal me."
Because their minds and intentions are firm and cannot be relinquished, it is said: "Sentient beings are entangled by conceit and stained by arrogance.

Regarding the phrase "deluded by views and unable to escape the limits of birth and death": the view of eternalism does not correspond with the view of annihilationism, and the view of annihilationism does not correspond with the view of eternalism; thus, one cannot escape this cycle of birth and death to reach the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, it is said: "Deluded by views, they cannot escape the limits of birth and death."
Those who have already attained and those yet to attain—both alike are subject to defilement.
They practice at the very root of disease; so too do those who study all that is to be learned.
Observe those who maintain the precepts, those pure ones of the holy life.
To gaze upon those who are sick and emaciated—this is called reaching the ultimate limit.

There are beings in the world whose minds are dominated by wrong views; they are greedily attached to sensual desires and cannot relinquish them. They seek purity through their lustful cravings, indulging in and habituating themselves to them. Within this state, they give rise to arrogance and do not reform themselves; this is called the second extreme. This, O worthy ones, is how people increase their attachments.

Regarding those who have already attained and those who are about to attain, there are those who have acquired the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and those who have not yet acquired them. Both of these types experience the defilements (*rajas*): first, the defilement of wrong views; second, the defilement of craving and desire. Being driven by the fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are unable to relinquish them. Therefore it is said: "Both experience the dust and grime."

Those who practice the roots of illness are the heterodox teachers and followers of divergent doctrines; they cultivate their respective arts to glorify themselves, as do all those beings who study various skills—whether it be training horses, driving chariots, or engaging in endless crafts—all of which they master completely. They maintain that by possessing such practices one attains liberation; therefore it is said: "and studying all that is to be studied."

Observe those who observe the precepts: there may be brahmins who uphold prohibitive vows; some observe the "crow-vow," raising their voices like crows; some observe the "owl-vow," prostrating at various times to imitate the hooting of owls; and some observe the "deer-vow," making their voices sound like deer. Therefore it is said: "Observe those who observe the precepts."
Regarding the "pure brahmins," those heterodox practitioners of other schools say among themselves:

"Those who practice the pure conduct in pairs shall attain liberation and reach the state of ultimate purity; furthermore, by serving fire, the sun, the moon, divine jewels, medicinal herbs, garments, palaces, and dwellings, they will eventually reach the realm of the unconditioned."
This is what is called "one extreme. There are beings in the world whose minds are dominated by wrong views;

they are greedily attached to sensual desires and cannot relinquish them. They reckon that desire is pure, and outsiders practice it without restraint or interval. This, O worthy ones, is how people increase their attachments. One who can understand this will not follow the current of saṃsāra.

Those with eyes behold; by "those with eyes" is meant the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who are able to observe through faith both the process of transmigration and its cessation. Therefore it is said: "that which is seen by those with eyes."
One who understands these two extremes is free from attachment and does not give rise to worldly afflictions; this is called the ultimate limit (*koṭi*).
One should contemplate them as bubbles upon water, and likewise as illusions or mirages;
by contemplating the body in this way, one shall not behold the King of Death.
"One should contemplate water bubbles, and likewise contemplate illusions and mirages" means that just as those water bubbles cannot remain for long:

formerly, there was a king’s daughter who was so beloved by the king that he never took his eyes off her. Once, when it rained and bubbles appeared upon the water, the girl saw the bubbles and felt great affection and admiration for them.
She said to the king, "I wish to obtain these water bubbles to use as a flower garland for my head."
The king said to the girl:
"Now, a bubble upon the water cannot be grasped; how can it be taken to make a flower garland?
The girl replied to the king:
"If we do not obtain them, I shall take my own life.
When the king heard the girl's words, he immediately summoned skilled artisans and addressed them, saying:
"Your craftsmanship is such that there is no task you cannot master; quickly provide water bubbles for my daughter to make a garland. If you do not, I shall have you all executed!"
The master craftsmen said to the king,
"We are not capable of taking bubbles to make garlands.
Among them was an elderly artisan who, confident in his own ability to take bubbles, stepped forward and addressed the king:
“I can take the bubbles and make them into a garland for the King.
The King was greatly delighted and immediately told his daughter, “Now there is a man capable of making a garland; you should go in person to observe him yourself.”
The woman followed the king’s words and looked outside; at that time, the old artisan said to the princess:
“I am not accustomed to distinguishing between the quality of water-bubbles; I pray that you, Princess, will take the bubbles yourself, and I shall fashion them into a garland.”

The woman immediately went to fetch the bubbles, but as soon as they reached her hands, they burst and could not be grasped; thus, throughout the entire day, she failed to obtain a single bubble, and becoming weary and exhausted, she abandoned her search and departed.
The woman said to the king:
"A bubble on water is false and cannot endure; I pray that Your Majesty will fashion for me a crown of purple-gold that shall never wither throughout the day and night."
A bubble upon the water deceives the human eye; though it possesses form and substance, it perishes as soon as it arises.

A mirage in the wild heat is likewise: through the exhaustion of craving, one loses their life. The human body is hollow and false, with little joy and much suffering; it is subject to decay and cannot remain long. It is transient and ever-changing, lasting but a brief moment in this world. If one does not fall within the sight of the King of Death, therefore it is said: "One should contemplate the bubble upon the water, And likewise contemplate the illusory mirage. If one contemplates the body in this way, One will no longer see the King of Death."
One should contemplate water bubbles, and likewise contemplate a mirage;
by contemplating the world in this way, one will not see the King of Death.

One who contemplates the world sees that the body of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) is thus impermanent and shall soon perish again. If one can extinguish these five aggregates, one will not encounter the King of Death.
Thus one should contemplate the body: like a king’s multicolored chariot, to which the foolish are attached;
one should skillfully seek to distance oneself from it.

Regarding "thus one should contemplate the body, like a king’s multicolored chariot": just as a king’s chariot is adorned with various colors, though it possesses form and appearance, it is not solid and cannot bear heavy loads. Therefore it is said: "Thus one should contemplate the body, like a king’s multicolored chariot."

That which the foolish are attached to, one should skillfully seek to distance oneself from; that which the foolish crave and habitually indulge in, the wise discard as if throwing away filth. Therefore it is said: "That which the foolish are attached to, one should skillfully seek to distance oneself from."
Thus one should contemplate the body as a king’s multi-colored chariot:
that which the fool is stained by and attached to, the wise person keeps far from.

The wise person knows its instability and does not take pleasure in it; they always desire to distance themselves from it as one avoids a fire. Therefore it is said: "The wise person keeps far from it."
Thus one should contemplate the body: it is the source of manifold illnesses;
when illness and folly conjoin, how can it be relied upon?

A person emerges from the womb due to causes and conditions from previous lives—whether they have many ailments or few, whether their physical form is handsome or ugly—for this reason it is said: "Thus one should contemplate the body: it is the source of manifold illnesses; when illness and folly conjoin, how can it be relied upon?"
One should contemplate the painted image, with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair;
the fool takes this as a causal support and does not seek to cross to the further shore.

Regarding "one should contemplate the painted image, with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair": various fragrant perfumes are used to bathe the hair, and the scent of these fragrant baths spreads far and wide; therefore it is said, "one should contemplate the painted image, with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair."

The fool takes this as a causal condition and does not seek to cross to the other shore. Enveloped by folly, he is unable to achieve detachment; lacking skillful means, he cannot reach the further shore. What is called "the further shore" is the extinction of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore it is said: "The fool takes this as a causal condition and does not seek to cross to the other shore."
One should contemplate the painted image with its mani-jewel-like deep blue hair;
the fool takes this as a causal basis, while the wise person regards it with revulsion.

A person of wisdom, through discernment, sublime contemplation, reflection, and calculation, does not give rise to conceptual attachment; therefore it is said: "the wise person regards it with revulsion."
They forcibly use colorful paintings to adorn their ugly and impure bodies;
the foolish take these as their conditions, yet do not seek liberation for themselves.
Once there was a family of noble lineage, possessing abundant wealth and many treasures, complete with the seven precious gems. The elder thought to himself:

"At this time, the young men of the Way have not yet severed their sensual desires; it would be appropriate for me now to invite them to my home and have my women serve them food, so that I may observe if any among them harbor lustful intentions."

He immediately went to the monastery to extend an invitation. The young practitioners then went to the elder’s house, where the women were adorned and dressed in new clothes; they all came out to pay their respects, giving rise to thoughts of reverence.

At that time, an arhat possessing the six supernatural powers perceived this immediately; he then transformed the corpse so that the bones, flesh, and blood were completely consumed, leaving the skull, hands, and feet each in a separate place.
At that time, the Arhat addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should concentrate your minds to seek transcendence from the world; do not gaze upon female forms and give rise to defiled thoughts.

Then the elder, beholding this auspicious omen, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He reproached himself inwardly, realizing his error, and prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he sought repentance for his transgression.
"I have now come to know the subtle and wondrous nature of the Dharma.
Each of the women felt ashamed and immediately returned to their houses.
At that time, the Arhat said to the elder:

“The Buddha-dharma is vast, expansive, and boundless; for you now to attempt to measure the Sage with the intellectual capacity of an ordinary person is not the correct principle. It is like comparing a handful of earth to Mount Sumeru, or wishing to measure the waters of the great ocean with a vessel of a *sheng* or a *he*.”
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“By force of effort, one paints forms to adorn this foul and impure body;
the fool takes this as his support, yet does not seek deliverance for himself.”
"Dividing the hair into eight parts, with earrings on both ears—
these are the attachments of the foolish, who likewise do not seek their own deliverance.
When the bhikṣu had spoken these two verses, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the elder and the women gave rise to virtuous minds of their own accord and paid reverence to the Triple Gem; subsequently, each attained the fruit of the Path.
Attached to desire and stained by desire, they did not investigate the conditions for the fetters (*saṃyojana*);
yet, by not giving rise to those fetters, they shall cross over the flood of sensual existence.

Regarding "those who are attached to desire and defiled by desire": among the various groups in the world, their inclinations differ; some have few desires, while others have a preponderance of desire. Those whose desire is excessive do not comprehend the Dharma of the Sages. Therefore it is said: "attached to desire and defiled by desire."

Regarding those who do not investigate the conditions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*): among the diseases caused by the fetters of greed, envy, and stinginess, these are the most grave; they penetrate the bones and reach the marrow, such that even a physician cannot cure them. One may accumulate wealth in the hundreds of millions yet be unwilling to give in charity, yet at the end of one's life, one cannot take so much as a single coin with oneself.

If there are sentient beings who practice greed and envy, their bodies will lack majestic power and they will consequently fall into poverty; their kinsmen will be discordant and they will be despised by others. Therefore it is said: "One does not investigate the conditions of the fetters."

Those who do not allow the fetters of birth to bind them and who seek to cross over the flood of sensual existence must understand that there are four types of floods, each with its own distinct nature.
What are these four? First, the flood of sensual desire; second, the flood of existence; third, the flood of ignorance; and fourth, the flood of views.

The various classes of sentient beings who are submerged in birth and death all do so because of these four; drifting through the four outflows (*āsrava*), they cannot free themselves and must continue to traverse the cycles of the five destinies. Therefore it is said: "One should not allow the fetters of birth to bind one; one ought to cross over the flood of sensual existence."
"Supreme is all freedom from desire; one should contemplate this great vision.
Thus there is liberation for those who were originally not yet delivered. Regarding "supreme is all freedom from desire":

"supreme" refers to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); "desire" refers to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). When one is no longer subject to the three poisons within these three realms, one attains eternal liberation therein. Therefore it is said: "Supreme is all freedom from desire."

One who observes this great vision should know that the person free from desire is the foremost disciple of the Buddha. The Buddha has four types of disciples, and among them, the Arhat is the most excellent, the most honored, the most noble, and unsurpassed. Therefore, it is said: "One should observe this great vision."

Thus, one who possesses liberation is a noble person whose practice is not for their own sake; they have attained eternal mastery over the four floods and no longer cling to the conduct of body and speech. Therefore, it is said: "Thus, one possesses liberation."

"Those not yet delivered" refers to the hardships of birth and death experienced in the past, which have never been transcended; one should seek skillful means to deliver oneself from these three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*), so as not to undergo further existence or create another body composed of the four great elements. For this reason, it is said: "those not yet delivered."
"Leaving the garden, he returns to the garden;
having escaped from bondage, he returns to bondage. One should observe such a person.
Formerly, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Garden at Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Kapilavastu with his attendant Ānanda to beg for food.

At that moment, the youth Nanda, from atop a high tower, saw the World-Honored One entering the city to beg for food from afar. He quickly descended from the tower and went to where the World-Honored One was; prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata’s clan is a noble family of the nation, a lineage of wheel-turning sage kings. Why do you debase yourself by carrying an alms bowl to beg for food?”
At that time, Nanda took the Tathāgata’s bowl and entered the house to prepare sweet foods and drinks.
After seeing Nanda enter the house, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"I shall now go toward the Nyagrodha Park; if Nanda comes out, do not take back the bowl."
"You must say to Nanda:
'Deliver the bowl yourself back to the Tathāgata.
Nanda received these instructions and followed behind to return the bowl; his wife followed after him once more and said to Nanda:
"Return quickly and do not linger; you must come before we eat.
Not long after he had set out, the wife sent a message again:
"Return at once and do not delay."
The reason for his earnestness was his fear that he might abandon the household life to study the Way.
Nanda carried it to the World-Honored One, personally holding up the bowl and presenting it to the Tathāgata, saying:
"I pray that you will accept it at once; I now wish to return home."
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Since you have arrived here, it is now appropriate for you to leave home, shave off your hair and beard, and don the three dharma robes; why do you again decline and wish to return home?"
At that time, the Tathāgata, through his awesome supernatural power, compelled Nanda to leave the household life for the path and confined him in a quiet chamber, not allowing him to return home.
As the days and months passed in succession, it was Nanda’s turn to serve as the duty-holder.
Upon hearing this, Nanda was inwardly delighted and thought:
"Now that I am on duty, I shall have leisure; taking advantage of this opportunity, I will escape and return home.
At that time, Nanda accepted his assignment and attended to the tasks of preparing water and sweeping the floor, performing every duty without omission.

At that time, the heavenly deity who guarded Nanda drew water until it was full, whereupon it spontaneously spilled onto the pure ground, causing the grass and soil to flourish even more; when he closed the doors, the doors opened of their own accord.
Nanda reflected: "I am of royal lineage;
my family possesses abundant wealth and many treasures, lacking nothing at all. I shall now flee back home.
Should anything be lost or damaged, I can compensate for it with goods. For now, I will take a secret, narrow path, for if I follow the main road, I will surely encounter the Tathāgata."
At that time, Nanda took off his three dharma robes and, changing into white lay garments, departed with a grinding heart.

Before he had traveled for long, he encountered the Tathāgata proceeding from that direction. Upon seeing him, Nanda ran toward a large tree, wishing to hide himself; however, by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, the tree was turned so that it stood behind Nanda, leaving him bewildered and with no place to settle himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One again employed his supernatural power to uproot that great tree and suspend it in mid-air.
Then Nanda entered the base of the tree and concealed himself by making his form invisible; the Tathāgata soon went there and met with him.
"Nanda! Why have you come here? Nanda remained silent, feeling ashamed and abashed, and did not answer.
The Tathāgata addressed Nanda a second and a third time, saying:
"Where do you wish to go? Why do you remain silent and not answer? Nanda replied:
"Return home and meet with your wife.
The Buddha told Nanda:
"If a person studies the Way but their mind is not focused, they will greedily cling to desires and disregard the calamity of burning the body in future lives."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Escaping from the garden, yet escaping the garden only to return to the garden;
one should observe such a person: having escaped bondage, they return once more to bondage."
"I shall now take you to tour the heavens; you should focus your mind and harbor no fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, took Nanda in his hand and led him to the heavens.
He saw a palace made of the seven treasures, intricately carved with gold and silver, attended by an incalculable number of jade maidens; there were only women, no men, and no husbands.
At that time, Nanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What celestial palace is this, so incomparably joyful?
Within its halls of the seven treasures, lutes and harps are played, and musicians perform various entertainments for mutual delight—something never heard of before."
"However, this goddess has no husband; I only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve my doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Nanda:
"Go there yourself and ask her about the truth of the matter."
"The heavenly maidens shall explain it to you themselves.
Having received these instructions, Nanda went to that celestial palace and asked the heavenly maidens with sincerity:
"You heavenly maidens naturally enjoy blessings; in palaces of the seven treasures, you delight yourselves with the five kinds of music. Where, then, are your husbands?"
The goddess replied, "Do you not know?

In the land of Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was Śākyamuni Buddha and his paternal cousin named Nanda. After his life has ended, he shall come to be born here in this celestial palace; that man is our husband."
Upon hearing this, Nanda rejoiced secretly to himself,
thinking, "The one being discussed is surely I.
He immediately returned to the Buddha's presence and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"These palaces, these jade maidens, and their entire retinue are all mine.
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Practice the holy life with joy; before long, you shall come here and receive such natural blessings."

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, took Nanda by the hand and led him to hell; on the way, passing beyond the Iron Ring Mountains, he saw a monkey that was blind in one eye.
The Buddha said to Nanda,
"Why is your wife Sundarī like this blind monkey?
Nanda replied to the Buddha:
"Stop, stop, World-Honored One! Do not speak of this further!
How could one compare that person to her?
Sundarī was the most exquisite among women; she was skilled in sixty-four arts, leaving no matter to which she was not proficient."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Nanda:
"A blind monkey compared to Sundarī, and Sundarī compared to the celestial maidens—by hundreds of millions of times, no analogy can serve as a comparison."

At that time, the World-Honored One took Nanda by the hand and led him to hell, showing him the immeasurable agonies of torture, flogging, and scourging; how sinners were boiled in the cauldrons of the eight great hells; and how each great hell was surrounded by sixteen subsidiary pits—mountains of knives, forests of swords, chariots of fire, and glowing embers—where they were scorched, roasted, and stewed in boiling oil, their suffering beyond description.
There was a great cauldron surrounded by hell-wardens; the broth boiled and the fire blazed fiercely, yet no sinner was to be seen.
Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wonder, World-Honored One!"
"All these hells contain prisoners; why is it that this cauldron is seen yet no sinner is found within?
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Go there yourself and ask the wardens of hell; they shall explain its origins and details to you."
At that time, Nanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to ask the warder:
"What is this cauldron that is empty and devoid of sinners? The warder replied:

"In Jambudvīpa, the son of the King of the True and Pure House has attained the Way; his paternal cousin, the son of King Amṛta, is named Nanda. He is a man of dissolute habits and excessive lust, who, relying on his noble lineage, treats the myriad people with contempt. After his life comes to an end, he shall enter this cauldron and remain there for the duration of kalpas before finally attaining release."
"What you wish to know is as follows.
Having heard this, Nanda’s hair stood on end; his body trembled and his complexion changed. He approached the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, O Teacher of Gods and Great Protector of the Two Realms, now that I behold these transformations, my fear redoubles."
He then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"Now I renounce the rank of the heavens, And shall not create the root of birth and death.
Seeking liberation from the suffering of hell, I pray you, preach the extinction of Nirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Nanda, establishing him in the unconditioned and leading him to the site of enlightenment.
Clothed in dark blue robes and shaded by a white canopy, The charioteer drives the single-wheeled chariot;
Beholding those fine motes of dust and defilement, He has forever severed his bonds.
Many people seek refuge in mountains, rivers, trees, and spirits;
in gardens, pavilions, and shrines, hoping to escape suffering and hardship.
People harbor fear and their minds are so deluded that they do not awaken; when encountering these objects before them, they offer prayers without distinguishing between the true and the false.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Yuezhi, there was a king named Wushao, under whose rule all throughout the world submitted without exception.
His mother instructed him, saying:

"Should you ever face the peril of death, take care not to circumambulate the Buddhist temples counter-clockwise; you must remember to circumambulate them clockwise. Be careful not to violate this instruction of mine."

At that time, the wicked young king mobilized his troops to attack the city of Pure West (Cunxi). With his own hand he grasped a sword and slew three hundred million people; it did not reach four hundred million, as he intended to reach five hundred million. Later, when he was defeated in battle, he fled on an elephant. Looking back, he saw a Buddhist stupa and recalled his mother’s instructions; he then turned the elephant to the right. When the enemy kingdom saw this, they all submitted and returned to their own country.
Seeing the thieves retreat, the king pursued them from behind; he then returned, destroyed the thieves, and captured the king himself. Thereupon, he recalled the Buddha’s words:
“He who takes refuge in the Buddha has found the most honored and supreme refuge, beyond which there is none.”
"If I do not turn to the right, how could I possibly defeat these rebels?
Therefore it is said: "Many people seek refuge in mountains, rivers, trees, spirits, gardens, pavilions, and shrines, hoping to escape suffering and calamity."
This is not the supreme refuge, nor is it one that brings auspiciousness;
those who take such a refuge shall not be liberated from all suffering.
But if one takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus, [one shall be liberated].
Cultivate the Noble Four Truths as they are seen by wisdom.
Born from the cause and conditions of suffering, one should transcend this root of suffering through the Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones, reaching the limit of the nectar of extinction.
This is the supreme refuge; it is not without auspiciousness.
For those who take this refuge, they shall be liberated from all suffering.
When a person cultivates the Path, there is only faith and integrity; when the faculty of faith is complete, the precepts will not be violated.

Any sentient beings who are able to take refuge in these Three Jewels shall have no wish that remains unfulfilled; they will be venerated by devas and humans, attain the Way for themselves, and furthermore receive blessings for eternal kalpas.
A person without a protector is like a tree without roots; if one has something to rely upon, what task will not be accomplished?
One should observe that which is to be observed; one should also observe that which is not to be observed.
Having observed, one observes again; having observed, one does not observe again.

What is called "contemplation" refers to the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as suchness (*tathatā*). When a practitioner clings to these, contemplating the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as suchness, they contemplate the present while contemplating the past and the future. The arising of worldly defilements (*kleśa*) stems from these three periods of time; thus one falls into the cycle of birth and death and fails to reach the Way. Therefore it is said: "One contemplates by means of contemplation that which should be contemplated."

"Regarding 'that which is not contemplated should also be contemplated': that which is called 'not contemplating' refers to not seeing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. One should thus contemplate and investigate these clearly, knowing them as the non-seeing of the Four Truths—the suchness of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Therefore it is said: 'That which is not contemplated should also be contemplated.'"

To contemplate and then contemplate again means that one is able, through faith, to discern suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; one reflects upon each of these individually to thoroughly investigate and master their meaning.

To contemplate and not contemplate again means that having already contemplated and already known [the truth], one no longer reflects further. Therefore it is said: "One should contemplate even when not contemplating, and contemplate again after having contemplated."
Contemplating and then contemplating again, one discerns the fundamental nature of that [body].
Calculating day as night, the precious body will soon perish.
Regarding "contemplating and then contemplating again," there are two kinds of contemplation:
The first is the contemplation of material wealth (*dhanānupaśyanā*), and the second is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārthānupaśyanā*).

Now, the contemplation of material wealth increases the fetters (*saṃyojana*), whereas the contemplation of the ultimate truth exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*) and accomplishes the practice of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Therefore, it is said: "One contemplates and then contemplates again."

Regarding "discerning the original nature of those": there are some whose human natures and karmic actions differ, and whose realms and dharma-teachings are manifold; the Sages discern each of these one by one.

There are those whose minds are awakened, those whose minds are not awakened, and those who are both awakened and unawakened; the sentient beings' dispositions for awakening vary in speed. Therefore, the Sages instruct them with the Way, urging them to practice diligently day and night without slackening. For this reason, it is said: "discerning the original nature of those."

Regarding "reckoning day as night": the natures and conducts of the various classes of sentient beings differ; some contemplate the roots of goodness, while others do not contemplate the roots of goodness. This is what is meant by reckoning day as night.

Regarding the phrase "the precious body will soon perish": worldly wealth and goods are the common law of the world; though gathered throughout one's entire life, they must inevitably decay and be destroyed. However, the wealth of roots of goodness never rots or perishes. Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states:
"One should exchange this non-precious body for a precious body, exchange non-precious wealth for precious wealth, and exchange a non-precious life for a precious life."
Therefore it is said: "The precious body will perish before long.
Though one observes, one does not observe repeatedly;
though one sees, it is as if one does not see; though one observes, one still does not see.

Regarding "observing without repeated observation": that practitioner contemplates sublime observation (*vipaśyanā*), yet the Path observes and knows that this practitioner likewise lacks sublime observation.
There are two types of persons who attain the concentration of contemplation (*cintāmayī samādhi*):
one person attains observation, while the other does not.
Furthermore, there is another guide who observes the practitioner: "Is there perhaps anyone here who is fit for the Noble Truths?
He contemplates and examines them thoroughly and finds that none are fit for the Noble Truths; therefore it is said: "He observes, yet does not observe again."

Regarding "observing yet not observing": there are many who cultivate and accumulate the practice of the Path through reflection; they further observe the events of the distant past, and while some may achieve penetration and others may not, they distinguish each one without confusion. Therefore it is said: "observing yet not observing."
What is seeing and what is not seeing?
What is it that speaks of seeing and not seeing?
By what cause does seeing and not seeing arise?
Regarding the question, "By what view does one see?

What is it that is not seen?"—the practitioner, while practicing the Dharma, conceives of it as being this eternal and pure dharma. That which is called "not seeing" refers to not seeing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; therefore, it is said: "What is it that is seen and not seen?"

Regarding the statement "what is seen and what is not seen": the practitioner perceives only a single object—whether it be an object of form, or an object of form, sound, odor, or taste; whether there is mental reflection or no mental reflection. Therefore, it is said: "What is seen and what is not seen?"

Regarding the reason why one sees and another does not see: it is like two people who have both fully cultivated their practices and are complete in their merits. Although they remain within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they harbor no fear or weakness; their minds seek to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) without hesitation or obstruction. Yet, the mind of one person is biased and fails to reach the ultimate goal. One does not see the severing of all outflows (*āsrava*), while the other does not see [the end of] remaining in various births and deaths. For this reason, it is said: "For what reason does one see and another not see?"

Regarding "because one emerges from views": by means of the Dharma of the noble ones (āryadharma), one personally perceives the essential meaning of transcendence; thus, whatever one aspires to will surely be accomplished, free from fear or hesitation. Therefore it is said: "because one emerges from views."
If one does not contemplate suffering, one should always deeply contemplate oneself in order to understand the root source of suffering; this is called the clear and wondrous contemplation.

"If one does not contemplate suffering" means that if a practitioner does not see that it is empty, non-self, and without a personal identity, and furthermore does not discern the various aggregates of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they will fall into ruin.

One observes for oneself the impurities and uncleanness within the body; from head to foot, there is not a single part to be craved. One does not conceive of "I," "myself," "form," or "my form," nor does one discriminate between the beginning and end of form. Therefore it is said: "If one does not contemplate suffering, one should always deeply contemplate oneself."

Because one understands the root source of suffering, this is called the "one who possesses clear and wondrous contemplation. What is understood here is the meaning of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. The body is a source of affliction from which ten thousand maladies overflow; when the practitioner contemplates with an undistracted and unerring mind, they deeply realize the root source of illness. The body dwells in the world as a composite of the four great elements; since countless kalpas past, it has not beheld the Great Illumination because it was enveloped by delusion and confusion. Now that I have been liberated from this, I shall no longer create the conditions for it.
Therefore it is said: "By understanding the root source of suffering, this is called clear and wondrous contemplation.
Who causes ordinary people not to perceive the foundation of all conditioned phenomena?
By observing through that [foundation], one leaves behind darkness and beholds the great light.

Who causes ordinary people not to perceive the root of all conditioned phenomena? Who has created this world of blindness and darkness that fails to behold the Great Radiance? Why do sentient beings wander aimlessly, failing to recognize the true path? Although the suffering of the four great elements, the aggregates, and the sense bases is manifest, the deluded are stained by attachment and do not believe it to be a calamity; they give rise to various false views, thereby increasing their worldly afflictions.

Because of that practitioner, one observes for oneself, contemplating day and night with the cessation of fetters as one's task. One leaves behind darkness and perceives the Great Radiance; the root of this Great Radiance is the absence of any root of darkness. Such a person does not recognize the Buddha, does not recognize the Dharma, and does not recognize the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; furthermore, they do not recognize True Suchness, nor the Four Truths of Suffering, Origination, Cessation, and the Path. They do not cultivate practices of purity regarding their objective spheres. Therefore it is said: "Who causes the ordinary person not to behold the root of all practices? Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, "The Chapter on Observation."
Udānavarga, Volume Twenty-Four; Udānavarga, Volume Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 29: On Evil Conduct Commit no evil;
Practice all that is good; Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
