"Commit no evil whatsoever" means that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, instruct future followers of the Three Vehicles that one does not attain the Way by practicing evil; rather, by cultivating goodness, one personally reaches the traces of the Path. Therefore, it is said: "Commit no evil whatsoever."

Those who faithfully practice all virtues—those practitioners universally cultivate all manner of goodness; they alone adorn themselves, being fully endowed with manifold merits. Seeing evil, they avoid it and constantly cultivate what is good. That which is called "good" refers to the wondrous medicine of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), which incinerates and extinguishes distracted thoughts.
Therefore it is said: "One should practice all that is good. As for "purifying one's own mind":

the mind is the root of action that brings about the source of transgression. One hundred and eight heavy roots—difficult-to-unravel knots—envelop the mind; when desire, anger, delusion, arrogance, and stinginess abound, they plant various defilements. One who possesses these ailments has an impure mind. Thus, the practitioner should hold fast to their resolve and train their own mind so that it does not harbor distracted thoughts. By persevering in this way, the root of the Path is established. Therefore it is said: "Purify one's own mind."

Regarding these teachings of the Buddhas: the Tathāgatas have expounded various prohibitions and precepts; the precepts serve to restrain the body, while their meaning serves to collect the mind. It is extremely rare for a Buddha to appear in the world, occurring only once in many hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, like the udumbara flower.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has left behind his instructions and teachings, handed down from sage to sage until the present day. One must not fail to cultivate the prohibitions and precepts, nor must one fail to practice benevolent giving. That I have attained Buddhahood and reign as king over the three thousandfold world system is entirely due to the cultivation of prohibitions, precepts, and benevolent giving.
Therefore it is said: These are the teachings of all Buddhas.
By practicing generosity one obtains the reward of merit;
by not harboring anger or resentment, one extinguishes evil with goodness, so that desire, anger, and delusion leave no remainder.

In the past, the uterine younger brother of Mahāmaudgalyāyana possessed abundant wealth and many treasures, fully endowed with the seven precious gems: gold, silver, *musāragalva*, *aśmagarbha*, pearls, amber, and coral; his storehouses were overflowing, and his servants and slaves were beyond counting.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana went to his younger brother’s house and said to him:
"I have heard that you are stingy and jealous, and do not delight in giving.
The Buddha constantly proclaims that when a person practices generosity, they obtain immeasurable retribution."
"You, my brother, shall now obtain immeasurable merit through this act of giving.
Hearing his elder brother's instruction, the younger brother opened the treasury to practice charity, establishing a new storehouse in anticipation of receiving its reward.

Before ten days had passed, his wealth and treasures were completely exhausted; the old treasury was entirely empty, and the new treasury yielded no return. Consequently, he became deeply distressed and said to his elder brother:

"Previously, when I was instructed and exhorted that giving yields great rewards, I did not dare disobey your teaching and exhausted my treasury in acts of charity, so that there were no poor people—whether of the past or the future—to whom I did not provide for.
Yet now, wealth and goods are spent, the old stores are empty, and the new stores have yielded no returns; could it be that I have been misled by you, my brother?"
Maudgalyāyana said to him:
"Stop, stop, son of good family!
Do not speak such words."
Do not let those of other schools with heterodox views hear these crude words.
If merit were to have a physical form, even the realm of empty space could not contain it; I shall now provisionally show you a small reward. If you wish to see it, follow me.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, by means of his supernormal power, took his younger brother in his hand and ascended to the Sixth Heaven.

There were palaces there composed of the seven treasures; bathing pools lay before and behind them, and fragrant breezes spread afar. The treasuries were overflowing beyond measure, and the retinue of celestial maidens numbered many tens of millions. They were exclusively women with no men, nor did they have husbands.
The younger brother said to Maudgalyāyana:
"What palace is this, so towering and magnificent?
No men are to be seen; it consists entirely of women."
Maudgalyāyana told his younger brother, "Go now and ask; you shall know it for yourself.
He then went and questioned him.
“O Goddess, you should know!
I have a question; I pray that you will provide an answer. The goddess asked:
“What doubt do you have that you wish to ask about?
The man replied, “What palace is this,
composed of the seven treasures, so lofty and magnificent, suspended in the void of space?”
"Who possesses such merit as to receive blessings therein?
I pray you resolve my doubts so that I may forever be free from hesitation.
The goddess replied:

"Do you not know? We have lived here for many years, and our blessings have been provided naturally so that we no longer suffer such hardships. If you wish to know about my husband, he has kept his intentions in his heart; I shall now explain them to you."

Within the borders of the kingdom of Kapila in Jambudvīpa, there is a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha endowed with supernatural powers named Maudgalyāyana. He has a virtuous younger brother, a wealthy elder who delighted in giving alms to relieve the destitute and aid the needy. After his life comes to an end, he shall come to be born here as our husband; this is the reward for his gift of the seven-jeweled palace and our own bodies.
Upon hearing this, the man was delighted and a virtuous mind arose within him; he returned to his elder brother’s place and reported the matter in detail.
Maudgalyāyana said to him, “What do you say, son of good family?”
"Does a noble person’s act of giving merit a reward, or does it not?
The younger brother, filled with shame and remorse, prostrated himself in repentance; he then returned to the world and practiced extensive giving without weariness.
Therefore it is said: "Generous giving brings forth the reward of merit.

Regarding those who do not harbor resentment or anger within: when a person harbors poison concealed inside, they watch for the faults of others and afflict their goodness; such a person as this should not be befriended. It is like fire covered by ashes;

though the eyes do not see it, treading upon it burns the feet. If one has no self-protection and rashly violates the precepts, though the mind may feel bold at the time, one does not realize the injury that follows.

Human injury has existed since antiquity; it may arise either from pre-existing resentment or from sudden anger. While those who act out of sudden anger may still be forgiven, those who harbor resentment beforehand are difficult to approach with sincerity.

Why is this so? For when people harbor secret plots, there will inevitably be injury and destruction; as the ignorant masses pursue one another, they ultimately bring about calamity. When outward conduct is not discreet while inward feelings are shared, they praise one another and become evil companions. When their affairs run contrary to their wishes, they meet with ruin and extinction; their families and property all enter the government treasury, and others loathe and envy them, finding no pleasure in hearing their names.
Therefore it is said: "One does not harbor anger or resentment within.

To extinguish evil with goodness, so that desire, anger, and delusion leave no remainder—what is called "goodness" here is precisely the Path-factors of the Noble Ones (*ārya-mārgāṅga*). By riding upon these Path-factors, one is like the waters of the four great rivers: once their flow is severed, there is no fear or difficulty. One extinguishes and crosses over the various classes of evil so that they do not arise again. When calamities, the spitting out of poison, and the arising of desire, anger, and delusion exist, one must uproot the three roots and plant the three karmas; if one looks upward to cultivate the contemplation of the Path and advances toward the Four Fruits (*catur-śrāmaṇya-phala*), what difficulty could there be in experiencing them?
Therefore it is said: "By means of the good, extinguish the evil; so that desire, anger, and delusion leave nothing remaining.
Walk alone and do not follow fools; if you wish to be in a group, follow the wise.
The wise extinguish their own evil, just as a crane selects the milk to drink from the water.

Walk alone and do not follow the foolish. What is meant by "walking alone" is that in a secluded and tranquil place, one’s mind is not distracted; one contemplates the roots of goodness and keeps mindfulness fixed before oneself. If one wishes to dwell together with others, one should associate with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and never associate with evil friends (pāpamitra). Therefore it is said: "Walk alone and do not follow the foolish."

Those who wish to join a group should follow the wise. In this world, there are many who aspire to emulate the superior sages—those who pursue the wise, who maintain the precepts, who are diligent, whose eloquence is profound, who are capable of expounding the teachings of the Way without succumbing to weariness. Therefore it is said: "Those who wish to join a group should follow the wise."

"The wise person extinguishes their evil" means that one who possesses wisdom understands the past and masters the present; whatever they speak or say is necessarily salvific. Day and night they diligently contemplate the Way and its arts, receiving the verbal teachings uttered by the enlightened ones. By means of wholesome merit, they eliminate all evils; therefore it is said: "The wise person extinguishes their evil."

Regarding the crane that selects milk to drink: long ago, there was a man who caught many cranes and raised them on milk until they grew large. As they were born in succession, their number became infinite. The method for raising cranes was to mix water with the milk so that they could eat it; however, according to the cranes' natural habit, when it was time to eat, they would exhale air through their nostrils, causing the water to separate into two parts, and consume only the milk. Thus, despite being wild and simple creatures, these birds were able to distinguish between the water and the milk, discarding the former to eat the latter.
Can the bhikṣus of today do otherwise?
They should select what is good and eliminate what is evil, just as that bird, the crane, deeply understands what is desirable and what is not.
Therefore it is said: "Like the crane choosing milk to drink."
Observing the manifold transformations of the world, one knows the traces of the arising and ceasing of phenomena;
the noble and holy do not delight in the world, and the foolish do not dwell among the noble.

Regarding "observing the manifold transformations of the world," what is called the "world" consists of three categories: [the world of sentient beings, the world of receptacle, and the world of time].
First is the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), second is the world of the aggregates (*skandha-loka*), and third is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

These three worlds are prison cells for storing illness; they are solid both internally and externally and cannot be cured by physicians. Internally, the four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously; externally, there are venomous creatures—vipers, snakes, centipedes, vipers, scorpions, tigers, and wolves—that bite and sting upon being seen. There are many such various transformations, each with its own distinct nature, as well as water, fire, thieves, bandits, and enemies who secretly come to inflict injury.
Therefore it is said: "Observe the various transformations of the world.
To know the traces of the arising and ceasing of phenomena means to know that there are two aspects to the arising and ceasing of those traces:
first, the traces of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and second, the traces of the aggregates (*skandha*).
To be able to extinguish such matters is to accord with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, it is called "knowing the traces of the arising and ceasing of phenomena.

The noble ones do not delight in the world, nor do the foolish dwell among the wise. The noble ones forever extinguish all evils and do not dwell among the common masses; as a crane flies high and does not delight in burial mounds, and as the *śiṅxing* (gibbon) loves purity and does not dwell in latrines, so too is the person of noble virtue: they do not dwell among the common masses to share their same light. The foolish love what is evil and do not dwell among the assembly of the wise.
Therefore it is said: "The noble and wise do not delight in the world; the foolish do not dwell among the wise.
Understanding and discerning the relish of mindfulness, contemplating the meaning of cessation, free from fever and the notion of hunger, one should partake of the flavor of the Dharma.

Regarding the understanding of the flavor of mindfulness and waiting: since undergoing countless cycles of birth and death, one has never yet attained this flavor of mindfulness and waiting. In the world, there are many sweet, exquisite, and superior flavors—such as sugarcane and grapes—which are beyond counting; one might enjoy them day and night without ever reaching satiety. Yet, through these, one cannot attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

As for the flavor of mindfulness and waiting, it has never before passed one's lips; were one to encounter it even once, hunger and thirst would vanish forever. As for all other flavors, they lead one through successive births and deaths, causing one to fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*), making it truly difficult to seek an end to such suffering.
Therefore it is said: "To understand and know the relishing of mindfulness.

As for the meaning of "contemplating cessation": that practitioner, with single-minded devotion, contemplates meditative concentration; the dharmas he attends to are never confused, and from beginning to end he does not lose their thread. Therefore it is said: "Contemplating the meaning of cessation."

Regarding "being without fever and without the perception of hunger": desire is fever, hatred is fever, delusion is fever, and hunger and thirst are fever. One who can sever this fever of hunger and thirst performs a most difficult feat;
even if one were to drink these four great oceans of water in an attempt to quench that thirst, such a thing has never been seen.
To eliminate this thirst so that it never arises again, there is only the pure flavor of the eight liberations; only by this can the root of these manifold cravings be extinguished.
Therefore it is said: "Without fever, without the perception of thirst."

Those who should partake of the flavor of the Dharma—this so-called flavor of the Dharma—is supreme among all gifts, for the gift of the Dharma excels all other gifts; it is supreme among all flavors, for the flavor of the Dharma excels all other flavors. One who attains this flavor never departs from the Dharmakāya and severs the afflictions of worldly hunger and thirst. If a person seeks liberation through study and practice, yet fails to obtain the essential flavor of the ambrosia, how can they sit peacefully in non-action?
It is exceedingly difficult for one who is not earnestly diligent to seek and attain the traces of the Path.
Therefore it is said: "One should partake of the flavor of the Dharma.
A person does not diminish their mind, nor do they destroy their intention.
By means of goodness, one eternally extinguishes evil; thus, one need not fear falling into the evil realms.

As for the person who does not damage their heart nor corrupt their intention: such a person first establishes their practice by initially training in wholesome dharmas. At the outset, their mind may be hesitant, wavering between faith and lack of faith; yet one whose will is courageous hears [the teaching] and immediately gains faith and understanding, whereas one whose mind is full of doubt does not penetrate the Dharma. Such a person must inevitably undergo the cycle of birth and death, passing beyond billions of Buddhas without receiving deliverance.
Even if one’s heart is impaired, as long as one’s resolve is not destroyed, the attainment of the Ultimate Way is exceedingly easy.

When a person desires to practice and study, they shall obtain it by focusing their intent; just as a commoner hears of a certain Dharma and finds many obstacles along the way that prevent passage, yet by maintaining a single-minded focus on its form and intent, they reach it.
How is this known?

It is because those who have attained supernormal powers can manifest forms according to their mental intentions; therefore it is said: "A person does not damage their mind, nor do they destroy their intention."

"By means of the good, one eternally extinguishes evil; thus, one need not fear falling into the evil realms. This means that when a person practices the path with earnest devotion, worldly roots of goodness appear before them. Although these are roots of goodness, they are mundane and subject to outflows (*āsrava*); yet, because such a person does not give rise to conceptual attachments or seek higher attainments through them, this person will ultimately never fear falling into the evil destinies.
Therefore it is said: By means of the good, one eternally extinguishes evil; thus one need not fear falling into the evil realms.
If a person wishes to refine their spirit, they must cultivate and polish it repeatedly.
The wise are easily adorned; such a one is called a hero of the world.
Those who can draw near to them will find peace and freedom from sorrow and affliction.

If a person wishes to refine their spirit, they must practice constant cultivation and polishing. Those of long-standing study may appear outwardly empty yet inwardly substantial; some may hide away in mountain thickets, while others may feign madness as they wander through the world. Though their conduct differs, the benefit they bring is one and the same. This does not concern the physical vessel, but rather the pure refinement of the spirit so that the concentrated mind does not err. The practitioner manifests expedient transformations by the thousands and changes by the hundreds, employing skillful means to guide sentient beings to the Chamber of a Hundred Refinements.
What is called this "chamber" is the city of Nirvana—empty, tranquil, and unconditioned.
Therefore it is said: "If a person wishes to refine their spirit, they must cultivate and polish it repeatedly.

The wise are easily adorned; they are called the heroes of the age. Those of swift and sharp faculties have speech that conforms to the rules. If one desires that those to be saved attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)—then the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of phenomena comprise the internal teachings, while the analytical knowledge of expression and the analytical knowledge of eloquence comprise the external teachings.
Therefore it is said: "The wise are easily refined and adorned; they are called the heroes of the world.

Those who can draw near to such persons will find peace and freedom from distress. Whether walking, standing, advancing, retreating, moving about, or returning, these people maintain dignified deportment at all times without losing their proper measure. They are like a multitude of flowers in full bloom, whose fragrance spreads far and wide.

Those who practice in this way are likewise so: when their virtue of precepts, learning, and generosity, as well as the gates of *dhāraṇī* and their concentrated mind, remain undistracted, they are able to draw near to them without transgression or failure, and thus they can accomplish the untainted (*anāsrava*) holy conduct.
Therefore it is said: Those who can draw near to him will find peace and freedom from sorrow.
Having forever stilled all faults, they are gentle and not impetuous;
they blow away all unwholesome dharmas, just as the wind sheds its leaves.

"One who has forever stilled transgressions" refers to one who is gentle and not impetuous; whose faculties are complete and do not overflow; whose speech is focused and correct, never being impetuous; and whose deportment and etiquette are never lost. Such a person has no peer and commits no transgression; therefore it is said: "One who has forever stilled transgressions is gentle and not impetuous."

"Blowing away all evil dharmas, like the wind removing its leaves": when a practitioner maintains their resolve with unshakable firmness, holding fast to faith so solidly that they do not transgress even by a hair’s breadth, they cast off all evil dharmas and advance daily toward the good. Day and night they polish themselves so as not to allow even a speck of defilement; just as iron produces rust that must be polished away for it to shine, and the human heart is heavily encrusted with impurities that require wisdom to illuminate—it is for this reason it is said:
"Blowing away all evil dharmas, like the wind removing its leaves."

Without cause, one fears such a person who slanders and defames the pure; yet evil soon gains its power, like smoke and clouds driven by the wind. Without cause, one fears such a person who slanders and defames the pure.

For among humans, cultivation and study take the removal of defilement as supreme; the practitioner who eliminates stains cultivates only purity. When merit is full, how could one fear not reaching the goal? One whose mind is free from stinginess and envy honors the root of the Path and awakens with clarity; this is because they have attained thorough penetration of the profound essentials.
A pure person is free from the fetters of defilement; yet the fool slanders them, calling them impure. By slandering a noble one, one incurs the karma of the Avīci Hell.
This results from the accumulation of merit through long-standing practice.
Therefore it is said: "Out of fear of that person, one slanders the pure. Seeking out evil, one reaps its power;

like smoke and clouds driven by the wind, worldly people cling to delusion and take evil for excellence. From this, calamities gradually enter the Great Mountain (Mount Tai), creating the karmic offenses of the hells, hungry ghosts, and various animals. Therefore it is said: "Seeking out evil, one reaps its power; like smoke and clouds driven by the wind."
In the conduct of people, each knows for themselves: that good is good, and evil is evil. Regarding "in the conduct of people, each knows for themselves":

when people's practices and inclinations vary, those who do evil know it as evil, and those who do good know it as good. Even among those who perform good or evil without self-awareness, the retribution received is doubled: the virtuous receive inexhaustible blessings, while the wicked receive double the punishment; the pure receive the fruits of pure conduct, and the impure receive the fruits of impure conduct.

At the time of death, good and evil are clearly distinguished. If a deity comes to welcome them, they will see palaces, mansions, gardens, and bathing pools; their spirits will not be confused, garments and ornaments will naturally appear upon their bodies, and celestial maidens will surround them in mutual enjoyment. They will further perceive that the light they emit shines forth without obstruction.

When a person who has accumulated evil deeds approaches the day of their death, their consciousness becomes disoriented; they see only great fires, swords, and halberds, as well as crows, wild foxes, rākṣasas, malevolent spirits, tigers, wolves, and other ferocious beasts. Furthermore, they see mountains of knives, trees of swords, thorny pits, and ravines, all surrounded by malevolent ghosts.
Therefore it is said: "Goodness is what makes one good; evil is what makes one evil.
When a person commits evil, they will later receive the retribution themselves; if one does not commit evil, there will be no cause for worry later.

Regarding the fact that when people commit evil, they later receive retribution for themselves: when a person commits evil, they invite calamity and misfortune upon themselves; it is not as if parents, brothers, or kinsmen can take their punishment upon themselves.

Likewise, if one does not commit evil oneself, one will not receive retribution later. Such a person, while alive, may encounter a sage and shall receive blessings; these blessings are not obtained by their parents, brothers, or kin on their behalf. Because their own intent is pure and they do not burden others, and because they have practiced purity themselves, they receive the retribution for themselves.
Therefore it is said: "When a person commits evil, they later receive the retribution themselves; having not committed evil, they have no cause for worry later.
Having realized for oneself what is pure and what is impure, why concern oneself with whether others are pure?
The fool does not discipline himself, like iron drilling into pure steel.

One who understands for oneself what is pure and impure has no need to worry about the purity of others; if one is oneself pure, one can also cause others to practice purity. But how can one whose own conduct is uneven cause others to attain pure conduct?
Therefore it is said: "Having realized for oneself what is pure and what is impure, why worry about the purity of others?

The fool does not discipline himself; he is like one who drills iron with pure steel. What the fool practices throughout his entire life never reaches its end, yet in a single day he commits deeds that cause him to fall into kalpas of eternal suffering. Even if he encounters sages and saints, he receives no salvation—just as when drilling iron with pure steel, even if the effort is exhaustive, the desired result cannot be obtained.
Therefore it is said: "The fool does not discipline himself, like iron drilling into pure steel.
If one sees with the eye what is not wrong, the clever person seeks skillful means;
the wise person lives well in this world and does no evil.

If what is seen by the eye is not perverse: suppose a person habitually practices and is single-mindedly devoted to evil; yet, when seeing forms with the eye, they do not give rise to visual consciousness, and whether the form is beautiful or ugly, their mind remains entirely equanimous. Even if they see a beautiful form, they do not give rise to defiled attachment; even if they see an ugly form, they do not harbor resentment. For this reason it is said: "If what is seen by the eye is not perverse."

A wise person who seeks skillful means perceives that the forms seen by the eye are not real; they are subject to decay and destruction, shifting and unstable. That which is born must come to an end, and even that which is permanent must perish. Fools take delight in them, but the wise laugh at such attachment. Therefore it is said: "The wise person seeks skillful means."

The wise person lives their life well and does not commit various evils; for the skillful means taught by the wise are manifold. They prevent evil before it takes form and cultivate merit spontaneously. Their conduct is not entangled with the world, and their teachings do not detract from the physical nature.

Moving through the world, they do not regard their own lifespan as long; seeing it short, they feel a sense of shame, and seeing it long, they do not boast of themselves. Completing their allotted lifespan in this world, they ultimately never engage in evil deeds.
Therefore it is said: "The wise live their lives well, committing no evil.
A merchant on the road is fearful; with few companions and much merchandise, he passes through dangerous places, yet there remains the anxiety that his axle might break.

Merchants traveling on the road are fearful when their companions are few but their goods are many. Long ago, there was a group of merchant travelers who ventured upon a journey through a vast wilderness full of perils; the roads were infested with bandits, leaving no way to escape. They carried great wealth and treasures but possessed no provisions, and their fellow travelers lacked weapons for self-defense. Since the travelers were few while the treasure was immense, they were gripped by fear and their consciousness burned with anxiety.
A certain clever man said to his companions, "Do not give way to fear; I shall devise a plan to escape this peril.
As their minds became resolute, they were able to remain unharmed.
Therefore it is said: "The merchant on the road is fearful, for his companions are few while his goods are many.

When passing through dangerous and difficult places, there is the anxiety of a broken axle; because the road is perilous and he does not meet with good companions, he abandons the great highway to follow a narrow path. Failing to reach his destination, his carriage breaks down midway, and the preceding companions do not look back, leaving the following companions behind as they abandon one another.

For this reason, the World-Honored One employed this as a metaphor, desiring that future generations may deeply discern between transgression and merit, so that those who receive his transformation have not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction, and those who propagate the teaching do not waste their efforts.
Therefore it is said: When passing through dangerous and difficult places, there is the anxiety that the axle might break.
If one has a body free from sores, one will not be harmed by poison;
for poison can do nothing to one who has no sores. Thus, when there is no evil, nothing is created.

It was just as when Devadatta was in Rājagṛha and conceived a malicious intent to cause harm; later, when the matter became manifest and was heard by the entire kingdom, King Ajātaśatru said to Devadatta:
"You should leave this country and need not remain here; there is no one among the sixteen great nations who does not know of this."
"How could this Devadatta commit such manifold evils and give rise to a heart of malice toward the Tathāgata?

Having heard this, Devadatta harbored grief within; his mind finding no peace, he returned to his native land. His old resentment remaining unextinguished and bound by the fetters of anger, he rashly entered the Bodhisattva’s inner palace and said to Gopī:
"I shall now take you as my first consort; I do not know if it would be acceptable to you, O noble lady?"
When Gopī heard this, she said to Devadatta, "I wish to grasp your right hand. Devadatta immediately extended his hand for her to take;
however, as she gripped his wrist, his bones shattered and blood flowed from his five fingers. At that moment, he became dazed and unconscious, regaining consciousness only after a long while.

Gopī said: "Except for the power of Siddhārtha, there is no one who can surpass me. If I were to grapple with you, your body would be shattered and mangled more severely than dust and mist; it would be like a strong man snapping a thousand trees with his fingers—what difficulty would there be in crushing you as I please?"

At that time, Devadatta proceeded further into the palace and sat upon the Bodhisattva’s couch. When the palace attendants saw him, they all felt resentment and jealousy; they immediately rushed forward, vying with one another to seize him and hurl him beneath the couch. He was instantly wounded in his left hip, rendering him unable to walk or move about. His family members carried him in a litter back to their own residence.
All the Śākyas were indignant and came to tell him:
"Devadatta, you should now change your ways and repent before the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, Devadatta privately devised a crafty ruse; he secretly fashioned iron claws and smeared them with lethal poison, appearing mild and gentle outwardly while harboring malice within.
At that time, Devadatta recalled what the Buddha had said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama constantly proclaims these words:
'One who has a body but no sores cannot be harmed by poison; since poison can do nothing to one without sores, there is no evil and nothing is created.'"
"I shall now go there and feign repentance; I will claw and tear his feet with my nails so that the poisonous gas flows out and he dies naturally.
The men carried him on a litter to visit the World-Honored One. When they were twenty-one *ren* away from the World-Honored One, he said to those around him:
"Set me down on the ground; I wish to proceed on foot."
He immediately descended to the ground.
At that very moment, fierce flames welled up from within the earth, enveloping his body as he was about to enter hell.
Therefore it is said: "One who has a body but no wound will not be harmed by poison; the poison can do nothing to one who lacks a wound."

To commit many various evils is certain to bring affliction upon oneself; to practice goodness and bestow benevolence is a most difficult thing. Regarding "To commit many various evils is certain to bring affliction upon oneself":

in the world there are many who spread evil and thereby harm themselves, failing to accord with the Noble Truths. They butcher and hunt fish, raise pigs and poultry, set out snares and nets to capture herds of deer, act as thieves and slay thieves to deliver them to the jailers, or belong to the Caṇḍāla caste and ply their trade with lutes and fishing lines. Such evil-doing sentient beings are beyond counting; those of this kind will certainly bring suffering upon themselves. Upon death, they enter hell and undergo immeasurable pain. Therefore it is said: "To commit many various evils is certain to bring affliction upon oneself."

Regarding the statement that "to bestow goodness and spread benevolent virtue is an exceedingly difficult matter": for a person to be able to examine for themselves the retributions of good and evil across past and future lives, to extensively give to those in dire straits, and to offer even the very flesh of their own bodies as gifts to others—this is indeed most difficult.
Therefore it is said: To bestow gifts and spread benevolence—this is exceedingly difficult.
How excellent is the one who cultivates goodness! How excellent is the one who commits great evil!
For the wicked person to do evil is easy; for the wicked person to do good is difficult.

Excellent is the practitioner of virtue! For a good person, the cultivation of virtuous conduct is as natural as it is spontaneous. Those who are inclined toward evil should not be associated with; those who do good are protected by all Buddhas and are beloved and respected by devas and humans alike. Wherever they go, they never part from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Therefore, it is said: "Excellent is the practitioner of virtue."

"Excellent indeed is the doing of great evil" means that when a person commits evil, it increases day by day without diminishing, just as creeping weeds grow of their own accord without being planted. Even if one were to scrape the ground clean of the old site, they still sprout without ceasing; therefore it is said: "Excellent indeed is the doing of great evil."

That it is easy for the wicked to do evil, yet difficult for a wicked person to do good, is like the Caṇḍāla caste, who constantly carry out dead bodies to discard them among the burial mounds; their hearts are always joyful and free from fear or restraint, and they find even greater delight in their own amusement.
It is also like a prison guard who maintains his shackles and fetters, committing evil day and night while considering himself honorable.

The noble and sagely person contemplates these manifold transformations as a great affliction; like one condemned to death who approaches the marketplace, with every step he takes he draws closer to the ground of death—how could such bitter suffering within the three realms be worth coveting or admiring?
Therefore it is said: "It is easy for the wicked to do evil, but difficult for the wicked to do good.
The fool considers himself upright, yet his evil is not yet matured;
when evil reaches full maturity, all sufferings likewise ripen.

The fool considers himself upright, just as one whose evil has not yet matured; the fool thinks his own conduct is exclusively correct and that all else is unlawful. Seeing those who practice virtue, he harbors hatred and envy toward them. Once the roots of sin are fully established and his deluded mind has reached full maturity, he finally realizes that what he has done was wrong.

Now, the evil I have committed was not done by my parents, nor was it created by my brothers or kinsmen; I must bear its retribution alone, and though I repent, it is of no avail. It was not wrought by the gods, nor by ghosts, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. I now know for myself the root of my transgression: I harbor no resentment toward heaven above, nor do I cast blame upon the earth below; I accept this punishment with a willing heart, knowing that there is nothing more to be done.
Therefore it is said: "The fool considers himself upright, as if his evil has not yet matured.

When evil reaches full maturity, one likewise undergoes all manner of suffering. A person who has accumulated sins enters hell to receive retribution; thirteen kinds of flames envelop their body, and though they die and are revived again and again, they cannot find death. They must repay their past offenses until they are exhausted without remainder, only then to emerge.

If they are reborn among animals, they are shrouded by ignorance and do not recognize the True Path; their dewlaps swell, their backs are broken, their noses are pierced, their heads are yoked, and their hands and feet are bound with shackles.

If one is born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), one suffers from hunger and thirst day and night; their belly is as vast as Mount Tai while their throat is as narrow as a needle. Their body is forty *li* long, with a thousand partitions for every inch.
If they are born among humans, they are poor, lowly, and wretched; their clothing does not cover their bodies and their food does not fill their mouths.
Therefore it is said: "When evil has reached full maturity, all sufferings likewise ripen.
When the wise perceive evil, they do not allow themselves to be ripened by it;
as long as evil is not yet ripe, the wise contemplate that evil."

When a wise person sees evil and is not ripened by that evil, it means that when a practitioner observes another committing evil, they reprove and admonish them at the proper time, saying: "This is not a sublime practice; wandering in saṃsāra, it is extremely difficult to seek liberation. It is the root cause for creating offenses within the three evil realms. Therefore, it is said: "The wise person sees evil and is not ripened by evil."
Just as evil is not yet ripe, the evildoer contemplates his evil; it is like a person who, having committed an evil deed, immediately feels remorse, thinking:
"Alas! What I have done was surely improper and is detested by others. Having now practiced this, could it not be that my own mind was mistaken?"
"From this day forth, I shall repent and regard evil as foul and impure.
Therefore it is said: "As with evil that has not yet ripened, the evildoer regards its evil;
so too does the worthy one regard its evil, until even the worthiness has not yet ripened."
If one speaks of those who are "mature through worthiness," it means that the worthy observe one another.

The worthy examine their own faults; this applies even to those who are not yet fully mature in worthiness. A person of worth maintains the precepts and is endowed with all virtues; they are widely learned, eloquent, and wise, with no deficiency in speech. Their words are gentle, and they always act with sincerity. They practice the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and have compassion for all beings. Seeing even a slight transgression, they feel fear; how much more so when it comes to committing a crime of the Avīci hell?
Therefore it is said: "The wise observe their own faults," up until the point where "the wise do not become complacent.
If one who is already mature in wisdom observes themselves with wisdom, the wise person examines and contemplates their own nature and conduct, thinking:

"The offerings I now receive are all the result of training accumulated in previous lives. Had I not planted merit, bestowed kindness, and practiced virtue in the past, by what cause would I have obtained this reward of fortune today?"

Now, those who do not exercise caution and earnestly practice their virtue will, upon receiving another form in the future, have no merit to rely upon; they shall once again drift through the cycle of birth and death. Only after long-term accumulation of expedient practices will they achieve success, yet the hardships encountered in the interim are beyond what can be known or calculated. Even passing by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they neither see nor hear them, falling away due to their own conduct until this present day, still not yet delivered.
Therefore it is said: "When one is mature through virtue, the virtuous examine one another.
Even if a person commits evil deeds, they do not do so repeatedly;
they take no pleasure in them in their mind, knowing that evil is suffering."

Although a person may commit evil deeds, they should not do so repeatedly; one who commits evil deeds must reform themselves, for once one has fully experienced the sufferings of the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions, it is extremely difficult to seek deliverance from within them.

Therefore, the wise regulate themselves with prohibitive laws and guard against evil before it occurs; thus, even if they receive retribution, it remains light. If they are in hell, the water in the cauldrons is cool and their suffering is slight, because they have repented and understood the root of their transgressions.
If they become animals, their burdens are not heavy and they are fed according to the season without added pain.
If they become hungry ghosts, there are four kinds of such ghosts; those born as noble and honored hungry ghosts find clothing and food provided spontaneously.
If one dwells among humans, one belongs to a wealthy and noble clan, free from any lack;
if one is born in the heavens, even as a reward for slight merit, one eats with the mouth covered, feeling ashamed of one's meager fortune.
Therefore it is said: "Though a person commits evil deeds, they should not do so repeatedly.

One who finds no pleasure in such thoughts and knows that evil is suffering—the practitioner who perceives evil and does not desire it—restrains his own mind and prevents it from scattering. Although a transgression may be minute, its retribution is like Mount Tai; though a fierce fire may be small, it consumes mountains and wilds. For this reason, the wise should always exercise caution and foresight, knowing that the source of evil is the root of all suffering.
Therefore it is said: "If one finds no delight in that mind, knowing that evil is suffering;
if a person can perform meritorious deeds, they should do so repeatedly.
If one takes pleasure in that intention, one will properly receive its karmic reward."

If a person can create merit, they should also do so repeatedly; for the reason why people in this life fall into poverty is entirely due to being misled by the fetters of stinginess from their previous lives.

Therefore, when the Sage addresses various categories of beings, he first prioritizes the bestowing of kindness. Even if one is poor, one must nonetheless reduce one's own share, however slightly, to compensate for past transgressions. Even if one possesses no wealth, one should employ oneself by exerting physical labor to serve others—repairing shrines and assisting in communal affairs—so that one’s meritorious deeds are not neglected day or night. Even a single snap of the fingers spent contemplating the good is sufficient; how much more so, then, to personally cultivate merit and virtue?

Therefore it is said: "A person can create merit for themselves; they should also cultivate it repeatedly. Regarding the phrase "one who aspires to that with a willing heart and properly receives its karmic reward":

when a person cultivates merit, it brings benefit to many. Seeing those who practice goodness, one rejoices on their behalf; immediately providing one's own wealth to encourage and assist them in making merit, one sees oneself receive blessings and a good reputation spread abroad. Those who see one will rejoice in their hearts and all pay respectful homage. Upon birth, one invariably encounters the sages and does not fall into the eight states of no leisure. Therefore it is said: "One who aspires to that with a willing heart and properly receives its karmic reward."

First, one should restrain the wholesome mind and hold fast to the root of evil; from this, one gives rise to meritorious deeds, for the mind otherwise delights in evil. Regarding "first, one should restrain the wholesome mind and hold fast to the root of evil":

one should fully maintain the wholesome mind without allowing it to be scattered. One should hold one's intent firmly before oneself as if carrying a bowl of oil, and remain trembling with vigilance as if avoiding the conflagration at the end of an eon. One should eliminate the impurities of the mind by means of [contemplating] impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, bathing it until it is pure. Therefore, it is said: "First, one should restrain the wholesome mind and hold fast to the root of evil."

Thus, one should cultivate meritorious deeds; for those whose minds delight in evil and who do not practice goodness to create provisions for future lives, they face the calamity of their bodies being consumed by fire at the end of life. Day and night they commit evil and cannot reform themselves. Therefore it is said: "Thus, one should cultivate meritorious deeds; for those whose minds delight in evil."
"Though the evil one commits may be slight, In future lives the suffering he undergoes is profound;
He shall receive boundless retribution, Like poison within his heart and belly.

Regarding the statement, "Though the evil one commits may be slight, in future lives the suffering he undergoes is profound": when a person’s will is not firm and their actions are indeterminate, whether they commit a sin to a small or great extent—whether consciously or unconsciously—they must inevitably receive the retribution and cannot escape its consequences. Lacking shame and remorse, they seek neither liberation nor the path to transcend the world. Therefore it is said: "Though the evil one commits may be slight, in future lives the suffering he undergoes is profound."

One shall obtain boundless retribution, as if poison were in one's heart and belly. Even if there is but a slight opening for dust and defilement to stain the mind, one will immediately undergo boundless transgression; or by provoking others to commit evil deeds, one thereby brings about the fall into boundless sin for oneself; or by alienating kinsmen and causing strife within the household—such sufferings and afflictions are beyond counting.
Therefore it is said: "One shall obtain boundless retribution, as if poison were in one's heart and belly.
Though the merit performed may be slight, one will later receive great fortune; one shall obtain a great reward, like planting seeds and harvesting fruit.

Regarding the statement that although one's merit may be small, one will later receive great merit: when a person performs meritorious deeds, it depends solely upon their intention, not upon whether their material wealth is much or little. If one bestows many things while harboring inner stinginess, the merit obtained later cannot even be mentioned;
yet if the objects bestowed are few but the mind is impartial and universal, extending widely to all without seeking for oneself, the merit obtained later is beyond measure.
Therefore it is said: "Though the merit performed be small, one will later receive great merit."

One shall obtain a great reward, just as one who sows reaps the fruit; later, one will receive the natural blessings of devas and humans, with a serene countenance, always dwelling in a central land rather than a frontier region. One’s words will be followed and used without offending the minds of others; possessing abundant wealth and many treasures, one harbors no malice or envy. If remaining at home, one cultivates virtue so that the clan is harmonious; if one should leave the household life, renouncing affection and love, shaving off beard and hair and donning the three dharma-robes, one disciplines the body to study the Way, eliminating thoughts of glory and hope. Transcending stages to attain realization, one exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*) and accomplishes untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*). With all virtues universally complete and merit fully perfected, it is like a farmer who, having sown much, obtains a harvest; his granaries and treasuries are filled, his heart is joyful, and he celebrates within himself that his efforts have not been in vain.
Therefore it is said: "One shall obtain a great retribution, just as planting seeds yields fruit.
To unjustly slight another who is without fault, or to unjustly invade one who is without malice—one shall, within the ten states of existence, surely go to those very realms.

To be harsh toward one who is faultless and to aggress against one who is without malice—this is like a person who, though devoid of anger, envy, or pride, is nevertheless targeted by a foolish and deluded person who directs their intent toward them with a mind of plotting harm. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are compassionate toward all; seeing those in sorrow and suffering, they deliver them from their hardships, giving rise to thoughts for all living beings as a mother loves her child.
Therefore it is said: "To be insolent toward one who has done no wrong, and to invade one who harbors no ill will.

Regarding the phrase "one shall then proceed to those ten abodes," the so-called ten abodes are: first, the Unrelenting (Saṃjīva); second, the Heat (Kālasūtra); third, the Great Heat (Mahāraurava); fourth, the Black Rope (Raurava); fifth, the Wailing (Pratāpana); sixth, the Great Wailing (Mahānaraka); seventh, the Equal Harm (Samghāta); eighth, the Equal Life (Utpala); ninth, the Animals (Tiryagyoni); and tenth, the Hungry Ghosts (Pretas).
If there are sentient beings whose malevolent minds are intensely blazing, they will not escape these ten states after the end of their lives.
Therefore it is said: "Regarding these ten categories of states, one shall surely proceed to them."
Painful sensations are harsh and violent; this form will surely decay and perish.
Tormented by manifold ailments, the mind becomes disordered and unstable;
one is separated from one's kin and all wealth and goods are exhausted.
Those who are plundered by kings, whose wishes do not follow their intent,
or who undergo countless transformations, being consumed by fire—
when their bodies perish and they lack wisdom, they likewise proceed to the ten realms.

All the verses above were spoken from the divine mouth of the Tathāgata: Devadatta, through his foolish teachings, incited Ajātaśatru to drink wine and drive a rutting elephant intoxicated toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned toward that elephant and spoke these verses:
"Do not say there is no evil when you have committed it; do not say there is no fault for what has been done long ago;
do not say there is no fault for what was done in secret— all of these have their evidentiary consequences."

When a person commits evil deeds, there are varying degrees of gravity; yet if their intent is intense and they do not relinquish it, being unable to distance themselves from it or seek the essential way out, they conceal and hide it, nor can they confess it to others.

For this reason, the World-Honored One instructed future generations that whether one acts anew or repeats old habits—even down to the most secluded and private places—the karmic retribution for good and evil cannot be hidden.
Therefore it is said: "Commit evil and do not say there is none; commit it repeatedly and say there is no sin.

To speak in secret of being without sin—all such things have their evidence. If a person intends to establish themselves in a secluded place to create the roots of various evils, although they may at that time escape the censure of the masses, they will nevertheless not escape the retribution of future lives.
Therefore it is said: "Secret and lewd speech is not without fault; all this has its own evidence.
Evil speech brings sorrow, long-practiced speech also brings sorrow, secret and lewd speech likewise brings sorrow, and its retribution also brings sorrow."
When a person first commits evil, their initial intention is so fervent that they do not realize it; at that moment, their mind is bold and they believe it is right to act thus.

At that time, the World-Honored One drew an analogy: just as when the sun first sets, the shadows of mountains, rivers, and trees all hang down until darkness falls, so too it is with these followers of delusion who cling to confusion. Having established the roots of unwholesome conduct through body and speech, on the day of their death, the heavy shadows of their various evils each follow them, gradually leading them to the dark chamber where they receive retribution.
Therefore it is said: "Committing evil brings sorrow; long-continued practice of it also brings sorrow; doing so in secret likewise brings sorrow; and its retribution also brings sorrow."
"He grieves here, and he grieves there; for those who commit evil deeds, there is grief in both places.
He grieves there as he undergoes retribution; only by observing their conduct can one know this with certainty.

What is called "grieving here" refers to grieving in the present life. What is called "grieving there" refers to grieving in future lives. What is called "grieving here" refers to before one has died or reached the end of one's life. What is called "grieving there" refers to after one has already died or reached the end of one's life. Therefore it is said: "He grieves here, and he grieves there."
Regarding those who perform evil deeds and grieve for both: they grieve here and receive retribution there; only by observing their conduct can one know this with certainty.
Regarding those who perform meritorious deeds and rejoice for both:
they rejoice here and receive retribution there; by observing their conduct, they are purified of themselves.

In the past, King Virūḍhaka raised an army and launched a military campaign against the kingdom of Kapilavastu. He crushed the populace and captured seven thousand people; those among them who had realized the stages of the Path, he buried up to their feet and ordered fierce elephants to trample them to death.
To explain the meaning briefly, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The King of Kosala is currently devoid of gratitude and reciprocity; he opposes the noble and rebels against the truth, committing crimes of the Avīci hell. Such as these shall themselves receive their retribution in seven days' time."

The royal lineage of the kingdom of Kosala shall be extinguished, with no further successor; the flames of the Avīci Hell shall burst forth, enveloping the king’s body and his attendants, as they all enter the midst of the Avīci Hell.

Upon hearing this, King Vairāṭa immediately prepared his fourfold army; the palace ladies and court beauties departed the city to avoid the calamity. He then proceeded to the Ganges River, where he unfurled sails and boarded a ship, believing that he had escaped the disaster.
At that time, the flames of the Avīci Hell came forth to meet them, and the king and his entire retinue, great and small, all entered the hell without anyone escaping.

Before King Virūḍhaka had yet fled from the calamity, he arrived within the city of Śrāvastī and heard from afar the sounds of performers playing music, singing, dancing, and laughing, enjoying themselves with the five kinds of sensory pleasures.
The king asked his attendants, "Whose sounds of laughter and merriment are these that reach even here?"
The ministers replied,
"This is the sound of musical instruments from the residence of Prince Jyotiṣka.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon him to come at once.

"While I am currently engaged in a military campaign, battling bandits and worrying over state affairs, Citra today enjoys himself with the five kinds of sensual pleasure. Should I be defeated by the bandits in battle, this man will surely hope to obtain the position of sovereign king."
When Prince Jeta heard the king’s summons, he immediately went out to receive him.
The king said to the prince:
"I am at war with bandits and my heart is filled with anxiety for the myriad nations, yet you are now merely indulging yourself in the five pleasures."
He immediately drew his sharp sword, severed [the head], and departed.

With his head cast away, Citra was reborn in the heavens; amidst the five kinds of music provided by the palace maidens, he enjoyed himself without realizing his master had been lost. He was surrounded on all sides by celestial nymphs, who likewise performed songs and instrumental music for their mutual entertainment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye how Prince Jeta was receiving blessings in two places, spoke these verses in the midst of the great assembly:
"He rejoices here, and he rejoices there; In both places, he rejoices because of his meritorious deeds.
He rejoices there as he receives the retribution; Seeing his own conduct, it is pure."
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke these verses to King Virūḍhaka:
"He who cooks here and he who is cooked there—both are cooked for their evil deeds.
He who cooks there shall receive the retribution; the practice one has performed will manifest its own proof."

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye that King Virūḍhaka was in hell, undergoing the fivefold torments of flogging, scourging, and other agonizing sufferings, spoke this verse:
"By performing merit and refraining from evil, All proceeds from the law of past actions;
In the end, one fears not the path of death, Like a boat crossing against the current."
In the past, before the Buddha had attained equal and perfect enlightenment, he was a bodhisattva named Sarvadatta. For the sake of a brahmin, he bound himself and went to the palace gate.
The King of the enemy state said,
"Are you now afraid of me?
At that time, Sarvamdada spoke this verse:
"Performing merit and refraining from evil— All arise from the laws of past actions.
In the end, one does not fear the path of death, Like a boat cutting across the current.

Long ago, there was a man-eating *piśāca* who ruled as king among men. He constantly consumed human flesh as his primary fare. Having captured ninety-nine kings during a military expedition against a neighboring state, he established twenty-one men as his regular provisions. These ninety-nine kings said to the *rākṣasa* king:

"In a neighboring kingdom there is a king named Sunetra, who delights in practicing generosity and cultivating the virtues of a bodhisattva; he does not refuse anyone who makes a request. Great King, if you are able to capture him, we would willingly accept death and harbor not the slightest regret."

At that time, the rākṣasa king immediately raised a host of spirits and went to watch for an opportunity; it happened that King Sunakṣatra was just then sporting in the bathing pools within his outer gardens.
There was a brahmin who took leave of his family to pursue studies abroad. According to the custom of the brahmins, when it was time to depart, he said to his parents:

"I am now leaving home to seek companions for my studies; as for the day of my return, no date has yet been set. Should my funds become exhausted, I shall borrow from the King, and I will repay you upon my return."
That person, having completed his studies and achieved success, returned home; however, seeing only an empty house and no people, he immediately asked his neighbors:
"Where are my parents, brothers, and sisters now?"

The neighbor replied, "After you studied under him, you failed to repay the king's wealth with any equivalent; consequently, you have been imprisoned by the king and are now in jail. If you wish to go and see him, now is the time."
The man thought to himself:

"My family is impoverished and my means are meager; I possess no wealth or treasures. If I were to go to the prison to visit my parents, I too would be seized and subjected to the same suffering, unable to escape the king's law. It would be best to change my appearance and disguise myself while remaining outside, to go secretly and seek what is needed so that once the official goods are fully repaid, I may finally be released."
The man thought again:

"There is a king in a neighboring country named Śobha who cultivates virtue and morality, and whose mind of generosity never ceases. I shall go to him and tell him my situation with utmost sincerity; he will surely not refuse me, and it will suffice to repay the king's property."
He immediately went there and begged from the king as he had been instructed.
The king said, "Excellent!"
"We shall provide for you; once you have finished bathing, we will grant you our gift. Please stay a moment and do not worry that we shall fail to keep our word.
The king went to the bathing pool and was captured by the ghost soldiers. The king immediately turned back to look, his face filled with grief and his tears falling.

The king of ghosts asked him, "We have heard that Your Majesty is benevolent and compassionate, providing aid to all without exception. Even though you have encountered this calamity, why do you grieve so?"

The king replied to the spirit, "In my life, I have practiced giving with never a regret. Just now, there was a brahmin outside begging for alms; I promised him but had not yet given it to him, and that is why I am so distressed."
The king of ghosts said to the king, "Your Majesty has maintained sincerity and faithfulness from the beginning without change; now I release you so that you may complete your act of giving.

Knowing then that the king’s heart had not failed in sincerity and faith, the king returned to his palace, opened the treasuries to bestow gifts according to the wishes of those people, and soon thereafter returned to the place of the king of ghosts to fulfill his pledge.
The King of Ghosts said,
"Do you not fear me? Why have you come here to face death?"
At that time, the Great King Sunakṣatra addressed the king of ghosts with these verses:
"By performing merit and refraining from evil, All proceeds from the laws of past actions;
In the end, one fears not the path of death, Like a boat crossing against the current."

Upon hearing this, the King of Ghosts felt deep shame within his heart; he changed his mind and reformed his conduct, resolving to cultivate the roots of goodness. He then addressed King Śunakṣatra, saying:
"What you have now spoken is rare even among human beings. I shall now release ninety-nine kings."

"I relinquish this position; I pray that Your Majesty shall govern and transform the realm through the Dharma. I shall lead my host of spirits back to our original dwelling. If we both remain in good health, we shall surely visit one another frequently."
Thereupon, they parted ways and each returned to their respective abodes.

The myriad people celebrated with joy, and the realm became pure and peaceful; together they practiced the ten wholesome deeds and refrained from cultivating evil karma. Because Sunakṣatra had accumulated virtuous conduct without ceasing, he later attained Buddhahood beneath the King of Trees and again spoke this verse:
"Performing merit and not committing evil Is entirely due to the law of past actions."
In the end, one never fears the direct path to death, Like a boat crossing a flowing stream.
The Twenty-ninth Chapter on Evil Conduct concludes. The *Udānavarga*, Scroll Twenty-five.
The *Udānavarga*, Scroll Twenty-six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty: The Pair of Essentials.
The night light illuminates the darkness until the sun has not yet risen.

The sun’s light spreads great brilliance; the night-light then becomes dark and dim. Having observed this meaning, the Tathāgata draws an analogy so that future generations may clearly understand the matter:

it is like the firefly, dwelling in the deep darkness, spreading its radiance to illuminate the distance, thinking to itself that its own light is unsurpassed. When the Sun Deity releases hundreds of thousands of rays of light as he rises in the east, at that moment the firefly’s light no longer exists; its color becomes dark and dim, appearing like pure ink. Therefore it is said: "The night-light shines in the gloom until the sun has not yet risen; when the sun’s light spreads great brilliance, the night-light then becomes dark and dim."
The *pratyekabuddha* spreads forth radiance; before the Tathāgata has appeared, the Buddha emits a great light, wherein there are neither *pratyekabuddhas* nor *śrāvakas*.

The practices of the non-Buddhist *brahmacārins* differ: some attain knowledge through observation, some through entering meditative concentration, and some awaken by hearing the teachings. These three types of people, while traversing the world, each claim themselves to be supreme.
Why is this so? It is because the Tathāgata has not yet appeared in the world.

Should the Tathāgata descend as a spirit into the world, emitting great radiance and spreading the transformative teachings, at that time the non-Buddhist Brahmins would naturally vanish; their path would no longer be practiced, and they would possess no further divine power.
Therefore it is said: "The observer radiates light; yet before the Tathāgata has appeared, the Buddha emits the Great Radiance, wherein there is neither observer nor śrāvaka."

To perceive what is not firm as firm, and to perceive what is firm as not firm—such a person does not attain firmness, because they have given rise to false views. Regarding "perceiving what is not firm as firm":

this refers to those classes of beings who are attached to birth and death; if they conceive the thought that dwelling in the world and delighting in the five desires for one's own amusement constitutes firmness, it is for this reason that it is said:

This is to conceive the notion of permanence regarding what is impermanent. As for conceiving the notion of impermanence regarding what is permanent: those of false views have long held to their convictions; they instruct one another and thus give rise to this discourse. We have heard in secret that the Buddha’s teaching speaks of *nirvāṇa*—where there is no birth and no extinction, and no perception of arising or ceasing; furthermore, there are no songs, praises, joy, or dance, nor the five clans of kinsmen, nor coming and going, advancing and retreating, gardens, pavilions, or bathing pools. Since none of these exist at all, what permanence could there be?
The Buddha said, "It is not so.
These people possess inverted and false minds that have not been extinguished; there is nothing more firm and solid than Nirvana, yet they instead revile it, claiming it is not firm."
Therefore it is said: "To conceive of what is not firm as firm.

As for the statement, "He does not reach the firm because he gives rise to wrong views": extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is free from all afflictions; it is serene, unconditioned, and immovable in its concentrated stillness, never subject to change. The fool, failing to understand this, considers it not to be the truth. Therefore it is said: "He does not reach the firm because he gives rise to wrong views."
One who knows the firm as firm, and knows the non-firm as non-firm, seeks that which is firm;
he takes correct governance as his foundation.
If there are sentient beings who understand the extinction of *nirvāṇa*—which is without arising and without ceasing—they likewise do not deceive or delude the world.

The abode of eternal quiescence of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is such that when sentient beings enter this chamber, they do not feel increased joy upon attaining honor and high status, nor do they feel added grief when beset by humiliation and disgrace. They differ in speech from those with inverted views and diverge in their destination from those of heterodox factions; they are as profoundly still as the great void, eternally at rest and non-arising. This is what the wise admire; it is not the practice of the foolish.

Those who wish to reach that chamber must traverse the path of the Eightfold Noble Way and seek to cross the vast precipices of the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby ferrying themselves across the perilous shores of birth and death. They settle their spirits in the tranquil state of non-action (*wuwei*) and look back upon the lingering torments of suffering. Alas, how profound is the proliferation of ignorance and delusion! Therefore it is said: "He who knows what is secure as secure, and what is insecure as insecure, seeks that which is secure, taking correct governance as his foundation."
"What the fool considers a fortress, Is instead bound by the nine fetters; Like a bird cast into a net, This arises from the deep-seated solidity of craving.

Regarding "what the fool considers a fortress": when a person lives in the world, their deluded mind is difficult to reform. Some say the accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) constitutes the fortress; others say the fundamental fetters (*saṃyojana*) constitute the fortress. Within this, they give rise to conceptualizations without distinguishing between the true and the false; thus, even though they have left the household life to study the Path, they instead practice deviant conduct. Therefore it is said: "What the fool considers a fortress."

Regarding "being bound by the nine fetters in turn": when a person cultivates the Path, they ought to renounce the household life. Yet, encountering evil associates who point out deviant paths, they abandon their former fetters only to be bound by the nine fetters in turn. Like a moth leaping into a flame without regard for future consequences, this arises from the deep-seated and firm nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Therefore it is said: "Being bound by the nine fetters in turn, like a bird falling into a net; this arises from the deep-seated and firm nature of craving."
All those who harbor doubts regarding this world and the world beyond can extinguish them entirely through meditative concentration; free from affliction, they cultivate the holy life.

As for those who harbor doubts, these practitioners of the path contemplate the perception of foulness and impurity, thereby removing their doubts, hatred, and envy. Upon hearing [the teaching], they attain faith without needing further deliberation; therefore it is said: "All those who harbor doubts."

Regarding "this world and the world beyond": "this" refers to the present life and "beyond" refers to future lives; "this" refers to the present existence and "beyond" refers to future existences. To not give rise to hesitation or doubt therein is to accord with a concentrated mind.
Therefore it is said: "In this world and in future worlds.

As for "one who can extinguish through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)," it means that the mind and intentions of one who has entered concentration are firm and stable, such that they are able to completely eliminate and prevent the arising of conceptual attachments; therefore it is said, "one can extinguish through meditative concentration."

One who practices the holy life without affliction is not troubled by the fetters and proclivities; with a resolute mind that is pure and always as if in single-minded concentration, the roots of virtue they cultivate transcend those of ordinary people. Therefore it is said: "Practice the holy life without affliction."
Free from dust and detached from dust, one who can wear this robe has no driver and reaches nowhere; this is not the dharma-robe.

When people cultivate the Way yet constantly harbor defilement, and the stains of lust, anger, and delusion do not leave their minds, they may don the *kāṣāya* but do not remove the three poisons; thus they do not reach the Way. Therefore it is said: "Free from dust and detached from dust."

Only those who are worthy sages can wear this robe; they block all evils and are able to don this robe of the True Dharma. Those who do not possess such qualities should not wear it. Therefore it is said: "Those who can wear this robe have no driver and go nowhere; this is not a robe of the Dharma."

If one can remove defilements, Cultivating precepts, wisdom, and concentration, Such a person should contemplate karma; This is who should wear the kāṣāya. Regarding "if one can remove defilements, cultivating precepts, wisdom, and concentration":

for a person’s practice of cultivation, the removal of defilements is the foundation. When the fetters of the three poisons are forever exhausted without remainder, even if one has attained arhatship, if one does not enter meditative absorption, one will only realize one's errors when confronted by neutral circumstances. By cultivating the precepts to remove defilements, one does not lose the mind of the Way; therefore it is said: "If one can remove defilements, cultivating precepts, wisdom, and concentration."

"One should contemplate karma; this one should don the saṃghāṭī robe. For one who has entered meditative concentration, there will surely be benefit; whatever the mind intends, there is no task that will not be accomplished. Among the devas, worldlings, Māras, and their followers, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings, there are none who do not revere and serve them. Therefore it is said: "One should contemplate karma; this one should don the saṃghāṭī robe."
Without gentle and mild speech, one’s reputation may still reach far;
though a person possesses a kind countenance, they may harbor a heart of craftiness and deceit.

Regarding "without gentle and mild speech, one’s reputation may still reach far": in this world, there are many who engage in conversation with others while harboring treachery within, appearing outwardly as if they were simple-minded. Therefore it is said: "Without gentle and mild speech, one’s reputation may still reach far."

There are those who possess a fine countenance yet harbor a mind of craftiness and deceit. Long ago, King Prasenajit was sporting in his pleasure gardens when he saw two brahmins practicing the Way by mortifying their bodies; they worshipped the sun and moon and sacrificed to water and fire.
The King, seeing that this man’s resolve in practicing the Way was so arduous, immediately went to the Buddha's presence and said to the World-Honored One:
"Just now, while traveling for an excursion, I saw two brahmins who practice the Way with such austere forms that they are most difficult to equal and have no peers."
The Buddha told the king:

"If one wishes to know whether another has cultivated virtue and perfected the observance of the precepts, one must observe their deportment while living together and examine their speech; only then can one discern whether they possess the precepts or not."

Upon hearing these words, the king felt deep shame within his heart; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet, and withdrew. Returning to the palace, he addressed his ministers:
"Go quickly to that place and summon the two brahmins to my rear garden. I wish to observe them closely to see if they truly practice austerities in pursuit of the Way and its virtue."
"Is it not that he has falsely assumed a reputation and his conduct is dissolute and improper?

Following these instructions, the minister summoned him to the garden. From atop the palace tower, the king observed his behavior from afar; realizing that the man was crafty and deceitful, falsely claiming to be a practitioner of the Way, he felt profound shame and remorse. His faith in the Buddha’s path flourished, and he became intensely devoted to it.
He then issued a decree to all the people within his realm: "Whoever serves those of external studies or heterodox paths shall be executed without mercy."

The king went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and repented for his previous failure. He vowed that from this day forward, he would provide the four requisites as offerings and revere the Triple Gem for the rest of his life, never violating this oath.
Therefore it is said: "A person may have a fine complexion, yet harbor a mind of craftiness and deceit.
One who can sever this, forever uprooting its source—the wise who eliminate all defilements—is truly called one of 'fine complexion'."

Regarding those who can sever this and forever uproot its root: the people of the world often harbor treacherous and wicked hearts; though they don the dharma robes, their inner conduct is not genuine. Only one who can sever this is truly worthy of the Gate of the Way. Therefore it is said: "Those who can sever this shall forever uproot its root."

The wise one who eliminates all impurities is called one of virtuous appearance; the person of wisdom practices the essentials of the Dharma and should take this as the Way. That which is not the Dharma is not practiced, for this is what the learner prizes. Their countenance is serene and radiant, such that all people look up to them with reverence. Therefore it is said: "The wise one eliminates his impurities, and is thus called one of virtuous appearance."
One cannot judge another’s character by their outward composure; one may perceive a person’s true intent upon a brief glance.
In this world, many are those who act contrary to their words, wandering aimlessly through existence like counterfeit brass that contains nothing but copper within.
Wandering alone without fear or inhibition, one may be inwardly defiled while appearing outwardly pure. One cannot judge a person’s intent by their composed appearance;

for there are many in the world whose countenances are serene and whose speech is eloquent and refined, yet whose inner hearts are hypocritical and whose minds and mouths are at odds. Though they are called human beings, their conduct is uneven; they appear like sages on the outside while harboring poisonous deeds within.
