Although one may briefly meet them and fail to distinguish between the wise and the foolish—just as one sees the light of a fire from afar at night, yet burns one's hand upon reaching out to seize it—so it is with these people: though they possess a pleasing appearance, they harbor blazing flames within. Therefore it is said: "One cannot know a person’s intent by their composed appearance, merely by a brief glance."

In this world, there are many who act contrary to the Way and wander aimlessly through existence. In the future, fools will become increasingly adept at craftiness and deception; gradually, they will come to slander the worthy and revile the sages. Employing ten thousand forms of villainy and intrigue, they delude the people of the world. When conversing with others, their countenance is not upright, yet their speech is composed in elegant phrases, their eloquence unimpeded, and they are capable of performing lawless deeds in the midst of the great assembly. When the multitude beholds them, there are none who do not rub their eyes in wonder. Therefore it is said: "In this world, there are many who act contrary to the Way and wander aimlessly through existence."

Just as with that counterfeit brass which contains nothing but copper within, a person of crafty deception employs many stratagems, using smoke to make the color of the copper surpass that of true gold, thereby deluding the people of the world to greedily seize their wealth. For this reason, the Tathāgata draws upon this as a metaphor: just as that counterfeit brass gains great worldly profit, so too is it with the treacherous and wicked person.

With sweet words and beautiful phrases, they entice donors to obtain offerings such that the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick—are never lacking. Although they receive these offerings, they shall later have to repay them by undergoing the retribution of molten copper, experiencing bitter suffering until their accumulated sins are exhausted. Therefore it is said: "Just as with that counterfeit brass, which contains nothing but copper within."

To travel alone without fear or hesitation while harboring impurity within and appearing unclean without is like the case of a treacherous person who frequently travels among the people with many followers; though everyone who sees him pays him respect, it is only later that one realizes he is not a true man, just as when a bandit’s cruelty has ravaged many villages, one finally knows he is no genuine person.
Therefore it is said: "Wandering alone without fear or dread, yet internally defiled and externally impure;
gluttonous and lacking self-restraint, wandering through the three realms of existence according to the seasons, like a pig kept in a pen, repeatedly receiving the womb."

Greedily devouring without self-restraint, though they practice the three turnings according to the season, they are like those deluded fools who serve as the leaders for others and receive their offerings. They nourish their own forms until their bodies become fat and robust, yet they cannot even turn over in bed. Donors and patrons visit them at all times; these fools feign sitting in meditative concentration and contemplation, thereby securing great offerings for themselves.

For this reason, the World-Honored One used it as a metaphor: like a pig being raised that lies down to eat without moving, unaware that in time it will suffer slaughter and dismemberment; so too, the casting off of one body and the taking up of another knows no rest.

Therefore it is said: "Greedily devouring without self-restraint, wandering through the three realms of existence according to the seasons, like a pig kept in a pen, one undergoes the womb again and again."
If a person can concentrate their mind and know moderation in eating, seeking only to sustain the body and nourish life while guarding the Way, they shall succeed.

Formerly, the Buddha spoke this verse to King Prasenajit. Because the King had cultivated the roots of virtue in past lives, his blessings manifested as a natural response: in his rear garden, sugarcane trees grew spontaneously, exuding sweet juice that flowed without ceasing day or night; furthermore, a single stalk of non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously within that garden, with hundreds of drooping ears that were inexhaustible when harvested.
The king accepted the blessed food and ate it without satiety; his body became so heavy that he suffered extreme distress from his labored breathing and was unable to turn over.
He then went to where the Buddha was, bowed low with respectful courtesy, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person can concentrate their mind, Knowing moderation in eating,
Seeking only to sustain the body And nourish life while guarding the Way."

Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he rose from his seat, took leave of the Buddha, and returned to the palace. He immediately commanded his cooks:
"When you present food before me, you shall only receive your meal after first reciting this verse."

From that time forth, he constantly took this as his practice; the King gradually reduced his food until his body became light and agile, and in his movements and comings and goings, he experienced no suffering or distress.
He observed purity and cultivated himself, yet his faculties remained incomplete and he felt no satiety regarding food—such are the conduct and practices of ordinary people.
The desireful mind increases further, like a house that has collapsed and is leaking.

One who contemplates purity while practicing for themselves, yet whose faculties are not complete—such a person, when first engaging in practice, lacks firm resolve in their intent. Internally contemplating their own hair, fur, nails, and teeth, they become attached to what is pure and give rise to lustful thoughts; thus anger is increased and ignorance grows. Failing to restrain the gates of the sensory faculties, they remain unsettled; through negligence and self-indulgence, they ultimately lose the light of the Path. It is like adding ghee to a blazing fire; clearly understanding this principle, how could it possibly be a sign of extinguishing the fire?

Now, those who wish to extinguish the fires of lust, anger, and delusion so that they never arise again should cultivate the perception of the foul and impure. Therefore it is said: "One who contemplates purity while practicing for themselves does not possess the full complement of the sense faculties."

Regarding food, there is no satiety; such are the practices of the vulgar. Those practitioners who never tire of begging, yet who, upon receiving alms, hide them away in bags without relinquishing their stingy minds—when they eventually pass away, they will undergo the conduct of the vulgar. Therefore it is said: "Regarding food, there is no satiety; such are the practices of the vulgar."

The desire-thought increases further, like a house that is dilapidated and leaking. When a practitioner clings to delusion and does not cultivate the roots of goodness, their desire-thoughts blaze intensely and they do not reform themselves; they shall again undergo the hardships of birth and death. It is just as when a roof is poorly constructed and not properly repaired—if it rains, water leaks through, drenching and splashing clean clothes until they are soiled. Human nature is like this: if the mind is not firm, it leaks lust, anger, and ignorance. Therefore it is said: "The desire-thought increases further, like a house that is dilapidated and leaking."
One should contemplate the practice of impurity, with the sense faculties free from deficiency or leakage;
knowing moderation in food, possessing faith and maintaining diligence,
one does not indulge the desires of the mind, remaining as unshakable as Mount Tai before the wind.

One should contemplate the practice of impurity; those whose faculties are without deficiency or leakage should control their minds so as to have no leisure even for eating or breathing. They observe this body, discerning each instance of the outflow of impurity, analyzing the thirty-six foul and unclean substances within the body. From head to foot, there is not a single thing to be craved. By withdrawing and gathering the faculties so that they do not leak away, it is said: "One should contemplate the practice of impurity, with the faculties free from deficiency or leakage."

Knowing moderation in eating and possessing faith while maintaining diligence, the practitioner who holds fast to this resolve attains untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*). One who eats excessively becomes dazed and cannot enter meditative absorption;
however, one whose faith is fervent and capable of practicing diligence will transcend the masses, advance alone, and soon receive its realization.
Therefore it is said: "Know moderation in food, possess faith, and maintain diligence.

To not indulge in the desires of the mind is like the wind blowing against Mount Tai; the practitioner’s intent remains undisturbed by manifold thoughts. Desire is the root of calamity and the master that gives rise to disaster and affliction. When one perceives the spirit of the body to be frantic and unable to receive the light of wisdom, death will arrive face-to-face with the agony of the body being consumed by fire. One should discern this principle: all such things are suffering and affliction.

One restrains the mind so that it does not give rise to the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects; externally one wards off the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and internally one gathers the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). Being pure both within and without, one does not leak out desires, remaining as firm and immovable as Mount Tai, unshaken by whirling winds. One’s mind is like a *vajra*, incapable of being destroyed or corrupted. Therefore it is said: "Do not indulge the mind in desire, for it is like the wind blowing against Mount Tai."
"Solitude is most delightful, yet people do not find joy therein;
those free from desire always dwell there, for it is not a place for those possessed by desire.

Regarding the statement "solitude is most delightful," the reason the Sages spoke these words was their desire to cause practitioners to swiftly attain the Dharma. Within the midst of quietude and stillness, the mind attains single-minded concentration; through contemplation and reflection, one does not waste a moment, and the response of the mind is like the echo of a person’s call. Therefore, it is said: "Solitude is most delightful."

As for those people who do not delight in that [state], such individuals are all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) whose minds are attached to sensual desires and cannot relinquish them; their minds are fixated on female beauty as something substantial, yet once they perish, they realize it was not real. Therefore it is said: "Yet people do not delight in that."

Regarding those who dwell constantly in the state of desirelessness, they are called "sages" because their lust, anger, and delusion, as well as all fetters, bonds, and attachments, have been suddenly and completely eliminated. They are as pure as celestial gold, without even the slightest blemish. When they travel through villages to teach and transform others, they carry their alms bowls at the appointed time to bring blessings and deliver sentient beings. According to the amount given, they offer prayers of blessing for the donors; when a donor hears their voice, the Way and its teachings penetrate their heart.

Should they encounter a Pratyekabuddha, he flies his bowl into the void and performs the eighteen transformations; though his form remains among the multitude, his mind dwells in the vast wilderness. Therefore it is said: "Those without desire dwell therein constantly."

That which is not the dwelling place of desire is so called because the minds of those attached to desire remain fixed upon it; it is like a person who has fallen into sin and is confined in prison, where, as the authorities do not pass judgment, they remain for years and years, and though they long to seek release, it is difficult indeed to obtain.

Those who are lewd and dissolute are likewise thus: enveloped by a deluded mind and confined within the prison of desire, they do not encounter the medicine of the untainted wisdom of the sages; therefore, it is exceedingly difficult for them to attain liberation and deliverance.
Therefore it is said: "It is not a place for those driven by desire.
Whether in a village or in seclusion, on high banks or level ground—wherever an Arhat passes, there is none who does not receive his blessing.

Wherever a True Person dwells, there will inevitably be auspicious responses; the Four Heavenly Kings, lords of the earth, constantly come to protect them. The region where they reside shall not suffer calamities or afflictions, for blessings can suppress evil and prevent various harms from arising—this is due to the majestic spiritual power resulting from a Sage residing therein.
Therefore it is said: Whether in a village or in solitude, on high banks or level ground, wherever the Arhats pass, there is none who does not receive their blessing.
Difficult to shift and difficult to move, like that heavy Snowy Mountain, they do not appear except to the virtuous, just as one cannot see in a dark room when shooting at night.

The minds of the noble and sagely cannot be moved; whatever they intend to accomplish, they surely achieve without difficulty. It is just as when various mountains produce excellent medicines, which one may take at will to distinguish and eliminate poisons. For this reason, the wise say that they are endowed with all virtues. Therefore it is said: "Difficult to shift, difficult to move, like that heavy Snowy Mountain."

If one is not virtuous, they will not manifest; it is like shooting arrows in a dark room at night. Without a good friend, or by failing to associate with a good friend, one hears evil but does not investigate its root, and hears good but does not praise its virtue. This is just like shooting arrows in the darkness within a dark room. Therefore it is said: "If one is not virtuous, they will not manifest, just like shooting arrows in a dark room at night."
"There are thousands of wise ones, yet the one of noble wisdom dwells in the forest;
the principles and meanings are most profound, discerned by the wise.

Regarding "there are thousands of wise ones, yet the one of noble wisdom dwells in the forest": this means that the wise possess discernment; having heard a single phrase of meaning, they can eloquently expound countless methods of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Their contemplation and discernment all arise from cultivation and refinement. Therefore it is said: "There are thousands of wise ones, yet the one of noble wisdom dwells in the forest."

The principles are extremely profound; that which is analyzed by the wise is the analysis of all phenomena without losing their proper sequence. The principles are so profound that they thoroughly elucidate those phenomena; one knows from whence they arise and from whence they cease. Analyzing these principles, not missing even a single detail—therefore it is said: "The principles are extremely profound; they are what the wise analyze."
There are many classes of sentient beings who, though not struck by arrows, nonetheless meet their end;
observing this principle now, it is something those without precepts find shameful.

Regarding the statement that there are many classes of sentient beings who, though not struck by arrows, nonetheless meet their end: what is meant by "meeting their end" refers to those who practice what is not the Dharma. Therefore it is said: "There are many classes of sentient beings who, though not struck by arrows, nonetheless meet their end."

Now, observing this principle: that which those who lack precepts find shameful is the sharpness and swiftness [of insight]—observing that what is permanent is actually impermanent, and that what is pure is actually impure. Those endowed with the virtue of the precepts praise such purity; yet when those who have violated the precepts hear this instruction, they claim it is slanderous and not a truthful teaching.

They do not even acknowledge their own names or lineages, nor do they humble themselves to praise others; they are like a skilled archer who distinguishes between the well-shot and emulates its excellence.
Why is this so? It is because one wishes to cause those who are evil to reform their conduct, and those who cultivate goodness to revere and honor the True Dharma.
Therefore it is said: "Now, observing this principle, that which is shunned by those who lack precepts."
"Observing existence, one knows fear; through change, one knows both existence and non-existence.
Therefore, one does not delight in existence; one should mindfully seek to distance oneself from it.

Regarding "observing existence, one knows fear; through change, one knows both existence and non-existence": existence is fearful and cannot be relied upon. If one does not depart from it as it truly is, [fear persists]. Therefore it is said: "Observing existence, one knows fear; through change, one knows both existence and non-existence."

Therefore, one should not delight in existence (*bhava*), but should instead be mindful of distancing oneself from existence. For a person who does not delight in the root of all suffering, yet fails to contemplate the karma that produced it, it is said: "Therefore, one should not delight in existence, but should instead be mindful of distancing oneself from existence."
Lacking faith and lacking integrity, one who breaks through walls to commit theft—
having severed all such hopeful intentions, he is called a hero.
"Lacking faith and lacking integrity" refers to those disciples of the Buddhas who do not possess a mind of sincere conviction.

Why is this? Because that person does not believe in the Buddha, does not believe in the Dharma, and does not believe in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; nor do they believe in suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. That which is the cessation of all these is Nirvāṇa. Such a person neither believes nor reverently honors [these truths]; therefore it is said: "Lacking faith, lacking reciprocity."

Regarding "breaking through walls to commit theft": those who practice this act break down the walls of the tainted triple world (*traidhātuka*) and engage in trade therein, hoping for blessings and prosperity; therefore it is said, "breaking through walls to commit theft."

"To sever that expectant mind—this is what is called being a hero. To sever the notion of gain and honor so as to be free from expectation, such a person among men is beyond reproach; therefore it is said: "To sever that expectant mind—this is what is called being a hero."
"Except for the conditions of one's parents, The royal family, and the two kinds [of kin], When one has completely extinguished them throughout the realm, One is a stainless brahmin.

Regarding "except for the conditions of one's parents": the reason the Tathāgata spoke these words was to demonstrate that the affection of the heart has been forever exhausted without remainder and will never arise again; therefore, it is said, "except for the conditions of one's parents."
Regarding "the royal family and the two kinds": this is discussed because the king manifests arrogance.
As for the "two kinds," they are: first, the precepts; second, wrong views. Once this arrogance is eliminated, it shall not arise again. Therefore, it is said: "the royal family and the two kinds."

Regarding the statement, "He who has completely extinguished his objective realm and is stainless is a brahmin": the reason the Tathāgata spoke these words was to demonstrate that his own pride had been forever exhausted without remainder and that he cultivated pure conduct; therefore, it is said, "He who has completely extinguished his objective realm and is stainless is a brahmin."
If a person has no dependence, They know that which is most cherished:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Contemplating these as their practice.
Regarding "if a person has no dependence": a practitioner who has no fetters or afflictions and does not store up [possessions] is therefore said to have "no dependence."

To know that which is esteemed as food: worldly people rely on food to preserve their lives; one should understand the origin and end of this solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Furthermore, the food of craving (*saṃkalpa-āhāra*) arises from mental conceptions and attachments like the hide of a living ox; the food of volition (*manaḥ-saṃcetanā-āhāra*) is like a mass of fire; and the food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is like a sword or a halberd. Just as a person who consumes solid food contemplates its origin and end—whether held in their own hand or placed within a bowl—one should reflect upon the process by which food comes into being.
From what does cessation arise?
By contemplating that all impure things are not to be craved or delighted in, it is therefore said: "Knowing that which is esteemed as food.

As for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), when one contemplates them as a practitioner, it is like those sentient beings who enter the three gates of liberation; they contemplate and recollect the Path, never letting it depart from the forefront of their minds. Therefore it is said: "Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—contemplating these as one's practice."
A bird flies through the void, yet leaves no tracks; likewise, the traveler is said to have no destination.

Regarding the statement that "a bird flies through the void, yet leaves no tracks": all birds flying in the void are called *phaṇindra* (phoenixes); within the void, no tracks are seen, for as they circulate and come and go, there is no fixed location. Therefore it is said: "A bird flies through the void, yet leaves no tracks."

As for that practitioner who says there is no destination: that practitioner contemplates this principle and finds that they have no knowledge whatsoever of the directions—east, west, south, or north—to which one might go; therefore it is said, "As that practitioner says, there is no destination."
Those who are able to sever the root of existence do not rely on what has not yet come to be;
they practice by contemplating emptiness and signlessness.

As for those practitioners who sever the root of existence: that which is discussed as "existence" refers to the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of formlessness. When these are forever exhausted without remainder and never arise again, it is therefore said: "Those who are able to sever the root of existence."
"Not relying on the unmanifested" means not knowing the changes of rise and fall regarding events that have not yet undergone transformation; therefore, it is said, "not relying on the unmanifested."

When one takes the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*) as the object of contemplation, one becomes attached to the three gates of liberation—the doors of cessation—and finds entertainment therein, unable to relinquish them. Therefore it is said: "One takes the practice of emptiness and signlessness as the object of contemplation."
Rare are those beings who do not follow the path; there are those who are saved and those who are not, and it is extremely difficult to escape death.

"Rare are those beings who do not follow the path" means that rare are those beings born in a central land, and even rarer are those beings who encounter the worthy and the noble; therefore it is said: "Rare are those beings who do not follow the path."

Regarding those who are saved and those who are not: although there are many sentient beings who seek to cross over the world, those who do so are nonetheless few. They do not know whether the root of birth and death exists or not, nor what is right or wrong; this arises from their base impurity and failure to comprehend the nature of conduct. Therefore it is said: "There are those who are saved and those who are not."

Regarding "death is exceedingly difficult to avoid": people crave life and see only what is before their eyes; they do not realize the suffering and affliction of approaching death, nor do they contemplate the practices for transcending the world. Therefore, it is said: "Death is exceedingly difficult to avoid."
All things are explained as equal; when one contemplates phenomena together with phenomena, all fetters and latent tendencies are completely severed, and there is no longer any feverish affliction.

Regarding "all things are explained as equal; when one contemplates phenomena together with phenomena": when a person dwells in the world, they observe right and wrong. Since phenomena are fully accomplished without being superior or inferior, it is therefore said: "All things are explained as equal; when one contemplates phenomena together with phenomena."

To have completely severed all fetters and afflictions so that no further feverish distress remains is as follows: when a practitioner reflects and deliberates, severing all fetters and removing all attachments and conceptualizations, they are no longer subject to the affliction of feverish distress; therefore it is said: "Having completely severed all fetters and afflictions, there is no further feverish distress."
Traveling the path, there is no further sorrow; throughout the day one attains liberation.
All fetters and afflictions are exhausted; there is no longer any further distress.

Regarding "traveling the path, there is no further sorrow; throughout the day one attains liberation": for one who practices the path, they cultivate virtue spontaneously; having brought all suffering and affliction to an end, the dust and defilements do not arise. Therefore it is said: "Traveling the path, there is no further sorrow; throughout the day one attains liberation."

When all fetters and latent tendencies are exhausted, there are no longer any manifold afflictions. Just as that practitioner maintains a firm resolve such that the fetters and latent tendencies are forever extinguished without remainder, it is therefore said: "When all fetters and latent tendencies are exhausted, there are no longer any manifold afflictions."
"No creating, no having created; the creator suffers the fever of affliction.
Neither creating nor not creating—what was before is likewise after.

Regarding "no creating, no having created; the creator suffers the fever of affliction": when a person has previously committed a transgression and deeply knows it to be contrary to the Dharma, they manifest it before others, seeking to reform and repent without concealment. If they are born again in a physical form, they will not suffer affliction. Therefore it is said: "No creating, no having created; the creator suffers the fever of affliction."

"Neither created nor uncreated; as it was before, so it is after" means that if a person commits a transgression and immediately reforms and repents, at the time of their death their spirit will not be confused. Protected by benevolent deities, they will not fall into the evil realms. Therefore it is said: "Neither created nor uncreated; as it was before, so it is after."

"It is excellent for the doer; having done it, one harbors no grief. Doing with joy and doing again, one is born in heaven to receive happiness. Regarding "it is excellent for the doer; having done it, one harbors no grief":

when a person cultivates wholesome conduct and is fully endowed with manifold virtues, they are honored by all people and followed by all as their model. After the end of their life, they are reborn in a good destination, the heavens. Therefore it is said: "It is excellent for the doer; having done it, one harbors no grief. Doing with joy and doing again, one is born in heaven to receive happiness."
Furthermore, they do not know how to debate, nor can they distinguish between the noble and the holy;
yet if they were to know how to engage in discussion, their speech would leave no trace of defilement.

Regarding "furthermore, they do not know how to debate, nor can they distinguish between the noble and the holy": it is like those practitioners who do not understand discourse and cannot differentiate the meanings of phrases; when in a great assembly, they do not know the proper decorum or etiquette, and they fail to distinguish between the wise and the foolish. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, they do not know how to debate, nor can they distinguish between the noble and the holy."

Furthermore, if one knows the discourse on debate, that which speaks of the stainless path—this stainless discourse removes all conceptual attachments; one harbors joy within and rejoices immeasurably, being fully satiated by the flavor of the Dharma heard, and does not fall into the afflictions of the evil realms, the hungry ghosts, animals, or hell. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, if one knows the discourse on debate, that which speaks of the stainless path."
When one speaks discourses that accord with the Dharma, one should raise the banner of the seers;
the Dharma-banner is the seer, and the seer is the Dharma-banner.
When one speaks discourses that accord with the Dharma, one causes the flavor of the Dharma to flourish and spread it among people, with complete phrasing, teaching one another in succession.

The "Sages" are the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they are said to possess the body of names and the body of phrases, distinguishing each part without error, desiring that the True Dharma endure long in the world.
Therefore it is said: "When one speaks in accordance with the discourse of the Dharma, one shall raise the banner of the ṛṣis; the Dharma-banner is the ṛṣi, and the ṛṣi is the Dharma-banner."
Some revile in silence; some revile in the midst of a crowd;
some revile without uttering a sound; there is no one in the world who does not revile.

Regarding those who revile in silence: within their hearts they burn with rage, cursing incessantly, wishing that the other person might encounter water, fire, or bandits. They contemplate these things inwardly without manifesting them outwardly; therefore it is said, "some revile in silence."
There are those who revile others in a crowd, shouting at the top of their voices without regard for the status of superiors or inferiors; therefore it is said, "There are some who revile in a crowd.

There are also those who revile without raising their voice, remaining among the assembly yet not addressing their insults face-to-face with loud cries; therefore it is said, "There are some who revile without raising their voice. In this world, there is no one who does not revile.

"One disparagement and one praise merely benefit one's reputation; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus cannot be known. One disparagement and one praise merely benefit one's reputation.

While various virtuous deeds and merits nourish the body, if one receives offerings, one does not take joy in them; if one suffers disparagement or humiliation, one does not feel distress. The past has already ceased, yet the wholesome mind is not interrupted; the future has not yet arrived and shows no signs of arising; the present does not abide but continues to drift and turn. Therefore it is said: "One disparagement and one praise merely benefit one's reputation; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus cannot be known."
Praised by the wise, whether in good or in bad fortune, the person of wisdom is without flaw;
through wisdom, concentration, and liberation, they are pure and transparent within and without, like polished purple-gold.

Whether praised or criticized by the wise, the one who perceives and sees extensively expounds a single principle beyond compare; all receive deliverance, their spirits saved and freed from suffering. This is like the Tathāgata, who when walking treads upon the void, four inches above the ground, while the patterns of his footprints appear vividly upon the earth; within them, insects, mollusks, and all forms of living beings receive his light and are delivered, remaining peaceful for seven days, forever free from all suffering and incapable of being harmed.

It is also like pure *cāmpeya* gold, which is clear and pure both inside and out, without any flaw or impurity. Therefore it is said: "Whether praised or criticized by the wise, the person of wisdom is without defect; through wisdom, concentration, and liberation, they are as clear inside and out as *cāmpeya* gold."
Just as Mount Sumeru is not moved by the wind,
so too is the person of wisdom unmoved by praise or blame.

Just as that Mount Sumeru stands firm and stable, never to be shaken by the wind, so the Tathāgata, dwelling in or having transcended the world, is not moved by the eight worldly dharmas of praise and blame.

There was a brahmin of vast learning and wide vision who encompassed all matters; upon hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world, he remained unmoved by either censure or praise. Holding his mind like the earth, he took no account of the good or the bad. He went to where the Buddha was and reviled the Tathāgata with a hundred kinds of insults; afterwards, he again praised the Tathāgata with a hundred kinds of words. Yet the Tathāgata’s mind remained firm and unshaken. Therefore it is said: "Just as Mount Sumeru is not moved by the wind, so too is the person of wisdom not moved by censure or praise."
As a tree that has no root—how could it have branches, let alone leaves?
The steadfast one who has untied his bonds—who could destroy his virtue?

Regarding the lines "As a tree that has no root—how could it have branches, let alone leaves": ignorance is the root and the source of all afflictions; craving gives rise to branches and leaves, thereby giving birth to false views. Therefore it is said: "As a tree that has no root—how could it have branches, let alone leaves?"

"The steadfast one is liberated from bonds; who can destroy his virtue? By "the steadfast one" is meant the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Having been freed from all fetters and attachments, he no longer undergoes the form of a womb-born existence, nor does he pass from this life to a future life. Therefore it is said: "The steadfast one is liberated from bonds; who can destroy his virtue?"
Stainless and without abiding, The body is a moat where the seeds of suffering are sown;
The Most Victorious One is free from craving, Which gods and men do not understand.

"Stainless and without abiding" means that all fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been abandoned forever, leaving nothing behind. Where there are fetters, there is abiding; where there are no fetters, there is no abiding. Furthermore, there is neither the moat of the body nor the seeds of suffering. Therefore it is said: "Stainless and without abiding, the body is a moat where the seeds of suffering are sown."

The Supreme One is free from craving, unknown to gods and men alike; when the Tathāgata sits in meditation, entering a state of tranquil samādhi and right reception, he extinguishes his physical form and remains self-concealed. Should any god or sage wish to know the whereabouts of the Tathāgata, this is impossible.
Therefore it is said: "The Most Victorious One is without craving; neither gods nor men understand this.
Just as a net covers a thicket of trees, so when there is no craving, how could there be anything else?
The Buddha possesses immeasurable conduct; since there is no track, whose track could he follow?"
Regarding the metaphor of the net and the forest, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain to you how craving is the root from which branches and leaves spread and entwine; reflect upon this well."
As explained at length in the sūtras, one transmigrates through birth and death, becoming attached to the five destinies.
Therefore it is said: "Like a net in a thicket. As for the phrase "no craving, much less anything else":

when the Tathāgata attained the Way, he was forever free from craving; having eternally severed the five destinies, he does not dwell in the three realms nor undergo the four modes of birth. Therefore it is said: "No craving, much less anything else."

The Buddha possesses immeasurable practices; since there is no trace, who can follow that trace? That which is called "Buddha" refers to one who awakens all dharmas, knowing nothing that is not known and reaching nothing that is not reached. He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment. His extensive exposition and preaching are without end; he is lofty and unsurpassed, beyond measure; he is profound and bottomless, unfathomably deep.

Where there are fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is a trace; where there are no fetters, there is no trace. When a person has feet, they can travel to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below. Those with the traces of fetters enter the three realms and roam through the five destinies, never leaving birth and death. Those without the traces of fetters do not reach the three realms or the eight difficult states.
Therefore it is said: The Buddha has immeasurable practices; being traceless, who can follow his traces?
If one does not desire birth, and through birth does not undergo existence, the Buddha has immeasurable practices; being traceless, who can follow his traces?

If there are those who do not desire birth, and because of that birth they do not undergo further existence—having cast off one body and assumed another form, passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of births and deaths, through immeasurable and incalculable cycles of birth and death—they now attain the Way. Having exhausted their past bodies, they no longer receive further forms or undergo various sufferings and afflictions. Therefore it is said: "If there are those who do not desire birth, and because of that birth they do not undergo existence; the Buddha has immeasurable practices, yet being traceless, who can lead by his traces?"

If one wishes to extinguish these perceptions, there will be no causes within or without, nor will there be any transgression of the perception of form; thus, in the four [realms], one shall not undergo rebirth.

Regarding "if one wishes to extinguish these perceptions, there will be no causes within or without": what is meant by "perceptions" refers to the perception of desire, the perception of form, and the perception of the formless. When the practitioner has eternally extinguished these and does not allow them to arise, and furthermore does not create the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms, being pure within and without and producing no defilement, it is for this reason it is said: "If one wishes to extinguish these perceptions, there will be no causes within or without."

Furthermore, there is no transgression regarding the perception of form; as for the four who should not undergo rebirth, it is like that practitioner who contemplates past form and past derived matter, future form and future derived matter, and present form and present derived matter, discerning each one individually as being without the four types of form.

Just as that Wheel-Turning Sage King rules over the four continents, his body endowed with the marks of a great man and all the secondary characteristics, those who observe him view him as no different from themselves. They do not give rise to thoughts of attachment because of his physical beauty, nor do they give rise to thoughts of aversion because of his physical ugliness. They do not perceive "this is me" or "that is not me," nor "this is mine" or "that is not mine. Furthermore, they do not perceive "is" or "is not," nor "both is and is not," nor "neither is nor is not. Being entirely free from thoughts of beauty or ugliness, they forever sever the four attachments and do not engage in them. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, there is no thought of form; one does not undergo rebirth through the four attachments."

Abandoning what precedes and abandoning what follows, abandoning the interval and transcending existence—abandoning all completely, one does not undergo birth and old age. "Abandoning what precedes and abandoning what follows;

abandoning the interval and transcending existence" means that by "what precedes," one abandons the past aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of attachment.
"Abandoning what follows" means abandoning the future aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and bonds of attachment.
"Abandoning the intervening existence" means abandoning the present aggregates, bases, elements, fetters, and bonds of attachment.

"Abandoning all" means that within this very life one attains the path of emptiness, rules over the three thousandfold world system and the ten directions, and by following one's own will, having accomplished what was to be done, one truly knows that one shall no longer undergo rebirth in a womb.
Therefore it is said: "Abandoning what precedes and abandoning what follows, abandoning the interval and transcending existence—abandoning all completely, one does not undergo birth and old age.
*Udānavarga*, Volume 26; *Udānavarga*, Volume 27.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 31: On Pleasure (Ratiparivarta). Verse 31:
To win brings the end of enmity; to lose brings self-contempt; to desist brings happiness.
There is no mind of victory or defeat.

To say that "victory extinguishes enmity, while defeat leads to self-contempt" means this: just as an enemy spies upon another day and night, harboring great resentment and hostility, carrying this sinful enmity from lifetime to lifetime without relinquishing it—even after passing through hundreds of thousands of bodies, the retribution for vengeance may finally cease—yet the one who suffers defeat feels self-contempt. Therefore, it is said: "Victory extinguishes enmity; the defeated feel self-contempt."

When one rests, there is happiness; there is no mind of contention or victory. All fetters and afflictions are forever exhausted without remainder, and thoughts of conceptual attachment never arise again. Furthermore, there is no mind of contention or victory—neither "I am superior and he is inferior" nor "he is superior and I am inferior. There is absolutely no sense of self or other. Therefore it is said: "When one rests, there is happiness; there is no mind of contention or victory."

If one harasses others while seeking peace and happiness for oneself, one will instead become their enemy and never escape suffering and affliction. Regarding the line "If one harasses others while seeking peace and happiness for oneself":

in this world, there are many who harbor deluded minds and harbor deep-seated animosity, provoking and harassing others while hoping for personal joy and prosperity for their kin. This is like planting bitter seeds while hoping for sweet fruit; it is a futile waste of effort that benefits neither the present nor the future.
Therefore it is said: "If one harasses others while seeking peace and happiness for oneself, one will ultimately create enmity and hatred, never escaping suffering.

Although killing in a sudden fight may still be somewhat excusable, harboring malice and secret plots is not to be trusted; such persons as these will surely head toward the evil realms. This is because they cling to folly and refuse to abandon it.
Therefore it is said: Thus one brings about enmity and hatred, and in the end does not escape suffering and affliction.
Those who delight in sensual desires and strike living beings with staves, seeking security therein, shall find no happiness in the next world.

Those who take pleasure in sensual desires—since all sentient beings crave pleasure and do not delight in suffering and affliction, and upon seeing suffering, their collective minds have no wish for it—yet they themselves commit killing and teach others to kill, they themselves engage in lewdness and teach others to engage in lewdness, they themselves speak falsehoods and frivolous speech and further teach others to speak falsehoods and frivolous speech, and they themselves take what is not given and further teach others to steal the property of others; therefore it is said: "They take pleasure in sensual desires."

"To apply the staff to living beings" means that one's conduct is unlawful and unjustly oppresses the common people; what the mind harbors takes inflicting injury as its foundation. Therefore, it is said: "To apply the staff to living beings."

In this world, one seeks security for oneself, yet finds no happiness in future lives. When people commit evil deeds, they do so entirely for their own sake; when they cast off this body and take on another form, they encounter all manner of suffering and affliction. Wandering through birth and death, drifting through the five realms of existence, the pain of their transgressions follows them wherever they are born. Therefore it is said: "In this world, one seeks security for oneself, yet finds no happiness in future lives."
If a person desires joy and happiness, they should not strike living beings with a staff;
by seeking happiness for oneself therein, one will also obtain happiness in future lives.

Regarding the line "If a person desires joy and happiness, they should not strike living beings with a staff": all sentient beings crave happiness and do not delight in suffering. Seeing those who suffer, one should give rise to a heart of compassion and pity, regarding them with the four immeasurables as impartially as one’s own infant. One should never harbor resentment or strike at sentient beings; while dwelling in the world, one should always seek peace and security for oneself and others.
"If I were to harass others today, I would suffer countless retributions in future lives.
Therefore it is said: "If a person desires happiness, they should not lay a staff upon living beings; by seeking happiness therein for themselves, they shall also obtain happiness in future lives."
Delight in the Dharma and delight in its practice; be careful not to practice unwholesome dharmas.
Those who are able to practice the Dharma well find happiness in this life and in future lives.

When a person dwells in the world, they should be intent on practicing the Dharma; they should select wholesome dharmas and discard those that are evil. Moving about and traveling, they should seek out virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and adopt their wholesome teachings. Wherever they go, they should promote matters of the Dharma. Therefore it is said: "Delight in the Dharma and delight in its practice; be careful not to practice unwholesome dharmas. Those who are able to practice the Dharma well find happiness in this life and in future lives."
One who protects the Dharma and practices the Dharma obtains a good reward for practicing the Dharma;
this accords with the teachings of the Law and Discipline, for one who practices the Dharma does not go to evil.

Regarding "one who protects the Dharma and practices the Dharma obtains a good reward for practicing the Dharma": being able to personally protect the Dharma so that it is not lost or neglected, one subsequently attains its merit. Therefore it is said: "One who protects the Dharma and practices the Dharma obtains a good reward for practicing the Dharma."

"This accords with the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya; practicing the Dharma, one does not head toward evil" means that those who practice according to the Dharma protect themselves by means of the Dharma. In whatever realm they are born, they do not encounter calamities or misfortunes. From their youth until their old age, they receive the full measure of their rewards. When their celestial merit is exhausted, they descend to be born among humans and again receive abundant blessings. Therefore it is said: "This accords with the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya; practicing the Dharma, one does not head toward evil."
"One who protects the Dharma and practices the Dharma is like a canopy covering one’s form;
this accords with the teachings of the Law and Discipline, and such practice of the Dharma does not lead to evil.

The practitioner of the path protects the profound Dharma and its subtle teachings, removing all hindrances (āvaraṇa). Just as one who encounters fierce, scorching heat obtains a fine canopy and thereby receives relief, it is for this reason it is said: "One who protects the Dharma and practices the Dharma is like a canopy covering one’s form; this accords with the teachings of the Law and Discipline, and such practice of the Dharma does not lead to evil."
Evil conduct leads one into hell; wherever one goes, one falls into the evil realms.
One sinks into calamity through unrighteousness, like a hand grasping a snake or a viper.

Regarding "evil conduct leads one into hell; wherever one goes, one falls into the evil realms": when a person commits evil deeds, these are not acts performed by parents, brothers, or kinsmen; they result entirely from the offenses committed by one's own body. Having committed the offense, one must personally suffer its retribution; no one else can take it upon themselves.
The views of the non-Buddhist heterodox teachers differ; they hold that while one person commits the transgression, another receives the retribution.
Therefore it is said: "Evil conduct leads to hell; wherever one goes, one falls into the evil realms."

To unlawfully bring oneself to ruin is like grasping a snake or a viper with one's own hand. It is just as when someone grasps a snake or viper—whether taking it by means of incantations, or by means of medicinal herbs, or having been taught by a master to handle such a malignant serpent—their hand is bitten by the snake after the incantation has ended; they die and enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, undergoing birth and death without end.
Therefore it is said: "One who acts contrary to the Dharma sinks into ruin, like a hand grasping a snake or a viper.
Whether by means of the Dharma or non-Dharma, these two matters do not yield the same retribution;
through non-Dharma one enters hell, while through the True Dharma one is born in heaven."

Whether by means of dharma or non-dharma, both matters receive the same retribution. These classes of sentient beings perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds, yet they do not realize for themselves the retribution of calamity or fortune; those who do good do not know that goodness has its retribution, and those who do evil do not know that evil has its retribution.

It is like a person who obtains food mixed with poison; having obtained it, they consume it, unaware that there is poison within. The toxic vapors spread and intensify, causing distress to their body.
It is the same with those who commit evil deeds: though it tastes sweet at the time, they later suffer its calamities, ultimately losing their lives and failing to reach a good destination.
A person with sight observes the food and knows that it is pure and contains no poison; thus, having taken it, they suffer no affliction thereafter.
Therefore it is said: "One does not receive the same retribution for both dharma and non-dharma; through non-dharma one enters hell, while through the true dharma one is born in heaven."
Giving and fighting occupy the same place; this is not praised by the wise or the virtuous.
The time of giving and the time of battle—these two matters are exactly equal.

Formerly, within the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Jyotiṣka (Most Victorious), and another elder named Durjaya (Invincible). These two were foremost in their stinginess and greed within the kingdom. They possessed abundant wealth and many treasures, complete with the seven precious gems; their elephants, horses, chariots, attendants, servants, and slaves, as well as their grain, food, fields, and enterprises, were beyond measure.
Each of their two gateways had seven layers of doors, and they commanded the gatekeepers not to allow beggars to enter their premises.

In the middle of the courtyards, iron cages were placed over them for fear that flying birds might peck at and gather the grain; the four walls of the dwellings were constructed of cast-iron enclosures for fear that rats might burrow through or gnaw upon the household goods.

At that time, the five great śrāvakas each went in succession to teach him; they emerged from the earth and instructed him with the gift of Dharma, yet the two elder sons heard this and neither accepted the teaching.

Later, the Buddha went there in person; sitting and reclining in mid-air, he emitted a great radiance. The Buddha preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the elder, yet although the elder heard it, his mind still did not fully comprehend it.

He thought to himself: "The Buddha has come to my house; I must not let him return to the vihāra empty-handed. I should enter the storehouse and take a white cotton cloth to offer as a gift to the Tathāgata."

He immediately rose and entered the storehouse to select one of the inferior items, but instead obtained a superior one; setting that aside, he took another and obtained one even better still. His mind and heart contended with one another, and he could not resolve the matter for himself.

On that day, the asuras and the Trāyastriṃśa devas fought together; sometimes the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated, and sometimes the asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye, saw the mind of the elder: at times the mind of stinginess prevailed while the mind of generosity was inferior; at other times the mind of generosity prevailed while the mind of stinginess was inferior.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Giving and fighting occupy the same place; this is not praised by the wise or the virtuous.
When one gives, it is as if one were at war; in these two matters, they are exactly equal."
Hearing this from afar, the elder felt deep shame within his heart, thinking, "What the Tathāgata has spoken refers precisely to my own person.

He immediately brought out fine cotton cloth to offer as a gift. The Elder Hard-to-Subdue (Durdharṣa) also brought out five hundred taels of gold to bestow as alms; their minds were opened and their intentions liberated, and each of them realized the path.

When a person encounters hundreds of thousands of changes, If they equally eliminate the enemy of pride, And at that time bestow a pure heart, Such a steadfast man is most excellent. Regarding the line "When a person encounters hundreds of thousands of changes, if they equally eliminate the enemy of pride":

A student living at home is attached to wealth and business; amidst the confusion of various affairs, the mind is not settled. If a person wishes to cultivate the Way, they should leave behind household affairs, remove pride, and refrain from giving rise to thoughts of attachment. Only then can they practice giving without expecting a reward. Humility and self-effacement are the foundation of cultivating virtue; looking down on others while esteeming oneself is a calamity that brings disaster. Therefore, one teaches people to dwell in a place of quietude, and only then can they cultivate the true Way.
Therefore it is said: "When a person encounters hundreds of thousands of changes, they should equally eliminate the enemy of pride.

To give at the proper time with a pure mind is what makes a man most excellent. There are five occasions for giving that yield five merits; by removing the mind of arrogance and self-importance, one’s intent remains constantly pure and free from defilement. Therefore it is said: "To give at the proper time with a pure mind is what makes a man most excellent."

A little patience overcomes much; the precepts overcome much indolence. One who possesses faith and practices giving will receive a good retribution in a future life. Regarding "a little patience overcomes much" and "the precepts overcome much indolence":

there are many sentient beings whose faith is extremely slight and whose anger is fierce and blazing, while their observance of the precepts and practice of patience are likewise very few. Yet, by being able to practice patience, one overcomes enemies; the person who upholds the precepts surpasses the indolent person. This is just as Anuruddha once gave a single gift to a *pratyekabuddha*, and for ninety *kalpas* never fell into the evil realms. Later, he was born into the Śākya clan as a paternal cousin of the Buddha; he left the household life to study the Way and attained the fruit of the Path.
Therefore it is said: "Patience overcomes much; the precepts overcome much indolence. One who possesses faith and practices giving shall receive a favorable retribution in a future life."
"How joyful is this great reward of merit! All that was wished for has been fully accomplished; One swiftly attains the foremost cessation And gradually enters the realm of the unconditioned.

Regarding "How joyful is this great reward of merit! All that was wished for has been fully accomplished": the cultivation of merit by people is entirely due to the conduct established in previous lives. If one encounters a field of excellence (a worthy recipient), even though the seeds sown may be few, the retribution obtained is immeasurable. Conversely, if in a previous life one provoked or disturbed the noble ones, or if the intent of one's giving was impure and lacked impartiality, then even if one receives a human form, its appearance will be ugly and one will be despised by others. Thus, it is said: "If one commits evil, one receives evil; if one performs merit, one receives merit. Therefore, it is said: "How joyful is this great reward of merit! All that was wished for has been fully accomplished."

"Swiftly attaining the foremost cessation and gradually entering the realm of the unconditioned" means that all fetters are completely eliminated and all virtues are universally perfected; pure like radiance, both internally and externally transparent, whatever one seeks within the ultimate truth is obtained immediately, and if one desires to enter forever into the state of voidness, it is attained at once without any doubt or obstruction.
Even if the followers of external heterodoxy and wicked Māras should come to destroy those who cultivate merit, they will spontaneously perish at that very moment, for there is nothing they can do.

Just as in the past, when the Demon King led eighteen billion followers—each with a hundred heads on a single body, their forms terrifying—with tigers, wolves, lions, venomous snakes, and evil vipers coming to frighten the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata’s power of merit caused the demons to be destroyed.
After the Māra-king had retreated, the World-Honored One then spoke this verse:
"How wonderful! Such great karmic reward; All that was wished for has been fully accomplished.
Swiftly attaining the foremost cessation, One gradually enters the realm of the unconditioned."
If one seeks skillful means and practices the giving of noble wisdom, exhausting the very root of suffering, know that such a person attains great fortune.

As for "if one seeks skillful means and practices the giving of noble wisdom": this refers to a practitioner who desires to train in the Dharma of the noble ones; with courageous diligence and an undistracted mind, they then accord with the Dharma of the noble ones. Therefore it is said: "If one seeks skillful means and practices the giving of noble wisdom."

"One should know that by exhausting the root of suffering, one attains great fortune. What is called "suffering" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). One who is able to extinguish these accords with the Way and its teachings; therefore it is said: "By exhausting the root of suffering, one should know that one attains great fortune."
Loving the Dharma, one sleeps well and awakens; with mind and heart pure and clean, one delights in the teachings spoken by the noble ones.

When a practitioner trains in and realizes the profound Dharma, clearly understanding and discerning the meaning and phrasing of what is taught, their mind becomes tranquil and free from all other thoughts. Entering meditative concentration with a single-pointed mind, they are not shaken by various evils. They cherish and practice the instructions of the noble ones, never abandoning them; this is what the wise practice, not that which fools discuss. Therefore it is said: "Loving the Dharma, one sleeps well and awakens; with mind and heart pure and clean, one delights in the teachings spoken by the noble ones."
If a person’s mind delights in dhyāna, they likewise delight in non-arising;
they also delight in the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as the seven factors of enlightenment,
those four bases of psychic power, and the noble eightfold path.

If a person’s mind delights in dhyāna, they likewise delight in non-arising. As for why that practitioner delights in dhyāna, it is because they desire to attain parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder; since there is neither arising nor ceasing, it is said: "If a person’s mind delights in dhyāna, they likewise delight in non-arising."

"Furthermore, one delights in the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) as well as the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga)": Stopping the fetters so that they do not arise is called "foundations of mindfulness," and because there is awakening and awareness, it is called "factors of enlightenment. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, one delights in the four foundations of mindfulness as well as the seven factors of enlightenment."

Regarding "the four bases of psychic power and the noble eightfold path": the dharma of the bases of psychic power also severs the fetters and latent tendencies, bringing about happiness and unconditioned ease in the present life; likewise, the noble eightfold path also severs the fetters and latent tendencies in the present life, bringing about happiness and wholesome benefit. Therefore it is said: "the four bases of psychic power and the noble eightfold path."

One who delights in the food of alms, One who delights in wearing the dharma-robes, One who delights in walking meditation, And one who delights in dwelling among mountains and thickets— Regarding "one who delights in the food of alms" and "one who delights in wearing the dharma-robes":

it is like that practitioner who, having attained the wisdom that severs all [defilements], discerns the perception of food without the mind becoming stained by attachment to the thought of eating. Whether the food is fine or coarse, the mind remains free from judgment of right or wrong. As for the dharma-robes, they are neatly arranged, not violating the regulations and attire established by the former sages. Therefore, it is said: "One who delights in the food of alms, one who delights in wearing the dharma-robes."

One should delight in walking meditation (caṅkrama) and take pleasure in dwelling among mountains and groves. As stated in the sūtras of the Buddha, a person who practices walking meditation attains five merits.
What are these five?

First, one is capable of traveling great distances; second, one possesses great strength; third, whatever one eats and drinks is naturally digested; fourth, one is free from illness; fifth, those who practice walking meditation quickly attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

A person practicing the Way attains the subtle Dharma of the Four Noble Truths of True Suchness; having awakened their mind upon hearing the Dharma, they immediately enter deep mountains and uninhabited places to practice the Way through meditative concentration, and thereupon attain parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Therefore it is said: "One who delights in walking meditation, one who delights in mountain thickets, having attained the state of peace and bliss, is unconditioned in the present life;
having transcended all fears, they have surpassed all worldly attachments."

"Having attained the state of peace, one is unconditioned in the present life" means that just as a practitioner delights in the true Dharma within the realm of *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, gradually proceeding until reaching the realm of *anupādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; therefore it is said: "Having attained the state of peace, one is unconditioned in the present life."

"Because they have transcended all fears and surpassed all worldly attachments" means that by perceiving the path of the tracks, they transcend all hardships and sufferings; having surpassed all worldly attachments and traversed beyond the three realms, they become a field of merit for the protection of the multitude. Therefore it is said: "Because they have transcended all fears and surpassed all worldly attachments."
Delighting well in mindfulness and waiting, Skillfully contemplating all phenomena,
Excellent is he who is harmless in the world, Nurturing and sustaining all classes of sentient beings.
Free from worldly desire and attachment, He has transcended all defiled and clinging thoughts.
To be able to extinguish one's own pride and arrogance—this is called the foremost happiness.

When the Tathāgata descended as an incarnation and came to the royal house, he observed that the world is impermanent and all phenomena are like illusions. He renounced his worldly sovereignty to study the Way in the deep mountains, practicing asceticism for many years. Sitting beneath the King of Trees, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment; for seven days and seven nights, he gazed at the tree without blinking.
At that time, the Tathāgata rose from his seat, went to the abode of the Dragon King Manasvin, and upon reaching his palace, spoke these verses.

Upon hearing these verses, the dragon’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened; his eyes were cleared so that he beheld the form of the Tathāgata, and with deep sorrow he shed tears, reproaching himself for his past transgressions.
Therefore it is said:
"One who delights in mindfulness and waiting, who skillfully contemplates all phenomena—how excellent!
Such a one is harmless in the world and nurtures all classes of sentient beings."
In this world there is no pleasure like that of freedom from desire;
transcending all defiled attachments and being able to extinguish one's own pride—this is called the foremost pleasure.
The pleasure of the elderly who uphold the precepts, and the pleasure of those who have achieved faith.
The joy of discerning the meaning and intent; the joy of not committing any evil;

the joy of the elderly upholding the precepts. Regarding the phrase "the joy of the elderly upholding the precepts": as for those who study the Way, even if they are advanced in years, they must not harbor a mind of retreat despite their hardships; nor should they be indolent, even if they are in the prime of youth and witness worldly glory. The Way resides in the mind regardless of whether one is old or young; it depends solely on being resolute and steadfast until the Way is attained. If one maintains faith, what can one not achieve?
Therefore it is said: "For the elderly, upholding the precepts is a joy.

Regarding "the joy of accomplishing faith": when a person possesses faith, they are difficult to be moved by four things. Even if one were to manifest the form of a Buddha, displaying various marks and signs of radiance, with the intent to deceive and distract them, one could not cause their mind to waver. Therefore it is said: "The joy of accomplishing faith."

Regarding "the joy of discerning meanings and purposes": a person's eloquence arises entirely from past deeds; it is only after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas that one attains such eloquence. Although they produce verbal teachings to discern various meanings, each point of their discourse maintains its proper sequence. They may elaborate from the meaning of a single phrase to a hundred thousand, yet they never utter coarse or vulgar words. Therefore, it is said: "the joy of discerning meanings and purposes."

Regarding "the joy of not committing various evils": if a person is free from evil, they will be reborn in the heavens or among humans to receive blessings; therefore, it is said, "the joy of not committing various evils."
"There is joy in having parents in this world; there is also joy in the harmony of a gathered assembly.
There is joy in being a śramaṇa in this world; likewise, there is joy in the tranquility of the will.

Regarding "there is joy in having parents in this world; there is also joy in the harmony of a gathered assembly," as stated in the sūtras of the Buddha: the gravity of parental kindness is such that it cannot be fully recorded. Even if a filial son were to carry his father on his right shoulder and his mother on his left shoulder, traveling across heaven and earth from birth until death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he still could not repay even one day’s worth of his parents’ kindness.

Why is this? It is entirely because the parents nurtured the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), expanded the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), enabled them to behold the light, and provided care by pushing aside the dry for them to lie upon and occupying the damp themselves, attending to them at all times.
Therefore, although a filial son wishes to repay his parents' kindness, he does not achieve even one part in a hundred thousand.
For this reason it is said: "In the world, there is the joy of having parents; there is also the joy of a harmonious assembly."

"In this world there is the joy of the śramaṇa; the joy of one whose will is tranquil is likewise. Having left the household life to study the Way, they sever all bonds of affection and abandon worldly affairs. They constantly practice the three karmas without losing their integrity, and are thus loved and cherished by hundreds of thousands of living beings, who provide them with offerings and whatever they require according to the season. These renunciant brahmacārins diligently discipline their bodies and exhaust themselves to seek the severance of fetters and attachments; their conduct is pure and they do not create the roots of evil. Therefore it is said: "In this world there is the joy of the śramaṇa; the joy of one whose will is tranquil is likewise."
The arising of the Buddhas is joy; hearing the Dharma and being able to receive it is joy;
the harmony of the Sangha is also joy; where there is harmony, there is constant peace.
Regarding "the arising of the Buddhas is joy": the appearance of a Tathāgata is extremely rare to encounter, just as the udumbara flower appears only once in many thousands of millions of kalpas.
At that time, when the multitude of living beings saw the utpala flowers, each was filled with joy and said to one another:
"The Tathāgata will descend into the world before long; how could such an auspicious omen appear in vain?"
"In the scriptures of antiquity there are established texts stating that if this flower should appear in the world, it will not be long before the Tathāgata appears in the world.
Thus, the devas and the people of the world rejoiced together, all preparing the requisites for making offerings, awaiting the sight of the Tathāgata’s radiant countenance and physical form.
Therefore it is said: "The arising of the Buddhas is joy.

Regarding the joy of being able to receive the teaching of the Dharma: when the Buddha first attained the Way, endowed with all the marks of perfection, he remained in silent meditative concentration for seven times seven days—forty-nine days—without expounding the flavor of the Dharma to sentient beings. Later, at the request of Brahmā, he then taught the sublime Dharma to the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. All living beings received his grace, and there were none who were not saved and delivered.
Therefore it is said: "To preach the Dharma and be worthy of receiving it is bliss;

the harmony of the Sangha is also bliss. When there is harmony, there is constant peace. The members of the assembly are not of one kind; they may be four, eight, or even innumerable. Among them, the Tathāgata’s assembly is the foremost.

Within the Tathāgata’s assembly, there are the four pairs and eight ranks of the twelve noble ones. Multitudes of sentient beings vie with one another to come and make offerings; those who cultivate reverence for the holy assembly obtain immeasurable merit.

Such a field of merit gives birth to the fruits of the Path; it is excellent, beautiful, and free from drought or frost. Whatever one’s wishes may be, there is nothing that cannot be attained. That which the Noble Assembly prizes above all is harmony; therefore it is said: "The harmony of the Saṃgha is also joy; in harmony, there is always peace."
The joy of perfecting the precepts; the joy of extensive learning and broad knowledge;
the joy of beholding the True Person; the joy of the path to liberation. Regarding "the joy of perfecting the precepts":

when sentient beings encounter one who upholds the precepts, they serve and make offerings to them, attending upon them at all times; subsequently, they obtain the retribution thereof, dwelling securely in the bliss of non-action and attaining freedom. Therefore, it is said: "The joy of perfecting the precepts."

Regarding "delighting in extensive learning and broad knowledge": furthermore, there are sentient beings who encounter those of extensive learning and receive their teachings, not losing a single instance of the body of names, the body of phrases, or the body of phonemes. They penetrate the principles and meanings, investigating and clarifying them; upon hearing them, they immediately awaken and do not need to receive them again. For this reason, it is said: "delighting in extensive learning and broad knowledge."

Regarding "beholding the joy of the True Person and the joy of the path of liberation": suppose there are sentient beings who, having planted roots of merit in past lives, encounter the worthy and noble ones and meet those Arhats, thereby attaining the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the meditative absorption of emptiness and stillness (*śūnyatā-praśama-samāpatti*).

If there are sentient beings who give to a true person (satpuruṣa), they shall receive retribution in their present life: wealth and treasures will accumulate, their wishes will be fulfilled according to their intent, and there will be nothing they do not achieve; furthermore, they will be forever untainted by the fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana).
Therefore it is said: "Beholding the True Person is joy; the path of liberation is joy.
The swift, cool waters are joy; the spontaneous gathering of the wealth of Dharma is bliss;
attaining the light of wisdom is bliss; extinguishing pride and being free from evil is bliss."

Regarding "the joy of swift, cool water": it is like a rapid river that is clear, tranquil, and cool; its sound is subtle, it does not harm living beings, and its taste is sweet and exquisite. It is what practitioners crave and through which they achieve much. Therefore it is said: "the joy of swift, cool water."

Regarding "the joy of the Dharma-wealth gathering spontaneously": what is called Dharma-wealth means that by assembling through the Dharma, one does not violate the principles of things, and thus cannot be encroached upon or deceived by government officials, thieves, bandits, water, fire, or calamitous changes.
Why is this? It is because one acquires wealth and profit solely through the True Dharma and does not wrong others; it is for this reason that it is said:
"It is a joy when the wealth of the Dharma gathers of its own accord."

"Attaining the joy of the clarity of wisdom and insight" means that just as a practitioner attains the foremost worldly knowledge (*laukikāgradharma*), they are able to fully discern all phenomena (*dharma*) and universally radiate light to awaken those they encounter; therefore, it is said: "Attaining the joy of the clarity of wisdom and insight."

Regarding "To extinguish pride and be free from evil is bliss": when a person harbors arrogance, they will inevitably look down upon others. Since time immemorial, the failure to bring one's virtuous qualities to completion has always resulted from the arousal of anger. Therefore, it is said: "To extinguish pride and be free from evil is bliss."

To behold the virtuous is joy; to assemble with them is likewise joy. Not associating with the foolish, one finds eternal joy by bringing past deeds to an end. Regarding the statement, "To behold the virtuous is joy; to assemble with them is likewise joy":

the noble and holy ones have perfected the fruits of the Path and are fully endowed with all virtues. These were attained through the long accumulation of practice and study in former lives. Those who respectfully serve such virtuous ones will subsequently receive immeasurable joy and wealth; their households will be harmonious and their clans will flourish daily. Therefore it is said: "To behold the virtuous is joy; to assemble with them is likewise joy."

"To not associate with fools, but to finish with them so as to be forever happy" means that virtuous people cultivate their conduct and seek out excellent companions; seeing those who are evil associates, they ultimately distance themselves from them. The reason for this is that those who are evil by nature ultimately possess no good deeds; they cause others to fall into darkness and fail to behold the Great Light. Therefore it is said: "To not associate with fools, but to finish with them so as to be forever happy."
Associating with the foolish, one passes through countless days;
living together with the foolish is difficult, like meeting with those one hates.
Living together with the wise is easy, like meeting with one's own kin.

Regarding "associating with fools for countless days": if a practitioner associates with fools, they will fall day and night into the cycle of birth and death; even if billions of Buddhas have passed by, they will not receive deliverance. Therefore it is said: "Associating with fools for countless days."

To dwell with fools is difficult, like being joined with those one hates; the suffering of being joined with those one hates arises entirely from ignorance. Because one does not follow a virtuous teacher nor associate with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), it is said: "To dwell with fools is difficult, like being joined with those one hates."

"It is easy to dwell with the wise, like meeting with one's own kin. This means that when those who possess wisdom associate with one another, they must surely reach a state of mutual joy upon meeting; they smile first and then speak, with harmonious countenances and pleasant expressions.
