Being pure and tranquil within and without, they are free from contention and dispute. Therefore it is said: "It is easy to dwell with the wise, like meeting with one's own kin."
The Honored One among Men is extremely difficult to encounter; his descent into birth is never in vain.
Wherever he may take birth, that household will surely receive blessings. Regarding the statement, "The Honored One among Men is extremely difficult to encounter;

his descent into birth is never in vain": he cannot be encountered even in hundreds of thousands of millions of *kalpas*. The one called the Honored One among Men refers to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. As for the place of his birth, his lineage is pure and his parents are authentic. His family is abundant in wealth and many treasures, fully endowed with the seven precious gems—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, agate, pearls, amber, and carnelian—and lacks nothing in terms of elephants, horses, or carriages. The land where he is born is harmonious from top to bottom, with all living together in mutual accord.
Therefore it is said: "The Honored One among men is extremely difficult to encounter; his birth is never in vain.

If he should take birth in a place, that household will surely receive blessings. As for the accomplishment of his kin, it occurs in the Central Kingdom and not in the borderlands or heterodox regions. Therefore it is said: "If he should take birth in a place, that household will surely receive blessings."
All shall attain peaceful sleep; the brahmin has attained parinirvāṇa.
Unstained by desires, he is completely liberated from all realms.
Having utterly severed inauspicious fetters and subdued internal feverish afflictions, he rests in peace.
Forever resting, they obtain sleep; their consciousnesses are entirely pure and clear.

Not long after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first delivered five people, followed by another five, then thirteen from the village on the riverbank, and thirty-seven from among the assembly of worthy men; in total, sixty-one people were enlightened by the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed his disciples:
"Each of you shall go forth in the four directions to teach and transform, delivering the people of Jambudvīpa.
I wish to go alone to the banks of the river."

Having ordained the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their thousand disciples, he next ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and subsequently King Bimbisāra, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having some minor worldly business, came to the city of Rājagṛha seeking lodging at the home of a great householder. It happened that the men and women servants of that household were each engaged in their respective tasks: some were splitting firewood and lighting fires; some were blowing on raw food to cook it; and others were spreading out mats, woolen rugs, and fine carpets.
At that time, the elder personally prepared a high seat, hung silk banners and canopies, and sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground.
Then, the elder Anāthapiṇḍika asked that elder:
"The preparations your noble house has made today to welcome guests are no small matter; do you intend to invite the king to visit your residence?"
"Is it that a son from a noble family wishes to take a wife,
or a daughter wishes to be married?
I wish to hear your intention."
The host replied:

"The culinary preparations I have now prepared cannot be fathomed by gods or worldly men, nor by kings, ministers, or the various officials; no men shall marry women, and no women shall go out their doors."
"The reason I have prepared these sweet delicacies and drinks is that at early dawn I invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to my home for a meal.

Upon hearing the name of the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, Anāthapiṇḍada’s hair stood on end; moved by both sorrow and joy, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. After a short while, he withdrew slightly from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I humbly hope, O World-Honored One, that you are at ease in your daily life and movements, and that you are in good health. Having heard that you were staying here, did you sleep well?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Anāthapiṇḍika, saying:
"All shall obtain a good sleep; The brahmin has attained parinirvāṇa.
Untainted by desires, He is completely liberated from all realms."
Having completely severed all inauspicious fetters and subdued internal feverish agitation, one attains restful sleep forever, and the mind-consciousness becomes entirely clear and transparent.
Be careful not to become attached to pleasure; you should instead proceed to guard your future conduct.
One should contemplate renouncing the world and observe matters of pleasure.

Be careful not to become attached to such pleasures; one should instead follow and protect those who practice the path. Indeed, when a person studies the Way, it is not accomplished without hardship; it must necessarily involve suffering before it is finally perfected. One should abandon mundane dhyāna and mundane liberation, and cultivate untainted dhyāna and untainted liberation. Therefore it is said: "Be careful not to become attached to pleasure; one should follow and protect those who practice."

"One should contemplate renouncing the world and observe the nature of happiness" means that when a person encounters minor pleasure, they should further seek out the roots of that pleasure so as to increase it; therefore, it is said: "One should contemplate renouncing the world and observe the nature of happiness."

"Worldly pleasures and the joys of the heavens— These are called the exhaustion of craving; Yet they do not equal even a sixteenth part [of true liberation]. Regarding "worldly pleasures and the joys of the heavens":

worldly pleasure refers to the bliss of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the heavenly joy refers to the bliss of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Throughout the long night of existence, sentient beings are deluded regarding the five destinies and fail to know how to receive the truth. They greedily cling to the retributions of worldly meditative merit, transmigrating through the five destinies in a cycle that begins again and again. Believing that they have attained the Way and will be eternally extinguished without further arising, it is for this reason it is said: "Worldly pleasures and the joys of the heavens."

This is called the "exhaustion of craving. Regarding the phrase "not obtaining even one-sixteenth": if there is a practitioner who first cuts off the root of craving so that branches and leaves are forever removed, who maintains resolve with trepidation to prevent evil before it arises, and who later attains the bliss of the outflows-free state with a mind wandering naturally—such a person has not yet obtained even one-sixteenth part [of this bliss].
Therefore it is said: This is called the exhaustion of craving; even sixteen [worlds] would not equal one-sixteenth of it.
One who can cast off the heavy burden and no longer create further burdens—since the burden is the suffering of the world—such casting off is the greatest happiness.

Regarding "being able to cast off the heavy burden and no longer creating further burdens," it is like a person carrying a heavy load through a perilous and difficult place. What they carry is neither essential worldly goods nor urgent necessities; it is not gold, silver, precious jewels, musaragalva, agate, pearls, or amber, but rather worldly items of no value.
A bystander advises them: "Observe what you are carrying; these are not true treasures. Why do you not discard them and seek something more authentic?"
That person immediately abandoned it and sought another who was genuine.
Observe that these sentient beings are also like this: burdened by the body of the five aggregates, they wander through the realm of desire, tumbling through birth and death, unable to escape.
The Sage said: "Why do you now carry this form of the five aggregates—a foul, leaking, and stinking place?
You should quickly cast it off and seek something lighter."
At that time, sentient beings immediately devised skillful means, relinquishing their forms in the desire realm and assuming bodies in the form realm.

Once they had assumed forms in the form realm, the sages again went there to teach and transform them, causing them to relinquish those bodies and attain the fivefold dharma-nature of untainted wisdom.
Therefore it is said: "One who can cast off the heavy burden and no longer create further burdens—this casting off of the world's suffering is the greatest happiness."

Having completely severed all cravings and desires, and extinguished all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as the root of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one will no longer undergo rebirth within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Just as that practitioner, through untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*), observes and extinguishes craving for the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*), craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*); and having eliminated the activities of body, speech, and mind—namely, the three bodily actions, the four vocal actions, and the three mental actions—so that they are forever exhausted without remainder; he understands the beginning and end of the arising of the five aggregates and no longer clings to the practices of the three realms of existence.

Therefore it is said: "Having completely severed all cravings and extinguished all conditioned formations, as well as having extinguished the root of the five aggregates, one shall no longer undergo rebirth within the three realms of existence."
Righteousness brings joy; friends share the joy of blessings;
the joy of their cessation is profound stillness. As this spreads from one to another to all people, suffering and joy are rooted in the same source.

Regarding the statement, "Yixing possesses joy; friends share in the happiness of his blessings," it is like a merchant who toils his body and endures hardship, braving dangers to procure precious treasures, and returns home in safety to the celebration of his clan. Among his kin, both male and female, young and old, there is none who does not rejoice, and his friends and companions all partake in the benefit.

If he were to open his heart and bestow these gifts universally upon all, so that they are no longer subject to manifold sufferings and take joy as their foundation, then even amidst the entertainments of his clan, they would find themselves unable to forsake him.

Therefore it is said: "When righteousness prospers, there is joy; friends share in the bliss of merit; that extinction is the joy of tranquility; as it spreads from one to another among people, suffering and joy are rooted in this."
Just as that brazier, blazing with fierce flames, gradually dies out until its destination is unknown; so too,
one who possesses such right view escapes the mire of craving and desire.
Departing, there is no fixed location, for one has attained the bliss of immovability.

It is like that furnace with its blazing, fierce flames; it is like the smith’s iron ball heated by fire, so intensely glowing that it is very difficult to approach. Thus, the Sage observes the classes of sentient beings who, burned and scorched by the fires of lust, anger, and delusion, remain unaware of their own condition.
Therefore it is said: "It is like that brazier, its flames blazing fiercely;

gradually it goes out until one knows not where they have gone. Just as a red-hot iron ball gradually cools until one knows not where the heat has gone, nor where the cold now resides, so it is said: "Gradually it goes out until one knows not where it has gone."

Regarding such people who possess right view and are freed from the mire of craving and desire: those practitioners attain equal liberation without further obstruction; having escaped the deep mire of craving and desire, they reach the shore beyond birth and death. Therefore it is said: "Such people who possess right view are freed from the mire of craving and desire."

When departing, there is no place of abiding; this is because one has attained the bliss of immovability. For those of such a kind, the spirit merges with the profound darkness and consciousness unites with the essence of emptiness; thus, they do not know east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below. When coming, they do not know from where they come; when departing, they do not know where they go. It is like a red-hot iron ball that gradually cools: one does not know where the heat has gone, nor does one know where the cold resides. Therefore it is said: "When departing, there is no place of abiding, for one has attained the bliss of immovability."
In the midst, there is no anger; there is change and nothing remains still.
Having removed sorrow, there is no grief; in tranquility, one contemplates the existence of the world.

Regarding "in the midst, there is no anger": what is called anger is that which defiles the human mind and prevents it from reaching the Path. Only those who are free from defilement can escape this heart of wrath and rage. Therefore, it is said: "In the midst, there is no anger."

There are those who undergo change and never rest; in the world, there are many types of conduct, and these conducts vary in their gravity and in their moral bearing. Some may possess a profound resonance with the Way such that, through the arrival of fortune, they do not create the afflictions (*kleśa*); others, however, though possessing knowledge, deliberately transgress and thereby give rise to worldly toil (*rajas*).

For this reason, the Sage issues admonitions to future generations, desiring that those who practice them may reform past errors and sever future calamities. Those who ardently seek learning should cherish and treasure these words; as long as they do not let them fall from their minds, they will be able to advance into the chamber of the Worthy and Holy Ones. Only then will they realize that the teachings of the Sage are worthy of veneration and that defiled dharmas are unfit to be approached.
Therefore it is said: "There is change and no stability.

Regarding "removing sorrow so that there is no grief": it is like that practitioner who has forever uprooted the source of sorrow and grief, becoming associated with the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), and serenely contemplates the transformations of the world as being like a phantom or a mirage.
Therefore it is said: Having removed sorrow, there is no more grief; in tranquility, one observes the existence of the world.
There is joy and no affliction for one who is well-versed in the True Dharma.
Even if they see that something has been lost, people still crave sensory forms.

There is joy and no affliction for one who has heard much of the True Dharma; like a person who has entered meditative concentration, they remain in tranquil meditation day and night, never departing from the state of samādhi. Taking emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their sphere of contemplation, although they may at that time undergo ascetic hardships of the body, their spirit remains tranquil and unconditioned, suffering no injury. Just as that practitioner is free from anger and regards all living beings with compassion as no different from themselves, it is therefore said: "There is joy and no affliction for one who has heard much of the True Dharma."

If one observes that there is harm and that every person is greedy for form (*rūpa*), a student should contemplate its root source: lust, anger, and delusion are the foremost of all calamities. These arise from the mind and intentions of desire and wrath, mutually defiling one another to create great affliction; thus, one cannot escape the source of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
Therefore it is said: Even if one sees that there is loss, people still crave form.

Without fetters, one lives well in this world; knowing the origin of the fetters through the Great Dharma, one should clearly perceive the flaws of the fetters. For every person’s mind is bound and attached.

They are likewise bound by the root of form. One who is free from fetters has exhausted lust, anger, and delusion; they no longer delight in the mundane roots of various fetters, nor do enmity or resentment arise within them. A person of wisdom discerns this and can sever this affliction; having removed it from themselves, they further treat others so that they too shall be without affliction. Furthermore, they do not harbor attachment to various forms, and their minds remain unmoved by gain or loss, defamation or praise. Therefore it is said: "One free from fetters lives well in the world; through the Great Dharma, one knows the source of fetters. People should clearly recognize the flaws of fetters, for every person is greedily bound and attached, likewise bound by the root of form."
"All sufferings arise from being humiliated; all pleasures arise from following one's own will.
Victory and defeat naturally arise, yet in the end, nothing is truly gained.

Regarding "all sufferings arise from being humiliated; all pleasures arise from following one's own will": when a person encounters misfortune, their mind finds no relief; they must watch the countenances of others, constantly fearing they might lose favor. Conversely, a person who acts according to their own whims attains whatever they desire as soon as it is thought of, like an echo responding to a sound. Therefore, it is said: "All sufferings arise from being humiliated; all pleasures arise from following one's own will."

Victory and defeat arise spontaneously, yet in the end, nothing is gained. This is like a person living in the world where nobility and meanness are not constant: one may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, only to later become a minor regional king; at one time honored and at another base, or high and at another low. Only the Way of the Worthy and Holy has neither honor nor meanness, neither height nor lowness. Therefore it is said: "Victory and defeat arise spontaneously, yet in the end, nothing is gained."
Those who wish to obtain happiness and long life should be able to endure even light retribution.
The patient person endures others; the impatient person dwells within the various realms of existence (*bhava*).

To state the essential point and briefly explain its meaning: where there is no harm, one brings about harm; where there is no affliction, one brings about affliction; where there is no anger, one brings about anger; where there is no enmity, one brings about enmity—it is no different from what was stated above.
Those who desire happiness and long life, Should remain free from delusion regarding delusions;
For while the deluded are confused by others, I am here entirely without delusion.
Those who desire happiness and long life, Should ultimately be free from all fetters and attachments.
One should eat with mindfulness as food, just as those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven always take mindfulness as their sustenance; thus, the body of mind has nothing upon which to rely.
Whether encountering suffering or joy in village or wilderness, one remains unburnt by either.
"Though one encounters the traces of contact (*sparśa*), how can there be contact where there are no traces?

Whether in village or wilderness, seeing suffering or joy, one who is not burned by either—whether a person practicing the Way dwells by a city or relies on a village, or stays in a desolate wilderness where no people dwell—if at times they encounter suffering that pains the hearts of the multitude, or at other times meet with pleasure yet do not take it as delight, they will not give rise to contact and the twelve kinds of ailments."
"That" refers to those six sense objects; "this" refers to these six sense faculties.
Therefore it is said: whether in the village or the wilderness, one perceives suffering and pleasure, yet neither "this" nor "that" burns one.

Although one may encounter the traces of contact (*sparśa*), if there are no traces, how can there be contact? When people dwell in the world, their minds are constantly heedless; first experiencing contact and subsequently feeling pleasure, they thereby increase the roots of transgression. At times, this gives rise to the experience of contact within those hells. Yet, where there is no contact, there are no traces, and likewise, there is no experience of contact in hell. Therefore it is said: "Although one may encounter the traces of contact, if there are no traces, how can there be contact?"
Wherever there is a worthy person, Who is not stained by the defilement of desire, Even when encountering suffering or pleasure, They do not give rise to a harmful mind.

Regarding "wherever there is a worthy person who is not stained by the defilement of desire": the sages dwelling in the world mostly remain in seclusion; they are not attached to thoughts of desire and do not give rise to the defilement of desire. Those so-called "worthy persons" are the Anāgāmins and Arhats.
Therefore it is said: "Wherever there is a worthy person, they are not stained by the defilements of desire.

Even when encountering suffering or pleasure, they do not give rise to harmful thoughts; though they encounter suffering or pleasure, they do not give rise to conceptual attachments. Therefore it is said: "Even when encountering suffering or pleasure, they do not give rise to harmful thoughts."
Udānavarga, Volume 27 and Volume 28,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Two: On the Mind and Consciousness The mind is light and difficult to guard; it dwells in the realm of desire. To subdue the mind is good;
through its subduing, one finds peace.

Regarding "light and difficult to guard": it is for this reason that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, appears in the world—to subdue the human mind and eliminate defiled and evil conduct. Just as those who practice the path constantly reflect upon themselves and give rise to mental discourse, they realize that what is called the "mind" brings about manifold calamities and causes people to enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore, it is said: "It is light and difficult to guard."

Regarding those who dwell within desire, the practitioner observes that the arising of illness always has its causes and conditions; he investigates the source of desire and finds it resides in the mind. It is just as when thieves rely on rugged terrain to commit robbery: were there no such terrain, they would have no means of causing harm.
Desire is likewise like this: the mind is its nesting place, and as it wanders and rushes about from one state to another, it brings about calamity and affliction.

Therefore it is said: "One dwells in desire. To subdue the mind is good; through such subduing, one finds peace. This means that if a person can subdue their mind, they will not be preoccupied with their own longevity; wherever they go, they will be honored by others. After the end of life, their outflows will be exhausted and their minds liberated, attaining the extinction of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore it is said: "To subdue the mind is good; through such subduing, one finds peace."
Like a fish on dry land, having left the deep abyss, its consciousness is filled with extreme terror as the hosts of Māra rush about.

Regarding "like a fish on dry land, having left the deep abyss": it is just as that fish, having lost the abyss, writhes upon the ground; its mind is afflicted with distress and lacks self-mastery. Therefore it is said: "like a fish on dry land, having left the deep abyss."

The mind-consciousness is utterly terrified, and the hosts of Māras rush about like fish leaping and struggling on the bank of the opposite shore, unable to find freedom; the mind is likewise, racing toward the various fetters and afflictions, unable to stop itself, and thus providing an opportunity for the various evils to seize it.
Therefore it is said: The mind-consciousness is extremely terrified, and the hosts of Māra rush about.
The mind runs to many places, like the radiance of the sun;
yet the wise are able to restrain it, as a hook stops a wicked elephant.

"The mind wanders to many places, just like the radiance of the sun" means that when the sunlight first emerges, it illuminates all four directions, reaching everywhere without exception; the mind is likewise, rushing toward the phenomena of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations, unable to restrain itself from flowing and racing about. It is like a wild elephant, fierce and difficult to control, which can only be subdued once it has been caught by an iron hook. Therefore it is said: "The mind wanders to many places, just like the radiance of the sun; the wise are able to restrain it, as a hook stops a wild elephant."
I now discourse upon this mind, which is unstable and invisible;
I now wish to instruct it, so take care not to allow any flaws or rifts to arise.

Regarding "I now discourse upon this mind, which is unstable and invisible": that practitioner of the path concentrates his intent and fixes his mind before him, admonishing and reproving his mind through various skillful means.

"From the very root of your mind, throughout incalculable kalpas, you have undergone birth and death; the number of times you have cast off one body and assumed another is beyond reckoning. At times you dwelt in the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions, and at other times you traveled between the heavens and the human world.
Now that I have become a person who has encountered the holy Dharma of the Buddha, you ought to abandon these fundamental thoughts of defiled attachment."
Having rebuked the mind with countless skillful means, he further addressed it:
"You are now fragile and unreliable; regarding this perceived body, you must bring an end to the fetters of craving."
Therefore it is said: "I now discourse upon this mind, which is unstable and invisible; I now wish to instruct you, so take care not to create any rifts."

"Let not your mind wander, nor indulge in heedlessness; I shall now restrain you, as one controls a wild and unruly elephant. 'Let not your mind wander, nor indulge in heedlessness' means that the mind, as a thing, is hesitant and unstable.

It clings to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, just as a monkey greedily clings to fruits and gourds, abandoning one to seize another without any single-pointed concentration. The mind is likewise: it gives rise to myriad distractions at will, creating manifold afflictions that cannot be relinquished. Therefore it is said: 'Let not your mind wander, nor indulge in heedlessness.'"

"I now restrain you, as one restrains a wild elephant. This means that I shall employ the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to restrain this mind and prevent it from wandering, just as one restrains a wild elephant so that it does not become unruly; therefore it is said: "I now restrain you, as one restrains a wild elephant."

Birth and death are without measure; coming and going have no beginning. Those who seek a dwelling repeatedly receive the womb. Regarding "birth and death are without measure; coming and going have no beginning":

when humans dwell within birth and death, they pass through kalpas that cannot be reckoned or recorded. Sometimes they are in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; the suffering therein is so immense it is difficult to calculate. Therefore it is said: "Birth and death are without measure; coming and going have no beginning."

Those who seek a dwelling repeatedly undergo the womb; their tracks of action are not extinguished, and they come and go without ceasing. Bound by attachment to the plump and white, and clinging to forms and colors, they repeatedly take birth in a womb. Therefore it is said: "Those who seek a dwelling repeatedly undergo the womb."
By observing this house, one no longer builds another dwelling; its beams and rafters are already ruined, and its towers and pavilions have collapsed.

"To observe this house" means it is precarious, fragile, and unstable, destined for decay and destruction according to the law of impermanence; even the Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans shall eventually melt away and rot.
As for "no longer building another dwelling," why is this so?

It is because one has understood the root source and the origin of illness; thus, one no longer undergoes rebirth in form to construct the chamber of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Therefore it is said: "By contemplating this house, one builds no further dwelling."
"The beams and rafters have already collapsed; the towers and pavilions have been shattered"—this is said to discuss the original source of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

That "the body is destroyed and the four great elements disperse, and all things do not remain joined for long" discusses the person who has realized the Way: having cast off the physical form, the spirit departs into the tranquil void. The limbs and the physical frame each return to their respective origins: earth returns to earth, water returns to water, fire returns to fire, and wind returns to wind. The spirit departs into non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and no longer fears returning to receive another form. Therefore it is said: "The beams and rafters have already collapsed; the towers and pavilions have been shattered."
The mind has already departed from formations; that which was in between has already ceased. The mind is fickle and restless, difficult to maintain and difficult to guard.

Regarding "the mind has already departed from formations": what are called "formations" are the foremost of all fetters. That all living beings sink into and are submerged by birth and death is entirely due to the creation of formations that leads to such calamities and transformations. When a Sage descends into the world, he diligently cultivates himself, severing the root of all formations so they do not arise again. Therefore it is said: "The mind has already departed from formations."

Regarding "that which has already ceased in the interim": the dharmas of the three periods of time have been forever exhausted without remainder; therefore it is said, "it has already ceased in the interim.
Regarding "the mind being light and fickle," as stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:

"I now declare that the nature of the mind is inherently light, fickle, and swift; in a single day and night there are nine hundred and ninety-nine billion thoughts, and in each thought there are different perceptions and differing actions."
Therefore it is said: "The mind is light and fickle. Regarding that which is difficult to maintain and difficult to guard:

at the very moment a thought arises, one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds. A mind mindful of the good reaches its object as swiftly as an echo follows a sound, without any obstruction; likewise, a mind mindful of evil responds like an echo to a voice. There has never been anyone who was able to guard it [with such ease].

It is as with the species of evil beasts, such as tigers, wolves, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; that one should wish to protect their minds so that they do not commit evil has likewise never been heard of before.
Therefore it is said: "Difficult to maintain, difficult to guard.
The wise are able to rectify themselves, just as a craftsman straightens an arrow.
When there is anger, they know there is anger; when there is anger, they know they have anger."

The wise are able to rectify themselves, just as a craftsman straightens an arrow. When a person practices the path, they first rectify their form; they constantly understand the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, non-self, and non-identity. Through the practice of the six recollections, they admonish themselves so that the body does not become crooked or deviant. This is like a skilled craftsman who is well able to treat an arrow so that it is straight, without knots, and capable of withstanding the enemy without difficulty. Therefore it is said: "The wise are able to rectify themselves, just as a craftsman straightens an arrow."

When there is anger, one knows there is anger; when there is anger, one knows there is anger. From this, resentment begets resentment. Since time immemorial, there has never been one who could extinguish resentment through resentment. One must certainly extinguish resentment; only after resentment is extinguished does one know that there is no resentment. Therefore it is said: "When there is anger, one knows there is anger; when there is anger, one knows there is anger."
This mind is self-created; it is not created by one's parents. To eliminate evil and attain concentration, perform meritorious deeds without turning back.

The various actions created by the mind bring suffering upon the body; whether one performs good or evil, this arises from the mind’s creation, and is not the doing of one's parents, brothers, kinsmen, servants, or slaves.

One who clearly examines this understands that these worldly afflictions arise from deviance; furthermore, by not failing to guard against them, one prevents the mind from becoming disordered. Therefore it is said: "This mind creates itself; it was not made by parents. Abandon deviance and resort to concentration; cultivate merit without turning back."
If a roof is not covered tightly, it will leak when the heavens rain; if a person does not reflect upon their conduct, they leak lust, anger, and delusion.

It is just as when people of the world construct palaces and dwellings that are not made secure; on days when it rains from heaven, there is no place that does not leak. If a person does not rectify their conduct, they leak the objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*); furthermore, if they do not contemplate the meditation on impurity, they leak forth the violent, overflowing waters of the three poisons. Therefore it is said: "If a roof is not covered tightly, it will leak when the heavens rain; if a person does not reflect upon their conduct, they leak lust, anger, and delusion."

In brief, one should summarize the essentials in verse: the same applies to delusion, the same applies to hatred, the same applies to stinginess and envy, the same applies to pride, and the same applies to the fetter of craving.
When a roof is constructed with great care, the rain does not leak; when a person reflects upon their own conduct, they are free from lust, anger, and delusion.

Just as a person of supreme diligence constructs a palace or dwelling so meticulously that the rain does not leak, so too does a person who reflects upon their own conduct eliminate lust, anger, and delusion, remaining without the leakage of various afflictions.

In brief, one should summarize the essentials in verse: the same applies to delusion, likewise to hatred, likewise to stinginess and envy, likewise to arrogance, and likewise to the fetter of craving.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
When one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, they immediately manifest in speech and action; thus, suffering follows as surely as a wheel follows the ruts of its track.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must first recite the verse on contemplating food before eating.

In the city of Śrāvastī, there were two beggars who went among the assembly of monks to beg for alms. It happened that they arrived just as the noble community had not yet recited the verse on contemplating food. Among them was one beggar whose jealousy ran high, and he gave rise to an evil thought:
"If I should later attain sovereignty as a king, I shall crush the heads of so many practitioners with my chariot wheels!

After he had spoken this verse, the beggar obtained immeasurable wealth from his alms; he went out to the side of the road and fell into a deep sleep. As hundreds of carriages passed through that very path, they crushed his head, and he died to enter hell, where he suffered immeasurable pain.
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
When one conceives of goodness within the mind, it immediately issues in speech and action; blessings and prosperity follow of their own accord, like a shadow following a form.
That second beggar thought to himself:
"If I should later attain wealth and nobility and become a king, I shall provide for this entire assembly of noble ones so that they never suffer from lack."
At that time, the beggar had obtained what he sought and went out to lie down beneath a tree, falling asleep with his consciousness serene and free from distracted thoughts.
At that moment, the kingdom lost its sovereign, and there was no longer any heir to continue the royal lineage. The ministers and officials gathered like clouds and deliberated together:

"Now the state has no ruler and no successor; we fear that before long the people will disperse, leading to the ruin of the nation and the destruction of our homes. Therefore, you lords, each of you, what plan do you wish to devise so that the country may remain intact and the people have no other destination?"
Among them was a wise minister, foremost in sagacity, who addressed the people:

"We have lost our sovereign and yet have no successor; it would be fitting to dispatch envoys to traverse the borders of the realm to find one who possesses the marks of majesty and is endowed with sufficient merit and fortune to inherit the royal throne."

He immediately dispatched an inspector, who saw a man sleeping beneath a tree; though the sun had shifted, the shadow of the tree did not move, covering the man’s body like a canopy above him. Upon seeing this, the messenger went to observe him closely, thinking:
"How extraordinary among men! What could possibly surpass this?"
"This man is precisely the one who should succeed to the royal throne.

He immediately summoned attendants to wake him and carry him on a palanquin, surrounding him before and behind as they escorted him to the royal palace; the people cried out "Ten-thousand-year Emperor! and the realm became peaceful and prosperous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having contemplated these two meanings, spoke this verse:
"The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
If one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, and immediately speaks or acts upon them, the suffering of transgression will pursue oneself, just as a wheel follows its track."
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign and the mind is the driver.
When one contemplates what is wholesome within the mind, it is immediately expressed in speech and action; blessings and prosperity then follow of their own accord, like a shadow follows a form.
"Mindfulness has no fixed abode; it is uninterrupted and boundless. Merit can suppress evil; the awakened one is the sage. Regarding "mindfulness has no fixed abode;

it is uninterrupted and boundless": if a practitioner of the path allows the mind to wander and relax, unable to maintain single-minded concentration, even if they hear the Dharma, it will not penetrate their heart and mind.
What is called "uninterrupted and boundless" refers to the perversion of precepts and the perversity of body.
Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness has no fixed abode; it is uninterrupted and boundless."

Merit can suppress evil; one who possesses awakening is a sage. Now, a person who accumulates goodness forever abandons the mind of lust, anger, delusion, and arrogance. For such a person, it is easy to tread the Path; from this point, blessings and auspiciousness will gradually lead them to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Therefore it is said: "Merit can restrain evil; the awakened one is the virtuous.
One should not, with an impure mind, harbor anger toward others.
Those who wish to know the Dharma should listen to what the Tathāgata has taught.
All those who eliminate arrogance, whose minds are utterly pure, and who can relinquish thoughts of harm, shall be able to hear the True Dharma.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly observe the three periods of time with their divine eye; they know that in future ages there will be ignorant and deluded sentient beings who, out of self-conceit, despise others and fail to serve the Triple Gem. When I have passed away, my Dharma will remain; you, son of noble family, must transmit my scriptures and precepts to later generations, so that all sentient beings who hear them shall receive salvation.

There was a bhikṣu in the Kukkuta Garden at the city of Pāṭaliputra, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of many tens of millions, as he ascended a high seat to expound the teachings of the Dharma. Among those who heard the Dharma, there were none who did not receive deliverance; according to their respective paths and destinations, each had their aspirations fulfilled.

According to the ancient customs of foreign lands regarding the proprieties of the internal Dharma, those who enter a temple to listen to the Dharma or pay homage to the Buddha must remove their hats.

At that time, there was a king whose head had naturally little hair and which was further afflicted by sores; moreover, his feet were clad in sandals. Relying on his own noble status, he wrapped his head in fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and entered the inner hall to listen to the sutras.
The king said,
"Monk, preach the Dharma to me. The monk replied:
“The Tathāgata has given this instruction: ‘If there is a sentient being whose feet are covered by shoes or sandals, do not preach the Dharma to them.

Upon hearing this, the king became enraged; he immediately removed his shoes and sandals and said to the bhikṣu, ‘Preach the Dharma quickly so as to please my mind! If you contravene my original intention, I shall have your head executed!’”
The bhikṣu informed the king:
"Furthermore, according to the prohibitions of the Tathāgata’s precepts, one must not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered.
Upon hearing these words, the king became even more enraged; brandishing his celestial majesty, he spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:

"You wish to humiliate me by moving back and forth before me now; therefore, I shall sit here with my head bared and listen to your exposition of the Dharma. If you cannot unravel the knots of my doubts, I shall take your body and divide it into three parts."
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately addressed the king with these verses:
"Not with an impure mind, nor toward one who is angry,
should one who wishes to know the Dharma taught by the Samyaksaṃbuddha [proceed]."
"Those who eliminate arrogance, whose minds are utterly pure, and who can relinquish thoughts of harm—only they may hear the True Dharma.

Upon hearing this verse, the king’s face flushed with shame and his countenance was cast down with remorse. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and sought refuge through repentance. Seeking to extinguish the transgressions of his body, speech, and mind, he knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"I wonder whether this verse was spoken by the divine mouth of the Tathāgata, or whether it was spoken by a venerable person who, having known my thoughts, spoke thus?
The bhikṣu told the king:
"This verse was indeed spoken by the divine mouth of the Tathāgata; it has been here for a long time, not merely now."
The King reflected to himself: "Excellent!

The Great Sage’s wisdom of the threefold transcendence penetrates all things without exception; he thus knew that among my followers there would be those with hearts of malice and harm. Now I repent deeply and shall not create such anew."

At that time, the bhikṣu gradually expounded the profound Dharma to him; immediately upon sitting there, all defilements were cleansed away and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, he was free from fear and apprehension.
The mind dwells in no rest and does not know the Dharma; it is deluded by worldly affairs and lacks right wisdom. Regarding "the mind dwells in no rest and does not know the Dharma":

the mind is like a rushing torrent, difficult to restrain and turn back. Just as water emerging from a spring flows downward day and night, and it would be difficult to make it flow back into the spring, so too such a person does not know the True Dharma; they likewise do not know when to approach and know, or when to abandon and know.
It is like a deaf person listening to the five musical notes, or a blind person holding a candle; therefore it is said: when the mind has no abiding or cessation, one does not know the Dharma.

Those who are deluded by worldly affairs and lack correct wisdom are like those practitioners who crave the pleasures of the world and believe in false, inverted views—whether they serve various deities, water, fire, the sun, or the moon, or perform sacrifices to their ancestors, parents, and brothers, hoping in their hearts to obtain the merit of the True Dharma. This is as difficult as a person attempting to establish a palace or residence in mid-air; it is exceedingly hard to achieve.
As the sutra states:
"To kill living beings for sacrifice is to bring harm upon oneself as well.
Therefore it is said: "Deluded by worldly affairs, one possesses no correct wisdom."
The thirty-six currents, along with the outflows of mind and intention, repeatedly involve false views, based upon the fetters of sensual desire.
Regarding the "thirty-six currents," there are thirty-six types of wrongness; as for the wrongness of the body (*kāyadr̥ṣṭi*), there are three, with one in each of the three realms.
There are three types of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): one in the desire realm, one in the form realm, and one in the formless realm.
There are twelve types of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): four in the desire realm, four in the form realm, and four in the formless realm.
There are twelve types of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): four in the desire realm, four in the form realm, and four in the formless realm.

There are six types of dogmatic adherence to precepts and observances: two in the realm of desire, two in the realm of form, and two in the formless realm. When these are combined, they total thirty-six. These cause worldly people to become deluded and fail to perceive right view; therefore, the wise guard against them before they arise.
Therefore it is said: "The thirty-six currents.

Together with the outflows of mind and thought (*citta-mano-āsrava*), these thirty-six perversions arise from the mind; they overflow in myriad ways and thus result in false views. Therefore it is said: "Together with the outflows of mind and thought."

"Repeatedly leaking false views, dependent on the fetters of sensual desire": these false views refer to the speculative views of eternalism and annihilationism. These two false views do not correspond with one another; the view of eternalism does not correspond with the view of annihilationism, nor does the view of annihilationism correspond with the view of eternalism. The perspectives of these two types of people differ from one another, and because of these false views, they are dragged into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Furthermore, three perceptions arise: the perception of greed, the perception of hatred, and the perception of ignorance. Therefore it is said: "Repeatedly leaking false views, dependent on the fetters of sensual desire."

"Abandoning the mind, one lets go of its roots; people turn according to their inclinations. To diminish one's reputation slightly, one is like a bird abandoning an empty forest. Regarding "abandoning the mind, one lets go of its roots; people turn according to their inclinations": there are many in the world who delight in the five sensory objects (*pañca-śabda*).

If the eye sees a form and visual consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); if the ear hears a sound and auditory consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); if the nose smells an odor and olfactory consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*); if the mouth perceives a flavor and gustatory consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-indriya*); if the body perceives the smooth or slippery and tactile consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*); if the mind cognizes mental phenomena and mental consciousness arises, it subsequently constitutes the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*). Therefore, it is said: "Abandoning the mind, one lets go of its roots; people turn according to their inclinations."

"To diminish one's reputation, like a bird abandoning an empty forest": when a person commits a transgression without regard for future consequences, the merit accumulated over many days is lost in an instant, leading to the censure of various donors and patrons:
"We originally called him one whose precepts were pure and complete; who would have thought that today we would see such flaws and gaps?"
Everyone treats them with contempt and no longer shows them respect.

It is like a flock of birds that constantly roosts in a lush forest, greedily coveting the fragrance and flavor of its five kinds of fruits and flowers; once the flowers and fruits are exhausted, each bird abandons it and departs. The person who violates the precepts is just like this: when merit is exhausted and sin arrives, they shall naturally be dispersed and cast out.
Therefore it is said: To diminish one's reputation, like a bird leaving an empty forest, dwell in solitude and cultivate yourself;
be careful not to follow the tracks of desire, lest you swallow a glowing iron ball and wail as you receive its retribution.

"To practice in solitude and self-cultivation, and take care not to follow the tracks of desire" means that one should always maintain upright and firm conduct of mind; one must not be ensnared by the hook of desirous thoughts. Desire causes people to become deluded and fail to distinguish between the honorable and the lowly. Therefore it is said: "To practice in solitude and self-cultivation, and take care not to follow the tracks of desire."

"Do not swallow hot iron balls, for one who wails while receiving their retribution suffers as if burned by fire, with pain piercing to the very marrow of the bones; upon death, they enter hell where there are ten thousand kinds of agonizing suffering—embracing hot copper pillars and swallowing hot iron balls. Wailing as they receive this retribution, they know not to whom they can appeal. Therefore it is said: "Do not swallow hot iron balls, for one who wails will receive their retribution."
One should rise but does not rise; relying on one's own strength, one lacks diligence.
Thus, one sinks into the lowliness of human form, being indolent and failing to understand wisdom.

Regarding "one should rise but does not rise": "form" refers to those who rise—the Buddha’s companions and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, by failing to cultivate meritorious virtues, though born at a time when such opportunities exist, one performs no beneficial deeds for others. Even if the heavens were to rain down the seven treasures filling the entire world, a fool, his mind deluded, would not gather those treasures. Constantly receiving a human form yet lacking far-sightedness, though called a "human," one is of no benefit to the age.

This is also like that: having encountered the age of a Buddha and being able to expound the profound Dharma, foolish people cling to their delusions and refuse to accept it; therefore it is said, "One should rise, yet one does not rise."

Regarding "relying on strength yet not being diligent": suppose there is a practitioner who possesses robust physical strength and is capable of receiving transformation, yet remains indolent and does not apply himself with great diligence. Therefore it is said: "relying on strength yet not being diligent."

To degrade oneself by assuming a human form yet remain indolent and fail to understand wisdom is to cast oneself into the cycle of birth and death while disregarding the calamities of future lives. Although one may encounter the era of a Buddha, meet with virtuous friends, and associate with sages and saints, if one is unwilling to receive wisdom and discern its underlying meanings, it is for this reason that it is said: "To degrade oneself by assuming a human form yet remain indolent and fail to understand wisdom."

"Disturbed contemplation and right contemplation both arise from the mind; one who can awaken to and know this mental contemplation finds that the deluded mind is repeatedly disturbed. Regarding "disturbed contemplation and right contemplation both arise from the mind":

what is called disturbed contemplation refers to the contemplation of desire, the contemplation of hatred, and the contemplation of ignorance. When a practitioner leaves behind these various forms of contemplation and practices right contemplation, this right contemplation stabilizes the mind, becoming transcendent, supreme, and the most honored among all concentrations. Unless one is a noble person (*ārya*) whose taints are exhausted and who is free from attachment, one cannot attain this concentration of contemplation. Therefore it is said: "Disturbed contemplation and right contemplation both arise from the mind."

One who is able to awaken to and understand the contemplation of the mind, yet whose foolish mind is repeatedly distracted, should as a student of progress practice the contemplation of the essential escape: the contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. By washing away the defilements of the mind and abandoning the eight worldly concerns, one cultivates a pure mind and understands that all marks and signs are each empty and tranquil. These spoken instructions are supreme and difficult to equal; one should practice the Four Truths accordingly day and night.

The deluded person clings to confusion and their mind is repeatedly disturbed; just as one might call a sweet elixir bitter, how could they expect a sage to pry open their mouth and force it upon them? Their persistent delusions are so difficult to reform that they remain thus.
Therefore it is said: "One who is able to awaken to the contemplation of the mind finds that the foolish mind is repeatedly distracted.
The wise contemplate in this way; the mindful person acts with single-minded dedication.
Alas! When the mind is free from attachment, only a Buddha can extinguish this."

The wise person contemplates in this way, and the mindful one is dedicated to practice. That which is called the exposition and subtle utterance of the wise, or the thorough clearing of doubts and the removal of difficulties so as to clarify the human condition for others; standing alone and peerless among the great assembly, he frequently asks the various groups, "Who has any doubt? I shall, with the fire of great wisdom, burn away your heaps of hesitation. Observing at all times so that his mind is not confused, this is the task undertaken by those in training. Therefore it is said: "The wise person contemplates in this way, and the mindful one is dedicated to practice."

"Alas! When the mind is free from attachment, only a Buddha can extinguish this. Those practitioners who attain the samādhi of meditative concentration completely relinquish all mundane, out-flowing (sāsrava) practices, and they likewise relinquish even the mundane roots of goodness, the liberative concentrations, and the states of mind."
"Who is this? Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can abandon it.
Therefore it is said: "Alas! The mind is without attachment; only the Buddha can extinguish this."
Contemplate the body as an empty jar; settle the mind like a standing city.
With wisdom, wage war against Māra; guard your victory and do not lose it again.
To "contemplate the body as an empty jar" means that just as an old, decayed jar is neither firm inside nor out, so that although it may hold things, they will not remain for long.
This body composed of the four great elements is likewise thus: it is constantly suffering and subject to decay, unable to remain for long.
Just like that which is worn out and dilapidated, whether it be beautiful or ugly, it ultimately returns to destruction;
it ends as a heap of ashes.

This precarious and fragile body is likewise: it receives both the beautiful and the ugly. When it receives that which is good, the various merits of virtue serve as ornaments for its body; when it receives that which is evil, it abandons virtuous conduct and defiles its mind, so that after the end of life, it lies abandoned amidst the mounds and graves.
Therefore it is said: "Contemplate the body as being like an empty jar.
To settle the mind as one establishes a city means that the purpose of building a city with firm walls and deep moats is solely to weary and repel the bandits who would plunder the people's property;
the mind is likewise, for it wears out and repels the entanglements of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).
When a city is firm and secure, enemies find no opportunity; when the mind is upright and not deviant, fetters find no opportunity. Therefore it is said: "Settle the mind as one establishes a city."

Regarding "one who fights Māra with wisdom": when one's skills and techniques are fully prepared and complete with the six arts (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one is then able to engage in battle with that sovereign son of heaven (*īśvara-devaputra*). Therefore it is said: "One who fights Māra with wisdom. Regarding "guarding victory so as not to lose it again": by overcoming lust, anger, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*) such that no further conceptualizations remain, one constantly binds the mind to the present without any other divergent thoughts. Therefore it is said: "Guarding victory so as not to lose it again."
To state the essential point: observing the world is likewise so.
Contemplate the body as a mass of foam; understand it to be like a mirage or a flame.
With wisdom, wage war against Māra; guard your victory and do not lose it again.

Just as a mass of foam arises and perishes in an instant, unable to remain for long, so too is this body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): when gathered it becomes a person, and when dispersed it becomes mere air. Originally derived from father and mother, these four elements, when traced to their beginning and end, are all empty and quiescent.

Pushing back, one does not see its front; searching forward, one does not see its rear. It arises and perishes, arises and arises; it perishes and perishes, perishes and arises. In arising, there is no seeing of arising; in perishing, there is no seeing of perishing. Yet ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) habitually practice in inversion and do not awaken to this. Therefore it is said: "Contemplate the body as like a mass of foam; understand it to be like a mirage or a flame. With wisdom, wage war against Māra; guard your victory and do not lose it again."
To speak in brief, the observation of the world is likewise so:
contemplate the seven factors of awakening with an even mind, without deviation;
one should abandon the deluded and confused mind and take delight in the patience of non-arising.
Having exhausted all outflows and being free from defilement, one attains parinirvāṇa in this world.

To "keep the seven factors of awakening in mind with an even mind, without deviation" means that just as a practitioner cultivates the dharma of the factors of awakening, contemplating them day and night without letting them leave their heart; therefore it is said: "To keep the seven factors of awakening in mind with an even mind, without deviation."

One should abandon the mind of delusion and folly, and delight in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If there are sentient beings who do not give rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, they will not reach the Path nor achieve any realization.

One must indeed abandon the mind of delusion and folly and remain unattached to perceptions of form; only then does one accord with the true joy of the Path through the relinquishment of the patience of non-arising. When the mind is free from birth and cessation, one enters the chamber of the Path. Therefore it is said: "One should abandon the mind of delusion and folly, and delight in the patience of non-arising."

"Having exhausted the outflows and being free from defilement, one attains parinirvāṇa in this world. This means that such a practitioner has exhausted all outflows and become free of them; their mind attains liberation and their wisdom attains liberation. Having attained mastery within the present life, such a person enters the realm of the unconditioned and attains parinirvāṇa. Being eternally tranquil and eternally extinguished, they are never born again. Therefore it is said: "Having exhausted the outflows and being free from defilement, one attains parinirvāṇa in this world."
One should guard one’s own mind, as a yak protects its tail;
by bestowing gifts upon all, one will never be parted from happiness.

"One should guard one’s own mind, as a yak protects its tail" means that when the mind acts in the practice of the Path, it creates endless complications; therefore, one must always restrain the mind so that it does not err. Just as that yak protects its tail day and night, fearing it might be severed—preferring to lose its life-force or its mate rather than letting a single hair of its tail fall to the ground.
It is the same for a bhikṣu practicing the Path: he would rather lose his life than violate the precepts.
Therefore it is said: "One should guard one's own mind, just as a yak protects its tail."

Regarding those who give to all beings and never depart from their happiness: they must indeed arouse a mind of compassion for all, regarding even their enemies as their own infants. Thus, asuras, garuḍas, caṇḍālas, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans will be unable to find any advantage over them; they will naturally receive boundless blessings and joy.
Therefore it is said: "One who gives to all never departs from that joy.
A single elephant emerges from among the herd; among elephants, he is the one with six tusks.
With a mind naturally equanimous in every thought, he alone finds delight in the vast wilderness."
In the past, the bhikṣu Kuśin was fond of quarreling and litigation, never finding joy therein, nor did he delight in the quietude of mountain wilds.

At that time, the World-Honored One went to him repeatedly to reprimand and admonish him, yet he did not accept the Tathāgata’s instructions. Although the Tathāgata preached the Dharma to him many times, he was unwilling to receive it and the Buddha then departed.
Not far from there, he saw an elephant alone in a secluded mountain, dwelling in tranquility and non-action. The elephant thought to himself:

"When I was among the great herd, I was troubled by the other elephants; when I followed the flock to graze, I obtained only inferior fodder, and when I drank water, it was turbid. Today, being here and not troubled by the other elephants, how joyful this is!"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"A single elephant emerges from among the herd; Among elephants, it is the one with six tusks.
With every thought, its mind is naturally equanimous; It alone finds joy in the vast wilderness."
After the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, he departed.
Not out of a lack of harmlessness, but for the sake of all people, he acted with a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings; thus, he harbored no resentment.

"To act for the sake of all people with a mind free from harm" means that one should completely eliminate all feelings of enmity, hatred, and resentment, and instead cultivate compassion for all classes of sentient beings; therefore it is said: "To act for the sake of all people with a mind free from harm."

One who practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings has no resentment; they regard others as their own body, without distinction. Whether hearing pleasant words or foul speech, such a person does not take them to heart. Being free from resentment and devoid of any intent to harm, they remain ever vigilant and respectful toward all sentient beings, never abandoning this practice. Therefore it is said: "One who practices loving-kindness toward sentient beings has no resentment."
If one has a compassionate heart and pities even a single person, one immediately attains all roots of goodness;
eventually, for the sake of all beings, the noble sages will proclaim this as the highest merit.

Regarding "if one has a compassionate heart and pities even a single person," as stated in the Buddha’s sūtras: suppose there is a person who gives to all sentient beings, yet adds a gift of compassion to a single individual—of these two, which merit is greater?
The bhikṣu replied:
"For one who practices loving-kindness and takes pity upon sentient beings, their merit is exceedingly great.
Therefore it is said: "By extending a heart of loving-kindness and compassion to even a single person, one immediately attains the roots of all goodness."

One should always act for the sake of all; those whom the noble and holy praise as supreme in merit find that the blessing of giving to even a single person is immeasurable, let alone giving to the entire multitude of sentient beings.

That merit is infinite, immeasurable, and beyond calculation; it is many hundreds of millions of times greater than anything that can be compared through analogy. Therefore it is said: "One should act for the sake of all; the noble and wise call this the highest form of merit."
Universally loving all, Compassionately mindful of the various classes of sentient beings, One who practices the mind of loving-kindness Will later receive unsurpassed bliss.

Regarding "universally loving all, compassionately mindful of the various classes of sentient beings": when a person practices loving-kindness, their resolve is impartial. Since the classes of sentient beings are more numerous than the elements of earth, one who can universally extend a compassionate heart to all sentient beings will, upon receiving a human body in the future, experience inexhaustible joy.
If one is born in the heavens, one will naturally receive blessings; looking east and gazing west, one will be attended by an incalculable number of jade maidens.

If one is born among humans, one will be born into a wealthy and noble family of the four castes, possessing all seven treasures in full without deficiency, with true and upright parents, never dwelling in lowliness or meanness.

Therefore it is said: "Extending universal kindness to all, taking pity upon the various classes of sentient beings, and practicing a mind of loving-kindness, one shall later receive unsurpassed bliss."
If, with a leaping heart, one practices all wholesome dharmas with joy and without indolence,
one will attain the state of peace and security.

If one acts with a leaping spirit, rejoicing without indolence, that practitioner stills lust, anger, and delusion; maintaining a firm resolve, they do not abandon their original vow. Whatever merit they obtain, they dedicate entirely to the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. They do not wait for this merit to seek the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King or the various minor kings; nor do they seek to become Śakra, Brahmā, or even Māra or the King of Māras. They seek only to attain the extinction of *nirvāṇa*, the unconditioned, the uncreated, and the dharma free from birth and death. Therefore it is said: "If one acts with a leaping spirit, rejoicing without indolence, and cultivates all wholesome dharmas, one shall attain the state of peace and security."
When the breath ceases, there is great joy; body, speech, and mind act in harmony.
Having attained equal liberation, the bhikṣu’s mind is tranquil and blissful;
all fetters are exhausted, and no further afflictions remain.

When one attains tranquility, joy arises; for those whose body, speech, and mind are in accord, the human mind uses this tranquility to eliminate all illnesses entirely, no longer engaging in the activities of body, speech, and mind. Whether it be practicing generosity, observing the precepts, restraining the mind, or undertaking the fast, all seek the Way of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Even if one leaves the household life to cultivate meritorious deeds, abandons worldly eloquence to practice the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and attains the dharma of the eight liberations—when a bhikṣu practices the Dharma without departing from the noble ones—it is for this reason that it is said: [the verse].
When one rests, joy is brought forth; body, speech, and mind are in accord.

What is called "knot" binds the human heart; these knots entwine one another like a moth wrapping itself in silk. When the human heart is thus bound, it does not perceive the Great Radiance. Only by removing those defilements can one see for oneself. Therefore, it is said:
All fetters are exhausted; there is no longer any defilement.
Even the sounds of the five kinds of music cannot please the mind.
It is not as good as once setting the mind upright and turning toward the Dharma of equality.

Even if the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments cannot please the human mind, for that practitioner whose will is fixed in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), who discerns the rise and fall and the destination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), even if the various devas were to perform songs and music in an attempt to cause this person’s mind to waver, it would not happen.
Why is this? Because the mind possesses right view and is free from inversion.
Therefore it is said: "Even the sounds of the five kinds of music cannot please the human mind as much as a single moment of a rightly directed mind turning toward the Dharma of equality."
The Supreme One attains a peaceful sleep, Nor does he conceive of a self;
All those with minds that delight in dhyāna Do not delight in the desires of the mind.

"The Supreme One attains a peaceful sleep, nor does he conceive of a self" means that a practitioner of the path does not conceive of a "self" or become stained by attachment to honor or office. Rather than taking a high bed within curtains and canopies with a mind bound by attachment, he would prefer to lie upon cold stones or roll about in the dust.
Therefore it is said: "The most excellent attain sound sleep, nor do they reckon that there is a self.

Those who possess a mind that delights in dhyāna and does not delight in sensual desires—the person whose mind does not shift or change when entering meditative concentration—remains silent and still at the moment of entry. Even if a thousand chariots thunder together or ten thousand peals of thunder shake the earth, they cannot cause the one who has entered concentration to depart from right reception (*samādhi*).
Why is this so? Because their minds have attained universal compassion.
Therefore it is said: "Those who possess a mind that delights in dhyāna do not delight in the objects of desire."
With a mind of supreme exultation, one does not perceive a self;
those whose minds delight in dhyāna do not delight in the objects of desire.

As for "with a mind of supreme exultation," this refers to one who perceives non-self and analytically discerns the four great elements arising from both the internal and external. Understanding each of these to be empty and unreal, it is therefore said: "With a mind of supreme exultation, one does not perceive a self; those whose minds delight in dhyāna do not delight in the objects of desire."
All fetters are forever exhausted; Like a mountain, they cannot be moved.
Untainted by defilement, One does not give rise to anger toward anger.

Regarding "all fetters are forever exhausted; like a mountain, they cannot be moved": it is as when that practitioner’s fetters are forever exhausted, being pure within and without and free from all blemish. His mind is like a vajra, incapable of being destroyed, and like Mount Tai, incapable of being shifted.

Why is this? It is because their resolve is extremely firm; they remain unstained amidst desire and unafraid in the face of calamity, for both body and spirit are empty and devoid of anything to which they might cling.
Therefore it is said: "When all fetters are forever exhausted, one is as immovable as a mountain; one is not defiled by what is defiling, nor does one give rise to anger toward what is provocative."
Those who possess such a mind— how could they know the traces of suffering?
Harmless and unstained, fully endowed with the precepts,
they are content with their food as well as their bedding and seats.
Cultivating the mind and seeking skillful means—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.

For those who possess such a mind, how could they perceive the traces of suffering? Just as that practitioner refines his mind, removes all defilements and attachments, and maintains a resolve to sever the fetters, advancing daily without indolence—at that time, how could he perceive any traces of suffering?
Therefore it is said: "How can those who possess such a mind know the traces of suffering?

One who is harmless and unstained, fully endowed with the precepts, neither harms himself nor harms others; he does not violate the sequence of what is taught in the precepts. Having cultivated virtue for himself, he further teaches this virtue to the people. Thus it is said: "Harmless and unstained, fully endowed with the precepts."

Regarding "knowing moderation in food and in bedding and seats": it is like that practitioner who takes measured food without greed or gluttony, merely seeking to sustain his life in order to practice the Way. This is like using grease to lubricate a cart; the purpose is to ensure that the heavy load can reach its destination.
It is also like applying ointment to a person's wounds; the purpose of applying it is to prevent new pain from increasing and to heal old sores.
Therefore it is said: "Knowing moderation in food, as well as in bedding and seating.

To cultivate the mind and seek skillful means—this is what is called the teaching of all Buddhas. A practitioner who grasps the essential meaning finds that what is most urgent in their practice is the *adhicitta* (higher mind); therefore it is said: "To cultivate the mind and seek skillful means—this is what is called the teaching of all Buddhas."
The practitioner contemplates the characteristics of the mind, Discriminating between thoughts and awaiting the cessation of mental activity;
By thus entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), One immediately attains joy and peace.

Regarding "the practitioner contemplates the characteristics of the mind": it is as when that practitioner knows the source of the mind; as soon as a thought arises, they cause it to cease so that it does not grow. They know the advancement and retreat of thoughts and the discrimination between good and evil. This refers to the practices cultivated throughout eternal kalpas. Therefore it is said: "The practitioner contemplates the characteristics of the mind, discriminating between thoughts and awaiting the cessation of mental activity."

Regarding the statement, "By attaining entry into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one obtains joy and peace": why is it said that one who enters concentration is called a person who has entered concentration?

Concentration possesses three meanings, of which *dhyāna* is foremost. It is like a king who governs the four quarters; he may indeed be rich in worldly wealth, yet he lacks the wealth of the Path (*mārga-dhana*).

One who practices *dhyāna*-concentration should be rich in the wealth of the Path and lack worldly wealth. What is called the wealth of the Path refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), the concentrations (*samādhi*) of *dhyāna*, and the roots of all virtues.
There are two meanings of "pleasure":
there is pure pleasure and there is impure pleasure.
As for impure pleasure, it refers to food, drink, clothing, bedding, and articles of adornment; incense, flowers, cosmetics, powders, silks, banners, and canopies—these are called impure pleasures.

As for those who possess pure bliss, they enter the meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and dwell in a state of profound tranquility, free from conditioned activity and devoid of other divergent thoughts;
this is what is called the bliss of purity. Therefore it is said: "By attaining entry into meditative concentration, one immediately obtains joy and peace."

Guarding the mind is self-adornment; envying others while cultivating oneself, one encounters sorrow without suffering pain—the wise dwell in discernment. Regarding "guarding the mind is self-adornment; envying others while cultivating oneself":

that practitioner constantly guards against the fetters and attachments to the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, not allowing various discursive thoughts to intermingle therein. Furthermore, they adorn themselves with the flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the seven factors of awakening. Therefore it is said: "Guarding the mind is self-adornment; envying others while cultivating oneself."

"Encountering sorrow, one does not suffer; the wise abide in discernment. This means that the practitioner who has entered the state of fearlessness is a wise person whose spirit is discerning and remains unshakable. Therefore it is said: "Encountering sorrow, one does not suffer; the wise abide in discernment."
When people do not guard their minds, they are harmed by wrong views;
harboring thoughts of frivolity as well, such individuals enter the path of death.

Regarding "when people do not guard their minds, they are harmed by wrong views": if practitioners do not guard against forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), and if there are sentient beings who cultivate deviant paths, they shall then proceed toward the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Those who do not practice wrong views are born among gods or humans, dwelling in the central lands rather than in the border regions or the eight states of non-leisure.
Therefore it is said: "If a person does not guard the mind, they will be harmed by wrong views."

Furthermore, those who harbor playful and frivolous intentions and thus tread upon the path to death—those practitioners who are deluded regarding the Way—all do so because they are shrouded by the latent hindrances (*anuśaya-āvaraṇa*). They are unable to catch even a glimpse of the radiance of wisdom; moreover, being further covered by the five hindrances of frivolity and obscured by heavy clouds, it is impossible for them to behold the light of wisdom.
