After their lives end, they will inevitably proceed along the path of death.
Therefore it is said: "Those who harbor thoughts of frivolity and playfulness are on the path to death.
For this reason, one should guard the mind, practice pure conduct with equanimity, keep right view ever before oneself, and discern the phenomena of arising and ceasing."

Therefore, one should guard the mind and practice the path of purity with equanimity. Such a practitioner constantly protects the mind and its intentions; they observe the laws of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and abandon what is improper. They know when it is appropriate to walk and know when it is appropriate to sit; whether advancing or retreating, moving or coming, they do not lose their decorum.
Therefore it is said: "For this reason, one should guard the mind and equally cultivate pure conduct.

With right view always preceding them, those who discern the dharma of arising and ceasing are like people who, having cultivated virtue, know themselves deeply; just as a householder with wealth can distinguish his own possessions, so too is it for one who practices the Way. Treading the straight path of the Eightfold Noble Path, they steer clear of the four turbid currents; grasping the torch of wisdom, they illuminate the dark chamber of the three poisons. Discerning the origins of arising and ceasing, they return to a single certainty without obstruction. In this, what difficulty could there be in attaining the Way?
Therefore it is said: Right view is ever foremost, discerning the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
The bhikṣu eliminates sleep; having exhausted suffering, he creates no more.
Subduing the mind with the medicine of discipline, he guards his heart so that it is no longer restless.

"A bhikṣu who eliminates sleep, exhausting suffering and creating no more"—this means that a practitioner of contemplation removes the affliction of the hindrance of drowsiness and sloth (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*), reaches the end of all suffering, and creates nothing new. Therefore it is said: "A bhikṣu who eliminates sleep, exhausting suffering and creating no more."

To subdue the mind through the application of medicine and to guard the mind so that it does not become restless again means that one must constantly protect the mind; if one’s aspirations are thus surely fulfilled, one can reach the state of a sage. Cultivating untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*) results from subduing the mind and removing defilements.
To practice heedfulness and not disturb others is the profound and essential task of a practitioner.
Therefore, it is said: "Subdue the mind with the medicine; guard the mind so that it is no longer restless."
"Sentient beings, deceived by their own minds, / All undergo the sufferings of hell. / To subdue the mind brings about happiness; / Guard the mind and do not let it wander again.

Regarding "sentient beings, deceived by their own minds, all undergo the sufferings of hell": being deluded and misled, they are driven by the mind to plant the roots of hellish retribution. For countless billions of kalpas, they endure immeasurable suffering—being slaughtered, cut, flayed, and torn asunder. Therefore it is said: "Sentient beings, deceived by their own minds, all undergo the sufferings of hell; to subdue the mind brings about happiness; guard the mind and do not let it wander again."

Guard the mind and do not let it wander; the mind is the gateway to all wonders. By guarding it so that nothing leaks away, one immediately stands at the gate of Nirvana. When the mind is upright, the Way exists; when it is crooked, there are heights and depths.

Sentient beings are deluded and ignorant, unable to distinguish the true from the false; thus they fall and fail to reach the Way. The deluded have their minds confused, claiming the Way resides in emptiness, yet they do not realize that the mind is the root of the Way—empty, silent, and still. It is the most supreme of all dharmas and the ultimate consummation of all practices. It is forever detached from the three realms of existence and does not dwell within the triple world; having crossed over all suffering and affliction, one will not be born again for the duration of one's life.
Therefore it is said: "Guard the mind and do not let it stray; the mind is the gateway to all wonders. By guarding it so that nothing is lost, one dwells at the gate of Nirvana."
Udānavarga, Volume 28 and Volume 29,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Three: On the Śramaṇa The bhikṣu begs for alms, yet receives without hoarding; praised by gods and men, he is born pure and free from defilement.
Regarding the bhikṣu who begs for alms and acquires nothing in excess: a bhikṣu who begs for food constantly reflects thus:

"What I now seek and obtain shall be sufficient for myself alone; I shall not retain any surplus to be reckoned as wealth. Should there be any remainder, I shall immediately give it away to others and not keep it for a long time."

As stated in the prohibitions of the Buddha’s Vinaya: when one's parents are advanced in years, aged, or bedridden with illness; or when fellow practitioners (bhikṣus) have long suffered from grave ailments and are unable to walk about—one is permitted to beg for alms, regardless of the amount, to provide for those who are aged or ill.
Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu begs for alms so as not to accumulate.

Praised by gods and men, born pure and free from defilement—this means that the bhikṣu practices few desires and contentment; when the time comes, he begs without storing or accumulating anything. The various devas protect him and extol his virtue; his fame spreads far and wide, such that there is none who does not hear and know of it.

Regarding this bhikṣu who is born pure and free from defilement, the reason why the various devas praise his virtue is that a person who upholds the precepts will, upon death, certainly be reborn in heaven; he increases the assembly of devas and diminishes the assembly of asuras. Therefore it is said: "Praised by gods and men, he is born pure and free from defilement."
The bhikṣu practices loving-kindness, cherishing and revering the Buddha’s teachings; deeply entering into śamatha and vipaśyanā, he attains peace once his conditioned activities have ceased.

The bhikṣu maintains his resolve and practices the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—pitying and caring for all beings; cherishing and revering the Three Jewels with unceasing faith, he deeply enters into the distinctions of the goals of śamatha and vipaśyanā, seeking alms wherever he may be and remaining to transform others in every place.

The reason for eliminating greed and restraining the mind is the desire to remove worldly glory and not covet gain or offerings; it is to exhaust the cycle of birth and death, extinguish all evil conduct, and cross over from existence to non-existence—this is called eternal peace.

Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness, cherishes and honors the Buddha's teaching, and deeply enters into śamatha and vipaśyanā, attains peace once his conditioned activities have ceased.
When the bhikṣu exhausts all cravings, abandons craving and casts off arrogance, and being without self, eliminates the notion of 'I' and 'mine'—who would not find this meaning intimate?"

When a bhikṣu has exhausted all cravings and abandoned craving to eliminate arrogance, that ascetic bhikṣu extinguishes all conceptual attachments—namely, attachment to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; and attachment to desire, attachment to form, and attachment to the formless. The pride of the three realms and the multitude of false inversions are completely and profoundly eliminated. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu exhausts all cravings and abandons craving to eliminate arrogance."

To eliminate the notion of self and abandon the ego—who would not find this meaning intimate? A bhikṣu practicing asceticism does not linger within the three realms; he understands that both the internal and external are entirely without a master. Those who calculate a self come haphazardly to seek blessings; though they may have their wishes fulfilled, they will inevitably fall later.
As for those on the stage of ordinary beings who do not perceive a self, they understand that the myriad things, both internal and external, are empty and quiescent: what, then, is "self"?

Who am I? That which is bound by others and subjected to abuse is entirely empty and quiescent, possessing nothing at all. When one is reviled by others, the sounds come and go; in the interval between them, both internally and externally, there is absolutely nothing.
Therefore it is said: "Abandoning the self by means of non-self—whom would this principle not endear?
One should know that this Dharma is the essential escape from the body; like an elephant facing the enemy, so should the bhikṣu practice."

One should know that these dharmas are the essential means of escape for the body. A practicing bhikṣu should extensively gather the various essentials, selecting and cultivating virtuous qualities to compensate for his deficiencies. Just as a person wishing to reach a destination must necessarily follow the path, and one seeking the lair of the Way must necessarily find its route, the path of essential escape is the suchness of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore it is said: "One should know that this Dharma is the means of escape for the body.

It is like an elephant confronting the enemy; when a bhikṣu practices this way, he is like that fierce elephant given strong liquor who charges wildly toward the enemy. Even though pierced by swords and arrows until death, he does not retreat, but only returns to his own camp once he has captured his quarry.
The reason for this is that one fears the driver above rather than external enemies;

a bhikṣu who practices the path is likewise: he must receive the harsh instructions from his teacher, internalize them within his heart, and reflect upon them repeatedly so as not to lose the traces of their meaning.
Therefore it is said: "Just as an elephant confronts the enemy, so does the bhikṣu practice his training.
A person does not live for an eon; he contends within with his own mind. Guarding the body and mindful of the Truths, the bhikṣu dwells in peace."

Now, when a practitioner of the path attains the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and cultivates them day and night, if they desire to remain for a kalpa or even beyond a kalpa, it will be accomplished according to their intention without difficulty. Free from all fetters and attachments, they constantly contend with the mind, preventing it from wandering at will and severing all cravings. They cast aside thoughts of right and wrong and part forever from desire; furthermore, they no longer perceive the nesting place of the three realms (*tridhātu*). Only then do they correspond to conduct that is without deficiency. Therefore, it is said: "Though a person does not live for a kalpa, if they contend within with the mind, guarding the body and mindful of the Truths, that bhikṣu shall find peace."
Regard relatives as friends; maintain a pure livelihood without admixture;
know what should be given when giving; likewise, let one’s deportment be complete.
When a bhikṣu is endowed with all these practices, he is able to reach the end of suffering.

The practitioner’s accomplishments all arise from friends; when their merit is perfected and virtue fulfilled, their fame spreads far and wide. Those who receive their teachings find new inspiration daily. Their practice is authentic and they do not cling to external things. Whatever gifts they bestow, they give to the Buddha, the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, their teachers, and their elders.
Why is this so? Because these individuals all possess dignified deportment, observe various rites and ceremonies, and understand the origins of suffering.

Therefore it is said: "Regard relatives as friends; maintain a pure livelihood without admixture; know what should be given when practicing giving; and likewise ensure that one's deportment is complete. When a bhikṣu is equipped with all such practices, he can then reach the end of suffering."
Do not recklessly offend with hands or feet; be moderate in speech and cautious in conduct.
Always find internal joy in a concentrated mind; one who maintains such practice is called a bhikṣu.

In this world, there are many people who are violent and do evil; they strike one another with their hands and fists, leading to injury, while internally they indulge the six senses, becoming attached to the phenomena of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures.

Although such a person may have attained the state of a practitioner, they do not accord with the practice of the Dharma; advancing, they lack the methods for cultivating the Way, and retreating, they lose the decorum of the noble ones. They are like those who carry out the dead, no longer fit for anything upright or proper.

These bhikṣus are also like this: they are able to focus their own minds so that their conduct is in accordance with the Dharma; sitting in dhyāna with a concentrated mind, they practice the Path during the six periods of the day without losing their fundamental practice. Therefore it is said: "Do not let your hands or feet commit transgressions; be moderate in speech and cautious in your conduct; always delight inwardly in a concentrated mind—one who maintains such practice is called a bhikṣu."
Delighting in the Dharma and desiring the Dharma, contemplating and finding peace in the Dharma, the bhikṣu relies upon the Dharma; upright and without waste.

The student who practices and discerns all dharmas, seeing the Dharma and attaining the Dharma, deeply enters into the contemplation of the Dharma—whether sitting or lying down, as various deities come and go—he contemplates and finds peace in the Dharma. The bhikṣu who relies upon the Dharma thereby attains parinirvāṇa; he benefits from the noble paths without waste, increasing day by day and never diminishing. He also causes the True Dharma to endure long in the world. Therefore it is said: "Delighting in the Dharma and desiring the Dharma, contemplating and finding peace in the Dharma, the bhikṣu relies upon the Dharma; upright and without waste."
One should train in entering emptiness; a bhikṣu should dwell in quietude, delighting in non-human places and contemplating the equality of all phenomena.

A practitioner who contemplates these five aggregates regards them as permanent, solid, and indestructible; unable to relinquish them, they give rise to worldly afflictions. However, a practitioner who discriminates the five aggregates and realizes that both the internal and external are entirely empty—even if situated in the midst of a wilderness, beneath a tree, or among graves—should contemplate the fundamental nature of dharmas and seek the fruit of the Path. First, one must practice emptiness before one may correspond to the true Path.

Formerly, while several practitioners were sitting in meditation and practicing the contemplation of emptiness within their room, Subhūti sought them out from outside and asked for the door to be opened.
The person inside replied, "Who are you?"
Subhūti replied: "The one whom worldly people conventionally name 'Subhūti'—what people delight in are lute playing, drumming, and performing music;
these are what people delight in. That which people do not delight in is meditative concentration, counting the breaths, and binding the mind to a single point; this is not what people contemplate."
Therefore it is said: "One should train in entering emptiness; a bhikṣu should dwell in seclusion, delighting in non-human places, and contemplate the equality of all phenomena.
One should restrain the five aggregates, subdue the mind like water, and through purity and harmony, experience the taste of ambrosia."

A beginner who contemplates these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) should see that they are all subject to decay and destruction, with not a single one worth craving. One should discern that all bases of support are entirely unstable; the mind should be impartial and equanimous, the countenance serene and pleasant, pure and flawless, reaching the end of all suffering. Therefore it is said: "One should restrain the five aggregates and subdue the mind like water; being pure and serene, this constitutes the taste of ambrosia (*amṛta*)."
Just as that most precipitous mountain is not moved by the wind, so too the bhikṣu who has exhausted all delusion is unshakable wherever he may be.

Just as Mount Sumeru is not tilted or shaken by the four winds, so it is with the bhikṣu who has exhausted delusion; he is not moved by the dharmas of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or subtle tangibles. Therefore it is said: "Just as that most precipitous mountain is not moved by the wind, the bhikṣu who has exhausted delusion is unshakable wherever he may be."
All name-and-form is not-existent; do not be deluded by it. One who neither clings nor craves is a bhikṣu.
Name-and-form and the six sense-bases are what the practitioner discards; "mine" and "not-mine" are entirely non-existent, and one does not approach dangerous dharmas.

The Dharma is of various kinds; some are true and real, while others are perilous. That which is called "truly authentic" refers to the various *pāramitās*, while that which is called "perilous" refers to worldly conventions.

A bhikṣu who is fully endowed with these qualities is called an arhat; therefore it is said: "Regarding all name-and-form, do not be deluded by what does not exist; by neither approaching nor craving them, one is a bhikṣu."

A bhikṣu is not defined by shaving his head; one who is arrogant, boastful, and lacks precepts is not a bhikṣu. Only by abandoning greed and contemplating the Way does one truly correspond to the title of bhikṣu.
One is not a "one whose mind is stilled" merely by shaving his head; one who is negligent and lacks faith cannot extinguish the manifold sufferings.
He was the foremost among śramaṇas.
Then, at the proper time, the World-Honored One took his bowl, adjusted his robes, and went directly to the place where the brahmin Pañcaśikha was begging for alms.
At that time, the brahmin saw the World-Honored One from afar and sighed to himself, saying:
"I am a mendicant, and you are also a mendicant; between us two mendicants, which one is superior?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"A bhikṣu is not defined by shaving his head; one who is arrogant and lacks the precepts is not a bhikṣu. Only one who abandons greed and contemplates the Way is truly worthy of being called a bhikṣu."
"Tranquility of mind is not [defined by] shaving the head; one who is heedless and lacks faith cannot extinguish the manifold sufferings.
Such a person is not a supreme śramaṇa.
When the brahmin heard this verse, he immediately offered all his wealth and possessions to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata did not accept it and said to the brahmin, "What I have now spoken cannot be praised by songs; for what reason, then, should I take the gift you have offered?"
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I do not know to whom this offering should now be entrusted?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Take now this offering you have received and place it in a clean location; either on ground where there is no grass, or in pure water.
At that time, the brahmin followed the Tathāgata’s instruction and immediately poured the offering into the water.
At that time, [the water] spontaneously surged forth from within, producing various kinds of sounds, and gradually a great radiance emerged from its midst.

Upon seeing this, the brahmin leaped for joy, unable to contain his exultation. The Tathāgata then preached the True Suchness and the Four Noble Truths; immediately, while seated there, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣu attains the concentration of loving-kindness and receives the teachings of all Buddhas;
having fully attained the track of cessation, he has no kin—be careful not to look upon them.
When the bhikṣu attains loving-kindness, he is liberated wherever he dwells; he discerns the myriad practices, reaching mastery in nothing that is not accomplished.

Furthermore, suppose there are people who see various classes of sentient beings—infantry, elephant troops, cavalry, and chariot forces—engaged in mutual combat and dispute; one who has entered into compassion feels pity for their plight and delivers these sentient beings to the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), just as a balanced scale is impartial and without duality.

Regarding the four firm minds attained toward the Tathāgata, they are unshakable; just as the most eminent householder and the bhikṣu never tire of beholding the Buddha, even if a manifested Buddha were to stand before them, it could not cause their minds to waver.

The practitioner attains the track of cessation where there are no further afflictions; knowing what is to be approached, they approach it; knowing what is to be followed, they follow it. Such is the trace of practice: the cessation of formations is its foundation.

To state the essentials briefly: these fetters and afflictions are fundamentally consumed by fire; thus, one gradually and successively severs the sources of all fetters and afflictions. In this way, there may indeed be a brahmin who attains even unto *nirvāṇa*.
With a mind of supreme joy and delight, further augmented by loving-kindness, the bhikṣu is full of serenity;
he exhausts emptiness until no root remains. That practitioner of the path leaps for joy without indolence;

hearing of pleasant things, he does not take them as cause for delight, and hearing of evil, he does not take it as cause for grief. The bhikṣu enters meditative concentration without confusion, constantly reflecting that from incalculable kalpas past, he has cultivated myriad virtues without losing the foundation of his practice. Having thoroughly exhausted the source of emptiness, it is boundless and shoreless. Therefore it is said: "With a mind of supreme joy and delight, further augmented by loving-kindness, the bhikṣu is full of serenity; he exhausts emptiness until no root remains."
Resting the body and resting the mind, Restraining the mouth is likewise virtuous.
One who abandons the world is called a bhikṣu; Crossing the abyss, they encounter no obstruction.

That practitioner maintains dignified deportment without failing its rules, guards against the four faults of speech without transgression, and ensures that his mind does not wander or run astray. The teachings he proclaims are free from coarseness or rudeness; he speaks with a preceding smile, making him perfectly attuned to human sentiment.
"One who has abandoned the world is called a bhikṣu. What constitutes a bhikṣu?

One who is said to be a bhikṣu is one who has departed from forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; who has removed lust, anger, and delusion. Therefore it is said: "He quiets the body and quiets the mind; he restrains his speech as well—this is good. One who has abandoned the world is called a bhikṣu; he crosses the abyss without obstruction."
Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no dhyāna. The Path proceeds from dhyāna and wisdom, whereby one attains proximity to Nirvāṇa.

As for human learning, it first begins with the recitation of the four Āgamas until the Tripiṭaka is fully mastered; only then is one designated as possessing meditative concentration (dhyāna), and this is considered mundane wisdom.

Regarding "no wisdom without dhyāna" and "no dhyāna without wisdom": the insight of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) must reach its destination without obstruction. If these two factors are fully possessed, one draws near to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore it is said: "No dhyāna without wisdom, no wisdom without dhyāna; the Path proceeds from dhyāna and wisdom, whereby one attains proximity to *nirvāṇa*."
In meditation, be without negligence; do not be disturbed by desire. Do not swallow molten copper to torment and scorch your own body.

Just as those who practice the path restrain their body, speech, and mind, being few in desire and content with what they have without excessive striving—even when obtaining clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for the sick—they merely sustain their physical forms and do not long for worldly glory. They maintain the proper measure in their deportment and etiquette, and always know moderation regarding their bedding and seating. Do not, in future lives, receive molten copper poured into your mouth. Therefore it is said: "In meditation, be without negligence; do not be disturbed by desire. Do not swallow molten copper to torment and scorch your own body."
One who can guard their own body and speech, guards the mind so that no evil arises,
and subsequently attains the dharma of the precepts— for this reason, they are called a bhikṣu. Indeed, when a person practices such conduct—
neither performing evil with the body, nor reviling with the mouth, nor harboring envy or jealousy in the mind— one who possesses these three qualities is a bhikṣu.

Therefore it is said: "One who can guard their own body and speech, and guards the mind so that no evil arises, shall later attain the Dharma of the precepts; for this reason, they are called a bhikṣu."
All who cultivate wholesome dharmas take the seven factors of enlightenment as their foundation;
this is called the sublime Dharma, and thus one is termed a bhikṣu of concentration.

Just as that practitioner skillfully cultivates the Dharma, first attaining the source of the exhaustion of suffering through the outflow-free state, he then obtains the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, gradually reaching the unconditioned and drawing near to nirvāṇa.

Therefore it is said: "All who cultivate wholesome dharmas take the seven factors of enlightenment as their foundation; this is called the sublime Dharma, and thus one is termed a bhikṣu established in concentration."
What is now being spoken of is that one knows for oneself the source of the exhaustion of suffering;
this is called the root of goodness, and such a person is an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) bhikṣu.

Within the present life, he observes and understands for himself, seeking skillful means to reach the limit of suffering. What is called "reaching the limit of suffering" is the extinction of Nirvāṇa. Therefore, with all faculties complete, he accomplishes outflow-free conduct; his practice is as he intends, without any failure or transgression.
Therefore it is said: "As is now being taught, one who knows for oneself the source of the exhaustion of suffering—this is called a wholesome dharma; such a person is an outflow-free bhikṣu."
Not by the power of moral discipline, nor by the meaning of extensive learning,
nor even by attaining a concentrated mind, nor by attachment to literary embellishments—
when a bhikṣu possesses that which he holds, he exhausts all outflows through his practice.

When a person practices, they do not seek liberation merely through diligence, patience, single-mindedness, and wisdom; nor do they reach the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) through extensive learning, understanding, and insight into internal and external phenomena alone. Rather, one must first attain mundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and only thereafter reach the sublime limit. Whether dwelling in the mountains, wilds, or secluded places, one encounters virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who explain the correct path and do not speak of deviant ways.

"Monks, you should know that this practice cultivates the outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas. Those who have thus reached the end of suffering are all Arhats whose outflows are exhausted; even those at the stages of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Anāgāmin still undergo various forms of suffering and affliction."

Therefore it is said: "Not by the power of observing the precepts, nor by the meaning of extensive learning, but by attaining a concentrated mind that does not cling to literary embellishments—when a bhikṣu possesses such [realization], he exhausts all outflows through his practice."
One should contemplate the bliss of perfect awakening and not associate with worldlings;
observing the phenomena of this present life, one should discern the five aggregates.
Just as those in training contemplate the bliss of perfect awakening and find joy therein, they do not associate with worldlings.
Why is this so? Because it does not belong to their sphere of experience.

One who contemplates these worldly affairs understands the nature of sentient beings—those born and those passing away, and the destinies to which they advance or retreat; one understands the origin of suffering and discerns the formation and dissolution of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Therefore, it is said: "One should contemplate the bliss of Right Awakening and not associate with the ordinary worldling; one should contemplate the affairs of this present life and discern the five aggregates."
If one acts and acts, one must surely exert oneself in self-restraint; yet even after leaving home and seeking liberation, the mind may still be defiled.
For those whose practice is lax and whose wearying thoughts are not eliminated, this is not the pure holy life—how, then, can they attain the Great Treasure?

Those who practice give rise to various conceptualizations, which trigger the root of fetters; some harbor discriminations and calculations regarding the burdens of this life and future lives, failing to liberate themselves from suffering. Monks, do not cling to these as being pure conduct.
Regarding those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the Dharma of the essential way out, I do not say that such persons are fit for deliverance.
Why is this so? Because they have not freed themselves from the bonds of attachment.
Bhikṣus, you should know that to speak of what does not exist as existing is to cultivate false views and is not the Dharma of True Reality. Why is this?

It is because all such afflictions arise fundamentally from the body of the five aggregates; with these afflictions present, one further gives rise to unwholesome conduct, and due to these various ailments, one fails to reach the end of suffering.
Monks, you should know how to investigate its source thoroughly and understand that impermanence is the nature of change.

When a practitioner contemplates this dharma, they see it as lacking solidity, lacking stability, and lacking any essential core. By understanding that there is no self, one understands birth and death; one is not thwarted or destroyed by the Māra of Death. Having attained victory over him, one no longer creates further existence (*bhava*). To exhaust all existence is called the "limit of suffering" (*duḥkhakṣaya*), and there is nothing higher than this.
"The mind attains eternal rest; the bhikṣu who restrains his mental activities, having brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, is then liberated from the bonds and attachments of Māra.

Just as that practitioner has eternally exhausted all fetters (*saṃyojana*), and since his mind no longer clings to or creates further formations (*saṃskāra*), the dharmas of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch no longer dwell within his heart. Knowing for himself that his transgressions are finished and he will not again receive a womb-born existence, he is forever separated from the realm of Māra and no longer associated with the dust of sensual desires. Therefore it is said: "The mind attains eternal rest; the bhikṣu who restrains his mental activities, having brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, is then liberated from the bonds and attachments of Māra."
When the mind attains eternal tranquility, the bhikṣu restrains his mental activities;
thereby he brings an end to old age, sickness, and death, and shall no longer undergo further existence.

Existence is the burden of birth and death; that one drifts and wanders through the five realms of rebirth is entirely due to the delusions of the mind, which have not exhausted their source. Therefore it is said: "When the mind attains eternal tranquility, the bhikṣu restrains his mental activities; thereby he brings an end to old age, sickness, and death, and shall no longer undergo further existence."
The practitioner who maintains resolute intent accomplishes much benefit; constantly seeking skillful means, they cross over by themselves.
By severing the root of craving, the bhikṣu restrains his mind in practice, so as to exhaust old age, sickness, and death, never again to undergo existence.
Craving is a malady that brings about much harm; within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are two types of craving:
first, craving for food, and second, craving for sensual pleasures.
In the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is craving for the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyānāsvāda*).
Therefore it is said: Having severed the root of craving,
with no more fetters or defilements in the mind, the bhikṣu who restrains his mental conduct brings an end to old age,
sickness, and death, and shall never again undergo existence.

What are called the "fetters" (saṃyojana) are the root of all conditioned activities that leak out various impurities and turbidities. Therefore it is said: "One whose mind is free from fetters, a bhikṣu who restrains his mental conduct, shall exhaust old age, sickness, and death, and will no longer undergo further existence."
By severing the roots of existence, the bhikṣu restrains his mental conduct;
having brought an end to old age, sickness, and death, he shall no longer undergo further existence.
Having crossed over birth and death, he shall not again receive existence.
The bhikṣu who restrains his mind and practices rightly brings an end to old age, sickness, and death;
he shall no longer undergo further existence and is thus liberated from the realm of Māra.
Having forever departed from the realm of Māra, he shall no longer abide in the realm of desire; being liberated and utterly liberated, he shall not undergo further existence again.

Having overcome the thorns of the forest, and having removed those who revile, he is like one leaning against Mount Tai; such a bhikṣu does not suffer. Regarding "having overcome the thorns of the forest": these are called forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). Furthermore, what else constitutes the "thorns of the forest"? [The answer follows: They are the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*). What are the six? They are the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. These are called the thorns of the forest. Having overcome them, he does not suffer. Regarding "and having removed those who revile": this refers to the six external sense bases. What are the six? They are the form-base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the taste-base, the tangible-base, and the mental-phenomena-base. These are called those who revile. Having removed them, he does not suffer. Why is that? Because he has abandoned all attachment. This is called a bhikṣu who does not suffer. Why is that? Because he has transcended all suffering. Therefore, it is said: "Having overcome the thorns of the forest, and having removed those who revile, he is like one leaning against Mount Tai; such a bhikṣu does not suffer. Thus it is taught. This concludes the *Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Who Does Not Suffer*. What is called the "thorn of the forest" refers to the afflictions of lust, anger, and ignorance, which constitute the very root [of suffering]; only the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to remove them.

Even if they revile me, I understand that they have no substantial form; within myself, I reflect that the body is a vessel of suffering, having no master either internally or externally. When one discriminates this body in this way, how could it be an object of craving or delight?
When one illness breaks out, four hundred and four illnesses arise simultaneously; this is called internal affliction of the body.

As for external afflictions, these include thorny thickets, the reputation of slander, physical disfigurement, and humiliation; or being beaten and struck—such things come from without. Or being harmed by vipers, snakes, and centipedes—all these are external matters that come to oppress the body.

It is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be moved by means of illusory spells or marvelous arts; likewise, for a bhikṣu who wishes to transcend the root of all suffering, there is only True Suchness and the Four Noble Truths.

That bhikṣu does not know suffering or pleasure; that which is called "not knowing suffering or pleasure" means that when suffering arrives, he does not regard it as acrid or painful, and when pleasure comes, he does not take delight in it.
Therefore it is said: "Having overcome the thorns of the forest and removed the insults, like one leaning against Mount Tai, the bhikṣu does not suffer.
Not dwelling on this world or the next, viewing the world as an illusion or a dream, the bhikṣu triumphs over both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin."

Just as a wise practitioner understands in their mind that this world and the next are subject to constant change and instability, it is therefore said: "One does not dwell on this life or the next; one views the world as an illusion or a dream. Such a bhikṣu transcends both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin."
Able to sever the root of craving, Exhausting the deep spring of desire,
The bhikṣu triumphs over both sides, Like a snake shedding its old skin.

The reason for employing this simile is to enable the practitioner to discern the depth and shallowness [of their afflictions], so that they may measure their correct practice in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One instructed them with the Way and its virtue, fearing that future sentient beings might not distinguish the root of craving; therefore, he expounded upon knowing its source.
Thus it is said: "One who can sever the root of craving and exhaust the deep spring of desire, such a bhikṣu transcends both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin."

To state the essentials briefly: desire, anger, delusion, and pride are likewise thus; for those attached to desire, one speaks of their desire; for those attached to anger, one speaks of their anger; for those attached to delusion, one speaks of their delusion.
One who can sever the five desires and cut off the root of desire,
that bhikṣu transcends both this world and the next, like a snake shedding its old skin.
It is as if a person whose body was bound by five fetters— sorrowful, distressed, and devoid of joy— later receives a pardon and is freed from peril.

For this reason, the Tathāgata provides this analogy, wishing to cause future generations to understand clearly and with certainty; therefore he says: "One who can sever the five desires and cut off the root of desire, that bhikṣu surpasses both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin."
One who can sever the five fetters and pull out the thorn of craving, that bhikṣu transcends both this world and the next, like a snake shedding its old skin. What are called the five fetters?

They are the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of sloth and torpor, the fetter of restlessness and remorse, and the fetter of doubt. These shroud the human mind so that it does not behold the light of wisdom; they leave people blind and dark, unable to see the radiance. They extinguish wisdom and cause one to be forever cut off from the various realms of existence, preventing one from reaching nirvāṇa.
Therefore it is said: "One who can sever the five fetters and pull out the thorns of craving, that bhikṣu triumphs over both worlds, like a snake shedding its old skin.
Regarding the phrase "pulling out the thorns of craving," there are three meanings for these thorns:

the thorn of desire, the thorn of hatred, and the thorn of ignorance. When these are completely severed without remainder so that they never arise again, one perceives the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing and severs the five hindrances.
Therefore it is said: "He has pulled out the thorn of craving.
One who possesses no worldly attachments and has further severed the roots of unwholesomeness—such a bhikṣu triumphs over both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin.

That practitioner has long been devoted to the practice of austerity; he cultivates the virtues of a bodhisattva, never ceasing throughout the day, and having left home to study, he does not crave worldly glory. Therefore it is said: "Those who possess no household affairs and have severed the roots of unwholesomeness—such bhikṣus transcend both this world and the next, like a snake shedding its old skin."
Those who are free from all burning afflictions (*paridāha*) and have severed the unwholesome roots—such bhikṣus transcend both this world and the next, like a snake shedding its old skin.

As for what are called "burning afflictions," there are three: first, the burning affliction of desire; second, the burning affliction of hatred; and third, the burning affliction of delusion. Among these three burning afflictions, hatred is the most severe; it burns like fire from the desire realm up to the stage of the first dhyāna.

The blazing fires of the three poisons burn from the realm of desire up to the formless realm; he who can extinguish these realms of the three poisons attains the foremost bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore it is said: "Those who are free from feverish affliction and have severed the roots of unwholesomeness—the bhikṣu excels both this world and the next, like a snake shedding its old skin."
Having severed desire without remainder, as one pulls out what is not firmly rooted,
the bhikṣu triumphs over both worlds, like a snake shedding its old skin.
When people are attached to desire, there is none who does not lose their life.
Why is this so? It is entirely due to the resulting of arbitrary mental judgments and deluded thoughts.
For this reason, the Sage first restrains lustful desire.
Therefore it is said: "Having severed desire without remainder, like pulling out what is not firmly rooted, the bhikṣu triumphs over both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin.
To state the essentials briefly: greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are likewise thus.
Craving arises and overflows, like a snake containing venomous poison;
the bhikṣu who triumphs over both [extremes] is like a snake shedding its old skin.

When a person follows the dictates of craving and cannot restrain themselves, they gradually proceed from the realm of desire up through the three realms of existence, transmigrating through the five destinies without escaping the four modes of birth.

Regarding the discourse on how a bhikṣu transcends both "that" and "this": "that" refers to the six sense objects and "this" refers to the six sense faculties. When a bhikṣu is able to extinguish both "that" and "this," it is like a snake shedding its old skin.
Those who possess the contemplation of the perception of cessation, And do not direct their minds toward internal [objects],
Such bhikṣus transcend both [this world and the next], Like a snake shedding its old skin.
As for "contemplation," there are three types of contemplation:
One who can extinguish the contemplation of desire, the contemplation of ill-will, and the contemplation of ignorance is called a true practitioner of the Way.
Therefore it is said: "He who has severed all conceptualizations and does not harbor them within his mind—the bhikṣu thus transcends both sides, like a snake shedding its old skin."
The bhikṣu upholds the precepts; Only when there is emptiness does he practice dhyāna.
The practitioner investigates its source; Non-action is the supreme bliss.

For a bhikṣu, the practice of conduct takes dignified demeanor as its foundation; the precepts serve to restrain the body, and the robes are the Dharma-garments. The rules of his conduct do not deviate from those of the former sages. When the mind is settled in the concentration of emptiness, it is then called dhyāna, yet he does not abandon conventional designations.

Just as that practitioner, upon receiving [the teaching], believes, understands, and discerns its meaning, seeking the state of unconditioned bliss where there is no affliction of hunger, cold, or suffering.
Therefore it is said: "One who maintains the precepts is called a bhikṣu; possessing emptiness, he practices dhyāna. The practitioner investigates its source; non-action is the supreme bliss."
The bhikṣu endures sorrow with patience; he arranges his bedding and seating. He should maintain mindfulness without negligence, severing craving for existence without remainder.

When the bhikṣu practices, he does not rejoice in dwelling in pleasure, nor does he suffer when encountering hardship. Regarding gain and loss, defamation and praise, his mind neither increases nor decreases. Dwelling in a secluded place, he sits upright with one-pointed concentration, his mind not wandering. He severs all fetters and afflictions, maintaining mindfulness free from conceptual attachment. Therefore it is said: "The bhikṣu endures sorrow with patience; he arranges his bedding and seating. He should maintain mindfulness without negligence, severing craving for existence without remainder."
"What is called a brahmin is not merely one who goes naked, dwells in the wilderness, or lies upon thorns;
such a person is not named a brahmin.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
From this day forward, please permit all your disciples to go entirely naked and not wear any clothing.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Alas! This is the delusion of a fool, contrary to the Dharma and Vinaya. This is the way of the brahmins, not the practice cultivated within our inner treasury.

Since people possess a sense of shame and modesty, there naturally exists the distinction between the honorable and the lowly, and the knowledge of parents and siblings; why then do you speak of wandering the world naked?"
At that time, there was another bhikṣu who approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
From this day forward, may you permit all practitioners to each keep their hair.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Ho! This is a perversion of folly that does not accord with the Dharma or the Vinaya; this is the way of the brahmins, not the practice cultivated within our inner treasury."
Again, another bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
May you permit all practitioners to smear their bodies with white ash.”
Again, another bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"From this day forward, may you permit the practitioners to practice breath-retention and abstain from food.
Yet another bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"From this day forward, I permit the practitioners to lie naked on the open ground.
The World-Honored One said:
"Ho! (Stop!)"
"It is a transgression for the foolish.
Then another bhikṣu prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"From this day forward, I permit all practitioners of the Way to bathe and purify themselves in the bathing pool.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One does not attain the Way by means of this practice."
Having cast off the body and being without attachment, not reciting heterodox words, and having eliminated both [extremes] through practice—
this is called a *brahman*.
Once, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Rṣipatana near the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, not many days had passed since the World-Honored One had ordained the five bhikṣus.

At that moment, there was an elder in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Yaśas, of noble lineage, possessing great wealth and abundant treasures; he was handsome and upright in appearance, peerless in the world.

Suddenly, within a single day, he attained extraordinary insight. He observed the men and women of his own household and saw that they were like dead bodies, not a single one worth cherishing; he viewed his own physical form as no different from those in a cemetery. He immediately rose from his seat and spoke thus:
"The delusions of ignorance are profoundly deep, such that one cannot distinguish between reality and illusory transformations."

At that time, the elder immediately left his home and fled the city. He took off his lapis lazuli sandals, which were worth ten thousand pieces of gold, and crossed the river to hasten toward the World-Honored One. Prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The affairs of the world are manifold and subject to many changes; all things are illusory transformations and cannot be relied upon. I now take refuge, desiring to seek the state of unconditioned peace and bliss."
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of noble family!"
"The Dharma of the noble ones is exceedingly vast and expansive; it is precisely that which your heart desires and delights in.
At that time, having heard the Tathāgata’s instruction, the elder was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him, namely: discourses on generosity, discourses on ethical discipline, and discourses on rebirth in the heavens; he spoke of the impurity of sensual desires and how the outflows constitute a great affliction.

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the elder immediately attained the pure Dharma-eye, with all defilements and dusts vanished while still seated. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and realized all dharmas, he rose from his seat and, taking refuge in himself, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“Indeed, O God among Gods!
"Listen; you may go forth from the household life into homelessness to study the Path.
The Buddha said to the elder, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His hair and beard fell away naturally, and he was spontaneously clothed in the dharma-robes; upon hearing the Dharma preached once more, he attained the path of an Arhat.

At that time, the parents, brothers, sons, and daughters of the elder’s household, with their retinues and stately carriages of elephants and horses, followed in pursuit to seek the elder Yashas. Upon reaching the riverbank, they saw the lapis lazuli sandals.
The father thought to himself:

"My son will certainly cross the river; there is no doubt about it. I know this because he has now left behind these glass sandals, worth hundreds of millions. I shall now cross the river and search for him wherever he may be."

He immediately crossed the river and, seeing from afar the World-Honored One’s radiant marks shining brilliantly, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
“Have you perhaps seen the youth Yaśas passing by while playing here?
By means of his supernormal power, the Buddha concealed the bhikṣu Yaśas so that the father could not see him. The Buddha then said to the elder:
“Rather than seeking your son now, it is better for you to seek yourself; simply sit down quickly, and I shall preach the Dharma to you.”
The elder sat down immediately, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; at that very seat, all defilements were cleansed away and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his samādhi so that the father might see his son. The father said to his son:
"Return home quickly; your mother is filled with grief and distress, fearing you will not return."
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Stop, stop, householder!
Do not speak such words."
"What do you think, householder?

Suppose there is a practitioner who was originally in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) with desire not yet exhausted, but later attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and leaves the stage of training behind. If one were to cause that person of no-more-learning to practice the dharmas of training—what do you think of this, householder?"
"Is this possible? The elder replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the elder:

“Your son has today attained non-attachment and dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Elder, you should know that having attained non-attachment, how could he return home to practice the five desires?”

Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately rose and prostrated himself before his son, bowing his body to the ground in homage. He took refuge in the True Man who is forever free from attachment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the elder:
"Having cast off the body, one has no dependence; One does not recite heterodox words; By means of the two practices, one eliminates [defilement];"
This is called a brahmin:
one whose conduct is pure in this life, who is without defilement in the next life, and for whom there is neither clinging nor abandoning—this is called a brahmin.

People who cling to false views do not change them even until death; those who hold the view of permanence are not associated with the view of annihilationism, and those with the view of annihilationism are not associated with the view of permanence. One who can relinquish these views and does not become attached to the three periods of time—for this reason it is said:
"One whose conduct is pure in this life and will be without defilement in future lives, for whom there is neither practice nor abandonment—he is called a *brahmin*."
If one relies on craving, yet the mind has no attachment; having already relinquished and rectified it, this is the cessation of the suffering of the end.

Although a person who first practices the path may still be at the stage of training, unable yet to discern and contemplate the fruits of the path with individual clarity so as not to lose their continuity, and unable yet to attain what has not been attained or achieve what has not been achieved—for this reason it is said: "If one relies on craving, yet the mind has no attachment; having already relinquished and rectified it, this is the cessation of the suffering of the end."
Those who have no attachments, who constantly practice right view, and always keep in mind the exhaustion of all taints—they are called brahmins.

It was as if a great elephant emerged from a small hole; wishing to exit through the city gate, it found the gate too narrow for the elephant. When the people saw this, they were each struck with amazement and said to that elephant:

"You have now emerged from a mere inch-long hole and come and gone without difficulty; yet, when you wish to leave the city, you are instead not permitted to do so. For this reason, the Sage used this as a metaphor:

although sentient beings may leave the household life to practice the Dharma, they are unable to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and achieve the state of being without outflows, nor attain liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom. Therefore it is said: "One who has no dependence on anything, who constantly practices right view, and always keeps in mind the exhaustion of all outflows—such a person is called a *brahmin*."
The fool accepts shaggy hair, as well as beds and bedding;
harboring a mind of greed and impurity within, what does he seek by adorning his exterior?

The fool does not realize for himself that he nourishes his hair; thus, those who shave their hair do so to remove the fetters (*saṃyojana*), not merely to shave the hair. Yet the foolish person persists in delusion, nourishing his hair to serve as an ornament.

The Dharma of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past has been transmitted from one to another; the practice of shaving the hair and beard and wearing the robes in proper order has existed since antiquity and is not something unique to this day.

Today, foolish people are greedily attached to bedding and requisites; however, within my Dharma, one is enjoined to maintain only the three robes and not to store anything in excess, making it a constant practice to dwell at the foot of trees or in cemeteries, as explained in detail according to the original text.

Internally harboring wrong views and giving rise to greedy and turbid thoughts, yet externally adorning oneself and claiming to be without flaw; though one abandons delusion for the sake of the Path, such a person is not free from confusion regarding the Dharma. Therefore it is said: "The fool accepts filthy hair, as well as beds and bedding; while harboring greedy and turbid thoughts within, what is the point of external adornment?"
Wearing tattered and coarse clothing, personally practicing the Dharma, dwelling in seclusion and reflecting—this is called a *brahmin*.

One who practices the path wears rough and unadorned garments, reflects upon the practice of the Dharma without seeking anything, and restrains speech and conversation so as not to incite strife between self and others; therefore it is said: "Wearing tattered and coarse clothing, personally practicing the Dharma, dwelling in seclusion and reflecting—this is called a *brahmin*."
Seeing the coming and going of delusion, falling into the moat and suffering pain;
wishing to cross alone to the other shore, not heeding the words of others, but solely extinguishing [the fires] so they do not arise—such a one is called a brahmin.

If a person clings to delusion and their mind does not awaken, nor can they transcend the stages to attain realization, remaining constantly in a state of suspicion and impurity, such a person is not one of pure conduct.
One who has severed all outflows (*āsrava*), exhausting them forever without remainder—such a person is called a *brahmin*.

Therefore it is said: "Seeing the coming and going of delusion, falling into the moat and suffering pain; desiring to cross alone to the other shore, not delighting in the words of others, but extinguishing [defilements] so they do not arise—such a person is called a *brahmin*."
Crossing the stream by cutting it off, being free from desire like Brahmā, and knowing through practice that [cravings] are exhausted—this is called a *brahman*.

If one could attain the Way simply by bathing the body with water, then all creatures of the watery realm would be called "attained to the Way. But it is not by bathing that one attains the Way; rather, it is by discerning all phenomena and scrutinizing their true meaning, becoming pure and flawless, so that the various fetters and the activities of the mind are forever exhausted without remainder. Therefore it is said: "Crossing the stream by cutting it off, being free from desire like Brahmā, and knowing through practice that [cravings] are exhausted—this is called a *brahman*."
It is not by bathing in water that many people can wash away defiled and evil dharmas; such a one is called a *brahmin*.
For even if a person bathes, they cannot remove the impurities within their belly; only when all evil dharmas are completely eliminated and no longer produced again is one truly named a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "One does not become pure by water; though many people bathe, only he who can eliminate base and evil dharmas is called a *brahmin*.
One is not a *śramaṇa* merely by shaving one's head, nor is one a *brahmin* by claiming auspiciousness;
rather, he who is able to extinguish all evils is truly a man of the Path."

What is called a śramaṇa does not necessarily mean one who has shaved off his beard and hair; rather, it is one who possesses right conduct within and accords with the Vinaya that should be considered a śramaṇa.

As for those who call themselves brahmins and claim that by reciting auspicious mantras they will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, they assume that everyone must be born there simply because they recite these mantras. However, what they mean by "reciting mantras to be born in the Brahma Heaven" is the ability to extinguish all evils and cultivate pure conduct.

Therefore it is said: It is not by shaving the head that one is a śramaṇa, nor by calling oneself auspicious that one is a brāhmaṇa; he who is able to extinguish all evils—he is truly a man of the Way.
Because he is non-dual, pure and without blemish, with all desires and fetters untied—he is called a brāhmaṇa.

Having completely abandoned all base and evil dharmas, whether in coming and going, moving about, or in every situation, his speech does not reach killing; he harms no one and causes no injury. Being pure and flawless, he is forever free from all bonds. Therefore it is said: "Because he is non-dual, pure and flawless, with the fetters of desire untied—he is called a *brahmin*."
To depart from evil is to be a *brahman*; to enter the right path is to be a *śramaṇa*. To cast off all my defiled conduct—this is what it means to leave the home life.

The conduct of a *brahman* consists in abandoning all unwholesome dharmas, becoming pure and transparent within and without, and ensuring that all defilements are forever exhausted. One harbors no expectations and does not hold oneself in superiority over others. With the mind settled and immovable, one awakens to the root of all dharmas. Having established the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and accomplished what was to be done, one will no longer undergo further existence. Cultivating pure conduct without omission, for this reason it is said: "To depart from evil is to be a *brahman*; to enter the right path is to be a *śramaṇa*. To cast off all my defiled conduct—this is what it means to leave the home life."
One who has no deluded mind, no pride, no folly or confusion,
no greed, and no notion of self— such a person is called a brahmin.
When a person lives in the world without harboring delusions, the brahmin speaks of himself thus:
"Once every hundred kalpas, within the great ocean, there naturally appears a delusive phantom that devours the people of the world.

One who has abandoned all pride and does not give rise to attachments—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—who is free from the eight worldly dharmas and is unstained by the world, is called a Bhikṣu, is called a Śramaṇa, and is also called a Buddha."
Therefore it is said: One who has no deluded mind, no pride, and no foolish confusion; who is without greed and without the notion of "I" and "mine"—he is called a *brahmin*.
I do not call one a *brahmin* merely because he was born from parents;
for such a person possesses many defilements. Only when these are extinguished does one become a *brahmin*.

What is called a brahmin is born of parents and possesses many defilements; yet, having left the household life and departed from all worldly affairs, he cultivates pure conduct and practices non-discriminatory giving—giving with equanimity and without dualistic thought, free from mixed intentions. Alternatively, when giving, he may seek to become a king or be reborn in heaven; this is called giving with mixed intentions.
One who gives without mixed thoughts does so entirely for the sake of all beings and not for themselves.
Therefore it is said: "I do not call one a brahmin merely because he was born of parents; he who possesses many defilements is not a brahmin, but he in whom these are extinguished is a brahmin."
With body, speech, and mind, pure and without fault, able to restrain these three modes of action—such a one is called a *brahmin*. His speech is gentle and never harsh;

he discerns the meaning and purpose as clearly as looking at a jewel in the palm of his hand. His voice is pure and pleasing to hear; he achieves much and, being pure and without fault, does not disturb or harm others. Therefore it is said: "With body, speech, and mind, pure and without fault, able to restrain these three modes of action—such a one is called a *brahmin*."
When reviled or struck, one accepts it silently without anger; possessing the power of patience, such a person is called a *brahmin*.

Being struck results in being struck, and being reviled results in being reviled—all such afflictions arise from a lack of patience. One who is truly patient is supreme in battle; patience is a sublime medicine capable of curing all maladies. If there is one who reviles you, remain silent and do not respond.
Therefore it is said: "When reviled or struck, one receives it silently without anger; possessing the power of patience—such a one is called a *brāhmaṇa*.
*Chuyao jing*, Scroll 29 and Scroll 30.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter on the Brahmacārin, Part Two:
If you are met with insults or deception, simply maintain mindfulness of keeping the precepts; keep your body upright and discipline yourself.
This is called a brahmin.

Furthermore, if there is someone who is insulted or deceived, they do not give rise to evil or harbor thoughts of anger; they maintain the precepts, possess great learning, and subdue their mental consciousness. Their body is upright, their shadow straight, and their mind is level as they abide in the Path.

Therefore it is said: If one is met with insult or deception, yet merely reflects upon maintaining the precepts, straightening the body, and self-disciplining—it is such a person who is called a *brahmin*.
Regarding what the world deems good or evil, long or short, great or small—if one neither grasps nor rejects these, it is such a person who is called a *brahmin*.

The worldly affairs of expedient means are manifold; yet, in wishing to examine human nature, one first gathers their speech. Whether they speak of good or evil, one does not harbor them in the heart; one perceives neither length nor brevity, neither breadth nor narrowness, and likewise perceives neither taking nor giving. One who fully accomplishes such practice is called a *brāhmaṇa*.
Therefore it is said: regarding the good and evil, the long and short, the large and small in the world, he neither takes nor gives; such a one is called a *brahmin*.
With the body as the root of action, and with speech and mind free from transgression, he who can master these three bases is called a *brahmin*.

One who does not kill with the body, does not revile with the mouth, and does not harbor envy in the mind—one who can fulfill these three practices amidst this world that boils like a cauldron—is truly called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "The body is the basis of action; when speech and mind are free from transgression, one is able to master these three spheres—such a person is called a brahmin.
One who does not rejoice upon coming nor grieve upon departing, who has left behind all attachments—such a person is called a brahmin."

That practitioner of cultivation maintains a firm mind, unmoved by praise or blame; seeing those who come, he does not rejoice, and even seeing those who depart, he does not grieve. Whether among a great assembly or apart from it, his mind is always equanimous, without fluctuation between high and low.
Therefore it is said: "One who does not rejoice at coming nor grieve at departing, who has left behind both the assembly and separation from the assembly—such a one is called a brahmin.
One who does not rejoice at coming nor grieve at departing, who is sorrowless and pure—such a one is called a brahmin.
If one sees those who are loved and cherished or those who are not loved and cherished, one should likewise not feel joy.
Why is this? For fear that the mind will become defiled and attached, thereby giving rise to the conditions for further existence.
If one sees a person going by and thinks to oneself:
"I have committed no offense against that person; being pure within and without, with the mind stilled and no [unwholesome] thoughts arising, such a one is also called a brahmin."
Therefore it is said: "He who does not rejoice at coming nor grieve at departing, who is free from sorrow and pure—he is called a brahmin.
Having severed affection and love, having left home and become desireless, with craving for existence exhausted—he is called a brahmin."

Just as that practitioner cultivates the Path, forever severing affection and love, leaving home to be free from desire, traveling afar without hindrance, exhausting all craving for existence, and eliminating the outflows of the three realms—one who is able to fulfill such qualities is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "By severing affectionate ties, leaving home free from desire, and exhausting all craving for existence—one is called a *brahmin*.
Having reached that state where 'that' does not exist, and where 'this and that' are non-existent, having abandoned all greed and desire—one is called a *brahmin*."

That which is called "that" refers to the six external sense bases; that which is called "not that" refers to the six internal sense bases. When a practitioner maintains his resolve and contemplates all internal and external phenomena as entirely empty and quiescent, he abandons greed and lust so that the six sense-faculties do not arise. One who is fully endowed with such fundamental practices is called a *brahmin*.

Therefore it is said: "When one reaches that state where 'that' does not exist, and through the non-existence of each and every thing, one abandons and leaves behind craving—such a person is called a brahmin.
When one reaches that state where 'that' does not exist, and through the emptiness of each and every thing, one is unstained by the three spheres—such a person is called a brahmin.

That practitioner who understands that both the internal and external are entirely free from fetters and afflictions, and who does not cling to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm—one who can fully perfect such a multitude of practices is truly called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "When one has gone to that state where there is no 'that,' and when all such states are empty, being unstained by the three spheres—such a person is called a brahmin.
One who can renounce household affairs, uproot craving and desire, and is free from greed and contented—such a person is called a brahmin."

A man who has left his home should not engage in worldly affairs; even if he has gone forth from the household life, if he does not cultivate the Dharma, violates the precepts, lacks diligence, and possesses little learning, one should likewise not associate with him in sitting or rising. Furthermore, one should not contemplate future gain and honor. Only one who can fulfill such requirements is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: One who can renounce household affairs, uproot craving and desire, and is free from greed with contentment—such a person is called a *brahmin*.
As is now known: one who has reached the end of suffering and possesses no further desire—such a person is called a *brahmin*.

Within the phenomena of this present life, one can discern that which is subtle and free from all evil; knowing that suffering is the primary source of all maladies, one who is able to sever it is truly in accord with the sublime.

One who, within the phenomena of this very life, does not associate with the mind of desire, whose anger and delusion are forever exhausted without remainder, and who is free from all bonds and attachments—one who can possess such qualities is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "One who knows as it truly is, having reached the end of suffering and no longer possesses desire—he is called a brahmin.
One for whom both evil and merit have been forever eliminated, who is without sorrow and free from dust—he is called a brahmin."

Even if one possesses merit—the roots of goodness and virtuous deeds of the mundane, tainted world—and thereby attains a human body, one still cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, and death because of these causes.

Furthermore, by committing offenses, one plants the seeds for the three evil realms and undergoes the cycle of birth and death. Both offense and merit are unworthy of craving; when both courses of action are forever eliminated and no further defilements remain, one who can fully practice this is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: One who has forever eliminated both the paths of demerit and merit, who is without sorrow and free from defilement—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
One who has forever eliminated both the paths of demerit and merit, and who is unstained in the three realms—such a one is called a *brahmin*.

Regarding merit and demerit, one is without desire and free from defilement; as for the bliss of the intermediate dhyānas and the bliss of the formless dhyānas, the practitioner relinquishes them all and remains unstained by attachment. Not clinging to the three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—one who is able to understand and fulfill this is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: When both the paths of demerit and merit are forever eliminated, and one is unstained in the three spheres, such a person is called a brahmin.
Just as when many flower petals pierce a mustard seed with a needle, one who is not stained by sensual desires is called a brahmin.

Just as the petals of a lotus flower do not receive dust or water, so too is it with that practitioner; because they have abandoned desire, they no longer cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. It would be as difficult to pierce a blue pea or a mustard seed with a needle as it is for such a person to be pierced by desire.
That practitioner is free from lust; to state the essential point briefly, he is not defiled by evil.
Therefore it is said: "Just as when a needle pierces a mustard seed amidst a multitude of flower petals, one who is not defiled by desire is called a brahmin."
With a joyful mind free from defilement, like the full moon, having eliminated all slander and defamation— he is called a brahmin.
Just as the full moon is pure and without blemish, free from the five obscurations, and surrounded by the host of stars, emitting great radiance that shines everywhere, so too is he.

That bhikṣu is a practitioner of purity who has forever eliminated the five obscurations and is no longer bound by the five fetters; his mind has attained liberation through the factors of enlightenment, and he is surrounded by various meditative concentrations and right attainments. Among them, he alone is supreme and free from all blemishes; having abandoned the eight worldly dharmas, he is already rid of praise and blame. Because he is able to fulfill these practices, he is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: With a joyful mind free from defilement, like the full moon, having eliminated all slander and malice—he is called a brahmin.
Like the clear and bright moon suspended in the void, unstained by desire—he is called a brahmin.

Just as the autumn moon is not obscured by five things, being pure and flawless while emitting great radiance that shines everywhere, so too is the bhikṣu who practices the path: he is not obscured by the five fetters of lust, anger, ignorance, and so forth. Because he is able to fulfill this practice, he is called a *brahmacārin*.
Therefore it is said: Like the clear and bright moon suspended in the void, unstained by desire—he is called a brahmin.
Avoiding strife, he does not contend; offended, he is not resentful; when evil comes, he responds with kindness—he is called a brahmin.

That person who has entered meditative concentration does not give rise to contention; with a single-minded focus in dhyāna, they await joy and peace. Guarding oneself and fully possessing the five practices is what is called "concentration.
Even if someone with malicious intent comes toward them, they always respond with kindness.
Therefore it is said: "Avoiding contention and not contending, being free from resentment when wronged, responding with kindness to those who come with malice—such a one is called a brahmin.
One who understands subtle wisdom, distinguishes the Way from what is not the Way, and embodies the practice of the supreme meaning—such a one is called a brahmin."

There are those who, upon hearing [the teachings], deliberate, calculate, and schematize all things, clearly discerning their meanings and purposes one by one; they know what should be pursued and pursue it, and they know what should be abandoned and abandon it, embodying and practicing the supreme meaning.
What is called the "supreme meaning" (paramārtha) is the extinction of nirvāṇa; one who is able to fulfill this dharma is therefore called a brahmin.
Thus it is said: "One who understands subtle wisdom, discriminates between the path and what is not the path, and embodies the practice of the supreme meaning—this is called a brahmin."
Those who dwell among humans, seeking alms for their own sustenance,
free from selfhood and attachment, not losing the holy life, and whose wisdom they proclaim is boundless— they are called brahmins.

There may be a son of noble family who, having gone forth from among the four castes to study the Way, abandons the mind of arrogance, leaves behind loftiness to follow humility, and does not cling to honor or hope, traveling and wandering throughout every place.

When there is the undertaking of Buddhist affairs and one reverently serves the Triple Gem, if one receives clothing, food, bedding, seats, or medicine for illness, one should then offer prayers of blessing so that the donor’s family may receive blessings in every successive life. Alternatively, by means of supernormal powers, one may soar into the void and perform the eighteen transformations; those donors who see this will all be filled with joy, and by receiving the Dharma from such a person, they shall all attain awakening. One who is able to practice in this manner is therefore called a *brahmacārin*.

Therefore it is said: "Those who dwell among humans, sustaining themselves by begging, who are without self and without attachment, who do not lose their holy life (brahmacarya), and whose wisdom is said to be boundless—they are called brahmins."
If one can renounce desire, leave the household life, and abandon craving, thereby severing the taints of desire—such a person is called a *brahmin*.

Just as that practitioner is able to completely sever desire, yet remains close to the gateway of the Path without abandoning attachment, so too there may be a *brahmin* who has not reached the ultimate goal; his desires are not yet severed and he remains attached to the five pleasures. Though he is called a *brahmin*, he is not free from desire.
All those in training who have eternally extinguished the outflow of desire (*kāśrava*) and no longer cultivate affectionate attachment, being able to fulfill this practice, are called *brahmins*.
