Therefore it is said: "If one can abandon desire, leave the household life, and renounce attachment, thereby severing the outflow of desire—one is called a *brahmin*."
To have compassion for others, causing them no alarm or fear; to refrain from harming and instead bring benefit—this is called a *brahmin*.

Of all essential practices, the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are the foundation. One should constantly bestow compassion upon sentient beings; seeing those who are fearful or afflicted by sorrow, one should go to comfort and transform them so they dwell forever in peace and security. To not harm others and to offer them sustenance—one who can fulfill such conduct is named a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: One who is compassionate toward others, causing them no alarm or fear, who does not harm but brings benefit—such a person is called a *brahmin*.
One who avoids resentment and does not resent, who inflicts no injury or damage, and who has cast away all perversity—therefore he is called a *brahmin*.

The practitioner maintains a firm resolve and distinct moral integrity; with an impartial mind, even upon seeing an enemy, they regard them as an infant, their compassionate heart being universally equal, uniform, and without duality.

Just as the mind of patience is like the earth and impartial as a scale, one regards all creatures—whether flying, crawling, creeping, or breathing—as one’s own body; one thinks of them as a father, one thinks of them as a mother, one thinks of them as a child, and one thinks of them as oneself, without any distinction.
One who is able to fulfill these various practices is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "Avoiding enmity and being without resentment, causing no injury or harm, and having removed all perversity—such a one is called a *brahmin*."
Neither in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present does he exist; without grasping and without abandoning—he is called a *brahmin*.

Just as there is a person who, in the future, commits no evil deeds—having not done them, not doing them now, and not intending to do them—and who, in the past, committed no evil deeds—having done them, not doing them now, and not intending to do them—and who, in the interval between them, commits no evil deeds—having done them, not doing them now, and not intending to do them.
One who is able to relinquish these various evil practices is therefore called a *brahmin*.
Thus it is said: "In what comes after, in what comes before, and in that which is between, there is nothing; neither grasping nor relinquishing—this is called a *brahmin*."
One who has abandoned lust, anger, and delusion, as well as pride and all evils—like a needle passing through a mustard seed—he is called a *brahmin*.

Just as a practitioner who wishes to defile his mind cannot reach the path of emptiness and stillness, yet by removing pride and all unwholesome dharmas, he gradually advances to the realm of *nirvāṇa*; it is like a needle passing through a mustard seed, which can never be obstructed.
That mind is likewise so: it is not constrained or obstructed by the fetters of lust, anger, and delusion. One who is able to fully practice this is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "One who has removed lust, anger, and delusion, along with pride and all evils—like a needle passing through a mustard seed—is called a *brahmin*."
The city is made secure by its moats; those who come and go suffer within them.
Desiring to reach the further shore, one refuses to accept the words of others;
only by extinguishing [the defilements] so they do not arise is one called a *brahmin*.

Birth and death have been endured for a vast duration, involving countless sufferings; only those who possess meditative concentration can transcend this hardship of birth and death. Having cast aside perverse doubts and intentions, they no longer waver; they abandon the fetters and latent tendencies of affliction and receive the fetters of purity.
One who is able to possess these qualities is therefore called a *brahmin*.

Thus it is said: "A city is made secure by its moats; those who come and go suffer within them. One who wishes to cross over to the other shore and refuses to accept the words of others—only he who can extinguish [the defilements] so they do not arise is called a *brahmin*."
If a person can sever craving in both this life and future lives, and their craving has been completely exhausted, they are called a *brahmin*.

As long as the root of craving is not exhausted, one does not reach the Path; only when the root of craving is exhausted can one truly practice the Path. Those who seek the Path but do not sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms do not reach the Path; only by severing the root of craving can one finally reach the Path. One who is fully endowed with these qualities is therefore named a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "One who can sever craving for both this world and the world beyond, whose craving has been utterly exhausted—such a person is called a *brahmin*.
One who has no expectations for either this world or the world beyond, being free from all expectation—such a person is called a *brahmin*."

Regarding what is called "hope": among all things in the world, everything is an object of human hope; yet because this hope has not been severed, one remains present in the world in this current body without having died. Even when one reaches the end of life in a future existence, with the body dead and the spirit departed, there is no further hope.
One who is thus endowed with such merit is called a *brahmin*. Therefore it is said:
"A person has no expectations regarding this world or the world beyond; because they have no expectations, they are called a *brahmin*."
Not recognizing even the devas and gandharvas, yet knowing the immeasurable contemplations—
such a one is called a brahmin.
While the Buddha, the Tathāgata, was sitting in meditation, neither the devas nor the people of the world could know where the Buddha was at that time.
There was a bhikṣu named Tāgisi who went to where the World-Honored One was and praised the Tathāgata with this verse:
"I take refuge in the Honored One among men; I take refuge in the Supreme One among men.
I wonder, O World-Honored One, by means of what dhyāna do you abide?"
“I only pray that the God among Gods will expound the meaning of his teaching.
The Tathāgata himself said:

“Within the holy life (brahmacarya), there is none who surpasses me. The reason I know this to be so is that while meditative liberation, right concentration, and fixed attention are still but the common dharmas of the world, such that even the devas, nāgas, and spirits cannot know my whereabouts, how much less could they know the wondrous gateways of manifold wisdom through which I perform the Buddha-work?”
"Can devas, nāgas, and spirits know my whereabouts?
For this reason it is said: "One who does not know himself, yet whom devas and gandharvas know through immeasurable contemplation—he is called a brahmin."
He personally recognizes his past lives and perceives the paths of gods and humans; knowing the source of suffering in birth, his wise mind is eternally tranquil.

He personally recognizes the events of countless kalpas of past lives and observes and knows the affairs of the hells and the heavens—something others cannot do. Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, can observe the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world as if looking at a bead in the palm of his hand. Knowing the source of suffering in birth, he thoroughly investigates its root; with swift and rapid wisdom, he quickly achieves the path of an Arhat, such that whatever he intends in his mind is accomplished without obstruction.
Therefore it is said: Having personally known past lives and seen the paths of gods and humans, knowing the source of the suffering of birth, the wise mind is forever stilled.
Knowing for oneself that the mind is liberated, freed from desire and without attachment, having accomplished the three knowledges—one is called a *brahmin*.

Just as that practitioner knows the thoughts in the mind, clearly discerning both those who are liberated and those who are not, they attain eternal liberation from all conditioned formations born of desire and conceptualization.

What are called the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are: knowledge of one’s own past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). One who is fully endowed with such practices is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: "Knowing for oneself that the mind is liberated, being freed from desire and unattached, having accomplished the three knowledges—one is called a *brahmin*."
Having personally known past lives and understood the causes and conditions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata Buddha is unattached; he is called a *brahman*.

At that time, the Tathāgata knew countless matters, observing the dispositions and conducts of sentient beings with complete clarity; he fully understood all who were born and all who died, just as rain from the heavens universally moistens the world. At that time, the World-Honored One’s observation of the classes of birth and death was likewise so; there were none among the born or the dead whom he did not examine and refine.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling alone in a secluded chamber together with Śāriputra.
At that moment, there was a person who had already passed away, whose spirit remained suspended in the intermediate state (antarābhava) without moving on.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Observe now this consciousness within the intermediate state (antarābhava): from where does it come?
And when it subsequently transmigrates, where will it dwell?”
At that time, Śāriputra immediately entered the meditative concentration of the fourth dhyāna and observed from where this person’s spirit had come,
and if it were to transmigrate, to what place would it go?
At that time, Śāriputra did not know from where this person had come or where he was going.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What you have now seen does not reach the realm of the Buddhas; the place from which this spirit has come—these countless worlds—is not something that can be seen by your supernatural power."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, “Observe again where this spirit shall be reborn.
At that time, Śāriputra entered into samādhi, yet he did not know where the spirit was heading. Śāriputra then arose from samādhi and approached the Buddha, saying:
"Today, having entered meditative concentration and surveyed the world, I did not know where this spirit was heading.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This spirit shall today pass through another hundred million worlds and will be born into such-and-such a family, with the surname of so-and-so and the given name of so-and-so."

What the Tathāgata perceives is not something that can be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; as for the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, only the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses this power of recollecting past lives.
Therefore it is said: "One who recognizes his own past lives, knows the causes and conditions of sentient beings, and is a Tathāgata Buddha free from attachment—he is called a brahmin."
Having completely severed all fetters, And being free from the fever of affliction, The Tathāgata, the Buddha, is unattached; He is called a *brahman*.

All sentient beings have severed all fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*). Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the fetters and proclivities, they still possess residual, similar fetters. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no such similarities; therefore, the Tathāgata, the Buddha, is without attachment.
Therefore it is said:
"Having completely severed all fetters,
one is likewise free from feverish affliction."
The Tathāgata, the Buddha, is unattached;
he is called a brahmin.
Among seers and nāgas, he is supreme; the Great Seer is most venerable.
One who has bathed before countless Buddhas is called a brahmin. As for what is meant by a "seer" (ṛṣi):
one who has attained the five supernormal powers, who is most honored among the multitude with none superior to him, and whose inner and outer being are pure and transparent, free from all blemishes.
The Immortal is also called the Elephant; it nurtures its physical form and is the greatest among beasts, possessing a resolute will that can repel all adversaries.
It undergoes countless ablutions; what are called ablutions are the eight liberations, the true bathing pool, which removes all dust and defilement so that no fetters remain.
The Tathāgata extends his hand; wherever his hand reaches, dust and grime do not adhere, and malicious persons find no opportunity to harm him.
Therefore it is said: "Among sages he is the supreme dragon; the Great Sage is most venerable. Having been bathed by countless Buddhas, such a one is called a Brahmin."
All things are exhausted and non-existent; having crossed the stream, one is free from outflows. Having transcended this shore from here, such a person is called a *brahmin*.
That practitioner has completely transcended all phenomena; with clear and precise discernment, he understands that all that exists in the world is ultimately nothing at all.
Regarding what is called "flood" (*ogha*), there are four names for these floods:
first, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*); second, the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*); third, the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*); and fourth, the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*).
Only after crossing these four floods does one attain the practice free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas still contemplate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, patience, warmth, and the peak dharma; although they may contemplate mundane dharmas with outflows where the fetters of the mind reside, there are times when, while intending to contemplate the outflow-free, they first contemplate the outflowing. For this reason, the Tathāgata’s profound treasury possesses a great deficiency.

The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, binds his mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) from existence to non-existence; regarding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), his contemplation has never lacked anything. He has attained all the *dhāraṇīs* and possesses powerful memory without forgetfulness, as well as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), great kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*), the three paths of unimpeded knowledge (*trivaiśāradya-mārga*), and the practice of the bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*). These are called the dharmas practiced by the Tathāgata, not the dharmas practiced by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore it is said: When all that exists is exhausted and gone, having crossed the stream and become free from outflows, one who has thus transcended the shore is called a *brahmin*.
Without meditation and without speech, and not even thinking of evil, with meditative wisdom purified—this is called a *brahmin*.

That practitioner does not dwell upon unwholesome meditations; for one who enters meditative absorption (dhyāna), there is no speech and no discourse, as they constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas.

Even if they encounter abuse or insults, they merely maintain their practice. If they attain the flavor-associated dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna, they hold fast to it with resolve and remain free from affliction. Because they are able to fulfill this practice, they are called a *brahmacārin* (Brahmin).
Therefore it is said: Without meditative absorption, without speech, and not even thinking of evil, with meditative absorption and wisdom purified—such a one is called a brahmin.
A bhikṣu wearing the shroud from the cemetery, contemplating that sensual desires are not real, sitting beneath a tree in a secluded place—such a one is called a brahmin.
There are four kinds of robes from among graves:

first, those worn when leaving one's home to become a renunciant student; second, those given as alms by donors which are accepted and preserved; third, those made of rags gathered from discarded refuse; and fourth, those from among graves that are filthy and impure.

When the Tathāgata first began his training, he donned his robes and contemplated that sensual desires are not real; he renounced sixty thousand wives, abandoned the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, and left the household life to study the Way in a secluded place. Sitting beneath the King of Trees, he subdued the Māra King and shattered eighteen billion hosts.
One who is able to possess these manifold virtues is therefore called a *brahmin*.
Thus it is said: "A bhikṣu clad in robes from the charnel ground, contemplating that sensual desires are not real, sitting beneath a tree in a secluded place—he is called a *brahmin*."
A person who has no conscious cognition, who neither speaks nor explains, whose body is cold and lacks warmth—this is called a *brahmin*.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, there is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not encompass; that he "neither speaks nor explains" means he has forever eliminated doubt and harbors no hesitation. With all afflictions and fetters forever exhausted without remainder, he has attained the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta-nirvāṇa*). Because he is able to possess these manifold practices, he is named a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: One who lacks conscious perception, who neither speaks nor explains, whose body is cold and devoid of warmth—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
Having abandoned the household life and being free from the fear of the home, having reached the nectar of extinction (*amṛta-nirvāṇa*)—such a one is called a *brahmin*.

Therefore, those who dwell at home settle among the people so that they may sustain their own livelihood; yet the body is but a house for the multitude of fetters. For this reason, the Sage teaches people to leave the home-life, to seek the nectar of extinction (*amṛta-nirvāṇa*) in seclusion and tranquility. One who is able to possess such manifold virtues is called a *brahmin*.
Therefore it is said: Having abandoned the household life and being free from the fear of home, having attained the extinction of ambrosia (amṛta)—he is called a brahmin.
Having severed worldly affairs and having no coarse speech in his mouth, one who is certain in the Eightfold Path—him we call a brahmin.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, his radiant marks resplendent, first turned the Wheel of Dharma for eighty thousand devas, two kings, seven brahmins, King Bimbisāra of Magadha and twelve thousand followers, and within the stone cave of the kingdom of Magadha, Śakra Devānām Indra and twelve thousand devas; finally, in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, he delivered Subhadra.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there shall appear in the world an arhat named Upagupta, who during that interval will deliver and liberate sentient beings beyond measure, expounding the unimpeded Dharma of the Eightfold Path.
Therefore it is said: One who has severed worldly affairs, whose speech is free from coarseness, and who is certain in the Eightfold Path—he is called a *brahmin*.
One who wanders alone in distant retreat, who remains hidden and formless, and who can subdue that which is difficult to subdue—he is called a *brahmin*.

Just as that practitioner gives rise to boundless conceptions and disperses limitless thoughts, with the physical body here while the mind is on the surface of the ocean, it is extremely difficult for anyone who wishes to observe the mind to discern its form.

In the mere twinkling of an eye, the mind and mental factors race forth, passing beyond tens of millions of billions of rivers and mountains; for this reason, it is said that they travel afar and wander alone.
Furthermore, some may ask: "The mind possesses ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), making eleven in total. Why, then, is it said that it travels afar and wanders alone?"
He replied:

"The mind constantly pursues causes and conditions, proceeding according to its prior impulses. When the mind is focused on forms and sounds, at that time there are no odors, fragrances, or tactile objects;
when the mind is focused on odors, at that time there are no forms, tastes, or tactile objects."
When the mind is fixed on flavor, there are no forms, odors, tangibles, or mental objects;
when the mind is fixed on the tangible, at that time there are no forms, sounds, odors, flavors, or mental objects;
when the mind is fixed on mental objects, the other five things are absent.

When the mind is present within form, it is the foundation of all phenomena (dharma), just as when a king travels, his retinue and ceremonial insignia are all fully present, yet he is designated only by the name "king.

This is likewise: although the ten factors of causal conditions are created by the mind and are all fully present, they do not receive that name; it is also like a bird flying through the air relying upon its six wings, yet it is designated only by the name "bird."

This is likewise so: the mind is formless and has no dwelling place; it is not something seen by the physical eyes of worldly people. It relies upon the five aggregates (skandhas), and when the aggregates disperse, it departs; it possesses no material substance. The difficulty of transforming the mind is like drilling wood with steel.

Therefore, the Sage left behind this teaching for future generations: those who wish to subdue the mind should apply the "hundred medicines" in the morning, the "hundred medicines" at midday, and the "hundred medicines" in the evening—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), along with tranquility (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and cessation (*nirodha*). By using these to treat the diseases of the mind so that they may be healed, one who is able to fulfill these requirements is called a *brahmacārin*.
Therefore it is said: "He who has gone far away and wanders alone, who is hidden and formless, who can subdue what is difficult to subdue—he is called a brahmin.
Formless and invisible, this too is invisible;
he who understands this verse knows that mindfulness has its source."
One who realizes that the fetters are exhausted is the supreme brahmin in this world.
That which is formless and invisible—what is it?
It is the mind.

Now, for the mind to give rise to affliction and for the body to invite calamity is like an elephant or horse that is stubborn, fierce, and untamable; a person with sight applies the whip and staff to make it aware of the pain, after which it becomes well-trained and docile.

The human mind is a source of affliction; it drags one into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Even if one attains human birth, one dwells in a lowly and base station, with an ugly countenance that provokes the envy of others.
Therefore it is said: "Formless and invisible, this too is invisible.
One who understands this phrase has a basis for mindfulness; having awakened to the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana), such a person is the foremost brahmin in the world.

The reason the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world is precisely to subdue this corrupt and evil mind. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, compassionately pity all beings; their vast mercy universally covers everything without exception, and though they dwell in the world, they remain unstained by it.
Severing the river of birth and death, able to endure and cross over, awakening oneself to emerge from the trench—
this is called a *brahman*.

Just as that practitioner, bound by the five desires, flows along the river of birth and death, it is necessary for the Great Sage to grant him guidance and skillful means so that he may reach the further shore from this shore.
The Tathāgata’s manifestation in this world is never without prior intent; he must first connect with those who possess the karmic affinity before finally entering parinirvāṇa.
The "ditch" refers to the ditch of arrogance; one who can cross this ditch will not be bound by arrogance.
One who is able to possess these qualities is therefore called a *brahmin*.
Thus it is said: "He who has severed the river of birth and death, who is able to endure and cross over, and who has awakened for himself and emerged from the moat—him we call a *brahmin*."
One should seek to cross over by cutting off the floods; the brahmin is one who is free from desire.
Internally observing all feelings, he is called a brahmin.
One who can understand this is truly a brahmin.
If a practitioner does not sever the flow of craving—the four currents and four abysses—is it not difficult for them to advance toward the Path?
Just as a river that overflows its banks inevitably causes injury, so too, O Brahmin, one who is greedy for sensual desires will go to an evil destination after death.
Therefore, the Tathāgata admonishes one to eliminate greed and explains that the root of desire is defiled and impure; one should sever all perversions so they do not flow and run wild.
Because one can fully possess these various practices, one is called a *brahmacārin*.

Therefore it is said: One should seek to cut off the stream and cross over; the brahmin is free from desire. Internally observing all feelings, he is called a brahmin. One who can understand this is truly named a brahmin.
First eliminate its mother; when the king and his two ministers have completely transcended the realm of sensory objects, he is called a *brahmin*. Regarding "first eliminating its mother":

the flowing and racing of affectionate craving serves as its source and root; the outflow-free consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is able to eliminate this affliction so that it is exhausted without remainder.
The King represents pride (*māna*); the two ministers represent the precept against stealing and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
"Exhausting the supreme realm" means that all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) can remove the afflictions of these various fetters.
Therefore, he is called a *brahman*.
For this reason it is said: "First eliminate his mother, then the king and the two ministers; having completely transcended all spheres of experience, he is called a *brahman*."
Do not strike a brahmin; do not release a brahmin. Alas, to strike a brahmin!
To release him is likewise alas.

One who is called a "brahmin" is one who has attained the path of Arhatship. One must not use the hand, a scroll, a sword, or a staff to harm such a true person. As for "not releasing a brahmin," this refers to a true person whom one should constantly provide with the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for sickness—ensuring these offerings never diminish.

"Shame on the brahmin who commits evil; shame also on the one who releases such an evildoer. One who does not withhold offerings of food, drink, bedding, seating, or medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm—because he is able to fulfill these practices, he is called a brahmin."
Therefore it is said: "Do not strike the brahmin; do not release the brahmin. Alas, to strike the brahmin! To release him is likewise alas!
Those who know the profound Dharma, whether old or young, do not question them;
they carefully observe the precepts with faith, like the fire-worshipping brahmins.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings.
At that time, the bhikṣus were not extensively learned; thereupon the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"Now these bhikṣus are largely indolent and their minds are not diligent. Furthermore, observing the matters of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—he knew that in a future age there would be bhikṣus who, driven by jealousy, hatred, and delusion, would not follow the teachings of the Way. They would give rise to slander, damage the Dharma of the Tathāgata, treat their teachers with contempt, and likewise show no respect for those who preach the Dharma."

Therefore, the World-Honored One, observing the future period of the Dharma’s survival, feared that there might be instances where the old and the young would treat one another with mutual arrogance and disrespect, failing to distinguish between honor and humility—the elderly relying on their seniority and the youth relying on their cleverness.
The elder stated:
"What I have witnessed with my own eyes is not within your knowledge; what you see now is like the light of a firefly.
The younger one then stated:
"Old, dull, and ignorant, my emotions have perished and my mind is blocked; how can I find a way back to knowledge?
The Tathāgata instructed him, saying:

"You should maintain the precepts for yourself, just as a fire-worshipping Brahmin maintains fires at five locations, serving them day and night without missing the proper times, making offerings of incense, flowers, and silken fabrics for every requirement."

Therefore it is said: "Those who know the profound Dharma do not inquire whether one is old or young; they carefully observe the precepts with faith, like the fire-worshipping brahmins. They take refuge in the Honored One among Men, just as they serve the fire-god."
Those who understand the profound Dharma taught by the Equally Awakened One, who examine it with discernment and maintain their precepts and faith, are like Brahmins who worship the sacrificial fire.

The Tathāgata appears but once in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; to encounter a worthy one or a sage is truly difficult to obtain. If a person can maintain the precepts and faith without losing proper decorum, they are like a Brahmin who worships the sacrificial fire.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, he admonished the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not recite the books of outsiders or that which is studied and practiced by those of heterodox schools. Why is this? [Because]..."
"What he has expounded is not the true meaning, nor is it the foundation of the ultimate path.

Therefore it is said: "Those who know the profound Dharma taught by the Fully Awakened One, who carefully observe the precepts with faith—just like the fire-worshipping Brahmins—they truly take refuge in the Buddha."
Among those outside their own teachings, the brahmin is supreme;
all taints have been exhausted by him, leaving nothing behind.
Or again, he contemplates feelings until they are all exhausted, leaving nothing behind.
Or again, he contemplates their convergence, seeing that all are exhausted and nothing remains.
Or again, he contemplates causes and conditions, seeing that all are exhausted and nothing remains.

Regarding those things outside his own dharma, that practitioner of the path contemplates and understands all phenomena; there is no matter to which he is not related, and no matter of which he is not aware. It is just as a brahmin who understands astronomy, geography, the stars, and portents, perceiving and comprehending them all, such that all taints are exhausted and nothing remains.

Contemplate all sufferings, whether pleasant or unpleasant, as they all return to extinction; contemplate their coming together as necessarily leading to separation, and how that which exists momentarily through causes and conditions likewise returns to cessation.
Just as with the internal dharmas, the brahmin remains on the surface;
even if they share the same bed and mat, he is like that *vāguluka*.
What are called "internal dharmas" are the four truths and suchness, analyzed in every detail without losing their proper sequence; yet the brahmin regards these internal things as being external.
Therefore it is said: "Just as the inner dharma is fundamental, the brahmin remains on the surface.
Even if one shares a bed and mat with him, such as the case of Bakula.

Since this bhikṣu Bakula went forth into homelessness, he has never spoken even a four-line verse of meaning to another. Even when sitting together, one would not hear him preach the True Dharma. From birth until old age, throughout eighty-one years at the Andhavana grove, he has never kept a śrāmaṇera disciple or any other attendants. He is pure and refined; his will is entrusted to the void, and his mind is fixed upon profound stillness.

Therefore it is said: "If one shares a bed and mat with such as that Pāṅgu, it is just like the internal phenomena while the brahmin remains on the outside; he knows birth and he knows old age, and thus he shall eventually reach death."

What is called the internal dharma does not deceive or delude people; it is consistently without deviation and consistently without perversity. Only the Tathāgata can transcend this realm, having exhausted his births and no longer undergoing further existence, knowing this as it truly is.
Therefore it is said: Just as with internal phenomena, the brahmin remains on the surface, knowing birth and knowing old age, until he must eventually reach death.
As the sun illuminates the day, the moon illuminates the night, armor and weapons illuminate the army, and dhyāna illuminates the practitioner of the Way;
so too, when a Buddha appears in the world, he illuminates all darkness.

Regarding the sun shining during the day: when the Son of Heaven of the Sun first rises, he emits hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, causing the stars and moonlight to lose their radiance;
yet when the sun sets, the moon and the stars all vie for brilliance together, each having its own illumination, though their lights differ.

It is like a great general’s troops facing two opposing enemies, raising their prestige and exerting their martial prowess to decide victory or defeat; their brilliant weapons flash and their bells and drums roar like thunder.

A person in meditative concentration can move mountains, fly peaks, stir up the dust of the ocean waters, and touch the sun and moon with their hands; yet, despite possessing such supernatural powers, they do not praise themselves.
Although these people possess such virtues, they do not equal the Tathāgata.

When a Buddha appears in the world, he is endowed with all marks and emits a great radiance that shines everywhere. Wherever this light reaches, day and night are indistinguishable; and for those who behold the light, deafness, blindness, muteness, and the agonizing pains of torture are naturally stilled.

Therefore it is said: As the sun illuminates the day, as the moon illuminates the night, as armor and weapons illuminate the army, and as dhyāna illuminates the practitioner of the Way, so does the Buddha appear in the world to illuminate all darkness.
The brahmin possesses none of these; though there is sorrow, he has no thought of sorrow.
Like that which turns according to his will, in each and every instance he extinguishes doubt.

The brahmin possesses none of these; his mind is fixed upon the sublime Dharma. Seeing joy, he does not take delight; seeing sorrow, he does not become dejected. Like that which turns according to his will, he constantly contemplates what is wholesome, and in each and every instance he extinguishes evil within himself. Having attained the practice of the Noble Truths, he discerns all the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Therefore it is said: The brahmin has no such thing; whether there is sorrow or the thought of sorrowlessness, he turns according to his will and extinguishes doubt in each instance.
He gives rise to all profound dharmas; the brahmin practices and enters meditative absorption, able to unravel the net of doubt and personally know its suffering.

When the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, first attained Buddhahood, for seven days he remained in meditative absorption, contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, discerning each one individually to know their arising and their cessation.
At that time, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi and spoke these verses:
"Having given birth to all profound dharmas, The brahmin practices and enters dhyāna;
He is able to unravel the net of doubt, And with his own body he knows its suffering."
"As it has been brought about by the practices and accumulations I have cultivated, today I have attained equal and perfect enlightenment; this is true and not false.

The brahmin entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), cast off all unwholesome dharmas, and completely destroyed the net of doubt. He attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all profound dharmas; his mindfulness was sovereign as he deeply understood the limit of suffering and deeply understood that the phenomena of the convergence of causes and conditions are provisional and not real.

To briefly recite its essentials: one should contemplate the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and further contemplate the law of cessation (*nirodha*). All phenomena arise from combination; all phenomena arise from sensation (*vedanā*). One should know that through their total extinction, one ceases to create outflows (*āsrava*).
Giving birth to all profound dharmas, the brahmin practices and enters into dhyāna, illuminating the entire world like the sun in the void.

Dharma can bring about the perfection of a person, whereas non-dharma does not; contemplating it day and night without letting it leave one’s breast, and ensuring that the actions of body, speech, and mind do not err, one who can accomplish such dharmas is able to illuminate all phenomena.
One bestows all that one has attained upon sentient beings, just as the rising sun abides in the void and shines everywhere; among those who behold it, there are none who do not receive its light.
Therefore it is said: "Having given birth to all profound dharmas, the brahmin practices and enters dhyāna, illuminating the entire world like the sun in the sky.
Having given birth to all profound dharmas, the brahmin practices and enters dhyāna;
he can repel the hosts of Māra’s enemies, just as the Buddha is liberated from all defilements."

Regarding the birth of all profound dharmas: the Tathāgata has attained equal and perfect enlightenment, being fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; his actions of body, speech, and mind are in accord with the untainted (*anāsrava*); he subdues the hosts of Māra at the appropriate time for advancing or retreating; and the Tathāgata, the one of equal and perfect enlightenment, is liberated from all fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana*).
Udānavarga, Volume Thirty.
